en: Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā (Karṇakagomin): Edited by Rāhula Sāṃkṛtyāyana. *Ācārya-Dharmakīrteḥ Pramāṇavārttikam* (the chapter on inference for oneself, *svārthānumānaparicchedaḥ*), together with the author’s own commentary (*svopajñavṛtti*) and the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) composed by Karṇakagomin. Kyoto, 1982 [Reprint].
Karṇakagomin’s Commentary on Dharmakīrti’s *Pramāṇavārttikavṛtti*.
He who has destroyed all bonds and states of existence, who stands perfectly established in liberation,
and in whom there arises a continuous stream of most pure knowledge extending to all that is knowable;
Having bowed many times today to the glorious Lord Mañjunātha, the pervasive one whose mind is ever-striving for the welfare of sentient beings, I wish to speak something from the *Vārttika*.
This entire merit belongs to the author of the commentary, that he speaks here even regarding this profound subject matter;
for once the rugged terrain has been cleared away by the tusks of Dignāga’s elephant, young elephants proceed with ease along the paths they have found.
If anyone, proud of their own virtues, treats me with contempt, let him know that this effort is not directed toward him;
for there may yet come someone who seeks this work, for there is no end to the diversity of minds among those born in this world.

For although the completion of a treatise without obstacle occurs through the accumulation of merit by performing prostrations to one’s chosen deity with body, speech, and mind—even without introducing a verse of homage at the beginning of the work—nevertheless, the Teacher introduced this verse of worship to a distinguished deity after considering both the benefit of others and the adherence to the conduct of the virtuous, on the grounds that such activity preceded by praise generates a superior degree of merit for the commentators and the listeners.
"With conceptual construction shaken off," and so forth.

When the term *Samantabhadra* is not understood through conventional usage as referring to a bodhisattva, then this is an offering to the Buddha, the Blessed One. And that [offering] is twofold: by way of praise and by way of prostration. By the word *namaḥ*, it is by way of prostration; by the remaining [words], it is by way of praise. Praise, moreover, is threefold: by way of the perfection of one's own welfare, by way of the perfection of the welfare of others, and by way of the means for the perfection of the welfare of others.

Since one who has accomplished his own welfare becomes capable of acting for the welfare of others, the accomplishment of his own welfare is first stated by the first half-verse. And this accomplishment of one's own welfare, characterized by the three bodies (*kāya*), is manifested as distinguished by three specific qualities: by the specific quality of the abandonment of obscurations (*āvaraṇaprahāṇa*), by the specific quality of profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), and by the specific quality of magnificence (*audārya*).

In this context, "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) refers to the minds and mental factors belonging to the three realms that function with the aspects of self and what belongs to self, as well as those that function with the aspects of apprehended object and apprehending subject. That very conceptualization is a "net" because its nature is bondage. Those forms whose nature has been "shaken off"—meaning destroyed along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and brought to a state where they no longer arise—are described as such. By this, the excellence of the abandonment of obscurations is stated. Furthermore, the excellences of profundity and vastness are expressed by the words "profound" and "vast."

He whose form is profound and sublime, with the net of conceptual construction shaken off—profound because it is not the domain of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others; sublime because it pervades all objects of knowledge and the welfare of all sentient beings; and whose forms are the three bodies—the Svābhāvika, Sāmbhogika, and Nairmāṇika—is that Blessed One whose form is profound and sublime with the net of conceptual construction shaken off. "Bhadra" means auspicious, characterized by worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Because he is "Samantabhadra" (Universally Auspicious) insofar as he brings about, for those who seek it, that [attainment] in its entirety and without remainder, according to their capacity; by this, the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpat*) is stated. And by the phrase "the light that radiates everywhere" (*samantasphuraṇatviṣ*), the means for achieving this perfection of the welfare of others is stated.

*Tiṣaḥ* means rays. Here, however, the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*) is [compared] through its common characteristics (*sādharmyeṇa*) to rays, in that it consists precisely in the apprehension of things as they truly exist. These teachings are called "rays" because they have as their object the means for achieving both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), just like actual rays. They are "all-pervading" (*samantaspharaṇya*) because the means for accomplishing the welfare of others (*parārthasādhanopāya*) is spread out—that is, pervaded—entirely toward those to be trained (*vinayebhyaḥ*), due to being explained in its totality. He whose rays of Dharma-teaching have become thus all-pervading is *Samantaspharaṇatviṭ*. Furthermore, because of its connection with the word *namaḥ*, the dative case is used throughout.

When, however, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is taken into account, this term "Samantabhadra" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the Mahāyāna as referring to a particular Bodhisattva; thus, this is a worship of a Bodhisattva. The meaning of the words (*padārtha*), however, should be applied as before. This, however, is the distinction: the state of having shaken off the web of conceptual construction (*kalpanājāla*) is to be understood from the abandonment of the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) of the Bodhisattva stages. Profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) is due to being beyond the sphere of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Magnanimity (*audārya*), on the other hand, is due to the greatness of the Bodhisattva.
The three bodies also exist in a corresponding manner for Bodhisattvas; however, they are established as belonging to Buddhas because of their attainment of excellence.

For there certainly do exist those who will grasp this treatise called the *Vārttika*; nevertheless, because of the abundance of defects in listeners, one might render even existing benefit as if it were non-existent. Thus, showing that the very state of having a mind cultivated by the practice of well-spoken words (*sūktābhyāsa*) is the cause for undertaking the treatise, [the author] speaks the second verse in order to express—by way of an indirect statement—that this defect of a listener’s fault is the cause for the loss of its great purpose, and therefore it ought to be abandoned: *na hi prayojanamanuddiśya prekṣāvantaḥ pravartante |* *ataḥ śāstrasya prayojanaṃ vaktavyam |* *tac ca dvividham—sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa ca |* *sākṣāt tāvat svaparasamayajñatāpādanam |* *pāramparyeṇa tu mokṣaprāptiḥ |* *etad dhi sarvaśāstrāṇāṃ prayojanam |* *atra ca kecit pūrvapakṣavādina āhuḥ—* *“na hy etac chāstraṃ prayojanavad, yasmān na kaścid asya kartā vidyate |* *akartṛkaṃ ca na kiṃcit prayojanavat dṛṣṭam |* *atha vā, saty api kartari, sa nityo ’mūrto ’karmāśraya iti na tatkṛtaṃ prayojanam upapadyate |* *athāpi mūrtaḥ syāt, tathāpi tasya rāgādidoṣaduṣṭatvān na tadvacanaṃ pramāṇam |* *pramāṇābhāvāc ca na prayojanasiddhiḥ |”* *atrocyate—yad uktaṃ “na kaścid asya kartā” iti, tad ayuktam |* *yasmād asyaiva śāstrasya vārttikākhyasya grahītāro vidyante ye tatpraṇetāraṃ parijñāya tadukte ’rthe ’bhiyogaṃ kurvanti |* *yadi nāma santi, tathāpi śrotṛdoṣabahulatayā santaṃ apy upakāram asantam iva kṛtvā, sūktābhyāsabhāvitacittatvam eva śāstrārambhe kāraṇaṃ darśayan, ayaṃ ca mahārthabhraṃśe hetudoṣas tyaktuṃ yukta ity etac ca vakroktyā kathayituṃ dvitīyaṃ ślokaṃ āha—* [The author then recites the second verse.]

"Generally, those attached to the vulgar," and so forth. Here, four kinds of defects in the listener are brought to light: poor wisdom (*kuprajñatva*), ignorance (*ajñatva*), lack of interest (*anarthitva*), and lack of impartiality (*amādhyasthya*). The word *prāyaḥ* ends in the vowel *o* and expresses abundance; thus, "generally" means "the majority of people. "Attached to the vulgar" (*prākṛtasakti*) refers to one whose attachment (*sakti*) is toward the "vulgar"—that is, toward external treatises (*bahiḥśāstra*). This is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (compound with non-co-referential members), justified by its semantic intelligibility. Alternatively, it may mean "one whose attachment is vulgar," in which case it is a *samānādhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (compound with co-referential members).
And because its object is the vulgar, the attachment is vulgar; by this, the defect of the listener—namely, his poor discernment—is stated.

"One of weak intellect" (*apratibalaprajña*) refers to one whose wisdom (*prajñā*) lacks the capacity to grasp the treatises (*śāstra*); this is to be connected with the phrase "generally [such] people. By this, their ignorance is stated. It is not merely that they have no interest in well-spoken words (*subhāṣita*), but rather, being overwhelmed by the impurity of envy (*īrṣyā*), they even hate the one who utters those well-spoken words. The meaning is that they both lack interest and harbor hatred. By this, their lack of interest and lack of neutrality are stated respectively. Here too, the phrase "generally [such] people" should be connected.

Others, however, explain that there is also a particle *prāyas* ending in *s*; and they maintain that it naturally occurs in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*) in the phrase "in abundance" (*bāhulyena*).

Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the mind’s resentment toward the prosperity of others. That very thing is a stain (*mala*) because it defiles the mind. The plural number is used due to the multiplicity of individual instances. Since this is so, for that reason, this work entitled the *Vārttika* is undertaken. "Benefiting others" (*paropakāra*) means the assistance of others; [it is derived] with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an instrument (*upakriyate 'nena*), or as "that which benefits others," thus *paropakāra*, according to Pāṇini 3.2.1 (*karmaṇy aṇ*). As for "benefiting others," we have not even the thought of it.

He asks, "How then is there an engagement in the composition of this treatise? and replies with the verse beginning "cetaś ciram," etc. "Cira" means for a long time; "vyasana" refers to a passion or devotion that has been increased by the practice of well-spoken words (*sūktābhyāsa*). That mind whose passion has been increased by the practice of well-spoken words is described as such. For this reason, his mind has become "anubaddhaspṛham"—that is, one in which a longing has arisen—for the composition of this *Vārttika*. Thus some explain it.

Others, however, explain it differently. At this point—when the question arises as to why this teacher Dharmakīrti provides an exposition of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* according to the method of a *vārttika* rather than composing an independent treatise himself—he says: "For the most part," and so forth. The summarized meaning of this verse is as follows: through reflection and compassion, my mind has developed a desire to compose an exposition of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*. Both reflection and compassion arise because the treatise composed by the teacher Dignāga is of limited utility.

And there is a lack of benefit due to the transgressions of kinsmen. Now the meaning of the words is stated: "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) means for the most part; the connection is that "people" (*janaḥ*) are those whose attachment is to the vulgar (*prākṛta*). In common worldly usage, the "vulgar" (*prākṛta*) refers to one who is low, whose lineage (*anvaya*) is corrupt. Likewise, the treatises of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) composed by others, which are refutations of the teacher’s treatise on ethics (*nītiśāstra*), are "vulgar" because they arise from perverted knowledge and possess a corrupt lineage. One who has attachment—that is, affection—for these is described as such.

Why, then, is he attached to the vulgar? He says: "one whose wisdom lacks capability. Therefore, taking even what is poorly spoken to be well-spoken, he becomes attached to the vulgar. Precisely because his wisdom lacks capability, being unable himself to understand the well-spoken words of the Teacher as they truly are, he perceives them as faulty and thus finds no benefit in those well-spoken words of the Teacher. Furthermore, he becomes hostile toward the Teacher; thus he says: "merely," and so forth.

Not only was he indifferent to the well-spoken words of his teacher, but being possessed by the impurity of envy, he even felt hatred toward the teacher Dignāga. How so? He was one whose passion for the practice of eloquent speech had been increased; for a connection indeed occurs even with that which is separated, according to the maxim: "Whatever has a relationship with something, it belongs to that thing even if it is far removed."

"Well-spoken" means that which is excellently stated; "eloquence" (*sūkta*) refers to the teaching of the Blessed One. "Habitual practice" (*abhyāsa*) therein, "increased passion" (*vivarddhita-vyasana*) for it, and "excessive attachment" (*atyartham āsaktatva*) to it—[these qualities belong] to the teacher Dignāga, and thus he is so described. By this, [the author] states that the teacher Dignāga has accumulated merit and knowledge; for only those who have accumulated merit and knowledge become ones whose passion for eloquence is increased through habitual practice.

Because [the author] possesses neither the capacity for wisdom nor a desire for the well-spoken words of the masters, being instead attached to the commonplace—for that reason, this *Pramāṇasamuccaya* is not a benefit to others (*paropakāra*). [The suffix] *-ghañ* is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*) in the rule "upakaraṇam upakāraḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.18). Considering that no superior (*utkṛṣṭa*) benefit arises from it, it is not a "benefit to others"; however, there is indeed some slight benefit, and that is precisely indicated by the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*). The word "iti" indicates a cause; for this reason, this is our concern.

"Even though this treatise possesses great significance, it has not yet become beneficial to many; therefore, how might I bring about its ultimate success?"—this is the form [of his resolve]. Furthermore, even a slight animosity toward the Teacher, who is like a Bodhisattva, is a cause of harm; thus, by correctly elucidating the Teacher’s system, I shall generate great respect for the Teacher and thereby turn back from that cause of harm. This is also compassion, characterized by the desire to separate [others] from suffering, as indicated by the word "also" (*api*).

In this context, by the second word "anubaddhaspṛham" (possessing a continuous longing), he states that reflection (*cintā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are the causes. That is to say, through these two—reflection and compassion—the mind possesses a continuous longing, meaning its desire proceeds as a stream for a long time, for the duration of this composition of the *Pramāṇavārttika*, which is a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.

Anticipating the objection—"If the Master Dharmakīrti intends to compose a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, why does he establish inference independently?"—he says "artha-anartha," etc., in order to dispel that doubt. "Artha" means the beneficial; "anartha" means the harmful. "Vivecana" is the discrimination between these two. Since that discrimination has its basis in inference, the analysis of the compound is: "that which has inference as its basis."

For, having ascertained benefit and harm through inference, one establishes benefit and harm respectively—through a continuous stream of cognition following upon that inference—for the sake of attaining or avoiding them by means of differentiation. Therefore, the discrimination between benefit and harm is based on inference. Regarding the phrase "because of disagreement with it" (*tadvipratipatteḥ*), some explain it thus: "because there is disagreement regarding that inference, [the author] speaks in order to establish it.
However, in this regard, the following must be considered.

If it is first determined thus—that [inference] is the basis for the discernment of what is beneficial (*artha*) and what is harmful (*anartha*)—that is not so; for the discernment of a third object, the indifferent (*upekṣaṇīya*), which is other than the beneficial and the harmful, is also dependent upon inference, and since the discernment of the beneficial and the harmful is not restricted [to inference alone], its dependence on perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not excluded. What, then, is this excellence of inference proclaimed that it should be explained at the outset? Alternatively, if it is determined thus:

"Because the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful (*arthānarthavivecana*) is based solely on inference (*anumāna*). Even so, this restriction is incorrect, because the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful is also based on perception (*pratyakṣa*). For it is the case that benefit and harm appear in perception precisely as distinct forms. And that perception—having its causes of error removed through the proficiency acquired by the excellence of repeated practice (*abhyāsātiśaya*)—generates a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that discerns benefit and harm.

For this indeed is the basis for the discernment of the beneficial and the harmful by means of perception: that having experienced the beneficial and the harmful in their distinction, one generates a determination regarding them in accordance with that experience.

Nor can it be said [that this occurs] later, because a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not grasp the actual nature of the thing; or, if it did grasp it, its status as a conceptual construction would be lost, since there is a contradiction in the fact that a cognizer associated with conceptual construction cannot have a clear manifestation of the object.

However, in certain cases where perception is unable to remove the causes of error due to a lack of clarity, certainty is sought through inference; this is not the case everywhere. Therefore, the determination of validity in perception occurs both intrinsically and extrinsically. Furthermore, this matter will be established in the second chapter, so it is not elaborated upon here.

Furthermore, it must necessarily be admitted that perception—which has had the causes of error removed through the power of repeated practice—serves as the basis for the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful, because it generates certainty in accordance with its experience. Otherwise, there would be no established status even for inference, since the mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, would not be certain. If smoke and so forth were themselves understood through another inference, there would be an infinite regress, because in that case too, another mark would have to be ascertained by yet another inference.

And if perception were not the basis for discriminating between what is beneficial and what is harmful, then that which was stated by the author of the treatise in another section—namely, "Because the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful are invariably preceded by correct knowledge," and so forth—would be contradicted. Likewise: "For one does not determine an object by means of these two," and so forth. Furthermore, it was said:
"From the recollection arising through the power of consciousness regarding things previously seen," and so forth (PVin 1.18).

Therefore, others explain it differently: the "object" (*artha*) refers to the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth composed by the Master Dignāga, because they are logical; whereas that which is composed by non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) is "non-object" (*an-artha*), because it is not logical. The "discrimination" (*vivecana*) between these two is their establishment according to what is logical and what is not, since this depends upon inference (*anumāna*). For it is only by relying on inference that the logicality or illogicality of the statements defining [the means of knowledge] is established, and not through perception (*pratyakṣa*), because perception is non-discursive (*avicāraka*).

That too is incorrect; for the validity or invalidity of definitional statements does not reside in their own form, but rather through their meaning. And that meaning is perceived as valid by means of inference in exactly the same way as it is by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As he will state:

"Direct perception, which is free from conceptual construction, is established by direct perception itself" (PV 3.123); likewise, "the determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is [established] through direct perception," and so forth.

Even he who thinks: "It is true that the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful is indeed accomplished through perception and inference; however, as for the claim that this discernment relies upon inference, since there may be dispute even regarding objects of perception, there is no basis for a definitive conclusion other than inference. Therefore, because of the primacy of inference, it is said to be the basis for such discernment."

This too is untenable; for it is established that only that which is ascertained is the object of perception, and since dispute is not possible regarding what has been ascertained, this [objection] is untenable.

But another says: the discernment of what is beneficial (*artha*) and what is harmful (*anartha*) arises from inference alone, not from perception. For those things whose results have already been experienced, or are currently being experienced, are not objects of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), because their result has already been accomplished. Therefore, one engages with beneficial and harmful objects that possess the capacity for future causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). And that capacity is not perceived among them by means of perception, such that they would become objects of purposeful activity.

Because the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished through engagement is yet to come, its capacity (*sāmarthya*, i.e., *kurvadrūpatā*) is also yet to come. Therefore, even regarding objects that are currently perceived, the determination of their suitability for future results occurs not through perception itself, but rather through the similarity (*sādharmya*) with an object that previously accomplished such purposeful activity; thus, the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful is achieved solely through inference.

That too is incorrect; for if that capacity (*yogyatā*, i.e., *kurvadrūpatā*) exists in objects as something belonging to the present time, then it would be ascertained by perception—even by one possessing an excellence of practice—just like a logical mark (*liṅga*). On the other hand, if it were future, then it could not be ascertained even by inference, because, as will be stated, there is no inference regarding a future object.

By this, that which is said—"the attainment of the object that is the locus of activity is indistinguishable for perception and inference"—should also be regarded as refuted. For the locus of activity is that which is capable of future causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), and it has been stated that such capacity is not determined by perception or inference. Furthermore, the locus of activity is held to be something delimited, yet a continuum (*santāna*) is not delimited by a single moment of perception or the like; so how could it be the locus of activity?

[Page 7] Now, it is argued that even though perception operates upon a single moment, by virtue of conceptual determination (*niścaya*), it has as its object a moment in common with others, and thus has a single continuum as its object; this is incorrect. For it is only by virtue of conceptual determination that perception is established as having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object through the very object that appears to it, and not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). This is because its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), just as perception whose object is a logical mark (*liṅga*) [is not ultimately the mark itself].

For instance, this appearing particular characteristic of smoke may be produced from grass, from leaves, or from something else; and because its specific differences are not determined therein, and because there is a determination for only a single moment, perception—even though its object is a particular characteristic—is established as having a universal as its object, since the ascertainment following upon perception conforms to the object of that perception.

Furthermore, it is not possible to establish perception as having a single moment as its object; for the moment that appears in perception is not ascertained, nor is it possible for it to be of the nature of either a preceding or a succeeding moment, since they exist at different times. Therefore, how could perception be established as having the general characteristic of a moment as its object through the non-determination of specific differences and the ascertainment of the mere moment?

Although the certainty "this is that very same [thing]" which arises subsequent to direct perception has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, it does not have a continuum (*saṃtāna*) as its object. This is because it apprehends both what was previously perceived and what is being perceived now, thereby failing to ascertain future moments; and furthermore, because its object is a form excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīya*). For this very reason, even when a moment appears, there is the certain cognition "this is a jar."

Now, if a real continuum capable of causal efficiency is not determined by perception and inference, how then do those two function as motivators [for action]? We reply: because they determine the mere nature of the thing itself.

For instance, having ascertained through direct perception that a thing such as fire is capable of performing a purposeful action like burning when it occurs in a continuous series in one place, one determines that this same thing, when perceived elsewhere—in another location and so forth—performs such an action by means of a continuous series alone. Furthermore, at another time, one who desires the result and seeks its specific nature, perceives fire and the like through both direct perception and inference, and proceeds to act based on the prior determination that "this is indeed that very same thing."

Therefore, the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the determination of the mere intrinsic nature of that object, not in the determination of its continuous occurrence, nor in the determination of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), since all of this has already been determined previously. Consequently, it is entirely logical that perception and inference are instigators [of action]. How then is it stated that the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful depends upon inference?

[...but it is not the object itself that is intended here, rather it is the Four Noble Truths. For we are seekers of liberation, and the Blessed One has stated that liberation arises from the vision of the Four Noble Truths. That vision is accomplished through the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Engagement in cultivation occurs through certainty regarding the Four Noble Truths. And since that certainty arises only from inference (*anumāna*) because [the truths] are beyond direct perception, it is inference alone that serves as the basis for discriminating between what is beneficial and what is harmful.

The "object" (*artha*) consists of cessation and the path because they are to be adopted; the "non-object" (*anartha*) consists of suffering and its origin because they are to be abandoned. Alternatively, the "object" is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and the "non-object" is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*); the differentiation of these two—their establishment according to their own nature—depends upon inference.

Furthermore, all cognition that performs the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful does not grasp the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather determines it; thus, it is indeed erroneous (*bhrānta*). Therefore, if the cognition of words and so forth is held to be the basis for discriminating between the beneficial and the harmful, it too is invalid (*apramāṇa*) precisely because it is erroneous. For this very reason, there is no possibility of its being explained here.

As for inference, even though it may be erroneous, its validity exists by virtue of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). However, if the validity of cognitions such as those derived from verbal testimony were accepted in this same way, they would be included within inference; and since that which does not possess the property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) cannot be a means of proof, the capacity to distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful belongs to inference alone. Now, one might object: if inference is valid by virtue of the necessary connection, then conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding eternal entities and the like would also be valid, because of their connection with objects such as momentariness. Or, if validity is based on a connection with the object as it is determined (*adhyavasita*), then the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel would also be valid.

For that [cognition] is indeed connected with the gem as it has been determined; therefore, even though there is an obstruction, since the object is determined as being related to a particular place and so forth, inferential cognition—which brings about the attainment of that object through the determination of the identity of the continuum based on its relation to that same place and so forth—is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but not every cognition.

The discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful consists in the form of comprehension; its mode (*ākāra*) is inference (*anumāna*), because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, the inferential mark (*liṅga*) itself is the inference; therefore, the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful has inference as its basis. Regarding the phrase "due to misconception concerning that" (*tadvipratipatteḥ*): it is because of confusion regarding that inference. To establish it—that is, to establish that inference by removing misconceptions—the author of the Sūtras says: "The property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmaḥ*), and so forth.

If it is asked: "If inference is to be established, why does [the author] establish only the logical reason (*hetu*) by means of [the statement] 'the property of the subject' (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth?"—this is not a fault. For since there is disagreement regarding inference by way of disagreement regarding the logical reason, its establishment occurs precisely by way of clarifying that [reason]. Furthermore, the cognition of inference arising from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics is indeed well-known in the world; therefore, disagreement is refuted by relying on that very common knowledge. Alternatively, when the word "inference" refers to the mark itself, then establishing the logical reason alone to refute disagreement regarding that [mark] is likewise without fault.

In this verse, the definition of the logical mark (liṅga), the restriction of its number, the reason for that restriction of number, and the exclusion of counter-examples are stated. "The property of the subject (pakṣadharma) being pervaded by a part of it" is the definition.

The property intended to be proven is a part of that [subject’s] side, and it is necessarily pervaded by that [reason]; this is the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). "Only threefold" is the restriction of number. "Because of the necessity of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)" is the cause for the restriction of number; the meaning is that inseparable connection is restricted to only these three. "Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those" is the exclusion of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); that is, fallacious reasons are other than those three types of valid reasons.

[Page 9] Now, if the pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) were grasped only in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then inference would not arise, because the pervasion of the reason (*hetu*) by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) would not be grasped in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). In that case, the definition "the reason is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) would be useless, as it would fail to produce cognition. Furthermore, even if pervasion were grasped through a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), inference would lack validity, because it would be of the nature of a memory (*smṛti*) since its object would have already been apprehended by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasped the pervasion.

Furthermore, it should not be stated that "the reason is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), because this is already understood by the very statement of its pervasion by the "portion of that" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*). Moreover, the capacity of a property of the subject to produce cognition arises through the force of its pervasion by the portion of that [probandum], and not merely by its existence in the subject; for otherwise, things such as a donkey present therein would not be reasons. Therefore, the definition "the reason is a property of the subject" need not be stated separately.
As it has been said:
"When the state of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*) exists, what is the use of the triad [of characteristics]?"
"If there is the property of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*), what is the use of the three [characteristics]?

Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) does not possess the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), because the apprehension of something else is a property of the person. Moreover, since a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) has the very form of the subject itself, and a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*) likewise does not depend on a subject by its own independence, a constructed (*kalpita*) characteristic of the subject cannot be a reason based on effect or essential nature, nor can it have the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, it must be stated that a reason is not merely a characteristic of the subject.

Likewise, if the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) were pervaded by the number three, then because the state of being a cause would be non-restrictive, the status of being a cause would be unavoidable elsewhere as well—such as in the case of the "conjoined" (*saṃyogin*) and so forth; thus, the restriction that "[a cause] is of only three kinds" would not be tenable.

Alternatively, if the state of being a cause were pervaded by the number three, then because the number three would be non-restrictive with respect to the cause, things such as the "effect" (*kārya*) and so on would also lack the status of being a cause; consequently, it would not be consistent to say that "only the effect and so on constitute the cause."

Furthermore: if there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between non-perception (*anupalambha*) and the probandum (*sādhya*), then even an unconnected reason would be a means of cognition; thus, the restriction that "it is of only three kinds" would not hold.

If, on the other hand, there is a connection, then because it would be included within either an effect (*kārya*) or an essential nature (*svabhāva*), the reason would still be of only three kinds—yet even so, this is not tenable. To say that "fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those" is not logical, because since another type of reason is absolutely imperceptible (*atyantaparokṣa*), its absence cannot be established by perception or other means; therefore, what was said is incorrect.

The reason (*hetu*) is that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds due to the restriction of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), while others than these are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

To this it is replied: although the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans is apprehended by means of a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), nevertheless, the specific determination that "the property to be proven exists here in the subject of the inference at this time" does not arise from the mere grasping of the pervasion; rather, it must arise from inference. Therefore, inference is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it establishes the object to be proven as connected to a specific place and so forth already apprehended; and that [inference] occurs only when there is the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and not otherwise.

Since the probans-property located in one place and so forth is not connected with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) located in another place and so forth, it follows that inference is simply the cognition of the property to be proven as delimited by a specific place and so forth, by the very power of the cognition of the probans as delimited by a specific place and so forth. It is not, however, the cognition of mere fire from mere smoke, because that [latter] is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Nor does the property of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) of the probans become established merely by the general understanding that "wherever there is the probans-property, there is the probandum-property," because the probans is not perceived as specifically being a property of the subject of the probandum, since it is stated in a general sense. Therefore, in order to bring about the cognition of the probandum as delimited by a specific location and so forth, the property of being a property of the subject must be demonstrated.

Therefore, what was stated—namely, that because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is already expressed by the statement "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," one need not say "and here there is smoke" for the sake of establishing fire in a specific location, since the meaning has already been stated"—is refuted. But if inference were thus a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then an inference lacking the property of the subject would also be a valid means of knowledge, because it would involve the apprehension of what was previously unapprehended. For example, inferring rain upstream upon seeing the swelling of a river downstream; or, "this child is a Brāhmaṇa, because his mother and father are Brāhmaṇas. As it has been said:
Even a river in flood, when seen at a lower level, necessarily leads one to infer the occurrence of rain situated above it as the regulating cause.
Thus, [the property of being directly perceived] is held to be the preeminent member of the reason;
yet that is rendered inconclusive by the observation of other properties previously mentioned.
The inference of a son’s status as a Brahmin from the Brahminhood of his parents is well-known throughout the world; it does not depend upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

If one were to imagine that the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) exists even there [in the case of a non-existent subject] due to affliction, then his definition would not coincide with the object to be defined.

"Just as that which is well-known in the world is followed by means of its characteristics, so too would the characteristic of the characterized be established; thus, it is not something previously unestablished that is being proven. To this it is replied: Why is it that the inference of rain occurs only upstream and not elsewhere? If you say, "Because the river's flood is related to that [rain]," then if this is the case, the inference of rain must occur at the place from which this river's flood has come, and not elsewhere, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, there can be the status of a prover (*gamaka*) only when the other party's connection to it is certain; otherwise, there would be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

Likewise, in the case of the statement, "This child is a Brahmin because his parents are Brahmins," here too, the property consisting of the Brahminhood of the parents is a related indicator (gamaka) for that very child whose Brahminhood is to be proven; it is not the mere Brahminhood of the parents [nor the Brahminhood of parents related to someone else], because such [other] Brahminhood does not serve as an indicator.

Therefore, since this [reason] also possesses the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), it is a means of cognition; thus, there is no need for the laborious postulation of *pakṣadharmatva*. Alternatively, that alone which is the cause of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is the logical reason (*hetu*). For example, smoke’s being an effect of fire, and a child’s being born from parents who are Brahmins, are the causes of the child’s Brahminhood; therefore, that alone is the appropriate reason. To postulate anything else would involve unnecessary complexity.

Likewise, there would be no inference of the rise of the ocean from the rising of the moon, because that [inference] would follow even before or after the rising of the moon. If it is argued that the inference occurs at the very time of the moon's rising, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been apprehended at that very moment;

If this is so, then the relationship with that very time constitutes the connection between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). In that case, that same time is the locus (*dharmin*), and the inference of the probandum occurs therein; since the rising of the moon is related to it, how can there be the fault of the probans not being a property of the locus (*apakṣadharmatva*)? Alternatively, if time is not accepted, then this inference is fallacious due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Or else, for the Buddhists, this inference does not exist because of the non-existence of time.

That is incorrect, because it is accepted that "time" is the designation for a specific great element (*mahābhūta*) which is the object of cognitions such as "forenoon" and so forth. In this same way, the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) should be applied in other cases as well.

Now, one might argue: "Granted that inference possesses validity when there is the property of being a characteristic of the subject, nevertheless, the definition 'characteristic of the subject' need not be stated separately, since it is already included by the statement of 'pervasion by a part of that' (*tadaṃśavyāpti*)."

True; however, this was stated for the purpose of excluding as a logical reason (*hetu*) that which, though pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), does not reside in the locus (*pakṣadharma*). For instance, smoke and the like observed in a kitchen or similar place would [otherwise] serve as a reason for inferring fire in the ocean.
But surely, a mark (*liṅga*) must be pervaded [by the probandum], and smoke located in a kitchen or similar place is not pervaded by the fire to be proven in the ocean.

True; however, by this mere statement of the definition—that "the reason is pervaded"—one does not obtain the understanding that "only where there is the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*) is there the inference of the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*). Therefore, the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is for the purpose of eliminating the suspicion that the inference of the probandum might occur elsewhere as well. Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), too, certainly possesses the status of being a property of the subject.

For when the very capacity to produce the perception of another thing, such as a patch of ground, constitutes the non-perception of that other thing, then since this capacity is of the same nature as the other ground and so forth, why would it not be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) for the non-perception? In the same way, [the property of] being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth is a property of sound and the like. Furthermore, even though non-perception has the form of a property of the person, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is indeed an effect of the other ground and so forth; its status as a property of that [ground] follows from its dependence upon it.

In the same way, although smoke and other such effects possess the property of being located in a particular place and so forth, it is merely by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that their very nature as related entities is established as "this is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).

The state of being a reason (*hetutva*) is pervaded by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), because that which has not known invariable concomitance is not a prover and thus lacks the status of a reason. Furthermore, invariable concomitance is pervaded by the two types of reasons: the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*). When there is a thesis to be proven consisting of either an affirmation or a negation, the effect-reason functions when another thing is affirmed, the essential-nature reason when that same thing is affirmed, and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) when there is a negation; therefore, the reason is pervaded by these three types, and thus it is of exactly three kinds.

However, it is not only the threefold reason that is a cause; for even the effect and so forth are non-causes when they are unknown. Furthermore, the capacity of the non-perception of the cause and the pervader to indicate [the absence of another] arises solely from their necessary connection (*pratibandha*). For it is precisely through that same necessary connection that the effect and the pervaded indicate the cause and the pervader; and it is through that very same necessary connection that the non-perception of the cause and the pervader indicates the absence of the effect and the pervaded.

Even in the case of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), when the very self of a jar or similar object—which is capable of producing an apprehension—is called "apprehension," and since apprehension is non-deviant from existence when all other causes are present, apprehension is here equated with existence; thus, in this case as well, the capacity to indicate [the probandum] is based solely on a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through identity (*tādātmya*). Furthermore, non-apprehension is not included within the category of effects (*kārya*) and other such reasons, because it does not depend upon a necessary connection with respect to its own probandum.

The cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) must arise from the presence of the reason (*hetu*) provided that it is dependent upon it. However, there is no such dependence when conjunction (*saṃyoga*) exists, because things that are not conjoined lack conjunction. Even for those things that are conjoined, their dependence does not arise from conjunction itself, since conjoined things arise from something else entirely. The same should be said regarding inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, dependence arises only through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). Consequently, conjunction and other relations—which fall outside the categories of effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—are not valid reasons, because they lack dependence and thus lack invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Now, if there is dependence upon that [logical mark], then that alone is the cause for its being a means of cognition; thus it is established that the reason is indeed threefold.

But even so, how can inference arise, given that non-conceptual perception does not grasp the property (*dharma*), the locus (*dharmin*), or their relationship, since it apprehends two real entities independently?

It is said: even by means of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), the apprehension of the relationship between property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) regarding smoke, location, and so forth, is nothing other than the appearance of one thing as being "on top of" another. And that [appearance] exists even in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); the only distinction between conceptual and its opposite is whether there is a verbal articulation (*ullekha*) or a lack thereof. Furthermore, that non-conceptual cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it produces affirmation and negation—such as "this is here" and "this is not here"—precisely with respect to the object as it has been apprehended.

Therefore, the determination of the essential nature of both the property-bearer (dharmin) and the property (dharma), as well as the determination of their relationship, occurs precisely through perception.

It has been stated that [the reason] is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). In the Sūtra, however, the "property of the subject" refers to the aggregate of both the property and the property-possessor (*dharmidharmasamudāya*). Since the status of being a property of such an aggregate is not established for the reason (*hetu*) from the perspective of the opponent, every such reason would consequently be unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, if it were established, inference would be rendered useless. Therefore, [Dignāga] says: "The subject (*pakṣa*) is the property-possessor (*dharmin*). This is because the term for the aggregate is applied metaphorically to its part. And the fact of being a part is the basis for the metaphorical application of the term for the aggregate; thus, the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is not called the "subject" (*pakṣa*).

Īśvarasena said: "One should simply state that 'the property of the subject (*dharmin*) is the logical reason (*hetu*),' because there is no purpose for [using] a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). To this, he replies with the words beginning "purpose," etc. He refutes this with the words beginning "no," etc. It is not the case that there is an absence of purpose; for one must consider that the metaphorical designation serves the purpose of excluding every [property] belonging to the subject. If the metaphorical designation were absent, the instruction would have to be simply "the property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*). And in that case, even a property of the subject in the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) would become a logical reason.

In the case of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), however, the property of every subject (*dharmin*) becomes negated. If one asks how this is so, he says: "Because it is a part of that" (*tadekadeśatvāt*). For instance, there is a metaphorical designation of a whole (*samudāya*) upon its parts. Being a part of that is the basis [for such usage], yet metaphorical designation does not apply everywhere. Since the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is a part of the thesis (*pakṣa*) because it is a constituent member of it, it is fit for metaphorical designation as the thesis; the employment of metaphorical designation is for the purpose of communicating its property.

And likewise, when there is the cognition of a substratum (dharmin) suitable for metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), there is the exclusion of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the reason] "because of the blackness of a crow" and so on is included. Now, if the meaning of the reason "because of being visible" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*) is "because of being an object of visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānaviṣayatvāt*), then this reason, being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), is already refuted by the very statement regarding the pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*); so what is the use of metaphor?

Furthermore, if the meaning of the reason is "because it produces visual consciousness," even then, that quality of producing it is simply existence; and since that [existence] also exists in sound, this [reason] is not merely a property of the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), according to some.

That is incorrect. For the capacity to produce visual consciousness is a specific property of existence (*sattvaviśeṣa*), and that belongs only to things such as jars, not to sound; therefore, the employment of a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) was made for the purpose of excluding it [from the category of sound]. However, even in the absence of a metaphorical designation, there is no status as a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) by virtue of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Nor is visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) pervaded by the impermanence of sound; so how could this [visibility] be its logical mark? This is not a fault. For it is pervaded merely by impermanence in general, and since that [impermanence] exists in sound as well, how could it be a non-reason (*ahetu*)?

[Regarding the passage beginning with] “by the expression ‘property’” (*dharmavacanena*) and so forth: since a property (*dharma*) is pervaded by its own constituent part (*tadaṃśa*), even by the mere mention of the property, because the property is dependent upon the locus (*dharmin*), it necessarily implies that locus. Therefore, when the establishment of the locus—that is, its reliance (*āśrayaḥ*, meaning its inclusion)—is accomplished, it is understood from the force of the term *dharmidharma* (property of the locus) that the mention of the "locus" (*dharmi*) here intends a close proximity (*pratyāsatti*). This is so when there is an intention to express pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The mention of the "subject" (*dharmin*) would be purposeless. Therefore, by the force of mentioning the subject, proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is established; and that proximity belongs specifically to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), because the reason is first presented in relation to it. Through that proximity, there will be the inclusion of the subject of the thesis. Why is the inclusion of the subject of the thesis not due to proximity? Because proximity exists not only for the subject of the thesis, but also for the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

In some cases, when an application is preceded by the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the existence of the reason (*hetu*) is first demonstrated even in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). If the establishment of the property-bearer of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) does not occur through proximity, then it will occur by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*); for by means of that very reason which consists in the pervasion of its part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), the existence of the property is established in the subject of the example. For it is thought that without an example, the pervasion of the reason by the property to be proven cannot be demonstrated. Therefore, by the exclusion [of the term] "property-bearer" (*dharmin*), there is the inclusion of the subject of the thesis alone.

Furthermore, one should not suspect that the mention of the "subject" (dharmin) is intended for the purpose of connecting it with the word "that" (tat) in the phrase "by a part of that," since the subject is already implied by the word "property" (dharma).

Thinking that where no further purpose is possible, that is the domain of *pāriśeṣya* (exclusion by remainder), whereas for the statement of the subject (*dharmin*) another purpose is indeed conceivable, the proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "Since its existence in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) is already established through its pervasion by that part [of the probandum], the repeated mention of the 'subject' might be suspected of being intended as a restriction, implying that only a property belonging to the subject of the example is the logical reason (*hetu*)."

Consequently, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that only properties such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) could serve as logical reasons (*hetu*), and not properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Therefore, a figurative application (*upacāra*) must be made. Furthermore, he asks: "Is this statement seen anywhere in a treatise on logic for the sake of establishing a restriction? To this, he says: "Only in the similar class," and so forth. In that regard, the definition of a reason according to the Teacher [Dignāga] is: "That which exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*), and is of two kinds [present and absent] in its absence (*tadatyaya*)."

Although the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is established by the restriction that "existence [of the reason] is only among similar instances" (*sajātīya eva sattvam*), the Teacher explained the statement "it does not exist there"—which asserts the non-existence [of the reason] in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). He did so so that non-existence might occur only where [the probandum] is absent, and not elsewhere, nor in the contradictory. Likewise here, the mention of the locus (*dharmivacana*) is suspected to be for the sake of a restrictive rule regarding existence.

[Objection: But surely, since that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) cannot be a logical reason, there is no need for a doubt regarding the restrictive rule; because a reason must be pervaded [by the probandum], and a property residing in one locus cannot be pervaded by a property of the probandum residing in another locus. Therefore, the inclusion of the subject of the probandum will occur simply through the force of stating a reason that is pervaded by a portion of that [probandum]. To this, he says: "By the force," and so forth.

From the force of what was just stated, there arises for listeners of keen intellect an understanding characterized by the apprehension of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) as the object [of the reason]; however, for those who would pursue that meaning on their own without the word, there would be a burden of comprehension. Therefore, by means of this mere metaphorical designation—namely, "the property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*)—which avoids the independent inference of the meaning not expressed by the word, and which is expressed by a term identical to "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*), the burden of comprehension is likewise avoided.
By the word *ca* (and), he says this: those who require instruction from another must understand this meaning from the statement of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

Since [the reason] is understood according to its definition, how could there be this doubt that "that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) is not a logical reason"? Therefore, the employment of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is for the purpose of removing the doubt regarding the restriction for those who follow the definition. In this context, because the use of words necessarily has the result of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), it must certainly be determined that, given the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) is the only possible compound and no other is possible.

And thus, because of the restriction that [the reason] must be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) alone, its pervasion by a part of that [subject] (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is contradicted; pointing out this contradiction in definition, he says:

Since being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) requires that the subject serve as a qualifier which excludes [the property] from anything else, a property that depends on such a qualifier does not extend to any other similar instance (*sapakṣa*) apart from that which has been made the subject. For indeed, whatever is qualified by the subject belongs only to the subject—just as Devadatta’s son [belongs only to him]. Because it does not extend elsewhere, there would be no commonality (*sādhāraṇatā*); rather, there would be a lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇatā*). This amounts to saying that it contradicts the pervasion by a portion of that [subject].

Because it is established that there is a pervasion by that part [of the subject] through their commonality; therefore, if it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there is no pervasion by that part, and if there is pervasion by that part, it is not a property of the subject—thus the definition is contradictory.

Now, if the pervasion of the probans by the probandum has not been apprehended in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). But if it has been apprehended, why does the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason in the example contradict the pervasion of that portion [of the reason] by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), since the pervasion has already been established even in the subject? Furthermore, when the momentariness of all things is to be proven, what positive concomitance could there be for the reason characterized as "existence" (*sattva*) in an example?

Therefore, because of the necessary connection with its own probandum, the reason is established as being pervaded by it; and since that [pervasion] is also established in the subject of the probandum through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case, there is no need for anything else, such as positive concomitance (*anvaya*). So how can this doubt be raised: that [the reason] is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because it does not occur elsewhere?

(Granted that although there is no arising of inference without the pervasion of the probandum by the reason in the subject of the thesis, nevertheless, without a means of valid cognition that grasps the necessary connection between the probandum and the probans in the example, the pervasion would not be established even in the subject of the thesis; therefore, this objection is appropriately raised.)

As for what was said—that this [objection] was raised with reference to the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) and with reference to a specific type of essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*)—that, however, concerns the inference of momentariness based on existence (*sattva*). For that [inference] is a means of cognition precisely through the operation of a proof that sublates the counter-example (*vipakṣabādhakapramāṇa*); we shall examine this in detail later. Therefore, for the sake of recollecting the proof of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) previously grasped, the occurrence of the reason elsewhere must be taken into account.

He addresses this with the words "no," and so forth. It is not the case that there is no non-occurrence elsewhere. Why? Because "non-connection" (*ayoga*) is the relation [in question], and the subject (*pakṣa*) is qualified by the exclusion of that. For qualification does not occur solely through the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), but also through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). This is because where the existence of a property in a given locus (*dharmin*) is doubted, the exclusion of non-connection is established by logical necessity.

Here is an example: "Caitra is an archer. For regarding Caitra, there is doubt as to whether archery exists or not; thus, when it is said, "Caitra is an archer," the alternative possibility of non-archery—which has been brought to mind by the listener's expectation—is excluded. In this case, the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is logically established.

Desiring to refute the position held by others, he says: "The connection is that because there is no non-occurrence elsewhere, there is no 'uniqueness' (asādhāraṇatā) due to the qualification by the exclusion of connection with another. Here too, the example is as follows: even though this word "archer" (*dhanurdhara*) is a general term—as in "Pārtha is the archer"—it functions here to denote one of preeminent quality through the force of the context and so forth; for since being an archer is already established in the case of Pārtha, there is no suspicion of non-connection (*ayoga*).

When there is a doubt regarding the possibility of another [person] possessing such excellence—namely, whether such excellence exists elsewhere or not—and one says, "Pārtha is the wielder of the bow" (*pārtho dhanurdharaḥ*), then it is understood that Pārtha alone is the preeminent wielder of the bow and no other. Therefore, in this case, the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is logically established. Similarly, when there is a doubt as to whether this property belongs to the subject (*pakṣa*) or not, and one says "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmaḥ*), it is understood that it is indeed a property of the subject and not a non-property.

And because the property (*dharma*) is dependent [upon the subject], it functions as a qualifier; thus, non-connection (*ayoga*) is excluded, not connection with another (*anyayoga*). Since the exclusion of connection with another is established through the pervasion by that part [of the reason] in the example, there is no doubt regarding the example. We shall explain this—that is, we shall point it out—in the fourth chapter (4.160).

Regarding the phrase "a part of that (*tadaṃśaḥ*) is its property (*taddharmaḥ*"), does the word *tat* (that) refer to the subject (*pakṣa*) and not to the property (*dharma*), because a property cannot possess another property? A part of that subject is its very property to be proven (*sādhya*). If it is asked how the word *aṃśa*, which is conventionally established as meaning a "portion" (*ekadeśa*), can denote a property, he replies: "By virtue of the speaker’s intention. Words do not possess denotative power through the force of the object itself, but rather by virtue of the speaker’s desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). Thus, the connection with the context is: "a part of that (*tadekadeśaḥ*) is a 'part of that' (*tadaṃśaḥ*)."

If it is asked, "Why is it so? he says: "Because the word 'pakṣa' does not denote the aggregate. If the word *pakṣa* were to express the aggregate, then a part (*aṃśa*) consisting of the property (*dharma*), which is one portion of the *pakṣa* whose nature is the aggregate of both property and property-possessor (*dharmī*), would exist. However, by means of the word *pakṣa* used figuratively, only the property-possessor is denoted; and since that [property-possessor] is a single entity, how could there be a "part" of it?

He explains [the term] by means of the passage beginning with "the pervaded state" (*vyāptaṃ padam*) and "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). Of that which exists as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there is pervasion—that which pervades and that which is pervaded—because they are cognized as the pervading and the pervaded properties (*vyāpyavyāpakadharma*). When it is intended to be expressed as the pervading property, then the connection is: "the very existence of the pervader, which is the object to be known" (*gamyasya*). In the phrase "therein" (*tatra*), this refers primarily to the sense of the locative case, not primarily to the sense of a substratum (*ādhāra*), because properties do not possess other distinct properties.

Therefore, this is the meaning: wherever the pervaded exists in a given subject (*dharmin*), there the pervader necessarily exists; thus, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the property of the pervader. However, it is not restricted in such a way that "only the pervader exists there," for that would entail the consequence of the reason being non-existent [in the subject], since even non-pervaders such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) exist there. Nor is it restricted to mean "it exists only there," for that would result in the fallacy of [qualities like] being produced immediately after an effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) not being valid reasons.

Furthermore, the reason would be "inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa*) because of its presence among the objects of cognition (*prameya*) despite their being eternal. However, when the state of being a pervaded property (*vyāpyadharmatā*)—that is, pervasion—is intended, then the pervaded exists only where the pervader exists in a given subject (*dharmin*), and not elsewhere. Here too, the restriction that "the pervaded exists only there" is not based on the consequence of the reason's absence, since even what is not pervaded may exist there; nor is it restricted to the sense that "the pervaded exists only there."

Because that which exists in only a portion of the similar instances (sapakṣa) would result in being a non-reason; furthermore, the common property (sādhāraṇa), such as "knowability" (prameyatva), would become a reason because it necessarily exists in eternal things. By the phrase "the existence of the pervader (vyāpaka) therein," the positive concomitance (anvaya) is implied; or by the phrase "the existence of the pervaded (vyāpya) only therein," the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is implied. Alternatively, the description of the properties of the pervaded and the pervader within the context of pervasion is for the purpose of demonstrating their necessity and lack of necessity respectively. Therefore, the reason is that which is pervaded, and not the pervader, because the latter lacks necessity.
Now, how can a property that exists without its pervaded be a pervader? For it would not be a pervader due to its lack of connection with the pervaded.

True. However, the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between two properties is determined only in a general sense. When the generality of impermanence (*anityatvasāmānya*) is ascertained as being pervasive of "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), yet that same [impermanence] is also observed in things not produced immediately after an effort, then the pervader is said to be "non-restricted" (*aniyata*). But if it is possible to ascertain that impermanence has the very nature of being produced immediately after an effort, then these two are mutually pervaded; thus, the reason (*hetu*) becomes truly pervaded (*vyāpta*). And this is the logical principle: that which is the subject of dispute is the probandum (*sādhya*), while the other is the means of proof (*sādhana*).

If, then, the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is merely that "it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by a part of that [subject]," then the reason would have two forms—namely, being a property of the subject and being pervaded by a part of that [subject]—whereas elsewhere it is stated to have three forms; how then is there no contradiction? To this, he says:

By this statement regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that part, both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are expressed; the sense is that pervasion consists in the nature of positive and negative concomitance. For it is said that whatever is concomitant with something, and ceases when that thing ceases, is pervaded by it. Since pervasion is of the nature of that [concomitance], the expression of pervasion denotes both positive and negative concomitance; therefore, because the two forms are expressed by the statement of pervasion, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, those two are ascertained due to the context of the "indicative reason" (*jñāpaka-hetu*).

And the ascertainment of those two is not by means of a single pramāṇa alone; rather, it is by whichever pramāṇa is its own respective determiner for each. And which pramāṇa belongs to which will be explained later.

[Objection: But since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), how can there be its negation (*vyatireka*)? If you say that its nature consists in the absence [of the mark] when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent, [we reply: No. For that very existence of the mark which occurs only when the probandum exists is itself the negation when the probandum is absent. Therefore, although there is identity between the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), their distinction is merely constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). Others maintain that the negative concomitance is the mark’s character of being non-existent when the probandum is absent.

And since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) consists in the form: "wherever there is the property of the probans (*sādhanadharma*), there is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)," therefore, that which was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila [is refuted].
"The rising of the sun that is yet to come is not joined with today's rising;
nevertheless, from today's rising, it is inferred that it will also occur tomorrow."
When the tip of smoke is seen in the sky, fire is inferred on the ground; yet the tip of the smoke follows the fire, and it does not reside upon the ground.

Thus, it has been refuted [by us] that "in this way, the mark does not follow the bearer of the mark through space and time; therefore, no part of its connection with the name is perceived as a positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," because the reason exists as a positive concomitance with the probandum (*sādhyānvaya*) exactly as it has been described. By this, the following objection is also answered: [The opponent argues: "If the reason is established by means of the object of inference (*anumeya*), then what is the point of stating the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? For the reason would already be established for the proponent (*vādin*) simply by the establishment of the object of inference. Alternatively, if the reason were established independently of the object of inference, then the statement of the example would be useless, since the reason would be established even without it. This is not so. For the object of inference is not established merely by the presence of the reason. Rather, the object of inference is established when the reason is shown to be pervaded (*vyāpta*) by the property to be proven (*sādhya*). And this pervasion is not established merely by the reason's existence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Therefore, the example is stated in order to demonstrate that very pervasion. Consequently, the example is not useless. Thus, the objection is refuted.
"In this case, the postulation of a relation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) must likewise be rejected;
for how could that which is not concomitant with something else be pervaded by it?

For this very reason, in order to refute such a pervasion imagined by others, the Teacher [Dharmakīrti] demonstrated the worldly pervasion (*laukikī-vyāpti*) with the words "the presence there of the pervader," and so forth. The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the relation is that which grasps the mark's (*liṅga*) dependence upon the probandum (*sādhya*). And that which grasps this dependence is precisely what grasps the pervasion consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because dependence upon the probandum is itself the nature of pervasion.

Therefore, from that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there arises the certainty regarding the absence [of the pervader and the pervaded]: namely, that where the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is impossible, there is the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*); and where there is the absence of the pervader, there is the absence of the pervaded. Consequently, as stated by Bhaṭṭa Kumārila:

"And because its object is a universal (*sāmānya*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) cannot occur in perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor can it be inferred previously, since there is no other previously known positive concomitance."
Now, if there were an inference based on positive concomitance (anvaya) that is devoid of any other positive concomitance,
then since this [inference] would be established without depending on it, what would be the use of positive concomitance elsewhere as well?
Furthermore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the logical mark (liṅga) with the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) cannot be established at all;
for even with great effort, that absence would not be understood due to a lack of cognition.

The argument that "as long as the limit of all opposing factors has not been determined, who is able to know from that the non-occurrence of the reason?"—that too is refuted. Furthermore, the connection is to be understood as follows: it must be stated that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And in this way, the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is indeed stated; thus there is no contradiction.

Therefore, what was stated by Aviddhakarṇa—namely, "We certainly accept inference as a valid means of knowledge because it is recognized by the world; however, the definition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is incorrect"—is refuted, because the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark is also recognized by the world, just as in the case of smoke and so forth.

Now, how can there be an ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*) by means of its respective valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that the mark (*liṅga*) is a universal (*sāmānya*)? For that [universal] cannot be apprehended by perception, since perception has only the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; and what is not apprehended cannot function as a mark. Nor can the particular, even if apprehended, serve as a mark because it lacks concomitance (*anvaya*). Nor is there an apprehension of the universal through inference, because its mark—being itself a universal in form—cannot be apprehended by perception, and if it were apprehended by inference, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Thus he says:
"Because of the infinity of marks, the things marked by them, and the inferences, there is no comprehension of even a single thing marked [by them], even in many thousands of yugas."

Now, if it is argued that the universal (sāmānya), which appears as a conceptual construction of the nature of the effect, is called the "reason" (hetu) for the effect and so forth because it is the basis for the perception of the effect and the like, and because of the determination (adhyavasāya) of it as such;
