That is incorrect; since that [exclusion] is also not distinct from conceptual construction, it does not persist in other instances—just like the conceptual construction itself—and how, then, could it be a universal or a logical mark (*liṅga*)? Therefore, it is precisely the form of smoke and so forth as excluded from what is of a different class (*vijātīya*), which is ascertained by perception due to the context of the "informative cause" (*jñāpaka-hetu*), that is called a "logical mark characterized as a universal" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-liṅga*) because its specific features are not determined. It is not, however, the exclusion from the dissimilar (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*) or the form of the conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*), because these are non-entities (*avastu*). Thus, this is the meaning:

By means of a determination (*niścaya*) arising in the wake of perception—which ascertains the form excluded from non-smoke—and by the non-ascertainment of specific qualities such as whether this appearing particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke is made of grass, made of leaves, or something else, the mark (*liṅga*)—which is a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) consisting of multiple particular characteristics—is established within the domain of perception. And just as the mark possesses a universal nature due to the non-ascertainment of its specific qualities, so too does the probandum (*sādhya*). Thus it is said: "Because it establishes merely the thing itself as excluded from what is not that [nature]..."
"It has been stated that the logical mark (liṅga) has a universal (sāmānya) as its object because it does not rest on particulars.

Thus, for such a logical mark characterized as a universal, its being an effect of the probandum (sādhyakāryatva) and its being of the same nature as the probandum (sādhyasvabhāvatva) are not contradictory, since it is a real entity (vastu). And since that logical mark is ascertained by perception and other means of valid cognition, everything is well-established.
With the words "These very ones" (*ta eta*) and so forth, he explains the phrase "that [reason] is indeed threefold" (*sa tridhaiva*).

"These very ones": those whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, whose nature (*svabhāva*)—consists of the effect, the essential nature, and non-perception, as they are joined with the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and with the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*). "From smoke" (*dhūmāt*) is the statement of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*); "fire is here" (*agnir atra*) is the result of the proof (*sādhyaphala*). However, this is not an application of the thesis (*pakṣaprayoga*).

But surely, that portion of space which is in contact with fire is perceptible; and that which is perceptible—consisting of light and so forth in the form of a portion of the sky—is not possessed of fire when it is seen as having smoke. Therefore, how can there be an establishment of smoke in a location through perception? Consequently, it is logical that smoke itself is the subject (*dharmin*).

Uddyotakara maintains that the relationship between the probandum and the probans is as follows: "This smoke possesses fire because it is smoke. However, even for him, since the smoke-part that possesses fire is imperceptible, and since the visible portion situated above does not coexist with fire, how can there be a perceptual ascertainment of the smoke-universal (*dhūmasāmānya*) in the subject (*dharmin*)? If it is argued that the composite whole of the smoke (*dhūmāvayavin*) is perceptible, we say no; for that [whole] does not exist apart from its parts.

The world’s conventional determination [regards] that [space] as a single entity; thus, even for such a portion [of space], its imagined unity is not prevented. Furthermore, it is the portion itself that the world apprehends as the "locus" (dharmin) with respect to fire, not the smoke. Therefore, if the inference of fire is desired, let the inference be made precisely with the portion as the locus; this is merely the extent of the matter.

However, some maintain that the previously mentioned refutation of the fault does not apply here. Alternatively, the subject (*dharmin*) is the observed location, and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is "possessing fire below," rather than merely "fire" itself. Since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has already been established with such a property to be proven, and smoke is established here through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could this not be an inference? As for the claim that the probans as an effect (*kāryahetu*) functions as a means of cognition only in relation to a specific place and so forth—that is entirely inconsistent, because the qualification of "place" and so on remains unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, because this probandum is established by the mere sight of smoke; or rather, when one has seen fire in a particular location and then removes doubt regarding its specific nature—such as whether it is *kiṃśuka* wood or something else—by means of seeing smoke, this should be understood as the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*). For at that time, both the locus (*dharmin*) and the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma*) are established through perception.

As for what is said—that inference [occurs] with respect to a subject (*dharmin*) that consists of both perceptible and imperceptible aspects—that is incorrect. Even if the reason (*hetu*) is established in the perceptible portion, there can be no inference of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) therein, because it is sublated by perception. In the imperceptible portion, however, inference might occur; yet in that case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, a property of a subject consisting of a perceptible form cannot be established by perception in the imperceptible portion, since perception does not operate upon that which is imperceptible.

Or, when the inference of impermanence is directed toward a sound that is perceptible by hearing, how then could the subject (dharmin) possess both perceptible and non-perceptible natures? This is trivial. "Because it is a *śiṃśapā*" is an example of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Umbeka, however, says here: "The capacity of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical reason (*hetu*) to produce cognition is utterly cast aside, because the relationship between the cognized and the cognizer (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is based on difference. For there can be no such thing as a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in that which is non-different. A *śiṃśapā* tree is not identical with the essence of 'tree,' because it is excluded from it. For whatever is excluded from something else is not of that same essence, just as a cloth is not of the essence of a jar. And since a *śiṃśapā* is excluded from *khadira* trees and the like, it is not of their essence."

Furthermore, if [the probandum] were identical with that [the probans], then at the very moment of perceiving the mark (*liṅga*), because there would be no distinction [between them], the probandum would be as unperceived as the mark itself; yet since the nature of the probandum would have already been grasped, its status as something to be inferred (*anumeya*) would be lost. Moreover, if the state of being a *śiṃśapā* were the indicator (*gamaka*) by virtue of identity (*tādātmya*), then, since identity is no different [in both cases], it would follow that the state of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) is also an indicator of the *śiṃśapā*.

Now, because it is not restricted [to the object], it lacks the capacity to indicate; therefore, restriction itself is the cause for the capacity to indicate, and not identity (*tādātmya*), since identity is observed even in the case of "tree-ness," which is deviant [with respect to being a *śiṃśapā*]. If it is argued that the *śiṃśapā* does not exist as having that very nature (*tadātman*) in a tree, then it would not be identical with it. In every way, the relationship of the indicated and the indicator exists only between two things [that are related]; however, in the case of difference (*nānātmya*), there is an absence of identity. Thus, the relationship of the indicated and the indicator must be rejected for both the exclusions (*apoha*) of "non-śiṃśapā" and "non-tree," or for the cognitions (*buddhi*) of those exclusions.

That is incorrect. For a *śiṃśapā* has the nature of being a particular kind of tree, and a particular kind of tree also has the very nature of being a *śiṃśapā*; thus, there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the two. Even though this identity exists, someone might be somewhat confused regarding the nature that is excluded from non-trees, [but not] regarding the nature excluded from non-*śiṃśapās*. Therefore, because the mark (*liṅga*), such as a *śiṃśapā*, is apprehended, there is no loss of its status as an object of inference (*anumeya*). And since a *śiṃśapā* does not have the nature of being merely a tree, tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*) is not the indicator (*gamaka*) for the *śiṃśapā*.
As for the objection regarding the absence of the probandum, the probans, and so forth, the author of the treatise himself will refute it; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

"Location" (*pradeśa*) is a statement of non-apprehension. "In a specific location" refers to the place indicated. "Somewhere" means in a place established for both the proponent and the opponent. "There is no jar" is the conventional usage of the absence of a jar that is to be proven. By the words "apprehension," etc., the reason is indicated. The "characteristics of apprehension" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa*) are the instruments of apprehension, such as the eyes, whose capacities are unimpeded. That which has reached these [instruments] is a specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) capable of producing a cognition bearing its own appearance.

The meaning is that the object is included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the production of its own cognition. From the non-apprehension of such an object, the conventional designation of its non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*) is established.

But how can that which does not exist in a certain place meet the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) there? For meeting the conditions for apprehension consists in being an object of cognition; and if that [objecthood] exists, how could there be non-existence?

It is said: if a thing that was previously apprehended were to exist under the very same conditions of causal totality (*sāmagrī*) as before, it would be perceived just as it was in the earlier time. Having thus mentally reflected upon the fact that the thing has attained the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), its negation is established on the grounds that it does not appear. This, however, does not apply to an invisible object, because there is no means to reflect upon its appearance, and because such an object is never apprehended at all.

If it is asked, "In the absence of the visible object, how is that very causal complex (sāmagrī) apprehended?", we reply: "Because there is the perception of one [of two] entities which are objects of the same cognition. Furthermore, the fact that the negated object possesses the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*) is ascertained by its own nature. To demonstrate that this very [fact] constitutes the possession of the conditions for perceptibility through the capacity for generating a single cognition, he says:

If a jar or the like were such that its existence were perceptible, it would necessarily be of that very nature; it could not be otherwise. Thus, it is never the case that such a thing is ungraspable; rather, it is necessarily known—this is the meaning. For this reason, the qualification "of that which has attained the conditions of perceptibility" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya*), which was stated, effectively means "of that existence which has attained the conditions of perceptibility. Here, however, the external referent is as follows: that by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).

"Perception itself is the defining characteristic. That which has attained this [characteristic] is "attained through the characteristic of perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), meaning its connection with cognition is non-deviant. That whose existence (*sattva*) is of such a nature is described as "thus characterized. The point is that when existence is of such a kind, cognition necessarily ceases upon the cessation [of the object]. All proof is pervaded by affirmation and negation; and the probandum (*sādhya*) being affirmed is divided by way of two types of necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Thus, showing that affirmation and negation depend upon three types of logical reasons (*hetu*), he says: "In that regard," and so forth.

Among those three types of reasons, two—the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*)—are proofs of a real entity (*vastu*), that is, proofs by way of affirmation (*vidhi*). The restriction "only these two" is intended; it does not mean "only these two are proofs of a real entity," because by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is also established through them. The third is the reason for negation (*pratiṣedhahetu*). Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as defined above is exclusively a reason for negation. However, one should not restrict it by saying "it is only this [one]," because exclusion is understood through the first two as well.

Someone says: "Exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is established by means of words and logical marks (*liṅga*); however, whatever exclusion there may be, it is all due solely to non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Therefore, non-apprehension alone is the single reason. This is incorrect. For first of all, this is not said with reference to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the operation of the means of valid cognition pertains only to the real entity (*vastu*). As it has been said: "Therefore, the validity of both [perception and inference] has the real entity as its object. Nor is this said on account of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), because conceptual determination pertains only to the real entity. Furthermore, there is no connection between the logical mark and exclusion.

[23] Furthermore, even one who thinks that in the case of non-perception (*anupalambha*), what is being established is the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent," and not a negation; and that this fitness is indeed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and likewise, when a location possessing fire is to be proven, the property to be proven is simply the location's possession of fire, and "because of possessing smoke" is the logical reason (*hetu*).

The claim that every reason (*hetu*) which is non-different from its locus (*pradeśa*) is necessarily a reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) is incorrect. For if it were so, even "donkey-ness" and the like would function as reasons for inference. If you argue that this does not occur because the donkey lacks the status of being an effect of fire, then since the very fact of smoke being an effect of fire is the basis for its probative power, how is it not a reason of effect (*kāryahetu*)?

But another thinks: "Non-apprehension, however, has a location as its effect; thus, when the conventional usage of 'non-existent' is to be proven, it is simply an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). Furthermore, the conceptualization of 'produced' has the word 'impermanent' as its effect; therefore, every reason is an effect-reason."

That too is incorrect. For the conceptualization of "produced" (*kṛtaka*) would, by virtue of being the cause of the produced, be an inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*) of that [producedness] alone, not of impermanence. If it is argued that it establishes impermanence because the produced has impermanence as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then in that case, the cognition of impermanence would arise from "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) itself, and not from the conceptualization of the produced. This is because impermanence is indicated precisely through the nature of being produced. Alternatively, there would be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), since something could be a conceptualization of the produced and yet not be impermanent.

The capacity to produce artificial conceptualization is not distinct from the artifact; furthermore, it does not exist before or after [the production of the artifact]. Therefore, it is impermanent. If, on the other hand, that capacity were non-distinct [from the artifact], then how could it not be an essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical reason (*hetu*) for proving impermanence? Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

But why are there only two means of establishing a real entity? He says: "The connection by way of essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the proof (*sādhana*). This is a compound [meaning] that which is established by way of essential nature. That is to say, being connected by way of essential nature; in other words, that whose essential nature is connected. When that [essential nature] exists, the sign (*liṅga*)—the object—does not deviate from the signified (*liṅgin*)—the object.

And from what does that essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) arise? He says: "Because of being of that nature" (*tadātmatvāt*), that is, because [the probans] has the nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāvatvāt*). Regarding its being of that nature—that is, the probans having the nature of the probandum—since the probandum itself is the probans, there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) would be merely a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "No," and so forth. [This is not so] because the various properties (*dharma*) constituting the probandum and the probans are conceptually constructed through the differentiation of their exclusions (*vyāvṛttibheda*), that is, through superimposition (*āropa*).

This is what is meant: a distinction between properties (*dharma-bheda*) is superimposed, and by means of that, a distinction between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabheda*) is established. For it is said that the certain [reason] is the indicator (*gamaka*), while the object to be ascertained is the indicated (*gamya*). Since the object of ascertainment is precisely that which has been superimposed, the distinction between properties is one superimposed through a distinction in ascertainment. And this we shall explain in the section on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3:163–73).

The Master Dignāga also stated this, as he says: "And likewise," and so forth. "All indeed" means that even in cases where there is a real distinction between the probandum and the probans, such as fire and smoke, because conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is impossible through the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), one infers by means of this; thus, the inferential mark (*anumāna-liṅga*), the object of inference (*anumeya*)—which is the subject of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—and their conventional usage take the form of diversity.

In other words, the linguistic convention of difference [is established] by means of a distinct form—consisting of the property (*dharma*) and the locus of the property (*dharmin*)—which is mounted upon the intellect and has entered into the appearance of the intellect. If, then, the linguistic convention of property and locus is merely imagined by the intellect, it follows that the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*) would result from a reason (*hetu*) that is itself imagined. Consequently, every fault that is attributed to a reason would apply here as well. As Bhaṭṭa says:
"Or, even if a difference exists, it is imagined by the intellect... (Ślokavārttika, Nirālamba 171–72).
It is postulated for the sake of conventional discourse regarding the property to be proven, the proving property, and so forth.
Therefore, when this proof is employed by you, as long as it is stated that "cognition arises in every case," there would be a state of refutation.

Here he says: "Distinction," and so forth. It is this very [distinction] that makes the object understood; however, the distinction consisting of diversity—namely, "this is the property" (*dharma*) and "this is the substratum" (*dharmin*)—is produced by the form of the cognition and is merely conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*) by the cognition. It is neither the object nor the logical mark (*liṅga*), for both are produced by the form of the cognition. To the question, "Why does the comprehension of the object not arise from a logical mark that is itself fashioned by conceptual construction? he says: "Conceptual," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since the various types of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—that is, specific conceptualizations—are independent insofar as they follow merely one’s own desire, they do not depend on [external] objects; because they do not arise directly from them, they do not have external objects as their objective support (*ālambana*).

Therefore, when a conceptual construction is imagined by those [desires] which are themselves non-objects, and that [construction] is taken as its object—that is, being an "imagined object"—if one were to admit the cognition of an object based on such a cause, there would be only the attainment of a non-object, and never the attainment of an actual object.

He states the second definition of the probans (*pratibandhalakṣaṇa*) with the words "of the effect as well," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of that nature" (*tatsvabhāvasya*), which refers to the nature of the effect, he says this in response to one who does not accept the validity of inference based on its arising from that [cause] (*tadutpatteḥ*). The connection is as follows: "these two cognitions of the inferable are valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*); "these two" refers to the logical marks (*liṅga*) of essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).

He says "two" because non-apprehension is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*); or rather, he says "two" with reference to what has been introduced: namely, the two cognitions of the inferable objects, which are essential nature and cause. "Even though they do not manifest that" means even though they do not manifest the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the inferable object; for they do not manifest that directly, as they do not arise from it immediately.

If one asks, "How then is there non-deviation? he says: "Because of its arising from those"—that is, because it arises indirectly from the two inferable [objects], namely the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the cause (*kāraṇa*). "Non-deviating from those" means non-deviating from the inferable objects. For this reason, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, what was stated by Aviddhakarṇa—that "valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the determination of an object not yet apprehended; hence, inference is not a valid cognition because it lacks the capacity to determine an object"—is refuted. This is because every discerning person seeking to act investigates a valid cognition precisely as that which points out an object that serves as the locus of action, and an object that serves as the locus of action is necessarily one capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, it has been stated that perception does not directly determine the capacity of a thing for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) to be accomplished through future activity; therefore, how could its validity consist merely in the determination of an object? Consequently, perception is a means of valid cognition because, by way of its arising with respect to its own object, it produces a certainty—such as "this is indeed that very thing which I previously apprehended as a continuous stream of causal efficiency"—and thus prompts action. The same applies to inference as well.

With the words "of perception also," etc., he states the pervasion (vyāpti): "only non-deviation from the object. When there is the possibility of an object previously ascertained as being capable of producing the intended effect, the validity of perception consists precisely in its existence [in that case]; otherwise, in the absence of that [object], because of the non-correspondence with the ascertained object, perception occurring when the object is absent would be deceptive. This is what is meant: when perception does not determine an entity that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, if even such a thing were to deviate [from its effect], there would be no valid cognition at all. And what else could constitute the non-deviation of one thing from another? [The text asks: "What other [basis] for the non-deviation of one thing, which is a distinct entity, exists from another, apart from its arising from that? There is none other; the meaning is that non-deviation is simply that very arising from it (*tadutpatti*).

Why? Because for things whose forms are not dependent and whose natures are not connected, there is no necessity of coexistence, and consequently, no necessity of non-deviation. Therefore, since perception arises precisely from an object that is ascertained by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it is non-deviant; and since this [capacity] also exists in inference, the two are equal—this is the intended meaning.

By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: that because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-figurative (*agauṇa*), it is difficult to obtain certainty regarding an object through inference (*anumāna*). If "non-figurative" is said to mean "non-metaphorical" (*anupacarita*), then inference is also indeed non-metaphorical, because its nature consists in a non-erroneous cognition (*askhaladbuddhi*).

Now, if the collection of both the property and the property-possessor (dharmin) were the object to be proven (sādhya), it would be impossible for the reason (hetu) to possess the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) or to have positive concomitance (anvaya). Therefore, in order to establish the property of being a predicate of the subject, the status of being the object to be proven must be metaphorically attributed (upacaritavya) to the property-possessor, and in order to establish positive concomitance, it must be so attributed to the property. Thus, because its object is metaphorical, inference itself is metaphorical.

That is incorrect because, in the world, when mere smoke is seen in a given subject (*dharmin*) as being pervaded by mere fire, the cognition of fire occurs in that very place; thus, what here is a mere metaphorical usage? In this way, the status of the whole (*samudāya*) as the probandum (*sādhya*) is established. As it has been said: "When the property alone is to be proven in the subject, the establishment of the intended whole is thereby accomplished. Furthermore, even if the word "probandum" is used metaphorically with respect to the object of inference, it does not follow that inference itself is metaphorical.

Now, if it is argued that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-derivative and non-erroneous, whereas inference (*anumāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge because it is erroneous, that is incorrect.

For even though the inference of fire is erroneous, it is observed in the world to be a valid means of knowledge—just like direct perception—because it arises from that [perception] and involves the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of external fire. If, on the other hand, even direct perception were not accepted as a valid means of knowledge, then there would be a contradiction with worldly consensus, since both direct perception and inference are recognized as valid means of knowledge by the world.

Now, it is not that the validity of perception and inference is being denied; rather, when faced with the challenge that neither a three-featured nor a four-featured logical mark (*liṅga*) is established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if inference is then cited as the proof, that same challenge applies there as well. Thus, the sūtras are entirely devoted to such challenges. Accordingly, the sūtra states: "If [the reason is stated] in terms of a particular, there is no general concomitance; if in terms of a universal, it is a proof of what is already established. (NS 2.1.39)

That too is incorrect; for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) has already been implied by the statement of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Nor can one be questioned by means of what is not a means of valid cognition, because it would be unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent.
[Note 1: *Pramāṇasamuccaya*. Note 2: In the margin:

Now, if inference consists of speech and is not a means of valid cognition for the speaker, yet one conveys [the meaning] to the opponent by means of speech, then questioning would be carried out by means of what is not a means of valid cognition.

That too is incorrect. For from the utterance of both [the speaker and the listener], the cognition of the object arises as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely because it determines the object; it is only that, since the speaker’s own comprehension has already been established, it is not [for him] a valid means of knowledge. But if it were not a valid means of knowledge for him, then it would not be a valid means of knowledge for either of them—so how could the cognition of the object arise from it? Furthermore, as for what was said—that "inference is refuted by means of an inference established for the opponent"—that too is refuted by this very point. This applies when [the word] functions as a signifier by virtue of its connection [to the object].

"And fire is not non-conjoined with any part whatsoever; nor is smoke [non-conjoined]. Therefore, by that [conjunction], the manifestation [of fire] is obtained from smoke. The objection raised against the opponent by Master Dignāga—that there would be the consequence of a relationship of signifier and signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) in every respect—is here also anticipated regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) with the words "If... and so forth. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Because it arises from the probandum, the effect is the signifier of the cause. Thus, a relationship of signifier and signified in every respect would result. Just as the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of fire are signified, its specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) such as being produced from grass or wood (*tārṇapārṇṇādi*) would also have to be signified.

Just as smoke possesses particular properties (*viśeṣadharma*), its general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and earthiness (*pārthivatva*) would also be indicative [of fire]. Why? Because there is a relationship of produced and producer in every respect. For instance, just as fire is the producer by way of general properties such as fire-ness (*agnitva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and existence (*sattva*), so too is it the producer by way of particular properties such as being produced from grass (*tārṇa*) or wood (*pārṇa*).

And just as smoke is produced as endowed with its own specific properties fixed to it, such as being smoky and pale, so too is it [produced] by means of general properties such as existence (*sattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*); therefore, just as there is a cause-and-effect relationship between these two, there would likewise be a relationship of the signified and the signifier. To this, he says:

"Not so," and so forth. There is no relationship of produced and producer in every respect; and therefore, how could there be a relationship of signifier and signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*)? If one asks why, it is because in the absence of those—namely, those specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) such as being produced from grass or wood—the smoke in its mere generality lacks that very rule of origination (*tadutpattiniyama*), which consists in the fact that it arises from those specific properties alone.

Likewise, in the absence of that [fire], there is no such rule of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti-niyama*)—in the form of "this belongs to fire alone"—regarding general properties (*sāmānya-dharma*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), which occur even when fire is absent. How could there be a relationship of producer and produced in every respect, such that there would be a relationship of signifier and signified in every respect?

Since this is so, therefore an effect such as smoke is "inseparable" (*avinābhāvi*)—that is, it does not exist without [its cause]—by means of as many intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) as it possesses, such as "smokeness" and so forth; here the third case ending is used in the sense of a specific characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). Where is it inseparable? In the cause; that is, within the domain of the cause. Alternatively, "in the cause" (*kāraṇe*) is a locative of support (*ādhārasaptamī*): it is inseparable from as many intrinsic natures as reside in the cause, such as "fireness," "substantiality," and so forth.

The meaning is that for those general properties residing in the cause, the cause is the signifier of the effect. What is the reason? Because of the restriction to being its effect (*tatkāryatvaniyamāt*). This is because of the existence of such a restriction as "only those general properties residing in the cause are its effect. For the effect never deviates from those general properties. Thus far, it has been explained that the general properties residing in the cause are what is to be understood (*gamyāḥ*).

Showing that the specific properties residing in the effect (*kāryagata*) are the indicators (*gamaka*), he says: “By those very [properties],” and so forth. The effect, too, is an indicator of the properties residing in the cause by means of its own inherent properties. Those specific forms, such as the state of being smoke (*dhūmatva*) or its paleness (*pāṇḍutva*), which do not occur in anything other than the [fire], do not exist without those general properties residing in the cause. Here too, the phrase “because of the necessity of being its effect” (*tatkāryatvaniyamāt*) is to be understood.
This is because there is a necessity of being an effect with respect to those very specific properties residing in the effect, in relation to the general properties residing in the cause.

If the relationship of the signified and the signifier were based solely on the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between general properties residing in the cause and specific properties residing in the effect, then there would be a relationship of producer and produced only in part. It would follow that only the general properties of fire are the producers, while only the specific properties of smoke are the produced. Since the relationship of producer and produced is intended to hold in every respect, this would contradict your own tenet. He refutes this [objection]: there is no consequence of a partial relationship of producer and produced.

Because it is accepted that a thing, being partless, is in every respect both produced and a producer; and because the relationship of the signified and the signifier is also intended in its entirety. Thus he says: "produced by that," and so forth. For if the particularity of the effect—which is produced by those specific properties residing in the causes—can be apprehended, since this falls under the jurisdiction of the indicative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*), then, because the apprehension of that produced particularity is intended, the specific properties residing in the causes possess the status of being the signified (*gamya*).

For instance, when the smoke of *aguru* is perceived, there certainly occurs an inference of that fire. Likewise, regarding the phrase "the particularity of the mark" (*liṅgaviśeṣa*), the particularity is the mark itself, namely the characteristic of smoke; since it is intended that the capacity to indicate (*gamakatva*) exists upon the perception of those [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) which have that [smoke] as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) or qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). For substance-ness and the other categories, when qualified by smoke, do not deviate from fire. [Objection: But surely it is smoke alone that is the indicator (*gamaka*) in that case, and not substance-ness and the others as qualified by it. Just as in the case of "because it is knowable while being produced," it is the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) alone that is the indicator, and not knowability (*prameyatva*).

This is true. However, some maintain that this statement is made merely to demonstrate the absence of deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Others, however, say: the inclusion of the universal (*sāmānya*) here is not because of the deviation of smoke; rather, for all cognizers, there is first a cognition of the perceived object in its universal form, followed by the determination of the particular (*viśeṣa*). And in that case, the universal which has been apprehended is not at all abandoned.

Therefore, by virtue of the cognizer’s own conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is the universal as qualified by the particular that becomes the signifier (*gamaka*), and not [the particular] due to its deviation.

This is correct; however, if this rule holds—that the cognition of a particular must be preceded by the cognition of a universal—then how is there a cognition of mere smoke that is devoid of [universals] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*)? Furthermore, the objection previously stated remains exactly as it was. Therefore, this is the sound solution here: because the particular characteristic of the mark (*liṅga*) is employed solely as a qualifier of the universal, it lacks the status of a logical reason (*hetu*); for it would possess the status of a reason only if it were employed as a reason itself, and not otherwise.

When, then, are the general properties residing in the logical mark (liṅga) non-indicative? To this he says: "unqualified," and so forth. When properties such as substantiality (dravyatva) and the like are intended as unqualified, they are not accepted as indicative because of their deviation (vyabhicāra).

With reference to the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: "The essential nature," and so forth. The word "reason" (*hetu*) carries over from the phrase "the reason for those [things]" (*teṣāṃ hetuḥ*). When the essential nature is the probandum (*sādhya*), what kind of thing is it? It is that which conforms to the mere existence of the entity; that is, when the presence of the reason conforms to the mere existence of the entity, the essential nature is the reason. The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of demonstrating independence from other factors. Why is the essential nature the reason only when it conforms to that mere existence? He says: "For the identity (*tādātmya*) of an object is indeed restricted to that which conforms to its mere existence."

That which is the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) exists only when that [probans] exists; it does not depend on anything else, nor is it a case of identity (*tādātmya*) with something that occurs later and is dependent on other causes. If one asks why, he says: "Because of its existence," and so forth. For there is no necessity regarding the subsequent existence of a property (*dharma*) that arises later, which is dependent on other causes, and which did not exist while that probans was present.

For that which follows later and is dependent on other causes need not necessarily come to be. What is the reason? Because causes can deviate from their effects. Since there is the possibility of an obstruction to causes, how could the effect necessarily arise from them?

But surely, no one accepts that the nature of the probans (*sādhana*) is identical to the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*); so how can it be said that "identity consists precisely in following the mere existence of that [probandum]"? The intention is as follows: even by those who accept the two properties called "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) as distinct, it must necessarily be admitted that there is "coming into being after not having been" and "ceasing to be after having been. Otherwise, producedness and impermanence would not belong to cloth and the like, just as they do not belong to the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

Therefore, let that which is the coming-into-being of an entity after not having existed be its "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), and let that which is the ceasing-to-be of an entity after having existed be its "non-endurance" (*anavasthāyitva*), which is its "impermanence" (*anityatva*). What is the use of postulating another universal (*sāmānya*)? [The opponent] says: "[Because of non-perception]... [p.30] "Non-operation," etc. Of what is there non-operation? Of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The plural number is used because there are many individual instances of the means of valid cognition. [Regarding the phrase] "dependent on scripture" (*āgamāpekṣa*)... [Note 1: In the margin. Note 2: The 12th leaf is missing.]
"It is said that [it] is established"—this is what is intended.

[The author] thinks as follows: because there is no distinction between cognition (*jñāna*) and the object of cognition (*jñeya*) in terms of their nature as awareness (*bodha-rūpatva*), a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception, which is of the nature of awareness, is established by itself; however, an object of cognition such as a jar, being insentient (*jaḍa-rūpatva*), depends upon a means of valid cognition. But since there is no distinction between the absence of cognition and the absence of an object of cognition in terms of their formless nature (*nīrūpatva*), how can it be said that the absence of cognition is established by itself, while the absence of an object of cognition is established through the absence of cognition? Furthermore, the absence of cognition is not established by anything else.

For indeed, since cognitions have the nature of being self-cognized, they lack association with a single [external] cognition. If there were a cognition within one's own continuum, it would be perceived; however, because it is not perceived, its non-existence is established by itself, and thus the absence of that cognition is accepted.

In that case, the non-existence of existence (*sattā*) would also be established. For even there, if existence were present, it would be perceived; since it is not perceived, it is determined that it does not exist. Consequently, non-perception would be useless for establishing non-existence. To refute the position that consciousness itself is the other object, he says "Now," and so forth. The establishment of the non-perception of a jar through the perception of the ground as distinct from the jar is what constitutes non-perception established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This is what is meant: because the state of apprehending a jar and the state of apprehending the ground are conjoined within a single cognition, when that cognition is one that apprehends only the ground, it then determines the absence of the state of apprehending a jar; thus, the non-apprehension of the jar is established by perception itself.

In that same way, why is non-existence not established by means of the existence of another? "In that same way" means as in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). The intention is this: because both the jar and the location are connected within a single cognition, why is the existence of the object to be negated not established through the establishment of the existence of the other—the ground, for instance, which is distinct from the jar? Now, one might ask: since non-existence consists in the cessation of an entity, how can it be said to be established by perception?

He thinks as follows: Non-existence (*abhāva*) simply does not exist at all; rather, it is only perception, which has existence as its object, that brings about the conventional usage of the non-existence of other things. Therefore, what was stated—that non-existence is cognized through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—is incorrect. For, first of all, the mutual non-existence of jars and so forth is not identical [to those things], because it would follow that when a jar is destroyed, a cloth or other thing would arise [in its place], since the non-existence of the cloth and so forth would have already perished. Alternatively, if non-existence were distinct [from the things], then there would be no mutual distinction between jars and the like.

For when a cloth, which is of the nature of the absence of a jar, does not exist, then the cloth would indeed be the jar. Or, just as the jar possesses the nature of a jar because it is distinct from the absence of a cloth, so too would the cloth and other things possess that nature, precisely because they are distinct from the absence of the jar.

Nor can difference be produced by the absence of these [entities] which are already mutually distinct, because such absence is incapable of effecting anything regarding that which is either already distinct or non-distinct. Furthermore, mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not possible among things that are non-distinct. Nor is difference produced by the absence of things that are already mutually distinct, since they arise as distinct from their own causes alone. Nor is the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) produced [by absence]. For the very arising of entities in their respective individual forms is itself their intrinsic difference; and that, precisely through its manifestation in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is the cause for the conventional usage of difference.

Therefore, that which is stated—"the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*)"—is refuted. Furthermore, the distinction between existence and non-existence is not based on non-existence, for that would lead to an infinite regress. If, on the other hand, the distinction exists by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*), then that same distinction would apply to non-existent things as well; so what is the point of postulating non-existence? Nor does it follow that an effect would be beginningless in the absence of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because [an effect] does not arise due to the absence of its cause. [Objection:

But surely, if antecedent non-existence exists, there would be the arising of the effect from the cause, whereas if antecedent non-existence did not exist, [arising would not occur] because [the effect] would already be present.

If this were so, the production of an effect would never occur, because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the contradictory [effect] is ever-present. Nor can the production of the effect result from the destruction of that [non-existence], for that would entail the absurd consequence of admitting the production of the effect even in the absence of prior non-existence. Nor is the production of the effect itself the destruction of prior non-existence, because that production is impossible due to the presence of its contradictory; for prior non-existence is not destroyed at the time the cause exists, yet it is destroyed at the time the effect is produced, just like the destruction of the cause.

Therefore, prior to its arising, the effect possesses neither the property of existence nor the property of non-existence, because it is non-existent and because a real entity is partless. Rather, when it arises, it is designated as "existent," and at other times it is said not to exist; thus, it is said that "the non-existent arises."

Furthermore, the Master himself will state that non-existence as destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is itself non-existent. And when something arises from another, the latter is called its effect and the former its cause. Since these arise as persisting for only a single moment, their perishability is established; and since they arise in their own respective natures, their mutual distinctness is also established. Therefore, even in the absence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest, linguistic usage based on the distinction between causes and so forth certainly occurs. Moreover, no mutual differentiation among prior non-existence and the others is ever perceived.

Because, in the case of a jar or the like, only its cessation—whether prior, posterior, or elsewhere—is perceived as non-different, even if a distinction of time is indeed cognized. For the universal "cowness" does not become manifold simply because it is perceived as related to multiple times and so forth. Furthermore, since cessation is formless, how could there be multiplicity in non-existence? For non-existence has the nature of the cessation of an entity.

This is said specifically with reference to that fool who maintains that an effect exists prior to its arising, after its arising, and elsewhere; against him, it is stated that "the effect is non-existent before, after, and elsewhere," which serves merely to negate the superimposition of existence.
By this, what was previously stated—that "these forms cannot belong to a non-entity" and so forth—is refuted.

For this reason as well, the following should be seen as refuted: since there is no relation—whether characterized by origination or characterized by opposition—between an entity and its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or its posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), because they cannot coexist. For this very reason, there is no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Nor is there a relation of qualifier and qualified precisely because of their non-coexistence, and because the nature of being a qualifier or a qualified does not exist in the entity itself; this [relation] is merely postulated by way of another relation.

It is like the case of the staff and the bearer of the staff. Furthermore, if the cognition "the prior non-existence of an entity" arises by virtue of the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*), then there would likewise be a cognition "the existence of prior non-existence," since the relationship is no different. Therefore, the cognition of prior non-existence and the like as being related to an entity when they are actually unrelated is nothing but an error.

Furthermore, there is no mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) among entities. For the cessation of a jar is not the cessation of a cloth (because it is not perceived as such), nor is it logical for that [cessation] to be related to the cloth simply because it exists in relation to it. If this were the case, then antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others would also be mutual non-existences, since they exist in relation to their causes and so forth. Therefore, there is only "non-existence of another" (*anyābhāva*), not mutual non-existence; thus, since there is no distinction between antecedent non-existence and the others due to this "non-existence of another," how can it be said that non-existence is fourfold? *Note: In the margin.*
And since the proof of selflessness has already been stated in the *Pratyakṣābhāvanirāsa*, it is not discussed here.

"But [it is argued: since non-existence is experienced as a non-entity, how can there be a determination by means of perception? This is not a fault, because for two things that coexist within a single cognition, the very apprehension of one by perception is the non-apprehension of the other; and that non-apprehension itself is the apprehension of its absence, for if it were present, its non-apprehension would be impossible. As it has been said: 'Existence is apprehension when all other causes are present and there is no deviation from that [apprehension]; non-existence is non-apprehension; and the apprehension of something else is non-apprehension.'"

Therefore, this is the meaning: when it is said that perception determines through non-existence, the sense is that it does not [positively] determine [existence]. And that non-determination of the existence of the perceptible is itself the determination of its non-existence. In this way, the fact that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in the wake of perception conforms to the object of perception is established. Thus, just like the conventional usage of the absence of apprehension, the conventional usage of the absence of the object is also established by perception; therefore, it is not proven by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Thus, for one who is not deluded, the non-perception of the perceptible does not deviate from non-existence; therefore, the conventional usage of non-existence is established by direct perception.

Nor is it correct to say that because non-existence cannot be established even for those things that are not perceived—on the grounds that their non-perception might be subject to deviation—it is impossible to employ them in conventional discourse. For if this were so, even perception would not be a determiner of non-existence. Since there is doubt, it is not logical that one thing [perception] should be the determiner while another [non-perception] should be the factor for conventional discourse. Therefore, because perception is a determiner, it brings about the conventional usage of the non-existence of a perceptible object just as it does its existence. fn. 1: "Non-existent" (Rong du med pa).

How, then, can the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding what is non-existent be something to be established? To this he says: "But when," and so forth. For in such a case, the non-existence of non-existent objects is nothing other than the non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of that which is capable of being perceived. At that time, even though the object of the conventional usage of absence has been established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there arises—due to delusion—a cognition of the subject (*viṣayin*) who is himself non-existent and not present, taking the form "it does not exist."

And such a word as "it does not exist" [indicates] the activity of a person, which is characterized by the absence of hesitation regarding coming and going; this is conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). A person who has not yet understood these [conventions] is set to engage in the convention of non-existence by means of the demonstration of the object—that is, by the demonstration of the perception of a place devoid of a jar, which is the object of the convention of non-existence. He states an example: "Just as," and so forth. A cow consists precisely of the collection of [features] such as the dewlap.

Therefore, in that case, it is not "cowness" (*gotva*) that is being established, but rather the linguistic convention of "cow. When a person of dull intellect, having applied the convention of "cow" to a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow), does not apply that same convention to a *bāhuleya* (a black cow) because he perceives it as lacking the form of a *śābaleya*, he is led to apply the convention of "cow" by being shown its underlying cause. For the convention of "cow" is based on the collection of features such as the dewlap and so forth, and is not based on the specific form of a *śābaleya*. Since that same basis exists in the *bāhuleya* as well, why should the convention not be applied there?
In the same way, even in a location devoid of a jar, one is led to engage in the conventional usage of "non-existent" by demonstrating the grounds for its non-perception.

Likewise, by that very [means] through which such conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is established, even the objection regarding the non-establishment of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) is warded off and rejected. For when non-existence is to be proven from the mark (*liṅga*) of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), if the mark itself were not to prove the absence [of the probandum] in the subject (*dharmin*), then it would likewise fail to do so in the example-subject; and since another example would be required there as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). However, when conventional usage is what is to be proven, there is no infinite regress, because one is merely re-applying at a later time that very same conventional usage which has already been set in motion.

[Objection: Surely, he who apprehends an object also apprehends the subject; how then can even linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) be something to be established? To this, he says: “The object,” etc. For in the world, such persons are seen who, despite having apprehended an object, have not apprehended its subject. For example, a Sāṃkhya who has initiated the linguistic usage of non-existence by thinking "there is no *rajas* in *sattva*" does not initiate that same usage regarding a lump of clay due to the absence of certainty regarding the cause; however, when the non-perception of the cause is demonstrated, he is led to initiate the linguistic usage of the absence of a jar.

The conclusion is stated with the words "In this way" and so forth. In the manner thus described, these two types of non-apprehension—of the perceptible and the imperceptible—are equal in having the negation of the conventional usage of existence as their result.

How is it that by means of both the absence and presence of the causes of its own [opposite], the nature of the conventional usage of "existent" (*sadvyavahāra*) is grasped by the word "own" (*sva*), while by the word "opposite" (*viparyaya*), the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asadvyavahāra*), which is contrary to the conventional usage of "existent," is grasped? The causes of these two are the "causes of its own and its opposite" (*svaviparyayahetu*). In this context, the cause of its own [existence] is perception (*upalabdhi*), and the cause of its opposite is the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*). The absence and presence of these two are the "absence and presence of the causes of its own and its opposite" (*svaviparyayahetvabhāvabhāva*). By means of these two.

This is what is meant: in the case of the non-perception of the unobservable, since perception—which is the cause for the conventional usage of "existent"—is absent due to the cessation of both direct perception and inference, there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "existent. In the case of the non-perception of the observable, however, because the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent"—which is opposed to the conventional usage of "existent"—is present, that [usage] proceeds; thus, by this, there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "existent. Therefore, the result is equally the negation of the conventional usage of "existent" in both cases.

[Objection: "But even when perception has ceased, since there remains doubt regarding the object, how can the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'existent' be precluded? To this he says: "In one case... Regarding non-perception whose object is invisible, because there is doubt about existence, the conventional usage of existence—which consists of certainty—is indeed precluded; however, the conventional usage of existence that is merely doubtful is not precluded. But in the other case, namely non-perception of the visible, it is the opposite; that is, from the reversal of doubt, which is certainty. The meaning is: "because of the certainty of non-existence."

If there is doubt regarding non-apprehension of the unobservable, how can that be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "In that case, the first," and so forth. Among those two types of non-apprehension, the first—the non-apprehension of the unobservable—is stated to be a means of valid cognition because of its utility, that is, its function, in negating the conventional usage of existence.

Where, then, does its lack of validity lie? To this he says: "But not... and so forth. The "observation of absence" (*vyatireka*) is the ascertainment (*niścaya*). By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), both verbal expression and conventional usage are understood. Since no ascertainment of absence arises from doubt, it is therefore not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for the second [type], however—it is non-apprehension whose object is something perceptible. Here, because it has the result of ascertainment—namely, that the result of this [non-apprehension] is indeed ascertainment—with respect to the observation of absence and so forth.

And that non-apprehension of a perceptible object is fourfold due to the differences in its formal applications (*prayoga*); this is the connection. "The contradictory" (*viruddha*) and "the effect of the contradictory" (*viruddhakārya*) constitute a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of dissimilar forms. The term "establishment" (*siddhi*), meaning "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) of that which has a perceptible nature, should also be connected here.

By this, two types are indicated: the apprehension of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and the apprehension of the effect of the contradictory (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*).

"The non-establishment of the cause and the nature [of the effect]" means the non-perception of the cause and the essential nature when they have reached the conditions for perceptibility—that is, when they possess the characteristics of being observable.

By this, both the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the essential nature are indicated; thus, there are four types [of non-perception]. "For the purpose of non-existence" means that its purpose (*artha*)—its objective—is non-existence (*abhāva*) and the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*). (It is so called because it has that as its purpose. 2*
fn. 2*: In the margin:

"Now, in the statement 'the establishment of two contradictory effects,' it is not heard that this refers to non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); how then can these two be considered non-perception? To this he says: "Whatever there may be," and so forth. This must be stated as a pervasion (*vyāpti*). There is no conventional practice of negation (*pratiṣedhavyavahāra*) produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*) that can be carried out without non-perception.

However, it has not been refuted that the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence is to be established by perception; this was already stated previously. To demonstrate that very pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). "That" refers to negation. It would be performed—that is, it would be expressed linguistically—in two ways: either through the affirmation of some object or through its negation. This holds even when an affirmation is being made of something.

Either a contradictory [thing] would be enjoined, or a non-contradictory one. In the case of the injunction of a non-contradictory thing, there is no contradiction regarding the coexistence of that which is being negated and that which is being enjoined; therefore, there is no negation of what is intended to be negated. As for the phrase "of the contradictory one also," and so forth: this [thing] would indeed be contradictory if its own contradictory were not perceived therein. He states this very point with the words "for thus," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has an unlimited cause," this refers to you [the opponent] who maintain that cold touch and so forth arise in a continuum as long as their cause remains unexhausted; it should be understood as occurring prior to the proximity of fire and other such factors. The understanding of contradiction arises because there is non-existence—that is, non-arising—when another thing exists, namely when fire and so forth exist; it does not arise from non-existence, for destruction would otherwise be causeless.

This is what is meant: when each preceding cold touch ceases by its own nature, there arises, in succession, each subsequent cold touch characterized by a progressive diminution corresponding to the increasing intensity of the fire, until finally there is a total non-arising of cold touch, which is then characterized by hot touch.

Therefore, even though destruction is causeless, because the cold sensation that had been proceeding in a continuous stream prior to the proximity of fire ceases by its own nature, and because another [sensation] that was about to arise in a continuous stream does not arise when fire is present, the understanding of a contradiction between fire and cold occurs in the world; however, this is not a contradiction in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). For this very reason, he says that it is "the understanding of contradiction" (referring to what was stated): "Furthermore, it is said that nothing such as fire can be called a 'remover' of anything else without the removal of its cause."

That is incorrect. Since destruction is causeless, how could it be the remover of a cause? If, on the other hand, you speak thus while accepting that destruction has a cause, then why does it not also remove the effect, just as it removes the cause?

Furthermore, if an effect cannot be ceased without the cessation of its cause, then how can that [subsequent] cause be a ceaser [of the first], as long as it does not cease its own cause? Since the same would apply to that cause as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and thus nothing would be the ceaser of anything. Nor is it appropriate to speak of this with reference to a continuum (*saṃtāna*), because if destruction possesses a cause, the very notion of a continuum is absent; therefore, this argument is trivial.
And that non-existence, characterized by non-arising when another thing exists, is designated as a cause of contradiction based on non-perception;
by this, the contradiction characterized by non-coexistence is explained.

Showing the second type of contradiction, he says: "The mutual apprehension," and so forth. Mutual apprehension (*anyonyopalabdhi*) is reciprocal cognition; its exclusion (*parihāra*) is their distinction (*viveka*). Those two whose established characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that is, their own nature (*svarūpa*), consists of that [distinction], are described as such. The state of those two is "the state of having a characteristic established by the exclusion of mutual apprehension" (*anyonyopalabdhiparihārasthitalakṣaṇatā*). That, or rather, is the contradiction. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). "Like permanence and impermanence" is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

But surely, even in the first type of contradiction there is mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*), and in the second as well there is non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). For it is precisely when two properties cannot coexist in one locus that the second type of contradiction is established; indeed, this is not claimed to exist between color and taste. If one asks why, then, two types of contradiction have been stated:

It is true that the distinction between the objects was stated for the sake of clarity. Some maintain that the former contradiction concerns only perceptible entities (*dṛśyavastu*), whereas the second concerns non-entities (*avastu*) as well as imperceptible objects (*adṛśyaviṣaya*). Alternatively, the former is a contradiction with another thing through the cognition of the absence of one in relation to the other; the second, however, concerns its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) by virtue of the absence of identity with another. Thus, there is a great difference between these two types of contradiction.

For instance, impermanence consists in the cessation of permanence, and permanence consists in the cessation of impermanence; thus, contradiction is established as residing in their very nature (*svarūpaniṣṭha*) through mutual exclusion alone. However, yellow is not of the nature of the cessation of blue, nor is blue of the nature of the cessation of yellow. This is because both are positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*), and because if blue were absent, it would follow that yellow must be present. Therefore, this is not a contradiction between these two. Nor is there a contradiction between them based on the non-deviation of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvāvyabhicāra*), since such a relation is not perceived.

For this very reason, the prescription of what is non-contradictory is stated. Even in the case of blue, this contradiction is with "non-blue" (*anīla*) in the sense of the exclusion of blue, not with a "non-blue" determined by the absence of blue; for there exists no such thing as a "non-blue" object distinct from yellow and so forth. How, then, is there a negation of identity with yellow and so forth when blue and the like are being perceived?

This is not a fault, because: when a single blue thing is perceived, if another [blue thing] were of a nature that is being perceived even while remaining unseen, it would be perceived in exactly that same way. Thus, having considered this "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), their identity is negated through the non-perception of their own-nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). And here too, regarding this contradiction, the phrase "and that [contradiction] is [known] from non-perception" must be supplied; therefore, the meaning is this: that contradiction consisting in mutual exclusion is to be ascertained solely through non-perception.

For it is thus: the contradiction between contradictories is said to be simply the non-appearance of one when there is the appearance of the other. And when the form of an entity appears, its absence does not appear. Therefore, because existence and non-existence do not appear as identical, their contradiction is determined. This same [principle] is to be determined in the case of permanence, impermanence, and so forth.

The non-appearance [of one thing] is said to be precisely the appearance of the other. Thus it says: "In that case as well," and so forth. "In that case" refers to the contradiction just mentioned. By the apprehension of one—by the apprehension of one contradictory thing—the non-apprehension of the other is indeed called the non-apprehension of the object to be negated. "Otherwise" means if the non-apprehension of the other is not stated by means of the apprehension of one; then, since the object to be negated would have its apprehension unnegated, its absence would remain unestablished even when the one is apprehended.

Consequently, there would be no contradiction at all for that which is being perceived. Therefore, since both types of contradiction are produced by non-perception, even those [reasons] such as the perception of the contradictory, when employed in a positive formulation, are essentially non-perceptions.

Now, it might be argued: "In the case of two contradictories, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is observed in the example as that which grasps the relationship characterized by contradiction. Yet, the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the relationship does not belong to the two related terms themselves. For instance, the nature of the perception that grasps the relationship between fire and smoke belongs neither to the smoke nor to the fire. Therefore, how can the apprehension of a contradictory be considered a non-apprehension, given that it appears in the form of an apprehension?"
Therefore, having observed fire and so forth— which are known to be incompatible with cold— in a given example, the absence of cold and the like is inferred upon seeing them in another location.

To this it is replied: If the relationship between the signifier and the signified were established by way of the relation of contradiction (*virodha*), then from the perception of fire there would be the cognition of cold, because those two alone are produced through the relation of contradiction. It is not so, however, because the absence of cold is not related [to fire]. Furthermore, when the cold is removed by the fire, how could there be a relation of contradiction? For contradiction cannot reside in both [terms simultaneously], as it lacks coexistence. Nor is there a contradiction between fire and the absence of cold, since they can coexist.

Nor can there be an inference of the absence of cold from fire, because fire is not invariably concomitant with the absence of cold; for even when fire is present, the presence of cold is observed. Therefore, just as the non-perception of cold occurs wherever fire exists, so too has its absence been established in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Consequently, the absence of cold in other instances of fire is inferred in exactly the same way.

Therefore, this is the meaning: even when fire is present in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), it is only at the time when cold is not perceived that fire possesses the quality of being contradictory; it does not possess it at other times. And since its status as a prover (*gamakatva*) is due to its being contradictory, it is said that its status as a prover is through the non-perception of something else. Consequently, the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) is of the nature of non-perception (*anupalabdhirūpatva*), because it is invariably determined by non-perception—just as the perception of a bare ground is of the nature of the non-perception of a jar.

e) Thus, even in the case of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*), the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) is indeed non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). For example, in the case of the Arhats: "The pot might be impermanent; it might be permanent. Here, the very perception of impermanence is the non-perception of permanence; therefore, there is no entity that possesses the nature of both permanence and impermanence.

Having thus established that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the means of cognition for the negation [of one thing] even when there is an affirmation of another object (*arthāntara-vidhi*), he says "of one," etc., in order to establish it also for the negation of another object. Why? [He asks] "of the negation," etc. Nor does it follow that the negation of another object occurs simply because of the absence of another object; for even in that case, when the negation of something else is to be proven, the reason would have to be the negation of either an effect or a cause. Or else, the reason would have to be the negation of that which is neither—an effect nor a cause. Among those [three possibilities], in those cases...

Since there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between that which is neither [cause nor effect]—being devoid of the nature of cause and effect—and the object to be negated, when that [connection] is absent, there is no absence of what is unconnected. "By another" means by that which is intended as the object of negation. Why should it follow that "it must not exist"? Even in the case of the non-perception of an effect, why would there be an absence of that [cause]? This is the connection [of the argument]. "The absence of that" refers to the absence of the cause; for causes are manifold, and those [causes] possess effects because of the possibility of deficiencies or obstructions [to their operation].

And this has been stated by taking the mere cause [as the subject]: the absence of a cause whose capacity is unobstructed is indeed understood from the absence of the effect; for it is the non-perception of both [the cause and] the effect that serves as the means of cognition. Therefore, it is the non-perception of the cause alone that makes known the absence [of the effect], as is understood through its connection with the word "of the effect.
*fn. 1*: In the margin.

If it is argued that the restriction [in the definition] is untenable because the non-perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is itself a reason for non-existence, he replies: "But the non-perception of an intrinsic nature is itself non-existence; it is not here that the absence of something else is being proved. Furthermore, when the negation of another intrinsic nature is to be proved, it is precisely the non-perception of the cause [that serves as the reason]; therefore, there is no contradiction."

What, then, is established there? He says: "Only," and so forth. "There" refers to the non-apprehension of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*); the "object" (*viṣayī*) is the cognition of non-existence and so on. "In this [non-apprehension] as well" means that when one states the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) through the non-apprehension of a property (*dharma*) that is its pervader (*vyāpaka*)—as in "there is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees"—then the non-difference (*abheda*) of the pervaded is also established. By the word "also" (*api*), conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is likewise included.

For when, on one of two elevated mountain regions, a forest of trees is visible but—due to its extreme density—the specific species of the trees cannot be determined; in that case, on the other part of the mountain, the absence of *śiṃśapā* trees cannot be ascertained because the *śiṃśapā* is not perceived. However, since a tree does possess the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), it is possible to ascertain its absence. At that time, the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is established through the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). fn. 1*: Cf. *tadā 'bhāvo 'pi*.

With the words "this" (*iyam*) and so forth, he explains the portion of the verse beginning with "the non-existence of an object" (*abhāvārtha*). Regarding "by the establishment of the contradictory" (*viruddhasiddhyā*): this means by the perception of that which is contradictory to its own nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhyā*). Regarding "as follows" (*yathā*) and so forth: where the cold touch is imperceptible in a given subject (*dharmin*), yet fire is seen from a distance—in that case, this formal argument (*prayoga*) is employed. By this example of the perception of the contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhyudāharaṇena*), one should understand that the establishment of the contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhasiddhi*) has been stated. The example beginning with "as follows" (*yathā*) refers specifically to a particular kind of cold touch.

Snow is accompanied by frost; cold pervades it, and fire is its opposite. In that case, fire, by excluding the opposite—cold—also excludes the touch of frost which is pervaded by it. Thus, this [inference] is included within the perception of the opposite of an essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) by implication. Furthermore, where fire is perceptible while the touch of cold and the touch of frost are imperceptible, this formulation should also be understood as applicable: [the exclusion of the effect of the opposite].
