By the non-establishment of the effect of that which is opposite [to the subject].

"Such as," and so forth. [The argument is: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of smoke. Fire, which is the opposite of cold, has smoke as its effect; that smoke brings fire into proximity, and that fire removes the cold. This application of the argument is to be understood in cases where the sensation of cold is imperceptible, while both the fire and the smoke are perceptible. Thus, first, the establishment of the effect of the contradictory has been explained.
Now: "The non-establishment of the cause and the state [of the contradictory]."

He explains this by means of the following illustration: "by the non-establishment of the reason" means by the non-perception of the cause. "For example," and so forth: when there is doubt as to whether vapor or the like above a large lake is actually smoke or something similar, then this formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be seen. For in that case, if there were fire in the motionless large lake, it would certainly be perceived due to its luminosity; since it is not perceived, the absence of the effect is established precisely because of the absence of the fire.

"By way of the non-establishment of its own-being" means by way of the non-perception of its own-being (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), [in the form]: "There is no smoke there, because it is not perceived. It should be understood that this refers to something that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). "By this" refers to the application of the non-perception of own-being. This is called the non-perception, which is the non-establishment of that which is both a pervader (*vyāpaka*) and an own-being (*svabhāva*). For example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because of the absence of trees. Tree-ness is the very own-being of *śiṃśapā*-ness; therefore, the *śiṃśapā* is pervaded by tree-ness.

But is it not the case that the negation of a perceptible object occurs only through the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), and not through the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth? For indeed, it is precisely the imperceptible cold touch and its imperceptible effect that are established as being negated; for if they were perceptible, there would simply be the non-perception of their own nature. Therefore, just as there is a negation of the imperceptible cold touch and so on, so too should there be a negation of things such as *piśācas*; to this he says: "In all cases," and so forth.

This is what is meant: just as in the case of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the absence of a jar or similar object—previously apprehended elsewhere—is established in a particular location, so too the absence of a cold touch (whose opposition is known elsewhere) and of an effect (whose causal status is known) is established in the subject of the inference (*sādhyadharmin*) through the apprehension of the opposite (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and other such means; however, this does not apply to that which is always visible. The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) refers to the establishment of absence when employed either by way of affirmation (*vidhimukha*) or by way of negation (*pratiṣedhamukha*); and by the term "absence," both the absence itself and the linguistic convention of absence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) are expressed.

Furthermore, regarding those causes and so forth whose non-existence is established by the non-existence [of something else], their non-establishment—being of a perceptible nature—is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). And the establishment of things contrary to them—that is, of things contrary to the object to be negated, such as those with a nature contrary [to it] and so forth—should be understood as having apprehension (*upalabdhi*) as its logical mark (*liṅga*). In this context, the phrase "establishment of things of a perceptible nature" is not to be construed [with the preceding], because the state of being perceptible is already obtained from the very word "apprehension. Rather, the connection should be made in this way: [the establishment of things contrary to the object to be negated is apprehension].

The establishment of those things intended as negatable which are contradictory to what is perceptible; for what reason? Because the non-existence of other [factors]—such as causes and so forth—that are imperceptible cannot be established. Thus, there is no establishment of contradiction and so on, because the nature of those intended as negatable is imperceptible.

[The opponent says: "In the passage beginning with *yadi*, etc., it is established that cold is absent through the perception of smoke, which is the effect of fire—the opposite of cold. It is also established through the perception of its cause. Why is the absence of cold not established through the perception of the cause of that fire which is opposed to cold—namely, wood and so forth?

"Of that which is contrary to it," and so forth, says the Master. That perception of fuel and the like—which serves as the cause for fire, which is contrary to that cold touch—is fallacious. When? When there is no contrariety between the two causes; that is, when there is no opposition between the causes of fire and cold. He provides an example, beginning with "For instance": for in this case, since mere wood, which is the cause of burning, has no opposition to frost and the like, which are the causes of cold.

Furthermore, regarding wood that possesses unimpeded capacity to produce fire: even if there is a contradiction with it due to the cause of cold, nevertheless, because such wood is ascertained precisely through the observation of its effect [fire], this would be a case of "contradiction by way of the effect" (*kāryavirodha*). However, when there is a contradiction between two causes and that contradiction is the indicator, there is the "non-perception of the cause" (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*). For example: "This person does not have specific symptoms such as horripilation. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), trembling of the teeth and so forth are included. The inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of excluding those effects of cold that are not specific.

For those [effects] can indeed arise from transformations caused by piśācas and the like. "One for whom a particular fire is present" means that person; the state of being such is "therefrom. Here too, the inclusion of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of including a fire of such a nature as is capable of removing the bristling of hair and so forth. For in this case, there is a contradiction between the fire, which is the cause of intense heat, and the cold, which is the cause of the bristling of hair and so forth.

Therefore, fire, by removing its own opposite—cold—also removes its effects, such as horripilation and the like. This application of the argument is to be understood when the cold touch and its effects, such as horripilation, are imperceptible, and one intends to establish the cessation of horripilation and so forth through the cessation of the cause of cold upon seeing the fire.

A person who is possessed of a specific quality such as horripilation caused by cold—wherever that person is located, that place is [the locus]. The mention of "place" (*pradeśa*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that this is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) of the inference "from smoke. For if the person were the subject (*dharmin*), the reason would not be a property of the subject, since smoke is a property of the place. And this formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be understood as being applied in cases where fire, the sensation of cold touch, and the specific quality of horripilation are imperceptible, and one seeks to prove their absence.

For in that case, by the perception of smoke—which is the effect of fire, which is incompatible with cold—one intends to establish the absence of horripilation and the like, which are effects of cold, which is incompatible with fire; therefore, such [an absence] alone is the probandum (*sādhya*). Indeed, smoke brings about the presence of fire, and that [fire] removes the cold; as that [cold] is being removed, it removes its own effects, such as horripilation. Thus, by implication, this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*).

The connection is with the phrase "this is the perception of what is contradictory to that" (1.32). The meaning is "the perception of what is contradictory to the cause. This has already been indicated by the non-perception of the cause itself, which is precisely the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*). Since, in both these applications as well, the understanding of the absence of the effect arises solely from the non-perception of the cause, this is stated as being simply the non-perception of the cause.

Thus, "this [is]" and so forth: although there are four types by way of the primary divisions, they become eightfold through the intermediate subdivisions of the preparatory applications (*prayoga*). For instance, from the perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) is stated as a subdivision; likewise, from the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*); from the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), the perception of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) and the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*); and the perception of the effect of the contradictory (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is of one kind. Thus, there are eight types.

[Objection: But surely, since smoke exists even when fire has long since perished in places such as a dwelling room, how is there no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the perception of an effect that is contradictory [to the probandum]? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth. In that case, even regarding the perception of a contradictory effect, dependence on place, time, and so forth is required. Here, there is dependence on time, as in: "It is not cold here at some time when fire was present. There is dependence on place, as in: "There is no cold in a certain region of the sky because of smoke, [namely] where fire is present from which this smoke has arisen."

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the dependence on specific conditions (*avasthāviśeṣa*) is intended. Having regard for that specific condition of smoke which has been observed in proximity to fire, the absence of cold is inferred even at the present time. Even in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), such as "there is fire here because of smoke," dependence on place, time, and so forth is accepted. The word "also" (*api*) serves to include this very point.

If it is objected that, since dependence on place, time, and so forth is a qualification of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the absence of a locus (*dharmin*), we reply: no. For it has been stated that the place itself serves as the locus, and [the reason] is a prover by virtue of its dependence on place, time, and so forth. Otherwise—that is, if there were no dependence on place and so forth—then the contradictory effect (*viruddhakārya*) would be deviant (*vyabhicārin*). For example, ash that does not depend on a specific place or time is deviant when used to prove the absence of cold (*śītābhāva*) while intending to prove non-cold. In this very way, it has been demonstrated that the perception of the contradictory and so forth constitutes non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

"Then what about... and so forth, says the opponent. "With equal qualities" means by means of a proximate and unobstructed [cause], just as when one sees a collection of causes such as earth, seed, and water, the effect—the sprout—is inferred. How does that [cause], which is called a "reason" (*hetu*), fall within the threefold [classification] of reasons known as essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)? It cannot be included in non-perception, because it is a proof by way of affirmation (*vidhi*). Because it is the essential nature of the cause, it is not the "reason of effect. And because it is the inference of one thing from another distinct thing, it is not the "reason of essential nature."

He states the inclusion [of the effect in the cause] with the words "by the cause," and so forth. By the phrase "by the complete [set]," it is meant that the effect is produced from as many a collection of causes as is observed; it is not by means of those [causes] having reached their final state, because the effect is already perceptible even before the sign (liṅga) is apprehended therein. Or, if it were imperceptible, there would be no possibility of determining the final state, and thus [the cognition] would be inference. Furthermore, for one who would be able to determine them, there is no inference, because those with limited vision cannot determine the final moments. That which is inferred as the arising of the effect is described as the nature (svabhāva) of the cause.

Why? Because it does not depend on any other entity. Therefore, this meaning is an essential nature (svabhāva), because it is invariably concomitant with the mere capacity for the production of an effect.

[Objection: "But when the production of the effect depends upon the final state, how can it be said to be independent of anything else? [The author] says: "That too"—namely, the production of the effect—"is dependent only on that which is present. That is to say, it does not depend on any object other than such a collection of causes (*kāraṇakalāpa*) as it is actually present; therefore, its nature (*svabhāva*) is necessarily connected (*anubandhin*) with just that. (Of what is this the nature? It is the nature of the complete collection of causes. This is stated with reference to the continuum (*saṃtāna*), not with reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). The meaning is that the generative continuum of the collection of causes is independent.

Even though the production of the effect is independent [of anything else], one might ask how it can be the "nature" (svabhāva) of the cause since it is a different entity; to this he says: "In that case," and so forth. Because, when the causes are complete, the possibility (*sambhava*) of the production of the effect is inferred from the complete cause as a logical mark (*liṅga*). "Possibility" (*sambhava*) means that which occurs from this; the meaning is that the capacity for producing the effect is inferred. He clarifies this very point: "Because there is an inference of the capacity of the complete [causes] to produce the effect. And this capacity is necessarily concomitant with the mere collection [of causes], because it does not depend on any other cause.

The opponent asks: "If, then, the capacity to produce an effect is invariably concomitant with that [capacity] alone, then the production of the effect is certain; why, then, is that [capacity] itself not inferred? To the question, "Why, then, is the effect itself inferred from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)?", he replies with the words beginning "the causal complex" (*sāmagrī*). The compound *sāmagrī-phala-śaktayaḥ* means: the capacities which are both the fruit and the capacities of the causal complex.

For instance, from a preceding complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there arises a subsequent efficient moment; and its excellence of nature (*ātmātiśaya*) is its power (*śakti*). Thus, the causal complex is the cause, power is the effect, and the transformation (*pariṇāma*) consists in the arising of a continuous succession of subsequent moments with respect to an effect that follows upon it and depends upon it. [If one argues that the cause can be inferred from this], there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*). Why? Because the possibility of an obstruction (*pratibandha*) exists.

He explains this with the words "For not," and so forth. It is precisely when they are complete—that is, when they are present—that causal substances produce their own effect. What is the reason? [The text says] "Because of the totality," and so forth. For those potencies whose birth arises from the totality (sāmagrī), there is a successive transformation; that is, the production of each subsequent, more distinguished moment from each preceding moment, because the arising of the effect depends upon that. And "in the interim" refers to the time of the transformation of the continuum (saṃtāna); for it is possible for an obstruction to occur.

[Objection: But surely even capacity (*yogyatā*) is dependent upon the successive transformations of subsequent moments, and since an obstruction is possible even there, how can there be an inference of it? [The author] says: "But as for capacity," and so forth. Because it does not depend on another substance—that is, because it does not depend on any other cause apart from the collection of causes already present—an inference of it is not contradictory.

He states that very inference: "Successively," and so forth. Taking each preceding moment as the material cause (*upādāna*), the arising of a subsequent efficient moment is the "transformation of successive potencies" (*uttarottara-śakti-pariṇāma*). With that as the reason, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is "capable of producing an effect. The subject (*dharmin*) is "this causal complex" (*kāraṇa-sāmagrī*). The reason (*hetu*) is "because of the absence of any other required condition for the transformation of potency"; that is, because there is no absence of another auxiliary condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) for that transformation of potency.

From what, then, does the production of capacity arise? He says: "The preceding," and so forth. That which has a "previously similar" cause—that is, a preceding causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*) of the same kind—is "that whose production of capacity has that much alone as its cause"; the state of being such is "therefrom. For this reason, that fitness is said to be independent of anything else.

Now, if it is said that the capacity (*yogyatā*) of a cause with respect to its effect is what constitutes "power" (*śakti*), then since the capacity would also be subject to deviation when the effect deviates, how can this be an inference? Alternatively, if it is said that there is merely the possibility of capacity, then the meaning would be: "the effect may or may not occur. Even so, how can this be an inference, given the presence of doubt?

To this it is replied: How is it that the opponent challenges this [inference] as being produced by a threefold reason? If this inference is established by the opponent, then the Teacher demonstrates that it is indeed produced by a threefold mark (*liṅga*). However, some maintain that this is not an inference in the ultimate sense; rather, it is "inferential" only in a secondary or figurative sense. Alternatively, if the capacity to produce an effect were inferred with absolute certainty, then because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it would not constitute a valid inference.

But when a possibility is inferred in the form "it might happen at some time or other," how could there be any deviation (vyabhicāra) in this case? Therefore, the meaning is this: if, in the course of successive transformations, there is an absence of continuity, then the effect may occur; otherwise, it does not. However, in the opponent's position—which maintains the inference of an effect with absolute certainty—there is indeed deviation.

Others, however, hold that—just as in the case of transformation—it is precisely that causal totality (*sāmagrī*) which is inferred, wherein, given the absence of an obstructing factor, there exists an absolute capacity for the production of the effect. They maintain that since the cognition of the capacity for producing the effect implies the effect itself as a qualifier, no separate inference of the effect is made. If it is asked how the absence of an obstructing factor is apprehended when the effect is inferred from the mere causal totality alone—and thus a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is alleged—the answer is: true.

For indeed, this inference belongs only to one who is able to know that; just as the inference of fire from smoke belongs only to one who is able to know that smoke is produced by fire, and not to anyone else, so it is in this case.

With the words "But then... and so forth, he again states the contradiction of the claim that "it is of only three kinds," namely: by means of something that is neither cause nor effect—by means of a non-essential property (*asvabhāva*) other than the object to be inferred, such as taste (*rasa*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the cognition of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth through smell and so forth is included. Here too, by the word "and so forth," touch and so forth are to be understood. For in the dark, having tasted the juice of a citron (*mātuluṅga*) and the like, having smelled the fragrance of a *campaka* flower, and having experienced the touch of fire; [one infers the presence of the respective objects].

In that case, their commonality of form (*rūpasāmānya*) is inferred; likewise, having seen the color of fire, its touch is inferred. Now, how does this [inference] fall within the three types of logical reasons (*hetu*) under discussion?

And since this is not an invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), there is no consequence of having to posit another logical mark (*liṅga*); thus he says, "That too," and so forth. The connection is: "That too is the cognition. For example, what is the case for the remaining [qualities] such as color (*rūpa*) which depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*)? That cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, which arises from taste (*rasa*) regarding that very same causal complex which produces taste—that is by means of the inference of a property (*dharma*). It is by means of the inference of the property of the cause of taste—which was previously the substratum (*apādāna*)—namely, its being the producer of color.

Therefore, this meaning is determined from the taste itself—that it is the cause for the production of a form that does not exist at the same time as it. For in this way, its status as the producer of a form coexisting with the taste is established, provided there were also a certain cognition of the form existing at the same time; otherwise, for past things belonging to the same time, there would be only one mode of inference, namely that arising from the mark of an effect.

Surely, there can be no inference of a form that is either subsequent to or simultaneous with the unexpressed cause of rasa, because such an inference would entail a fallacy when inferring an effect from a cause; furthermore, even in the case of inferring the capacity for producing an effect, there could be no inference of a form simultaneous with the rasa, and because there is an absence of any cognition resulting from an inference based on another inference.

Therefore, that which is said—namely, "when there is the cognition of past things, then the effect is the sign of that; thus it is born from a sign that is an effect, being 'born from an effect-sign' (*kāryaliṅgajā*); but when there is the cognition of simultaneous things, then the effect is the sign for that inference of the property of the cause, and thus it is 'born from an effect-sign' (*kāryaliṅgajā*)"—is refuted. [In this regard, others maintain... Furthermore, since qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth are established in a composite substance (*avayavidravya*), it is logical that there is a cognition of those [qualities] even when they are absent therein.

For Buddhists, this is not the case because they do not admit a whole (*avayavin*) distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities], and thus there is no absence of a subject (*dharmin*). Furthermore, if inference were possible without a subject, it would follow that one could infer form and so forth from taste in all instances. Moreover, the collection as a whole would become the probandum (*sādhya*), and the reason (*hetu*) would become a property not residing in the subject (*apakṣadharma*). Nor is it logical to infer the property of the cause, since taste is not understood to be an effect of form and the rest. And this is not stated while remaining undecided regarding the position of momentariness.

For if form (*rūpa*) and the rest were momentary, they would produce effects of their own kind, not effects such as taste (*rasa*), because there would be no apprehension of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). There can be no conventional usage of inference and the object of inference (*anumānānumeya-vyavahāra*) regarding moments, because their relationship cannot be ascertained. However, if the conventional usage of inference and so forth is based on continua (*santāna*), then since it is not established that the continua of form and the rest stand in a mutual cause-and-effect relationship, how can there be the conventional usage of inference and the object of inference?

He thinks as follows: it is not the case that there is an inference of color and so forth in every instance of sourness; rather, it occurs in a substratum (*dharmin*) such as a mango. And in that case, the rule of mutual inseparability (*avinirbhāga-niyama*) among color and the other qualities is indeed perceived. That [rule] must be caused by a necessary connection (*pratibandha*); otherwise, there would also be a rule of mutual inseparability between jars, cloths, and so forth. Furthermore, their necessary connection is neither identity (*tādātmya*), because they are perceived as distinct, nor is it origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because they exist simultaneously.

Nor is there a co-inherence in a single object for them; for first of all, there can be no co-inherence in a single object for things that are not already inherent by virtue of the power of inherence, because inherence itself would be non-existent [in that case]. Furthermore, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even for things that are already inherent, since they are produced as such from their own causes alone. Since the capacity to indicate [the probandum] is expressed precisely through such production, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) consists in dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*). And for one who has ascertained this necessary connection, there is inference with respect to another [unperceived] time.

Even though no composite whole exists here, nevertheless, because the object of the cognition of a mango and so forth possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*), there is an inference of its color-form and other qualities from its taste.

But even so, how can these [qualities] be dependent upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*)? For it is not by the same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that form produces form that it produces taste and the rest, since that would entail the consequence of their mutual non-difference. Nor does it produce one by means of another [nature], for that would entail the consequence of a difference in its own intrinsic nature.

This is not a fault, because here form does not previously possess the capacity to produce a single effect—such that this fault would arise—but rather possesses the capacity to produce multiple effects simultaneously; for it is observed that [the cause] arises as such. Furthermore, the causality of a cause does not consist in the mere absence of its effect, such that if multiple things were produced from one, it would follow that the one is [itself] multiple; rather, in the world, the causality of a thing consists simply in its existence prior to the arising of the effect.

Just as its status as a cause exists prior to the production of a single effect, so too is it observed to be the case regarding the production of a complex (kalāpa). Alternatively, by whichever very nature a form produces another form, by that same [nature] it also produces taste and so forth; however, the difference between their intrinsic natures is caused by a difference in the conditions (*upādāna*), not by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). For instance, although touch exists in air, because color and so forth are absent, there is no production of color and so forth. And although color and so forth exist in fire, because taste is absent, there is no production of taste.

Even though [taste] and other qualities exist in water, because odor is absent there, odor does not arise; therefore, it is established that taste and the rest have their own specific causes, namely taste and so forth. And a specific cause is a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), which is of the same genus or exists within an undivided continuum. From this difference in material causes, there follows a difference in the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of visible form and the other qualities.
As for what is further stated—that there is a collection of multiple potencies therein, whereby visible form produces visible form by one potency and taste and the rest by others—[this is incorrect].

That is incorrect. Even if one accepts that a single entity produces multiple effects by means of multiple powers, the consequence of its being multiple remains unavoidable, because the multiple powers themselves possess multiple natures. Furthermore, since the powers are non-different from the entity, if there were a distinction among the powers, it would follow that the nature [of the entity] must also be distinct. Alternatively, if the powers were distinct, it would follow that the nature [of the entity] could not be the causal agent. Nor can an entity become a causal agent through the possession of power, because that which lacks power cannot possess power.

Even for that which is capable, what is the use of a connection with a power (*śakti*), since it is an agent by its very nature? Furthermore, a power would not be an agent because it lacks a connection with [another] power. If you argue that, being a power itself, it does not require another power, then why should an entity (*bhāva*) also require a power, given that it too is capable?

The Mīmāṃsaka also maintains that power (*śakti*) is simply the excellence of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity, and that it is both distinct and non-distinct from it. It is distinct from the entity because when the entity is perceived, the power is not perceived; yet, because the production of an effect would otherwise be inexplicable, it is non-distinct from the entity, for otherwise the entity could not function as a causal agent (*kāraka*). As it has been said:
"The powers of all entities are postulated through the presumption of their effects."

That too has been refuted, because it is contradictory for a single power (*śakti*) to possess both distinct and non-distinct forms. Furthermore, by means of presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*), one should postulate that the non-distinct power belongs only to that entity which exists prior to the effect; thus, the prior existence itself is the power. And since that [prior existence] is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), why is the power not itself perceptible? It is simply determined through the observation of the effect. Therefore, because one infers the properties of the cause from the effect—such as taste and so forth—this [inference] is included within the category of inference based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).

"As in the case of the transformation of fuel in smoke. Just as when there is an inference of the causal complex of fire and so forth from smoke, there is likewise an inference of transformations of the fuel such as ashes and embers; it is just like that.

But is it not the case that this is an inference of a contemporaneous effect from a cause inferred through the effect of taste, and not an inference of the property of the cause? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). When there is a cognition of color (*rūpa*) from taste, it is the cause itself that is of such a nature; thus, the relation of producing color is what is inferred. When that [relation] is being inferred, another effect, which is a qualification of it, also becomes ascertained. However, another effect is not to be inferred after the cause has already been inferred.

Why is this so? He says: "For" (*hi*), because. That whose power (*śakti*) has proceeded and is unobstructed is "possessing proceeded power" (*pravṛttaśakti*). Being such, and being that material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of color-form (*rūpa*), it is described as such. Being a cooperative condition (*sahakāripratyaya*) for that [material cause], it produces taste (*rasa*) from the cause of taste. And when such a cause has been inferred, there is by implication an inference of color-form (*rūpa*), because color-form and taste are dependent upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*). A specific transformation of fuel (*indhana*) consists of ashes, embers, and so forth.
Its material cause is wood, and its auxiliary condition is fire; just as that [wood] produces smoke, so too are visible form and taste dependent upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*).

[The author] establishes this with the words "For thus" (*tathā hi*), etc., referring to the *sūtra*: "Because the activity of capacity... The commentary on this begins with "of its own cause," etc. "Of its own cause" means that without the proximity and suitability for the production of the taste—which is itself the fruit—by that which is the cause of the taste, namely the production of the taste itself, the taste does not arise. "That very [activity]" refers to the activity of capacity. The commentary on the phrase "another cause" begins with "the material cause of form," etc.

The cause of the activity of the material cause (*upādāna-hetu*) of form—namely, those atoms of form comprised within the prior characteristic (*pūrva-lakṣaṇa*) that are directed toward the production of form—is its own activity. Because the material cause of form is directed toward its own effect by means of the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-hetu*) which is the cause of taste, that activity of the cause of taste is also said to be "of such a nature" (*tathoktā*), insofar as it has the habit of acting together with the activity of the material cause of form toward the production of form.

Since this is so, therefore, from a cause that is "as it is"—that is, accompanied by the causal operation (*upādāna-karaṇa*) consisting of the capacity [to produce] that has already come into play, and which is subsumed within the preceding moment—the taste (*rasa*), which is intended as the logical mark (*liṅga*), when it arises, makes known the very same kind of cause; thus, while making [the cause] known, it makes known the color (*rūpa*) existing at the same time. Therefore, the meaning is this: such a cause is indeed determined through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not otherwise.
*fn. 1: Pramāṇa-Samuccaya.*

Furthermore, there is no inference of an effect subsequent to an inferred cause; and since the determination of the property of the reason (*hetu*) occurs solely through its being a producer of the effect and not otherwise, he says for that very reason: "In that case also," and so forth. By this means—that is, by this gateway—in the inference of color and other qualities from taste and other qualities, there is the cognition (*gati*) of past [qualities] and those existing at the same time. The past [qualities] are those coexisting with the material cause (*upādāna*) of the taste; the simultaneous [qualities] are those coexisting with the taste which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*). There is the cognition of these.

There is no inference of future things by means of a present mark (*liṅga*), because of the possibility of deviation. For a future thing may not come to be, as it can be obstructed by other causes; since an obstruction might occur there, [the mark] would fail. Furthermore, the inference of tomorrow’s sunrise from today’s rising is not a true inference, because of the absence of a restrictive mark (*niyāmaka-liṅga*); it is like inferring tomorrow’s sunrise from seeing a donkey today. Therefore, even in this case, the cognition of color and so forth from taste and so forth is an inference based on the mark of an effect (*kārya-liṅga*).

And because a reason is a means of cognition only insofar as it is dependent upon the probandum, for that reason there is no other type of reason—such as "conjunction" (*saṃyogin*) and so forth—that serves as a means of cognition beyond the threefold reason. Why? Because there is no necessity of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) for a nature that is not restricted to the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).

This is what is meant: first of all, there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of things that are not already in contact; and even for those that are in contact, what is the use of conjunction, since they arise in contact from their own causes? Therefore, [the reason] does not possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum] by virtue of conjunction, because it is unobstructed, like the case of two jars. Likewise, there is no inherence (*samavāya*) of things that are established separately.

Even for things that are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), what need is there for inherence (*samavāya*), since they arise from their own causes in a state of being positioned one above the other? Therefore, there is no capacity to indicate [the probandum] through inherence either, because it lacks dependence on the probandum; furthermore, he will state later that inherence does not exist. For this very reason, it was previously stated in the context of the inference of taste and so forth that the two types of co-presence (*ekārthasamavāyin*) do not exist. And the contradictory [reason] is included within non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

And as for that which was stated by the Naiyāyikas: "Inference is *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.5). Among these, *pūrvavat* is the inference of an effect from a cause, and it has been demonstrated that this is fallible (*vyabhicārī*). *Śeṣavat* inference is the inference of a cause from an effect, and this is indeed accepted by the author of the treatise. *Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference, however, is the inference of something in one locus after having observed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans in another locus.

Just as, having observed that Devadatta’s arrival at another location is preceded by motion, one infers the sun’s arrival at another location through its movement—this too arises solely from the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅga*), because arrival at another location is the effect of motion. The Master himself will state in the third chapter that all inference is indeed "based on general observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, what was cited by Uddyotakara as an example of inference based on general observation—namely, the inference of the rising of Mount Valakāta—that too arises solely from the mark of an effect, as stated in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*.
fn. 1*: It is established that there is no other means of cognition (*gamaka*) than the three types of reasons (*hetu*).

By this—namely, by stating that the inference of color and so forth from taste and so forth arises from an effect as its logical mark (*kāryaliṅgaja*)—the following is included: the emergence of ants carrying their eggs elsewhere is their migration; the leaping up of fish is a transformation of the fish; and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the flashing of lightning and the croaking of frogs are included. Regarding the phrase "inference of rain and so forth," here too, by the word "etcetera," the inference of wind and so forth is stated; for that too arises from an effect as its logical mark, through the inference of the property of the cause.

He says this very thing: "In that case as well," and so forth. "In that case as well" refers to instances such as the swarming of ants. "The transformation of the elements (*bhūtapariṇāma*) alone is the cause of rain"—here the particle *eva* (alone) is displaced [in the sentence structure]. The transformation of the elements is indeed the cause of rain; it is the cause of the swarming and other such characteristics of ants and the like. Therefore, just as from a certain kind of transformation of the elements the cause of rain arises for ants and others, so too, by inferring the cause of that kind, there is an inference of rain occurring at the same time.

In other cases, however, it is the capacity that is inferred, and not the actual occurrence [of the effect], because there is deviation due to the possibility of an obstruction. Therefore, even from a complete collection of causes, there is no inference of the effect; there is only the inference of the capacity.

Regarding those Mīmāṃsakas and others who infer an effect even from an incomplete cause, [the author] says—showing that they are utterly excluded from correct reasoning—"But by an incomplete reason," and so forth. "Incomplete" means deficient. The meaning is that inference based on the *śeṣavat* [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Why is it incapable? The explanation of this is: "For only when [the causes] are complete," and so forth. First of all, there can be no inference of an effect in any way [from an incomplete cause].

The phrase "the complete [causes] themselves lead to the inference of capacity" is also expressed by the word "also" (*api*). Because that which is incomplete is absolutely incapable, and because there is incapacity even through the successive transformation [of the causes], there is not even a partial inference of the effect. This is the explanation of the example "like the inference of passion from the body. Regarding the words "just as," etc.: "body" (*deha*), "senses" (*indriya*), and "intellects" (*buddhi*) form a *dvandva* compound. [The argument is: "This person possesses passion and so forth, because he possesses a body, because he possesses senses, and because he possesses intellect."

Thus, from the body and so forth, there is the inference of attachment (*rāga*) and the rest; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and others are included. In the Sūtra, however, the mention of "body and attachment" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). For the sense faculties and such alone are not the cause of attachment and the rest; rather, attachment and the rest are preceded by the fixation (*abhiniveśa*) upon "self" and "what belongs to self. That which is the fixation of "I" and "mine" with respect to the self and what belongs to the self is the prior cause of those [afflictions] such as attachment; therefore, they are described in that way. The phrase beginning with "unreasonably" (*ayoniśas*) is a further justification of this very point.

The source (*yoni*) of things consists of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth, because it is the cause for the cessation of the perception of [inherent] connection. One who praises or relies upon that is *yoniśaḥ*. Alternatively, the suffix *śas* is applied in the sense of repetition according to the rule "after a numeral or a singular word, when there is repetition" (*saṃkhyaikavacanāc ca vīpsāyām*), as in "one attends to each and every source" (*yoniṃ yoniṃ manaskaroti*). Such mental attention (*manaskāra*) is "proper mental attention" (*yoniśomanaskāra*), which is the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*). Its opposite, the knowledge of a self and so forth, is "improper mental attention" (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), because all faults such as passion arise preceded by that.

[Objection: But surely the body, the sense organs, and the intellect are also causes of attachment and so forth, since attachment and so forth are not observed in those who lack them. [Reply: To this he says: "Even though the body and so forth are causes," meaning that they are causes only when they are accompanied by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). Regarding the probandum, which is attachment and so forth, there is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) consisting of pieces of stone and the like, which are devoid of attachment and so forth; even though the presence of the reason—the state of possessing a body and so forth—is not observed in that counter-example, because there is no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary, this is an inference *śeṣavat* (inference from the remainder), and from this there arises doubt, not certainty.

And just as this which has been stated immediately above is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too, from the mere non-observation of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the inference of other causes based on the observation of a general effect—that is, a mere effect—is a semblance of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), meaning it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Of what sort? Like [inferring] passion and so forth from speech.

Now, one might object: "Since every speech is an effect of passion and so forth, how can there be a commonality among those effects? To this he says: "For not... and so on. The movement of the lips is "spanda" (vibration), and because that necessarily occurs at the time of speaking; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other things occurring at the time of speaking, such as facial distortions and the like, are included. "The mere desire to speak," which is the unqualified intention to speak, is the "commonality. Those [movements] such as vibration for which that alone is the cause are described as such; the state of being that is "tadbhāva," and from that [state].

If it is argued that this very desire to speak is itself passion (*rāga*), because passion is of the nature of attachment—this is what [the opponent] thinks—the Master says: "Since it is desired, nothing is contradicted. Because the desire to speak is the longing for the effect, which is speech, nothing undesirable is involved. Furthermore, the desire to speak is not passion; rather, it is produced and projected by that adherence (*abhiniveśa*) which is the view of a self, belonging to a self, and so forth, characterized by permanence and pleasure. The wise declare that passion is the mental clinging directed toward objects of tainted phenomena—that is, having the five aggregates of grasping as its objective support.

It might be thought: "Loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and so forth are admitted for those considered to be free from passion (*vītarāga*). Since these have sentient beings as their object (*sattvālambana*), they proceed from the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and, by proceeding through attachment to sentient beings, are by nature characterized by clinging (*abhiṣvaṅga*); therefore, even those free from passion would follow as being possessed of passion. To this he says: "Compassion and the rest are not thus. Compassion and the rest of those free from passion do not have sentient beings as their object, because they can also occur otherwise.

(“Because [speech] directed toward dharmas is also possible”) — we shall explain this immediately hereafter. Here, the connection is as follows: when an inference of passion is being made from speech, there is no comprehension from speech alone. This is because, just as one who is passionate speaks, so too does one who is dispassionate—that is, even one whose passion has been destroyed. An inference of passion is not from speech alone; rather, it is from a particular kind of speech, that which is produced by passion itself. To this he says: “Nor from a particular [kind of speech].”

What is the reason? Because intention is difficult to discern. For one who is dispassionate may act as if passionate, and one who is passionate may act as if dispassionate; thus, intention is difficult to discern. Consequently, due to the confusion of conventional usage, there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in all such statements—both in speech in general and in specific speech adduced as an indicator (*liṅga*) of passion and so forth. Therefore, there is no inference of passion and the like even from a particular [instance of] speech. Regarding what was stated—that "one who is dispassionate speaks in such a way"—he anticipates the following response:

"Regarding 'purpose' and so forth: linguistic utterance is conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). For one free from passion (*vītarāga*), there is no fruit in the utterance of speech; thus, the sense is that there is no deviation between passion and speech. [The opponent says: "No," [says the Teacher]. There is no absence of purpose, because linguistic discourse is for the sake of others (*parārtha*).

"It is not logical," and so forth, says the opponent. For one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) is not attached to others, and there is no engagement for the sake of others without attachment; this is the sense. This is not so, because engagement occurs even through compassion (*karuṇā*). If it is argued that "this very compassion is attachment," then we grant that this naming of compassion as "attachment" is accepted. If it is further argued that "compassion is also a fault consisting of attachment because it arises from the error of perceiving a self in sentient beings (*sattvadarśanaviparyāsa*)," he replies with the words beginning "without error" (*abiparyāsa*), and so forth.

He states precisely that [compassion] arises from non-perversion: "Even in the absence of the grasping of a self," and so forth. "Merely by perceiving a particular kind of suffering" means merely by defining the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). "Produced by the power of practice" means that compassion indeed arises from preceding moments of a similar nature. Connecting this also with scripture, he says: "For thus," and so forth. By the word "etcetera," those [types of compassion] without an object are included. Compassion having sentient beings as its object belongs to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); that having phenomena as its object belongs to the noble ones (*ārya*).

The [four immeasurables] are without objective support (*anālambana*) for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are free from the attachment to the grasped and the grasper. In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), loving-kindness and the others—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—are intended [to have these four as their objects]. Now, one might object: "Are they not practiced by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) as having sentient beings alone as their objective support? Then how can they be said to have phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth as their objective support? To this, he says:

And these—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—function through the practice of their own kind, because they arise by the power of preceding similar moments. However, there is this distinction: as long as one perceives sentient beings, they have sentient beings as their object; as long as one perceives phenomena (*dharma*), they have phenomena as their object. "They do not depend on passion" means that they do not operate toward sentient beings with underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
But has this point not already been stated immediately before, namely, that [compassion] arises through the power of practice merely by seeing a particular instance of suffering?

True. The distinction is that now [the mind] engages with all things by relying solely on compassion (*karuṇā*). If it is asked, "In that case, even when the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) has ceased, do passion (*rāga*) and the other afflictions still arise through habituation (*abhyāsa*), just as compassion does? he replies: It is not so; passion and the others do not function through habituation to their own kind, such that they would continue to arise even when the view of self has ceased. This is because they do not exist in the absence of the misconceptions regarding a self and so forth (*ātmādiviparyāsa*).

For one who is compassionate, the undertaking for the sake of others is not fruitless; because there is no error—due to the absence of clinging to a self and so forth—there is no self-interest at all. This is not a fault, because the welfare of others alone is intended as the fruit. If it is asked, "Granted that the welfare of others is intended, how can it be the fruit? he says: "By desire," and so forth. It is characterized by desire (*icchā-lakṣaṇa*), meaning it is the object of desire. That which is desired is, in short, the fruit.

If it is asked, "How can there be activity even for the sake of others in one who is devoid of the cognition 'I am'?"—the answer is no. Some say that activity occurs because of the presence of non-afflicted knowledge (*akliṣṭajñāna*). Others say it is due to the manifestation of a pure mundane mind (*śuddhalaukikacitta*) through the power of yoga. Still others say it is because [the Buddha] appears in such a way to those to be trained (*vineya*).

"In every way" is the conclusion. If the desire to speak in one free from passion (*vītarāga*) is established by means of speech, and if compassion is [thereby] asserted, then he is called "one with passion" (*sarāga*). In every way, because there is no superimposition of what is unreal, one who is free from passion and so forth is faultless; for passion and the like, which are of the nature of faults, must necessarily exist [if there were such superimposition]. Therefore, in proving that one free from passion possesses faults by means of something other than passion and the like—namely, the desire to speak and so forth—nothing undesirable occurs.

One might think: "Since passion and so forth are observed in the speaker himself, then by the mere observation of their presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there will be an inference [of them] even in those who are considered to be free from passion. To this he says: "In the speaker himself," and so forth. "An inference of that elsewhere" means that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in inferring passion and so forth in one who is considered free from passion. Whatever specific quality whatsoever is observed in the speaker himself, there would follow the undesirable consequence of inferring all of that in others as well.

Because the specific qualities observed in the self—such as being dark or fair—are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the phrase "inference of something other than passion" (*ananyānumāna*), this refers to the inference of a quality residing in the self that is distinct from passion. As for the word "here," what certainty is there that there is no deviation even with respect to passion and so forth, which are intended as the probandum? None at all. Because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between passion and speech. Since there is no inference from the observation of the self, therefore, speech should lead one to infer the excellence of the instrument [of speech] and the speaker's desire to speak.

The compound *karṇaguṇas tālvādīnām pāṭavādiḥ sa ca vaktukāmatā* is a *dvandva* [compound]; this is indeed a dual form in the accusative case. For speech is not observed in stones and the like, which lack the capacity to produce passion (*rāga*). He says “passion,” etc., because that very capacity is inferred from speech. Regarding the phrase “in the inference of that,” there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the inference of mere capacity.

For instance, just as there is an absence of the capacity to produce passion in things such as stones, so too there is an absence of that capacity in respect to all human qualities; therefore, if one were to infer the capacity to produce passion from the non-perception of speech in such cases, the same would apply to all human qualities.

Now, if it is thought: "The capacity for the production of passion (*rāga*) is indeed the single cause of both passion and speech; and when that [capacity] is inferred, passion is also inferred by implication. Therefore, it is only the capacity that is inferred, not all the personal attributes (*puruṣadharma*) of a person"—to this he replies with the words beginning "of passion" (*rāgasya*). Since passion is of no use regarding speech, because sound is produced solely from the activity of the palate and other organs, how can the power of passion—the power of passion—be useful for speech?

Now, if it is maintained that even the latent capacity for passion (*rāga-śakti*) is utilized toward the production of speech at the time of the operation of the palate and other organs, then, because they depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), passion itself would also be produced at the time of the production of the first phoneme. Furthermore, since that passion possesses a continuous flow (*santānavāhitva*), it would follow that passion alone is what is utilized in the production of the second and subsequent phonemes. To this he says: "For if the capacity were utilized, then that [passion] itself would be utilized. And it has already been stated previously that there is no utilization of passion.

Alternatively, for those who are free from the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātma-ātmīya-abhiniveśa*), speech is of no use. How then could that power—namely, the power of passion (*rāga-śakti*) known as latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) characterized by the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self—be of use with respect to speech? This is because for those free from passion (*vītarāga*), there is an absence of attachment to a self and so forth. For if a power were to be employed with respect to speech, then that very passion would be employed; for all those who possess attachment to a self and so forth are indeed passionate.
And it has been stated that such speech does not exist because it lacks utility; for the desire to speak is a general cause, as mentioned in this context.

The passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth is the conclusion (*nigamana*). "Invariably concomitant" (*nāntarīyaka*) means necessarily inseparable from the cause, because of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), that is, because [the effect] is dependent upon that cause. Nothing else—that is, what is not so connected—is [established] even if the reason is not observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), because for one of limited vision, non-observation alone does not constitute certainty. For one who perceives everything (*sarvadarśin*), however, there would be certainty through the cessation of observation; for his knowledge pervades all objects of knowledge. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "For one who perceives everything" (*sarvadarśana*).

Furthermore, he states—beginning with "In some cases, thus"—that non-existence is not determined by mere non-perception. [The phrase] "previously seen in that manner" refers to things seen in a certain way. Then, the word *bheda* (difference) is connected to each term: "by difference of place, time, and processing (*saṃskāra*). Processing refers to such things as sprinkling with milk. [The object] might become otherwise than the mode previously seen. To ask "What is it like?", he says: "Just as myrobalans (*āmalaka*). This is an illustration of the difference in processing.

And it is not the case that [sweet fruits] are thus abundant, for sweet fruits are not seen in abundance because bitter fruits are seen in abundance. It is not the case that [sweet fruits] do not exist at all now, because sweet fruits are not seen in abundance; rather, the possibility of a sweet fruit is not denied in some instances. Likewise, there is the occurrence of the *piṇḍakharjūra* (date palm) according to the difference of place, and of flowers and so forth according to the difference of time.

He states this by means of the example of the *āmalaka* fruit: just as *āmalaka* fruits change through processing with milk and other substances, so too the mental continuum (*cittasaṃtāna*), which is susceptible to passion and the like, becomes fit [for liberation] through the formative influence (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the practice of reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, through such practice, consciousness that has selflessness (*nairātmya*) as its very object is called "clearly manifest dispassion" (*vairāgya*), because passion and the like do not arise due to the disappearance of the clinging to a self and so forth resulting from the vision of selflessness.

Furthermore, knowledge that takes as its object the momentariness of all phenomena and so forth appears with clarity and is called omniscience, because it is free from all ignorance. Therefore, the increase in clarity resulting from the cultivation of reality (*tattva*)—precisely by means of the direct perception of reality—subverts the nature of cognition that is susceptible to passion and other afflictions. Consequently, even that which was previously perceived otherwise may, through the power of causes, become otherwise.

Therefore, even if one has not observed speech in someone who is free from passion, it does not follow that there can be no speech at all in every person free from passion; such is not a certain conclusion. Consequently, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is uncertain, one cannot infer passion and so forth from mere speech. For this reason, it is appropriate to say: "A speaker like me," meaning one who, like myself, possesses improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). He states this very point with the words beginning "In the arising of passion," etc. To the question "What, then, is this [improper mental attention]? he says: "The self," etc.

The view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) is the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). The inversion [of perceiving] permanence, pleasure, and so forth, is improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). This is a copulative compound (*dvandvasamāsa*), or else it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning that the view of a self itself is improper mental attention. In that case, even if "one like me" is used as a qualification for the speaker, the citation of the statement is pointless. The meaning is that the example of the reason "because of the statement" is useless. For at that time, whoever like me is endowed with the specific conditions for the arising of passion is one who possesses passion (*rāgī*).

The reason would be simply "as I [have seen]," because from mere non-perception there is no certainty. Therefore, the non-perception of the reason in the absence of the opposite (vipakṣa), when the opposite has not been observed, is not a cause for the ascertainment of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the logical mark.

Regarding PV(SV) 1.13, one might think: "The reason (*hetu*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because it is observed in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, speech is not observed in one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). Therefore, due to this non-observation, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—the absence of the probandum where the reason is absent—is established. To this, he says: "And not by mere non-observation" [is there] the non-deviation of the reason in the dissimilar class. Why? Because deviation is possible; that is, because deviation is possible. That which has possible deviation is "one for whom deviation is possible"; its state is "possibility of deviation," and [the non-deviation is not established] because of that.

Even if [the reason] has not been observed in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), nevertheless, since its presence there is not contradictory, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is suspected, as in the case of the cooking of rice grains contained within a pot (*sthālītaṇḍula*).

To support this very example, he says: "For not," and so forth. Even when those things inside a pot are seen to have been cooked in abundance, cooking is not established by the mere fact of being inside the pot. The inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding specific [additional] factors, as he will say later: "But it would be thus. Why is there a lack of proof? Because of the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Those which are seen to be cooked and possess such a nature are of a similar nature to them.

The cause of ripening is the same for those very things that have been ripened; "those which are ripened" refers to them. Otherwise, however—that is, if that qualification were absent—the phrase "there is a remainder" would mean that there exists an undetermined object (*anirṇīta-viṣaya*), which is to say, a remainder. And that [reason] is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).
(PVSV 1.14)

He asks—“What then? and so forth—to determine whether the *śeṣavat* inference intended here is that which consists of inferring a cause from an effect as stated by the Naiyāyikas, or something else entirely. He states the essential nature of *śeṣavat*: “Of which,” and so forth. That inference for which the exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is established merely by the non-perception of the reason—which is not itself a means of valid cognition—is called *śeṣavat* because that reason is a cause of doubt, that is, because it produces uncertainty.

What is the reason? Because that negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is uncertain, one might suspect its occurrence even in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Why, then, is it not certain? He says: "negative concomitance," and so forth. How can there be doubt even when there is non-perception? He says: "not all," and so forth. Is it not the case that only the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the means of cognition?

Since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established by mere non-perception in this way, therefore, one who desires the exclusion of the probandum through the exclusion of the one [the probans]—that is, the exclusion of the means of proof (*sādhana*)—must also accept some essential connection (*pratibandha*) between those two, the probandum and the probans, characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), and not merely non-perception. Otherwise, if no such connection were accepted, the reason would be non-informative (*agamaka*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would remain unascertained.
(PVSV 1.15)

For this reason—namely, because of that cause—the Master Dignāga described the ascertainment (*niścaya*) regarding all three forms of the logical reason (*hetu*), namely the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), in his *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and other works, by means of the passage beginning with "But the unestablished (*asiddha*) is a proof for neither [of the two]" (*asiddhas tu dvayor api sādhanam*). To the question "By the exclusion of what? he says: "The unestablished," and so forth. Because it belongs to the class beginning with "ādi," the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the instrumental case; thus, the meaning is "by the counter-example" (*vipakṣeṇa*).

In this context, the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is described by means of its opposite, the unestablished (*asiddha*). The ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is described by means of its opposite, the contradictory (*viruddha*), which has a contrary meaning. The ascertainment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is described by means of its opposite, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), which is characterized by deviation.

And by describing the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has indeed been shown. For, when there is no necessary connection, there can be no ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance. Therefore, demonstrating that very connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), and thereby challenging [the opponent's position], he states the ascertainment: "In that case," and so forth, explaining that specific defect for the removal of which the aforementioned ascertainment was stated.

"Of those that are contradictory and those belonging to the contradictory side" means: of the contradictory [reasons] and of those belonging to the contradictory side; those belonging to the contradictory side are those whose presence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is certain, while their presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is doubtful. These are indeed "doubtful inconclusives" (*sandigdhānaikāntika*), but they are designated thus according to what is established by others. The connection with the context is "by way of the non-ascertainment of the negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*). The connection is "the exclusion of the inconclusive. Therefore, the meaning is: "of the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*)" and "of its side."

And regarding the category of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*): [the term] "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the *śeṣavad* and so forth" excludes that which is doubtful with respect to both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). That whose presence in the similar class and its absence from the dissimilar class is established by mere non-observation is the *śeṣavat*.

Regarding the statement "But what is well-known [is accepted] by both," he now explains the Master’s text beginning with "by both. The phrase "by both" means that there is a negation of whatever is established for neither the proponent nor the opponent. By the word "well-known" (*prasiddha*), the connection is that there is a negation of those two types of reasons—the *śeṣavat* (probative by elimination) and the *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon)—which are both doubtful. He asks, "Doubtful about what? and replies, "Even in the case of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)," because in the case of the *śeṣavat*, there is doubt regarding the dissimilar instance.

But for that which is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), [the reason] exists neither in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) nor in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, by his statement regarding certainty, the Teacher also certainly intends a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Otherwise, if there were no necessary connection between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), and if the Teacher intended a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based merely on the non-observation [of the reason] in the dissimilar instances, then the statement of the property of difference (*vaidharmya-vacana*)—which was asserted as the counter-position to the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its deviation from the dissimilar instances—would be purposeless; this is the underlying intention.

But where was it promised by the Teacher? He says: "That which... and so forth. This has been stated in the *Nyāyamukha*: that both must be stated, namely similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). To the question, "In opposition to what was each stated? he says: "The statement of the probans (*sādhana*) [is] in opposition to the contradictory (*viruddha*); the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is in opposition to the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). And if it has non-perception as its result—that is, if the statement of dissimilarity has mere non-perception as its result—then [it is valid].

He explains this very point with the words "If," and so forth. By the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the non-observation of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is made known. That non-observation is understood even when the dissimilarity is not explicitly stated, because non-observation—characterized by the absence of observation—is established even prior to the statement of dissimilarity. Therefore, the statement of dissimilarity is purposeless.

If it is argued that there is a misconception regarding the observation of the reason in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), and that the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is for the purpose of removing that [misconception], he replies with "Not so," and so forth. "Of that" refers to the person being instructed, prior to the statement of dissimilarity. There is no misconception regarding the observation of the reason in the dissimilar instance until it is overturned by the statement of dissimilarity. Therefore, just as there is no misconception when the reason is observed in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), but rather a forgetting of it, this [forgetting] is recalled by the statement of similarity (*sādharmya*).

If it is argued that memory is produced by verbal expression through the mention of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) when there is no perception, [the author] says "perception," etc., in order to refute that very example: "Perception which is not being apprehended and not being remembered is not a factor for the comprehension of the probandum; this is correct. In that case, regarding perception, the instilling of memory—that is, the production of memory—by means of verbal expression is appropriate. However, it is not appropriate for the purpose of non-perception (*adarśana*). This is because non-perception is the absence of perception in the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) of the reason; that [non-perception] is sublated by perception.

In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of seeing the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—the absence of seeing is already established; therefore, the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) for the sake of establishing that, i.e., for the sake of establishing the absence of seeing, is pointless. The intention [behind this] is as follows: since seeing might be forgotten due to its being beyond the senses (*parokṣatva*), a statement for the purpose of remembering it would be appropriate. However, the absence of seeing consists in the cessation of seeing, and that manifests precisely from the non-experience of seeing. And for that which is manifesting, what is the use of memory? Thus, the statement for the sake of establishing that is pointless.

Indeed, for a person who does not perceive [something], there can be no certainty that "the reason does not exist in the counter-example" based on mere non-perception alone; for even when things are remote in terms of space and so forth, they may still exist despite being unperceived. If it is argued that the statement of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-vacana*) is for the purpose of producing the certainty that "it does not exist," that is not so. Because a thing being negated does not necessarily cease to exist simply because of a statement lacking valid means of cognition (*apramāṇaka*). How, then, is it understood that it does not exist? To this he says: "Just as... and so forth.

This is what is meant: the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason with its own probandum is precisely that which apprehends its dependence upon the probandum; and that which is intended here is "observation" (*darśana*), namely, the observation of the reason only where the probandum exists, which is itself everywhere the non-observation of the reason in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

The meaning is this: for that very person in whom the perception grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans has occurred and is now remembered, the recollection is produced by means of the statements of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) once the [respective] perceptions and non-perceptions have been cognized; it is not so for anyone else. As it has been said: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is demonstrated by means of the two examples," and "if it does not exist, it is made known."

In whatever manner—that is, by way of the necessary connection with its own probandum—if that logical principle is made known or remembered through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the connection, such that the reason does not exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), then it is understood that [the reason] does not exist there; but not without that connection.

He states the first portion of the verse beginning with "yadi" (*yady*): If one, while not perceiving [an object], does not conclude that it is non-existent based on mere non-perception, then one will likewise not conclude [non-existence] from a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) when that statement lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). For even that statement of dissimilarity merely makes known the non-perception itself; it does not convey anything further as a remainder.

It might be thought: "The absence of the reason (*hetu*) caused by the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is made known by the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); therefore, there is a distinction [between the two]. To this, he says: "And not one," and so forth. "Non-perception of one" means the non-perception of the probandum. "The absence of the other" means the absence of the proof (*sādhana*). The point is that [this would follow] only if there were no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), if cessation occurred without a necessary connection, then by the cessation of a cow, there would necessarily be the cessation of a horse as well.

Now, suppose it is thought: since the Master Dignāga stated that "the reason does not exist in the dissimilar instance," certainty follows from that very fact; therefore, he says "na ca" and so forth. Because that teacher made the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-vacana) that "[the reason] does not exist," it would follow that the non-existence of the thing itself occurs in that manner, due to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). For if that statement were authoritative, the proof of the probandum (sādhya) would result from the mere thesis (pratijñā) alone.

Therefore, how can the exclusion of the inconclusive [reason] be achieved by stating a dissimilarity? It cannot at all. Consequently, one who desires the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example must state the logical justification for that exclusion; for there is a principle that the means of valid cognition which grasps the necessary connection between the probandum and the probans [must be stated]. "Of this" refers to the person to be convinced. Thus, the certainty arises that the probans is excluded [from the counter-example].

The opponent [objects] with "nanu" and so forth. He thinks that because there is no perception [of the reason] in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), the exclusion of the reason is unestablished; this is precisely the correct principle. If the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) were based on non-perception, then why would inference *per modum residuum* (*śeṣavat*) not be fallacious?
