What, then, is such [an inference]? He says: "Just as," and so forth. "These fruits" refers to those other than those already consumed.

And this is the statement of the subject (*dharmin*): "these [fruits] are indeed ripe" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). "Thus they are sweet or sour" is the predicate. "Because there is no difference in their form" is the reason (*hetu*); that is, because they possess the same form—such as redness and so forth—as the fruit that has already been consumed. Or, "because they originate from the same branch" is the reason; "like the one already consumed" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Why would there be a lack of deviation (*avyabhicāritva*) for the *śeṣavat* inference if one were to accept the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception? To this he says: "In this case also," and so forth.

In this case, regarding the *śeṣavat* inference, when the entire remainder of the fruit—other than that which has been consumed and endowed with specific characteristics such as its form—is made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no perception of the reason (consisting of the specific form and so forth) in the absence of the probandum; thus, there is exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), and consequently, there would be non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*). For indeed, apart from the fruit that has been made the subject and that which has been consumed and taken as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the occurrence of the aforementioned reason does not exist in a third category, which constitutes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

"Contradiction by perception," and so forth. Some, such as Īśvarasena and others, maintain that there is a suspicion of contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) even for an inference based on the method of residues (*śeṣavat*), because it is possible to have a perceptual experience of a fruit produced from a single branch that is either unripe or tasteless; thus, they claim that [the reason] is fallacious. The meaning of this is that a logical reason (*hetu*) does not lead to a conclusion through mere positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) alone, but rather only when its object is not contradicted (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*).

Because there is no sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) regarding that object which has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*) and is imperceptible (*parokṣa*). If it is argued that there is no suspicion of sublation by a functioning perception, but rather the possibility that at some time there might be sublation by the perception of odor, [the author] replies: "In that way," and so forth. If one suspects that sublation by perception might occur in such a manner, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is because, in other cases, there is no rule guaranteeing the absence of sublation by perception even when a reason (*hetu*) is intended [to be valid].

The point is that even when a relationship [between the reason and the probandum] is accepted, the suspicion of sublation (*bādhāśaṅkā*) does not cease for the opponent. Therefore, one who denies the existence of an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) must accept that an established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) serves as a sublater. If there were sublation by a non-occurrent [reason], that is, by a means of valid cognition that has not even functioned, there would be no confidence (*anāśvāsa*) anywhere; there would be no certainty regarding the capacity to indicate [the probandum] (*gamakatvaniścaya*) in any logical reason, because a sublater could always be suspected.

For one who maintains that there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), there is no lack of confidence regarding the reason (*hetu*) in every case, because when a reason is connected to the probandum (*sādhya*), even the suspicion of sublation (*bādhā*) is absent. However, prior to the formulation of the reason, there might be a suspicion of sublation; for this very reason, the statement of the reason is uttered when [the presence of the reason] is doubtful. Furthermore, there exists no established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the "remainder" (*śeṣavat*). Therefore, it is established that if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is based on mere non-observation, then even the "remainder" would be non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).

[Objection: But surely, by the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), when there is the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) and the reason (*hetu*) is absent, the mere existence of that absence would be the indicator. To this he says: "But the absence... and so forth. That absence of the reason from the heterologous instances (*vipakṣa*) is indeed established—that is, certain—as the proof. Thus, [the proof] depends upon the ascertainment of the reason's being thus, namely, the ascertainment of the non-existence of the reason where the probandum is absent. This he means to say: for us, as for you, the absence is not [established] merely from the non-perception of the object.

However, when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), the exclusion of the probans from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*)—that is, its absence where the probandum is absent—is an intrinsic property (*svagato dharma*) of the probans. Furthermore, whatever is the nature of the probans necessarily depends upon its own ascertainment, because it is a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*). If it is asked, "How then, according to your view, can the *śeṣavat* [inference] be fallacious? he says: "But due to non-perception," and so forth. This refers to cases where, even though the absence of the probans in a certain portion of the heterologue is established, the probans remains unconnected to the probandum.

In the absence of that [reason], because the non-existence of the probandum is not established in all cases of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), doubt arises; therefore, that very lack of exclusion from the counter-example is the "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) of the *śeṣavat* [inference].

The phrase "kiṃca" (furthermore) serves to aggregate another fault. If [the absence of the probandum] were established through non-perception (*adarśana*), then even a purely negative reason (*vyatirekin*) would be a valid logical mark (*hetu*). Of what sort? For instance, [the argument]: "This is not soulless," and so forth. This has been stated by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), because it would entail the consequence of being devoid of breath and other such functions. Since it possesses breath and the like, it must possess a self (*sātmaka*); and this reason—never being observed in anything possessing a self, yet being excluded from all things devoid of a self—is called a "negative-only" (*avyatirekin*) reason, characterized by its absence when the property to be proven is absent.

For instance, in the case of objects such as jars—which are devoid of a self and lack an essence—whether they are perceived or unperceived, there is no observation of breath and so forth, meaning no observation of the expansion and contraction of inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*). In the case of those that are perceived, the non-observation of breath and so forth occurs precisely because their nature is not apprehended, since they have met the conditions for perceptibility. In the case of those that are unperceived, it is due to their belonging to the same class [of things]. Therefore, the absence of a self is pervaded by the absence of breath and so forth.

In a living body, however, by the cessation of that [breathing], there is the cessation of the absence of possession of breath and so forth; thus, through the cessation of selflessness (*nairātmya*), there would be the cognition of a self. If it is asked, "How then is this a cause for doubt according to you?", he says: "Because the self is invisible," and so on. Since the non-perception of the invisible self does not establish its absence in things such as jars, selflessness is not established in jars and the like. Therefore, because of this reason, there is no exclusion of breath and so forth from what is selfless. The meaning is that since selflessness itself remains unestablished—being doubted due to the absence of breath and so forth—it cannot serve as a probans.

If it is argued that because the Buddhist has accepted selflessness (*nairātmya*), the absence of a self in jars and other things is established by virtue of that very acceptance; [we reply: if the Buddhist’s own acceptance is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how is the existence of a self established in a living body? For that too is held by the Buddhist to be devoid of a self. Since the acceptance of selflessness regarding the living body lacks a means of valid cognition, the self is thereby established for it.

If this is so, then for another person as well, how could the proof of selflessness (*nairātmya*) regarding things other than a living body—such as a jar—be established without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*)? For it is not the case that for a Buddhist, one’s own acceptance (*abhyupagama*) is a means of valid cognition in some instances and not in others. Furthermore, by means of mere acceptance, one distinguishes between things possessing a self and those lacking a self; thus, jars and the like have been accepted as lacking a self both by the opponent and by us. Therefore, they are without a self.

We have accepted that the living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*), whereas you maintain that it is indeed selfless (*nirātmaka*). By thus analyzing [the case] and asserting that vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth do not exist in those things that are selfless—thereby claiming that these [breaths] are indicators (*gamaka*) regarding the existence of a self—you, the opponent, have admitted that the self is known through scripture (*āgamika*) and not through inference (*anumeya*). Therefore, even though a self is not observed in jars and the like, since the absence of a self whose nature is by definition invisible cannot be established, there is no exclusion (*vyatireka*) of vital breaths and so forth from anything that is selfless; thus, [your reason] is non-indicative (*agamaka*).

To begin with, the cessation [of breath and so forth] from the self is not established at all. However, even granting that for the sake of argument, it is said: "even when that [breath] ceases, and even when the self ceases in some instance"—that is, even when [the self] has ceased in observed things such as jars—there is no obstruction of the breath and so forth, because there is no necessary connection between them and the self. Since the cessation of breath and so forth is not established by the cessation of the self even in all unobserved cases such as jars, the reason lacks probative force because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

If one accepts the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based merely on non-perception, there is this further fault; thus he says: "And that which... and so forth. To the question "What, then, is that?", he says: "Likewise, [the reason] exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*)," and so forth. This passage belongs to the Master (Dignāga), and regarding that, it was stated: "The property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is understood as being ascertained by both the proponent and the opponent. By this, there is the exclusion of [reasons] that are unestablished for either one of the two, as well as those that are unestablished in their locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Just as the four types of unestablished (*asiddha*) reasons are excluded by the ascertainment of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), so too are the various forms of the unestablished eliminated by the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in cases such as "existing in the similar instances" (*sapakṣa*) or "not existing in them. This is because the types of unestablished reasons, such as those unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*), cannot possibly occur in relation to the similar instances and so forth. He says that this application of the unestablished need not even be mentioned, and explains it with the words beginning "only non-perception," etc. (*anupalambha eva*, etc.).

Since there is doubt regarding the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) precisely when there is non-perception (*anupalambha*), how could that [doubt] not exist when there is perception? For if the reason were perceived in the counter-example, that doubt would be absent. Therefore, by implication, a reason whose exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful—on account of the reason being non-perceived—is indeed accepted [as faulty]. Consequently, what is doubted is unavoidable; that is, an exclusion that has been made the object of doubt cannot be set aside.

If it is argued that because of the phrase "it should be cited as appropriate," the doubt raised by this statement is not actually precluded—this is not so. For immediately following that, there is the statement beginning with, "But that which expresses the certainty of both [parties]," and so forth. The passage here is the example: "Only that word which expresses the three-fold character (trairūpya) as certain for both parties is a proof or a refutation; however, one that expresses what is established for only one party or what is doubtful does not require further proof, and so on. This is the text that serves as the illustration in this context.

Whether it be the proponent or the opponent, he who states that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful (*sandigdha*) offers neither a proof (*sādhana*) nor a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). A reason whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful is uncertain for both parties regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); therefore, its statement is not a proof.

Since only a reason certain for both has been declared [as valid], one who—despite the absence [of the reason]—suspects its non-exclusion from the counter-example due to doubt about its cessation, denies the status of a reason to such a "doubtful-vyatireka" by attributing to it the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Furthermore, if exclusion were intended to occur through non-perception, then a specific, unique property such as audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) would become a cause for exclusion. Why? Because it is not perceived in either permanent or impermanent things. He explains this with the words "of audibility also," and so forth. For if exclusion were accepted as resulting from mere non-perception, and since audibility is indeed not perceived in either permanent or impermanent things, it would follow that it is a cause for their exclusion; that is, it would be a cause for the negation of both the permanent and the impermanent.

If it were indeed the case that audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) were excluded from that [permanent entity] simply because it is not observed there, one might ask: "From what [reason] does it follow that it is the cause for its exclusion? To this he says: "For not... For there is no exclusion other than the exclusion of that [entity]; thus, there is the exclusion of the permanent and the impermanent. If it is asked, "How is it that even for you, audibility is not the cause for exclusion?", he says: "But non-exclusion... and so forth. This is because there is no certainty of exclusion based merely on non-observation of something from certain permanent or impermanent things.

And there is uncertainty because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with either one [of the two] is not ascertained. This must necessarily be so; otherwise, if a property (*dharma*) is ascertained as being absent in a certain locus (*dharmī*), how could that [property], while existing, not cause one to understand the absence of that very thing in which its presence was previously ascertained? Its absence would indeed be understood.

If it were suspected that even for "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*), which is excluded from both the permanent and the impermanent, there would be sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when proving the exclusion of both, [the author] provides the explanation of the verse beginning with "even so" (*athāpi*). When proving the exclusion of both—namely, the exclusion of the permanent and the impermanent—by means of audibility, there exists a sublation by another means of valid cognition. He states this with the words beginning "mutually" (*anyonya*): those whose nature consists of mutual exclusion are "such" (*tathā*).

For instance, impermanence is simply the exclusion of permanence, and permanence is simply the exclusion of that [impermanence]. Likewise, non-existence is simply the exclusion of existence, and existence is simply the exclusion of non-existence. This is because the affirmation of one occurs through the exclusion of the other; since the second, being its opposite, is affirmed, there is no negation of it.

This is what is meant: when audibility is excluded from the eternal—meaning that [the property of being audible] would exclude [the eternal]—it would establish that very thing as impermanent; and since that same [audibility] is excluded from the impermanent, it would exclude the impermanent while establishing the eternal. Thus, affirmation and negation would occur simultaneously for a single entity, which is illogical. Therefore, because affirmation and negation are mutually contradictory at the same time, there can be no negation of anything whatsoever.

For a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is characterized by the cessation of a negation (*pratiṣedha*), and a negation is simply the cessation of a positive injunction; since these two are mutually contradictory, how could they both exist simultaneously in a single thing? Therefore, there is no certainty regarding exclusion from anything whatsoever on the grounds of "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*). [The proponent of the established doctrine] says: "Not now. [This means: "Now," that is, when sublation (*bādhā*) is impossible. Because it is not seen in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the reason is absent there. This being so, non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because sublation is impossible.

If it is argued that "let there be invalidity only in the case of audibility itself, and not elsewhere, because there is no sublation [of the reason] in other cases," he replies with the words beginning "tathā" (in that way). Even elsewhere, the sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible for the non-perception that establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason. Why? Because of the definition, and so forth.

The definition [of non-perception] is that it is the basis for the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Since the non-perception of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is endowed with this definition, if there is no possibility of sublation (*bādhā*) in that case, then that very definition—the nature of that non-perception which establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—would be undermined as a definition whose scope is universal. Consequently, there would be no confidence in establishing negative concomitance through non-perception in all cases; there would be no certainty regarding its being a means of proof (*gamaka*).

If this is so, then even regarding the object of inference (*anumāna*), one might observe in some cases a contradiction between perception and inference; for instance, when it is argued that "sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound" (*śabdatva*), its eternity is sublated by inference. Likewise, [the claim] "sound is inaudible because it exists, like a pot" is sublated by perception. Consequently, since there is no distinction in the definition [of the reason] in all such cases, would it not follow that there is a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) even in inference? [Response: This is not so. For in those cases, the reason is indeed fallacious (*asiddha*). It is only when a reason is established as being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) that it can lead to the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*). However, in the case of "sound is eternal because it is audible," the reason is not established, because audibility is absent from the subject. Similarly, in the case of "sound is inaudible because it exists," the reason is not established, because existence is absent from the subject. Therefore, since the reason is not established, there is no sublation of the probandum by either perception or inference. Thus, there is no lack of confidence in inference. Furthermore, the fact that a reason is sublated by perception or inference occurs only when the reason is actually established; it does not occur when the reason is unestablished. Hence, there is no lack of confidence in inference.

This is not as stated, because in an inference arising from the non-perception of an effect or of an essential nature (*svabhāva*), there is no contradiction with perception or inference; for that which could constitute a contradiction with perception does not possess the characteristics of such [an inference], and thus it lacks the definition of that inference.

If there is no sublation (*bādhā*) in an inference possessing the characteristics as previously stated, then two reasons endowed with the characteristics of a reason that establish mutually contradictory objects, having descended upon a single subject (*dharmin*), are called "the non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) by the Teacher; [if you argue] that this was not mentioned [by him], he states by this [passage] that such an admission is lost: since the non-erroneous contradictory is not mentioned regarding the object of inference, how can there be a loss of what was admitted? To the question, "Where then did the Teacher state it?", he says: "And the object," and so forth.

Regarding this non-erroneous contradictory [reason] (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), [the author asks]: "And what [is it]? and so forth. Here, in order to prove the existence of air (*vāyu*), the Vaiśeṣika has stated the sūtra: "Tactile sensation exists, and yet it is not perceived among those things that are seen. The meaning of this is as follows: whatever is a quality (*guṇa*) is dependent upon a substance (*dravya*). For example, color and so forth. And the tactile sensation that is neither produced by heat nor hot nor cold is a quality. Therefore, there must exist a substance that serves as its substratum.

Furthermore, this [quality] is not a property of the perceived elements such as earth and the rest, because they possess qualities such as touch that is produced by heating (*pākaja*) and is neither hot nor cold. When the Vaiśeṣika has thus stated, "Therefore, that of which this is a quality shall be wind," the Master Diṅnāga said in response: "If a negation of the perceived [elements] is made on the basis of mere non-perception, that too is not tenable. Demonstrating that the [Vaiśeṣika's] statement contradicts this, the author of the *Vārttika* says: "The perceived," and so forth.

If cessation were to occur through perception, then by the same reason—that it is not perceived when not seen—the logic regarding the non-produced touch that is neither hot nor cold would be untenable. The meaning is that the "inconsistency" described by the Vaiśeṣikas with respect to earth and the other elements, of which the Teacher has stated the illogicality, would instead be consistent and indeed logical.

He explains that with the words "If," and so forth. As the Teacher stated in the *Vāyuprakaraṇa*: "If the Vaiśeṣika were to effect a negation of touch [in air] based merely on its non-perception in relation to the perceived [elements] such as earth and so on, that too would not be logical. If the Teacher also intended a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based merely on non-perception, then how could it be illogical? The negation of touch would indeed be logical. What is the reason? Because here too, the absence [of the probandum] is admitted to be established through the non-apprehension of the reason.

"Is it not so? and so forth says the opponent. Because of the condition of being accessible to perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), the non-perception of a touch that is neither hot nor cold (*anuṣṇāśītasparśa*)—which is not produced by fire—in earth and the other elements is indeed logically a negation [of its existence]. "It is not logical," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). For what reason? That earth and so forth which are perceived as endowed with a touch other than the neither-hot-nor-cold are visible; and elsewhere, even if not perceived in a particular place and so on, earth and the rest possess that very same nature, being endowed with such a touch.

The term *dṛśyaś ca tatsvabhāvaś ca* is a dvandva compound. That very thing is the object (*viṣaya*), and that alone is *tanmātra*; this is a compound formed according to the rule *sup supā*. Because there is no prohibition of touch (*sparśa*) therein. For if there were a prohibition in that case, there would indeed be certainty; however, this Vaiśeṣika states the prohibition of touch by grasping earth and the other substrates (*dharmi*) in a general and non-specific manner.

Whatever exists, such as earth and so forth, all that is devoid of both hot and cold touch. Furthermore, there is no attainment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti*) of touch in earth and the other elements alone. Nor is there a rule of a single touch for earth and the others, because within that generality of earth and so forth, even though they remain earth and so on, a difference in touch is observed among specific instances such as cotton, stones, and leaves. For instance, the touch of cotton is different, characterized by smoothness, while that of stones and the like is different, characterized by roughness and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of this too": since there is the possibility that a touch which is neither hot nor cold might occur in some particular type of earth-substance, it is improper to deny the existence of such a touch merely because it is not observed everywhere in earth and the other elements.

As for what is said: "Because earth and the rest are uniform everywhere, the touch that is neither hot nor cold must likewise be uniform; however, the difference in qualities such as smoothness that occurs despite the presence of earth and the rest is caused by the dense or non-dense nature of the conjunction of the atoms of earth and so forth."

That is incorrect. For since there is no contiguity among non-dense [atoms], there is no conjunction. Therefore, just as there is density in the conjunction of stone-atoms, so too it would be for cotton-atoms; how then could there be a distinction such as smoothness? Consequently, even if conjunction exists, stone-atoms are inherently of one nature and cotton-atoms are inherently of another, and the distinction of smoothness and so forth is caused by that very nature. It is not produced by the density or lack of density of the conjunction.

And likewise, just as there is a distinction in touch—such as smoothness and so forth—due to the distinction of earth and the other elements, so too a distinction in the "neither-hot-nor-cold" [touch] might be possible. Now, let it be granted that there is no inference of air (*vāyu*) regarding an unperceived object; however, in the case of a perceived object, since a "neither-hot-nor-cold" touch that is visible is not observed to belong to earth and the other elements, an inference of air from that [touch] would indeed follow.

He thinks as follows: If the quality-nature of touch and so forth were established, then there would be an inference of the substance wind; however, that very [quality-nature] is unestablished. For us, it is simply a particular kind of touch, perceived independently, that is called "wind. But Master Dignāga, not accepting a wind distinct from touch, stated that the opponent’s inference regarding it is invalid; thus, there is no fault. Therefore, this remains established: by stating that there is no negation based on mere non-observation when positive and negative concomitance have not been ascertained, the Master has accepted the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

If it is asked, "Who then is being thus rebuked? he says: "Thus," and so forth. "Thus" means by the arguments just mentioned. A certain student of the Teacher—who is ignorant of the Teacher's treatises—speaking of non-existence on the grounds of non-perception, is the one being rebuked.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) that would follow if non-existence were accepted merely because something is not seen, he says: "Because of differences in place and so forth. By the word "and so forth," differences in time and preparation (*saṃskāra*) are meant. Even among substances belonging to the same genus, various powers (*śakti*) characterized by taste, potency (*vīrya*), post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), and so on, are seen to be distinct. In this regard—among substances possessing multiple powers—it is not logical to determine the existence [of a certain power] elsewhere, such as in another place, simply because it was seen once in a substance of a single nature.
This is just like the determination of the nature of a substance exactly as it has been observed.

With the words "If" (*yadi*) and so forth, he explains this very point: if it is maintained that there is non-deviation from the probandum for a reason that is unconnected to its own probandum merely because it is not observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), then the form of a substance perceived in one place would have to be inferable in another place as well, on the basis of the generality of the substance; for in that case too, there is at that time the mere non-observation of the reason in the dissimilar instance.

And this is not logical, because in a certain place some substances are seen to have specific tastes and so forth; yet they are seen again "otherwise," that is, in a different place, as the opposite of the form in which they were previously observed. By the words "such as" (*yathā*) and so on, he states the subject: *vīrya* is the power to remove defects; *pariṇāma* is the transformation [of digestion]. The analysis of the compound is: those whose taste, potency, and transformation are distinguished. "Not elsewhere" means in any place other than that particular field (*kṣetra*).

Just as [substances] differ due to the particularity of place, so too they possess distinct tastes, potencies, and post-digestive transformations (*vipāka*) due to differences in processing (*saṃskāra*). Processing refers to the irrigation with milk and other substances. And because those [plants] from that specific location are seen by other people to be endowed with such distinct tastes and so forth, it is established that all [plants], even those not from that location, are identical in their true nature—namely, in their form and other qualities—and thus possess the same essential character as they were perceived to have.

What is the reason? Because other qualities—the specific distinctions such as *rasa* and so forth—depend upon other causes. However, in the absence of a cause for distinction, there would be an inference of a single nature. Whatever Vedic [text] has an unseen author, that too is preceded by human refinement and has human effort as its cause. This is the probandum (*sādhya*). Since there is no difference between those sentences intended to be human and those intended to be non-human, this is stated as the logical reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever entity possesses a nature non-different from another must have the same cause, just as one instance of smoke is of the same genus as other instances of smoke. And sentences considered to be authorless (*apauruṣeya*) possess a nature non-different from human-authored sentences; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*). For, in whatever ways the Vedicists maintain that the Vedas possess a distinction—namely, by the removal of poison and so forth—all those ways are observed to have their causes in human beings. Indeed, even the mantras of the Śabaras and others are seen to effect the removal of poison and similar results.

If, on the grounds of the similarity of their intrinsic nature as sounds, it is inferred that even [the Veda], whose author is unseen, is of human origin, then in that case, because one perceives the continuum of one's own mind, all mental phenomena are known. Therefore, as long as there is the nature of consciousness, so long is everything dependent upon the five sense faculties and conceptual; and as it is now, so it will be in the future state, and as it is for me, so it is for others as well. Thus, by virtue of being mind and by virtue of being dependent upon the sense faculties...

Anticipating the objection—"Since the mind of every person is always associated with passion and so forth by virtue of being the cause of speech and other such functions, why is it not inferred that [the mind] has a restricted object, rather than being all-encompassing?"—he says: "Not so," and so forth. Just as sentences do not have specific causes that are impossible [to identify], persons likewise do not have specific causes that are possible; for it is due to the impossibility of such specific causes that [the inference is blocked]. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) after "speech" (*vacana*), there is the inclusion of [qualities] such as dependence on the sense faculties and the nature of being a mind.

From that sign—namely, speech and so forth—which possesses a similarity with [the subject] by virtue of some slight or partial commonality, one might infer for men a similarity in every respect, whether as being possessed of passion and so forth, as having restricted objects, or by some other characteristic.

He asks: "How is the occurrence of a specific cause [of this] possible? He replies: "Because a distinction is observed in all mental qualities (*caitoguṇa*). For even those qualities such as passion (*rāga*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), which function very slowly with respect to grasping their own objects, become more intense after some time. Furthermore, their respective objects become clearer; thus, a distinction is observed. But how does that [distinction] arise? He replies: 'From cultivation (*abhyāsa*), because a distinction in wisdom and the other qualities is perceived through that [cultivation].'"

[Objection: Let it be granted that there is an excellence [of qualities] through the practice of mental qualities such as wisdom (*prajñā*), since this is observed; however, since omniscience and the like have not been observed, how can they exist? To this, he says: "In the same way," and so forth. For other specific qualities, such as omniscience, are also possible. And because of the power of practice, when the aspect of selflessness and the conceptual cognition (*sāmānyavikalpa*) grasping all objects become vividly manifest, that itself is dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the state of omniscience (*sārvajñya*).

Therefore, there would be an inference of the impossibility of the distinctions of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and omniscience based on three modes: if conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the object of selflessness or regarding all objects were impossible; or, even if it were possible, if there were no distinction among the qualities of the mind; or, even if there were a distinction, if the cause of that distinction were not known. However, since conceptual construction regarding objects such as selflessness is indeed possible, and the cause of its distinction—namely, repeated practice—is known.

Therefore, just as when there is no deficiency in the causal conditions, one infers the capacity of this collection of causes, such as the seed, for the production of a sprout based on that capacity; likewise, when there is no deficiency in the causal conditions, it is possible for the knowledge whose object is selflessness—and which has all things as its object—to become clear due to a specific kind of practice that is continuous over a long period of time. Thus, there is an inference of the possibility of both dispassion and omniscience. Such, then, is our inference of possibility.

But when non-existence is to be inferred, there exists for you no reason that subverts that property [of being a person]. The connection is: "Because of its absence, men do not have reasons whose specific [concomitance] is impossible. But how is there an absence of a subverting [reason]? He says: "Because dispassion (*vairāgya*) is not observed. This is an elliptical expression, meaning also because an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) is not observed. And since a relationship of subverter and subverted between the reason and unobserved dispassion is not established.

It might be thought: "The impossibility of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth in [those who possess] speech and the like is not directly inferred—such that a subverting reason (*bādhaka-hetu*) would have to be sought—but rather, passion (*rāga*) and so forth are inferred in those who are considered to be free from passion. Once they have been so inferred, the object [of inference] is established; for even if dispassion is unseen, passion is in contradiction with it. To this he says: "Passion," etc. For there is no effect of passion and so forth that is non-deviant [from them]. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), non-omniscience is included.

For it is thus: beginning from the acquisition of linguistic convention, in proportion as there is thorough knowledge of an object, so too does the capacity for speech regarding that object arise. Therefore, if someone were to possess a cognition whose object is everything, who could prevent their capacity for speech from having that [entirety] as its object?

It might be argued: "If his excellence consists in characteristics such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth, why is it not perceived by us? To this he says: because even if those excellences characterized by dispassion and so forth were present, they cannot be seen in another's continuum (*parasantāna*). Nor can there be a rejection [of their existence] simply because such things are not perceived; to this he says: because such remote (*viprakarṣin*) things are not fit for rejection.

It might be argued that just as persons are not subject to refutation, so too are their statements; to this he replies: "Not so," and so forth. What is the reason? Because [the Veda] possesses observable distinctions. For it is held that the distinction of Vedic statements is indeed observable. Now, if it is not held—meaning, even if a distinction were admitted despite its being unobservable—there would be a contradiction in asserting that Vedic statements, which are distinguished by that unperceived distinction, belong to a different genus from worldly statements.

It might be thought: "The specific qualities of the Vedic [texts], such as being difficult to hear and difficult to pronounce, are indeed perceptible; therefore, they must be distinct from those [qualities] belonging to human compositions. To this, he says: "Of those specific qualities," and so forth. "Elsewhere" means in the case of human compositions. It is not only because it contradicts the acceptance of heterogeneity for unperceived specific qualities that the imperceptibility of these specific qualities is untenable; for this further reason as well: because there is a contradiction between the nature of what is perceived and the nature of what is unperceived. Indeed, two contradictory natures cannot coexist in a single entity.

If it is argued that the specific features (viśeṣāḥ) are indeed directly perceived, yet are not ascertained solely because of the presence of a cause for error—just as the potency of poison and the like is not perceived—he replies: "Because of the absence of a cause for error. For in the case of poison and such things, the perception of a similarity in form (*rūpasādharmya*) is the cause of error; this, however, does not exist in the case of Vedic [words]. If it is asked how this is known, he says: "Because of the absence of sublation (*bādhaka*), error is not established."

If, while no specific error regarding Vedic [words] is observed, a further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on their specific [nature] were to arise as a sublater of that error, then there would be certainty regarding the error and its cause; however, that does not exist. Therefore, when it is to be proven that Vedic [words] are non-distinct from worldly words, there is no proving means of valid cognition.

In that case, what is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding persons, by virtue of which there is a fault in attempting to prove the equality of all qualities? To this he says: "Regarding persons," and so forth. The very observation of excellence in the domain of wisdom and other qualities—which is preceded by practice—is itself the subverting argument. For if the mind of a person were such that detachment (*vairāgya*) were impossible, then no specific excellence could be produced through practice; yet such excellence does exist. Therefore, because the observation of such specific excellence acts as a subverting argument, [the case of persons] is not the same [as the case of the elements].

Regarding what was stated in the inference concerning Vedic statements—that there is an absence of a non-perceptible nature in words that are themselves perceptible—this fault would indeed arise if the particularity were of the nature of an intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*). However, [the author] says "of that which has become an extrinsic state" (*parabhāvabhūtasya*) because it is actually an extrinsic state (*parabhāva*). "Having gone to an extrinsic state" means having become an extrinsic state; the meaning is that it is of a different nature (*anyasvabhāva*). "Because it is not a particularity of that" (*atadviśeṣatvāt*) means because it is not a particularity of the sentence (*avākyaviśeṣatvāt*).

Since there is no distinction between these statements, therefore all of them—whether considered human or non-human—are of an undifferentiated nature; that is, they are produced by persons (*puruṣakriyā*), meaning they are created by persons (*puruṣaiḥ karaṇam*), or else, the meaning is that not even any worldly [statement] is not produced by a person.

Thus, having stated the contradiction with the treatises and the contradiction with valid cognition for one who—merely because the teacher [Dignāga] did not see it—desires the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the reason from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he speaks of the mutual inconsistency among the non-Buddhists (*atīrthika*), beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). "Earth-consciousness" (*mṛdacetanā*): this is the Lokāyata doctrine. "Self and earth-consciousness": this is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). From the word "etc. (*ādi*), substances such as milk and so forth are included.

Even though non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) has been stated by the opponent as a means to establish the non-existence of those [entities], it is held by the proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) and others not to be a prover of that non-existence, because mere non-apprehension is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*). Yet, if that very same non-apprehension is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge for negating the self and so forth, how could it prove the absence of the reason—that is, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the reason from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)? Furthermore, if this Vaiśeṣika and others were to rely upon non-apprehension as a means of knowledge regarding the absence of the reason, their doctrine of the self would become baseless and without support.

In this regard, because non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is possible as a means of proving non-existence: for indeed, there is no apprehension of the self (*ātman*) by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since its eternally imperceptible nature is accepted. Now, it might be argued that there is indeed apprehension of the self through inference (*anumāna*); to this he says: "its effect," and so forth. Precisely because the self is imperceptible, its mark (*liṅga*)—which would consist in the nature of its effects—is not ascertained; therefore, there is no apprehension [of the self] through inference.

If it is argued that just as there is inference for the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, even though they are always imperceptible (*nityaparokṣa*), so too will there be [inference] for the self (*ātman*), he says: "Of the sense faculties," and so on. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the seeds of memory (*smṛtibīja*) and the like are included. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone is the effect, because it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatva*). For instance, even when form (*rūpa*), light, and mental attention (*manaskāra*) are present, consciousness is absent in states such as when the eyes are closed; yet it arises again in states when the eyes are opened.

The effect of consciousness is established as depending upon other causes; therefore, by virtue of its establishment through such dependence, the existence of the sense faculties and so forth is asserted.

This is what is meant: that which this occasional cognition depends upon is inferred to be some cause of this cognition, and that very thing is designated as the "sense faculty" (*indriya*). However, it is not of such a nature that the sense faculty is inferred as being endowed with specific material qualities such as corporeality; this is the meaning. "In this way" means that the inference of the sense faculty occurs through the impossibility of explaining the occasional effect of cognition otherwise.

Likewise, the inference that "there exists some [entity] which has pleasure and so forth as its effect" does not support any point for the proponent of the self (*ātmavādin*), because it is established that such an entity is merely the nature of the self. This is because the proponents accept that pleasure and so forth possess a cause by means of some unspecified particular cause; yet the self is not of such a nature, since it is accepted as being characterized by eternal agency, enjoyership, and so forth. Furthermore, there is no effect-as-evidence (*kāryaliṅga*) for the self as it is thus accepted.

And this being the case, there would be only the non-apprehension of the self. Therefore, why has the proponent of the self (ātmavādin) been refuted—that is, rejected—by one who denies that self by means of that very non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of perception and inference? Since non-existence does not follow from mere non-apprehension, how could a reason that lacks a proof [of its negative concomitance] establish the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of reasons such as "possessing breath" and so forth from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)?

The Cārvākas maintain that consciousness is indeed the power of the primary elements (*bhūta*). Furthermore, since clay arises from the primary elements, the materialist (*lokāyatika*) asserts that consciousness exists even in clay, despite its being unperceived. As he says: "From those primary elements, consciousness arises—awareness is like the power of intoxication [in fermented grain]. Moreover, this is asserted on the basis of that very same lack of evidence, namely, non-perception (*anupalambha*).

He states the exclusion [of the reason] from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) regarding "non-perception" and so forth, which have been presented as logical marks (*liṅga*) to prove non-omniscience and other such qualities: "Even though curds and the like are not perceived in milk and the like, [one] desires them"—this refers again to that very same Sāṃkhya, who, having stated "The eyes and so forth are for the sake of another because they are composite," asserts the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by noting that "compositeness" is not observed in things that are not for the sake of another, such as a rabbit's horn. Thus, first of all, there is a mutual contradiction in this [position].

Nor is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason established by mere non-perception. For what necessity is there here that composite things must necessarily exist for the sake of another, such that—by the establishment of their being for another on the grounds of their being composites—the Sāṃkhya’s thesis of their being for the sake of the Self (*ātman*) would be proven? As for what was said—that curds and so forth are not perceived even within milk and so forth—that is not correct; because there is indeed perception of curds and so forth within milk and so forth. To the question "What is that [perception]?", he says: "Inference."

And he states the inference: "Because [the effect] does not arise from that which lacks the capacity. For if the capacity for curds and so forth did not exist in milk and so forth, then curds and so forth would not arise from that milk which lacks such capacity. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is not capable of producing something does not arise from it, just as a barley sprout does not arise from a rice seed; yet curds and so forth do arise from milk and so forth. Therefore, there exists in milk and so forth the capacity for curds and so forth. This is an argument by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) that resembles the "effect-reason" (*kārya-hetu*). And it is held that curds and so forth arise from the capacity itself, because of the non-difference between cause and effect.

"Then," and so forth, says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). Is that very entity which is subsequently perceived as curd and so forth the power (*śakti*), or is it something else entirely, a different object from the curd? If it were the former, then—just like the curd and other things whose forms are already accomplished—it would be perceived even during the state of milk, because there would be no difference [between the two states]. If, on the other hand, it is "something else"—that is, if the power is an object distinct from the curd and so forth—then how could another thing exist by means of the existence of something else called "power"? [In that case,] that curd and so forth would not exist.

This is the intended meaning: because of the capacity to produce curd and so forth, there would be a mere metaphorical designation of "curd" and so on for milk and the like. To disregard non-perception as a means of valid cognition and then, conversely, to accept that very same perception as a means of valid cognition—this is the mutual contradiction of these proponents of the self (ātmavādin) and others; such is the conclusion.

Since there is no distinct [entity] other than mere non-perception, therefore the connection consists of that alone. A nature that is connected with the mere existence of the reason, when intended as the probandum, would—by its own cessation—exclude the very thing that constitutes its own nature, which has been presented as the reason. The word "or" (vā) refers to the alternative to be mentioned later: just as a tree, when ceasing, excludes the *śiṃśapā* tree.

Why? Because it is well known that only a particular entity possessing branches and so forth is designated as "śiṃśapā. Therefore, that tree is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of what is called a śiṃśapā. How could an entity called a śiṃśapā exist by abandoning its own nature, which is the tree? What is the reason? Because the nature itself—the very essence of the tree—is the existence [of the śiṃśapā], since it has the form of a śiṃśapā.

For this reason, because of the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) of that probans which is its very nature—such as a *śiṃśapā* tree—with the nature intended as the probandum, such as "tree," there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) precisely because of the aforementioned kind of connection. The word "or" (*vā*) implies the phrase "the cause, while being withdrawn. The phrase "it would withdraw the effect" is the subject under discussion. Why? Because of non-deviation; the meaning is: because the effect does not deviate from its cause. He explains this with the words beginning with "the cause" (*kāraṇam*).

"Otherwise" means: if the effect were not to cease when the cause ceases, then that which is considered the effect would not truly be the effect of that cause at all. Therefore, the cause, in its cessation, necessarily brings about the cessation of the effect. Although smoke does not necessarily cease when the fire in a bedroom or similar location ceases, the meaning is that its production from anything other than its observed cause is not intended here. For this very reason, he says: "But it is established," and so forth.

Once the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established, it restricts the nature of the effect to the cause; that is, by making it non-deviant through the principle that "when [the cause] exists, [the effect] occurs, and when it does not exist, [the effect] does not occur. In both ways—either through identity (*tādātmya*) or through origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—it is precisely because of this essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) that the absence of the reason follows from the absence of the probandum.

"Otherwise" means if a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) were not established. [The opponent might argue: "By the cessation of one thing—the probandum (*sādhya*) which is not connected—there is the cessation of another. How could there be the cessation of the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*) which is unconnected? It could not be so. For instance, because a person is 'not possessing a horse' (i.e., devoid of a horse), it does not follow that he must be a mortal human; why not also be a cow-possessor? Likewise, by the presence of one thing, how could there be the presence of another probandum that is not essentially connected (*svabhāvena asambaddha*) to the reason? There would be no such presence. Why? Because..."

"Must one who possesses a cow necessarily also possess a horse? (p. 76) Since this is so, therefore, by virtue of a natural connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) alone—precisely because it is connected to the entity intended as the probandum—the reason brings about its own probandum; but not through a [mere] relation. This is because there is no relation residing in two terms (*dviṣṭhasambandha*) between cause and effect due to their non-simultaneity, nor between the pervaded and the pervader due to their identity. And that [natural connection] is the *svabhāvapratibandha*.

The "characteristic of the nature of that" means either characterized by the nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāva*) or characterized by its origination from it (*tadutpatti*). This very essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), known as inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), is demonstrated by means of examples based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

This is what is meant: the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is the apprehender of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because by that same [means] one grasps the dependence of the probans upon the probandum, and thus the absence [of the probans] when the probandum is absent is already grasped. It is merely that the means of valid cognition which apprehends their inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is shown by means of two examples because it has been forgotten. And since, through the manifestation of that very means of valid cognition, the absence of the probans in the absence of the probandum becomes certain via the recollection of the inseparable connection.

Therefore, in the case of a dissimilar example (vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta), a real substratum (dharmī) characterized as an effect or an essential nature—which would necessarily and invariably serve as the locus for this reason—is not accepted; however, in the case of the non-perception of an essential nature (svabhāvānupalambha), such a substratum is indeed accepted.

For in that case, the perception [of the reason] through its opposite must be demonstrated. What is the reason? Because the substratum (*āśraya*) is not accepted, he says: "And in the absence of that," and so forth. In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the cause (*kāraṇa*)—the mark (*liṅga*) called the "effect" which is pervaded by them does not exist; thus, even from the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), which is devoid of a substratum, there is the comprehension of that [reason], namely, the comprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). (||28||)

What is the reason? "Because," and so forth. In the case of an essential identity (*svabhāva-hetu*), the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*)—that is, its being pervaded by the probans—is made known. In the case of an effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*), the state of being the cause (*hetubhāva*) of the probandum—that is, its causality—is explained. "To one who does not know that" refers to a person who does not know that state of existence [of the probandum] or that state of being the cause [of the probandum].

He explains this with the words "For those [properties] have been seen," and so forth. The fact that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has that nature—that is, its being of the same essence as the probans (*sādhanasvabhāvatva*)—is made known through its necessary connection to that alone; that is, through its necessary connection to the probans alone. Since impermanence is established precisely at the time the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is established, its being of that nature—that is, its being of the same essence as the probans—is due to its necessary connection to the mere state of being produced. It is by means of such a [nature] that its having that nature is made known, and not by means of an impermanence that arises later from some other cause.

Regarding the phrase "just as some are mistaken," he says "who" and so forth, demonstrating that [the reason] possesses only that [essential property]. The meaning is: whatever reason produces a produced thing (*kṛtaka*) by its very nature, it produces it as something that is necessarily impermanent. By this means, the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is made known through an example; it is not merely a matter of observation. "Otherwise" means if such valid cognition is not demonstrated; then, from the existence of a single property—that is, from the existence of the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma*).
Since there is no rule that it must also be accompanied by some other property to be proven (sādhyadharma), there would be a suspicion that the probans deviates from the probandum (sādhyavyabhicāra).

Even if a proof is indeed to be demonstrated by means of an example, what is established thereby? To this he says: "By that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is an invariable concomitance with that alone," meaning an invariable concomitance with the mere fact of being produced (*sādhanamātrānubandha*). How is this made known? He says: "Whatever is the cause of the produced, from that very [cause] the produced is so born; that which is born is perishable, having the property of abiding for only a moment. The meaning is that it is perishable precisely by virtue of its momentariness, and not after having endured for another period of time.

But how is it that it has arisen in such a way from its own cause alone? He says: "from another," meaning from a cause of destruction other than its own cause. This is because its existence as such is denied—that is, its nature as impermanent is denied—as will be explained later. The connection [of the sentence] is: "nor is the state of being a cause for it established by a means of valid cognition."

The fact that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) stands in the relation of being a cause (*hetubhāva*) or a reason (*kāraṇatva*) toward the means of proof (*sādhana*) is explained by the principle that the means of proof exists only when that [property] exists; in this manner, the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is demonstrated by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To the question, "Of what [property] to be proven is the causal status demonstrated? he replies: "Of another object (*arthāntara*), namely, that which is distinct from the means of proof. Thus, when the state of being that [property] and the state of being its cause have been established by the valid cognition shown through the example.

When the nature of the probandum is established as being that [same] nature, and when the cause is established as being the nature of the probans—meaning, when the causal relationship is established—the connection with the context is: "In the absence of fire, smoke does not exist. The word "that" (*sa*) refers to the fire which has impermanence as its nature. Of that [fire] and of the smoke, respectively, there is the nature or the cause; the word "and" (*ca*) signifies a conjunction.

Since this is so, how could that smoke, which is a product, exist without its own nature—impermanence—and its cause—fire? It could not exist at all. Thus, when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated in the form of an unindicated subject, the negative concomitance is established even in the absence of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Therefore, as it was said by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara:
"The negative concomitance of the mark is indeed obtained from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)."

"The claim that 'it would not be understood even by those who have exerted effort because of a lack of understanding' has been refuted. Thus, for the sake of making known the existence of that [object] and its causal status to one who does not know it, an example must be stated."

Furthermore, for those for whom the presence [of the probandum] and the causal status [of the reason] are already established—just as their being mere properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) have been ascertained by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—the reason is indeed sufficient for those wise ones regarding that presence and causal status. For what purpose? It is for the sake of ascertaining the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Since that object is already established for the person to be convinced (*pratipādya*) by himself, what is the use of stating it? "At that time" refers to the time when the positive and negative concomitance have been ascertained.

Even when an example is presented for the sake of a deluded person, there is a lack of correspondence (*vaidharmya*) even in that presentation of the example; for the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established by the aforementioned method even without a substratum (*āśraya*). Therefore, thinking, "What is the use of relying on an example as a substratum?", the Master rejects the substratum in works such as the *Nyāyamukha*.

For it is objected in that very context: "If the opponent then accepts that space and so forth are eternal, how can there be the exclusion of 'being produced' from what is eternal? To this, the Master, rejecting the [invalid] locus (*āśraya*), says: "In that case, there is no doubt at all, because [the reason] does not occur there due to the absence of that [locus]."

This is what is meant: for one who has grasped the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is established there—in space and so forth—due to the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). And the absence of the non-eternal is established because the eternal is non-existent; such is the sense. Since the necessary connection is stated by means of two examples, for that reason, when the logical reason (*hetu*) has its relation known, it follows from the statement of either one of the two examples, whether of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

Even in the second case, even if only one of those two is not stated, recollection arises through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Connecting this also with the words of the Master (*ācārya*), he says: "As it has been said," and so forth. This passage is from the *Nyāyamukha*. Therein, the word "or" (*vā*) refers back to the preceding alternative. "By either one" means by the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) or by the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). "From the demonstration of both" means from the demonstration of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). This is also in that same treatise.

Thinking that, in the case of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*) and the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*), the demonstration of the presence of the effect when the cause is present and the presence of the cause when the effect is present is being made respectively by him [the opponent], the Master, by means of an implication (*arthāpatti*), states the proof of the second—respectively the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) or the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—through the statement of one, whether it be the positive or the negative concomitance. He says exactly this with the words: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

When it is stated that "whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent," it is clearly ascertained by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that this property called impermanence is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that which is produced, and that it is invariably concomitant with it—that is, it is invariably concomitant with mere production.

[Objection: But surely a cause is also invariably present in its effect, yet that [cause] is not the nature of [the effect]. To this he says: "not a different thing" (*anarthāntara*). How is it invariably concomitant with that? He says: "because of the necessity of its existence" (*tadbhāvaniyamāt*). The meaning is: because whenever there is the state of being produced, there is necessarily the state of being impermanent.

Now, is it not the case that the nature of impermanence—which is invariably concomitant with being produced—is not ascertained by perception, since there is no certainty that "this is momentary"? Therefore, how can it be said to be "seen through a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇadṛṣṭa*)? If you argue that it is "seen through inference" because a produced thing is necessarily subject to destruction due to its independence regarding [the cause of] destruction, that is incorrect. For even if destruction were causeless, it would only be causeless at the very moment the destruction of a jar or the like is perceived, and not at other times. So how could there be momentariness? Or, if [you claim] that the jar's destruction exists even prior to its arising because it persists for only a single moment—

Now, one might object: just as there is production from its own causes with the property of persisting for only a single moment, so too there could be production with the property of persisting for multiple moments; for causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) are observed to possess diverse potencies. Furthermore, if destruction were to occur only occasionally or at some particular time, then because it would depend on that specific time and substance, its independence would be lost. [On the other hand,] because it does not depend on a cause of destruction, otherwise—[if it did depend on such a cause]—destruction would not occur even in the second moment, since it would depend on that time and so forth.

Now, existence characterized by causal efficiency is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity; and since succession and simultaneity are excluded from eternal things, existence, being excluded [from them], remains only in momentary things. Thus, the property of being produced, which is conjoined with existence, possesses the capacity to prove [momentariness].

That too is incorrect. If [all things] were momentary, there could be no apprehension of succession; for the very same moment of cognition that apprehends the prior object does not apprehend the subsequent one, and that which apprehends the subsequent one does not apprehend the prior one. How, then, can there be an apprehension of succession? Only one who apprehends a subsequent object immediately after the apprehension of the prior object could be a perceiver of succession, and if that were so, he would have to be momentary. Furthermore, for that Buddhist for whom time itself does not exist, how can there be an apprehension of succession?

Because objects at different times are not perceived [as distinct], and in the absence of time, succession is nothing other than the form of multiple objects; thus, even for that which is eternal, its status as an agent of succession is not contradictory. Just as an eternal entity possesses multiplicity of form due to its agency of succession, so too it would be for a momentary entity. Alternatively, if—as in the case of a moment—there were non-existence of the eternal entity in a second moment due to the absence of an effect, [then it would be momentary].

That is incorrect because time does not exist. Or, even if there were a perception of succession, how could existence be pervaded by both succession and simultaneity? For causal efficacy is possible through another mode besides succession and simultaneity. Nor can the non-existence of another mode be ascertained simply because it is not perceived among perceptible things; for if that were so, the ascertainment of non-existence would occur only in specific places and times, and not at all times. Furthermore, the ascertainment of non-existence cannot result from the non-perception of an imperceptible thing, because of the resulting doubt.

Therefore, Śaṅkara and others argue: "Even if succession and simultaneity are incompatible with permanent entities, since existence does not cease [in them], how can existence have momentary nature as its essence?

Or, even if existence were pervaded by succession and simultaneity because no other mode is possible, nevertheless, the incompatibility of succession and simultaneity in permanent entities is not established by perception or other means, because permanent entities are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). And if that [incompatibility] is unestablished, then the cessation of existence in those [permanent entities] is not established; and if that is unestablished, there is no proof that existence has momentary nature as its essence.

Furthermore, from existence (*sattva*), there would be an inference of succession and simultaneity, because [existence] is pervaded by those very two; however, there is no inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) therein, because the capacity for successive agency is impossible. To this it is replied: succession and simultaneity are indeed established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For simultaneity is the coexistence of entities, whereas succession is their state of being prior and posterior. And that [succession] belongs to successive [entities], which are non-different; its manifestation is a single manifestation. However, that single manifestation is followed by the manifestation of another; it is a manifestation of succession, not of a single [entity], because otherwise there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the definition].

True. Even in that case, when there is an appearance of one [moment], there is not [an appearance] of the other; for if it were present, there would be a simultaneous appearance. Therefore, when two successive [moments] are grasped by two cognitions—the preceding and the succeeding—the succession is indeed grasped, because they are non-different. It is merely established as the "grasping of succession" through the arising of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the sequence—such as "this follows immediately after that"—by means of the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the previously experienced object.

Even if successive [moments] are perceived, since no conceptualization of a sequence arises in any way, it is established that there is no perception of a sequence; for this very reason, even when a single [successive thing] is perceived, it is said that there is no perception of a sequence.

Furthermore, how could there be a perception of a sequence even for one who asserts the existence of time? Because all effects would exist at a single time. If it is argued that the sequence of effects arises from the sequence of the limiting conditions (upādhi) of causes belonging to different times, that is incorrect, because time is unitary. For this very reason, there is no such thing as an eternal entity.
If it is argued that time possesses a sequence because it has a prior and posterior form, [the response follows].

Now, if even that [time] possesses a sequence, then there would be an infinite regress if it were dependent on another time. Alternatively, if its sequence exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then a sequence would likewise belong to many effects that are devoid of auxiliary causes. For us, however, time—which has the great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its object—is indeed well-known in the world as the referent of notions such as "prior" and so forth. And because of its differentiation, the perception of sequence and so on is perfectly logical. Furthermore, the status of being an agent for an eternal entity is not possible through any other means.

For, if it were to produce a single effect or multiple effects by means of another mode at one time, it would follow that it is non-existent at other times due to the absence of an effect. Furthermore, if it produces the effect repeatedly, there is no possibility of another mode [of action]. Alternatively, if it does not produce the effect by another mode at one time, nor does it produce it repeatedly, then it would be non-existent, because it is never a producer.

Therefore, since a jar or similar object is established by perception as performing purposeful action through either successive or simultaneous means, and because it is recognized as "this is that very same thing," it is indeed perceived as non-momentary. Furthermore, when its capacity for producing a particular effect exists, it exists at that very time, neither before nor after, because that effect is absent [at those other times]. And this capacity is non-different from the entity itself; the same should be understood regarding the production of each subsequent effect.

And because there is a distinction in categories (*padārtha*) due to the difference in causal capacity (*sāmarthya*), the restriction of succession and simultaneity applies only to the momentary. Therefore, wherever there is existence (*sattva*), even when succession and simultaneity are perceived, there is necessarily the perception of momentariness. This very restriction of succession and simultaneity that applies to the momentary is precisely what constitutes their impossibility in eternal things. Consequently, it is stated that the eternity perceived in things such as a jar is contradicted by existence; thus, the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) with respect to both succession and simultaneity for an eternal entity is established.

Just as existence (*sattva*) is pervaded by momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) in the case of perceived objects such as jars, so too it is in the case of unperceived objects because there is no distinction [between them]; having thus apprehended the pervasion through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), one determines their existence, and accordingly, there is the inference of their momentariness. However, if their existence were not determined, then—due to the suspicion that they might be non-existent like a rabbit's horn—there would be no cognition of their momentariness. Nor is the inference redundant in that case either, because momentariness is established therein precisely by a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).

For a person who has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is understood by the mere ascertainment of existence; therefore, the raising of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) would be futile. This method of grasping the pervasion has been explained in detail in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, and thus it should be understood from that very source.

However, those who—having established that momentariness pervades existence everywhere through the non-existence [of anything] contrary to existence—thereby infer momentariness from existence itself, for them there would be no arising of an inference at all; because momentariness would already be established everywhere through the very act of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the subject (*dharmin*) is not established, since the entire threefold world is not perceptible, and the reason (*hetu*) is likewise unestablished.

Furthermore, if the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) were established for the entire subject (*dharmin*) under consideration by virtue of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), then, because the probandum (*sādhya*) would also be established, there would be no arising of the inference. Moreover, since no other subject is established, how could a subverting proof operate? This argument is trivial. Therefore, it is established that this property called momentariness is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of "producedness" as qualified by existence, and is necessarily concomitant with it alone; or else, the intrinsic nature of this momentariness is necessarily concomitant with "producedness" alone, as perceived by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Alternatively, even for a reason such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) that is not qualified by the term "existent," there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) when proving momentariness. For if the very same nature (*svabhāva*) that exists in the first moment were also present in the second moment, then it would be a case of "coming into being after having not existed," just as in the first moment; and from that, momentariness follows. Or, if in the first moment there is only the birth of the produced thing and no persistence, while in the second moment there is only persistence and no birth—even so, momentariness would result.

Because there is no difference between birth and that which is born, nor between duration and that which endures. Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be duration in the second moment without birth. If there is birth, then there is no duration, because duration occurs only from the second moment onward. Since this applies everywhere—namely, that there is only arising and no duration—it follows that things are indeed momentary.
