And since arising is produced by causes, it is precisely there that "being produced" (kṛtakatva) resides, not in duration. Therefore, because being produced is contradictory with non-momentariness, the reason is not inconclusive.

The pervasion of this "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) by "momentariness" has been explained in detail in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. Consequently, even though producedness is not included within [the category of] existence (*sattva*), its pervasion is seen through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus he says: "Its nature is necessarily concomitant with that alone, as it is seen by valid cognition, because of the necessity of its being so; for when there is the state of being produced, there is the necessity of the state of impermanence."

Thus, for a person who knows that state—that which is produced is non-eternal—there arises, through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the certainty that "in the absence of non-eternality, there is no production," because for one who possesses such knowledge, production cannot exist in the absence of its own nature, which is non-eternality; for production would then be identical to that [non-eternality]. What is the reason? Because of the non-difference between the probandum and the probans. "Otherwise" means if production were to exist even in the absence of non-eternality.

In that case, there would not necessarily be the realization that "in the absence of that [permanence], the absence of being produced entails impermanence. The word "tathā" (likewise) connects with what is to be said later: just as there is an understanding of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) in an application based on similarity (*sādharmya*), so too there arises a recollection of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in an application based on dissimilarity. "In the absence of that" means when it is stated that "in the absence of permanence, being produced does not necessarily exist. From that very application of dissimilarity, for a person who understands the presence of that [property]—that is, for a person who understands that the probans has the nature of the probandum—[the recollection of concomitance occurs].

If it is asked, "How does it indicate that [the probans] has that as its nature? he says: "For instance," and so forth. This property called impermanence is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of this produced thing (*kṛtakatva*), because in the absence of that [impermanence], producedness would not exist. "Otherwise" means: if impermanence were not the nature of the produced, then in the absence of that [impermanence], producedness would not exist; since this [consequence] is impossible, for this reason, through the realization that [producedness] has that as its nature—and thus through the realization that producedness has impermanence as its nature—there occurs the recollection of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

This is what is meant: the very existence of the reason in the probandum itself is its non-existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); thus, there is identity between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), as well as their mutual pervasion (*anyonyavyāpti*). Therefore, through the cognition of positive concomitance in the reason, there is the cognition of negative concomitance, and through the cognition of negative concomitance, there is the cognition of positive concomitance; this is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). Consequently, the statement [from the *Nyāyamañjarī*]: "For Kīrti, who accepts [the force of implication], the restriction to two [types of concomitance] is not lost," is refuted.

Alternatively, this is not a means of valid cognition at all; rather, there is no fault in the fact that a single sentence, employed either through the method of agreement (*anvaya*) or the method of difference (*vyatireka*), conveys both [meanings] solely by virtue of convention (*saṃketa*).

Having explained the two-fold comprehension through the application of either [the positive or negative concomitance] in the case of the essential nature as the reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he says "likewise," etc., regarding the effect as the reason (*kāryahetu*). By the word "where" (*yatra*), which is a pronoun, there is a universal inclusion; when it is stated that "fire is necessarily present there," from this very statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the certainty arises that smoke is the effect of fire. What is the reason? Because fire is necessarily present where there is smoke. Otherwise, if fire were not the cause of the smoke, then—since fire would be a different entity—there would be no necessary connection (*anubandhaniyama*) between it and the smoke.

In smoke, there is no necessary connection (*anubandha*), because there is an absence of a rule (*niyama*) regarding its pervasion (*vyāpti*). Consequently, the entity that is the nature of smoke would possess independence (*svātantrya*). Therefore, due to this independence, even in the absence of fire, there would be no non-existence of the nature of smoke, because its deficiency [would not follow]; yet such is not the case. Thus, smoke must be accepted as an effect. For when smoke is admitted as an effect, the cause—fire—necessarily exists therein. This [point] is precisely what is meant by the word "this" (*idam*).

"Existence when there is another thing" means that when the [thing] considered to be the effect exists, there is the imposition of its own nature—that is, the presentation of its essential form. For the effect as well, "existence when that exists" means existence precisely when the cause exists; this is what constitutes being an effect. And this state of existing only when the cause exists is present in smoke. Therefore, for a person who has recognized through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that smoke is the effect of fire in this way, it follows by implication that "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist."

Now, he explains the understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), beginning with "In the same way" (*tathā*) and so forth. When it is stated that "where there is no fire, smoke does not exist," from this statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), for one who has recognized smoke as the effect of that [fire], the understanding of positive concomitance arises by implication in this manner: "wherever there is smoke, fire necessarily exists."

Otherwise, if it were not stated through the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) that smoke is the effect of fire, then in the absence of that—namely, in the absence of fire—the certainty of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), namely that "smoke would certainly not exist," could not occur. Therefore, this is established: when there is a distinct entity, that which necessarily does not exist in the absence of another is the effect of that other; and thus, from the statement of negative concomitance, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is understood.

On this point, the opponent states an objection: "But surely," and so forth. [The argument is that] the effect of both the eternal and the non-eternal would be an effect of an eternal or non-eternal object; its existence (*tadbhāva*) constitutes its essential nature (*tattva*), yet even in the absence of that [nature], it is not known whether auditory cognition is the effect of an existent sound—since it is a specific property of sound alone—or rather the effect of something non-eternal. Thus, [the reason] is inconclusive.

Consequently, the cognition arising from hearing (*śravaṇajñāna*) has neither the eternal as its object-nature nor the non-eternal as its object-nature; nevertheless, that cognition does not arise when those [objects] are absent—that is, when both eternal and non-eternal objects are absent. This means it is excluded by their absence. To explain: first, it does not arise in the absence of an eternal object, because it is absent in non-eternal things such as jars and the like. Furthermore, it does not arise even in the absence of the non-eternal, because it is absent in eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like. "It is certainly not the case that it does not arise," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*).

It is not possible to understand that audibility does not exist in the absence of permanence; rather, if there were the certainty that it exists through the absence of that [impermanence], then it would necessarily be its effect. However, there is no such thing as "it does not exist in the absence of that. Why? Because from that audibility, there remains doubt regarding those two very states: permanence and impermanence.

Otherwise, since audibility has been ascertained as being absent from both permanent and impermanent entities, how could there be doubt regarding sound through the consideration of its presence? Therefore, there is indeed no exclusion of audibility from both the permanent and the impermanent.

To the question, "How then is it said that audibility does not exist in either the permanent or the impermanent because it is unique (asādhāraṇa)? he says: "But only," and so forth. Because there is no ascertainment of the existence of audibility among permanent or impermanent things, it is said that audibility does not exist in the permanent or the impermanent.

Now, Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara argue: "If audibility were observed in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) when impermanence and so forth are to be proven, then there would be doubt regarding sound because of its audibility, just as there is from the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*). But this [audibility] is not observed in either the similar or the dissimilar instances; therefore, it results in non-comprehension (*apratipatti*). Alternatively, it might be argued that the entity "sound" is sometimes permanent and sometimes impermanent, and audibility is a property of that entity; therefore, doubt is said to arise concerning sound.

That is incorrect; for in that case, it would be the nature of the object itself (*vastudharmatva*) that serves as the cause of doubt, not audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*). To this it is replied: If it were established that wherever there is audibility, there is the absence of both the permanent and the impermanent, then there would be no cognition of the permanent or the impermanent. However, since audibility is absent in things such as jars—which are joined with impermanence and so forth—it follows that sound is absent [from those things]. Therefore, because of its audibility, there is indeed doubt regarding it.

But surely, audibility consists in the capacity for auditory cognition, and a permanent entity lacks such capacity because it is contradictory to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); so how can there be doubt on this basis? For [audibility] would result in the certain determination of impermanence alone.

He thinks as follows: if the mere capacity [to produce cognition] were the reason (*hetu*), then that would simply be existence (*sattva*); thus, there would be no fault, because that [existence] is common to both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar ones. The same should be understood regarding [reasons] such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*). Now, if the reason is that capacity which [belongs] toward the cognition of hearing, and that is not established as being pervaded by impermanence anywhere, how could impermanence be established from it? Because it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), this very sound is established as being pervaded by impermanence.

For by that very same subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), impermanence is established therein; thus, audibility would be redundant. In this way, one should understand the non-informativeness of those reasons which are "over-exclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*).

Therefore, this is established: in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the relationship of cause and effect between the probandum and the probans must be stated by means of two examples; it is not merely a matter of observation and non-observation. For in this way, through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), the cognition of the second [term] would arise from one [term]; otherwise, it would not. Thus he says: "But when... and so forth. In that case, there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) at all—namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—because of the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

And when positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself is not established, how then can there be an establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by implication, such as "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist"? Likewise, since mere non-observation is what is being indicated through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum is not established; how, then, could there be a recollection of positive concomitance by means of that? "As stated" refers to the characteristics of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). When one [of these] exists—that is, when the mark consisting of an effect or an essential nature (*svabhāva*) exists—for the sake of establishing the other: for the sake of establishing the cause by means of the mark of the effect, and for the sake of establishing the essential nature by means of the mark of the essential nature.
In the absence of that—that is, when the aforementioned necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is absent—it is impossible for one thing to be established through the existence of another.

(30) "The absence of the cause's own nature" refers both to the absence of the cause itself and to the absence of the nature of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). For this reason—namely, from the cause just mentioned—the logical reason (*hetu*, i.e., the *liṅga*) [is employed] for the negation of an effect or of that which is pervaded, and by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), also for the establishment of the conventional usage of negation (*pratiṣedhavyavahāra*) as the probandum (*sādhya*).

What is the reason? Because those very two—the cause and the pervader—when present, exclude their own dependent effect and their own nature; thus, by one who wishes to establish the negation of some object, whether it be an effect or a pervaded [property], the cessation of the cause or the pervader must be stated as the logical reason (*hetu*). By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is also established. Why is this so? Because, as the passage beginning with "for if there is no necessary connection" (*apratibandhe hi*) indicates, [the exclusion of the cause or pervader would not otherwise be possible].

The meaning is that there is no other obstacle besides those two. "Yukta" means logical or appropriate; thus, the sense is "of that which is perceptible. And regarding the phrase "of that," the non-perception of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the probans for negation. This is not a probans for negation itself, but rather it is called a "probans for negation" because it is the cause of the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that constitutes the object of that negation.

What is the reason? It is because the probans for negation—namely, the non-apprehension of such [an object] which is perceptible—is itself of the nature of a negation. The probans consists of both the non-apprehension of the cause and the non-apprehension of the pervader. "Of both" refers to the negation itself and the conventional usage of negation. (31)

Thus, this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), though briefly stated as threefold, is further stated in many ways, just as it was previously divided into eight types in this very context. To the question "In what manner?", he says: "That which is opposed to each of those" (*tattadviruddha*), and so forth. By the word "that" (*tat*), the triad of essential nature (*svabhāva*), cause (*kāraṇa*), and pervader (*vyāpaka*) under discussion is grasped. Opposed to that triad—essential nature and the rest—the "opposed" (*viruddha*) is likewise threefold, consisting of the divisions of the opposed to essential nature, the opposed to the cause, and the opposed to the pervader.

That which has "the contradictory" as its beginning is "that which begins with the contradictory" (*tadviruddhādi*). By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the effect of the contradictory (*viruddhakārya*) and the effect of that which is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakārya*) is intended. "Of those" refers to *tadviruddhādi*. "The non-comprehension and comprehension of those two" means the non-comprehension of that [the probandum] and the comprehension of that which begins with the contradictory. The distinction between these two constitutes the difference in formulation; therefore, it is stated in many ways due to this difference in formulation.

In that regard, by way of the non-perception of the [object] itself, three non-perceptions are subsumed: non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). By way of the perception of what is contradictory to it, there are likewise three: perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), perception of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*), and perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). By the word "etcetera," one should include the perception of the effect of the contradictory (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*) and the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*). In this manner, there is a summary of the eightfold non-perception previously mentioned.

With the words "Indeed, it is of three kinds," etc., he states the meaning of the verse: the connection is that "the non-apprehension of a reason whose existence is capable of being apprehended" (upalabhyasattva) means [the non-apprehension] of a reason that is fit for apprehension. The phrase "whose existence is capable of being apprehended" also applies to the pervader and to one's own self. The connection is that this threefold reason for negation is said to be of many types according to its formal application (prayoga). To the question "In what way is it according to formal application?", he says: "by way of the formal application of the distinctions between the non-comprehension and comprehension of those respective contradictories and so forth."

This very point is analyzed by the passage beginning with "by the non-perception of its arrival" (*tasyāgatyā*) and so forth. "By the non-perception of its arrival" means by the non-perception of its own nature, its cause, or its pervader (*svabhāva-kāraṇa-vyāpakānupalabdhi*). "By the perception of what is incompatible with it" means by the perception of what is incompatible with its own nature, its cause, or its pervader (*svabhāva-kāraṇa-vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). "By the perception of an effect incompatible [with it]" means by the perception of an effect incompatible [with it] (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*). The phrase "by such various types of formal applications" (*ityādibhedaprayogaiḥ*) refers to the various formal applications such as the perception of an effect incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), and so on, as was stated previously in the investigation of the divisions of non-perception (*anupalabdhiprabhedacintā*) [in verse 1.6]. (32)

Since it is thus a signifier by virtue of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), therefore: either through the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which is the restrictive factor that establishes the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between the probandum and the probans; or through the essential nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), which is the restrictive factor. The meaning is that the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the mark—whether it be an effect or an essential nature—does not exist without the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Furthermore, there is no inseparable concomitance with the probandum for an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, because it is a cause of doubt.

If, however, there were such inseparable concomitance, then since the probandum would already be established in that subject (*dharmin*) by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determines that concomitance, how could this [uncommon reason] function as a signifier?
Therefore, that which is stated by that venerable teacher [is as follows].
The term *avinābhāva* (inseparable relation) also encompasses all possible meanings;
it does not, for us, bring about the apprehension of a relationship suitable for inference.
If that which is an inseparable relation is not subsequently distinguished [from other cases],
then it would exist even in the case of the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason], and thus it would be no cause [for certainty].
"For that which is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) has been made one's own by that [subject] alone;
it follows that the reason would be reduced to a fallacy (*prasajyate*) because it is known only as 'it does not exist without [the probandum]'.

This is refuted. For "inseparability" (*avinābhāva*) itself is the restriction (*niyama*), since it is understood as "it does not exist without the probandum. If this is so, for what purpose is the term "restriction" (*niyama*) mentioned again? True; it is for the sake of refuting the opinion of others. For he [the opponent] desires a restriction other than inseparability. As Bhaṭṭa said:
Thus, having refuted the relations asserted by others,
the relation called "restriction" (niyama) is now stated according to our own view.
There are two possible courses for relations such as that of cause and effect: they may be either restricted or unrestricted. Of these, only restriction serves as a basis for inference.
All these non-restrictions (aniyama) are indeed not the cause for the arising of inference;
for nothing whatsoever fails to be inferred solely on account of restriction (niyama).
Therefore, it is determined that the relation here is exclusively one of necessity (niyama); it is intended as the relation of the indicator alone with the indicated, as was previously established.

"The cognition of the members that necessitate [a conclusion] regarding those possessing such members is an inference, based on the correct recollection of the rule through the observation of a single member"— this has been refuted.

In the absence of a relationship such as that of cause and effect, there could be no restriction at all, because for things that are unconnected, there is no necessity of coexistence. Furthermore, since mere paleness and the like are not the effects of fire, and since a logical mark (*liṅga*) functions as a means of cognition only in dependence on place, time, and so forth, how can it be said that there are only two ways [of establishing a relationship] even when the relationship of cause and effect exists?

Now, it might be argued: even by one who accepts relations such as the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), as long as the restriction of the probans (*sādhana*) to the probandum (*sādhya*) is not ascertained, that [relation] is not a factor for the cognition of the probandum; therefore, even though the causal relation exists, it is only this [restriction] that is accepted as the relation, because only that is a factor for cognition. To express that, it is said: "That alone is a member of inference (*anumāna*); the others are merely causes for its manifestation."

That is incorrect. For restriction (*niyama*) is precisely dependence upon that [the cause]; and that [dependence] has as its very nature identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*). Therefore, the ascertainment of restriction is nothing other than the ascertainment of identity and origination; it is not, however, an ascertainment of restriction through observation and non-observation, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [Objection:

But surely, just as there is deviation regarding the ascertainment of restriction in the case of observation and non-observation, so too would there be deviation in the ascertainment of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

That is incorrect, because it is accepted that the determination of the causal relation occurs precisely through two specific instances of observation and non-observation; and this very point will be stated right here. Furthermore, as for what Umveka says: "When smoke is observed in fire hundreds of times, a cognition of necessity arises—'This smoke is invariably present in fire'—due to its otherwise being impossible (*anyathānupapatti*). In this case, the observation of smoke in [what is not] fire would be a sublater (*bādhaka*), but since such does not exist, there is the necessity of smoke in fire."

That is incorrect. For if there were no causal relationship (*kāryakāryatva*) [between smoke and fire], then the observation of smoke in the absence of fire would be a mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which as a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) cannot constitute a sublation. Since smoke might thus be suspected of existing even in the absence of fire, how could there be a necessary restriction (*niyama*) of smoke to fire? Therefore, it is established that [the restriction is possible] only through a restrictive factor consisting either in the relation of cause and effect or in essential identity (*svabhāva*).

The rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvaniyama*) is established through the ascertainment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth; it is not [established] from non-observation, nor from observation. The rule of invariable concomitance is not ascertained merely from the non-observation of the reason in the absence of the probandum. Nor is it from observation; that is, it is not from the observation of the coexistence of the probandum and the probans.
Therefore, the invariable concomitance of one thing with another thing is due solely to its arising from that (*tadutpatti*).

Otherwise—that is, if there were no production from that [cause]—what necessary connection (*avaśyambhāvaniyama*) could there be between the mark (*liṅga*), which is not the self of the other, and those things intended by others as the probandum (*sādhya*)? However, if the mark is not a separate entity (*anarthāntara*), then the property to be proven must be admitted to be invariably concomitant with that [mark] alone; otherwise, if one were to admit that impermanence has as its cause something other than the cause of "being produced"—such as the cause of belching and so forth—then what necessary connection would there be to that property? It would be like a dye on a cloth.
The redness that arises subsequently, caused by saffron and other dyes, once the cloth has been finished. (33, 34)

In this regard, just as there is no rule of necessity [regarding the production of the effect], so too, if impermanence were intended to have a cause that is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), not only would this fault [apply], but another fault as well; thus he says, "Moreover," and so forth. There would be a distinct property called "permanence" caused by something other [than the produced thing]; for it would be different from that which constitutes its own nature, such as being "produced. This is because, if one accepts that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has a cause that is a distinct entity, two things are entailed: the non-production [of the property] despite the completion of the proof (*sādhana*), and the fact of having a different cause.

And this is not possible without a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). For it is not logical that when that probans (*sādhana*) has its intrinsic nature established, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—if it were unestablished or possessed of a different cause—could have that same intrinsic nature. It is indeed logical for a previously established mark (*liṅga*) to have a different cause as its intrinsic nature; for this is precisely what is recognized in the world as the difference between entities: the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), which is the conjunction with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmayoga*).

In this context, accomplishment and non-accomplishment are two contradictory properties. Furthermore, that which is the cause of differentiation—the differentiation of causes, namely the differentiation of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—is to be understood here as the cause of differentiation. By this, both the nature of differentiation and the cause of differentiation have been explained.

The appearance of difference, however, is the grasper of difference. If those two—the causes of the superimposition of contradictory properties—are not themselves differentiated from the object, then no entity would have any difference from any other object; consequently, the entire world would be a single substance. If it is argued that unity is indeed accepted for everything because there is no distinction in the three *guṇas*, the author replies: "And therefore," due to this oneness, there would be simultaneous arising and destruction.

The meaning is that upon the arising of one thing, there would be the arising of all, and upon its destruction, the destruction of all. Furthermore, every cause would have utility as a cause for every effect. This is because [you] do not admit simultaneous arising and so forth. Consequently, it would not even be the case that "all things are one. Now, if a mutually distinct nature is accepted through differences such as utility and so on, this would either be a different name for those very distinctions, or it would be the application of the designation "one" to many things. What is the reason? Because, having admitted that objects are mutually distinct, you nevertheless designate them as such; that is, by using the designation "one."

Now, it might be argued: "Impermanence is the connection with existence occurring between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). And this [impermanence] is indeed already established at the time of the production of the produced thing; it is merely that, having perished, it is not manifested at a later time. That too is incorrect. For as long as subsequent non-existence has not arisen, how can there be an impermanence existing in the interval? Even when subsequent non-existence has arisen, how could this [impermanence] exist in the interval? Or else, the nature of being produced would belong to the entity itself, since [impermanence] is non-existent.

The opponent begins with "nanu" and so forth. [He argues: Even if non-momentariness (*anityatā*) has a cause that is not a different entity (*anarthāntara-hetutva*), and even if it does not depend on a cause of destruction according to your own view, [non-momentariness] would not be established during the time of the entity's existence; for non-momentariness is not established while the entity exists. Therefore, he considers that non-momentariness comes into being at a time subsequent to the entity. [The response is: This lack of its own nature (*atatsvabhāvatā*) is the same [in both cases]. Just as there would be establishment [of non-momentariness] even if it had a cause that is a different entity, so too, since those two are distinct, this lack of its own nature is the same even if it has a cause that is not a different entity.

He replies with the words beginning "no," and so forth: "Completion" (*niṣpatti*) is said to be the acquisition of a previously non-existent nature, whereas impermanence (*anityatā*) consists in the cessation of an entity; therefore, since completion itself is non-existent, how could there be the production of contradictory properties? If, then, impermanence is not a real entity (*vastu-sat*), how can there be a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya-lakṣaṇa*) between the probandum and the probans? To this he says: "For that very entity [is impermanence]. This means: that which has its stability in a single moment is itself [impermanence].

The very nature of cessation (*nivṛtti*) is what is called impermanence, and that alone is the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the reason and the probandum; for impermanence is not a distinct entity or a formless state. Thus, by such statements as "impermanence belongs to the entity," no positive form is predicated of the entity; rather, it is expressed that its observed form does not exist, because if another property were being predicated, it would follow that the cessation of the entity itself is not being demonstrated.

If impermanence were simply the entity itself, how could there be a difference in expression such as saying that "impermanence is a property (dharma) of the subject (dharmin), namely sound"? To this he says: "Even though there is a difference in expression," and so forth. We shall explain later the reason for this difference in expression—the distinction in the expressive words—based on the relationship between property and property-possessor.

By this, that which is also stated by Uddyotakara and others—who maintain that the destruction of the cause occurs at the very time of the production of the effect, just as there is the downward and upward movement of the ends of a balance scale—is refuted. [They argue: "If [destruction occurs] at the time of the production of the effect, then the relation of cause and effect would not exist, because the destruction of the cause is the very production of the cause. Thus, from the statement that 'destruction is indeed existence,' it follows that the effect is produced together with the cause. Furthermore, if destruction were indeed existence, then the entity would have no existence even in its first moment."

The cessation of an entity occurs through its destruction, yet destruction as it is understood in the world is not the entity itself. Furthermore, because destruction would exist at all times, the entity would have to exist perpetually. If, on the other hand, the destruction of the cause were distinct from the arising of the cause, then impermanence would not possess the nature of being produced (*kṛtaka*). Moreover, if destruction were a separate entity that arose, there would be no cessation of that moment; how then could there be momentariness?

That is refuted. For destruction is of two kinds: that which consists in the cessation of an entity (*bhāva-nivṛtti-rūpa*) and [the other] which is an entity (*bhāva*). Therefore, an arisen entity performs its function, and at the time of the effect, the destruction consisting in the cessation of the cause is indeed well-known in the world. This [destruction] is not accepted as having the nature of an entity (*bhāva-svabhāva*), nor is it held to be either non-different or different from the arising of the cause, because it is formless (*nīrūpatvāt*); rather, one merely performs a negation of its difference or non-difference. And so he will say:
"For this alternative would apply to an entity, since a positive injunction follows the reality of the thing" (1.281).

Therefore, the claim that there is no cessation of the moment when something distinct [from it] has arisen is refuted; for since cessation occurs in the very first moment at the time of the arising of the second moment, an entity that persists for only a single moment is designated by the word "destruction. This destruction, being of the nature of an entity (*bhāva-rūpa*), is essentially of the same nature as its cause. And because it ceases at the time of the production of the effect, it does not exist at a time different from the effect; nor does it exist at all times, because the entity itself is non-existent [at those other times].

Alternatively, by means of the two [terms] expressing the property and the property-bearer—namely, "this is perishable" (*vināśvara*) and "this has destruction" (*vināśo 'sya*)—one and the same entity, which is excluded from non-perishability, is denoted through the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions; thus, it is entirely consistent that the entity itself is called "destruction."

If, then, impermanence is indeed the very nature of the entity (*bhāva*), then since that [impermanence] must also be perceived when the entity is perceived, why is it not ascertained in exactly that same way? To this he says: "That," and so forth. Even while seeing—that is, even while directly perceiving—the nature called impermanence, which has the property of existing for only a moment, one does not determine it; that is, one does not ascertain it. This is the connection [of the words].

Why is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) the property of abiding for only a moment? He says: because it arises from its own very cause with such a property of abiding for only a moment. Furthermore, why does one not determine [this] even while seeing it? He says: "because of the notion [of permanence]."

One whose intellect is dull due to the latencies of ignorance regarding permanence and so forth, which have been habituated throughout beginningless saṃsāra, is described as such; otherwise, why would there not be certainty for all beings regarding an object perceived [as it is]? By this, it is stated that although yogis may have a similar perception, because they lack dullness of intellect, there arises the certainty of momentariness.

If, then, due to ignorance there is no determination of impermanence even when an entity has perished, one might fear that the determination of impermanence would not occur; anticipating this, he states the external cause of error as well: "by the apprehension of existence," and so forth. That which is the apprehension of existence alone, and not of non-existence, is by that "apprehension of existence."

This is what is meant: because the preceding moment perishes at the very time the succeeding moment arises, there is no interval between the two moments due to their non-existence [simultaneously]; thus, because they are not perceived as distinct, there is always—in the second and subsequent moments as well—the apprehension of existence alone. Consequently, there is the "state of being such" (*tathābhāva*), which is the state of existence (*sadbhāva*) of that which was previously seen. Regarding this, there is a doubt (*śaṅkā*) of the form "Could this be that very same thing?"—a doubt that arises even for one who is deluded, since one sees "this is that very same thing.
Deceived or cheated by that [doubt], one does not ascertain [the difference].

"In that case, one might argue that even for fire and smoke, there could be no ascertainment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), because their difference would not be perceived due to the lack of an intervening absence. To this, he says: ‘Because of the arising of another similar [moment],’ and so forth. Furthermore, the perception of another similar [moment] is observed to be the cause of the delusion of difference, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like. This point should be understood in detail in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, where it is analyzed.
(Pramāṇavārttika 1.225)

Because of that, another [moment] arises which is similar to the preceding moment in every respect; deceived by this, one does not determine the subsequent moment as being different from the preceding moment, but rather thinks, "This is that very same thing. Therefore, there is no perception of the destruction of the preceding moment, nor a perception of the arising of the subsequent one. However, because fire and smoke are absolutely dissimilar, even when they occur in immediate succession, their difference is apprehended, and thus the determination of the causal relationship occurs. The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to indicate an alternative possibility.

Therefore, the meaning is this: if there is a deviation [in the inference] upon perceiving existence, or if there is deception due to the arising of a similar subsequent [moment], then for the opponent, there is always indeed deception.

Alternatively, [the author] asks: "But why is it that one does not determine [an object] even while seeing it? He replies: "By the perception of existence (*sattopalambhena*). Previously, one who was deceived by the perception of existence—[a deception consisting in] the superimposition of a previously seen state upon what is being perceived as lacking that [state]—does not determine it. If that were so, then determination would occur at the very moment of seeing the first instant, because there would have been no prior perception of existence; anticipating this objection, he says: "Or, deceived by the production of a similar subsequent [moment]. The word *vā* (or) has the sense of *ca* (and).

And because one is deceived by the arising of a second moment that resembles the first moment, one does not reach a definitive conclusion. [The author] says "one of dull intellect" to show that even for yogins, there would be no certainty [otherwise]. Thus, because of the presence of external and internal causes of deception, ordinary persons do not reach a definitive conclusion. However, for yogins, even though they perceive similarity, certainty certainly arises due to their sharp intellect. Therefore, this is established: even while seeing the nature of momentary existence, one who is deceived by the arising of a subsequent similar [moment] does not reach a definitive conclusion.

Now, if an entity were momentary, there would be a manifestation of the preceding and succeeding moments as distinct; since they do not so manifest, how can it be said that one does not determine [the object] even while seeing it? Or, if it is argued that because momentariness is not distinct from blue and so forth, it is apprehended when blue is apprehended—

This is correct; however, this point is now being examined: Is this blue non-momentary, or is it of the nature of a moment, or is it a continuum? In that regard, if it were non-momentary, then how could there be an appearance of momentariness within the appearance of blue? If, on the other hand, it is of the nature of a moment, then surely this very [nature] is unestablished; so how can it be said that there is an appearance of a moment within the appearance of blue? Furthermore, because a moment does not appear, there is no appearance of blue in the form of a continuum.

Now, [it might be argued that] when there is the appearance of mere blue, there is also the appearance of momentariness. That is incorrect; for perception’s grasping or non-grasping of an object occurs through appearance or non-appearance, and not otherwise. Thus it is said: "Whatever it grasps, it does so by means of its appearance. And it has been stated that there is no appearance of moments.

If momentariness were not distinct from blue and so forth, then because momentariness would already be ascertained, inference would be rendered useless. However, some one says: "Momentariness is simply the state of being the object of a single cognition, because there appears a state of being the object of a present cognition that is excluded from being the object of preceding and succeeding cognitions; thus, each moment is indeed distinct from preceding and succeeding moments. What is experienced and ascertained by perception is merely referred to by inference; therefore, inference is not useless."

That is incorrect. For if a single cognition were non-momentary, then its object would also have to be non-momentary. If, on the other hand, that [cognition] is momentary, how is this known? If you say it is because it too is the object of a single cognition, then the realization of momentariness would result in an infinite regress. Now, if the manifestation of a moment of cognition is admitted, why is it not likewise admitted for a moment of the object? Otherwise, even a single moment would be manifold, since it would be the object of multiple cognitions.

But Bhaṭṭa Vāsudeva says: "The non-appearance [of objects] precisely due to the destruction of preceding and succeeding moments is itself the appearance of their non-momentariness; therefore, every perception grasps only momentariness, and it is merely by means of the inference of momentariness that [the object] is established as being erroneous."

This too is untenable; for since the thesis is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no possibility for an inference (*anumāna*) to arise. Furthermore, even non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) direct perception would be erroneous, and because [the inference] depends on the apprehension of a relation (*sambandha*). Moreover, it contradicts the text [of Dharmakīrti], which states: "Even while seeing... Therefore, it is incorrect to say: "Even while seeing, one does not determine."

To this it is replied: Just as there is a sequence of preceding and succeeding among the moments of objects (*arthakṣaṇa*), so too is there such a sequence among the moments of cognition (*jñānakṣaṇa*). Therefore, by that preceding moment of cognition, only the preceding moment of the object is apprehended, not the subsequent one; and by the subsequent [moment of cognition], only the subsequent [object] is apprehended, not the preceding one. Since these two do not appear within a single cognition, how could there be an appearance through differentiation such that "this is other than the preceding"? Thus is the objection raised.

The manifestation of a thing’s own nature (*svarūpa*) is itself the manifestation of its distinction from other things, just as the manifestation of Mount Sumeru is distinct [from others]. And since this occurs even for a momentary entity (*kṣaṇa*), how could there not be a manifestation of its distinction? Furthermore, this is because of the cognition that "what was seen is being seen now. For the nature that was previously seen is one thing, and the nature being seen now is another. To explain: the first observer perceives only the nature of the thing as it is currently being seen, and not as it was previously seen; thus, there is indeed a difference between these two.

It is not the case that there is no perception of distinction—like that between a jar and a cloth—due to the absence of an interval caused by the non-existence of preceding and succeeding moments that are exclusively similar. Nor is it the case that there is non-difference because of the non-appearance of distinction; for even in the case of mother-of-pearl, when one proceeds with the thought "this is indeed my silver," there is no non-difference [of the two] simply because of the absence of a perception of the distinction between the mother-of-pearl and the silver.

Therefore, just as in this case of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), the very appearance of the shell’s own nature is itself the appearance of its distinction from other things, so too it would be for a single moment. The only objection that might arise is: "Why is the preceding moment not remembered through its distinctness? To this, it has already been stated: it is not remembered because people are deceived by the production of subsequent moments that are similar [to the preceding ones].

But even so, the moment (*kṣaṇa*) does not appear, because an entity is not perceived as having a duration equal to the time taken for the passage of a single atom; rather, if there is no appearance of [the entity] in a single moment, how could there be an appearance of a non-momentary [entity], since it does not appear at every moment? Furthermore, since an entity as it arises is apprehended by perception as being devoid of prior and subsequent forms, how can there be an apprehension of its momentariness?

Nor is it perceived as non-momentary, precisely because it does not appear as connected with earlier and later times in the present perception; for the non-appearance now of that very nature which was connected with the earlier time is itself destruction, and the appearance of a different nature is itself origination. Thus, how can it be called "non-momentary" when the destruction and origination of preceding and succeeding moments do not appear? Nor is this present [entity] of the nature of multiple moments; for if multiple moments were possible at this time, it would possess a form such as "grasped" and so forth, and its nature would not be redundant.

For it is not by means of a certainty produced through direct perception that one determines "this exists right now"; rather, [the determination] is "it exists at this time. However, it is by means of inference that "it exists right now" is established.
Therefore, it remains established that even while seeing, one does not ascertain [the object], and so forth.

Now, if there were a certainty through direct perception that "it is always similar," then the cognition "this is that very same thing" would be an error; yet, since the recognition "this is that very same thing" arises at all times in a firm form, how can it be an error? To this, Bhaṭṭa says: [1]
fn. 1: *Ślokavārttika*, in the section on the "Eternity of Words" (373, 374): "Because it exists at that time and because it is additional, [the cognition] has been established.
Wherever the mind is firmly settled on the thought that 'it is exactly the same as the eternal,' there the recognition [expressed as] 'that' is understood to be an error."
In this case, a firm cognition arises that [the object] is indeed permanent;
its validity is established by the fact that it is not contradicted by the existence of that [object].
In that regard, due to differences of place, time, and so forth, there is a limited occasion [for its existence];
for the existence of the present has not passed away from the previous cognition.

Nor is there always a certain determination of similarity through inference, because such [an inference] is sublated by perceptual recognition (*pratyakṣapratyabhijñā*), and because inference does not arise when recognition is present. Nor is recognition invalid due to the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*); for as long as this [recognition] lacks validity, inference does not arise, and as long as inference does not arise, this [recognition] lacks invalidity—thus there is the fault of mutual dependence.

To this it is replied: By the word "that" (*sa*), the nature associated with a previous time is made the object; and by the word "this" (*ayam*), that associated with the present time. There is a difference between these two, and not a lack of difference in any way, because the entity possesses a single nature consisting of its form at the present time and its future form. Therefore, since only difference appears when there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), how could this [recognition] subvert the inference of momentariness?

Alternatively, the object's connection with a prior time is simply non-existent now, because that prior time no longer exists. Or, if it were existent, it would necessarily be connected to the present time and could not be connected to a prior time due to contradiction; thus, [the opponent's position] is untenable. Therefore, that portion of cognition which grasps the non-existent connection with a prior time is erroneous; otherwise, it would grasp the object's clearly manifest states such as childhood and so forth, yet it does not do so.

Therefore, how could there be sublation by inference from that erroneous cognition which, through the superimposition of a previously perceived form, apprehends "this is that very same thing"? For perception arises as the grasper of an object only where the operation of the sense organ occurs. Now, regarding existence at a previous time, what operation could occur now? It is non-existent because it has been set aside [in the past]. Nor can that [past existence] be grasped as non-different [from the present]; so how could a cognition that apprehends the identity of existence at the prior and subsequent times be a perception?

And when something perceived in the state of childhood is recognized through direct perception in the state of old age, permanence does not appear within that recognition. Rather, only the identity "this is that very same thing" is determined. Nor is this identity [the essence] due to the difference between the states of childhood and old age. Furthermore, the postulation of permanence and so forth does not arise from the impossibility of accounting for the apprehension of identity; for such apprehension can occur even due to the cause of an illusion arising from the production of successive similar [moments], as in the case of hair that has been cut and grown back again.

Nor does recognition here arise from a distinct universal of "hair-ness," for that would entail the consequence of producing a cognition of the form "that is here. Nor does it arise from a non-distinct [universal], because otherwise there would be a persistence [of the universal] elsewhere, whereas the forms of the persisting and the excluded are mutually exclusive due to their absolute difference through their successive conjunctions. Consequently, the recognition "these are those very same hairs" is a delusion caused solely by the arising of similar [moments] in succession. Thus, in the case of jars and the like, the emergence of inference is indeed appropriate, given the possibility of doubting its non-delusory nature.

Nor does there arise the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), because it is not by means of inference that the invalidity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is produced; rather, it is known [as invalid] precisely from its own cause, since it is produced as something inherently lacking validity. This is because [recognition] grasps [an object] as "seen. For the state of having been seen (*dṛṣṭatva*) does not exist in the prior state, since at that time [the object] had only the nature of being currently perceived (*dṛśyamāna*). Nor does it exist now, nor does the connection with the prior time belong to the object currently being perceived, because that which was previously [perceived] no longer exists at present.

Therefore, by superimposing the quality of being "seen," the recognizing cognition (*pratyabhijñā*) arises as non-authoritative precisely because it is erroneous. Furthermore, the emergence of inference (*anumāna*) is not caused by the lack of authority in this [recognition], but rather by the presence of a counter-reason (*pratibandhi*) regarding the probandum; thus, it serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*) of recognition. This detailed analysis of the refutation of recognition has been set forth in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, and should therefore be understood from that very source.

Therefore, this is established: although one perceives that very nature of momentary existence as its intrinsic character (*svabhāva*), one does not ascertain it because one is deceived by the arising of a similar [moment] immediately following, and thus fails to determine the destruction of the preceding moment.

But how is it understood that one who is deceived by the arising of a similar [moment] does not determine [the destruction]? To this he says: "The final," and so forth. The final moment is that moment which does not link up with another similar moment; because of the certainty that the observer of that [final moment] has perished, it is understood that even previously this [entity] perishes at every moment, though it is simply not determined due to the aforementioned cause of deception.

"But surely, even for one who perceives the final moment, how can there be certainty regarding non-existence, since at that time there is still the perception of existence? For one who perceives only existence cannot understand its absence. To this he replies: "Afterwards," and so forth. We do not say that certainty arises from the mere perception of the final moment; rather, having perceived the final moment, [certainty] arises afterwards... [when] that effect of his is no longer perceived.

Furthermore, when smoke arises from the proximity of fire, wood, and so forth, its non-perception does not occur when horses and the like are removed; rather, its non-perception occurs when the fire and other such factors are removed. Thus, through the combination of perception and non-perception, the status of being a cause is established without doubt in those very factors that are intended as causes. And since this aforementioned definition of an effect exists in the case of smoke, therefore smoke arises from fire alone.

Furthermore, regarding smoke that exists at all times in the presence of fire, its non-origination from fire is sometimes asserted on the grounds that it is produced by something existent or non-existent, or because it is causeless, or because its cause is invisible. Among these, we shall explain in the third chapter (*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.4), under the section beginning with "If it is argued that everything is incapable," that the first position is not tenable. Nor is it causeless; this too he will state in that very same place. Nor is smoke caused by an invisible factor, because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth.
*Note 1: Leaf 37 is missing.*

Now, it might be argued: "This is the nature of the invisible [cause], that it produces smoke only when in proximity to fire and the like, and only at the time of burning camphor and such substances does it produce it endowed with fragrance and so forth, and not otherwise. To this we ask: has the production of smoke ever been observed without fire, such that you would speak thus? If you say no, then how is smoke not the effect of fire, given that it exists whenever fire exists? Furthermore, to claim that at the time of the smoke's production, fire—though always perceived—is present only by mere chance (*kākatālīyanyāyena*), is a false designation.

Alternatively, that very nature of the invisible [entity] is such that if it is not assisted by fire, why does it produce smoke only when fire and other factors are present, and not before or after? Therefore, it is only when fire and other factors are present that its non-inherent nature becomes a producer of smoke, and not otherwise; thus, even in that case, smoke would ultimately be produced by fire alone.

Furthermore, just as smoke is understood to depend on [causes] such as place and time because it does not arise without them, so too, since it is observed never to arise without fire, who could deny its dependence on fire? And that dependence is nothing other than being its effect. Just as smoke is accepted as being produced by [fire] because it exists only when that [fire] is present (though it may be invisible), why is it not likewise accepted that it is produced by fire because its existence is observed at all times only when fire is present?

To whatever extent a thing is observed to arise only when certain factors are present, to that same extent all of those factors possess causality, since their prior existence is equal in each case. Thus, since smoke is produced by a causal complex including fire, non-perception, and so forth, how could there be any deviation from fire?

But another says: "Granted that there is a causal relationship between fire and smoke, nevertheless, they are not apprehended by a single cognition because they exist at different times. Furthermore, it is not the case that the preceding non-conceptual [cognition] apprehends the preceding thing-in-itself as having the nature of a cause; for the effect, being yet to come, is not perceptible. Likewise, the subsequent [cognition] apprehends only the subsequent thing-in-itself, but not as having the nature of an effect, since the cause, being past, cannot be apprehended."

Nor can it be grasped by conceptual cognition, for this same objection applies equally there as well: no one has ever apprehended that "this has arisen from that," and for that very reason, it is not grasped even by memory, because there was no prior experience of it.

To this it is replied: First of all, because the effect is non-existent in its unarisen state, it lacks connection with the cause; and even in its arisen state, it is likewise [without such connection], because it is independent. Similarly, in the states of the effect’s completion or non-completion, it is simply not connected to the effect. Furthermore, there is no relationship of cause and effect between these two, because they exist at different times. This designation—“this is the effect of that” or “this is the cause of that”—is merely a conceptual construction.

Therefore, being an effect consists precisely in obtaining its own nature from the cause; likewise, for the cause, being a cause with respect to the effect consists precisely in its prior existence. And since that acquisition of self-nature and that prior existence are non-different from the entity itself, they are indeed apprehended by perception. Thus, how could the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) not be graspable by perception? It is merely when the effect is seen that one employs the conventional designation, "this is the effect of that" or "this is the cause of that. For a causal relation is not possible between two things that are not related as cause and effect.

Nor can their status as cause and effect be established as non-different through the relation of causality, because that would involve a contradiction. Nor can it be established as different, because that would entail the consequence that they lack the nature of cause and effect by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). For even in the case of things that are cause and effect by their very nature, what is the point of postulating a separate entity called "causality," since they possess the form of cause and effect precisely through their own nature? Therefore, the causal relation between these two consists simply in their being prior and subsequent.

When that preceding entity is apprehended, its nature as a cause immediately followed by its effect is indeed apprehended. Furthermore, when the subsequent entity is apprehended by a later cognition as being immediately after its cause, it is apprehended precisely as having the nature of an effect; for that immediate succession possesses a nature non-different from the [cause]. For this very reason, there also occurs the recollection, "this arises immediately after that," because the immediate succession has been experienced.

But Aviddhakarṇa says: "The state of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) is established when, having seen one [instance], a second and subsequent ones are seen. However, for the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), there is no persistence of a perceiver. Furthermore, there can be no recollection of the invariable concomitance of another object with what was experienced, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."

That is incorrect; for the first and subsequent objective moments are apprehended by the first and subsequent moments of cognition, and because memory is possible through the causal relationship between those factors falling within a single continuum. How the causal relationship functions in the case of momentariness has already been explained and will be further discussed [in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.33].

But even so, since the moments themselves are not ascertained, how can there be an ascertainment of the causal relationship? Nor can that be ascertained by means of a continuum (*santāna*), because a continuum does not exist as something distinct from the members of the continuum (*santānin*). There are only the members of the continuum occurring at prior and subsequent times; and since one moment exists when another does not, there is only the appearance of a single moment. How, then, can there be an appearance of a continuum? And in the absence of that, how can there be a causal relationship?

That is incorrect, because there exists no entity consisting of a single atom, since [atoms] lack a gross nature. The appearance of a continuum is merely the appearance of those [atoms] belonging to a continuum which appear without interval; and in that case, because one determines unity through similarity while failing to discern the distinction between moments, there is no ascertainment of the causal relation among the moments occurring within a single continuum.

However, as for those [moments] occurring in distinct continua, because they are of a different nature due to the progression of the continuum, there is no determination of that [causal relation]; therefore, it is said that the determination of the causal relation between the fire-continuum and the smoke-continuum occurs because the smoke-continuum is perceived as being preceded by a fire-continuum—this is trivial.

But Adhyayana says: "If the causal relation is grasped between two particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can there be a relationship of signifier and signified between two universals (*sāmānya*), since they are distinct?
That too is incorrect, because a universal is accepted as having the nature of many particular characteristics. As it has been said:

"Because it establishes merely the thing as excluded from what does not possess its form, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is said to have the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, since it does not rest upon particulars.

(Pramāṇasamuccaya) Therefore, the apprehension of the relationship of universals is precisely the apprehension of the relationship of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); it is not something other than that.

In this regard, for the Buddhist who maintains the theory of inference, all the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) existing in the three worlds would have to be apprehended as being pervaded by fire; for if even one were not apprehended, the reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Yet perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not able to do this, because its object is restricted to what is present before it. Nor can the pervasion of other particular characteristics with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) be grasped through inference, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

That is incorrect because: perception apprehends smoke as distinct only when the specific fire is present; it determines that the nature of smoke—which is excluded from non-smoke—is the effect of fire alone, which is excluded from non-fire. Just as it is here, so too in other places, such as another location, it determines that this very nature is produced by fire alone; otherwise, it would not be grasped by perception as being connected with fire.

In this way, if smoke were produced by both fire and non-fire, its cognition would occur as being connected to both; it does not, however, occur as being connected to fire alone. Yet, it is so cognized. Therefore, since there is the certainty that even in other cases this very form belongs to fire alone, how could there be any deviation of smoke from fire? Furthermore, this inference belongs only to one who is able to discern that form as distinct from steam and the like, and not to anyone else.

Even for one who maintains that the universal concomitance (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is apprehended, the inference [of fire] occurs only through the determination of the smoke-universal as being restricted to fire, because of the suspicion of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) based on the observation of the smoke-universal in places such as cowherd huts where it exists without fire. And this determination of the smoke-universal as restricted to fire is possible only after first determining individual instances of smoke connected with fire. Furthermore, it is not possible for anyone by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the smoke-universal as qualified by every individual instance of smoke connected with fire across all locations and so forth.

Nor is the universal "smoke" apprehended as qualified by a specific instance of smoke connected with fire in a kitchen or similar place, because there is no continuity of that specific instance elsewhere. And that universal smoke which does persist [everywhere] is not invariably concomitant with fire. Therefore, the objection is equal for those who maintain that the pervasion is grasped through a universal: how is it that the specific universal "smoke" is apprehended as being pervaded by fire everywhere?

Now, if there is no subverting evidence against smoke being produced by fire elsewhere, and that very same thing is recognized through the cognition "this is that very same [thing]," then that universal is accepted; for us as well, since the cognition "this is that very same [thing]" arises, that [universal] is accepted—so what is the difference between us two?

This is all [mere words]. Demonstrating this very point, he says: if that smoke were to exist in the absence of that—namely, in the absence of fire—it would transcend its state of having a cause and would become causeless. Or rather, if that smoke, which is perceived as being connected with fire, were to exist in the absence of that—namely, in the absence of fire—it would not be perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having a cause, namely, as being connected with fire; yet it is so perceived.
Therefore, it is not merely from seeing it thus many times, but even once, by virtue of the aforementioned direct perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).

What is the reason? Because fire does not arise even once—not to mention repeatedly—from that which lacks a cause; for oil never arises from sand, even once. With the words "of the effect," etc., he states the meaning of the verse; "for not," etc., is the justification for this very point. By this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated: for one who asserts deviation, smoke would exist even without fire. And by this, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is stated. Therefore, because it exists without fire, fire is not its cause; thus, it would be causeless—this is the intended sense.

If it is argued that smoke is not causeless because it has as its causes such things as the accidental summit of a mountain, which are different from the causes of fire—this is not so, for the same logic applies even when another distinct cause is postulated. For instance, if that other cause were absent—even in the absence of that other cause—the fire would still arise; thus, that other cause would likewise not be the cause. Furthermore, is that fire and that other cause of the same nature as the production of smoke, or are they not?

If it has the nature of not producing [smoke], then how could smoke arise from that fire or from anything else? Since they do not have the nature of producing that [smoke]—that is, since they have the nature of not producing smoke—smoke would simply not exist. Why? Because for that which does not have that nature, and which by its own nature does not produce smoke, there would be no production of that smoke; thus, that smoke would lack a cause.

Alternatively, if the other [thing] had the nature of producing smoke, then both would possess the state of being fire, because fire is characterized by the nature of producing smoke. This will be explained further below.

One who asserts deviation [of the logical reason] certainly does not say, "It is that very same [smoke]," and so forth; nor is it said that smoke produced from fire arises from something else. For if that very same [smoke] were to arise from something else, there would be the consequence of its being causeless, because such a thing—identical in its essential nature as a property produced by fire—would be arising from another source.

The proponent of the established doctrine [responds] with the words "from something of a different kind," and so forth. [The opponent asks: "In that case, is the cause held to be similar to the effect, such that you say, 'How can that which arises from something of a different kind be of that same kind? [The proponent replies: "No, because the meaning is different. For when smoke—which has been observed to be produced by fire—is produced from something dissimilar, how is it that it becomes "of that same kind"? That is to say, it possesses a nature identical to the properties produced by fire.

This is what is meant: just as there is a specific nature (*tādṛśatva*) among the various types of smoke—such as that produced from grass or leaves—relative to one another, so too there is a specific nature among the various types of fire—such as those produced from grass or leaves—that generate smoke, precisely relative to one another. Therefore, when a particular type of smoke is observed arising from a particular type of fire, such a type of smoke arises only from such a type of fire; whereas smoke produced from a different [type of] fire is of a completely different nature, like steam and the like.

[Objection: But surely, by means of a moment of smoke produced from fire, there arises another such moment of smoke; therefore, even from something other [than fire], such [smoke] comes into being. [Reply: No. For it is only another moment of smoke produced from fire that becomes similar to a moment of smoke produced from fire, and not any other. Indeed, even if there is a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of similarity due to steam and the like, it does not actually possess that similarity. Furthermore, for a moment of smoke produced by a moment of smoke, it is only a moment of smoke produced by a moment of smoke that becomes similar, and not any other. Therefore, since such [an effect] arises only from such [a cause], how can there be any deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? By this [it is established].
If all things were momentary, how could they have their existence dependent upon anything else,
given that their being would arise from nothing other than their own fully manifest causes?
Therefore, just as the production of smoke from smoke that is not produced by fire [is impossible],
by what means could the production of that [smoke] from the head of Śakra be prevented?

This is refuted. For the first moment of smoke produced by fire is of such a nature that it is produced by another moment of fire; likewise, the second moment of smoke produced by that first moment of smoke is produced by another moment of smoke. This remains the case for the third and subsequent moments as well. Thus, even with respect to the moments, there is no deviation for such [a causal series]. He states this very point: "For what arises from such [a cause] must be of such [a nature]."

Even if [the effect] were to arise from something different—even from that which is dissimilar to fire—if it were to possess a nature identical to smoke produced by fire, then because there would be no restriction upon the capacities of those causes, the distinction between causes would not differentiate the effect. Since there would be an absence of such a restriction on the capacities of both similar and dissimilar causes—namely, that a similar cause produces only a similar result and a dissimilar cause produces a distinct result—the diversity of the universe would become causeless.

If it is argued that there is no lack of cause because production occurs from some cause or other, he says: "Or everything from everything," and so forth. If production occurred even from that which lacks the capacity [to produce it], then everything would be born from everything; but this is not the case. Therefore, and so on. "That is not smoke": "that" means that fire which possesses the observed form from which smoke is seen to arise; the meaning is: from a fire that is of a different genus (*vijātīya*) than that. (35, 36)

And likewise, if there were causelessness, smoke would have to exist either eternally or not at all. What is the reason? Because an entity that lacks a cause does not depend on anything else for its own production; that is, it does not depend on other causes. If it is argued that even without dependence on other causes, it occurs only occasionally by its very nature, [the author] says: "For [it arises] from dependence."

This is what is meant: since that which is unestablished does not exist at all, how could it have occasional occurrence by way of its own nature? However, that which is established does possess a nature; the objection is merely raised as to how that very establishment occurs only at certain times. He explains this very point with the words beginning "for he" (*sa hi*). "It would never not be" means it would exist at all times. Why? Because when that [cause] exists—that is, when the nature of smoke exists—there is no deficiency due to the lack of dependence on other causes, just as in the case of the desired time. Furthermore, the phrase "even then" (*tadāpi ca*) means that even at the time when it is observed, smoke would not exist, because there is no distinction from the time when smoke is absent.

Dividing the latter half [of the verse], he says: "Because of dependence" (*apekṣayā hi*). This means in dependence upon a suitable place and time. For, since there are two times for an effect—namely, the time of its existence and the time of its non-existence—it is because of the connection with the suitability and unsuitability of that existence, i.e., the production of the effect, respectively. The mention of "time" is intended as an illustration; the same should be stated for place and substance as well. However, this is not accepted in the [opponent's] sense.

In that case, since capacity (*yogyatā*) and incapacity (*ayogyatā*) belong equally to those two times and places—wherein the effect exists and wherein it does not—it would be impossible to establish a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the presence or absence of that [effect] in them. For the time of the effect itself possesses the presence of the effect, while for anything other than that, there is the "other," namely the absence of the effect; thus, a restriction is untenable. Both those times—the time of the existence of the effect and the time of its non-existence—would have to possess the effect, because of the similarity of their capacity; or else, neither would possess it, because of the equality of their incapacity. Therefore, capacity belongs only to the time of that [effect's] existence. It is by depending upon that [capacity] that entities become occasional (*kādācitka*).

Granted that there may be suitability regarding the desired place, time, and so forth; yet, by that alone, the status of being a cause is not established. To this he says: "And that," etc. Since this is so, if there were no cause, there would be either perpetual existence or perpetual non-existence, but such is not the case.

"Therefore," and so forth. That by the exclusion of which something functions is what it does not depend upon; and that in relation to which it is dependent is what it does depend upon. If it is asked: "Even if it occurs in a certain place and so on, how is it still dependent upon that? he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
