"Occurring in such a way" means occurring in one place while excluding another; a functional entity (*bhāva*) necessarily depends upon a place and so forth. If it is argued: "But no benefit is conferred upon that entity by that place and so forth," he says: "The benefit produced by that," and so forth.

"Because a restriction [of the form] 'in that [place] alone' is untenable" means: because it is impossible to establish a restriction such as "it must not exist in that place and so forth. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the mention of place and time; it is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes substance (*dravya*) as well. "Seen once in a certain place and so forth" means: having been seen by the aforementioned perception in the presence of certain things, it is not seen again when there is a deficiency of even one of those very things.

"Otherwise" means: if smoke were not of that nature—namely, being produced by a specific causal complex such as fire—it would not exist at all elsewhere than in fire; or, if it did exist there, it would not be smoke. This is because smoke is a specific nature produced by that, namely, produced by fire.

Likewise, the cause—the fire—also possesses the nature of producing such an effect, which is the nature of fitness for producing smoke; this causal fitness exists even in the state devoid of smoke. Therefore, the definition [of the probans] is not yet established. Thus, when the mutual dependence of fire and smoke as having a restricted nature has been established by perception, [the definition follows].

If it is maintained that this smoke exists even from something other than fire, then that nature which produces smoke does not belong to that non-fire. For when smoke arises from what is not fire, at that time a nature that produces smoke has arisen precisely for what is not fire. And how could that which is the nature of what is not fire be the nature of fire? Consequently, because fire would have a nature that does not produce smoke, it would not produce smoke even once. Furthermore, smoke itself would not possess the nature of smoke; thus he says, "And not," and so forth.

That which exists apart from fire is not smoke. What is the reason? Because it arises from a non-fire that possesses a nature incapable of producing smoke. And if its nature were such that even a non-fire were admitted to possess a nature capable of producing smoke, then that [non-fire] itself would be fire, because its form is that of a producer of smoke; by this means, smoke is shown to be non-deviant [from fire]. (37)

"Having the nature of fire" means "if it has the nature of producing smoke. That [Śakra’s head] would indeed be fire, because it possesses the nature of producing smoke. Now, suppose that Śakra’s head does not have the nature of fire; in that case—that is, on Śakra’s head—why would it not [produce smoke]? He says: "Because of smoke," and so forth. For (*hi*) means "because. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has the nature of being the cause of smoke. Why is this so? Because it possesses a distinct capacity for that.

Likewise, by means of the power that produces smoke—which functions as the instrument—the [fire] is distinct and dissimilar from other things such as fireflies. If it were admitted that smoke arises—that is, its production occurs—from something that is not smoke, meaning from what lacks the nature of fire, then that smoke would be causeless, as was stated previously.

The opponent says, "The body," and so forth. "Now" means: if one does not admit that a single thing, such as smoke, arises from something of a different class (*vijātīya*), how can there be the production of a single effect from distinct causes that are mutually heterogeneous? He explains how this occurs with the words, "Just as," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), light, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and others are included. This being the case, consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises both from the nature of the eye and from the nature of non-eye factors such as form and mental attention; yet, this [consciousness] is not without a cause.

The opponent thinks: "In this way, smoke might arise from fire, and yet it might also arise from something other than fire, such as the peak of Mount Śakra; nevertheless, it will not be causeless. He refutes this with the words beginning "Not at all" (*na vai*). In the case of the eye and so forth, each individual member—possessing that nature, namely the nature of being a producer—is not indeed a producer when independent of the others. For if it were so, then because of the deviation of the cause in each individual instance, it would be causeless. Rather, it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer; it possesses that nature, meaning it possesses the nature of being a producer.

By the statement that "the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer," its nature as such is already established, because that which lacks this nature is not a producer. Why, then, is it stated separately as "of what nature"? True; however, it is stated for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). It means that the nature of being a producer exists only in the state of the causal complex, neither before nor after, nor separately. Regarding the phrase "with their presence determined by the capacity of their own causes": the collective meaning is that all other causes, when assembled for a single effect, constitute the cause.

Some, however, read the word *vā* [in the text], [interpreting it as]: "The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, or it is of that nature. But here, the word *vā* serves no purpose; thus, this is simply a faulty reading. If, having stated "the causal complex," visual consciousness were to arise even from another causal complex, then because it would arise from something different, it would follow that it is causeless. Rather, that very [specific] causal complex is inferred by means of the effect. The point is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since [the effect arises] from the individual causes and not from anything else.

It might be argued as follows: "Only the very first moment of smoke is produced by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of fire and so forth, yet that [first moment] cannot serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) because it is not ascertained. Furthermore, the connection (*pratibandha*) with smoke that is grasped belongs only to the cause of the preceding smoke. How, then, can there be an inference from that [connection] regarding the causal complex of fire and so forth? To this he says: "And that very [complex], etc. Because the continuity of the effect is established by its own nature, the basis is the primary cause; for without the causal complex, the continuum of smoke itself would not exist.

Then, having unified the series of smoke as being the effect of fire, there is an inference of the causal continuum of the burning [fire] and so forth; for one who perceives only the immediate range cannot discern through the analysis of individual moments.

It might be argued: "One infers precisely the [actual] fire, yet there is no purpose for one who seeks causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) by means of that [inferred object]. This objection has already been answered by the very act of posing it. The meaning is this: that same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), proceeding as a continuum, is the cause for the persistence of the nature of the effect and for the occurrence of the continuum of effects, because each subsequent moment of smoke arises in dependence upon each preceding moment of fire and so forth.

For there is no such restriction that only one single moment of smoke is produced by fire and not another; rather, as long as the fuel has not been completely reduced to ashes, the production of moments of smoke is not contradictory.

Therefore, just as a continuous series of smoke is produced by a fire that functions as a continuum through the generation of successive moments of burning—and this [series] is determined by direct perception—likewise, when one determines such [a series] elsewhere, the inference of a continuum of fire capable of performing a causal function for one who desires that object is not contradictory. Furthermore, the nature of smoke whose continuum of burning has been interrupted is entirely different from that of smoke situated in a dwelling house or similar place where the continuum of burning has not been interrupted. Since people do not clearly perceive the distinction between these two, how could there be any deviation [in the logical reason]?

Alternatively, it is explained otherwise: [The opponent objects,] "Is it not the case that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct from its constituent parts (*samagra*)? And since that [complex] is a single entity, only a single effect can arise? Otherwise, because each of the constituents possesses its own capacity, there would be a multiplicity of effects, or else they would produce the single effect only successively; yet this is not the case. Therefore, how can it be said that [the complex] produces a single [effect]? Anticipating this objection, he says: "And that very same [complex]," and so forth. "That very same causal complex" means that the constituents themselves (*samagra eva*) are designated by the term "causal complex. For what reason? Because, by virtue of the persistence of their own nature—that is, through the presence of their own essential form—they serve as the basis for the effect.

He thinks as follows: If the production of an effect were due to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) alone, then the individual members of that complex would lack causal agency. This would contradict direct experience. Furthermore, if the members of the complex were themselves causal agents, there would either be an excessive multiplicity of effects, or they would produce a single effect only in turn. Nor can the members possess a uniform nature by virtue of the power of the complex, for that would entail the non-existence of the complex itself. Therefore, those members, having arisen from their own causes as being restricted to the production of a single effect, are designated by the term "complex."

Nor is there any obstacle to many things performing a single effect. Nor is it our view that the cause itself becomes the effect, such that the multiplicity of causes producing a single effect would be contradicted. Just as a single effect is seen to have its cause in the prior existence of multiple factors, so too is it for multiple effects; or, just as those very same complete factors produce a single totality characterized by conjunction, why should they not likewise produce a single effect?

This is of little consequence. Since that [cause] is productive of a totality (*sāmagrī*), for that very reason there is the non-sequential production of the auxiliary causes; the meaning is that there is no production in succession. With the words "And as for... and so forth, he raises the objection regarding production from a heterogeneous cause and refutes it. The meaning is that he demonstrates here precisely what was stated previously: that such a thing does not arise from something of a different nature. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [examples are given]: an arrow from a cow's horn, a scorpion from a cow's dung. "Even in that case" means even when an effect arises from a heterogeneous cause.

"Even when designated in such a manner": even though things such as the water-lily (*śālūka*) produced from a dissimilar source are designated as "water-lily," they nevertheless possess a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) compared to that water-lily which originates from its own seed—that is, from a water-lily characterized as its own seed. As for the plantain tree (*kadalī*), which arises from both a seed and a bulb (*kanda*), it is likewise [differentiated]; and because of the difference in causes, it is mutually distinct [from other types].

And this difference is not something to be established; thus he says: "Clearly," and so forth. Or, regarding the discernment of the entity's difference: "an aspect well-discerned" means an aspect ascertained through differentiation from causes that have similar aspects. (38, 39)

Existence only when that exists is positive concomitance (*anvaya*); non-existence only when that is absent is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). "Positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatireka*) refers to these two together. That which is the nature of an effect, observed to follow a particular cause that it must follow—that following nature is the cause of that [effect]. The analysis of the compound is: "that of which this [following] nature is the cause. This means that the effect follows its cause because that [cause] is its cause.

But when it is stated with reference to the cause, then the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that which is to be followed—such as fire—is the cause of that which is intended to be the effect—such as smoke; that is, it is the cause of that [effect]. And since, in this way, there is a restriction of the intrinsic natures of cause and effect through their mutual non-dependence, for this reason, there is no possibility [of the effect] arising from a different cause, that is, from something of a dissimilar class (*vijātīya*).

Therefore, because the causal relation is established through the aforementioned perception and non-perception—that is, through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)—it occurs by means of that establishment of the causal relation. Consequently, the comprehension of that [relation] consists in the comprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); it is not otherwise. Thus, apart from the ascertainment of the causal relation, there is no comprehension of positive and negative concomitance through mere perception and non-perception alone.

What is the reason? Because the comprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which is dependent solely upon perception and non-perception, is contingent upon the perception and non-perception of [the reason] in its entirety. For perception establishes positive concomitance only if the reason is perceived in every instance of the similar class (*sapakṣa*); likewise, non-perception would establish negative concomitance only if the reason were not perceived in every instance where the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is absent.

Just as the fact that smoke is a product is established once in a single instance, and thereby its status as such is established everywhere; likewise, it is false to claim that the certainty of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) will arise everywhere simply because [the reason] is observed in some instances of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and not observed in others of the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*). For even if permanence is observed in some cases of incorporeality, such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth—this being stated according to what is accepted by others—in other cases, such as pleasure (*sukha*) and the like, it is not so.

"Otherwise"—that is, if impermanence were not established—then the observation of the reason, *amūrtatva* (formlessness), in a single instance of the example would not prove its existence everywhere. Therefore, such observation is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Likewise, since formlessness is not observed in some things like jars even though they lack permanence, yet it is observed again in pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth which lack permanence, the non-observation of the reason in one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is not a proof for the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Consequently, the determination of both positive and negative concomitance occurs only through the determination of the causal relationship between the reason and the effect. (40)

The opponent says, "Intrinsic nature," and so forth. [He asks: "Now, since the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been established for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), how is the inseparable connection with the probandum established for the intrinsic-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)?

[The author replies: "But was not the inseparable connection for the intrinsic-nature reason already established previously by the statement: 'Even the existence of the intrinsic nature is a reason that follows from the mere existence [of the probandum]'?"

True. However, he thinks as follows: "The inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been described as occurring solely within a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as it truly is; in that case, the fallacy of being a mere part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*) would not arise. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*), likewise, anticipating that the charge of being a part of the thesis will be avoided by means of the subsequent proof of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), restates the previously mentioned inseparable connection as depending solely on that [exclusion], beginning with the words: "The inseparable connection also exists in the case of an intrinsic nature," and so forth.

In the case of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a reason (*hetu*), there is also an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). In what [probandum] (*sādhya*)? In that which follows upon mere existence (*bhāvamātrānurodhin*). The passage beginning with "For he who... is the explanation of this very point. "The inseparable connection of the entity" refers to [the reason] such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Because in the absence of that—namely, in the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) which follows upon mere existence—there would be an absence of the entity that has been presented as the reason. What is the cause? Because of the non-difference between the probandum and the proof (*sādhyasādhanayor abhedataḥ*). He explains this very non-difference with the words beginning with "That which is... (*ya eva*).

That very nature which begins with "whatever is produced" and conforms to the mere state of being produced is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). Since that very nature, by its own essence and without depending on any other cause, is in reality and from the perspective of ultimate truth the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), how could that entity exist while abandoning its own self, which is the impermanence inherent in its intrinsic nature?

"In that case, it is precisely this," says the opponent. "The indication of the subject (*pakṣa*) is the proposition (*pratijñā*). Its referent is the aggregate of the property and the property-bearer (*dharmadharmisamudāya*); a part of that, consisting of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), would be the logical reason (*hetu*). For instance, as long as one says 'sound is impermanent because of impermanence,' it is equivalent to saying 'it is impermanent because of being produced' (*kṛtakatvāt*); and thus, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*). (41) fn. 1: *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.33.

"This is not a fault," says the proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntavādī*). This is because [the text begins with] "all things" (*sarve bhāvāḥ*), and so forth. Here, the collective meaning is as follows: by the first verse, the seed for the conceptualization of properties (*dharmakalpanā*) is stated; by the second, the conceptualization of properties itself; and by the third, the avoidance of the fallacy of the thesis being a part of its own proof (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*) is explained. "All things" (*sarvabhāvāḥ*)—derived from the suffix *dhinuṇ* in the sense that they "undergo exclusion"—possess an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from both their own-nature (*svabhāva*) and other-nature (*parabhāva*). All things are excluded from their own-nature—that is, from their own-form (*svarūpa*)—and from other-nature, whether of the same class (*sajātīya*) or a different class (*vijātīya*). This is because of the establishment of their own-nature; that is, because they abide in their own-nature.

Is it not the case that a cow is distinct from a horse and so forth by way of genus (*jāti*), and a white cow is distinct from other horned individuals of the cow species by way of quality (*guṇa*)? In this manner, the differentiation of all entities down to the ultimate atom is produced by qualifiers such as genus and the like, and not by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

To this it is replied: First of all, a distinction is not produced among entities that are already non-distinct by means of a universal (*jāti*) and so forth; for whether [the universal] produces a distinction in something already distinct or non-distinct, it is in both cases incapable of performing any function (*akiñcitkaratva*). Nor is it [produced] among things already distinct, because that would be redundant (*vaiyarthyāt*). Nor is the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of their distinction produced, since the establishment of the conventional usage of distinction follows simply from their appearing as distinct in their own nature within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore: the distinction of universals (*jāti*) and so forth from one another and from their possessors cannot be established through anything other than those [universals] themselves, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And if this distinction exists by way of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of things, why is it not simply accepted as belonging to the entities themselves? What is the use of postulating universals and the like? As for the Digambara who thinks: "If there were no mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of entities, there would be only one thing consisting of all natures due to the confusion of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); therefore, difference alone must exist, otherwise the mutual non-existence of entities would not be possible. [This is his view.]

This too has been refuted by him, because it is impossible for non-existence (*abhāva*) to produce a distinction among existing things (*bhāva*). Nor is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) possible for things that are non-distinct and produced from causes. If they are distinct when produced, how can mutual non-existence be possible? It has already been stated: "If they are distinct when produced, how can there be a conceptualization of mutual non-existence? Now, if the claim that "all things are distinct" is based on inference, then the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because all things are not objects of perception (*pratyakṣa*). For this very reason, this is not considered to function through perception.

But another says: although things are indeed distinct by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they nevertheless possess properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, because these are perceived. Nevertheless, non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-vijñāna*) apprehends only existence (*sattāmātra*) in cows and the like, not their distinction. For the apprehension of distinction is precisely the apprehension of a particularity (*viśeṣa*) relative to something else, and a particularity is not apprehended without conceptualization; thus, it is the object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), not of non-conceptual cognition. As it has been said:
Particularities, however, are cognized by conceptual cognitions;
and some of these reside in each individual substance, while others are established in many.
"He conceptualized that which has arisen as having the nature of both exclusion and inclusion;
however, that which has arisen with respect to a cow and a horse does not differ from perception.
Therefore, there is no appearance of distinct objects in non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*).

As for the one who says: "Even by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), difference is not grasped; for the grasping of the difference between entities is caused by the grasping of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). And since difference is mutual non-existence, and non-existence is not graspable by perception—since perception does not determine that 'there is a horse in the cow'—perception grasps only pure existence (*sattāmātra*)," this was stated by Maṇḍana.
The wise say: "Direct perception is an affirmer, not a negator;
therefore, the scriptural teaching of non-duality is not contradicted by that direct perception.
Both of these [positions] are untenable, because existence-in-itself does not appear [in perception], since cows, horses, and so forth appear only in their own specific forms. As it has been said:
This is logically consistent, because a distinct form is perceived for each individual substance;
for it is not understood that there is no difference merely because one is unable to describe it.

As for the one who says: "There is no difference at all among entities. For instance, the nature of a cow is exactly the same whether a horse is produced or not; it is precisely that and nothing more, since there is no such thing as a *jāti* (universal). How, then, can there be a difference based on this? Or, even if there were a difference, it is not graspable by perception, because one does not perceive [perception] in the form: 'this is different from that. Such a function is absent in perception," as he said: "For this [perception] is not capable of performing so many functions."

That too has been refuted: the very arising of cows, horses, and so forth in their own respective natures constitutes their difference, and they appear directly as such in their own natures; and that such an appearance is what is called the "appearance of difference" in the world—this is merely a trifle.

Therefore, because things situated before one are established in their own respective natures—by this reason, one who apprehends difference through perception apprehends it by means of a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*). Consequently, the result of the means of valid cognition that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that "all entities possess the nature of exclusion. Furthermore, since it will be demonstrated that universals (*jāti*) and so forth do not exist as separate entities, it follows that there is no ultimate relationship between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*). Thus it has been stated.

[Objection: Is it not the case that things are called "homogeneous" (sajātīya) because of their connection with a universal (sāmānya)? And if the universal does not exist, how can one speak of "exclusion from the homogeneous"? [Reply: This is not so. It is not by virtue of a connection with a universal that produced entities possess a common form; rather, they are established as such through their own causes alone.

Therefore, as for what Uddyotakara says: "The universal 'cowness' does not exist in the cow prior to its connection with cowness, such that it would be redundant to say 'this is indeed a cow' because of its connection with cowness; rather, the entity is connected with cowness at the very moment it exists. Prior to the connection with cowness, the entity does not exist. And that which does not exist cannot be designated as either 'cow' or 'non-cow.'"

That is refuted. For at the very moment an entity exists, it is already established as having the nature of a cow; what, then, is the use of its connection with "cowness" (*gotva*)? Nor can dissimilar things attain a state of similarity through their connection with a universal (*sāmānya*), because for them, the universal itself does not exist. It is accepted that a universal is the state of being similar among those things that are already similar. Furthermore, if it is admitted that entities become similar by virtue of a universal, then so long as they are not joined with that universal, the entities would not be similar.
As long as things are not similar, there can be no connection with a universal; thus, there would be a circular dependency. Therefore, things are produced as similar solely from their own causes.
Consequently, since the difference between a *vāhuleya* cow and a horse is equal [to that of two cows], and no other universal is admitted, where could "exclusion" (*apoha*) be postulated?

This is refuted, because the conceptual construction of "exclusion" (*apoha*) occurs only with respect to universals (*sāmānya*), and because those things that are not similar are conceptually constructed as having the nature of the excluded.

As for what is further stated: "The appearance of a universal in non-conceptual cognition arises precisely from the appearance of [the object] as 'similar'; otherwise, like a brindled cow (*bāhuleya*) and a horse, there would also be a perception of difference between a brindled cow (*śāvaleyā*) and a spotted cow (*bāhuleya*), since they are distinct in every respect. Yet, the cognition 'they are similar' does occur; therefore, this very [cognition] constitutes the universal."

Thus it has been said: "The non-conceptual cognition grasps the object as having a dual nature. Alternatively, if the universal (*sāmānya*) is not grasped by conceptual cognition, then it must certainly have been grasped by non-conceptual cognition as well, because it appears inseparably from the conceptual [cognition]. For instance, those very individuals such as the *śābaleya* cow that are grasped by the cognition "this is a cow" [are the same as those grasped by non-conceptual perception].

It is precisely those [particulars] that appear in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*); it is merely that one grasps some exclusively as non-conceptually constructed while others are grasped as conceptually constructed. Thus, there is a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa-bheda*), not a difference in their appearance (*pratibhāsa-bheda*). Therefore, the claim that "the universal (*sāmānya*) appears even in non-conceptual cognition" is also refuted; for certain similar things appear by virtue of their own causes alone. Furthermore, the nature of a universal is dependent upon its manifestations (*vyakti-paratantra*), and non-conceptual cognition does not grasp the dependence of a real entity.

Since it apprehends the object independently, how can it be said to apprehend a universal (*sāmānya*)? Furthermore, a common form does not appear simultaneously in many [individuals] in the same way that it appears in each one individually. For this very reason, conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), which apprehends a common form among things that are entirely distinct from one another, is erroneous, as it is sublated by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*). Alternatively, if it were to apprehend a universal already apprehended by non-conceptual perception, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because it would be apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitvāt*).

Now, if it is argued that conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) has the status of apprehending what was not previously apprehended because it causes one to grasp [an object] through conceptualization, then memory and so forth would also have the status of apprehending what was not previously apprehended; for they too would not possess the status of apprehending what was already apprehended, since their objects are those being remembered. Alternatively, if it is argued that conceptual cognition has the status of apprehending what was not previously apprehended because it apprehends a thing as qualified by a genus (*jāti*) and so forth—even so, if the state of being qualified by a genus and so forth is a real property (*dharma*) of the thing, then it has already been apprehended even by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); how then could there be the status of apprehending what was not previously apprehended? On the other hand, if it is merely a conceptual construct (*kalpika*), then how can that which apprehends it [be said to apprehend something real]?
Validity [of cognition] arises because its object is superimposed; therefore, it is established that universals (*jāti*) and the like do not exist at all.
How then is it said that "entities possess the nature of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*)? This designation is made by way of imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*), so there is no fault. Thus:
"Those who imagine that the universal to be expressed is the exclusion of the non-cow (*agonivṛtti*)."

The claim that "by the term *agopoha* they have clearly stated nothing other than the actual entity that is 'cowness'" (*gotvavastu*) has been refuted. For it will be explained later that what is being negated is the ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) cowness, not the conceptually constructed (*kalpita*) one.
(Ślokavārttika, Apohavāda, v. 1)

If, in the ultimate sense, there is no relation between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmin*), how then is there a distinction between cognitions such as "sound is produced" and "sound is eternal," given that their object is the single nature of sound?
Or, if these [cognitions] are without objects and arise solely from the seeds of mental impressions (*vāsanā*),
how could there be comprehension or activity regarding external things?

Alternatively, if activity proceeds from the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the external object, even so, since the very determination of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is identical to that of "impermanence" (*anitya*) due to their non-difference, how can there be a difference in cognition? [The opponent argues: Since "produced" and "impermanent" are non-different, there is no real difference in cognition because there is an absence of a difference in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of them; to this, he says: (42)

"Because," and so forth. Since all things are excluded from everything else, therefore, based on whatever [exclusion]—such as from the eternal, the unproduced, and so on—the objects such as sound and the like are excluded; the distinct properties, such as impermanence and being produced, which are based on that exclusion (the exclusion of the locus), are conceptualized and superimposed by mental constructions (*vikalpa*). What remains? Those which penetrate its specific features. This means those which penetrate the specific features of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—namely, the nature of the exclusion from the unproduced and so on—and whose habit is to penetrate them, meaning their habit is to manifest as non-different from them.

This is what is meant: by way of the [conceptualization] "it is not unproduced," it is the very nature of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the conceptual construction of "produced" that has been awakened; therefore, when a conceptual construction arises as "produced," being non-different from its own form, it apprehends the specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound precisely as excluded from the "unproduced," but not as "impermanent. Likewise, by way of the [conceptualization] "it is not permanent," it is the capacity of the latent impression of "impermanent" that has been awakened; therefore, the conceptual construction [arises].

When [the cognition] arises as "impermanent," one apprehends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sound itself, which is non-different from its own form and is excluded from what is permanent; it does not apprehend it as "produced. Therefore, there is a difference in cognition. And because it is sublated, the object appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not external; since conceptual construction has the appearance of an external object solely by the force of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), the object appearing as an external form to the conceptual construction is called its "own form" (*svākāra*). It is not, however, a superimposition of the external upon the own form due to similarity. As it is said in the *Nāmanimittaprakaraṇa*: [1]
fn. 1: Pramāṇavārttika 3.12:
"The operation [of cognition] toward an object would occur through similarity and error, but not at all times;
furthermore, there is no spatial error in cognition, because the arising of consciousness is uniform."

"Of such a [cognition] characterized by the appearance of an external object"—by this [the following objection] is addressed: "Or rather, the apprehension of one's own form as being identical to that which is absolutely dissimilar to the external object is intended to mean a similarity produced by the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*). Just as a cloth, though dissimilar to a jar, when determined as being distinguished by the absence of trees, is determined to be similar to a jar insofar as it is 'not a tree,' because the exclusion of trees is common to both the jar and the cloth;

likewise, the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), though absolutely dissimilar to the external object, is determined as being [identical to] the external object due to the apprehension of a similarity produced by the exclusion of others."

That has been refuted. For conceptual cognition appearing as an external object arises from its own causes alone. Nor is similarity produced among dissimilar things by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because such exclusion is ineffective in producing either difference, non-difference, or similarity. Furthermore, no similarity exists that is itself excluded from others; for even among similar things, how could similarity be produced by the exclusion of others? It is because similarity exists by way of their very own nature (*svarūpa*).

Nor does it occur that first there is the appearance of its own form, and subsequently there appears the superimposition of an external object—which is intent on grasping a similarity produced by the exclusion of others—within that [form]. For when the nature of a mirage has not first appeared, the superimposition of water caused by the grasping of similarity is impossible; and prior to the superimposition of an external object, there is no superimposition of a graspable form upon one's own form, because conceptual construction itself would be non-existent. If it were to exist, it would be of the very same nature as cognition, and thus it would not be dissimilar to the external.

Furthermore, since there is an absence of similarity produced by the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*), how could an external form be cognized? As for inference, its operation does not presuppose the grasping of the exclusion of others, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established through its connection with that [exclusion]. And when the non-apprehension of specific features (*viśeṣa*) by conceptual cognitions is perceived, then the operation occurs solely in a positive form; for, due to the determination of the thing's own nature as being affirmed, the exclusion of others is cognized by implication (*arthāt*).
Therefore, for us as well, the word-meaning is indeed a positive entity (*vidhi*). Furthermore, that which is superimposed as being external is connected with both affirmation and negation.

But surely, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) appears as grasping a determinate form; thus, by conceptualizing an object as devoid of other forms, it conceptualizes a determinate object. Consequently, since the determination of a determinate form has exclusion (*anyanivṛtti*) as its object, how can it be said that the word-meaning is exclusively a positive entity?

That is incorrect, because there is no cognition [of the thought] "I am conceptualizing the exclusion of another. Furthermore, that which does not appear when being conceptualized cannot be the object of that conceptualization. If one conceptualizes a restricted object while conceptualizing only the exclusion of other forms, then there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): for the other form would also have to be understood by way of the exclusion of another, since it too would possess a restricted nature.

If, on the other hand, one conceptualizes the other form as a positive entity (*vidhirūpa*), then the determination of its restricted nature is not preceded by the ascertainment of the exclusion of others.

And it is not the case that, as in the thought "I see an object possessing a universal," there is no appearance of the qualifier-qualified relationship between the genus (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*); nevertheless, because they follow from specific cognitions, the Naiyāyikas and others have postulated the perception of an individual qualified by a universal. Similarly, even though there is no [direct] cognition in the form "I conceptualize exclusion," it is logical that the external form is superimposed upon the aspect of the conceptualization—though directed toward the exclusion of others—because otherwise the superimposition of something similar to the external would be inexplicable.

For conceptual construction arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone, even in the absence of similarity, having determined an external form. As it has been said: "Its nature is produced from the latent impression deposited by the experience of that [object], and its essential character is the determination of that [external] state. Likewise, the nature of the latent impression of conceptual construction is such that it appears in this manner."

Nor can a cognition that superimposes an external form have as its object the exclusion of other things, even if it is caused by a similarity produced by the cognition of another thing. For the cognition of water in a mirage does not have similarity as its object, because its object is the superimposed water. Furthermore, the specific form of entities is not produced by the exclusion of others, because exclusion, being a non-entity, lacks causal efficiency; rather, those forms arise from their own causes alone.

Nor is the determination of a restricted form the object of the exclusion of others, because this [determination] has a restricted form as its object; for this very reason, it is not apprehended by perception as being preceded by the exclusion of others.

Furthermore, he will state that it is not logical for the exclusion of others to be a manifestation of a distinct entity. Nor is it logical for it to be inexpressible as either identical to or different from [the object], for in that case it would be a mere non-entity, like the horn of a hare. Moreover, it could not be accessible through direct perception because it lacks any form (*nīrūpatvāt*). Nor is it accessible through inference, because no inferential mark (*liṅga*) exists due to the absence of a relationship. Furthermore, its postulation cannot be based on the impossibility of an otherwise restricted form, because there is an absence of any exclusion of others that possesses a restricted form.

And how can things that possess a determinate nature have that determinate nature through the exclusion of others? For they arise from their own causes as possessing determinate natures. Therefore, the exclusion of others is understood only preceded by the ascertainment of a determinate nature. For instance, when "jar" is said, it is understood by implication that "it is not a non-jar"; thus, this is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpaka-vikalpita*) and does not exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Therefore, this is established: by means of both the word and the inferential mark (*liṅga*), a real entity is presented in a positive form, and by implication (*arthāt*), there is the negation of anything else. And so he will say: "When those [entities] themselves are understood from words, the exclusion of others is also understood," and so forth (1.128).
Consequently, that which was stated by Kumārila—
But in your position, a word does not function by means of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha);
for here, it is not mere negation alone that is apprehended in the manifestation [of cognition].
However, from words such as "cow," "gavaya," "elephant," and "tree," verbal cognition proceeds by way of a determination in a positive form.

Therefore, it is established that only in those words where there is a connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) does this [negation] function as a factor for the non-exclusion [of others]; elsewhere, it is understood as its own nature. This is because even a word-meaning in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is accepted. How, then, is there a distinction between the Buddhist view and the views of others? Or how is it said that the object of both words and logical marks (*liṅga*) is *apoha*? (43)

Surely there is indeed a great difference [between us], since conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) is accepted by our opponents as having an ultimately real object, whereas by the Buddhists it is accepted as having a mentally constructed object. Furthermore, the "exclusion" (*apoha*) is so called because the imagined form (*ākāra*) is based upon exclusion; or else, it is so called because "by means of this [cognition], something is excluded. Alternatively, the mere negation of others (*anyanivṛtti-mātra*), which is implied by the sense of the object, is called "exclusion" (*apoha*). However, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is called "exclusion" (*apoha*) in the sense that "in this [particular], other things are excluded."

Therefore, properties whose distinctions are conceptually constructed in dependence upon objects that are excluded from one another are made the objects of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*). To show that for this reason conceptual cognitions have distinct objects, and that words which have those same objects are also not synonyms, he says: "Therefore," and so forth. And since the distinctions between properties are thus imagined, therefore that specific particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*) which is established in dependence upon the impermanent things to be excluded is the characteristic of impermanence; by whichever property and by whichever word [it is expressed].

Just as by the word "impermanent" [the object is indicated], sound is also called a "property" (*dharma*) because it denotes a property; yet it cannot be [indicated] by another [word] through that same capacity. By another word than "impermanent," such as "produced" (*kṛtaka*), it is to be cognized in relation to a different object to be excluded. Therefore, the determination is distinct. For that reason, conceptualizations do not have a single object, nor are words synonyms.

Therefore, what was said—that there is no relationship of indicator and indicated between two things that possess identity (*tādātmya*), and that there is no connection between two things that possess a conceptualized form (*vikalpitārūpa*) yet stand in the relation of indicator and indicated—is refuted. This is because it is precisely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as excluded from the non-produced (*akṛtaka-vyāvṛtta*) that falls within the scope of the logical reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*). Since that which is known as "produced" (*kṛtaka*) functions as the indicator, and since its nature is a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*) excluded from the eternal (*nitya*), there is identity (*tādātmya*) [between the indicator and the indicated].

By the words "For all indeed," etc., [the author] states the meaning of the verse while refuting the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*): those things whose stability is in their own nature (*svarūpa*) are "thus" [described]. For all entities indeed have their stability in their own nature; they do not mix themselves with another, nor do they make them one. What is the reason? Because that which is being mixed with another would result in the loss of its own nature (*aparatva*), since it would incur the status of being that other.
It might be argued: "In all things, cognition is of a nature that excludes [others] (*vyāvṛttātmikā*)."
It arises as having a dual nature, and without that, it is not tenable.

Therefore, particulars consist of a universal nature and the universal consists of a particular nature; thus, the entity has a dual form. In this regard, there are two possibilities: either the non-difference of the single form from the distinct [particulars], or the non-difference of the distinct [entity] from the single [form]. To refute the first position, he says: "Of those"—that is, of entities—it is impossible to say that their "distinct" form, which is of a single nature and thus non-distinct, is not their own form, their very essence. Why? Because at that time, one must consider "of that"; for that non-distinct form does not belong to them precisely because it is non-distinct [from them].

Furthermore, regarding the claim that there is non-difference for that which is distinct from a single [entity], he says: "For that very thing would be so, because of the existence of the non-different. If the form is apprehended as non-existent, then that very non-different form would belong to them, not a different one. Why is this? Because of the existence of that very non-different form. Now, it might be argued: "Their difference is indeed admitted. To this he says: "Because of the absence of a different object with a manifold form that is distinct from that non-different self."

Now, it might be argued: "The very distinction that belongs to the particular (*viśeṣa*) is itself the non-distinction of the universal (*sāmānya*)," as it has been said: "But for one who asserts a distinction of the universal, [that distinction] must be accepted after being demonstrated through its particulars. To this, he replies: "And because distinction is contradictory to that very [universal], since it is impossible for that single entity to be manifold."

Now, [it might be argued that] the distinction of the universal is through its particularity (*viśeṣa*) and not by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*). In that case, because the inclusive (*anugata*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*) forms are not mutually connected, there would necessarily be a difference between them. Regarding this, he says: "And that [universal], being of a single form, is established within itself—within its own essence—as unmixed with the form of the individual (*vyakti*). Since it is not perceived as having a mixed form when it is actually unmixed, it is nothing but false. If it is argued that this falsity does not apply because the universal is in some way non-different from the individual, he says:
"This is not so, because superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and the like are impossible in the cognitions of horses and so forth."
"It is certainly not the case that the distinctness of genus (*jāti*) and so forth exists apart from the individual (*vyakti*).

This is incorrect. For if there were identity, by whichever form it is distinct, by that very same form it would be non-distinct; this is a contradiction. Furthermore, distinction and non-distinction do not appear simultaneously within a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, if non-distinction is apprehended by one [cognition] while distinction is apprehended by another, how could the cognition apprehending that [non-distinction] not be erroneous? This is because it apprehends [the object] otherwise than its actual state, and because that [object] possesses a single nature.
Alternatively, due to the lack of mixing, a single form would not possess the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), as it would be a separate entity, like a jar.

Uddyotakara, however, says: “The inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) regarding cows and the like must arise from a cause distinct from the individual bodies (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, because it is a specific [cognition], like the cognition of ‘blue’ or ‘sword. And that cause is called a ‘universal’ (*sāmānya*) because it produces identical manifestations.
(1) [fn. 1: Cf. Nyāyavārttika 2.2.65.]

In this case as well, it is shown that the state of being similar is not produced for similar things by means of some other entity, because they are already established as such; nor is it produced for dissimilar things. Thus he says: "Another entity"—namely *sattā* (existence), *gotva* (cowness), and so forth—is not the universal (*sāmānya*) of those distinct individuals, because it does not possess their nature. Since those individuals have dissimilar forms, and a universal is held to be the state of being similar (*samāna-bhāva*).

Alternatively, because it does not possess that nature [of the individuals] and because it is a distinct entity from the individuals, it is like unity. Now, if it is argued that even though it is a distinct entity, it is the universal (*sāmānya*) of those [individuals] because it inheres in many of them—then there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it applies to dualities and other effect-substances (*kāryadravya*), for duality also inheres in multiple substances; by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), plurality (*bahutva*) and the rest are meant. Likewise, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) inheres in multiple substances.

Furthermore, since a product-substance (*kāryadravya*), designated as a "whole" (*avayavin*), inheres in its constituent substances (*ārambhakadravya*), it follows that [the whole] would have the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to duality and so forth. To the objection that "only that thing is a universal in the presence of which distinct particulars become similar, and not everything," he replies: "No. For by means of which other entity, characterized by oneness, are other dissimilar and distinct things not made similar—that is, not unified? Because such an entity is useless for producing the state of being both distinct and non-distinct, or similar and dissimilar.

Furthermore, since things such as those located in different places appear [as distinct], how could they be identical? At most, the particulars (*bhedāḥ*) would merely possess that [property], meaning they would possess a single common attribute. Just as the elements (*bhūtāni*) and the planets and constellations have a long cord tied around their necks for the purpose of worship, and by means of that single cord they "possess" it at the neck yet do not become one, so too it is with the individual manifestations (*vyaktayaḥ*).

[Objection: But surely, because a quality (*guṇa*) is corporeal, it is logical that there be a cognition of its possession [by a substance]; however, this is not the case for a universal (*sāmānya*) in respect to individuals, because it is incorporeal. [Reply: No. For we accept that [the universal] is inherent (*samaveta*) in them, and that it exists as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). Just as even when there is a single relation with a horse, individual instances are not identical—and for that very reason they are not the objects of a non-different cognition; they are not the objects of a non-erroneous cognition having a single form—just as the elements (*bhūta*), which do not have the nature of a single quality, are not the objects of a cognition having the form of a single quality. It is just like that.

It is established that even when there is a relation to many things, a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) cannot be their universal (*sāmānya*), because that would lead to the absurdity [of universality] in cases such as duality and so forth; yet, things are perceived as "similar. Therefore, the cognition—which unifies these two distinct entities by means of a single form, thinking "this pair is of one nature"—manifests with the universal as its object. It is precisely the very nature of those two distinct entities themselves that appears as a single form.

The cognition does not appear in such a way as "these two are related by means of a single universal," whereby a universal as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would exist. The phrase "like the elements" (*bhūtavat*) is a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); the meaning is that the cognition does not grasp the elements—which are related to a single quality—in that manner.

Alternatively, it is not the case that the cognition whose object is a universal appears in the same way that the elements are related to this [single quality], namely, as "two distinct things related by a single relation."

Now, it might be argued: "The universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the individuals (*vyakti*). And since a qualifier, by producing a cognition colored by itself within the qualified (*viśeṣya*), does not appear as a separate entity from the individuals, [it is non-different]. But even if it is a qualifier, it cannot be identical with the qualified—just as a staff-bearer is not identical with the staff. So how can there be an appearance of non-difference? Furthermore, because they are one in their aspect of non-difference, the relation of qualifier and qualified cannot exist. Therefore, the perception of the non-difference of the universal from the individual is nothing but an error (*bhrānti*). If it is argued that this is not an error because such a perception occurs at all times, he says:
For that which is perceived through one form and is then perceived otherwise is false; however, that which is always understood through that very same [form] is not so.

That is incorrect; for [the universal] would then be non-different from the individual. Furthermore, one must admit a distinction in cognition between "cow" and "cowness. Nor is the apprehension of a relation between the genus and its possessor—like that between lac and crystal—an error, because the perception of a crystal that is not red as being red is indeed erroneous. Thus, the grasping of identity between the genus and its possessor is erroneous; the intellect perceives only the universal.

If it is argued that for one who perceives that [inherence], because inherence is subtle, there is the error consisting in the apprehension of individuals as non-different from the universal—[we ask] how is she "one who perceives that"? From what is there the certainty that this cognition perceives a real universal? Because its object is always the non-difference of individuals, it has no seed; thus it is seedless, and yet it is an error, which is impossible. For an error arising from delusions cannot be produced without a cause.

It is like the error regarding water and so forth. This error, which unites entities that are actually unconnected, must have a cause; that which is its cause is the universal (*sāmānya*). To this, he replies: those very particulars (*bheda*) which have a single effect—namely, the cognition of that universal—are "those having that single effect," and they are the seed of the error. And this will be demonstrated later.

Nor is it logical that a delusion of a single form regarding individuals arises through the superimposition of a universal upon what is perceived; for similarity is the cause of such delusion, yet a universal is absolutely distinct from individuals, since the universal lacks the form of color and shape while individuals possess the form of color and shape.

Now, it might be argued: "The superimposition upon particulars is not caused by similarity, but rather we say it is an error consisting in the determination of identity—'this is that very same thing'—with respect to things that are absolutely distinct. If this is so, then even without a cause for error, if they become objects of an erroneous cognition of a single form simply because they are related to a single [universal], [then our point stands].

In that case, for those things which possess number, conjunction, and—by the word "and so forth"—disjunction and the rest, and which exist as a single entity, there would arise a delusion of a uniform form when they are joined with the quality of oneness; yet such a delusion does not occur. Therefore, even in the case of individual particulars, there is no delusion caused by oneness. For this reason—"that" meaning therefore—just as the universal is intended to be distinct from the individuals, so too, because it is not present in the cognition of the universal and because it does not appear [in that cognition], the universal is not something other [than the particulars].

Or, even if a universal (*sāmānya*) exists, because that universal also abides within its own self—that is, within its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—it is unmixed with anything else, namely with the form of the individual (*vyakti*). Since it does not abide in the individuals, the meaning is that it does not have the nature of a property (*dharma*). Therefore, because they are established in their own respective natures, these entities such as pots are distinct from others—both from what is considered similar by virtue of having an identical form, and from what is considered dissimilar—and are separate by way of their own nature, because they are of a single form by their very essence (*prakṛti*).
This is what is meant by "because they are established in their own respective natures."

He states the meaning of the second verse: "From whatever [respects] those entities are distinct, that distinction is their differentiation (*tadbheda*). Therefore, although their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct, they are cognized as possessing manifold properties—such as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth—by means of words that have been applied through conventional designations (*saṃketa*) to indicate those distinct natures. This occurs even though there is no multiplicity of nature within a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For a single particular characteristic does not possess a plurality of intrinsic natures.

To the question, "How then is there a multiplicity of properties? he says: "Taking the distinction from this and that" (*tatas tato bhedam upādāya*). From whatever [things] they are excluded, taking the distinction from each of those and relying upon it, those words which have been established by convention for the purpose of manifesting each respective distinction—that is, each distinct intrinsic nature (*bhinnasvabhāva*)—are restricted to being denoters of this distinct intrinsic nature. Therefore, a single word does not imply all distinct intrinsic natures; thus, even though those words do not individually imply all distinctions, [they function accordingly].

Because they enjoin a single distinct [entity]—that is, because they enjoin the nature of each individual distinct thing—they are restricted solely to that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). That which is determined by the word as a nature distinct from others is that particular characteristic; they are restricted to that, meaning they have that as their sole object.

[Objection: But surely the object that appears in a word is determined as being external; it is one thing, namely the universal (*sādhāraṇa*), while the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is another, non-universal thing. How then can [words] be said to be "based upon that" (the particular)? To this he says: Since an object is excluded from even a single [instance]—from whatever [thing] it is excluded by words and thereby made an object of them—it possesses a differentiation (*bheda*) within that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is itself differentiated from many [other things], namely from that which is not its cause and that which is not its effect. It is on account of this that they are said to have that [particular] as their object, but they do not have that [particular] alone as their object.

Alternatively, those [cognitions] have as their ultimate basis the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that property which is the locus of exclusion; they culminate in the attainment of that very [characteristic]. What is the reason? It has already been explained that even from a single [entity], there exists its differentiation [from others]. Summarizing, he says: "Therefore"—because there is exclusion from the similar and the dissimilar, therefore for a single entity, however many are the forms of others, there are accordingly, in relation to them, exclusions from those other forms; these are conceptualized as distinct properties (*dharmabheda*) in relation to the other forms.

It is so called because by means of these [reasons], that which is of a different class (*vijātīya*) is excluded. What is the reason? Because with respect to that excluded object, which is a subject (*dharmin*) not established as a positive entity (*avidhibhūta*), there is an effect that is impossible for it; and for whichever intended subject that effect is impossible, it is "that whose effect and cause are impossible" (*tadasambhavikāryakāraṇa*). This is due to its difference from that [impossible effect and cause]. Therefore, because it is excluded—due to being different from what does not have that effect and what does not have that cause—as many as are the exclusions (*vyāvṛttayaḥ*), so many are the linguistic designations (*śruti*) applied for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), by way of excluding what does not have that effect and cause.

That which has that intended effect and cause is "that-effect-and-cause. For example, sound has auditory consciousness as its effect and effort as its cause; that which is not like this is "not-that-effect-and-cause. The analysis of the compound is: those whose purpose (*artha*)—namely, the purpose consisting of activity and cessation for the sake of conventional usage—is achieved by excluding that [non-that-effect-and-cause].

He states the object [of the definition]: that for which effort (*prayatna*) is the cause is called "produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*). By this, the term "sound produced immediately after effort" is intended to exclude lightning and the like, which have a different cause—that is, no cause consisting of effort. That for which auditory cognition is the effect is "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*); by this, the term "audible sound" is intended to exclude that which does not have such an effect. Since all linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) are based on purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and since purposeful action is characterized by the relationship between cause and effect, this same exclusion of things that do not possess such effects or causes should also be applied to words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth.

With the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he explains the third verse. Because distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti-bheda*) and verbal expressions (*śruti*) are restricted to their respective distinctions, therefore—even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a single substratum (*dharmin*)—a particularity (*viśeṣa*), namely a property (*dharma*) characterized by being produced (*kṛtaka*) and so forth, is conceptually constructed and perceived as belonging to that substratum (the meaning of *dharmiṇā* is explained as *nāmnā*, which means "by the word"). That [particularity] cannot be [perceived] by anything other than that [word].

Therefore, because it is to be made known by a word other than the intended one—such as "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and so forth—by another word such as "impermanent" (*anitya*) and so forth, the reason is not a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*), since the words "impermanent" and "produced" have different meanings. (44) The opponent asks, "How so? and so forth. [The response is: "By both the word and the logical mark (*liṅga*). Although the logical mark is the subject under discussion here, the mention of the "word" is for the purpose of demonstrating that [the Veda] is devoid of an object, just like the logical mark; thereby, the authority of the Veda is refuted.

Now, it has been stated that an object is communicated by means of a word or a logical mark (liṅga) in a positive form (*vidhi-rūpa*); so how can this doubt be raised—that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is what is communicated—and how is this understood?

This is not the case. "Exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) is defined as that by which something is excluded; thus, it refers to the very form superimposed (*āropita*) as having an external nature. Therefore, how is it understood that it is precisely that [superimposed form] which is communicated by word and logical mark through a positive formulation, and not the actual nature of the thing (*vastu-rūpa*)? Alternatively, "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) is that in which something is excluded; thus, it refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

How is it known that this very [object] is presented and determined by means of words and logical marks (*śabda-liṅga*) through a positive formulation (*vidhi*)—that is, in a positive form—and not rather that the actual nature of the thing, characterized by the state of an ultimately real subject (*dharmin*), is being presented?

The response beginning with "of another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarasya*) is as follows: The meaning is this—if the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) were ultimately real and entirely non-different, then since the object would be cognized in its entirety by a single [cognition], there would be no application of another means of valid cognition or another word, because it would lack validity as apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*). Yet, there is indeed the application of other words and so forth; therefore, the relationship between property and property-bearer is merely conceptual (*kalpita*).

Although the imagined relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmin*) has already been established by the very refutation of the previous [notion of] generality, nevertheless, there is no fault in establishing it once more by this different method; demonstrating this very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth.

Regarding the term "of one": since the reality of an object's nature (*arthasvabhāva*), which is devoid of any distinction between property and subject (*dharmadharmivibhāga*) and is partless, exists as a perceptible entity by its own very form, what other unperceived part could there be? What other nature (*svabhāva*) could remain unseen that is distinct from the nature already perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such that it would have to be examined by means of those instruments of knowledge known as inference (*anumāna*)? The plural number is used because of the diversity of individual instances (*vyakti*).

"Everything indeed is perceived because an entity is partless; therefore, it should not be subject to investigation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the explanation beginning with "one," and so forth. For the single nature of an object is partless, and that must first be accepted as being perceived, since it is upon that [perceived basis] that inference operates. What is the reason? Because a proof is impossible when the locus (*dharmin*) has not been previously established by a means of valid cognition; for the logical mark (*liṅga*) would be impossible due to the fallacy of having an unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Therefore, the locus must be something already well-established.

This is what is meant: there would not even be the occurrence of the *liṅga* (the mark), let alone the ascertainment of the *liṅgin* (the possessor of the mark) through the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example, when "impermanence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), sound is established by perception; because its own nature (*svarūpa*) is established by that very means of perception, there is the establishment of all its aspects. Why? Because there is no absence of any other unestablished nature—that is, no other nature apart from the nature of sound remains unestablished.

Alternatively, if the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is unestablished, then it would lack that intrinsic nature—that is, it would lack the intrinsic nature of sound—because there is a contradiction in one and the same thing possessing both an established and an unestablished intrinsic nature.

He states this very point with the words "for not," and so forth. *Yoga* is the acquisition of a property not previously obtained; *kṣema* is the preservation of a property already obtained. That which possesses both *yoga* and *kṣema* as one is described thus [as having "identical *yoga-kṣema*"]. This means it has identical properties. A nature (*svabhāva*) that does not always share the same *yoga-kṣema* with another is one that has distinct *yoga-kṣema*. It is not logical for that nature to belong to something whose *yoga-kṣema* is distinct from it, because the conventional usage of difference is based solely upon that [distinctness]. Thus, diversity is established through such a determination.

"Otherwise" means that if this cause of differentiation were not accepted, then—as was stated in the context of the discussion on whether "this is indeed the cause of difference or non-difference"—it would follow that the conventional usage of non-difference (*abhedavyavahāra*) would be impossible. Since this is so, therefore, with respect to a perceptible subject (*dharmī*) such as sound and the like, because its entire nature is determined—that is, because the nature of the subject is understood in its totality—there is no scope for the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), namely inference (*anumāna*), which would otherwise be rendered objectless (*nirviṣayī*). (45)

If it is argued that the same fault applies to you as well, he says: "No," and so forth. By means of a cause for error—such as the arising of another similar [moment]—which serves as the causal basis, another quality, such as stability (*sthiratva*) and so on, would be joined to or superimposed (*samāropyeta*) by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "just as" (*iva*). It would be joined just as the form of silver is joined to mother-of-pearl. How? Because of the perception of a similarity (*sādharmya*) between the form of mother-of-pearl and the form of silver, such as their whiteness (*caikacikya*) and so on.

The form of the mother-of-pearl itself, whose specific qualities have not been determined, is said to possess a similarity of form because it is the basis for a similar cognition; however, there is no such thing as "similarity" that exists as a common property shared by both.

This is what is meant: if another quality were not superimposed by means of the cause of error, then I too would be at fault; however, it is indeed superimposed. Therefore, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates for the purpose of excluding that superimposition. Some hold that, because the object has been experienced and ascertained, another means of valid cognition would not operate since it would merely grasp what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*); but since the object has been experienced yet remains unascertained due to superimposition, inference (*anumāna*), as another means of valid cognition, operates for the purpose of excluding that superimposition.

That is incorrect, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) has no established connection with exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). Nor is it the case that until the exclusion of the opposing position (*pakṣa*) is first effected by the reason, the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) would remain doubtful; for the reason is connected with the probandum, and where the probandum is absent, its opposite is also absent due to contradiction. Therefore, the logical mark, ascertaining its own pervader in a positive form (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*), precludes the superimposition of anything else by implication (*arthāt*).
But even so, how can there be a negation of that [non-momentariness], since the superimposition of non-momentariness persists even when the inference of momentariness has been set in motion?

True; however, once the object of non-momentariness has been negated by means of inference, it is demonstrated that this appearance of a non-momentary form is not produced by that [object], but is rather superimposed due to the arising of a similar subsequent [moment].

Therefore, for that very person who has experienced [an object] but lacks certainty regarding its momentariness and so forth, an inferential cognition proceeds to establish that certainty. Because there is no contrary superimposition (*viparīta-samāropa*) and because of the absence of [factors such as] lack of habituation (*abhyāsa*), the experience is not incapable of producing certainty. Even in that case, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the sake of certainty, because by the certainty regarding one aspect, it is certain in its entirety. Furthermore, there is no object that appears such that not even a single nature (*svabhāva*) of it remains uncertain. Therefore, even in that instance, when one means of valid cognition operates, the non-operation of the other would indeed occur.

The commentary beginning with "yadi" [is as follows]: The analysis of the compound is: that whose nature (*svarūpa*) is such that every reality (*tattva*) has been seen. Likewise, by a cause of error characterized by the production of a subsequent similar [moment], which obstructs certainty—that is, which hinders the certainty [of the object] exactly as it was perceived—[qualities] such as stability and so forth belonging to another moment would not be superimposed (*saṃyojyeta*), nor would they be projected. Just as, even when mother-of-pearl is apprehended in its specific form, the form of silver might be superimposed due to its similarity to white [objects], in that case, the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) would find no scope.

It might be thought: "The superimposition of silver upon the mother-of-pearl does not occur through the perception of a specific form; rather, such a determination arises simply from seeing that universal form which is common to silver. To this, he says: "Not so" (*na hi*). For two forms are not possible in the mother-of-pearl: one form common to silver, and another distinct form characterized by its specific determination. Why? Because it would follow that there would always be a cognition appearing as variegated (*śabalābhāsā*) by way of both a universal and a particular form.

Or, [it is] "due to non-apprehension through distinction": because if there were no apprehension through distinction—that is, through differentiation—such that one could think, "this is the universal" and "this is the particular," the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of duality would be impossible. This is because the conceptualization that "there are two forms in the mother-of-pearl" would be untenable; for if one were to construct duality without a difference in appearance, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), whereby one might construct duality even in other things intended to be unitary. Furthermore, it would entail the consequence that the subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), such as "this is not silver," would never arise. Therefore, since two forms are impossible in the mother-of-pearl, [the object is not a single entity].

Seeing the specific form of the mother-of-pearl, a person sees only its particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), not the universal.
