Because the conditions for certainty—such as repeated practice—are absent, he fails to ascertain it; yet, seeing that specific form of the mother-of-pearl, he thinks, "I am seeing the universal," namely the universal form of silver. Thus, from this conceit of grasping the universal form of silver, there arises for that observer the superimposition (*samāropa*) of silver upon the mother-of-pearl.

Alternatively, one thinks, "I see that which is the commonality—the identical form—of the mother-of-pearl and the silver. From that perception of form, there arises for this observer the superimposition of silver. For instance, since the form of this [object] is exactly the same as the form of silver that I previously apprehended, there occurs the cognition: "This is that very same silver."

Just as there is the superimposition of silver, so too, with respect to a perceived subject such as sound, because of the production of successive similar moments—due to the arising of a second moment that resembles the first through the cause of non-delusion—a person who fails to perceive the difference between the preceding and succeeding moments superimposes that state [of identity] upon it; that is, by superimposing existence, there arises the delusion of stability.

Therefore, as many as are the superimpositions (*samāropa*)—such as permanence and so forth—which are the "other-natures" (*parabhāva*) of this [object] whose nature consists of momentariness, selflessness, and so on, and which arise from their respective causes; and as many as are the superimpositions that arise from whatever cause corresponds to them, those [cognitions] which exclude them become, by implication, the exclusion of that superimposition. As they arise, these are valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) designated as inference (*anumāna*). The plural number is used because of the diversity of individual instances. They would be fruitful; they would be purposeful.

However, those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which have as their result the exclusion [of others] and the negation of superimposition (*samāropa*), do not function toward the communication or illumination of a portion of an object (*vastvaṃśa*) that is not already cognized; for that portion of the object is already seen when the partless substratum (*dharmin*) is being perceived. What is the reason? Because it is impossible to perceive a partless thing through a single part. (46)

Since this is so, therefore, although every quality—that is, the entire nature—of an entity perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed perceived, nevertheless, because of the presence of error, it is not ascertained. Thus, for the sake of that ascertainment, inference (*anumāna*) proceeds in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*) as a means of proof; this has been stated quite clearly. Therefore, another means of knowledge does not function toward what is already seen by direct perception for the purpose of grasping what was not seen. Rather, its operation is solely for the sake of ascertaining what is seen. By this also, the positive sense is clearly stated, while the negation of others follows by implication. (47)

"Grasping the real entity," and so forth. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction with respect to perception (*pratyakṣa*). And when the grasping of a real entity is admitted by means of inference (*anumāna*), since the subject (*dharmin*)—such as sound—is partless, the determination of its single property characterized as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) entails the determination of all properties of that subject; thus, the intention [of the author] is that other inferences, such as for "permanence" (*nityatva*), would then be rendered futile.

Apoha is that which is superimposed as something external; it is so called because by means of it, the object is excluded (*apohyate*). If that [exclusion] is accepted as being established by inference—whether as that which is excluded in this [process], namely the eternal exclusion (*nityāpoha*), or as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is admitted to be grasped by inference because it is non-different from its own form—then the fault just mentioned does not apply.

The phrase "not only," and so forth, is the explanation. The connection is with the words "in some case, regarding a subject perceived through direct perception" (*kvacit pratyakṣadṛṣṭe dharmiṇi*). The meaning is: "regarding some subject perceived through direct perception. The term "in some case" (*kvacit*) is used because not every subject is perceptible. By the reasoning just stated, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntarāvṛttiḥ*).

In that case, inference (*anumāna*) is also held to convey a real entity (*vastu*), such as sound and so forth, by way of a positive affirmation (*vidhi*). It is a determination of the real entity, not [a mere] exclusion of objects nor an exclusion of superimpositions (*samāropavyavaccheda*). "In that case" means when the nature of the real entity is apprehended in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*). When there is the ascertainment of one property (*dharma*), because it is non-distinct from that—due to its non-distinction from the ascertained property—there is the ascertainment of all properties; thus, there is no further operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), meaning no further application of another inference. If it is argued that even though there is non-distinction, there is no ascertainment of all properties, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.

"In that" refers to the property (dharma) ascertained by the first inference. "Its nature" means that it is not logical for something to be unascertained while possessing the nature of a property already ascertained. Explaining how this fault does not apply to the theory of exclusion (*apoha*), he says: "But when," and so forth. When, however, an inference—while performing a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a real entity (*vastu*)—indirectly effects the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*), rather than doing so directly because its function is that of a cognizer; by this, the following objection is refuted: "If there were merely the exclusion of superimposition, there would be no engagement with another object in practical discourse (*vyavahāra*), because that [other object] would not be ascertained by the inference."

Since the exclusion of one superimposition of "unproducedness" by means of your single inference of "producedness" does not constitute the exclusion of another superimposition of "permanence," for that purpose—that is, for the sake of excluding other superimpositions—another [inference], such as that of impermanence and so forth, is set in motion.

Therefore, the external object is not grasped by conceptual cognitions in its own form, but rather the external object is grasped only as unified with their own internal aspect. And since that [object] is unreal and is excluded by this [cognition] from what is other, it is called *apoha* (exclusion).

This being the case, another person, whose intention is not understood, says: "But surely," and so forth. First, an error (*viparyaya*) proceeds by superimposing a form contrary to that [reality]. Then, preceded by that error, there occurs a determination of an unperceived object through a logical mark (*liṅga*). This is not an absolute rule, because inference is possible even in one who is free from error. Thus he says: "Just as," and so forth. "Suddenly" (*akasmāt*) means from that which has arisen unexpectedly. It refers to the cognition of fire from smoke in some place quite abruptly.

For, in that case, when fire is apprehended without cause, the superimposition of non-fire is not possible. Therefore, "that" [means] for this reason, exclusion is not performed everywhere by implication through inference.

"The answer has been stated," says the Teacher. For, regarding the operation of inference as something that grasps the essential nature of a real entity (*vastu*), the following response was given: if the substratum (*dharmin*) is apprehended by perception, then because its properties (*dharmas*) are non-different from that substratum, all [properties] would be apprehended, rendering inference useless. Alternatively, if a difference between the property and the substratum were admitted, there could be no relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) with the substratum, precisely because their difference is admitted.

Furthermore, impermanence and the other properties do not arise from the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), nor does the subject arise from impermanence and the other properties. Consequently, it has already been stated that there is no cognition of a property that is unrelated to that subject, because inference is impossible in a case where there is no relationship of cause and effect between them. This is the point being made here.

Since this is so, therefore, even in that case where fire is cognized from the accidental perception of smoke, there is indeed for the person who perceives that [smoke] and perceives the location a non-ascertainment of its nature—that is, a non-ascertainment of the nature of possessing fire. And that [non-ascertainment] is rendered indeterminate precisely because of error, due solely to the apprehension of the location as being equivalent to one devoid of fire. He states this very point with the words "If that," and so forth.

Alternatively, how could there be a non-determination of its intrinsic nature? Rather, there would necessarily be determination because of the absence of error. Yet, non-determination does occur. Therefore, the apprehension of a subject (*dharmin*) does not grasp the actual nature of the thing; thus, it has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object.

Furthermore—“And he,” and so forth. “He” refers to the person (*puruṣa*). By means of a cognition that is “distinguished from that”—that is, distinguished from fire—he determines that place, even though it possesses fire, as being “distinguished from that” in its form. With what kind of cognition? With one that is “freed from the cultivation of the existence of fire,” meaning devoid of the possibility of fire’s presence. How can such a person be said to be non-erroneous? He is indeed erroneous, because he perceives that which is not [fire] as being that.

For instance: as long as one does not perceive smoke in that particular location, one determines it to be similar even to another location devoid of fire. If, despite there being some experience [of fire] elsewhere, there were a certainty regarding this [specific case], then doubt would necessarily arise; and doubt, by its nature, rests upon two opposing sides. Since that doubt necessarily touches upon the subject as well as its opposite, how could the exclusion of the other (the absence of fire) be established by the logical mark (*liṅga*) even when doubt has been removed?

Furthermore, one who necessarily understands the object of inference solely through the logical mark (*liṅga*) would be subject to error or doubt regarding that object of inference; for it is because he is free from both the superimposition of its form and from doubt that a person, being free from the superimposition of a non-fire form and from doubt, does not follow the logical mark when apprehending that [object], namely, the apprehension of fire. He would not rely upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), nor would he take heed of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that logical mark.

To the extent that one pursues [an object] and attends to it, the practitioner—possessing doubt regarding the superimposition of its form—removes that superimposition by the force of the logical mark (*liṅga*), or removes doubt in some instances; therefore, in all cases, the exclusion of superimposition is effected through the apprehension of its own pervader (*svavyāpaka*). (48)

Therefore, [inference] has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object, that is, the exclusion of others; this was stated, but not directly. "Otherwise" means: if the apprehension of inference were desired to occur without superimposition (*samāropa*), then, given that the subject (*dharmin*) has been established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what further nature (*rūpa*) could there be for that unestablished subject—distinct from the already established essence—for the sake of making which known the inferential mark (*liṅga*) would operate?

[Objection: Surely, an entity would exist when doubt or error arises. As it has been said: "And these conceptual constructions do not arise and perish without being cognized. Nor can doubt regarding the superimposition of that form [of the object] be postulated by following a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the sake of its apprehension, even in the position where no certainty arises; for it is possible to follow a logical mark for the sake of certifying the probandum (*sādhya*).
Otherwise, if the locus (*dharmin*) were established, what would remain unestablished beyond this? (PV 1.49cd)

By this [statement] as well, the cognition whose object is the subject (*dharmin*) would have a conceptually constructed object; however, the superimposition upon the subject is not thereby established. Thus, how can it be said that the exclusion of superimposition follows from the meaning of that inference? True; however, this is the intended meaning: as long as there is no certainty regarding the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the inference does not arise, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, the certainty regarding smoke as being related to a specific location that possesses fire—namely, "this very [place] is [it]"—is itself an error, because it is a determination of something otherwise. For the error here is not merely of the form "fire does not exist here"; rather, it is the error consisting in the misconception that "this is other than the place possessing fire. Therefore, even in this inference, there is indeed a negation of the superimposition (samāropa) that "this place possesses fire" rather than being "merely a place."

Granted, then, that an inferential mark (*liṅga*), which functions within its own domain to exclude that [superimposition], performs the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) by means of that superimposition. But as for this conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) which arises subsequent to perception—since it occurs even when no superimposition is present, how could it perform the exclusion of others? Furthermore, according to your own view, it must necessarily be accepted that its object is the exclusion of others, because its object is a universal (*sāmānya*) and because, in your system, a universal is characterized by the exclusion of others. (49)

Therefore, he says: "In some cases," and so forth. Even when some [object] such as a form (*rūpa*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the cognition that arises subsequent to it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object; for this very reason, it is conceptual (*vikalpaka*). That which functions with respect to an object in which no other part—the aspect of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogyākāra*)—has been superimposed (*asamāropita*), even though it has the exclusion of that [object] alone (*tanmātrāpoha*) as its domain.

Therefore, this is the meaning: conceptual cognition, which apprehends the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) devoid of superimposition through a differentiation of verbal forms, is erroneous; thus, it merely determines the external object as being devoid of that superimposition, but it does not grasp the actual nature of the external thing. Consequently, conceptual cognition has as its objective domain the mere exclusion (*apoha*) of other superimpositions, which consists precisely in the constant determination of the external [object] as such alone.

Alternatively, that which is both non-superimposed and a distinct part [of the object], when present, causes conceptual cognition to arise; that cognition has as its domain the exclusion of everything other than that [distinct part]. That which is this non-superimposed distinct part becomes the object of the exclusion of everything else.

This is what is meant: even where a superimposition has occurred, the negation of that superimposition is not established by means of words or logical marks (*liṅga*), because of the absence of a [necessary] relationship. For this very reason, it is not produced; furthermore, because destruction is causeless, [the negation] is merely due to the cessation of the subsequent [cognition] following the prior superimposition. When there is the ascertainment of impermanence and so forth through words and logical marks, and consequently no further superimposition arises, the negation of superimposition is thereby accomplished.

Likewise, even when [the object] is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), who can prevent the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) by another conceptual construction? Therefore, it is not the case that there is a discrepancy in the statements—whereby an entirely different kind of exclusion of superimposition was stated previously, while now a different one is being stated.
Consequently, this [objection] is refuted:
that "prior to hearing the word 'cow,' there would have been a cognition [of the object] as 'not a cow'."
"By which the word 'cow' is employed for the purpose of excluding the non-cow.
(Ślokavārttika, Apohavāda 92).

When the operation of both word and logical mark is conceived as consisting in the exclusion of others by generating a certain cognition regarding their own object, then it is established that their activity occurs solely in a positive form. Therefore...
"If this word 'cow' is capable of excluding others,
then another sound must be sought as the producer of the cognition of a cow regarding the animal; thus [the objection] is refuted."
Likewise, it is also said:
"Even if the application of words and logical marks is not tenable when divorced from exclusion (apoha),
nevertheless, the cognition of the knower does indeed rely upon a real entity."

fn. 1: *Ślokavārttika*, *Apohavāda* 92. (p. 129) That is precisely what we accept. It is not the case that the operation of negating other things belongs to the word or the logical mark (*liṅga*) regarding the object presented by the word or the logical mark; rather, it belongs to the object itself.

Therefore, as Kumārila says: "Because negation is formless and because there is no differentiation [within it], there is neither the relation of logical mark and marked (*liṅga-liṅgibhāva*), nor is it expressible by words."
There would be no relationship of signifier and signified between two exclusions (*apoha*), because they are non-entities,
just as in the world there is none between a sky-flower and a hare’s horn according to your own view.
Furthermore, if the meaning of a word is conceived as being merely negative in form, [it follows that it lacks causal efficiency].

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is expressed by the word "non-existence," would be of a different kind [from what it is]. (36) If exclusion (*apoha*) were the denotable object, then all words expressing distinct universals (*sāmānya*) would be synonyms when based upon particulars (*viśeṣa*). (42) 1
fn. 1: *Ślokavārttika*, *Apohavāda*.

Likewise, if the differentiation of the exclusion (*apoha*) were due to the differentiation of the objects to be excluded (*apohya*), then that [differentiation] would be merely figurative (*aupacārika*). Furthermore, since an exclusion that is devoid of form (*nīrūpa*) does not possess differentiation through the differentiation of its substrata (*dharmin*), how could it be differentiated by exclusions existing externally? Regarding this, he says [in verse 2]:
"But surely, the differentiation of the exclusion will be established through the differentiation of the objects to be excluded."

Its distinction does not arise from itself, nor is it [derived] from another; rather, it is metaphorical. Furthermore, since even the substrates that come into contact with it do not differentiate it in reality, the claim that it would be differentiated by the external objects to be excluded (*apohya*) is an excessive conceptual construction. (47, 52)

This is refuted, because mere exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not an object of words and the like. (fn. 2: *Ślokavārttika*, *Apohavāda*). He explains the verse beginning with "that which" (*yad*) and so forth. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), words and so forth are included. "It has no mark" (*liṅga*) means that this is a certain cognition whose nature is devoid of a mark (*liṅgarūpa*). It exists [only] when there is superimposition (*samāropa*); for indeed, when form and so forth are perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there can be no superimposition of a contrary aspect at that time. Therefore, how could it have exclusion as its object?

With this much, the first half of the verse has been explained. To explain the second half, he says: "Because there is an absence of that certain knowledge regarding the object of superimposition (*samāropa*); it [the cognition] has as its object the exclusion of that [superimposition]. This is the connection with the subject at hand. He states this very point: "In whichever particular distinction (*bheda*) a person has a superimposition, there is no certainty regarding that distinction—the object of superimposition—such as 'it is unstable' or 'it is without self. (50)

What is the reason? It is because there exists a relationship of sublation between the mind of ascertainment (*niścaya*) and the mind of superimposition (*āropa*). This is due to the fact that there is a relationship of sublation between a cognition of ascertainment and a cognition of superimposition that is its opposite. Demonstrating precisely this relationship of sublation, he says: "For not... [The connection is as follows: even if an entity is perceived as distinct from everything—both from those of its own class (*sajātīya*) and from those of other classes (*vijātīya*)—it is not recognized through every aspect exactly as it was seen; that is, it is not ascertained in such a manner. The word "not" connects with "is ascertained."

What is the reason? Because in some cases, such as [the determination of] momentariness and so forth, there is the possibility of an intervention. This occurs when one has reached the cause of error; for example, even though one perceives a shell that is excluded from everything else, there is no certainty regarding its being a shell because the cause of error—the similarity to silver—is possible. However, in respect to that aspect where the cause of error does not exist, there arises for this perceiver a subsequent conceptual certainty based on memory.

Although there is no difference in the perception of it—meaning there is no difference in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding all its aspects—it is "based on memory," meaning it has the nature of recollection (*smṛti*).
[Objection: But since it does not arise with the mental apprehension "that," how can it be of the nature of memory?

[Reply: True. It is called "of the nature of memory" because it takes as its object that which was the object of non-conceptual [perception], having unified it with its own [present] form. And since the object remains free from superimposition even though there is no difference from perception, therefore the relationship of sublated and sublator is understood between superimposition and ascertainment. Consequently, due to this relationship of sublated and sublator, it is understood that the activity of this ascertainment—which is the exclusion of superimposition—is the absence of superimposition.

Granted that there is an activity directed toward the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa*), nevertheless, such activity does not have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). To this he says: "The exclusion of others is precisely the exclusion of that [superimposition]; the exclusion of others is indeed the exclusion of superimposition."

Therefore, because it functions free from superimposition, not only is the determinate cognition "sound is impermanent" a domain of the exclusion of that alone (*tanmātrāpoha*) according to the previously stated reasoning; even that determinate cognition which arises subsequent to perception is a domain of the exclusion of that alone, and does not, by its own nature, determine the intrinsic character (*svabhāva*) of the real entity. What is the reason? For it is observed that even when there is a determination of some aspect such as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*), there is no apprehension of another aspect such as "momentariness."

If, however, the determination of the nature of a thing were made by a certainty arising subsequent to perception, then, since a thing is partless, such a determination of its nature would be impossible; and because it is impossible for there to be another aspect [of the thing] that is not determined. (51)

Since the operation of a determination (*niścaya*) or of a word occurs solely through the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a real entity (*vastu*), and not by way of grasping the actual nature of the entity itself, therefore, for as many superimpositions of parts or superimpositions of other forms as have occurred or have not occurred regarding a single [entity], there are just that many determinations and just that many words which operate toward their respective objects for the sake of excluding those [superimpositions]. For that reason, those determinations and words have distinct domains and distinct objects, because—by virtue of their own respective causes—they have as their object an external thing that is non-different from their own determined internal forms. Thus, this [is established].
That which resides in a cognition superimposed by the intellect does not follow from another object or cognition;
nor does it produce the intended object, and thus it cannot be said to be the denotable meaning in reality.
Furthermore, if even "intuition" (pratibhā) were to have external objects as its domain, [it would be subject to the same critique].
If the external world is determined to have a single nature, how can there be diverse appearances?
Or, if these [appearances] are without objects and arise solely from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*),
how could there be cognition and activity directed toward external things?

If it is held that activity [of conceptual thought] always occurs through an external resolve (*adhimokṣa*) upon its own part [the mental image], then it follows that the object of the word is unreal, because one acts through such an error; this is refuted, since conceptual thought is accepted as having a constructed (*kalpita*) object. (52)

fn. 1: *Ślokavārttika*. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: when the nature of a real entity (*vastu-svarūpa*) is grasped by means of a cognition (*buddhi*) or a word (*śabda*). When it has been pervaded by a single word and made its object in all its aspects (*sarvākāra*), then regarding that single [entity] which is pervaded by a single cognition of a determinative nature (*niścayātmikā buddhi*), there is no other aspect of that entity that exists as an object to be communicated. Alternatively, it is not the object of another word or cognition that communicates that entity. (p. 132)

For this reason, words that function subsequently with respect to an object already perceived would be synonyms, like the words *vṛkṣa* and *pādapa*. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a single object [for all cognitions], because there would be no occurrence of a cognition that follows distinct objects, such as "the taste is sweet," "it is oily," "it is heavy," or "it is cold. (53)

Introducing [the argument] in order to refute the ultimately real distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*), he says: "Even for whomsoever... and so forth. For even that Vaiśeṣika for whom various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—that is, qualifiers such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and the like—are distinct from one another and from their substratum, and for whom an object such as a jar possesses these multiple adjuncts; for that very object which is differentiated by those distinct adjuncts, the cognition consisting of ascertainment (*niścaya*) apprehends it through affirmation alone; and that cognition is distinct with respect to each individual adjunct.

And by demonstrating the difference in objects for cognitions, the difference in meanings for words is also demonstrated by implication. He explains this with the words "Even that which... and so forth. The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the rest, are mutually distinct from one another and distinct from their substratum; thus they are distinct from that which possesses the adjuncts (*upādhimat*). Based on those means—that is, based on the distinct adjuncts—the mention of "words" (*śruti*) is merely illustrative; the same applies to cognitions as well. "In the support of those"—that is, in the supports of the adjuncts—"and in that very place"—that is, in the adjuncts themselves—they "function"—that is, they operate as denoters. "Therefore" (*tat*) means for that reason.
This would entail the undesirable consequence that terms such as "this" (*ayam*) and so forth would be synonyms, characterized by having the same referent.

To this, he replies with the words "of that too," and so on. If the possessor of attributes (*upādhimat*), whose nature is non-different from those potencies which are the causes or factors for the assistance provided by various kinds of attributes, is apprehended—that is, determined—in its entirety by a single certain cognition, then what distinction could there be among the collection of assisted attributes? What specific attribute would remain undetermined? All of them would necessarily be determined.

But surely, even though a relationship exists between fire and smoke, it is observed that when fire is ascertained, smoke is not necessarily ascertained; likewise, when a substratum (dharmin) is ascertained, its property (dharma) may not be ascertained.

But surely this very non-perception would not exist; for if the nature of fire were grasped in its entirety by a determinate cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*), it would be determined precisely as the cause of smoke and so forth, and thus smoke and the rest would also be determined. Therefore, its nature is not grasped by a determinate cognition. In that case, even by a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), there would be no grasping in its entirety, because since smoke does not appear [in that cognition], its being an effect [of fire] is not grasped.

This is not so. For the fire’s causality with respect to the production of smoke is said to consist solely in its prior existence (*pūrvabhāva*). And since that [prior existence] appears in perception, how could there not be a grasp of the fire as the cause of that [smoke]? Therefore, this is the meaning: in the ultimate sense, there is no mutual dependence between fire and smoke, because there is no relation between them in their states of being already produced and not yet produced. It is merely said that they are cause and effect on the grounds that smoke occurs only when fire exists.

However, because a property and its locus are mutually dependent, if the locus were ascertained in its entirety, there would be a direct ascertainment of all its properties; it would not be a case of implication by way of meaning (*arthād ākṣepa*).

But when the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is one that determines an external object and not a grasper [of itself], then—since the object determined by it can be distinguished from others—it is logical that it implies other properties (*dharmas*) by implication (*arthāt*). Furthermore, if there were mutual dependence, as long as there is no determination of the property (*dharma*), there would be no determination of the substratum (*dharmin*); and as long as there is no determination of the substratum, there would be no determination of the property; thus, there would be the fallacy of circularity (*anyonyāśrayatva*).

But surely the relationship between the qualifier (*upādhi*) and the qualified (*upādhimat*) is said to be nothing other than the relationship between the locus (*āśraya*) and the located (*āśrayin*). And that [relationship] exists only for two things that exist at the same time; moreover, there can be no relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakārya-upakāraka-bhāva*) between those two because this [relationship] requires a difference in time. So how can it be said that "if one thing qualified by a single qualifier is grasped, everything is grasped"?

True; however, others maintain that the relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*) is one thing, while the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) is another. For instance, although the substance of a jujube fruit is produced by its own causes, it is nevertheless assisted by the bowl [that holds it]. Therefore, this relationship of beneficiary and benefactor is asserted to exist between two things that arise at the same time; it is with this intention in mind that this was said.

Alternatively, when a property (*dharma*) is being ascertained, it necessarily implies the cognition of its substratum (*āśraya*) precisely because it is dependent upon that substratum; and this applies to all properties that are so dependent. Therefore, the relationship between property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is merely conceptualized, since it functions through the operation of verbal testimony and other means of knowledge. Furthermore, on this view, there is no redundancy in employing other means of knowledge for the conceptualization of the difference or non-difference of properties, because—being unreal entities—their difference or non-difference does not exist in an ultimate sense.

Furthermore, since other properties must be postulated by means of other valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), how could there be a postulation of the difference or non-difference of properties in their absence? This is trivial.

With the words "Even if" (*yady api*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the verse: Even if it is admitted that for other words—that is, for other cognitions—the objects possessing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have distinct limiting adjuncts as their respective causes during comprehension, nevertheless, that object possessing those adjuncts (*tadvān*) is grasped—that is, made an object—by the words and cognitions. For that possessor of adjuncts, which has a nature consisting of the capacities that serve as the basis for the assistance of the various adjuncts, there is no differentiation within its own self, that is, within its essential form.

Furthermore, if there is apprehension even by way of a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there must be apprehension in its entirety; when that is the case, what limiting adjunct could possibly remain undetermined for it? Rather, every one of them would necessarily be determined. Why? Because it is apprehended as being assisted by all its limiting adjuncts.

If it is argued that through the medium of a single attribute (*upādhi*), it is only the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the substrate of attributes (*upādhimat*) that is apprehended, and not the state of being assisted by the attribute, he replies with the words "For not... and so forth. The connection is as follows: "For the state of being assisted by the attribute is not something else that remains unapprehended. This is because for that [substrate]—which is being apprehended in its own form—the state of being assisted is non-different from its essential nature. Since this is so, for this reason, "of this" means of the substrate of attributes.
That very apprehension which occurs by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*) or essential nature is itself the apprehension by way of being assisted.

Let it be granted that, by means of a single attribute (*upādhi*), there is a perception of the possessor of attributes (*upādhimat*) as having the nature of benefiting all its attributes. But how can there be a perception of the attributes themselves, which are distinct from that [possessor]? To this, he says: "Of those two," and so forth. This means that between the collection of attributes and the possessor of attributes—which stand in a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor—there is a mutual connection within their own essence; that is to say, because the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor is identical with their very nature.

Consequently, when there is the cognition of one thing whose nature is that of a benefactor, both are apprehended due to their connection; that is, there is the apprehension of both the qualifier and the qualified.

He explains this [passage] beginning with "of that which has become its very self" (*ātmabhūtasya*), and so forth. For instance, when the substrate possessing attributes (*upādhimat*) is apprehended, its state of being a benefactor (*upakārakabhāva*), which is its very self, is first apprehended; and when that is apprehended, the state of being an effect (*upakāryabhāva*) of the attributes, which is also its very self, is apprehended as well, because the apprehension of the state of being a benefactor is inseparable from the apprehension of that [self]. Therefore, for this reason, since both the attribute and the substrate possessing the attribute are apprehended within a single cognition, even when that substrate possessing the attribute is apprehended as qualified by a single attribute...

The apprehension of all adjuncts (*upādhi*) follows as a necessary consequence; that is, because it is inseparable from the apprehension of the adjuncts. "Otherwise" means that if the adjuncts were not apprehended, [the substrate] would likewise not be apprehended. Even if one were to say, "[It is apprehended as] the possessor of adjuncts (*upādimat*) which is assisted by the adjuncts," it still would not be apprehended.

If it is argued that the capacity to assist is apprehended only with respect to that very adventitious property (*upādhi*) which at that time serves as the ground for the application of the term "cognition," and not with respect to the assistance of other adventitious properties, [the author] replies: "For it is not something else," and so forth. That nature which is not apprehended as assisting another adventitious property is not distinct; rather, everything is indeed apprehended, because a non-entity (*avastu*) is partless.

One might think: "The apprehension is merely that [the substrate] is an 'auxiliary' (*upakāraka*) with respect to that which possesses the limiting adjunct (*upādhimat*), and not that 'this is its auxiliary'; therefore, there is no apprehension of the limiting adjuncts. To this, he says: "And also not," and so forth. "Apprehended in such a way" means apprehended as simply an "auxiliary. In that case, there would be no apprehension of the limiting adjunct, which is the effect of the auxiliary. Why? Because it would follow that even that auxiliary would not be apprehended as "an auxiliary."

This explains that because [the two] are related, there is no apprehension of the benefactor as such without the apprehension of the second related term; thus, even the term "benefactor" is not apprehended [in isolation]. He provides an illustration of this kind: "like the relation of owner and owned. For indeed, there is no apprehension of ownership without the apprehension of the owner. Therefore, although a single cognition or word functions by way of one limiting attribute (*upādhi*), there is nonetheless the apprehension of all limiting attributes and of the substratum of those attributes in its entirety.

Therefore, even in the theory that there are limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are distinct entities, the same undesirable consequence applies; namely, even in the claim that these adjuncts are indeed separate things, it follows that other words and cognitions would become synonyms. (55)

With the words "But even so" (*athāpi*) and so forth, the opponent raises a further objection: "Those powers by which the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) assists the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), those powers are distinct from the possessor of power. Therefore—due to this distinction—this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not follow. [The opponent explains: "If one perceives the non-difference of a single power that assists a single adjunct, there would be a perception of all powers; and from that perception, there would be a perception of all adjuncts. This undesirable consequence, however, does not exist [in our view]."

He states the reply: "In the assistance of the factors," and so forth. The "factors" (*dharmas*) are the substrates (*upādānas*); regarding their "assistance," if one accepts that there is a difference between those powers and the possessor of those powers, then what do those powers become for that possessor of powers? They become nothing at all; the meaning is that they are not related to it. This is because if there is no assistance from them to the possessor of powers, then [there is no relation]. Alternatively, if assistance is desired for the sake of establishing a relationship, [then the following applies].

In that case, other powers distinct from [the primary] power must be admitted as its auxiliaries; and for those [auxiliary] powers by which it assists, another assistance must be postulated in order to establish their status as related entities. Since another power would have to be postulated there as well, there would thus be an infinite regress.

He explains this with the words beginning "If," and so forth. "With respect to each limiting adjunct" (*pratyupādhi*) means for every individual adjunct. The capacities (*śaktayaḥ*), which are the modes of assistance, do not constitute the very self of that possessor of adjuncts; they are not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Rather, they are distinct from it. Nor do they experience assistance—that is, they do not assimilate it—from that possessor of adjuncts. If so, why are they called "the capacities of the possessor of adjuncts"? Why are they designated as such? Because there is no relationship [between them].

For the sake of establishing a relationship, if one accepts that there is an assistance rendered by those powers (*śakti*) which assist the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—distinct from the possessor of the adjuncts (*upādhimat*)—then this possessor of the adjuncts assists the powers that assist the adjuncts. If those [powers] are held to be identical with its own self, then this possessor of the adjuncts, while assisting the powers that assist the adjuncts, is one and partless (*anaṃśa*) by virtue of those powers being identical with its own self.

With the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, he establishes apprehension by means of the entire essence. When a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is apprehended, there is the apprehension of a distinct power that assists that [adjunct]—namely, the power that assists the limiting adjunct. "In its apprehension" (*tad-grahaṇe*) means in the apprehension of the power that assists the limiting adjunct. "Its assistant" (*tad-upakārī*) means that which assists the power assisting the limiting adjunct.

Of what nature is it? It is that in which all the powers that assist the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have become its own self; that is to say, such a state (*bhāva*) has been grasped, and it causes all those powers that assist the limiting adjuncts to be grasped. And these powers, once grasped, cause the limiting adjuncts that they assist to be grasped; thus the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains as before. What difference would there be from that which was called "uncertain"?

Now, lest this fault should arise, those powers that assist the [primary] power are also held to be distinct from the entity possessing the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). In that case, the powers that assist those [secondary powers] must also be postulated as distinct, and likewise those that assist them; thus, because there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of limiting adjuncts, their powers, and the powers that assist those adjuncts—due to the lack of a finality in a series of ever-further powers—the connection of the object would never be established.

For in this way, the relations [of the substrate] are with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are distinct from its powers (*śakti*); and those [relations], too, are only with powers that are distinct. Thus, each subsequent power is connected to each preceding power—which are indeed distinct—resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), but not with the possessor of the adjuncts (*upādhimat*). Consequently, that single possessor of adjuncts is never perceived even once together with those powers that assist the adjuncts—that is, together with the nature of the assistance provided by the powers.

The meaning is that the powers belonging to the powers of the adjuncts (*upādhi*) are themselves the nature of that [entity], because those powers are not distinct from it. "By virtue of possessing that" means by virtue of possessing the power of the adjunct's assistance. Therefore, since it is apprehended as possessing the adjunct, the postulation of an adjunct is entirely redundant; this is the intended sense.

Thus, first of all, when the operation of words and cognitions occurs with respect to that which possesses the adjunct (*upādhimat*), the aforementioned fault applies. When, however, they occur with respect to the adjuncts themselves, another fault must be stated; therefore, he introduces the position regarding the adjuncts (*upādhipakṣa*) in order to state that [fault], beginning with "If, moreover," and so forth. If words and cognitions were to adhere to adjuncts—which are distinct qualifiers devoid of a basis in a single, absolute entity—by taking them as their objects of comprehension, then that possessor of adjuncts would not be included by those words and cognitions, because it would not be made an object of them.

By way of the apprehension of that [object], which is to say by way of the apprehension of the possessor of attributes, there is the apprehension of every attribute through even a single cognition of a word.

Regarding this, he states the fault with the words "tadāpi" and so forth. "Of that which possesses the adjunct" (*tasyopādhimataḥ*). "Because of non-inclusion" (*anākṣepāt*) means because of non-demonstration. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to that which possesses the adjunct. To the question "How is it useless?", he says "arthakriyā" and so forth. Having placed purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) at the forefront, one engages [with things]; thus, it is that conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) for which purposeful action is the basis (*āśraya*) or the objective support (*ālambana*). Every single conventional practice of those who act with foresight has as its object that which is beneficial or harmful.

And that [exclusion] occurs through two modes—affirmation and negation—since there is no third mode. This instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, qualifiers such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in that [practical] context; rather, it is the specific individual (*vyaktibheda*) which is capable and is expressed by the word itself. Therefore, what is the point of employing words for the sake of [inefficacious] universals? And since this is so, the specific individual capable of causal efficiency is not expressed by words.

Consequently, intended adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as "cowness" and so forth, would not be adjuncts; they would not be qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is because, when a word or a cognition operates toward some substratum of an adjunct by means of that adjunct, there is an absence of a subordinate member—that is, an absence of a qualifier—relative to that [substratum], namely the primary object (*pradhāna*), which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). It is in relation to that primary object that they are thus called "adjuncts. This is the established principle regarding adjuncts according to logic.

But when it is the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) themselves that are expressed by the word, then, because that which possesses the adjuncts is not implied—and thus not communicated—by the word, those adjuncts do not constitute parts of any principal entity; the meaning is simply that they do not exist at all. If it is argued: "Even if only the adjuncts are being enjoined, there is no fault, because the possessor of the adjuncts is indicated and thereby delimited by those very adjuncts which are pointed out by the words; thus, the fault of the uselessness of employing the words does not arise."

That same consequence regarding the apprehension of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) applies equally here. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "He, for his part," and so on. "He" refers to the substrate of the adjuncts (*upādhimat*). By the phrase "due to being inseparable," it is meant that because there is no deviation between the adjunct and the substrate of the adjunct, even when characterized by a single adjunct, it is characterized in its entirety because it is partless; thus, the consequence of apprehending all adjuncts remains as it was.

It might be thought: "This undesirable consequence applies where the word directly denotes the possessor of the attribute (*upādhimat*), but not where it does so by virtue of the object's nature. To this he says: "For what difference is there here?"—namely, whether words should directly convey this possessor of the attribute.

Whether the adjuncts (*upādhi*) are indicated by the tallness or indicated by the word, they would indicate the possessor of the adjuncts (*upādhimat*); what difference is there? None at all. For instance, that possessor of the adjuncts is determined at that time—namely, at the time of indication—by the power of the adjuncts as "the benefactor of all," meaning the benefactor of all the adjuncts. And thus, as before, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of grasping all the adjuncts; therefore, what was said regarding "indication by means of what is indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇa*) is of no consequence, because it is afflicted by the faults previously mentioned.
Because there would be an infinite regress if the powers that assist through their substrates were distinct [from them], therefore powers are not distinct. (56)

Therefore, when that substrate possessing the limiting adjunct (*upādhimat*) is accepted as being assisted by one particular adjunct, there are distinct capacities (*śaktibheda*) that assist the other adjuncts. Consequently, those [capacities] which do not exist as something other than the nature that assists the single adjunct—those which, while the substrate is perceived, would remain unperceived—are in fact not different from it. For this reason, upon the perception of that substrate, there is the perception of its entire nature, including all the capacities that assist the various adjuncts.

As for the Bhaṭṭa who thinks: "Dharmas are indeed distinct; therefore, when a single dharma is determined in a locus (*dharmin*), there is a determination of all dharmas because of their difference. He says this:

"That which persists among those things whose nature is appearance and disappearance is the *dharmin*, or else it is that in which cognition [of the *dharmin*] occurs prior to the grasping of the dharmas. (152)

"In a substratum possessing infinite properties, when one property is determined, the word would be merely a means [to that end], but not a determination of all [properties]. (178) This [position] is also refuted precisely because it entails the same faults that arise for both sides. (57)

fn. 1*: In the *Ślokavārttika*, *Pratyakṣapariccheda*, [the author] raises the opponent's objection with the words beginning "yadi" (*if*). Even when an object has been grasped in its entirety by a single determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*), another [cognition]—that is, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)—is for the purpose of removing error.

With the words "It might be thus," etc., he explains this very point: when there is the apprehension of a partless, indivisible entity, what other part could there be at that time, during the apprehension of the partless entity? There is nothing that is not apprehended; indeed, everything is apprehended. However, although it is apprehended, it is not ascertained due to error; therefore, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) proceeds.

With the words "If this is so," and so forth, the proponent of the established doctrine [Siddhāntavādin] states: that subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which is desired for the purpose of removing error is established as having exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its object—that is, as having the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object—by the reasoning previously stated. It is "like that," meaning like the subsequent means of valid cognition. Therefore, the other cognition of certainty occurring at the prior time, which arises from the means of valid cognition occurring at a later time, that too has exclusion as its object. What is the reason? Because it functions with respect to an object that is free from superimposition (*asamāropa*).

He explains the verse beginning with "tat tarhi" [then, in that case] as follows: Since it has the result of excluding the superimposition (*samāropa*) of another aspect, it is established that [the cognition] has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object by way of negating the superimposition about to arise. Likewise, even a preceding determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*) has the exclusion of others as its object. For what reason? Because it operates upon an object where no superimposition exists. He says this very thing: "In whichever aspect there is the apprehension of this [cognition]. For this reason, it is established that the initial determinate cognition, which operates in the absence of superimposition, has the exclusion of others as its object.

Furthermore, by one who desires another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even when an object has been grasped by a certainty, for the sake of removing error, it would have to be admitted that the object of the certainty is not yet certain; otherwise, error would be impossible. And that is incorrect, as he says: "Moreover," and so forth. How can that form which is not determined by certainties be the object of those certainties? It is not at all.

What is the reason? Because this alone is the realization of an object by means of determinations (*niścaya*): namely, the determination of that object. If that which is intended as the object of determination were undetermined—just like other aspects (*ākāra*)—then it would be apprehended by those [determinations] in the same way as that which is not intended as the object of determination.

"How so? and so forth begins the opponent's argument. Even for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), who maintains that a second means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required for the purpose of excluding superimpositions regarding what has been grasped by perception—whether he intends that an aspect not yet ascertained is grasped by perception, or whether grasping occurs precisely through the force of ascertainment—the same logical consequence applies: how can a form that is not being ascertained be said to be grasped even by perception? Thus, the difficulty is equal for both sides.

He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "no," etc.; the intended meaning is that [perception] is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). "That" refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Even when it is said that it grasps an aspect such as blue and so forth, that grasping is not by way of ascertainment (*niścaya*), but rather by way of appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Since a partless entity appears in its entirety, there is a grasping in every respect (*sarvathā*). "Therefore" (*tad*) means for that reason.

The apprehension or non-apprehension of perception does not occur respectively by virtue of certainty or uncertainty; rather, it occurs by virtue of appearance or non-appearance. Therefore, when there is no certainty, the establishment of something as apprehended by perception is not contradicted by mere appearance. It is not the case that for determinations—as it is for perception—there is apprehension by mere appearance even of an aspect that is not certain, nor non-apprehension by mere non-appearance; such is the connection [of the argument].

If one asks why, he says: "Something," and so forth. Just as when one sees a person and, although determining his humanity, acts with uncertainty toward another, such as a thief, there is a difference in activity and thus a difference in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). For instance, through the determination of humanity, a conventional usage corresponding to that—such as trust—is observed; however, because of the lack of determination regarding thievery, a corresponding usage—such as fear—is not observed. Therefore, that which is grasped by a determination is that whose difference in activity corresponds to that determination.

And since there is no distinction in non-activity corresponding to the lack of ascertainment, there is no apprehension of that [form]. "Because it is thus," and so forth. "Of this" refers to the form (*ākāra*). "Otherwise" means: if its apprehension were not established by virtue of ascertainment, then even in the case of a single form that is intended to be ascertained, there would be no apprehension of it as "this" through the act of ascertainment. (58, 59)

"What, then, is the reason? asks the opponent. "Because it is 'differentiated from everything,' that is, because it is excluded from both similar and dissimilar [entities]. "In that very way" means that, according to experience, there is no conceptual determination (*niścaya*) regarding all particularities (*bheda*) that is merely mnemonic (*smārta*). For this reason, the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) maintains that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must operate with respect to another particularity in order to exclude other forms. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) replies: "Due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes. For mere experience is not the sole cause of determination; rather, factors such as repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) are also auxiliary causes. Determination occurs only with respect to that form where these [auxiliaries] exist, and not elsewhere.

[Objection: But surely, even regarding a momentary form, since it is perceived at all times, there is indeed habituation (*abhyāsa*), and thus there would be certainty. [Response: Here, "habituation" is intended to refer to an object that has been both experienced and ascertained; however, because a momentary thing is subject to the occurrence of causes of error, it is neither experienced nor ascertained. Therefore, how can there be habituation with respect to it? Consequently, this remains established: only with respect to that form where there is habituation is there certainty.

Regarding PV 1.60, he says: "And therefore," and so forth. Even though a particular—characterized as blue or the like, excluded from everything else, devoid of parts, and partless—is apprehended by perception in its entirety, that particular for which there exists a cooperative condition for its ascertainment (avasāya), i.e., its definitive determination (niścaya), is what is cognized; that is, it is definitively determined.

He explains with the words “Even though” (*yady api*) and so forth. Regarding all distinctions such as momentariness and the like, the phrase “to that extent” (*tāvatā*) means by mere experience alone. This is because the experiential cognition (*anubhavajñāna*) depends upon other causes for the production of ascertainment (*niścaya*). He states this very point with the words “For experience” (*anubhavo hi*) and so forth. “According to the habituation to conceptual construction” (*yathāvikalpābhyāsam*) means that it produces [the result] by means of whatever kind of habituation to conceptual construction one has, acting as its cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). He provides an example with the words “Just as” (*yathā*) and so forth.

Even though there is no difference in the perception of the form of the dead woman, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the mendicant, the lover, and the dog arise respectively as [the notions of] a corpse, a beloved, and food, according to their respective habitual practice of such concepts. And it is not only the habitual practice of conceptualization that acts as the auxiliary cause; rather, there is another as well—this he states with the words "In that case" (*tatra*), etc. Even in that case, despite the lack of difference in the perception of the form, there is the clarity or sharpness of the intellect (*buddhi*). Just as for yogins, through the clarity of their intellect, the determination of momentariness and other such qualities occurs by mere perception.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), desire, capacity, and so forth are included; thus, "and so on" means beginning with these. They are the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for the arising of the ascertainment of difference from experience—that is, from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). If one asks: "In that case, when the aforementioned causes do not exist in many instances of ascertainment, how can there be a sequential occurrence (*krama-bhāva*) of those ascertainments? [The author] says: "And of those very [causes]," and so forth. "Of those" refers to the causes of ascertainment; [the sequence arises] due to the differences in the degrees of proximity (*pratyāsatti-tāratamya*).

That certainty for which the cause of certainty is most proximate arises first. By the word "first" (*ādi*), there is a sequence among certainties based on the distinctions in the degrees of intensity. He provides an example with the words "just as," etc.: when a teacher is like a father, then, although there is no difference between one person’s being a progenitor and his being a teacher, upon seeing the father approaching, one determines, "My father is coming," and not [that] "the teacher [is coming]," because the cause for the certainty of fatherhood is most proximate.

[Objection: But even when there is practice in the conceptualizations of momentariness and selflessness, for those who do not perceive reality, the ascertainment of momentariness and so forth does not arise from perception; therefore, he says: "That too," and so on. [It arises] when the cause of error is absent, but not from the mere presence of an ascertainment-condition. Since this is so, when the cause of error is absent and the auxiliary conditions are complete, the ascertainment arises from perception, but not from it alone. Therefore, it is not the case that [the object] was not experienced, and so forth.
And therefore, this remains established: that the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) is apprehended by means of both words and logical marks (*liṅga*).

Now, if even this exclusion were non-different from the object-entity (*padārtha*), then once it had been made the object of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or word, other [means or words] would be redundant, because [the object] would have been ascertained in its entirety.

Now, even if they are distinct, since they are dependent upon that [single entity], when a single object characterized by the exclusion of one [particular] is ascertained by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then by the logic previously stated, all exclusions would be ascertained; consequently, other means of valid cognition and so forth would not function. Therefore, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is the same. That is not so. For there exists no mutual exclusion among entities (*bhāva*) that is either non-different or different. It has already been stated, and will be stated again, that they have arisen as distinct solely from their own causes. (60)

To the question, "How then do designations such as 'exclusion of others' (*anyavyāvṛtti*) and cognition proceed? he says: "In that case also," and so forth. Even in that case—where the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—those words which express a property (*dharma*) or a substratum (*dharmin*), as well as the determinations (*niścaya*) whose objects are both, conform to linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). The distinction between the objects of property and substratum for these [words] is constructed by following convention; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no exclusion at all. This is the meaning.

He explains this with the passage beginning "In that regard, the exclusion of others" (*tatrānyāpoha*). It is not the case that the cow’s exclusion from the horse is a separate property (*dharma*), nor is the subject (*dharmin*) excluded from the horse something entirely distinct. Nor is it that the cow is characterized by an exclusion; rather, as he will state, the exclusion itself is the excluded thing.

If the exclusion of non-horseness from the horse were distinct from the substance of the cow, then the exclusion of the horse itself would also have to be excluded by the substance of the cow, because they are non-different. Consequently, since the cow is excluded from that exclusion of non-horseness, it would follow that the cow possesses that very nature [of being a horse], just like the horse, due to the consequence of its becoming the nature of a horse. For in this way, the cow is excluded from the exclusion of the horse—which is characterized as non-horseness—only if it possessed horseness. And thus, because the cow would have attained the nature of a horse, the exclusion of the cow from the horse would be non-existent, since the cow and the horse would be one and the same.

Regarding what was stated by the Jains and the followers of Jaimini— "If there were no exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), everything would be one and of a single nature"— this was said in response to them: if the exclusion of others were a separate entity, then cows, horses, and so forth would possess oneness.
fn. 1*: Ślokavārttika.

(p.144) Nor is the exclusion of the non-cow non-different from the cow, because it would follow that there would be no cognition of "cow" when there is the exclusion of the horse; furthermore, it would follow that upon the destruction of a cow, a horse would arise, since the exclusion of the horse would have already perished. Therefore, exclusion does not exist at all.

Therefore, as it was said by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: "Is this non-cow (agopha) a distinct entity when the cow is distinct? If it is distinct, is it dependent or independent? If it is dependent, then, because of its dependence, it is a quality (*guṇa*); thus, by the word 'cow,' the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) would be denoted, and not the substance 'cow. In that case, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression 'the cow stands. If, on the other hand, it is independent, in what sense would there be the meaning of the genitive case [in the phrase] 'the exclusion of the cow' (*gor apohaḥ*)?"

If it were non-different [from the individual], then it would simply be the cow itself; thus, there is nothing undesirable [in that]. As for the claim that "this exclusion (*apoha*) is, with respect to each object, both unitary and related to many, and that is precisely what constitutes 'cowness' (*gotva*)," that has been refuted. Since there is no such thing as the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), an entity is merely produced from its own causes in its own form and is excluded from others; and it is this exclusion from others that is conceptually constructed for it. Furthermore, since there is no exclusion in an ultimate sense, that which is the exclusion is itself the excluded. This is because a single thing is made the object of both [the exclusion and the excluded] by two [distinct conceptual operations].

Furthermore, it is precisely that [entity] as excluded from others (*anyavyāvṛtta*) which constitutes the probans (*liṅga*), the probandum (*liṅgin*), the relation (*sambandha*), and the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpaviṣayatva*). For conceptual construction, having superimposed upon the person its own form as non-different from the [object] excluded from others, causes the person to engage with that [object]; thus, because it performs this function so effectively, that very [exclusion from others] is the external referent of the word (*śabdārtha*).

As for what Kumārila says: "Perhaps the exclusion (*apoha*) of an entity might arise from just one thing, or from all things. If it were from just one, then—just as the substance 'cow' is designated by the word 'cow' through the exclusion of the horse—so too would it apply to a lion and so forth, because the exclusion of the horse exists as the cause for the application of the word 'cow' even in those cases. He states this as follows: "Therefore, since they have the nature of the exclusion of the horse, every single thing such as a lion, while bearing that non-exclusion of the cow as its cause, is called a 'cow'. (1*)

Now, the exclusion (*apoha*) of the substance "cow" is from everything else. In that case as well, if horses and so forth are to be excluded individually, then because the objects to be excluded are infinite, the exclusion itself would not be established. Furthermore, because the objects to be excluded are distinct, a distinction in the exclusions would follow. Consequently, even with respect to a single individual, there would arise a cognition of multiple universals, just as there is with respect to different species such as horses and the like.
Therefore, a single universal denoted by the term "cow" is not established.

Nor is it possible for all of them to be excluded in their collective form (*samudāya-rūpa*). For a collection would have to exist as a single unit, yet it is impossible for those things to be excluded to possess such unity or singularity. Nor does there exist a collection distinct from them; and if it were not distinct, the problem of infinite regress (*anantya*) remains as before. Furthermore, they cannot be excluded in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), because a universal is not a real entity (*avastu*); and if they were to be excluded [as a universal], they would consequently possess the nature of a real entity. fn. 1: *Ślokavārttika* 57. 2: Ibid. 60.
That is incorrect because, since all entities arise each with its own specific nature, their exclusion from everything else is already established by their own causes.

Now, if it is asked how this [exclusion] is known, one must consider: does a cow appear in perception as having the nature of past, future, or present horses and so forth? If you say "no," then how is it that the exclusion of all those [others] is not established by perception? For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exclude other things by grasping them with its two hands; rather, its exclusion of others consists precisely in the manifestation of an object of a determinate form. Therefore, the very apprehension of an object of determinate form within perception is the apprehension of the exclusion of everything else.

And having ascertained its own object, it ascertains everything that is not thus by way of its otherness; therefore, a simultaneous negation of all else is made in a general and undifferentiated manner. This is because a universal has the nature of an unascertained particularity. As it has been said:

"Because it establishes merely the thing as excluded from what does not have that form, the [inferential cognition] is declared to have a universal as its object, since it is not established through a distinction of the mark (*liṅga*). (Pramāṇasamuccaya)
Therefore, the reality of something to be excluded (apohya) is indeed accepted [by you].

Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that being an object of exclusion implies reality, since even non-existence (abhāva) is an object of exclusion, yet it has been stated that this [non-existence] lacks reality. Consequently, the notion that "cowness" (gotva) exists in a single individual through the "exclusion of non-cows" (agopoha), which is characterized by the simultaneous exclusion of all [other things], and that various conceptualized universals—such as "non-horseness," "non-lionness," "non-buffalooness," and so forth—are established through the exclusion of each horse and other animals respectively, and that words function by means of these [universals] to denote them, is quite insignificant.

If there is no difference between exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and the object denoted as excluded (*vyāvṛtta*), how can there be a difference between the word and the cognition [expressing] "exclusion" and "excluded"? For instance, "exclusion" is one word, while "excluded" is indeed another word. Likewise, there is also a difference in cognition: when "exclusion" is stated, only the property (*dharma*) is understood; when "excluded" is stated, the substratum (*dharmin*) is understood. Therefore, he says: "from the word," and so forth. The cognition that arises from a word expressing either the property or the substratum is "verbal apprehension" (*śabdapratipatti*).

The expression “the word and the cognition of the word” is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (a single remainder of dissimilar items). The meaning is that there is no difference between the distinction of the word and the cognition that arises from the word. [This refers to] the convention (*saṃketa*), which is the establishment of the relationship between the name and the named; because of the distinction of that convention. And the distinction of convention will be demonstrated immediately thereafter (in verse 1.63) with the words “the exclusion of other distinctions,” and so forth. The ellipsis to be supplied is: “there is no distinction of the denotable object (*vācya*) in reality between the two words ‘property’ (*dharma*) and ‘subject’ (*dharmin*). (61)

The opponent objects with the words "But surely... and so forth: "If there is no difference in what is to be expressed (*vācya*), why is a distinction in convention (*saṃketabheda*) not logical? To this he replies: "Of the two," and so forth. This genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), because of the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65], and because of the optionality provided by the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā* [Pāṇini 2.3.64] which applies when both [agent and object] are applicable—specifically, by the restriction *karmaṇi* [Pāṇini 2.3.66]. The meaning is that a single object is denoted by two words, namely the word for the property (*dharma*) and the word for the substratum (*dharmin*). If a single thing is to be expressed by two [words], then the convention is redundant.

Likewise, in the phrase "tathā ca," since there is no difference between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*), the genitive case in "the cowness of the cow" (*gor gotvam*) expresses a distinction (*vyatireka*). This is because that genitive case, being a marker of distinction, functions by relying on a real difference in entities, as in the expression "Devadatta’s water-pot. Thus, it has been argued that in the absence of such a convention, and consequently in the absence of the genitive case expressing distinction— *fn.

First, setting aside the fault regarding the absence of case-endings (*vibhakti*), he says: "Of the two," and so forth. Even though two words—one denoting the property (*dharma*) and one denoting the property-bearer (*dharmin*)—express a single object, the case-ending is "distinct" (*vyatirekin*). That is, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses distinction. The word "iva" (like/as if) is displaced [in the sentence] and indicates that the meaning is "as if distinct. This is due to a slight degree (*leśa*) of difference caused by a difference in conventional designation (*saṃketa*) regarding the expressed object; it is not, however, due to an ultimate difference in the thing itself.

As he explains with the words beginning "Indeed, [it is] not [dependent] on words," etc.: "[Dependent] on the nature of the object" means dependent on the external particular (*bāhyasvalakṣaṇa*). What is the reason? Because, if [words were dependent] on desire—that is, by the power of human will—there would follow the undesirable consequence that they do not apply even to non-existent things. "They" refers to words whose application is bound to desire; in whatever manner they express a distinction, they may function in two ways: in the case of a distinction, as in "the king's man"; and in the case of a non-distinction, as in "the self is indeed the seer of the self."

Thus, although the object is non-different, words applied by being so designated express that object as if it were differentiated, without obstruction, by assuming a semblance of difference. This is because, in reality, there is no difference in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For this reason, he states "cow" (*gaur*) as denoting the substratum (*dharmin*), and "cowness" (*gotva*) as denoting the property (*dharma*). Even though these two denote the same thing, they are used for the purpose of conveying a certain aspect of the object, namely, the cow as excluded from non-cows.

For the purpose of manifesting "cowness" (*gotva*), which has the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*) as its cause: when the convention (*saṃketa*) is established in this way—that the mere exclusion of non-cows is what is to be conveyed by the word "cow"—the case ending is not distinct from its referent. Thus, there occurs the genitive case in the form "this [thing] has cowness" (*asya gotvam*). The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is "that of which there is a distinct referent" (*vyatirikto 'rtho 'syāḥ*). It appears as if presenting the property (*dharma*) as a separate entity from the substratum (*dharmin*).

"Even when there is no difference in meaning" means even when the property is not distinct [from the substratum]. What is the reason? Because of the habitual observation of such usage. When there is a difference in entities, because of the habitual observation of the use of the genitive case, as in "Devadatta’s water-pot" and so forth.

This is what is meant: let there be a difference between the entity and its property, or let there not; in any case, the use of the ablative case-ending (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) follows merely the speaker’s whim. Simply through the habit of observing such usage, the word makes the object appear as if distinct. "To that extent" means merely by the employment of the case-ending. "In all cases" means even when there is no difference in the object itself.
