In expressions such as *gaur gotvam* ("the cow is cowness"), there is no ultimate difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).

Therefore, even in other cases where there is no difference in the object, because there is no necessary connection for a word that functions by expressing exclusion (*vyatireka*) when it is employed according to the will of a person, we observe that words function by the power of human intention even in the absence of such an external denotable object. Thus he says: "Just as," and so forth. A single entity is expressed by the singular number in a certain context, as in the case of "you" (*tvam*).

Even though there is no distinction—that is, even though there is no distinction in their oneness—that very same entity is expressed by the plural "you" (*yūyam*). Therefore, since the plural is observed even when referring to a single thing, it is understood that the application of words does not correspond exactly to the objective reality. If it is argued that the plural is used even for a single person because of the extended rule (*atideśa*) "some [grammarians] [use the plural] for *yuṣmad* when it refers to a superior," this must be considered further.

Is it that the sentence of extension (*atideśavākya*) effects a plurality for a single entity, or is it that the mere plural ending, which was not previously applicable, is being prescribed? First, it cannot be the former position, because an actual thing (*vastu*) cannot be established by a mere verbal expression. As for the second position, it is already established that the application of words occurs solely through the force of [the speaker's] intention. Thus, the fault regarding the absence of case-endings has been refuted.

He introduces that very [point] in order to avoid the fault of the absence of convention: "But because of the absence of purpose," and so forth. There is an absence of purpose because a single [entity] is denoted by both the word for the subject (*dharmin*) and the word for the property (*dharma*). Yet, that purpose certainly exists: there are other distinctions relative to "cowness" (*gotva*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), earthiness (*pārthivatva*), and so on; their exclusion is their non-acceptance.

Those two—rejection and non-rejection—are, respectively, the purpose (*pada*) or motive for that distinction in convention (*saṃketabheda*) between those two words denoting the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*), which distinction conforms to the desire of the cognizer—that is, it follows the wish of the hearer.

This is what is meant: when a cognizer, having no further desire for the form excluded from others, seeks to know a cow-individual as excluded from a horse alone, then—as long as one does not superimpose an exclusion from the horse as a distinct entity and likewise express it through a worldly term denoting a property (*dharma*) preceded by convention—so long is it impossible to communicate the object sought by the other. Therefore, for that purpose, it is said: "this [cow] is non-horse."

For in this way, because the subject (*dharmin*) is not the primary focus, there would be no implication of a form excluded from others, nor an exclusion from just one thing such as a horse. Yet, if one were to say "it is not a horse" at that time, then by that very expression, the form excluded from others would also be implied. And how could one who speaks of what is not sought after when what was sought after is not being inquired about not be considered insane?

Furthermore, when one desires to know a cow-individual as excluded from a horse—its form being characterized by exclusion from others—even then, as long as the individual is not presented to the other as qualified by the exclusion from horses, having been superimposed as the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*), and is not expressed by a worldly term denoting the subject preceded by a convention, so long the object desired to be known cannot be communicated. Therefore, for that purpose, it is said: "This is not a horse."

For in this way, by virtue of the primacy of the subject (*dharmin*), there occurs an implication of a form excluded from others, and the individual cow (*go-piṇḍa*) is thereby described as being excluded from horses. It is not, however, explained in that manner as "it has non-horseness," because that would entail the failure to imply the form excluded from others that is actually sought after by the inquirer. And how could one who speaks of a matter not sought after not be a madman? Furthermore, all verbal usage is preceded by convention (*saṃketa*), and convention is itself preceded by an object constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it is logical that even through conceptual thoughts, the cognition of the relationship between property and subject (*dharma-dharmin-bhāva*) occurs by means of this very same door.

Therefore, what was said—that while there may be a distinction in the application of words denoting the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) based on whether they exclude other differences or not—the question of how the conceptualization of the property and the property-bearer is understood is thereby refuted.

Clarifying this very point through its application, he says: "When this," and so forth. "The cognizer" refers to the hearer. Therefore, "exclusion from others"—that is, from horses and the like—refers to another [animal] such as a buffalo; "the nature excluded from buffaloes and the like" means a nature that is independent of existence (*bhāva*), that is, independent of being (*sattā*). In the case of a specific individual, a cow, one desires to know merely the exclusion from horses: "Does it have a form excluded from horses?"

"For the purpose of making known that which is thus" means: in accordance with what the cognizer desires to know, for the purpose of making known the mere exclusion from the horse—which is "thus" constituted—one makes known (prabodhyate) or reveals (prakāśyate) non-horseness by means of a word for which a convention has been established regarding the mere exclusion of the horse, while other exclusions have been set aside. [One reveals it] thus: "This individual possesses non-horseness. The exclusion from the horse and so forth is the basis for the other exclusions, such as the differentiation from buffaloes and the like.

The cognizer is one who has no further desire for those [other exclusions]. "That" refers to the composite whole (*piṇḍa*). This means that he wishes to know the substance "cow" as conjoined with the exclusion of the horse through an exclusion that does not reject other internal distinctions. That is to say, he is one by whom other internal exclusions, such as the buffalo and so forth, have not been abandoned. Regarding that very thing in which other internal distinctions have not been abandoned—that is, regarding that very exclusion of the horse—speakers employ a word denoting the substratum (*dharmin*), saying, "This is not a horse. To the question, "In what manner do they employ it? he says: "For the sake of manifesting it in that way."

[This is] for the sake of manifesting the exclusion of the horse (*aśvavyavaccheda*) whose other differences have not been rejected. Others read: "for the sake of manifesting in that way the very exclusion of the horse whose other differences have not been rejected. Even then, this is the meaning: they employ—that is, they express—precisely that exclusion of the horse, which consists in the form of the horse's negation, by means of the word that expresses the locus (*dharmin*), namely, by the statement "this is not a horse."

For what purpose? For the sake of manifesting that which is of such a kind while not excluding other distinctions—that is, for the sake of manifesting [the object] by means of a word denoting a property (*dharma*) which does not exclude other distinctions. Precisely for this reason, in the phrase "by which," in the case of a word denoting a property mentioned previously, other distinctions are excluded; thus, having formed the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) in a general sense, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) should be applied. This is subsequently connected with the phrase "of the operation of the word" (*śabdavṛtteḥ*). Otherwise, it would have to be "because other distinctions are excluded.
In this same way, the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) should be understood for other words of this same class.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence of two words with distinct causes [of application] in a single substratum. The relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) is the relationship between that which is to be excluded and that which excludes. An example is: "His cow-ness is white" (*gotvam asya śuklam*). Because the word for a quality (*guṇaśabda*) possesses the gender of its denotation, it takes the neuter gender. Others read it as "white" (*śukla*), [in the masculine].

And they explain it as follows: For the word *guṇa* (quality), when employed as referring to quality alone—having set aside other distinctions—is masculine; whereas for words such as *śukla* (white) and others that function solely with respect to quality, [the gender] belongs to the quality itself. But for those [words] that function with respect to that which possesses the quality (*tadvat*), the gender belongs to the thing denoted (*abhidheya*). Thus, between these two [types of words], which both function with respect to a mere property (*dharma-mātra*), there is neither grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) nor the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).

He asks, "Why is there no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? and answers with the words beginning "tanmātra" (*in that alone*, etc.). This explains that coreferentiality and so forth belong only to the object as it appears in cognition; it does not belong to the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because that is inexpressible. It is merely through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) that it is said to apply even to the external. Furthermore, if a single cognition produced by two words were to arise with respect to a single substratum (*dharmin*) appearing as endowed with two properties, then coreferentiality would exist.

In this case, however, there is a relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the cognition—which is characterized solely by the particularity of "cowness" (*gotva*) and excludes other differences—and that which serves as its substratum (*tadāśrayabhūta*). This is because [the cognition] does not appear as a single entity with a non-different substrate (*dharmyabheda*), being the very basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The meaning is that the cognition does not manifest after having grasped a single substrate as conjoined with both "cowness" and "whiteness."

Or rather, regarding the phrase "of that which has it as its basis": that very *gotva* (cowness) is the basis for that cognition; because the individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*) does not appear as identical with that specific [cognition], which—by means of that specific [aspect] consisting solely of *gotva*—has excluded all other properties. For when one employs the expression "this has *gotva*," a cognition arises that apprehends the property as having a distinct form. Therefore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Because it excludes other properties and because the cognition has no further expectation regarding other distinctions, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified [between the two words].

However, in the second case—the position that the word expresses the substratum (*dharmin*)—there occurs grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or the relationship of qualifier and qualified, as in "the white cow. He states the cause for this coreferentiality with the words "In that way," and so forth. "In that way" means according to convention (*saṃketa*); that is, by the reason of following the convention of the word for the substratum with respect to a real entity whose other distinctions have not been excluded. "Joining" (*yojana*) is the synthesis [of the two words] upon a single substratum.

"Phenomena whose cause is exclusion are 'exclusion-phenomena' (*vyavacchedadharmāḥ*); and since they are gathered together, they are 'all-inclusive exclusion-phenomena'—this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. By means of those phenomena acting as instruments, [the object] possesses divisions; that is, because the single substratum (*dharmin*), which possesses many divided properties, appears to the intellect through the presentation of words. In other words, the intellect appears by presenting the substratum possessing many properties as if it were one."

However, the subject (*dharmin*) manifested as an appearance in cognition is not a single entity in reality, because the distinction between property (*dharma*) and subject (*dharmin*) constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is unreal. Some also read "of one alone" (*ekasyaiva*); in that case too, it should be understood that this is logical only by virtue of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer.

Thus, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established. And because the word denoting the subject (*dharmin*) functions without excluding other distinctions, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) arises from the very fact that the cognition produced by it depends upon those unexcluded other distinctions—as in "the cow is white" or "the cow is blue. The word "and" (*ca*), as before, refers back to the previously stated reason.

This alone is the pervader of all linguistic usage, and not anything else imagined by others, such as universals (*sāmānya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth, because those [concepts] are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus he says: "This very difference," and so on. This very difference between two words denoting a substance (*dravya*) and a state (*bhāva*) is characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other properties (*dharmāntara*). "Everywhere" means: in the case of a universal and that which possesses a universal; in the case of a quality and that which possesses a quality; in the case of an action and that which possesses an action—in every object, the word denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) is the one expressing the substance.
The word *dharma* denotes an entity (*bhāva*). For this reason, there is no difference whatsoever in the ultimate sense between the referents of those two words, *dravya* and *bhāva*.

He explains this with the words "Therefore," and so forth. By means of being the object of a determinative cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*), there is no distinction whatsoever. For instance, just as when "cowness" (*gotva*) is mentioned, there is a determination regarding the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyavaccheda*) in that very [referent], so too when "cow" (*go*) is mentioned—although what is expressed is the exclusion of the non-cow along with other differences that have not been rejected—nevertheless, the determination pertains only to the exclusion of the non-cow, while regarding the other differences, there is merely a non-rejection.

And that very same thing is the referent of the word (*śabdārtha*) wherein a verbal ascertainment (*śābdo niścayaḥ*) occurs; thus, there is no difference in the expressed object (*vācya*) between two words—one denoting a property (*bhāva*) and the other denoting a substance (*dravya*). Rather, they differ merely in whether they exclude other distinctions (*bhedāntara*) or not. He states this very point: "One [word] refers to that alone," and so forth. "One" refers to the word for a property (*dharmaśabda*); "that" refers to what is excluded from non-cows (*agovyavacchinna*). That property-word by which other distinctions are excluded is described as such.

The word *anya* (other) is a term for a substratum (*dharmin*) which, without negation, conveys that very same aggregate through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus, there is no difference regarding the determination of the substance; rather, the difference consists merely in negation and non-negation. Since this is understood in the same way for "Devadatta goes" and "Devadatta is going," there is no difference whatsoever; this should be applied similarly in other cases as well. (63, 64)

Even that fourfold application of words—divided according to genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and relation (*sambandha*)—is subsumed by this very distinction of properties inherent in the object; thus he says: "desiring to make known," and so forth. Desiring to make known the ultimate [object], characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions, [he uses] either a *taddhita* [derivative], meaning one ending in a *taddhita* suffix, or even a *kṛt* [derivative], meaning one ending in a suffix designated as *kṛt*.

Or if one were to express [the object] by means of another word—either a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) distinct from a primary derivative (*kṛt*) or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), or an underived word (*avyutpanna*) such as "white" (*śukla*)—then there would be no further distinction [of the object] other than the specific characteristic of either excluding or not excluding other distinctions.

He explains this with the words beginning "to this extent" (*etāvantam*). "To this extent" refers to the characteristic of having excluded other distinctions. The connection is that [the speaker] might also indicate [the object] by means of a primary derivative (*kṛt*).

When the root *pac* (to cook) denotes an action such as placing [the pot] on the fire that resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*), and the suffix *ghañ* is applied to that very same [action], then by the word *pācakatva* (the state of being a cooker), the relation between the action and its factor—the inherence (*samavāya*)—is expressed. Thus, the word *pāka* (cooking) has the same meaning as the word *pācakatva*. Both of these convey an object that excludes non-cookers, having set aside other differences [between them].

But when the action residing in the object (*karmastha*)—namely, the transformation (*vikṛti*)—is the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook), then how can the word *pācakatva* (the state of being a cooker) denote a relation? This is because *pācakatva* and *pāka* (cooking) have different meanings. Or rather, [how could it denote the relation] by means of something other than a primary derivative (*kṛt*) or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), such as a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth? The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "In order to make known that which has become thus, and to make known the exclusion of other differences, one should show it by means of a convention established by oneself," for example: "Devadatta sleeps" (*devadattena śayyate*) or "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklatvam*).

In this case as well, the very same meaning that belongs to the word *śāyaka* (the shooter) is the very same meaning for *śayyate* (is shot), with other distinctions excluded. Likewise, the very same meaning that belongs to "the white cloth"—which is the exclusion of what is non-white and has other distinctions excluded—is the very same meaning for "the whiteness of the cloth," with other distinctions excluded.

"By the mere mention [of it]" means: by the mere expression of the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) residing in a single substratum (*ekadharmin*), which consists of the distinction between what is rejected and what is not rejected; that very entity, though in reality distinct from other objects, appears as if divided into the forms of property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*). However, it does not actually become so—this is the connection [of the sentence]. What is the reason? Because the terms "property" and "substratum" have been established as conventions (*saṃketa*) solely for the purpose of making known that single entity as it truly is, namely, as possessing the distinction between what is rejected and what is not rejected.

Or rather, "merely by such a designation" means that by the mere designation of a property (*dharma*) that is a distinct entity, the essential nature of that [subject] becomes in the ultimate sense indeed a distinct entity; for the term "property" has been established as a convention in order to make known that very thing which is thus constituted—namely, that which is independent of other distinctions and excluded from others.

"Now, [the opponent] says: 'But surely... and so forth. It is said that there is a relation; that is, the relation between the action of cooking and the agent, the cook, is characterized as inherence (*samavāya*). For it is observed that a nominal suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) following a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix expresses a relation, as it has been stated: 'In compounds, *kṛt* derivatives, and *taddhita* derivatives, there is the expression of a relation. And the word 'cook' (*pācaka*) ends in a *kṛt* suffix; it is not the mere action consisting of cooking itself that is expressed by the word 'cook-ness' (*pācakatva*)."

This is what is meant: the action is indeed distinct from the agent, and the relation between the two is likewise distinct. Consequently, even though the root *pac* denotes an action residing in the agent, the meaning of *pāka* and the word *pācaka* are not identical. He refutes this with the words "not indeed by the cooking," and so forth.

The agent designated by the word "cook" is said to be something entirely distinct from the act of cooking itself, being conjoined with a real, substantial activity (*vyāpāra*) consisting of the process of cooking that resides within the agent. This is the kind of independent agent, separate from the action, who is described by the Vaiśeṣikas and others as one in whom the relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*) is a real entity. However, such an independent agent, existing apart from the action, will be refuted.

The point is this: if action or the agent is not distinct [from the substance], how could there be a relation that could be expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*)? Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of this" (*asya*), one must supply the words: "that which is the denotation of the word *pācaka*—the mere entity (*vastumātra*) excluded from what is not a cook, yet not excluding other differences—that very thing denoted by the word *pācaka* is also expressed by the term *pācakatva*. This is because it is precisely that [entity] which excludes other differences that is being denoted.

But the relation is not denoted, because it does not exist as a [real] entity. Precisely that which was stated as the referent of the word "cook" is also the referent of the word "cooking," as indicated by the word "also" (api).

Another explanation: [the phrase] "not indeed by cooking" (*na vai pākena*) uses the word "cooking" (*pāka*) to denote, according to the position of those who advocate the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), a distinct and separate agent of cooking (*pācaka*) who serves as the locus of the action—exactly as it is described by the opponent, such that he would be the locus of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*). Since such a thing is unestablished, what is expressed instead is the exclusion of the non-cooker (*apācakavyāvṛtti*), by way of rejecting other differences. He states this very point with the words "but that which... and so forth.

The word *yat* refers to that which is to be expressed, characterized by the exclusion of non-cooks (*apācaka*) and having other internal differences rejected. The word *asya* refers to that very same thing denoted by the word *pāka*, which was immediately presented following the word *pāka*; it is also denoted by the word *pācakatva*. It is not a [real] relation, because such a relation is unestablished. These are therefore false conceptual constructions, being unstable and arising from what lacks the force of real entities (*avastubalāyāta*). (65)

But how is it understood that action does not exist as something distinct [from the substance], nor its inherence [in it]? To this he says: "Just as... and so forth. "Or its inherence" means the inherence of the action and the factors of action (*kāraka*). And because there is no difference between exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛttimat*), for that reason, the object of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—that is, that which possesses a universal (*jātimat*)—is denoted by words. Thus, whatever fault exists in the position of "possessing that" (*tadvatpakṣa*) would also apply to the exclusion of others; therefore, the description of the position of "possessing that" has been rejected. For if one were to admit the separateness of the universal and that which possesses it, then the fault mentioned regarding the position of "possessing that" would indeed occur.

"Of that which is qualified by it" means that because words denote an object qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), [the fault] "stated regarding the position of [the word] possessing that" applies; that is, what was stated regarding the position of [the word] possessing that [universal]. For instance, if a word, having denoted a universal, were to apply to that which possesses it, it would be non-independent (*asvatantra*). Consequently, since the word would be controlled by the universal—which serves as the ground for the word's application—it would not entail the mutual differences residing in the individuals; thus, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with them.

Furthermore, there would be the fault that the application of a word to that which possesses [the property] is merely metaphorical (*upacarita*), and so forth. Thus, having stated that the word functions by means of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the objection that "the sound (*dhvani*) functioning in that which possesses [the property] is not independent" would follow as a universal consequence. That too is a description of the position that [the word refers] to that which possesses [the property]. By this [statement], [the objection] has been countered and rejected on the grounds of the non-difference between the exclusion and that which possesses the exclusion. For, in that case—namely, in the position that [the word refers] to that which possesses [the property]— [The objection: "If the word were to denote the exclusion itself, then since the exclusion is a non-entity (*avastu*), the word would have a non-entity as its object. Consequently, because the exclusion is a non-entity, the word would be incapable of producing any activity toward an object; thus, verbal cognition would become non-functional. To this we reply: No, for we do not say that the word denotes the exclusion alone. Rather, we say that the word denotes that which possesses the exclusion by means of the exclusion. "Having taken up another object" means having taken up a real entity that is a universal (*sāmānya*) [as the basis], [and applying it] to another object which possesses that [universal]. Because it does not directly denote that which possesses the universal, there is a lack of independence (*asvātantrya*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the faults of non-co-referentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇya*) and metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) are included.

But in the case of the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because there is identity between the exclusion and that which is excluded, the application of a word to one object does not depend upon taking up another object; therefore, there is no fault such as lack of independence (*asvātantrya*). Thus he says: "And not," and so forth. The exclusion from other entities is not different from that which is excluded; for it has just been stated that this is because one of two words—one denoting the property (*dharma*) and the other the property-bearer (*dharmin*)—denotes a single particular exclusion.

"How so? and so forth, asks the opponent. "Now" refers to the identity between the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses the exclusion (*tadvat*). Because a single excluded particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not persist [as a universal], and because it is not conjoined with other things, how could that exclusion—which is of the very nature of that particular—be a universal (*sāmānya*), given that like the particular itself it does not follow through [to others]? It certainly could not; yet, it is observed as a universal.

With the words "In that cognition," etc., the proponent of the established doctrine [the Siddhāntavādin] explains: In a conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) of a universal (*sāmānya*), because it appears in a single form, that which is excluded by this [cognition]—namely, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) itself—is called the "universal. This is what he says: Exclusion is not a single entity existing as the very nature (*ātmabhūta*) of the excluded particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); rather, the universal is merely the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises by its own nature subsequent to the experience of the excluded particular characteristics.

When entities perform a single function, [the cognition] arises as if displaying a single form; by the power of that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), a universal (*sāmānya*) is postulated. Furthermore, by this [explanation], it is shown directly that even though [particulars] are devoid of universals, they are the objects of words and so forth.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "Not at all anything," and so forth. The intended meaning is that [the universal] does not exist as a real entity (*vastubhūta*). If so, how is there the conventional usage of universals, co-referentiality, and so on? To this he says: "By words," and so forth. That conceptual cognition which has words as its basis—acting as its cooperative cause—is produced by the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) such that it joins together even properties that are not actually conjoined, making them appear as if they had a single form. It is by virtue of the appearance of a single form in that cognition that there is a universal.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established by virtue of the appearance of a single substratum (*dharmin*) endowed with two properties (*dharma*). Furthermore, this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth is established as pervading the non-existent. To explain how its object is non-existent, he says: "Of objects," and so forth. Because there is no conjunction of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the conventional usage of a universal is non-existent in its object. And because there is no difference within a single particular characteristic, the conventional usage of co-referentiality is non-existent in its object.

[Objection: But surely this entire conventional usage proceeds by way of dissimilarity; how then can it have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object? To this he says: the connection is with the phrase "the objects of all that conventional usage, such as 'universal' (*sāmānya*), etc., are its basis. [This refers to] those things whose nature consists in having effects corresponding to that [usage] and causes corresponding to that [usage], by means of which [nature] acting as an instrument.

"From others" means from those things that do not possess that same causal efficiency; objects distinguished from these serve as the basis for all conventional usage regarding universals and so forth. For this reason, it is said that the object [of conceptual cognition] is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). However, the exclusion of others does not appear therein, because only the external object appears in a single form by way of a positive entity (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, since a person impelled by a determinate cognition is led to engage with a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is excluded from the undesired—by avoiding what is undesired, for this reason too it is said that the object is the exclusion of others; yet this is not out of regard for how it appears, because the positive entity itself appears.

Therefore, as for what was said by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: "Is the referent of the word 'cow' a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*)? If it is a positive entity, is it a cow or a non-cow? If it is a cow, there is no dispute. If it is a non-cow, then to say that the referent of the word 'cow' is a non-cow is an extraordinary feat of verbal skill! If, on the other hand, it is a non-entity, that is incorrect; for upon hearing the word 'cow,' there is no consensus among those being addressed regarding a non-entity."

Furthermore, the meaning of a word is understood through comprehension, yet no one understands non-existence from the word "cow. Likewise, regarding this exclusion (*apoha*) expressed as "it is not a non-cow," does it have the cow as its object or the non-cow as its object? If it has the cow as its object, how can there be the non-existence of a cow in the cow itself? If, on the other hand, it has the non-cow as its object, how can there be a comprehension of something else based on an exclusion whose object is something else? For when a *khadira* tree is being cut, the cutting of a *palāśa* tree does not occur. Now, if you say that the negation of "non-cow" applies to the cow—namely, "it is not a non-cow"—then by what means was "cow-ness" ever presented as "non-cowness" such that it must now be negated?

fn. 1*: Cf. *Ślokavārttika*, *Apoha*; *Nyāyavārttika* 2.2.71. [Objection: "The [objection] has been refuted; since the word 'cow' has the cow as its object, the dispute arises solely because its object is imagined (*kalpita*). Or, just as the negation of a cow occurs even when there is no superimposition (*samāropa*), it was stated previously; therefore, this [argument] is trivial. Consequently, it remains established that the meaning of a word is indeed a positive injunction (*vidhi*)."

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In that regard," and so forth. That subject (*dharmin*) which appears to conceptual cognition is said to be such because it does not depend, in its own nature, upon an external reality. It is "one, excluded from many" by virtue of appearing to cognition; for, through the appearance to cognition resulting from the presentation of a single subject excluded from many, a single subject is established as being excluded from many.

The meaning is this: although [an object] is excluded from many [other things], conceptual exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are imagined therein as distinct properties (*dharmabheda*). That very real property-bearer (*dharmin*) is made the object of words; for speakers utter words in order to produce a conceptual appearance (*vikalpapratibhāsa*) of that which is so constituted. And since the conceptual appearance, excluded from others, is made the object of words, the meaning is that its status as a positive object (*vidhiviṣayatva*) is established.

It is not only by means of words that [the particular] is made an object, but also by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); thus he says: "By the experience of that," and so forth. The connection is as follows: the experience of each respective particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is "the experience of that"; the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by that is a capacity; its awakening is that which conforms to the production of an effect; and those conceptual constructions whose birth arises from that [awakening]—by them it is made an object. By what kind of [conceptual constructions]? By those whose objects are determined to have that very nature.

The state of being that [external object] is what is determined (*adhyavasita*). That external state which appears in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is precisely that which is determined as its own nature. Those conceptual constructions for which such an object is the domain are "those [constructions] characterized in that way. This means they proceed by unifying the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpita*).

The reading *adhyavasitatadbhāvārtha* is an alternative; it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "an object whose nature has been determined as that [other]. The connection is: even though it is a single thing, it is "an object whose nature has been determined as that" because it is excluded from many [others]. Therefore, by virtue of the appearance in cognition (*buddhipratibhāsa*), there is the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth. And precisely within that appearance in cognition—characterized by either the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions—it is conventionally used. Thus, *vyavahāra* (conventional usage) is derived from the object (*karman*). It is the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) themselves that constitute the conventional usage.

This is what is meant: it is being elaborated that those two—the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*)—which are established as appearing in cognition, are inexpressible in terms of identity or difference from one another. Thus, it is stated that the fault which was mentioned regarding the positions of ultimate identity or difference between property and property-possessor—namely, the futility of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, characterized by [the property's] independence and so on—that fault does not apply here.

He states another fault regarding the two positions of identity and difference with the words "For not," and so forth. A property (*dharma*) is not other than the substratum (*dharmin*). Why? Because it is not denoted as a distinct entity; for by the two words "property" and "substratum," that which is excluded [from others] is denoted as one and the same. Nor is the substratum itself the property. Why? Because, just as in the case of words expressing that [substratum], there would follow the undesirable consequence that words expressing the property would also imply a further exclusion. Just as in the case of words expressing the property, [the substratum] would likewise entail the implication of another exclusion.

Likewise, because [the word] conveys its intended object through its activity; for by the word "property" (*dharma*), there is no conveying of a particular that has excluded other particulars. This refers to the non-establishment of a distinct convention: the word "property" conveys an exclusion that has excluded other particulars—this is the non-establishment of that distinct convention. This aforementioned inexpressibility of property and property-bearer in terms of identity or difference was stated with respect to the object appearing in cognition within the referent of a word; however, regarding the "real entity" (*vastu*), that is, the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Precisely because it does not exist [as a real entity], it is inexpressible in terms of identity or difference; however, the object of words and so forth is established according to how it appears. [The opponent] says, "But surely," and so on. "Observed" means perceived in linguistic usages. In the expression "the cow-ness of the cow," there is a genitive case. By the word "and so forth," one includes such constructions as "cow-ness is situated in the cow," or "the word 'cow' applies to the cow by means of the cause that is cow-ness," and the inclusion of various other case endings. This is because there are many properties, such as cow-ness, substantiality, and so on. "In that regard" means among those many properties.

The proponent of the established doctrine states: "If there were no difference between the property and the property-bearer, and no ultimate difference, then the observed distinction in expression—such as 'cowness,' 'substantiality,' and 'earthiness'—would not exist, nor would there be mutual distinction among the properties themselves.
This has already been explained here, because it was stated previously that "the operation of words is certainly not dependent upon the intrinsic nature of their objects," and so forth.

Furthermore, in order to establish [the point] by means of a further injunction regarding the qualified subject, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth. For those proponents whose words are governed by the thing itself (*vastuvaśā*), that is, dependent upon the thing (*vastvāyattā*), and not dependent on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣāparāśrayāḥ*)—that is, those words for which the speaker's intention alone is the primary basis (*paraḥ pradhānam āśrayaḥ*)—there would be no genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), nor would there be differences in number (*vacanabheda*) and so forth. Thus, the objection concerning the genitive, the differences in number, and so on—the phrase "and so on" (*ādi*) including such examples as "the state of a cow is 'cow-ness' (*gotva*)," and so forth.

The objection regarding the absence of secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita-pratyaya*) is valid against those who maintain that words denote real entities (*vastu-vādin*). These words, such as the genitive and others, are intended to be applied—despite the non-difference of the entity—in certain cases, because they are tied to the entity; that is, they are dependent upon the entity, just like smoke and so forth. For smoke, being tied to fire, is capable of making fire known, but it cannot be employed to convey water by way of the opposite.

In that case, if words were tied to real entities (*vastu*), this objection would apply: "If there is no distinction [between the word and its referent], how can there be the genitive case and so forth? (vv. 66–67). He says "But when... and so on, to show that this very objection does not arise. Whatever speech (*vacas*) is employed by speakers in whatever manner—whether to express a distinction or a non-distinction—and which is determined (*viniyamyate*) by them as a signifier (*vācaka*) independent of an external object; that speech functions as a signifier accordingly, in that very way.

He explains this with the words "For not... and so forth. When there is a distinction of entities (*vyatireka*), the grammarians' established rule is that the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) occurs, and when there is plurality, the plural suffixes such as *jas* and others occur. This too does not function by itself through the mere presence of an entity independently of the intention of a person; rather, it functions solely by the power of convention (*saṃketa*). He says this very point with the words "But those [suffixes] there... and so forth.

However, those such as the grammarians employ the genitive case and the plural number in that context—namely, where there is distinction (*vyatireka*) and plurality (*bāhulya*)—according to conventional usage; thus, from the genitive and so forth, such a cognition arises. A cognition of distinction and so forth occurs for others as well, because they observe such linguistic usage. But it is not by the force of the thing itself that there is a restriction of the genitive and other cases to distinction and plurality. The same applies elsewhere.

Even though there is no distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmī*), and even though the entity is a single unity, the genitive case, the plural number, and so forth are employed by speakers in their respective ways as causes for cognition, according to the requirements of the situation. This is based on the distinction between the property and the property-bearer characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other differences—such as "somehow"—and based on the multiplicity indicated by the difference in exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) among properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). Thus, these grammatical forms become the grounds for understanding exactly as they are applied.

In this regard, since it is established that words are based solely on intention (*icchāmātra*), and because they function according to human will—operating by the power of that will and not revealing the actual nature of things—the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear from words. Rather, there is an awakening of conceptual construction (*vikalpaprabodha*), meaning the arising of conceptualization, for each person according to their habituation; that is, according to the habituation to a particular convention (*saṃketa*). This means that the causes of conceptualization in the mental continuum of the listener correspond to those conventions.

Thus, regarding the application of such words to their expressed objects—such as the consideration of the genitive case and so forth in the sense of "distinction"—for the Naiyāyikas and others, the determination of things occurs "by virtue of that," meaning by virtue of the word; they accept a thing as distinct [from its properties], arguing that because there is a genitive case in "the cowness of a cow," the universal must therefore be distinct, and so on. This is merely a display of dullness, a demonstration of ignorance regarding the established nature of the relationship between words and their meanings.

The opponent says, "In that way," and so forth. "Having established conventions in that manner regarding properties (dharma), subjects (dharmin), and so on" means that the terms *dharma* and *dharmin* are established by either excluding or not excluding other distinctions; and by the word "and so on," terms such as *dravyatva*, *pārthivatva*, and others—expressed in the plural—are established through different exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).

Nor, however, is the plural number used because of a real distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*), nor because of a real difference in the sixth case-relation (*ṣaṣṭhīvastubheda*), nor because properties such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth are distinct in an ultimate sense. Why is this so? Because the response begins with "In that way," and so on: "Because such conventional usage would be impossible. This means that if there were a real distinction between the property and the property-possessor which are the objects of conventional usage, and if properties were mutually distinct from one another in an ultimate sense, then conventional usage regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth would be impossible. (68)

He explains this very statement of the opponent’s objection, beginning with "for not" (*na hi*), as follows: Since the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), which are the objects of conventional usage, are real entities (*vastu*), one must admit that they are either identical to or different from one another, because there is no other possible mode for a real entity; thus, these two alternatives are presented.

This is for the purpose of exposing the faults in both positions—that [the universal] is distinct [from the individual] and that it is identical with its true nature (*tattva*). Otherwise, if the opponent were to adopt the position of distinction based on the statement "because of the difference between the distinct thing and its counterpart," the presentation of the position of identity would not be appropriate to the context. The phrase "connected with that" refers to the relationship between the universal and its possessor. Alternatively, if it is accepted that words function according to the actual state of things, then universals and the like are logically consistent. We shall explain this very point immediately below.

"Based on the entity" (*vastukṛta*) means that the distinction in the application of words—such as the singularity or plurality of entities, and the distinction in the application of singular or plural endings—is established. For instance, the word *dārāḥ* ("wife") is accepted as being always plural and feminine. When this word *dārāḥ* refers to a single woman, it is because of the establishment of difference [between her and other women]. Conversely, when many cities are denoted by the singular term *ṣaṇṇagarī*, it is because of the establishment of non-difference. What is the basis for this? There is no external basis whatsoever.

Because of the establishment of difference and non-difference in such cases as "the nature of the beginning" (*ādiśabdātmikatā*) or "a garland of clarity" (*prasādamālā*), [one might ask]: what is the basis for the genitive of distinction (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī*) in the expression "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*)? Now, if it is argued that by the word "reality" (*tattva*) it is meant that the nominal derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*) "spaciousness" (*khatva*) arises from the sentence "the nature of space," that is not so.

For the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) does not have the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*); rather, it has the sense of "being" (*bhāva*). Furthermore, there is no purpose in demonstrating the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*), since the distinction [between the two] is already shown by one or the other. On this point, some say that because all linguistic usage is pervaded by both the derivative formation and the explanatory sentence (*vākya*), both were stated in order to demonstrate that pervasion. Others explain it differently: [they ask] what is the basis for the distinction in the expression "the intrinsic nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*), and likewise, what is the basis for the abstract suffix in the expression "spaciousness" (*khatvam*), which denotes a distinction?

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "yad" (when). "When" (*yadā*) means at which time. Others read the word "yat" (which), in which case the meaning is "because. The sense is: "Because it is so, there occurs the plural form in *dārāḥ* and so forth; otherwise, due to [the object's] being a single unit, only the singular would be appropriate. Even for a single woman or for sands (*sikatā*), there are many capacities (*śakti*); therefore, the diversity of capacities is the cause of the plural number. "Everywhere" (*sarvatra*) refers even to cases where the singular is intended, such as in *vṛkṣaḥ* and so forth.

Because there is no object that possesses a single power, since every [object] has multiple powers; if this were the case, the effort [expressed in the rule] "the singular number is used for a single thing" would be useless, because even though there is a difference in powers, there is no difference in the substance (*vastu*), as the substratum of the powers is non-different. If you argue that in other cases where the singular number applies—such as in *vṛkṣaḥ* (tree) or *paṭaḥ* (cloth)—the singular is used [because the object is one], then here too, in the case of *dāraḥ* (wife), the singular is used because there is no difference in the substance of the single woman.

Since this is so, the differentiation in the application of words does not depend on the power of real entities. Therefore, this rule for the application of words—being established as devoid of reality and not based on external objects—demonstrates the independence of human will in the employment of language.

If it is argued that there exists a single collection (*samāhāra*) of the six cities—whether consisting of action or quality—and therefore the singular number is used, he replies: No, for the cities themselves are not "anything" [as a distinct entity], since a substance (*dravya*) that is a whole composed of the cities is not admitted; how then could there be a collection of those cities, whether consisting of action or quality, on the basis of which such a thing would be designated? This is because action and quality are dependent upon a substance. What, then, is a substance? He says: "palaces," and so forth. A city is a collection of houses and the like.

Furthermore, since it is not admitted that dissimilar components such as palaces initiate a [single] substance, how could their collection—the collection of palaces and so forth—be a substance called a "city"? To the extent that a city is held to be a collection of palaces, gateways, persons, and so on, that city cannot be a substance because those palaces and other components do not possess conjunction (*saṃyoga*). It is maintained that substances initiate another substance only when they are assisted by conjunction. There is no conjunction among the detached palaces, persons, walls, and so on, by which a city produced from the palaces and other parts could be a substance.

It might be thought: "Even if there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of palaces and so forth in their entirety, nevertheless, since there is a mutual conjunction among those very things such as palaces and persons, the city will exist as having that conjunction as its nature. Even so, the substantiality (*vastutva*) of the city remains unestablished, because conjunction belongs to the category of qualities (*guṇapadārtha*). To this he says: "Not conjunction," and so forth. The city does not have the nature of conjunction.

Likewise, since heterogeneous substances such as wood and bricks do not originate a [new] composite substance (*kāryadravya*), even a palace is not of the nature of a substance; rather, it is held to be of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). And since conjunction is a quality (*guṇa*) and qualities themselves are devoid of further qualities, how could there be a conjunction belonging to the palace, by virtue of which the city would consist of that conjunction?

He says this very thing with the words "of the palace," and so forth. Furthermore, because it is not conjoined with another [entity], the city is not a conjunction; by the word "and" (ca), this is added: because the previously mentioned palaces and so forth, being separate, are not conjoined, the city is not a conjunction. Thus, since there is an absence of conjunction for the palaces and so forth in both ways, the city's nature as a conjunction is refuted.

If it is argued that the city will consist of whatever number belongs to the palaces and so forth, he says: "For that very reason, there is an absence of number. Because the palace consists of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), for that very reason there is an absence of number in the palace, since qualities (*guṇa*) are devoid of [other] qualities; for number is also of the nature of a quality. That which is both "that" (conjunction) and "conjunction" is *tatsaṃyoga*; the meaning is that it is a conjunction whose essence is the palace. If it is argued that the city is that existence (*sattā*) qualified by that conjunction and by the persons [inhabiting it]:

What qualification can there be for this existence (*sattā*), which is unitary, eternal, and unsurpassed? For palaces, men, and the like do not qualify existence, because it cannot admit any further excellence (*anādheyātiśayatvāt*). Therefore, existence is without qualification. The intention [of the objection] is that if it were a city, then cityhood would apply everywhere. And "because of the unity of existence" means that existence is one and all-pervasive throughout substances, qualities, and actions.

"Even though there is a plurality of cities" means even though there is a plurality of collections of palaces and so forth that serve as the basis for the designation "city. Otherwise, since the city under discussion consists of existence (*sattā*), how could there be a plurality of cities? If it is argued that "the substance"—meaning the palace, the person, and so forth—and the existence (*sattā*) which possess mutual concomitance constitute a city, then in that case, the cognition of a "city" would not occur everywhere, because palaces and such do not exist everywhere. Furthermore, the opponent considers that the use of the plural number is established due to the plurality of palaces and other components.

He states the reply: "The non-recipient," and so forth. What kind of assistance can there be between existence (*sattā*) and a palace (*prāsāda*), which are respectively non-recipients and non-providers of benefit? For the meaning of "cooperation" is twofold: characterized by the production of a distinguished moment within a continuum through the conferral of mutual excellence; and characterized by the performance of a single effect by those things that have arisen already capable due to their own prior causes. It is not the former [kind], because excellence cannot be conferred upon existence.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because just as pure existence (*sattā*) alone is incapable of producing the cognition of a city, so too it would remain incapable even when accompanied by palaces and the like; or, if it were capable, it would produce that cognition even when alone. Furthermore, if the city were the mutual conjunction of these two [existence and palaces], then even a single city would possess a manifold nature, since its essence consists of the palaces and so forth. Consequently, because there is a plurality of conjunctions—namely, those between men, and those with existence—the singular number "city" (*nagaram*) would be incorrect. By the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), a conjunction whose essence is the palace is intended.

Regarding the phrase "of such things," this refers to persons existing in conjunction with one another; when there is a cognition such as "an object" or "a city," and a word is to be produced, there exists a single, undivided power (*śakti*). If it is argued that this undivided power is the cause for the singular number, we say no. Why? Because the power is not distinct from the essential nature of the thing (*vastu-svarūpa*); since it is not distinct from the entities such as the persons themselves, it possesses multiplicity just like them. Therefore, how could there be a singular number based upon it?

Alternatively, if it is accepted that power (*śakti*) is distinct from the essential nature of the entity (*vastusvarūpa*), then because the form of power would not be assisted by the existence of the conjunction with the *puruṣa* and so forth, there could be no dependence of power upon the *puruṣa* and others. Consequently, the relationship "power belongs to the *puruṣa* and others" would not exist; such is the intended meaning.

Now, if it is maintained that even for a power (*śakti*) distinct [from the possessor], there must be a benefit (*upakāra*) conferred by the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth, in order to establish its dependence upon them—then, when such a benefit to the power is desired as being produced by the person and so forth, one must consider whether this initial power by which the person and others first benefit the [primary] power is itself distinct from that [primary] power or not. If it is distinct, there would be an infinite regress; if it is not distinct, [the same problem remains].

Even if one accepts that the first [case-ending] is based on the singular number in relation to the capacity (*śakti*), there would be the consequence of non-distinction (*avyatireka*). And if there were non-distinction, there would be multiplicity just as with the thing itself (*vastu*); thus, the consequence of using the plural for many [things] remains exactly as it was. This argument is trivial. Furthermore, if one postulates a capacity (*śakti*), the genitive case—based on distinction—as in "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*) would not be possible. The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is also mentioned by the word "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) only figuratively, because the genitive is the cause for its application.

Therefore, this is another point: the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *khatvam* based on a relation of distinction (*vyatireka*) would not be possible. For, according to the etymological derivation that "the nature of space (*kha*) is *khatva*," the abstract suffix arises precisely because it is based on a relation of distinction.
(Pāṇini 1.4.21).

Alternatively, the connection and the division of the text should be made according to what is appropriate. Regarding the term *khatvam* ("the state of being space"), there should be the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) "there would not be its existence or arising based on a distinction" (*vyatirekāśrayā*). [Regarding the phrase] "the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of space," there would not be a genitive case; for there is no intrinsic nature or entity other than the object denoted by the word "space" that could serve as the basis for a genitive of distinction (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī*) or for a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) respectively.

If it is argued that there exists a universal called "space-ness" (*khatva*) which serves as the basis for the exclusion [of non-space], he replies: "Not in that case," and so forth. Because space is of a single nature, the universal "space-ness" does not exist in it. Even though existence (*sattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*) exist in space, nevertheless, those two are not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of space, because they are common to jars and other things. Nor do existence and substantiality serve as the basis for the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the term "space-ness," because those two are not the cause of the word or the cognition of "space."

It is accepted that the cause of the cognition and verbal designation corresponding to [an object] is the nature (*svabhāva*) which serves as its basis; nor are qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth [the cause]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), oneness, priority, and so on are included. Thus it is said: "the nature of space. Since a quality such as omnipresence, being a distinct entity from the substance, cannot logically be its nature—that is, it cannot logically be the nature of space—because it is not tenable for one distinct entity to be the nature of another distinct entity. Furthermore, if omnipresence and the like were the nature of space...

In that case, since those qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) would have the nature of space, it would follow that they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). For, if their essential nature as qualities were simply space itself and no other nature existed, they would be without intrinsic nature. And if they were without intrinsic nature, space would likewise lack a distinct intrinsic nature; this is the intended meaning. If it is argued that even omnipresence and the rest possess a nature distinct [from space], he says: "Of that too," and so forth.

The analysis of the compound *tasya* [is as follows]: "its nature" (*svabhāva*) means that it has another entity (*arthāntara*) such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth as its nature. Regarding the term "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*): if that other entity which is intended to be the nature of omnipresence and so forth were itself to have the nature of yet another entity, then it too would necessarily have the nature of another entity. Otherwise, because that [second entity] would not be distinct from omnipresence, it would likewise lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). And in that case, by searching for further and further natures, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and consequently, not even a single established nature would exist.
The intention is that there is no apprehension of the first [category], which has the nature of space, and therefore that very thing constitutes the absence of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

In this way, there is a group of the six categories (*padārtha*)—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), examples such as "a row of palaces" and so forth are to be understood.

How can there be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is no distinction? For a "universal" (*sāmānya*), which is expressed by the word "group," is not possible among those six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*). This is because universals are admitted only in the case of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*). Likewise, neither number (*saṃkhyā*) nor conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is possible, since these two, being categories of quality, exist only in substances.

"How so? and so forth [is] the opponent. Now, if one does not accept that space has a nature distinct from other things, then since the object denoted by the word *kha* (space) and the object denoted by the word *bhāva* (nature) would be non-existent and indeterminate, how could there be a designation as "its own nature" (*svabhāva*) using a term implying distinction? The meaning is that it would not be "space" alone; rather, because there would be no basis for distinction, a designation without distinction would be the only logical course.

He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "of space" (*khasya*). "Of space" means: by way of [space] being a different object from the common nature of earth and so forth—which belongs to that object denoted by the word *kha*—through the non-consideration of other unmentioned particulars, and through its exclusion [from them]. The nature that is the basis for the application of the word *kha* is unique to other substances; thus, when there is a desire to know it, it is expressed as "the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of space," or "spatiality (*khatva*)," in such a way that it may be understood: "this is the intrinsic nature of space, not of anything else."

By this rejection of other exclusions (*bhedāntara*), since a single excluded form is not being denoted, something else has been stated as the cause for the expression of exclusion (*vyatireka*). By that, the designation "the absence of a jar" and so forth becomes established. Others, however, say: when the word "nature" (*svabhāva*) conveys the nature of space, it conveys it merely by the exclusion of [other] natures, but not by the rejection of other natures; whereas the word "space" (*kha*) conveys that very same thing without rejecting other forms.

Therefore, [the opponent argues that] because of a slight distinction characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), this intrinsic nature of space is designated as distinct by saying "this is the nature of space" or "spaciousness" (*khatva*). To this, [the author replies: "This is not very well-founded, because there is no cognition of the exclusion of other distinctions.

Thinking that by stating "the form which is the basis for the application of the word 'space' (*khaśabda*) is spoken of in this way without reference to a form common to other objects," the opponent has effectively stated that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is the denotable object, the other party says [the following], beginning with "But not all... and so forth. However, [the author] does not say "all," etc. [as the opponent might suggest].

"No," and so forth, says the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin). That which is excluded from everything and consists of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that very form is what is presented by words in a cognition arising from words. "No"—this is the connection [to the previous argument]. Why? Because if that specific characteristic were to appear in verbal cognition just as it does in sensory cognition, it would follow that it is not beyond the senses; that is, it would follow that it is perceptible. If one asks, "Then what is done by the word? he says: "Only," and so forth. "This one" refers to the communicator.

Deceived by the determination of identity between the perceived object and the conceptual construction, and with the intention "I shall cause [the listener] to understand such a unique object," one—by means of the word acting as an instrument—imparts to the conceptual construction in the listener an aspect superimposed as being external to its reflection. What kind [of aspect]? One that is unmixed with the nature of that [external object], and whose form is not grasped as a real entity. To show that this is also the view of the Master Diṅnāga, he says: "As he said," and so forth.

When a word such as "heaven" (svarga), whose referent is unperceived, is uttered, there arises for the listener a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) of the object; that is, a conceptualization whose nature is determined by an external object, but which does not grasp the actual external form itself.

By this, [the author] demonstrates that even this Teacher intends the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) to be the word-meaning. In this way, when a reflection of a conceptual construction has been produced in the listener by means of a word, neither the person to be informed nor the informant has, respectively, apprehended or communicated the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

For if the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were conveyed by a word, then even upon hearing words such as "heaven" (*svarga*), there would be no difference in the mental appearance for the listener compared to those who have experienced it, or compared to those who perceive heaven through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, the listener would also possess a cognition of the form of the particular characteristic of heaven and so forth.

And since there is no comprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) from a word, this listener, although not comprehending the intrinsic nature of an entity from the word, nevertheless—being one who determines (*adhyavasāyin*) that very reflection of conceptual construction as being such [an entity], that is, as having the unmingled nature of the real object—determines it to be the specific characteristic and is satisfied, thinking, "I have indeed comprehended the specific characteristic itself. What is the reason? Precisely because it is of such a nature.

Even though the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not directly apprehended, the cognition of the word-meaning occurs precisely because it has the form of the determined (*adhyavasita*) specific characteristic. And since the word-meaning is understood through the determination of the specific characteristic, it is said in this way that "the word expresses its own form. This is because of the statement that "the unique form, which is the basis for the application of its own word, is expressed by not referring to a form common to other objects"; it is not, however, because it generates a consciousness in which the form itself appears.
Therefore, it is established that the meaning of the word is the injunction (vidhi), because its object is unreal; this is the distinction from the view of others.

[The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose forms are exclusively excluded. Because of the non-connection of those entities (*bhāva*), and of "another"—that is, of a universal (*sāmānya*) distinct from the entities.

"It has been stated," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). To the question "In what manner was it stated?", he replies: "The non-association of things that are unassociated and mutually excluded with a single dissimilar entity; for example, the non-association of individual cows with the single nature of 'non-cow'—that very [non-association] is [the universal]. The commonality (*samānatā*) of the various cows, which are excluded from that nature of being a non-cow, is 'cowness' (*gotva*). Other universals (*sāmānya*) are to be understood in the same way.

This is what is meant: the word "of the similar" (*samānām*) is a genitive in the sense of the agent; therefore, the meaning of "generality" (*sāmānyam*)—as in "the state of being similar"—is that entities which have arisen with a common form, excluded from those of a different class, constitute the generality. And it is precisely this generality that possesses the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*), the nature of the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), and their relationship, because it is a real entity (*vastu*). Furthermore, because it performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*), it is the object of purposeful activity and the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), according to its determination (*adhyavasāya*), but not the mental image (*jñānākāra*), because that is the opposite of these characteristics. (69)

Thus, having refuted the indirect criticism regarding the position of superimposition (*samāropa*), and having set aside the indirect criticism regarding the position of exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) precisely because such exclusion is not admitted, and having established that entities which are indeed excluded from others are determined as a unity and constitute the universal (*sāmānya*), [the author] says "Moreover... and so forth, in order to remove the criticism stated by others even with respect to the universal as a mental form (*buddhyākāra*).

Depending upon entities that are distinct, or depending upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is excluded [from others], a cognition arises that manifests as a single object. By means of this—by its own nature, by its own form, as a single form—the "other-nature," namely the particular characteristic that is mutually excluded, is concealed or covered. Why is it qualified as such? Because it is a concealment (*saṃvṛti*); for it is by means of this that the particular characteristic is concealed.

Having their various meanings concealed—that is, with their various meanings veiled—they appear as if non-different, as if mixed together, even though they are inherently distinct, by means of a certain form such as "cowness" which is conceptually constructed through the exclusion of dissimilar things. By this, [the following objection] is refuted:
"The form of the cognition residing in the cognition does not follow after other objects or cognitions, nor does it produce the intended object;
therefore, that too is not denotable in reality," and so forth.

Therefore, by the power of the intention of the intellect (*buddhi*), and by the power of superimposing a single form, the universal (*sāmānya*) is proclaimed as "all-pervasive. This means that the form superimposed by the intellect alone is called the universal. Just as it is conceptualized and superimposed by that [intellect], so too is that universal non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Now, if it is admitted that the appearance is non-different [from the individual], how can it be said that the universal is non-existent? No; because that which is intended to be different from the individuals appears as non-different. Furthermore, if there were non-difference in every respect, then—just like the individuals—it would lack continuity, and thus the cognition of a recurring [universal] would be nothing but an error. Moreover, if there were both difference and non-difference, there would likewise have to be an appearance of both forms simultaneously. Yet, in whatever cognition there is the appearance "this is a cow," there is not at that same time the appearance "the cowness is here."

Now, it might be argued: that which persists while another does not persist must be distinct from that other, just as the non-blue is distinct from the blue. And since the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) persists in another individual despite the non-persistence of the particular *śāvaleyā*, it must therefore be distinct from it. In that case, the perception that apprehends the cowness as non-different from the *śāvaleyā* would be erroneous, because it apprehends what is actually distinct—as established by another means of valid cognition—as non-different. Furthermore, it is impossible for a single entity to possess both difference and non-difference in the very same form, due to their mutual contradiction.

Nor is there a distinction between things by way of their specific forms (*viśeṣarūpa*) and non-distinction by way of their universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*). For if this were so, the specific forms would possess a single location and so forth, which they do not. Furthermore, there would be no difference in appearance between the universal and the specific, because they would be non-different in every respect. Alternatively, if there were a difference, then since the inclusive (*anugata*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*) forms would not be conjoined with one another, it would follow that they are absolutely distinct.

And if that [universal] were non-different from each individual, how could there be a single universal? Nor is it logical to claim that a single universal exists because, upon seeing a second or subsequent individual, there arises the cognition "this is that very same one," even though it was not apprehended during the perception of the first individual; for the component of memory denoted by "that" cannot arise in the absence of a previously experienced object, namely the universal.

Consequently, just as it was not apprehended in the first individual, so too it would not be apprehended in each instance of the second and subsequent individuals; how then could the cognition "this is that very same thing" arise? Nor is it reasonable to postulate the apprehension of a universal in the first individual—whether by a non-conceptual or another kind of cognition—on the grounds that such recollection ("that") would otherwise be inexplicable, because there is no appearance of a recurring form [in the sensory perception].

Nor is it logical that its apprehension therein occurs by way of its nature as a *dharma* (property), because a universal (*sāmānya*) possesses a single, recurring form. Nor can it be said that its apprehension by perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*) occurs by way of its relation to preceding and succeeding individuals; for this would entail the undesirable consequence that perception would arise in the form "this is that very same thing. Furthermore, perception is held to be characterized by the ascertainment of a present object, whereas the preceding individual is not present.

Therefore, since a mistaken cognition of a single form—namely, "this is that very same [thing]"—arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) when there has been a prior experience of one particular instance excluded from non-cows and a subsequent experience of another instance excluded from non-cows, it is logical to postulate that very [exclusion] as its cause, and nothing else. Furthermore, because this cognition is mistaken, it is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*).

He explains the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "buddhiḥ" (cognition). [The phrase] connects with the statement "cognition is conceptual. "From those" refers to those of the same class; "different from those" means their exclusion (*vyatireka*). Those which possess this are "those excluded from others" (*tadanyavyatirekiṇaḥ*), meaning they are differentiated from those of a different class. "Its own latent impression" (*svavāsanā*) refers to the nature of the latent impression of conceptualization; "conforming to" (*anuvidadhatī*) means following that capacity for producing a non-differentiated cognition with respect to things that are actually distinct. That is, it imitates it.
