For in this way, its own cause is imitated by it: if a single form arises even with respect to distinct things. "Of these" refers to the objects (*padārtha*). "Having superimposed" means having projected [it] upon the objects, thinking that there is a single form of entities themselves; thus they produce those entities. It displays them as if they were non-distinct; that is to say, it shows them as if they possessed a single form.

[Objection: But if it is maintained that conceptual construction arises through the force of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by an experienced object, how can a conceptual construction having a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) arise, given that the universal has not been experienced? To this, he says: "And that... and so forth. Those entities for which there is a single [common] goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and a single means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—for example, for jars and the like, the single goal to be accomplished is the holding of water and so forth, and the means of accomplishment is the lump of clay and so forth—they are "those with a single goal and means. Their state (*tadbhāva*) is "that-ness" (*tayā*). By means of that, which functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

For those who discern things from others that do not accomplish what they are capable of accomplishing, that is their *prakṛti*, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is characterized by the generation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a single form, even though [the things] are distinct by nature. Or rather, it is the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) which is the cause of such a conceptual construction; its very nature is such that it projects this specific form onto something else. This is how cognition appears. That is to say, it appears as apprehending a universal that is non-different from the individual instances.
Therefore, as for what is said: "If one were to say that this non-differentiated cognition is merely mnemonic (*smārta*)."

"Surely, even in the case of the son of a barren woman, there exists the possibility of being remembered"—this [objection] is refuted. For distinct experienced [objects], by virtue of their capacity to produce a cognition with a non-different form regarding their own objects through their performance of a single effect, possess the capacity to generate a faint memory of their own objects that has a clear form [as experienced], just as an object experienced with a clear form possesses the capacity to generate a faint memory of its own object. "Arising from that" (*tadudbhavā*) means that whose arising occurs either directly or indirectly from the specific natures of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the conceptualization of phonemes (*varṇavikalpa*), according to their respective order. And this cognition, "this is that," is called a conventional construction (*saṃvṛtti*).

The suffix *ktin* is employed here as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), [deriving the word] from the notion that "by means of this cognition—by its own nature, which is its own manifestation—the form of another thing, the form of a real entity, is concealed. And those entities are [said to be] "concealed by that" cognition; that is, their differences are concealed, meaning their manifoldness is hidden. "By some form" refers to that which is superimposed by conceptual cognition; they thus appear within conceptual cognition. *fn. 1*: Ślokavārttika, Anumānapariccheda 160.

(p.169) "Therefore, for these... and so forth. The connection is as follows: by people who conform to the appearance in cognition—that is, the form of a conceptualizing cognition—a single form presented by that cognition is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*). Of what is it said to be the universal? Precisely of those revolving within cognition. The connection is: "of these [things] revolving within cognition."

Having experienced the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), these entities—which exist within the intellect and possess the form of a jar, yet appear indistinctly in conceptual cognitions such as "this jar is white," "it is black," or "it is something else"—are precisely what constitute the commonality (*sāmānya*) related [to those cognitions]. This is because the specific characteristics do not appear in the common cognition and are therefore not related to it. The phrase "of the qualifiers existing within the intellect" means that they flash forth as if external, i.e., they appear as if they were outside.
And he states the cause for its appearing as if external: "because of the grasping of a specific form" (*ākāraviśeṣaparigrahāt*).
Some say that there is a determination of the external because of the clear imitation of the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the conceptualization of an external object.

But this is incorrect; for it has already been explained that the superimposition of externality is not caused by similarity. Therefore, the "specific form" is the form of a jar or the like; its "grasping" is the experience (*anubhava*), and from that, there is an appearance as if it were external.

This is what is meant: a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), arising through the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of a jar or similar object, determines its own form as non-different from the external jar and so forth, but it does not actually grasp it. Therefore, doubt sometimes arises regarding the object designated by a word because of this lack of grasping. In that case, however, the conceptual construction determines its own form—which is [subjectively] non-different from the external—precisely from its own cause; it is not due to similarity, because there is no such thing as a corresponding external object and because there is no actual grasping.
Now, one might object: even for those [particulars] residing in the intellect, what other form appears apart from their own essential nature that could constitute a universal?

True. Regarding this, some say that their unity arises because they are not distinct from a single cognition. Others, however, say that each of them possesses the nature of a universal in relation to its own individual manifestation. Both of these views are incorrect, because there is no appearance of a single [common] form; rather, others accept a universal merely because of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those [particulars] as having a single form. It is with reference to that intention that it is stated thus.
However, the Master’s intended meaning is that the appearance is "identical," not that it is "one"; as he will state [in verses 70, 71, and 72].

Alternatively, let it be as stated [in verse 1.109]: "The appearance of cognitions is distinct, yet they are said to be identical because of the apprehension of that [appearance]. If the universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed the form displayed by conceptual cognition belonging solely to those [appearances] revolving within the intellect, and since that [form] is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpatva*), how can it now be called the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*)?

"It is that very thing," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). That very appearance, established by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), is called "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), because it is derived through the perception of an object as distinguished from others.
If the form of conceptualization is the universal (*sāmānya*), how is there the perception of external things as having a common nature? As it has been said:
"Or rather, these [cognitions] are without an object, existing merely as a result of mental impressions (*vāsanā*)."
"How could there be practice and engagement with external objects?

To this, he says: "That very [object]," and so forth. Grasping that which is the appearance in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhipratibhāsa*), that conceptual cognition appears as if it were grasping a real entity (*vastu*). Why? Because of the natural delusion of conceptualizations; by their very nature, due to the delusion of grasping an object as non-different from their own form.

If so, why is it said that its object is *apoha*? To this he says: For that conceptual cognition, by virtue of its determinative function (*adhyavasāya*), arises with respect to individual particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) which are distinguished from others; thus it is understood to have "exclusion" as its object. This is due to its effect, however, and not because it takes the nature of exclusion itself as its object.

But the opponent, his intention unknown, says: "Now," and so forth. The meaning is that [the objects] external to the universal are the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). For in this way, the inclusion of both external and internal [objects] is accomplished. [The opponent asks: "How can there be a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) regarding those [particulars], since they are distinct from one another for a discerning person, and [conceptualization] does not occur with respect to them—that is, with respect to the particular characteristics? [The author] answers with the words "The commentators," and so forth. For they, while establishing the object exactly as it exists, distinguish it in such a manner.

"The appearance in conceptual cognition is one thing, while the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is another. Practitioners do not discriminate in this way; rather, those practitioners, regarding the very appearance of conceptualization—which has its own objective support—as being the external particular characteristic capable of causal efficiency, think: "The object of perception is the particular characteristic; the object of conceptualization is [the universal]. This very point is clarified [as follows].

Having unified those two appearances of the universal, they resolve that this very particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is what is made an object by conceptual cognition and what is denoted by the word; thus, having formed such a conviction, they engage with the object that performs a causal function.

This is stated according to the intention of those who engage in conventional discourse—that is, according to their own intentions—when it is said that "a conceptualizing cognition arises with respect to distinct entities," because one acts by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object. By saying this, it is not meant that the external object is superimposed upon one's own internal form; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of acting toward one's own internal form alone, just as in the case of superimposing water onto a mirage. Nor is it the case that one's own internal form is superimposed upon the external object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of acting solely out of a desire for the result of the superimposition, just as in the case of one seeking water when experiencing an illusion of water.

Now, what is meant by the "unification of the perceived and the conceptualized"? If the perceived were non-different from the conceptualized, there would be no engagement with external objects. If the conceptualized were non-different from the perceived, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be the referent of words. Furthermore, the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized cannot occur through perception, because perception does not have the conceptualized as its object; nor can it occur through conceptualization, because conceptualization does not have the perceived as its object. Moreover, since the perceived is absent in the case of the past and so forth, how could there be a unification of the two?

To this it is replied: When there is an experience of an object, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises with its form through the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) thereof; this [conceptualization] determines its own form as non-different from the external, but it does not actually make it non-different. Therefore, because the object of the conceptual construction is determined as having the nature of the perceptible (*dṛśya*), the unification of the perceptible and the conceptual is spoken of. That which is fit to be seen is "perceptible" (*dṛśya*), or that which can be seen; thus, even the object of conceptual vision is called "perceptible. By this, the perceptibility of even a future object indicated by scripture is established, as is the case for non-existence (*abhāva*).

Therefore, a cognition of non-existence apprehends its own form—which, though positive in nature—by superimposing it upon the non-distinction from the absence of the object; thus it is said to have non-existence as its object, but it does not grasp non-existence itself, because all conceptual constructions are devoid of [external] objects.

"By virtue of performing that function," and so forth. It is not merely said that conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) arises with respect to particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) and their distinctions by the force of that [perceiver's] intention; likewise, it is said that speakers communicate through words objects as distinct from those that do not perform that function, by means of performing that function. If it is asked, "Why do commentators not realize the identity between the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpya*)? he says: "Because of the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*), etc. For the appearance of the perceived is vivid, whereas that of the conceptualized is not.

Because for that which is bound to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), clarity is impossible. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that even when the visible object has ceased, the conceptual construction does not cease; and because [the object] performs or does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*). "Those who contemplate reality" (*tattvacintaka*) refers to the commentators who follow logic (*nyāya*). This is a genitive of the remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*): "those who contemplate reality. It means they are contemplators of reality, not of unreality; for while there is a requirement for the mere exclusion of other related entities, the relationship of action and agent is not intended to be expressed here.

Alternatively, one may form a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) of the word *tattva* with the noun derived from the root *cint* ending in the suffix *ac*, and then apply the suffix *kan* as a pleonastic marker (*svārthika*). Consequently, the prohibition of a genitive compound by the rule "nābhyām" (Pāṇini 2.2.15) and so forth need not be suspected here. [The phrase] "of the perceived and the conceptualized" (*dṛśyavikalpayoḥ*) is understood from the context.

“If,” and so forth, says the opponent. The determination of a universal among external things conforms to the intention of the cognizer; in that case, let the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) also not be a universal. Why? Because “it is not so. That is to say, there is no such cognition on the part of those engaged in linguistic practice that “the exclusion of others is what is expressed by the word. The Teacher, too, demonstrating the parity [of the two cases], says: “Certainly not merely,” and so forth. “There is no such cognition” means [no cognition] in the form of the exclusion of others.

Even though you accept a universal (*sāmānya*) through such forms as being distinct from the individual (*vyakti*) and so forth, there is nonetheless no cognition [of it]. For the Vaiśeṣikas and others, it is distinct from its substratum (*āśraya*); for the Sāṃkhyas and others, it is non-distinct; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of [properties] such as being fully present in each individual is intended. In that regard, first of all, the difference of the universal does not appear at all, because the cognition "this is a universal" does not arise. Even in the case of non-difference, only the individuals would appear, not the universal.

Furthermore, the fault inherent in both positions—namely, difference and non-difference—would apply. Nor is it logical for that [universal] to be fully present in each individual; for if it were so, it would belong to only one related entity within a single individual, rather than to many. And this is not the case, because a universal relates to many, according to the definition: "A universal (sāmānya) is the state (bhāva) of those things that are similar."

Now, if it is argued that because it is recognized (*pratyabhijñāna*) in other individual instances (*vyakti*), it must belong to them, even so, as a perceiver of the qualities of the elements (*bhūtaguṇa*), it would be related to many things rather than being fully present in each one individually; for it is not perceived as being related to many within each single instance. Or, if it were so perceived, there would have to be an appearance of multiple instances therein. If it is then said that it is fully present in each one because it does not appear in the intervals between instances, [we reply:]...

Therefore, how could its relation to multiple things be established in a single instance by this much alone? Furthermore, it has already been stated that recognition (pratyabhijñāna) is not possible with respect to a universal. Consequently, it is established that neither its subsistence in each individual instance, nor its eternity, unity, and omnipresence, appear [to consciousness].

If there is an equal lack of apprehension in worldly practice regarding both a real universal (*sāmānya*) and exclusion (*apoha*), then what is the basis for this [exclusion]? To this he says: "Only," and so forth. The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the state of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) being devoid of those of a different class; that is stated to be the cause for a cognition that possesses a non-differentiated form.

What is the reason? Because that *anyāpoha*—characterized by the exclusion of what is heterogeneous—is present in all distinct entities, and because there is no contradiction in such an *anyāpoha* being the cause of a universal cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*). For instance, just as one perceives a single tree as excluded from non-trees, so too does one perceive another; thus, a cognition with a single form arises therein. And there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against this.

He states the third reason: "And of conventional usage," and so forth. "Because it is seen to be so" means because it is seen to be based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). And this will be demonstrated by the passage beginning with, "And the word 'sound' is said to function by way of excluding what is other than that. The meaning of the sentence is as follows: just as this conceptual cognition appears in a single form, so too there exists no external universal corresponding to it. Therefore, the intention is that a real, ontological universal is not the basis for conceptual perception.

And he states the reason for the non-existence of a universal: "Because," and so forth. "Individuals" refers to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). They do not "follow along" (*anuyanti*), that is, they do not intermingle. By this, the acceptance of a non-distinct universal is refuted.
To refute a distinct [universal], he says: "Something else that follows along. That which is intended as a universal form, distinct from the particulars, does not appear in perceptual cognition.

[Objection: But surely, even regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) that appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), this same fault of non-continuity (*ananvaya*) and so forth is equal in both the positions of difference and non-difference; how then can it be accepted as a universal? [Response: To begin with, a common form (*sāmānākāra*) indeed appears. As long as it is not understood to be devoid of difference and non-difference, its very status as a "decoration" (*alaṅkāra*)—that is, its presentation as a non-entity—is precisely what constitutes its being a universal. For this very reason, it is said that it exists according to its appearance (*yathāpratibhāsam*).

They "enter into" (anvāviśanti) means they become mixed. If there were mutual entry, then due to the attainment of a single form, there would be an absence of distinction; for that reason, it would follow that the universal itself does not exist. Therefore, the meaning is this: the property of being the basis for a cognition of a single form among distinct things that are similar is the universal; [if there were mutual entry], that [basis] would cease to exist due to the absence of such distinctions. Furthermore, the phrase "and other than" is an explanation of "other than the individuals," namely, "distinct from them."

Thus, by that form [of non-perception], when the conventional designation of the absence of a universal—which has met the conditions for perception—is to be proven in relation to a cognition of a universal, the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is stated. Furthermore, a universal that does not meet the conditions for perception should not be admitted; for how could a universal that does not appear [to cognition] cause another—that is, a possessor of the universal—to be grasped or designated by itself, through its own universal form?

The connection with the context is: "How [can one thing be designated] by its own form as another? It is accepted that, by the power of the universal (*sāmānya*), there occurs a single designation and cognition regarding individuals. Therefore, the collective meaning is that the universal must indeed be accepted as meeting the conditions for perception. Thus, first of all, because it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for being an object of apprehension, a single entity related to many does not exist.

"Let it be granted that one thing may be related to many; nevertheless, its nature as a universal is not tenable," he says with the words "And not," and so forth. "By them" means by the distinct individuals (*vyakti*). "Is stated" refers to duality and the like. Since it has already been stated that there is no such over-extension (*aprasaṅga*)—namely, that even conjunctions, effects, and substances would result in having the nature of a universal—it is not simply because one thing is related to many that it is a universal; rather, a single universal is that which is the cause for non-differentiated designation and cognition, whereas duality and the like are not all [such].

If it is argued that this is because the aforementioned cognition of words lacks a basis [in a real universal], then how could there be the occurrence of a single-mode cognition—the functioning of a cognition with a single form—in one particular individual when it has not been brought to a state of uniformity by a universal residing in another?

The opponent replies: "Because of its connection with them. That is to say, due to the connection with those individuals, the cognition occurs in other particulars even though they are distinct from the universal.

The Teacher [Vasubandhu] says: "Number. This locative case is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*bhāva-lakṣaṇā*). When number exists—that is, when there exists a composite substance (*avayavin*) which is an effect—then, because the suffix *san* occurs in relation to conjunctions and so forth (due to the word "etcetera"), they too would result in being universals (*sāmānya*); such is the collective meaning. If it is argued that because number and the other [qualities] do not have the nature of a universal, the occurrence of a single-form cognition in a substance does not take place by their power; [the response follows].

Now, is it not this very nature of the universal that is being investigated? What is this "nature of the universal"? Since the specific characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) itself is not perceived as distinct from number and so forth, [the opponent's position] is not clear; such is the meaning. He states this very point with the words "In that regard," and so on. When asked, "In that regard, what is this nature of the universal?", you replied: "When there is a relation between one [entity] and many, there occurs a non-different cognition regarding the individuals. Therefore, because of the occurrence of that cognition, the definition of the universal is: "The universal is a single entity related to many."

In this regard, we state the following regarding the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): there exist multiple related factors for those effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including duality (*dvitva*) and the rest—from which there would arise a cognition of a single form (*ekākārapratyaya*) even with respect to the substances that serve as their substrata. What is the reason? Because the cause [for such a cognition] exists.

For it is accepted that the arising of a single cognition from a universal occurs precisely because of the cause consisting in a connection with many [individuals]. And this state of being related to many exists even in the case of substances and so forth, which serve as the cause for a single cognition. Therefore, because the single cognition arises [in their case], number and the rest possess the nature of a universal (*sāmānyātmatā*). "Otherwise" means: if, despite possessing the aforementioned definition of a universal, the nature of a universal is not accepted for number and the rest, then let it not be accepted for anything else either that is considered to be a universal. What is the reason? Because there is no difference [between them and those cases].

And likewise, if substances and so forth were to attain the nature of a universal, there would be a confusion of the forms of substances, qualities, and the rest. The connection is as follows: the universal is the appearance of a single form within a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), which is merely an appearance within cognition itself. And because it is of the nature of cognition, it is indeed real, just like cognition itself. As it has been said: "A universal is indeed a real entity; for it will be the form of cognition.
And that cognition, being of the nature of a real entity, arises with respect to the objects denoted by words."
"Therefore, only the real entity itself would have to be imagined as the denotable object, being non-excluded by cognition.

He refutes this with the words "that is not so," and so forth. That universal which is asserted to be of the nature of cognition—since it is not distinct from that cognition, like the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition itself—how could it go toward something else, an external [object]? The meaning is that it cannot be a universal for those [external objects].
He explains this with the words "of cognition," and so forth: because that which is of the nature of cognition does not exist in those [external] objects.

True. There is no real concomitance (*anvaya*) of the nature of cognition across individual instances; rather, because that [nature] is determined (*adhyavasāya*) to exist within the mental image (*buddhipratibhāsa*), and because there is a determination of an external object, there is thus a conventional usage of a universal (*sāmānya*) through error. This is precisely what the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) accepts. However, the author of the treatise intends that individuals which, by their very nature, produce a single effect and are excluded from those that do not produce such an effect, serve as the cause for a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) of that kind; thus, that cognition is held to be based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

But the opponent does not accept such a basis (*nimitta*). Therefore, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) interrogates the very basis, beginning with the words "In that case" (*tatra*), and so forth. In that regard, since the individual instances (*vyakti*) are non-entities, and since the opponent does not admit that these instances—which by their very nature are excluded from what is of a different class (*vijātīya*)—have a single effect, what is the cause for the arising of cognition? It is nothing at all. For the opponent does not accept that distinct instances, though excluded from what is of a different class, are the cause of a single conceptual cognition (*ekapratyaya*).

Furthermore, there exists no real entity that is a universal (*sāmānya*). If a cognition of a universal were to arise without a basis—that is, without a cause—it would occur everywhere; consequently, the single-form cognition "cow" would also occur with respect to trees.

He states another meaning of the passage beginning with "not distinct from cognition" (*jñānād avyatirikta*), starting with "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) and so forth. Previously, by the term "another object" (*arthāntara*), the external was mentioned; now, "another cognition" (*jñānāntara*) is being indicated. For this very reason, he asks: "How [is there apprehension] of another cognition? Of what kind of cognition? Of that which arises from another individual instance (*vyaktyantarabhāvin*). The meaning is: of the conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) produced by another cow-individual, as distinct from the conceptual cognition [produced] in relation to one cow-individual.

For a universal would exist either by pervading multiple cognitions or by pervading external individuals; however, for that which appears in cognition, neither of these two is possible. Thus he says: "And therefore," and so forth. "Another individual" refers to the external [object].
"Therefore" is the conclusion.

He explains [the meaning] with the words "for not," and so forth. "By something" means by way of a general form (*sāmānyarūpeṇa*). "The apprehension of these in that manner" means the apprehension of objects as being "similar."

[Objection: Surely even the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) must state the basis for this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because if it were produced without a support, it would follow [absurdly] in all cases. To this he says: "Mutual exclusion" (*itaretarabheda*), and so forth. The "designation" (*saṃjñā*) is the act of establishing a convention (*saṃketakriyā*). That which is its object is "mutual exclusion. It is "of such a nature"—that is, mutual exclusion characterized by the reciprocal differentiation of entities—which is the seed of this false conceptual construction. The "designation" is the act of establishing a convention; that which is its object is that mutual exclusion whose fruit is the communication [of the object].

He explains by means of the words beginning with "of which" (*yasya*). For the sake of communicating that mutual exclusion (*itaretara-bheda*), a convention (*saṃketa*) is established. Therefore, [the phrase] "from the things to be accomplished" (*sādhyebhyaḥ*) means from those things that are not its effects; having cognized the entities to be accomplished as distinct from those that are not their effects, the convention is established on the grounds that one might act toward those things that have that effect by avoiding those that do not. This aforementioned mutual exclusion is the seed—that is, the cause—of the false conceptual construction (*mithyā-vikalpa*) which appears as a single nature and possesses a single form.

"Grasping that very [object]" means grasping the differentiated as distinct; this is stated by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). However, there is no actual grasping of a real entity (*vastu*) by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This conceptual construction, which has the form of a universal (*sāmānyākāra*), arises from the nature of its own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*); that is, from the intrinsic nature of the predispositions for conceptualization. Thus, it appears with a single form. (74)

But how can there be a single effect—consisting of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) with a single form—from individual particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) which are themselves distinct? By the phrase "by that," meaning by virtue of having a single effect: because they are distinguished from others that do not produce that effect, the non-difference of the individuals is stated. This is because of the statement: "The non-connection with one [thing] is the commonality of those things excluded from it."

He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "prakṛtiḥ" (nature). "Nature" (*prakṛti*) means intrinsic character (*svabhāva*). "Recognition of a single form" (*ekākāra-pratyabhijñāna*) is the single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*). "Cognition of experience" (*anubhavajñāna*) is the cognition of the object (*arthajñāna*). The term is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "single reflective awareness" and "cognition of the object," because the rule regarding the prior placement [of the shorter word] is not invariably fixed. Although the word "cognition of the object" (*arthajñāna*) has fewer syllables, its prior placement was not made. The analysis of the compound is: "that of which these are the first" (*te ādī yasya*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), effects such as burning and houses are included.

The term *ekārtha* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is a single object" precisely because it is a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) and so forth. Regarding its accomplishment—that is, its establishment—even though there is difference, that is, plurality, certain things are fixed by their own nature (*svabhāva*), that is, by their very essence, like the sense faculties and so on. Alternatively, even though there is absolute difference, certain things have arisen as similar from their own causes and others as dissimilar; this has already been stated. In that regard, those things which have arisen as similar produce a cognition of a single form through that very nature, even without a universal (*sāmānya*), just like the sense faculties and so on.

In this context, the phrase "restricted to the accomplishment of a single unifying cognition" is presented as the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), whereas the phrase "the accomplishment of a single object such as the cognition of an object" is presented as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because it is established for both [parties].
fn. 1: Pāṇini 2.2.34.

For this very reason, it is analyzed at the outset: "Just as the sense-faculty," and so forth. The connection is that just as the sense-faculty, light, and mental attention produce a single visual consciousness (*rūpa-vijñāna*). This illustrates what is established by the force of reality (*vastu-bala-siddha*). [The phrase] "the self," and so forth, relies upon the tenets of others (*para-siddhānta*). "Eternal, atomic, and swift" refers to the mind (*manas*) having the nature of an atom. "Their conjunctions" refers to the conjunctions of the self, the sense-faculty, the mind, and the object, because of the statement: "The self is conjoined with the mind; the mind with the sense-faculty; and the sense-faculty with the object."

The compound *ātma-indriya-manorthāś ca tatsannikarṣāś ca* is a *dvandva*. [It refers to] the self (*ātman*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*), the objects (*artha*), and their respective contacts (*tatsannikarṣa*). The opponent’s position is that these—the self, the sense-faculties, and the objects—produce cognition when assisted by their respective contacts. Even in the absence [of one of them], [the effect] is restricted to its existence; that is, it is restricted to having a single effect. For the opponent does not accept a universal (*sāmānya*) called "the state of being a producer of visual cognition" belonging to the eye and the other [faculties]. [Note 1: Nyāya-bhāṣya 1.1.4]

Now he explains the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*). [The phrase] "such as *śiṃśapā* trees" refers to *śiṃśapā*, *khadira*, *nyagrodha*, and so forth; even though they lack mutual concomitance (*parasparānanvaya*) and even in the absence of a common universal (*sāmānya*) such as "treeness," they produce a single-form recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the form "tree. Or rather, the point at issue is that *śiṃśapā* trees and the like produce purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) achievable by wood—such as fire, houses, and so forth—which is distinct from mere recognition.

"According to the conditions" means as follows: when they obtain the auxiliary condition of fire, they produce burning; when there is a convergence of conditions favorable to a house, they produce a house. By the word "etcetera," effects such as chariots and so forth are included. However, even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities, water and the like are not by nature capable of performing the causal function accomplished by wood, because they do not have that as their effect. Regarding this point, he provides an example: "like the ear and so forth in relation to the cognition of form.
Just as the ear, sound, and so forth are not capable of producing the cognition of form, by the word "etcetera," [the incapacity] regarding the cognitions of taste and so forth is also implied.

This might be argued: "The fact that many things each perform a single effect cannot be established without a universal (*sāmānya*). To this, he says: "Fever," and so forth. "Together" means accompanied by other individual instances. "Each" means in their individual forms; they are observed to produce a single effect, such as the alleviation of fever, just like medicinal herbs. The word "or" (*vā*) refers back to the previous example. And there are no others, such as curd, cucumber, and so on [that would serve as counter-examples].

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "yathā" (just as). In that case, when the pacification of fever and so forth is to be performed, they do not depend upon a general property called "medicine-ness" (*auṣadhatva*). What is the reason? Because, despite their difference, they possess that nature; that is, because they have the essential nature of performing the effect of pacifying fever and so forth. If there were an incapacity in the particulars (*bheda*), there would be a dependence on a general property. But that is not the case, even though there is no distinction in that [general property] and no distinction among the particulars—such as curd and *trapusa* (cucumber). Others explain the compound *dadhitrapusādayaḥ* as a copulative (*dvandva*) meaning "curd and *trapusa*," where *dadhitrapusa* refers to curd that has only slightly begun to coagulate.

In those [individuals], such as the specific instances of *guḍūcī* and so forth, which are of such a nature and perform a single effect—[the word] "something" refers to that which is either distinct or non-distinct [from them]. As it has been said:
"Even in the case of an object being produced (*nirvartya-karman*), the universal (*jāti*) is the means (*sādhana*);
for the sake of the accomplishment of its own substratum, it is the instigator of the action."

The meaning is that, because of that very same generality, the effect characterized by the pacification of fever and so forth would be one and the same; therefore, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says: "That is incorrect, because the universal (*sāmānya*) is without distinction. Because it is unitary and eternal, the universal is undifferentiated; thus, it cannot perform that specific effect, namely, the effect of pacifying [fever]. Otherwise, since the universal would be without distinction, even when there are differences in the fields and so forth of those individual instances such as *guḍūcī*, it would follow that their effects—such as the pacification of fever—would likewise be without distinction. Regarding the phrase "quickly," etc.: for those produced in a specific field, there is a quick pacification, whereas for those of the opposite [conditions], there is a slow pacification.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as "longer" and "quicker" are included. Furthermore, there would be no gradation (*tāratamya*) in the quality characterized by health and so forth in the body resulting from the administration of *gūḍūcī* and other substances—which differ according to the preparation of the field (*kṣetra*) and other factors—because the universal (*sāmānya*) is a single unity. If it is maintained that a particularity (*viśeṣa*) of the universal arises through the distinction of the field and so forth, then, if a particularity is admitted in the universal, there would be a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*), because difference is defined by particularity. Consequently, there would be a loss of its essential form; for the single essential form of the universal would be lost.

Furthermore, because of the reason of permanence, since the universal does not assist the individuals, it does not produce an effect; this is how the argument proceeds. For if the universal were to assist [the individuals], then, due to its eternity, it would possess no specific quality that could be imparted by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), and thus, being independent of others, it would not require auxiliaries. Consequently, that universal would produce its own effect all at once. Alternatively, if it does not produce it, then it does not have the nature of producing it. Since there is no difference between its state of non-production and its state of production, it follows that it would not produce the effect even at the time of its supposed activity. This is the sense.

However, he states that there is no such fault regarding the production of effects by individual instances (*vyakti*), which are impermanent, with the words "The individuals, however," and so forth. *Saṃskāra* refers to treatments such as sprinkling water and the like. Those [individuals] whose arising is characterized by such [treatments] are "thus [qualified]. That which possesses a distinction (*viśeṣa*) is "possessing a distinction" (*viśeṣavat*); this refers to an effect characterized by the alleviation of fever and so on. Furthermore, it is not logical to say that it is precisely that intermediate generality (*avāntarasāmānya*)—characterized by qualities such as rapid efficacy—which resides in those individuals that performs the action possessing the distinction.

For even when medicinal herbs are employed, there is the consequence that the effect would arise for any man [who uses them]. "Like that" means like a particular individual (*viśiṣṭavyakti*). "Some" refers to those of the same class (*sajātīya*), such as the single act of recognition and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the fetching of water from a single source and the like are included. "From those that do not produce that" means they are said to be non-different from those that do produce recognition and so forth because of their difference [from others], and not because of a connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*).

Having established non-difference by way of the effect, he states it by way of the cause: "or by one," and so forth. Just as the various instances of a jar produced by effort are said to be non-different from those not produced by effort because they are distinct from what is not produced by effort; for although there is a difference in the effort for each individual jar, nevertheless, due to its being the cause of a single act of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), that [effort] too is considered one. This will be demonstrated further below.

"But what [is the case]? and so forth begins the opponent's argument. That universal (*sāmānya*) which has "difference" (*bheda*)—meaning exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or cause (*nimitta*), is that by which the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is to be cognized as "common" because it is excluded from those things that do not produce that effect and those things that do not have that cause. Otherwise, [if it were not so], it would be something else entirely; that is, a form revolving within conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) which is other than the particular and is incapable of performing a causal function (*anarthakriyākārin*). It is by means of that universal characterized by difference that [the particular] is to be cognized as "common."

But surely, since it was previously stated that a universal is spoken of precisely because those entities existing within the intellect—while conforming to their appearance in cognition—assume specific forms and manifest as if external, the persistence of doubt remains exactly as before.

True; however, this is raised for the purpose of establishing an additional fault. He says "What follows from this? (kiṃcātaḥ) in order to make known that fault. With the words "If [it were] otherwise," etc., he states the intention of the question: if the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is what is to be cognized, how can it be the object of conceptual construction? For it is by the force of the intention of a conceptualizing cognition that the universal characterized by difference is established, due to the influence of that cognition's intention, according to the statement: "That which exists is proclaimed as the universal."

If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were to be cognized as identical with a universal (*sāmānya*) of such a nature, then it would become the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). But this is not tenable. Alternatively, if it is argued that what is cognized as identical is a form entirely different [from the particular], existing only within the transformation of the intellect (*buddhiparivartin*), [the author] states the fault in this case as well: "Or how could there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) from something else? For causal efficiency is not possible from a form that merely appears to the intellect.

Consequently, because they are said to be non-different from those things that do not produce that [effect] due to their exclusion from them, the establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*) by way of its effect is untenable. Furthermore, since the form existing within cognition is common [to many], yet no universal such as impermanence is perceived in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the particular characteristic would lack that nature—that is, it would not possess the nature of impermanence and so forth. And because impermanence and the like are not perceived in the particular characteristic, these properties such as impermanence would lack the status of being real entities (*vastudharma*).

He refutes [the objection] with the words "no," and so forth. The position adopted here is that the conventional usage of terms such as "universal" (sāmānya) and the like applies only to a form appearing within cognition. Thus he says: "The object appearing in cognition," and so on.

And this is the summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*). Its explanation is as follows: it is connected with the phrase "this cognition which is conceptual" (*vikalpaka*). Although its object is not that [particular], meaning although its object is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the real thing (*vastu*), it is "as if having that as its object," as if having the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object. That whose own form (*svarūpa*) has "the state of that determined upon" (*adhyavasitatadbhāva*), meaning whose own form has the external state superimposed upon it, is such [a cognition]. And because it has the state of that determined upon, it is therefore thought to have the particular itself as its object.

If it is asked, "How is it that [the universal] has as its very nature the state of being determined as that [particular]? he says: "Because its nature originates from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of that. The meaning is this: the experience of that particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), the latent impression deposited by it, and the origination—i.e., the arising—from that [impression] constitute the nature (*prakṛti*) or essence of that universal, by virtue of which it comes to have a nature whose state is determined [as the particular]. Those things such as jars, etc., which produce non-different effects.

They are the causes of the cognition of a single form because they are produced from them through a continuous succession; thus, [the cognition] appears as if it were grasping a non-distinct object. However, there exists no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*)—whether distinct or non-distinct from the individuals—which could be grasped by it. In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, its "identical form" (*samākāra*) consists in the exclusion of others: that is, the difference (*bheda*), the distinct nature (*bhinnaḥ svabhāvaḥ*), from those things considered of the same class which are other than them—that is, from those of a different class. This is the analysis of the compound: that which has as its identical form (*samāna ākāro yasya*) this very difference in the ultimate sense.
Precisely because it arises from that [object] and because it turns away from that [object], the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is called its "identical form" (*samāna ākāra*).

In this regard, regarding the cognition just mentioned, "as if one" means as if it were following after all individual instances (*sarvavyakti*); "as if performing a causal function" means as if it were performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). If one asks, "But why does it appear in such a way? he says: "Of those engaged in worldly practice," and so forth. This is because those engaged in worldly practice proceed by determining (*adhyavasāya*)—that is, by conceptualizing—the very portion of the conceptual construction (*vikalpāṃśa*) as being external, as being unitary, and as performing a causal function. Others read the text as "by those engaged in worldly practice" (*vyavahāribhiḥ*).

Because of its connection with the preceding term "adhyavasāya" (determination) in the phrase "by those engaged in worldly transaction" (*vyavahāribhiḥ*), the third case ending alone is employed, and not the sixth. This is because of the prohibition of the sixth case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā*. Otherwise—that is, if there were no determination of an external object regarding the conceptualizing aspect—then even when such a conceptualization has arisen, there would be no activity directed toward that which performs a causal function. That reflection within the conceptualization, too, appears as performing a causal function by virtue of the determination of the person engaged in worldly transaction.

And if it is asked: "Why then is the conceptual reflection (*vikalpaprativimbaka*) itself not the reality (*tattva*), appearing as if distinct from that which performs the function and that which does not? he says: "Nor... and so forth. That conceptual reflection is neither reality nor a real entity (*vastu*). What is the reason? Because, when examined, its failure to perform a causal function (*anarthakriyākāritva*) renders it irrelevant to [the definition of] deviation (*vyabhicāra*). We shall demonstrate this immediately hereafter.

In this regard, those objective forms (*arthākāra*) which, by way of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), appear in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*)—those objects appearing in conceptual cognition are grasped as being "the same" through that universal characterized by difference. [The phrase] "excluded from something" means through exclusion from what is of a different class (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*). For instance, even though the various individual trees appearing in conceptual cognition possess an external form that is merely determined (*adhyavasita*), they appear as if excluded from non-trees. The same applies to others.

The connection is made by changing the gender and number [of the words], such that it means: "the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not apprehended as being similar to that. What is the reason? Because the particular characteristic does not appear within that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in which the universal (*sāmānya*) appears.

Thus far, the conventional usage of the "universal" has been explained with respect to the object appearing in cognition. Now, he states the conventional usage of "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words beginning "those very... Those very objects appearing in conceptual construction...

Being as if excluded from something—just as varieties of lotus, being excluded from non-lotuses, appear again as possessing exclusion from what is non-blue—and because a single substratum (*dharmin*) appearing as conjoined with two exclusions manifests, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Furthermore, this conventional usage of "universal" (*sāmānya*) and "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding objects appearing to the intellect, which has just been discussed, is performed with a purely false object. Why? Because even though the forms of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) are themselves non-existent, they are presented by the conceptualizing intellect through their conformity to a single form, and through a nature of the property (*dharmasvarūpa*) that conforms to two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). The convention of a "universal" arises because [the object] appears with a single form;
and the convention of "co-referentiality" arises because a single [entity] appears with multiple forms.

If every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has only a false object, why are conceptual constructions such as impermanence and selflessness—which arise by way of [reasons] like "being produced"—considered valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while eternal conceptual constructions are not? To this he says: "And all this," and so forth. The connection is: "all is a distortion" (*viplava*). "Distortion" (*viplava*) means error (*bhrānti*). "This" refers to that which has the form of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so on. It is produced by the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by the very perception of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); for, through a succession of causes, all conceptual constructions arrive at their objects by way of the perception of real entities.

For instance, even conceptual constructions such as "permanent" and so forth arise solely from the perception of a real entity (*vastu*), because they are dependent upon the perception of a continuous succession of similar moments. In that regard, although all conceptual constructions are equally dependent upon the door of perceiving a real entity, those conceptual constructions of impermanence and so forth—which have their birth bound to that [entity]—are non-deceptive with respect to the real entity, even though they do not manifest that [entity] itself and do not manifest its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because the superimposed forms such as impermanence and so forth actually exist in the real object, it is merely that [the object] does not appear in its form as a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, conceptual construction is called an error. Just as in the case of the illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel, there is non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) despite the failure to grasp the true nature of the jewel, because the luster is connected to the jewel and because the illusion of the jewel arises based upon that luster.

But it is not so with conceptual constructions such as "permanent" and so forth; for even though these arise by way of the perception of a real entity (*vastu*), they superimpose a form that does not actually exist in that entity. Thus he says: "not of others," and so on. This is connected with the phrase "correspondence to the real entity (*vastu*) regarding other conceptual constructions such as 'permanent' and so forth. "Even though there is an origination from the differentiation of that" means: even though there is an origination from the non-differentiation of the object.

Just as when one has perceived a particularity characterized by momentariness and so forth, there occurs a pursuit of that [particularity] through the determination of it as some kind of generality—by grasping a generality whether distinct or non-distinct from the particular—due to the superimposition of stability and other such qualities upon that [particularity]. This is like the cognition of a gem that arises because of a similarity such as brilliance in the light of a lamp; that cognition does not correspond to the actual object, the gem, because even though the gem is determined through a causal chain, the cognition is not directly connected to it.

And since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have only false objects, they lack causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) with respect to the objects of those conceptualizations; therefore, that which was stated—namely, "how could there be causal efficacy from anything else?"—is established as proven.

If it is asked: "How then is a universal, characterized by the exclusion of what does not produce that [effect], established with respect to objects that are the referents of conceptual constructions? We say: No. For those things which appear as if external—because they perform a single telic function—appear as if distinct from those that do not perform that function. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "impermanence and so forth are not perceived in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and therefore it lacks that nature," he says "nor indeed... and so on, in order to refute that: because there is no such thing as "impermanence" apart from the fluctuating entity itself.

By which [reason] there would be no connection between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and impermanence. Rather, the entity is indeed momentary, because the particular characteristic itself has the nature of impermanence; in this same way, "selflessness" (*anātman*) and so forth are also to be understood. Therefore, when the particular characteristic is apprehended by perception, impermanence is already apprehended; it is merely not ascertained due to the presence of causes for error. Consequently, the function of inference consists solely in its ascertainment. Thus, it is established that the cognition of impermanence regarding the particular characteristic is simply the ascertainment of that [already perceived fact].

If the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is impermanent, how can there be a cognition of this object as "impermanent" or "this has impermanence," in the form of a subject (*dharmin*) and a property (*dharma*)? To this he says: "momentary," and so forth. Of such a specific characteristic—that is, of that which is of a mobile nature—because it does not persist for more than a single moment, its apprehension as lasting for only one moment leads to the following thought for those who perceive the final moment at a later time: "This is impermanent," and so on.

When there is an intention not to exclude other distinctions, one says "this is impermanent"; when there is an intention to exclude other distinctions, one says "this has impermanence. In this way, the cognition of the relationship between a subject (dharmin) and its property (dharma) arises.

Since [these properties] are constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), how can there be a relationship between a property and its locus (*dharmadharmibhāva*) with respect to external reality? To this he says: "taddharmatām" and so forth. The meaning is that conceptualizations (*vikalpāḥ*) enter into the state of being that property—that is, the state of being the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—and thereby determine (*adhyavasyanti*) the specific characteristic. Following words for which conventions have been established based on differences in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there are properties (*dharmāḥ*) of various forms as well as those of a single form; these are both "properties" and "distinctions" (*vyatireka*), forming a copulative compound (*dvandva*). These various properties include impermanence, being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth.

They demonstrate that a single property, such as impermanence, belongs to many things like pots, and that the exclusion [of others] is the impermanence of those pots and so forth. The word "entities" (*vastu*) is to be supplied [as the object]. Nor is reality established by the various properties and so forth posited by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because conceptual construction does not grasp real entities. For this very reason, he says: "they demonstrate."

If it is argued that, because they grasp what is not a real entity (*avastu*), those conceptual constructions would consequently be without a basis, he says: "And not those... "Not" [means]: conceptual constructions do not lack a basis, because their basis is the perception—the direct experience (*anubhava*)—of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in its aspects such as impermanence, which is the differentiation of the object of conceptualization and which reveals various properties (*dharma*) and so forth. For instance, having perceived the ultimate reality—the particular characteristic in its form of impermanence and so on—conceptual constructions, arising through the power of that perception, proceed by determining (*adhyavasāya*) the perceived aspect.

And because conceptual constructions proceed by verbalizing exactly what has been perceived—such as the aspect of impermanence—and do not follow after something else, like the conceptualization of permanence and so forth, therefore that which was stated—that "their nature is non-substantial"—is refuted. Thus he says: "No. These [aspects] such as impermanence and so forth do not have a non-substantial nature. Why? Because it is precisely the intrinsic nature of those things that appears and manifests in that way as having the nature of impermanence and so forth; that is to say, because of its determination (*adhyavasāya*).

If impermanence and so forth appear as the very properties of the real entity (*vastu*), then what is the error (*vibhrama*) produced by conceptual construction? To this he says: "But of the real entity," and so forth. The apprehension of a single real entity in manifold forms, and of many things as one, as well as the apprehension of property and property-bearer as distinct, is an error; that is to say, it is a delusion. What, then, is the reason that the apprehension of oneness and so forth is an error? To this he says: "Of that [entity], whether one or many," and so forth.

Of a particular instance such as a jar, which performs a single function and accomplishes a single effect such as the fetching of water; likewise, regarding future desires to know—that is, regarding desires to know that it performs a single function; for the purpose of making known its existence—that is, for the purpose of making known its performance of a single function; because its status has been so established; because it has been fixed in a single form, such as a jar, for the sake of facilitating linguistic convention; and likewise, of even one thing that performs multiple functions.

Just as in the case of a jar—which performs functions such as visual cognition and the holding of water—there is an inquiry into its nature as it exists, and for the sake of making known that nature, it is established in such a way to demonstrate its possession of multiple functions; because it is situated as having been so fashioned, and because it is defined by such forms as being visible, earthen, and impermanent. In the same way, this should be stated accordingly in other cases as well. It is not from a difference in the thing-in-itself (*vastubheda*) that there is an establishment of multiple properties in a single entity.

What is the reason? Because it is impossible for that very same single entity to possess multiplicity. Consequently, the apprehension of multiplicity in what is single is declared to be an error. Likewise, the establishment of unity in what is multiple occurs only by way of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what is not its effect, and not due to any non-difference in the entity itself; thus he says: "because multiplicity cannot belong to what is one. Accordingly, the apprehension of unity in what is multiple is an error. In this way, even the apprehension of a distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is indeed erroneous.
What is the reason? Because a separate universal has already been refuted [in the passage] beginning with "Individuals do not follow after another," and so forth.

He says—“of these,” and so forth—in order to show that properties (*dharma*) are indeed distinct from the property-possessor (*dharmin*), and therefore the referent of a word will correspond to the actual state of things: “Because of the difference in the nature (*prakṛti*) or intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*) of those properties such as impermanence, if one accepts that the referent of a word corresponds to the actual state of things, then coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible in cases such as ‘blue lotus’ or ‘sound is impermanent. This is because qualities such as blue and so forth, as well as universals such as lotus and so forth, possess a mutual difference in their intrinsic essences.”

Since there is no occurrence of words denoting those [distinct things] within a single substratum, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is impossible. Therefore, the implication is that the determination of word-meanings does not correspond to the actual state of things.

With the words “of that which has those as its limiting adjuncts” (*tadupādheḥ*), etc., he anticipates the opponent’s intention: since those properties such as blue (*nīla*) are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of a single substance, there is no fault because that one [substance] is denoted by two [terms], namely, a quality (*guṇa*) and a genus (*jāti*). Thus, the fault of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not exist. He states the reply: “not providing assistance,” etc. The substance does not provide assistance to the properties such as blue, which are intended to be its limiting adjuncts.

For no assistance whatsoever is rendered by the quality of blue or the universal of lotus-ness to the substance; and consequently, since they provide no assistance, it is impossible for qualities such as blue—which cannot have their occurrence imposed upon the substance—to be dependent upon it. Thus, qualities such as blue are not limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because they lack dependence. Otherwise, it could not even be said that "this is its adjunct."

If it is maintained that the dependence of properties (*dharma*) upon a substance (*dravya*) is a dependence on a real entity, then even in that case of dependence, one must admit that [the property] is produced by the substance; otherwise, dependence on a substance would be impossible. Furthermore, the producer must be admitted to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*), because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) belongs only to the momentary. Consequently, because of the non-coexistence of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) considered as effects and the substance considered as the cause, [they cannot exist simultaneously].

There is a simultaneous non-denotation of the two—the qualifier and the qualified—which are of the nature of real entities (*vastu*), because at that time the specific property intended as the cause has ceased. The term "of one" refers even to the qualified [entity] which possesses limiting conditions (*upādhi*). This is an elliptical expression (*adhyāhāra*) for demonstration; in that case, the referent of the word would not have a real entity as its object, because the word denotes only a specific property superimposed by the intellect.

It might be thought: "Let that which has perished, as the qualified object, be the object of the mental appearance for the word referring to it; however, as for a qualifier that is actually existent, let the word denoting it have the real entity itself as its object. To this, he says: "The mental appearance," and so forth.

That designation whose object is a mental appearance is "such"; its state is "being such. When that [state] exists, let every designation—even one intended to have a particular as its object—be likewise nothing but an object of a conceptual mental appearance. What is the reason? Because when a single thing possessing distinct limiting conditions—that is, possessing various qualifiers—is apprehended, it does not appear [as such] in the cognition.

For in that case, one must admit a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) that supplies [the missing element] when that which possesses the adjunct (*upādhimat*) has perished; and at that time, since that which possesses the adjunct is absent, the adjunct itself is also absent, because there is no dependence [of the one upon the other]. When that single [entity] possessing distinct adjuncts does not appear, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)?

However, when it is accepted that both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) appear in the conceptualizing cognition, then a single cognition arises which apprehends a single substratum (*dharmin*) as grasped by two imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*); thus, coreferentiality is not contradictory.

With the words beginning "upakāryā" (the object of assistance), he anticipates the opponent's intention. [The opponent argues: "There is no fault in this, namely, that there is the superimposition of a cognition upon a single [entity]," and so forth. However, because an auxiliary condition (*upādhi*) that exists simultaneously with its possessor has an already established nature, it lacks dependence; therefore, it is not an auxiliary condition. If it is argued that its prior state of dependence constitutes its very nature as an auxiliary condition, he says: "No," and so forth.

For that which is unestablished—being like the horn of a hare—cannot possess dependence or the status of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Since there is no dependence for that which is either entirely existent or entirely non-existent, one makes the dependence of limiting adjuncts a mere conceptual superimposition; thus, in the conventional usage of dependence, why is it that the same superimposing cognition is not likewise followed in the conventional usage of the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*)? "In every way" (*sarvathā*) means by every manner, such that just as the cognition conforms to the conventional usage of dependence, so too should that same superimposing cognition conform to the conventional usage of the qualifier and the qualified.

For it is logical to conform to that [distinction], because it is impossible to engage in conventional discourse without relying on the appearance of an object as presented by cognition. Furthermore, when a thing is apprehended by means of a single word or a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), all its inherent properties are necessarily implied by the force of the thing itself; thus, the futility of other words and so forth—which was previously stated in the passage beginning "of a single nature of an object that is perceived," etc.—is established.

In the view of those who maintain that [universals] are real entities (*vastuvādin*), it would exist in accordance with the appearance in cognition. What is the reason? Because the appearance in cognition is devoid of a real object (*nirvastuka*), there is no occasion for the faults that arise from the causal efficacy of real entities. By using the plural number, he says this: not only is there no occasion for the fault of the other [particulars] being redundant, but likewise there is an absence of a separate universal (*sāmānya*), because it is impossible for limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to be dependent on something else.

The absence of the relation between qualifier and qualified [is established] because a single entity possessing distinct substrata does not appear in cognition; and as for the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that was previously mentioned, its occurrence here is likewise impossible. He states this very point with the words "That is non-different," and so forth. For indeed, the form appearing in that cognition appears as non-different. Therefore, having supplied the words "so that the universal is not contradicted by experience," the connection is made with what is to be said hereafter.

When "blue" is said, although the single form of blueness is made an object by way of the exclusion of the non-blue (*anīla-vyāvṛtti*), the conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-buddhi*) effects the exclusion of doubt regarding that very form of blue, and not regarding any other form. Therefore, the form appearing in that cognition has an uncertain aspect and so forth, because the aspect of the lotus—defined by the exclusion of the non-lotus—is not ascertained. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: since certainty has not arisen regarding that particular aspect, another aspect remains there; and because the word "lotus" is employed with reference to that [aspect], it appears as something to be grasped by the cognition that has arisen, being accompanied by an expectation for that [other aspect].

By this, the cause for the relationship between qualifier and qualified has been stated. Regarding co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he says "distinct," and so forth. Even when there is a synthesis—that is, a presentation—of distinct word-meanings characterized as "blue lotus" and so on, [it is because] that which is grasped by two properties, though non-distinct in its nature as a single substratum, appears in conceptual cognition as the form of a mental image; thus, universals and the like are not contradictory, in accordance with how they are perceived.

Therefore, as for what is stated by Bhaṭṭa: "If one grasps apoha as merely the exclusion of others, then because the exclusion of non-lotuses is absent in the exclusion of non-blue things, and because the exclusion of non-blue things is absent in the exclusion of non-lotuses, there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified between those two properties; and because that [relationship] is absent, there can likewise be no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two words that denote them."

Nor can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two things denoted by the words, because they are distinct. Nor can coreferentiality be mediated by the locus in which the two exclusions (*apoha*) reside, because an exclusion, being a non-entity, lacks the property of being something that can be contained within a locus. Furthermore, it has been refuted [by others] that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of the word and that no other locus is admitted; for even if the two exclusions were present in the particular characteristic, there would still be no coreferentiality of the two words, since their having a single object is not perceived.

Since it is accepted that one's own internal form, which is distinct from external objects, constitutes the object of words and so forth, it follows that in words such as "blue lotus," the expression of the word-meaning is indeed accepted; thus, everything is well-established.

The connection [of the sentence] is to be understood by changing the construction of the words as follows: "Even the distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) of this mental appearance (*buddhipratibhāsa*) is not contradicted according to how it is perceived. He states that very point with the verse beginning "from many," etc.: because the mental appearance arises from many objects. Why is there a distinction among the many objects? It is merely said so by virtue of the person's conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). Regarding that mental appearance, when there is a desire to know its affirmation or negation in relation to the distinction from a single object—

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Is sound impermanent? It is not visible; thus that very object which has become a manifestation in cognition is demonstrated. To the question "In what manner?", he says: "Having rejected," and so forth.

Alternatively, the connection is that even the distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is not contradictory for this entity. Why? He says: when there is the possibility of a distinction from multiple external objects, regarding the distinction of that [entity] from one [of them], in the inquiry concerning affirmation and negation—such as "Is sound impermanent? or "Does it not possess visibility?"—that very same external entity is demonstrated; this is the connection. By what means is it demonstrated? He says: "Having rejected," and so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having prompted by means of the word *dharma*, one establishes it as if it were a distinct property (*dharma*). For instance, when the prompting is made by the word *dharma* in the statement "impermanence is not visible," a property such as impermanence is established as if it were something distinct. He asks: for what reason? He says: because it appears thus to the cognition; that is, because when there is prompting by the word *dharma*, it appears to the cognition which apprehends the property as if it were indeed distinct.

"Without distinction" means that, without rejecting any particular differences, another external nature—one whose internal distinctions have not been rejected—is established as the subject (*dharmin*) and is demonstrated by means of a word.

This is what is meant: having first raised an inquiry with the word "property" (*dharma*) and presented it as if it were a distinct property, and then again raising an inquiry with the word "subject" (*dharmin*), another nature is established as the subject, and thus that very same external object is demonstrated. For example: "impermanence of sound," or "sound is impermanent and not visible. [This is done] "by way of a portion of existence and non-existence."

Because of the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions, the conceptual cognition appears as if it possesses distinction—appearing as if it were distinct in form with respect to the property and the property-bearer. However, there is no actual distinction in the real entity (*vastu*). Cognition is not distinct by virtue of a distinction in the real entity. Why? Because of the aforementioned fault; for it is impossible for properties to be dependent upon a property-bearer that provides no assistance.

Likewise, [one might think that] impermanence is the probandum (*sādhya*) and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the probans (*sādhana*), and thus there is a distinction between the probandum and the probans; therefore, he says "tathābhūta" and so forth. The connection is as follows: by means of the statement of the multiplicity of such distinct properties (*dharma-bheda*)—whose internal differences have been rejected—the distinction between words and the distinction between the probandum and the probans are established.
