He asks: for what purpose are those phenomena—which have that [exclusion] as their inherent nature and basis, which consist of the various appearances of phenomena that are reflections in conceptual cognition—produced? He says: "For the sake of its own nature," and so forth; that is, for the sake of the realization or the attainment of that very excluded (vyāvṛtta) real entity (*vastu-svabhāva*).

Because they are connected to the object through a conduit (*praṇālikā*), he states a summary verse for the sake of easily grasping the very subject at hand, beginning with "its own nature" (*tatsvabhāva*). The conceptual cognition (*vikalpikā dhīḥ*) which is known subsequent to the experience of that objective nature (*vastusvabhāva*)—the word "also" (*api*) being displaced in its order—is, even though it does not possess the object [directly], as if it were directed toward that object. By virtue of its determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is established upon the exclusion (*bheda*) from those things that do not produce that effect;
thus, because it arises through the power of that experience and because it accords with the excluded object, it is said to be "established upon that."

When the cognition has become such as this, that objective form which appears within it—as if external due to the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized—appears as if one and common across individual instances of the same class, and as if excluded from others of a different class. Yet that [form] is indeed excluded [from being real], because the nature of cognition is luminosity (*āloka*). That form of cognition is without reality (*nistattva*), that is, devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Why? Because it does not constitute a factor for valid investigation (*parīkṣānaṅgabhāvataḥ*).

Therefore, it has been stated that only that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is a factor of investigation (*parīkṣāṅga*), because by virtue of not being a factor of investigation, it is incapable with respect to causal efficiency. And since the form appearing to cognition (*buddhipratibhāsi rūpa*) is devoid of reality (*nistattva*), he says that the conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) directed toward it proceeds only with regard to a false object (*mithyārtha*).

"Objects," and so forth. "Qualified by cognition" means that they have ascended onto the conceptualizing intellect; being thus qualified by cognition, they possess the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-rūpa*) because their nature consists in the exclusion from what is of a different class. For example, lotus-objects possess the form of exclusion from non-lotuses. By this—namely, by way of that final form of exclusion, which is "lotus-ness"—they appear as if non-different, but not in an ultimate sense, because the form of the cognition is unreal. By this, the cause for the conventional usage of a universal has been stated.

"Excluded from others, yet those very same [things]" means that those very objects, being distinguished by cognition and possessing the nature of being excluded from others, further appear as excluded even from other things of the same class—just as those very same varieties of blue are excluded from what is non-blue. And this is because a single object, embraced by two exclusions, appears [to consciousness].

The seed of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has been stated. He states that very point with the words "of these" (*teṣām*), and so forth. The connection is as follows: "the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of those objects appearing in cognition is extended. In the word "of these," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) with reference to the linguistic usage. Of what kind is this object? It is "false" (*mithyārtha*). He states by means of the instrumental [phrase] "by those which have become instruments": "commonality," and so forth. "Common locus" (*samānādhāra*) means the state of having a common substratum (*samānādhāratva*); this is because the designation emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāva*).

The conventional usage of universals is extended by means of cognitions and designations whose objects are universals, whose objects are coreferentiality, and whose domain is universals; by other [means], the conventional usage of coreferentiality [is extended].

Although, in this context, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consists solely of verbal cognition, nevertheless, by attributing to them an instrumental function (*savyāpāratā*), both cognition and words take on the form of instruments (*karaṇa*). There is no fault here, because it is precisely the activity of those two—characterized by the manifestation of the object—that is intended as "linguistic usage," just as in the case of saying that cognition is either the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or the result (*phala*). And all such linguistic usage, characterized by cognition and naming, has its basis in the mutual exclusion (*parasparavyavaccheda*) or mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of things.

Because it arises by way of both [exclusion and affirmation] regarding objects that have been excluded, that linguistic usage is said to have "other-exclusion" (*anyāpoha*) as its object on account of its dependence upon mutual non-exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), and not because its object is the exclusion of others; for this linguistic usage has affirmation (*vidhi*) as its object.

Conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) is not the basis for the acquisition of a thing (*vastulābha*) nor for the attainment of a thing (*vastuprāpti*). Nor is it all discourse; rather, it is that discourse in which there exists, through a lineage of succession, a connection with such a real entity (*tathābhūtavastu*). He provides an example, saying: "as in the case of the aforementioned inference. The "aforementioned inference" refers to the conceptualization of inference previously described. It does not apply elsewhere, such as in the conceptualization of permanence and so forth, because even through a lineage of succession, there is no connection with a real entity there, since a real entity does not possess the nature of being permanent and so forth.

Although inferential conceptualization and other [conceptualizations] are equal in being erroneous—since they both determine an object through their own internal appearance as if it were the actual object—it is said: "Just as with the light of a jewel. Just as the cognition of a jewel in the light of a jewel is erroneous, so too, although the error is equal in the case of the light of a lamp, the apprehension of the radiance of a jewel as being the jewel itself is concordant (*saṃvādika*) when the jewel is what is to be attained, but the light of the lamp is not. In the same way, the conceptualization of [an object] as stable and so forth is concordant; this is the meaning.

If the conventional usage of "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth applies only to objects that are established within cognition, then there would be no activity toward external objects because the conventional usage of "universal" and so forth would be absent from them; therefore, he says: "In that regard," and so on. The word "therein" (*tatra*) introduces the sentence, or it functions as a delimiter (*nirdhāraṇa*). Therein, among the individuals (*vyakti*), those individuals which perform a single function are delimited. Even though they are many, they have a single effect; for example, various types of jars have the single effect of fetching water and so forth. Thus, they perform such an action for the sake of what is not their non-effect.

The exclusion from others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) is that which serves as the basis for those cognitions and designations by means of which even a manifold entity is led to be treated as a unity; that is to say, it attains the status of a conventional universal (*sāmānya*).

The word "thus" (tathā) refers to the dependence on the immediately preceding general property (*sāmānya*). Even a single entity performs multiple functions; for example, a jar performs the functions of producing visual consciousness, carrying water, and so forth. In the *Tadbhāvadīpana*, regarding the illumination of its status as a performer of multiple functions, [the author] uses the reason of its distinction from things that do not perform those functions to show various properties, such as "the jar is visible," "it is earthen," and so on. By this, the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) is demonstrated as existing only with respect to external objects.

If the conventional usage of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth regarding external objects were ultimately real, then [the following consequence] would follow; therefore, he says: "stated according to how it is perceived. In accordance with conceptual cognition, the referent of a word—the universal characteristic—is stated as it is perceived, even though it does not exist ultimately. This is because this referent of a word and its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are impossible in a real entity.

To summarize what was introduced—that the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) concerns an object appearing in cognition—the author says "property," and so forth. "This is the property, this is the property-bearer" is the establishment [of these two]; and their distinction is such that "this is its property, characterized by being produced (*kṛtakatva*), etc.," while their non-distinction is such that "this is produced. And because this is superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it does not examine the reality of the object; the analysis of the compound is: that by which the reality of the object—that is, the thing-in-itself—is disregarded.
Just as in the world, even though [an object] has ascended into the intellect, it is perceived through the force of its being determined (*adhyavasita*) as having that nature.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: that distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth is exactly as it is according to worldly consensus; thus, the arrangement of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) is postulated by the wise. For what purpose? "For the sake of entering into the ultimate truth" (*paramārthāvatārāya*), that is, for the sake of fathoming the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things such as impermanence.

But what is the reason that the conventional usage of oneness and so forth is impossible with respect to a real entity? He says: "They do not conjoin," and so forth. Ultimate objects do not conjoin by themselves; therefore, there is no conventional usage of a universal (sāmānya) with respect to a real entity. Nor are they differentiated by properties such as being produced, because it is impossible for that single entity to possess [multiple] onenesses individually.

Therefore, when among those many objects a single form is determined in one object, or multiple forms are determined in a single object, that is a delusion—an error of conceptualizing cognition—because ultimate objects neither merge nor are they divided; they do not differ.

For that reason, this [conceptual] generality belongs to many [individuals]. Likewise, as for this distinction between properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*), and this very usage of difference or manifoldness (*nānātva-vyavahāra*), it exists in the object of cognition (*buddhy-artha*), not in the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because the appearance in cognition is unreal (*alika*). If it is asked, "How then is there a distinction of properties such as 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth in that particular? he says: "And of that very [particular]," and so on. It is by means of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) that a distinction of properties is conceptually constructed (*prakalpyate*) for that very particular.

Why is the relationship between the signifier and the signified established through the distinction of imagined dharmas, rather than by the mere perception of the real entity? To this he says: "sādhya... and so forth. Because in the conceptual construction that "this is the probandum" and "this is the probans," there is an abandonment of the perception of the real entity. Alternatively, why is it that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, as qualified by the universal, is not apprehended by inference just as it is by direct perception? To this he says: "sādhya... and so forth. Because in the conceptual construction of the probandum and the probans, there is an abandonment of the perception of the real entity.

How could there be a grasping of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as qualified by a universal? [The opponent might object: "The particular is to be grasped as conjoined with the universal"; thus, masters such as Ācārya Dignāga have asserted that the particular is grasped as conjoined with the universal. Dispelling this doubt, he says: "The particular," and so forth. The meaning is that even in this statement—"the particular conjoined with the universal is cognized"—it is not the particular itself that is indicated as the object of apprehension; therefore, one should not understand it in that way.

However, it should be understood that even in this case, it is only external particulars that are determined—though not actually apprehended—as being conjoined with a universal characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

Others, however, read the text using the masculine gender: "the particular (*bheda*) conjoined with the universal is what is apprehended. In that reading as well, the meaning is: "the particular conjoined with the universal is what is apprehended"; even in this statement, it is not the specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is to be understood [as the object].

If it is asked, "What is the reason that it must be understood as being only there [in the particular]?", he says: "Similar," and so forth. A single form (*ekākāra*) among many is a "similar form" (*samānākāra*). The state of having multiple properties (*anekadharmatva*) within a single thing is a "differentiated form" (*bhinnākāra*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the forms of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmī*) is intended. That particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not in any way an object of apprehension (*grāhya*).

What is the reason? Because it is impossible for many distinct properties—such as being produced, impermanence, and so forth—which are themselves distinct entities, to coexist within a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Indeed, it is not logical for a single entity to possess multiple forms of reality, because a particular characteristic is partless (*niraṃśa*).

Summing up, he says: "That form," and so forth. "That" means therefore; "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct from everything else and unique. Thus, there is no verbal expression (*śruti*), that is, no word, nor is there any conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), that expresses that particular characteristic in its unique aspect. The word "no" (*na*) connects to the subject at hand. The meaning is that there is no grasper of the particular characteristic by way of its own unique nature. What is the reason? Because both words and conceptual constructions function only through universals (*sāmānya*).

By stating that there is no scripture (*śruti*) that establishes such [a thing], it has been asserted that words are not applied to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, he raises an objection with the words "But what then," and so forth. Those which are made objects by convention are "conventional" (*saṃketinaḥ*). Therefore, they say: "Convention is remembered for the sake of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). At that time—namely, at the time of linguistic usage—that specific characteristic does not exist wherein the convention was established.

Because even a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is momentary, there is no persistence of that very same form at another time; or, if it were not momentary, there would be no conventional designation (*saṃketa*) because of the absence of cognition [of it], and thus there is no persistence of its being an object [of cognition] at another time—how much less so in the case of particular characteristics distinguished by different places and times? For this reason, the ellipsis is to be supplied: "a convention is not made with respect to that particular characteristic.
He explains this with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*).

"Api nāma" means "how indeed might it be? "Prāk" (previously) refers to the connection made at the time of the convention; this is how the syntax connects. "Ekatra" means in one and the same particular (svalakṣaṇa); "paścāt" (later) means at the time of practical usage. For what reason is this not tenable? He says: "tasya," etc. "Tasya" refers to that [word] perceived at the time of the convention, because it does not encompass (*anāskandanāt*) the various differences of place and time during the state of practical usage and so forth. Because of its non-continuity (*anugamāt*): for a difference seen in one place cannot possibly exist elsewhere. (94)

"Distinct" according to the Vaiśeṣika system, and "non-distinct" according to the Sāṃkhya system. It is "pervasive" because it extends over individual instances of the same class; it is a "universal" (sāmānya). Therefore, there is no fault of the object's non-existence at the time of linguistic usage. There is no fault of the word-referent being absent at the time of usage, because the universal is the referent of the word, and since that [universal] is a single entity, it exists both at the time of the convention and at the time of usage.

In the sense of "how indeed," the word *api* is used [in the phrase *kathaṃ nāma*]. With the intention: "At the time of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), having cognized objects capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*) from a word that has been uttered, how might a person proceed toward their accomplishment—that is, toward the accomplishment of causal efficiency?"—expressive words are associated with those objects.

He explains with the words "not indeed," and so forth. "Addiction" (*vyasana*) is an intention that is independent of any result; this refers to when people, while establishing a convention or employing words for a conventional object without actually creating a convention, engage in all such linguistic or other activities—whether they be objects of attention, worthy of apprehension, undertakings, or practical transactions—for the sake of a result, and not without a result. Why? Because an undertaking that is fruitless is to be disregarded by those who act with foresight, and is therefore not to be grasped.

The word *tad* means "therefore. This practitioner, when employing [a term] for some intended object—that is, when establishing a convention—is fit to seek only the result; that is to say, he ought to rely solely upon the purpose (*prayojana*). And the phrase *tac ca* refers to the result, which consists respectively in the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, as is appropriate in each case.

Since the human goal (puruṣārtha) is intended to consist precisely in the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, a person—having understood the object to be the means or the non-means for those two desired results—would, with the intention "I shall act toward the means to the desired and desist from the means to the undesired," or "I shall cause others to do so," employ words; and the listener, too, would attend to that injunction.

It is indeed reasonable that the application of a word [should be] "I shall cause another to engage in conventional usage," because the application of a word has another as its purpose. But what is the utility of a word for one's own engagement in activity or cessation from activity? True; however, this presentation is made on the grounds that one who, through the habit of employing words, understands [the meaning] by oneself, might sometimes understand it in this way. Otherwise, it would be something to be disregarded—because the application of a word would be something to be disregarded in the absence of a result. Such being the established principle, a universal (*jāti*) is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); therefore, it is not the object of a word.

He explains this with the words "For not," and so forth. A genus (*jāti*) is not capable of performing such acts as carrying or milking; consequently, for one who desires carrying, milking, and the like, an injunction regarding the genus is fruitless, and thus the employment of a word for that purpose [the genus] would be useless.

Even as regards the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by one’s own apprehension that is described as belonging to the universal (*jāti*), a person does not act for its sake, because that [apprehension] is already established through the very use of the word. If it is argued that the use of the word will be for the sake of apprehending the universal alone, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. "Such" refers to the context of carrying, milking, and so on; for it has been stated that the use of a word that is fruitless is to be disregarded. And this is so when the universal is the object denoted.

In the case of the sentence "Bring the cow," there would be no comprehension of the sentence-meaning [if it were based solely on the exclusion of others]. This is because the universal *gotva* (cowness) lacks connection with the action [of bringing], nor can there be comprehension of the sentence-meaning through *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indication by indication), since such a process is not observed. For there is no comprehension of universals from the words; nor is there a subsequent comprehension of particulars from those universals, and then of the connection from those particulars—thus, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would be of a highly delayed nature. Now, even if *apoha* (exclusion) is the denoted object, how can there be comprehension of an external object, given that *apoha* is formless? Nor is it logical to apply a word to a portion of cognition, because such a portion does not perform any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
True. However, it will be demonstrated that the application of a word to that [particular] is logical precisely because it appears as having causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Nevertheless, even so, since that part of cognition is a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can it be denotable by a word?

To this it is replied: first of all, the part belonging to itself (*svāṃśa*) indeed appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as non-different from the external object. Its appearance does not, however, result from its being grasped by the conceptual construction—lest there be the consequence of determining it in its entirety—and furthermore, such [total determination] is not admitted.

Nor is its apprehension merely a conceptual determination of it as having an external nature, because it is not apprehended in its actual mode of being; and if it is not apprehended, how could there be an appearance of it? However, if it is the specific particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition itself, then an appearance is logical, since its own part possesses the nature of consciousness.

Therefore, if the nature of the specific characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-svalakṣaṇatva*) is not admitted for the own-part (*svāṃśa*), for nescience (*avidyā*), and for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then there would be no manifestation at all. Furthermore, how could the own-part be delimited by a conceptual construction that is of the nature of non-cognition, since this [delimitation] is a property of cognition? Consequently, precisely because it possesses the nature of the specific characteristic of cognition, the own-part manifests within conceptual construction; that [own-part], being non-different from the external object, is established as the object of conceptual construction.

Since that very form which is cognized is determined by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as being non-different from the external object, for this very reason conceptual construction is said to have a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, and not a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because neither the object nor its own part [the cognition] is grasped in its own nature. Therefore, even the own-part—the particular characteristic of the cognition—which is superimposed as having an external nature, possesses the character of a universal. And so he will say: "If it were an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition, then [the fault of] universality would follow; since that is accepted, it is equal [to the external object] by virtue of having the nature of the excluded object (*apohya*). (PV 3.9)

And it is indeed logical that this [universal] is denotable by a word. [The opponent says: "It is a case of 'indication of the indicated' (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) and so forth. [The author replies: True, the universal does not perform a causal function; rather, only the individual (*vyakti*) does. However, because the individual cannot be directly expressed by a word, the word is applied to the universal and thus indicates the universal. Through its connection with that universal indicated by the word, the individual is also indicated.

This is untenable; for when the word "cow" is uttered, it is not the universal *gotva* (cowness) that is perceived, but rather the individual cow itself that is determined. Even though this is indeed the case, it is nevertheless stated [by the opponent] that "it is not impelled by the word," and so forth.

Even if there were indeed a relationship between the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), how could [the word] apply to a specific individual (*vyakti-viśeṣa*) that is not enjoined by the word? It could not at all. For even though a relationship exists between a staff and the bearer of a staff, no prudent person, when told "cut the staff," cuts the bearer of the staff. The meaning is that, because it is not enjoined by the word, application toward the individual when the universal is enjoined is not logical.

If it is argued that because [functions] such as carrying or milking are impossible in the genus (*jāti*), activity will nonetheless occur toward the individual (*vyakti*) even though it is not directly enjoined by the word, he replies with the words "Nor also... and so forth. If a speaker were to enjoin an action that is possible for one thing toward an object in which it is impossible, he would be a babble-er of incoherent speech for the listener. However, activity does not arise from an enjoined [word] that is incapable [of denoting the intended object] toward something that is capable, just like an injunction to milk a bull. For when someone says, "Milk the bull," since milking is impossible in that case, [no activity occurs].

When a cow other than a bull is possible [as the referent], the listener proceeds to milk it; for him, there occurs only this thought: "This speaker is uttering an incoherent prattle. It might be argued: "Let there be no application [of the word] to a female cow because of the absence of a relation [between the word] and the injunction regarding a bull; however, when the universal (*jāti*) is enjoined, there will be application to its individual instance (*tadvyakti*. To this he replies: "And not," and so forth. Because even if a different entity—the universal—is enjoined as the related [referent], [the word does not apply] to the "different entity," namely the individual instance.
But surely this point has already been stated in the passage beginning with "even when [an object] not enjoined by a word exists, there is a connection," and so forth.

True. However, this is introduced again for the purpose of providing further exposition. He sets forth that very point as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "the relation is indefinite," and so on. That staff whose relation [to the possessor] is indefinite is described as such. For instance, even in the absence of the person possessing the staff (*daṇḍin*), the existence of that [staff] is found in the staff itself; therefore, it is so called. "There" means in the case of the staff-bearer. "If it is argued 'no'" means that when the staff is mentioned, no activity [toward the bearer] occurs. The intention is that when the universal (*jāti*) is mentioned, however, there is a cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) because the relation is fixed.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says "that," and so forth. "That" refers to the fact that the lack of a fixed connection is equal even in the case of a universal (*jāti*). If one asks how this is so, he says: "of the individuals," and so forth. This might be argued: just as words such as "brother" and the like, while denoting their own referent, imply a second [referent], so too do words for universals. To this he replies: "But words such as 'brother,' etc. By the word "etc.," words such as "son" and the like are included. The meaning is that because they are denotable by relative terms, they are established only in dependence upon another relative. "They would imply another" means they would imply a second [relative], such as a brother and so on.

And "implication" (ākṣepa) is the generation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the form of a second related entity; it is not, however, mere presentation, because a conceptual construction arises even when the related entity has perished. Nor is there a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) in that case. He says, "If they were denotative of the related entity, then this fault would arise," beginning with the words "gone away" (*apeta*), etc.

There would also follow the undesirable consequence that even for those universals (jāti), such as "Pāṇḍava" and so forth, which are related to individuals that have departed and perished, there would be a constant persistence [of the universal] through its relation to those departed individuals, because of the words denoting those universals. For their persistence by way of being related to departed individuals would only occur if there were a persistence of the individuals themselves, even though they have departed.
Alternatively, it follows that there would be a constant persistence of those individuals who have departed from their related universals, because of the words [denoting the universals].

(p.198) [The opponent says: "At all times," and so forth. If it is argued that because the capacity for that relation is perceived at both the time when the individual is absent and the time when it is not absent, the following of the individual is indeed intended—this explains that just as words such as "brother" and the like, while denoting their own primary referent, imply the related party without qualification, so too do words expressing a universal (*jāti*).

He states the answer: "At all times" (*sarvadā*). "At all times" means that the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) would fail to function with respect to a particular individual capable of carrying a load, milking, and so forth, during both the time when the individual is present and the time when it has departed. If one asks for what reason, he says: "Because [the universal] is accompanied," and so forth. This is a locative dual. Because there is no specific implication of that particular [individual] which is capable of causal efficiency, whether the universal is in a state of being accompanied by an individual or not accompanied by one. This is what is meant.

Just as past and future individuals are implied by a word for a genus (*jātiśabda*) by virtue of being the nature of the word’s referent, so too there is no distinction regarding the manifestation of a present individual elsewhere as the nature of the word’s referent.
If it is argued that this is not a fault because the cognition of the individual follows from the injunction of the genus associated with that individual:

"Let it be so; however, that individual too, as a qualifier of the universal—that is, as a qualifier of the specific property—is already implied by the injunction of the universal. Therefore, the universal alone is not the denotable object. Rather, the possessor of that [universal] (*tadvān*) would have to be the denotable object; thus, another position would be adopted. And we shall state the fault in that case immediately hereafter. This is the intended meaning. (95)

This was stated while accepting the relationship between the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*); however, he says "nor... and so forth, because the relationship itself does not exist. What is the reason? Because there is no mutual assistance, as they stand in a relation of neither being produced nor producing one another. Therefore, due to the absence of a relationship, even the indication of the individual (*vyakti*) by means of the expression of the universal has been refuted. This is because of the absence of a result, meaning the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Even for one who maintains that the universal is non-different from the individual, there would have to be an appearance of the individual in verbal cognition just as there is in perception. Furthermore, defining that [universal] by way of its "distinctive portion" (*bhedāṃśa*) is also untenable. With the words "In this way," etc., he raises another alternative position. "Possessing that" (*tadvān*) means possessing the universal (*jātimān*). "Enough" (*alam*) means capable. "Therein" (*tatra*) means in that which possesses it (*tadvati*). "And he" (*sa ca*) refers to the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). This is the explanation of the passage beginning with "And that word," etc. "Therein" (*tatra*) means in the individual; what is the use of another universal imagined as an intervention (*vyavadhi*) or an interposer (*vyavadhāyaka*)? And "because of infinity" (*ānantyāt*) refers to the opponent.

"This infinity is equal" is the reply. He explains this very point with the words "It might be so," and so forth. "Even in that which possesses it" means even in that which possesses a universal (*jāti*). Since it must be the individuals themselves—qualified by universals and the like—that are expressed, for this reason the connection of the word must be established "in them," that is, in the individuals. Why? Because that which has not had its connection established is not denoted. The genitive case here is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*); the meaning is: because of the non-denotation by that word whose connection has been established. Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

Alternatively, because a meaning that has not had a relationship established with a word cannot be denoted by it—this "relationship" being what is referred to—it is impossible to establish such a relationship with that which possesses the universal (tadvat), due to its infinity. Therefore, this position is untenable. If it is argued: "Because the relationship of the word is established with the universal (sāmānya) that is related to that [particular], and since the universal is related to the particular, the relationship is effectively established with the particular as well."

The answer to this has already been stated: even though a connection exists for a universal, there is no cognition of another individual based on a convention established for one genus; furthermore, it has been stated that no connection exists between a genus and its possessor. For even when a connection exists, there is no comprehension of the person with the staff from the word "staff"; likewise, it has just been explained that there is no connection whatsoever between a genus and its possessor. (96)

Thus far, by the words "all entities" (*sarvabhāvā*) and so forth, the author of the *Vārttika* has explained his own intended position regarding the scope of the indicative signs of injunctive words (*vidhiśabda*). Now, with the intention of showing for what purpose the teacher Dignāga stated that the universal (*sāmānya*) is characterized by differentiation (*bheda*), he asks: "Moreover," and so forth. He thinks as follows: just as the word "cow" is conventionally established when the nature of being a cow (*gotva*) is not [otherwise] perceived from the word "cow," so too [is it here].

The opponent asks: "Why is the convention not established for that similarity characterized by exclusion (*anyāpoha*), which consists in the difference of those things performing the intended causal function from those things that do not perform that intended causal function—since all those performing the intended function are alike in being distinct from those that do not? He states this as follows: "Whatever causal function... and so forth.

With reference to, that is to say, intending, the accomplishment—that is, the production—of an object characterized by burning, cooking, and so forth, this person employs, that is, applies, words toward objects that accomplish the intended purposeful action. Because those things which accomplish it (i.e., the intended purposeful action) are distinct from others that do not accomplish it, those things which accomplish it are non-different [from one another] due to being excluded from everything of a different class. Therefore, since there is no difference among these objects in that very respect, why is a word not applied to that which is characterized by the exclusion of others?
The intention of the question is that there might be a cognition, by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), even of that which is qualified by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

Regarding the phrase "like that" (*tadvat*) and so forth: the fault that was stated by the teacher Dignāga regarding the position that [the word] possesses a universal (*jāti*), namely, "because that which possesses [it] is not independent" (*tadvato nāsvatantratvāt*) and so on—since that same fault applies here, that fault arises. Therefore, the word is not applied to a particular characterized by the exclusion of others. He accepts that this is a fault of non-existence (*asattva*). However, having accepted that it has been demonstrated that "this fault does not exist at all," he says this: "The universal is redundant. The meaning is that another universal is not tenable.

He explains by means of the words "it might be" (*syāt*) and so forth: even when a real entity (*vastu*) is accepted as the referent of a word, though it is excluded from others that do not perform that function, there is no distinction between this position—that [the referent] possesses such exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—and the position that it does not possess it. He says this very thing with the words "For who," and so on. You have called it "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), while the opponent has called it "universal" (*jāti*) and so forth; what difference is there here in the object to be expressed? None at all, except for the difference in terminology.

"Let it be so," says the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*). [The opponent asks: "Is the universal (*jāti*) something else that is a real entity (*vastubhūta*)? Why, when the fault is equal, is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) accepted [as the basis of cognition] while the universal is not accepted as a real entity? To this he replies: "For even the universal... and so forth. "In the absence of that" means in the absence of exclusion; "of this too" refers to the universal that is a real entity. Since there would be no differentiation among entities, the universal—which by its nature inheres in multiple objects—would be non-existent. Furthermore, it has already been stated that differentiation is not produced by the universal.

Therefore, difference must necessarily be admitted. That [difference] consists in the exclusion of one thing from that which does not produce its effect; and the non-difference of other things—which do produce that effect—from that same thing which does not produce its effect. Let there be a cognition of those things characterized by that [exclusion] as being qualified by non-difference. It is called "cognition" because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) of cognition, but it is not cognition itself. Alternatively, the word "cognition" (*pratipatti*) may be derived in the instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*), considering that entities are cognized by means of this exclusion acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "for its own sake" (*svartha*): if the object denoted is either qualified by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) or qualified by a universal (*jāti*), then the defects such as infinity (*ānantya*) and so forth, which were raised against the position [that the individual is the denotatum], would apply, because it is impossible to avoid them. If it is asked, "Since the defect is equal [in both cases], why is the universal (*jāti*) itself not accepted [as the denotatum]? he replies with the words beginning "artha-antara" and so forth. "Artha-antara" refers to a real entity (*vastubhūtā*) that is the universal. If it is argued that the purpose of the universal is to produce a non-different cognition regarding things that are different, he replies: "tad-arthasya," meaning of that which is to be accomplished by the universal.

"By another" means by a non-difference characterized by the exclusion of what does not have that effect. For if that object is established even by a universal (*jāti*), why abandon the universal and accept [only] exclusion? To this he says: "That," and so forth. "Of its acceptance" means of the acceptance of exclusion. For it has been stated that if that [exclusion] were not accepted, the conceptualization of a universal would not even exist. (97)

Now, since exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) must necessarily be indicated by the word, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth. A sound (*dhvani*) is called such by the speaker because the listener proceeds by means of the exclusion of what is other than the intended object. The particle *ca* has the sense of the word *eva* (only), and its position is displaced; it should be understood immediately after the phrase "by the exclusion of that which is other. "By that" means by the sound. "From those" refers to those objects not intended; the meaning is: "being expressed without [proper] exclusion" when there is no exclusion of that intended object. [The question is: how then would the listener proceed?

He explains this very point with the words "the word," and so forth: "The speaker employs [the word] with the intention: 'How might the listener proceed toward objects that accomplish the intended purposeful action, by avoiding what is undesired and by excluding what is not intended?'"

If the exclusion of others were not expressed by the word, then activity would be permitted toward that which is intended to be communicated as well as toward that which is not intended. And if that were the case, it would follow that the employment of the name—the verbal expression for that intended object—would be useless. For instance, when "bring it" is said, a mere thing is implied; therein, the word "fire" is employed in the phrase "bring fire" in order to exclude what is not intended.

If, however, even when that [word] is employed, the non-bringing of fire is not excluded, then there would be no purpose in uttering the word "fire. Since the word "bring" also excludes non-bringing, it would follow that both bringing and non-bringing are permitted; therefore, since both engagement and withdrawal would be permitted, the mention of its name would result in futility—this is how it connects with the preceding argument.

Thus, when there is no mention of words because of disregard for the injunction (*codanā*) regarding either a single intended object such as fire or a single performance characterized by bringing it and so forth—given that there is no expression of the exclusion of others—or alternatively, because of disregard for the injunction regarding activity and cessation as will be stated later; that is, because of disregard for the injunction of a single operation characterized either by engagement or by withdrawal—the remainder is to be explained as before.

And in this way, there would be the abolition of linguistic usage (*śabdavyavahāra*), but such is not the case; therefore, [the argument] begins with "necessarily" (*avaśyam*) and so forth. "And that" (*sa ca*) refers to the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*). "In those other than that" (*tadanyeṣu*) means in those things that have the same effect as the one in question, but which are different from what does not have that effect; [the term] is non-different [from them]. Because all [things] are excluded from what does not have that effect, the exclusion possesses the characteristic of a universal (*jāti*), namely, the state of being excluded from multiple objects. "That" (*tam*) refers to the exclusion; how qualified is it? It is "that which has a fixed acceptance" (*niyatābhyupagama*).

Because if that [universal] were not accepted, it would follow that the universal does not exist at all. That which has a fixed denotation—that is, a fixed expression—is "that which is so. If there were no such denotation, the employment of words would be fruitless. The meaning of the universal is characterized by the continuity of cognition and verbal designation across individuals; it is established as such because it is "that by which [the universal] is proven" (*prasādhyate 'nena*).

The meaning is this: having abandoned such an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), the conceptualization of a separate entity—a universal—is merely a stubborn adherence to what is useless; it is nothing but a clinging to a non-entity, for there is no other reason for it. Why is that? Because this universal cannot be associated with the characteristics of being eternal, all-pervasive, and so forth, according to how it is conceptualized. This is the intention of the Master Dignāga in his statement regarding the "exclusion of others" (*anyavyāvṛtti*). (98)

"No," and so forth, says the opponent. "It is certainly not the case that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not produced by the word; rather, it is indeed produced. For what purpose, then, was the universal (*jāti*) mentioned? To this he replies with the words beginning "pravṛtti" (activity): for the universal is the object of that activity which belongs to one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). It is by stating that [object] that we have mentioned the universal.

The proponent of the established doctrine [Siddhāntavādin] begins with "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) and so forth. If there is an exclusion that is the denotatum of this word; or if there is an exclusion of this possessor of a universal (*jātimat*) that is the denotatum of the word—[the opponent asks]: "Is it not the case that the purpose of words is simply this much: the engagement [of the listener] with what is desired by means of the exclusion of others? [The Siddhāntavādin replies: "In that case," meaning when the engagement with what is desired must be effected through exclusion, or regarding that object of engagement (*pravṛttiviṣaya*), what need have you for some other, additional universal?

"Is it not so? and so forth, says the opponent. "It has been said," says the Teacher. "For thus... is the demonstration of its illogicality. "That" refers to the universal (*jāti*). Because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the universal is not fit for purposeful activity. Nor is the universal cognized from the word "cow. This has already been explained in the passage beginning with, "In that regard, the universal is unfit for causal efficiency" (*Pra.vin. Saṃkṣepa*). If it is argued that a person’s engagement with a substance capable of causal efficiency will occur by means of the universal, he says: "By means of that," and so forth.

[The opponent asks: "Even if a connection exists, how could one act toward that which is not enjoined by words? and so forth. [The author] says: "If it is argued that the possessor of the universal (*tadvān*) alone is enjoined by means of the universal (*jāti*," he replies: "In the case of enjoining the possessor of that," etc. The word "obstruction" (*vyavadhāna*) has been stated; this is to be connected by changing the gender of the term [from neuter to masculine]. It was stated that there is an obstruction therein by way of the general [category]. Why is that [possessor] not directly applied? [The author answers with the verse beginning: "But why is there an obstruction by another therein? and so forth.

It might be thought: neither the universal (*jāti*) alone nor the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the basis for the application [of a word]; for the universal alone lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and the individual alone cannot be the object of verbal expression. Therefore, the universal and its possessor together constitute the object of application; it is these two taken together that have the status of the word-meaning. To this, he says: "Of the universal and its possessor," and so forth. "In being the object of application" means when they are accepted as the objects of application which is based on words.

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Why are exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*) not accepted as objects of purposeful action? The implication is that both exclusion and its possessor are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that exclusion, being of the nature of a word, is a conceptual construction of the intellect and therefore lacks reality, and thus—because it is not a means toward causal efficacy such as carrying or milking—it cannot be an object of purposeful action; [we reply: this lack of being a means applies equally to the universal (*jāti*), for that too is incapable of carrying, milking, and so forth.

If it is argued that there is no fault characterized by the absence of purposeful action, because the possessors of the universal (*jātimat*) are the means toward causal efficacy, just like that [exclusion]; [we reply:]...
"It is the same," and so forth, says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). "That" refers to the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsādhanatva*).

Thus far, having explained that Master Dignāga asserted that even an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) which does not exist has the status of a word-meaning by way of the principle of an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*), he further states that the word-meaning is indeed a positive entity (*vidhi*)—beginning with "And [it is] a grasp of what is present" (*avasrugrāhaś ca*). If it is asked: "If its object is a non-entity (*avastu*), how does it cause a person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to act? he replies: "That [is] through delusion," and so forth. "That" refers to the verbal cognition; through the power of delusion, it causes the person to act.

To the question "How is it precisely an error?", he says: Because even though it is not a causal agent (*akāraka*), the external object is determined as a causal agent (*kāraka*) since its own appearance is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyāyogyatva*). If one asks, "In that case, how is there correspondence with the real entity (*vastu-saṃvāda*) in the case of inference and so forth?", he says: "Correspondence with the real entity," and so on. When there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) regarding that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), [correspondence occurs]. But from what does this necessary connection itself arise? It arises through the production of the real entity—that is, through the production of the real entity to be proven acting as the cause. Otherwise, if such a connection did not exist...

There is no correspondence whatsoever with verbal cognition and the like. If it is argued that "there is non-erroneousness because of the arising from a real entity," this might be so if one considers that verbal and other cognitions arise from a real entity and thus correspond to that entity—assuming thereby the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader. But this is not the case. Even when there is arising from a real entity, such cognitions are erroneous because they do not manifest that [entity]; that is, they do not manifest the actual form of the entity, yet through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [cognition], there is a determination of the entity. Thus, their nature is that of error.

The meaning is that, because there is no contradiction between the production of the form of an object and error, the reason (*hetu*) has a doubtful exclusion (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*). An illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel indeed accords with the actual jewel. While justifying this very point of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he says: "vitatha... and so forth. This is what he means: if there were a contradiction between error and correspondence, then the proof that error corresponds to a non-entity would be non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to the probandum; however, that is not the case.

Because the characteristic of error is a false appearance (*vitathapratibhāsa*), not non-correspondence (*avisamvādana*). This is because [the latter] is invariably concomitant with that; that is to say, it is because [the cognition] arises from the thing itself (*vastu*) as its inseparable concomitant. This correspondence does not depend upon the appearance. It does not depend on an appearance residing in the thing, because even that which lacks such an appearance corresponds precisely by virtue of being connected to the real object.
Therefore, this remains established: even though a verbal cognition has a false appearance, it is a correspondent provided there is a connection with the real object.

Now, if it is further maintained that verbal cognition corresponds exactly to the object itself, then, regarding the external object, for one whose mind is directed toward the thing as it exists—that is, toward the object as it is—there would be a superimposed cognition; in other words, there would be a cognition produced by the word that is otherwise than the actual object.

If such activity is admitted, then the universal must be accepted as the apprehended object of that verbal cognition, because there is no prompting by a word regarding the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). And since that apprehended universal is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is no activity toward that universal which is the object of conceptual cognition. Otherwise, if activity were to occur elsewhere—that is, toward the individual (*vyakti*) other than the universal, even though it is not prompted by the word—there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that the word "cow" would apply even to an individual horse because there is no relation between the universal "cowness" and the individual horse, this is not so; for it has already been stated that application is impossible when something is indicated by a word that does not denote it, even if a relation were to exist.

Now, if it is argued that it is not the mere [universal] that is enjoined by the word, but rather "that which possesses it" (*tadvat*), then, when the acceptance of "that which possesses it" is admitted, the faults such as the uselessness of the universal (*sāmānyavaiyarthyādayaḥ*) have already been stated. It has been said that the universal is useless because the word should be applied directly to the individuals themselves; what is the use of a universal? By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of faults such as infinity (*ānantya*) is intended. [The opponent claims: Only the genus (*jāti*) is denoted by the word.

Since that universal (*jāti*) is inherent in individuals (*vyakti*), it cannot be apprehended in isolation; therefore, it is apprehended as unified with the form of the individual. He raises this very doubt [with the words] "the universal," and so forth. If it is argued that cognition—which appears as if fused [with the object] through its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—causes one to engage with the individual that performs a causal function, then at that time neither the universal nor its possessor is apprehended in its own form; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

What is the reason? Because even for a single universal (*sāmānya*), its own state of being—which is its unmingled form—is not apprehended by a cognition that is erroneous due to its close adherence to a false appearance. Consequently, since one must admit the activity of such an erroneous cognition, the view of the proponents of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is nothing other than the position of the opponent.
(99) "In this way," etc., says the opponent; "of the concomitant" refers to a universal that is to be understood through multiple individuals.

"This is not a fault," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). Because of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), even though there is a difference—namely, a mutual exclusion (*parasparavyāvṛtti*)—up to the point of fetching water, one observes that those various similar causal efficacies (*arthakriyā*), such as cognition and so forth, perform their functions by virtue of being properties of the real entity (*vastudharma*). Having observed this, a person may indeed join together objects with those sounds—which consist of internal verbalization (*antarjalpa*)—and whose scope is that distinct nature (*svabhāva*) which is excluded from other things that do not produce that effect, thinking, "This is that very same thing."

The word "api" (even/also) is placed out of its logical order; its meaning is "even upon seeing another. The collective sense is this: even when there is the perception of an object different from—i.e., distinct in character from—that previously seen object, one might perform a recognition by superimposing identity due to deception, namely because [the new object] performs a similar purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

But how can things that are distinct perform a non-distinct purposeful action? To this he says: "This has been stated," and so forth. [It was stated in verse 1.75: "In the accomplishment of a single purposeful action, such as a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) or a cognition of an object... (1.75).

Because this has been stated previously in such passages as "one [single] among those that are similar," for a person who perceives other distinct things, [the word] "from others" means from those that do not perform that function; thus, entities (bhāvas), by their very nature as real objects (vastudharmatayā), through their very existence, produce a false cognition (mithyāpratyaya) having the form "this is that very same thing"—such is the connection.

To specify what kind [of object], he says "that," and so forth: that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from those non-effects which belongs to objects that perform a single causal function—that exclusion is the object (*viṣaya*) of the verbal expression (*dhvani*); by that [expression] it is "conjoined" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), meaning "associated" (*saṃsakta*), that is to say, "accompanied by verbal designation" (*sābhilāpa*).

If they produce [cognition] by way of the nature of things (*vastudharmatā*), why do they not do so at all times? To this he says: "By their own experience," and so forth. That which is the self-experience of those entities previously arisen—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) characterized as a capacity for the production of recognition—its awakening is its orientation toward the production of an effect; and the awakening of that [impression] occurs again from the experience of objects belonging to that same class.

Since awakening has such a characteristic, it does not occur at all times; therefore, the possibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) does not exist perpetually. "Having a mixed difference" means that the difference between the two individuals perceived previously and subsequently is "mixed," that is, unified by something [the conceptual thought]. "Otherwise" means: if, by superimposing unity upon distinct things through their similarity—namely, their having a single effect—one does not accept that recognition is an error even when applied to distinct things, but rather [accepts it] because of their connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*), then [recognition] would not possess a mixing of difference.
The synthesis of differences would not result in a cognition possessing a single form; that is to say, there would be no cognition of a single form regarding many things.

For even those who possess a staff (*daṇḍin*) are not apprehended as a unity merely because they are joined with a single staff. He explains this very point [with the words] "just as in the case of those with staves" (*yathā daṇḍiṣu*). He clarifies that very same point with the word "for not" (*na hi*). "There" (*tatra*) means among those with staves. "Elsewhere" (*anyatra*) means in another person with a staff, distinct from one particular staff-bearer. That substance which is the staff, having been seen in one staff-bearer, would likewise be present here in the second staff-bearer; however, it is not by way of that [staff] that one thinks, "this is that very same staff-bearer. Or rather, [the phrase] "just as in the case of many through the connection with a single staff" [is to be understood].

Just as this [notion] does not occur with respect to each individual staff such that one perceives, "This is that very same staff," so too, because individuals are connected to a single universal (*sāmānya*), there would not be the perception "This is that very same [individual]," but rather [the perception] "This belongs to that [universal]."

If it is argued, "Let it be so," he replies with "Not so," and so forth. The conclusion is given by "That," and so forth. "One" means that even for a person who perceives a single [form] common to many individuals, cognition is not tenable as having a single form, just like the connection of differences (*bhedasaṃsarga*). The "connection of differences" is the state of having a single aspect; a cognition possessing that is not logical. However, for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), this is not a fault; thus he says "through delusion," and so forth. The meaning is "by the power of error."

If it is argued that a single, real universal (*sāmānya*)—existing as a single form in the manner of "it is thus"—is the cause of recognition, and that therefore [recognition] cannot be a delusion due to the absence of such a thing; [we reply: those very excluded entities (*vyāvṛttā bhāvāḥ*) are the performers, by nature, of that single object such as cognition. Experience itself is the door, that is, the cause; for by its very nature or essence, it is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) because it serves as the cause for the result of delusion, which is the fruit of error.

[Objection: But surely, if an error such as that of water in a mirage were to arise without similarity [to water], there would be an over-extension of the principle. And if similarity is admitted, why not admit a universal (*sāmānya*) as well? To this he says: "In the case of mirages, etc. The first word "etc. includes [the error of] a rope and so forth; the second includes the error of a snake and so forth.

The phrase "those two alone" means that even though they are distinct, the two entities in the form of water and mirage are the causes—the producers—of that experience which serves as the basis for the reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) in the form "this is that very same water," which possesses an undifferentiated form.

This is what is meant: there is no similarity whatsoever among dissimilar things. Even for similar things, it is their own nature (*svarūpa*) that is similar which serves as the cause of error, not "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) itself. For instance, the cognition consisting in the experience of water deposits an impression (*vāsanā*) that reflects the form of water. And just as that impression is awakened again by the experience of the specific individual (*svalakṣaṇa*) of water, so too is it naturally awakened by the experience of the object known as a mirage, because that [mirage] has that very same nature.

Therefore, just as a cognition that reflects the form of water is said to arise from the experience of water, so too does it arise from the experience of a mirage. Consequently, these two entities called "water" and "mirage" become the causes for the error of water by way of being experiences of those respective objects. Nor does this lead to an over-extension [of the principle], because although they are equal in their non-watery nature, the specific nature of the mirage arises from its own causes as something possessing similarity; it is not the case that something becomes similar merely through a connection with similarity, as was stated in the section on *sāmānya* (universals) according to the established logic.

Having thus refuted the view of Uddyotakara and others, he says "na hi" and so forth in order to refute the Mīmāṃsaka position. For instance, in the cognition of water, two things appear: the universal of water (*jala-sāmānya*) and its connection with a particular place and so forth. Therefore, when a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arises stating "it is not [there]," it is the connection with the place and so forth that is subverted, not the universal of water. Consequently, the cognition of water has the universal as its very object; hence it is said.

In that case, there is no distinct, separate generality (*sāmānya*) such as "water-generality" within the mirages; nor is there [a generality] in the form of water. Or, if the existence of a water-generality were admitted, then the cognition apprehending it would be one that grasps an existent object, because it would grasp a generality that is a real entity (*vastubhūta*).

Now, it might be argued: "The cognition of water has as its objective support (*ālambana*) precisely the water-generality residing in other places and times; it is not an error. To this it has been said: "In all cases, the external objective support exists, though its nature is otherwise in terms of place and time. (Verse 1)

fn. 1.: *Ślokavārttika*, *Nirālambanavāda* 108. [Objection: "How then is there the cognition of water in a mirage? It is an error because of the superimposition (*samāropa*) there of the universal 'water' (*jala-sāmānya*) which resides in another place and so forth. To this he says: "abhūta... and so forth. It is an error because of the superimposition there of the form of water (*jala-ākāra*) which does not exist in the mirages.

"No," and so forth, says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). That cognition of water does not apprehend that generality—the generality of water situated in another location. Why? He says: "And whichever form," and so forth. This cognition of water superimposes upon those mirages a certain form—that is, the unreal form of water. To the question, "Why is even that which is being superimposed an object (*viṣaya*)? he replies: "Of that which has not been made an object," and so forth.

This is what is being said: at the time of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that universal (*sāmānya*) which has not been made an object cannot be superimposed upon it, just like any other form. For another form, such as fire and so forth, is not superimposed there, because it is not an object at that time. And whatever form is superimposed as non-different from the external, only that appears as having the status of an object.

And that form of water being superimposed there upon the mirage-ripples does not exist, because it is sublated; therefore, the cognition of water is not "universal" (*sāmānya*), in the sense that "this [cognition] has a universal as its object. Likewise, like the mirage, the cognition of water that superimposes the form of water even upon real water is non-universal. The opponent replies with the words "If [it were] real," etc.: There is indeed another universal of water; when that is apprehended, there is the superimposition of it—the superimposition of water—and not otherwise. If the superimposition of water upon real water could occur without a universal of water, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): the superimposition of water would occur even in the case of fire and so forth.

"It exists," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). When there is the apprehension of true waters—which possess the capacity to perform a single effect such as drinking or immersion—why is the attribution of "water" not accepted? If it is argued that without a universal (*sāmānya*), distinct things would simply lack the power to produce a single effect, he replies: "And necessarily... and so forth. This has already been demonstrated in the section [of the *Pramāṇavārttika*] beginning with: "The means for accomplishing a single purpose, such as a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*) or the cognition of an object" (3.72).

Others, however, explain the passage beginning with "for there is no other generality whatsoever" by taking the word *sāmānya* (generality) to mean "similarity" (*sādṛśya*). Their interpretation is not very coherent, because [the phrase] "since it is perceived as such" and so forth would lack expressive power; for similarity is certainly not perceived in the form of water.

"From that" means from the power of a single cause. "Those very [particulars]" means that among those things possessing the aforementioned powers, it is the manifest individuals (*vyakti*) themselves that are joined [with the cognition], and not the universal (*sāmānya*). "From others" means from those things which do not have that effect. "Of such a kind" means having a single form. "According to the state of being" (*yathābhāvam*) refers to the positive concomitance (*anvayībhāva*) in the sense of not deviating from the nature of the object. Just as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists devoid of a universal, why does the conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) not cognize it by transcending that [particular]? Why, then, does it superimpose an unreal universal upon it?

The meaning of the phrase "according to the state of being" (*yathābhāvam*) is expressed by the words "unmixed" (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*), and so forth. "Unmixed" means not having attained a single, unified form. A "distinction" (*bheda*) is a mutual difference; that entity which possesses such a distinction is described as such. This [conceptualization] is powerless. Why is it that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are incapable of grasping things as they truly exist? Because they originate from ignorance (*avidyā*). Grasping the reality of things is knowledge (*vidyā*); because it is the opposite of that, conceptual construction itself is ignorance. The word "origin" (*prabhava*) is used here in the sense of "power" (*prabhāva*); the meaning is "by the power of conceptual construction."

If it is argued that since non-apprehension of an object as it actually exists is the very nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and because it is by nature erroneous, it is not logical for the delusion of conceptual construction to consist in the destruction of a real universal (*sāmānya*), he replies with the words "And not," etc. Here, the internal distortion is said to be the very nature of conceptual construction itself; the meaning is that this is the very nature of conceptual construction by which it becomes a delusion without depending on any external similarity.

The error consisting of the appearance of hair and so forth is the delusion of hair and so forth. Just as that [delusion] becomes erroneous by relying on an internal distortion (*viplava*)—which consists merely in the apprehension of an unreal form while being independent of external objects—so too is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) [erroneous], because it apprehends the form of an unreal universal (*sāmānya*). This is the intended meaning here. It is not, however, intended here that the "internal distortion" is the seed of error because [the error] arises from it; this point will be clarified later.

Regarding the statement, "But [the opponent] says it arises from ignorance (*avidyā*)," here the word "ignorance" refers specifically to the seed of the appearance of duality within a mental continuum where the obscurations have not been abandoned. Consequently, "arising" means origination; likewise, even internal distortion (*viplava*) has that very same thing as its seed. Since all cognitions possess such an arising from ignorance, the author says: "Because of arising from ignorance, there is distortion," and so forth. If distortion—that is, error—resulted from the arising or production of ignorance, then it would follow that even visual cognition and the like are distortions.

With the words "No," and so forth, he states his own intention: "Of that"—meaning of ignorance—cognition that superimposes a general form is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because that is its defining characteristic. He says this with the words "For it is indeed a conceptual construction," and so on. "That" refers to ignorance. "By nature" means by its very essence. With the words "It is not thus," and so forth, he dispels the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). This is because those [sensory cognitions] are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) due to having the form of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, they are not erroneous by their very nature like conceptual constructions; rather, for some, error occurs through a physical disorder of the sense faculties and so forth.

Having explained [the nature of ignorance] according to the system of external objects, he now speaks according to the system of internal cognition, beginning with the words "And not... and so forth. He says this: "Granted that the meaning of the word 'ignorance' (avidyā) is conceptualized in whatever way it may be formulated by the objector, even so, there is no fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because [that consequence] is accepted. Nor does this fault of being erroneous apply even to those cognitions such as visual perception and the like, because they too are distorted. He states exactly that with the words "of the non-dual" and so forth. The self-cognition (*ātmasamvedana*) of visual and other sensory consciousnesses is itself non-dual; it is considered non-dual because duality does not exist therein.

For instance, blue and other such objects—which are intended as the apprehended (grāhya) and which appear as distinct at the same time as consciousness—are not ultimately real, because they cannot withstand analysis as being either one or many. In relation to those [objects], the status of consciousness as the apprehender (grāhaka), which takes the form of an agent, is also unreal; however, its nature as self-cognition (*samvedana*) is not unreal, because that is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is argued that self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is also erroneous because it is not distinct from the form of the apprehending subject which is itself erroneous, we say no. For if it were non-existent in its own nature, there would be no manifestation at all, like a rabbit’s horn. Furthermore, even error must possess reality in its own nature; otherwise, its status as an error would be impossible. Since cognition whose sole nature is the awareness of its own form is precisely what constitutes self-awareness, how could self-awareness not be real? Alternatively, the appearance of duality is the error, and error is grounded in reality.

It is like the error of [perceiving] two moons and so forth. Reality (*tattva*), moreover, is the non-dual (*advaya*) which is the opposite of duality, and that is precisely the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvidrūpa*). It is not, however, the mere absence of duality, because [such an absence] would be non-existent; thus, how could it not be cognition? ... Therefore, regarding the aforementioned objection... and those [appearances] which... because they manifest in the form of grasped object and grasping subject, we shall state in the third chapter (p. 211) that these too are erroneous. For this very reason:

Even though self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) of those things possessing the appearance of duality is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the distinction between valid and invalid cognition (*pramāṇāpramāṇavibhāga*) is not established as seeing reality (*tattvadarśitva*). If one asks why, he says: "Of all," and so forth. *Viplava* means error (*bhrāntatva*). *Tadābhāsa* means the semblance of a valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). The *vyavasthāvibhāga* refers to the systematic distinction between these two. The *āśraya* is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the seed of error; its *parāvṛtti* is the removal of obscurations (*āvaraṇavigama*).

The prefix *ā* denotes a limit (*maryādā*). The connection [of the words] is as follows: "the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇyavasthā*) exists because, until the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), there is a correspondence with what is intended as suitable for causal efficiency at all times. Causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is characterized by cognitions manifesting as burning, cooking, and so forth. That which is "suitable" (*yogya*) for that [efficiency] is also "intended," because it is desired by the person. The analysis of the compound is: "because of the correspondence (*samvādana*) with that."

The restriction "because of correspondence with what is intended" means that [validity] arises from correspondence with what is intended, but not *only* from correspondence; for even from a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), correspondence may sometimes fail to occur due to a deficiency in the conditions for cognition. The phrase "because of correspondence with what is intended as capable of purposeful action" is an illustration; it should also be understood as "because of non-correspondence with what is intended in that way."

Thus, the cause for the establishment of what constitutes a fallacious means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) has been stated. [An objection: In the Vijñānavāda, since external objects do not exist, how can there be a correspondence with that which is intended to be capable of causal efficiency? [Response: This is not a fault, because the word "capable" (*yogya*) is used to designate a cognition—such as the appearance of water in a mirage—which is indeed capable of producing another cognition appearing as burning, cooking, and so forth. Thus far, the establishment of validity has been explained for visual and other sensory cognitions, as well as for those produced from signs such as smoke, which manifest fire and the like.
