Regarding the cognition of non-self (*anātman*) and so forth, which is produced by such logical marks as "being produced," he says: "It is false," and so on. Because the cognition of non-self and so forth proceeds by superimposing a general form (*sāmānyākāra*), it is false. Nevertheless, it possesses validity because it is conducive to tranquility (*praśama*). Tranquility is the abandonment of passion (*rāga*) and the like. For those who grasp an object through its general form as non-self and so forth and cultivate that [meditation], once the cultivation is perfected, passion and the like are abandoned through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of non-self and so forth.

But for whom is even a false perception seen to be conducive to tranquility? To this he says: “The notion of ‘mother,’ etc. Even though the notion of ‘mother’ toward one who is not a mother is false, it is a cause for the non-arising of passion. It is by virtue of this similarity that this is an illustration; however, the notion of ‘mother’ and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By the word “etc.,” the inclusion of the notions of ‘sister’ and so on is intended. And here, the suffix *-vat* is used in the sense of the genitive case.

Even when external objects are perceived, since there is no real entity corresponding to a universal (*sāmānya*), if every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is erroneous, then—just as a conceptual construction of water arising from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a mirage is erroneous because it lacks the universal of water—likewise, a conceptual construction of water arising even from a real body of water is erroneous, because that [real water] is also devoid of the nature of water (*jalatva*). Since both proceed by apprehending something as what it is not (*atasmims tadgraha*), why is it that one [conceptualization] accords with the object while the other does not? To this he says: "The mirage," and so forth.

The phrase "and of another" refers to the cognition of water regarding a non-existent body of water; because the universal of "water-ness" (*jalatva-sāmānya*) is absent, rays of light and water are distinct entities. The connection [of the sentence] is: "even though there is no difference in their arising from that [universal]. Regarding the phrase "even though there is no difference in the delusion": just as there is a delusive conceptualization of water due to the superimposition of the universal of water upon a substance consisting of rays devoid of water, so too is there such a conceptualization even regarding a real body of water. Since this [conceptualization] consists in apprehending something as what it is not, it lacks the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as drinking and so forth.

In that [cognition], the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of water is suitable, while that of a mirage is unsuitable; this is because of their respective origins in the case of real water and in the case of mirages. Consequently, there is, respectively, correspondence (*samvāda*) and its opposite—the latter being non-correspondence—in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of water regarding real water and regarding mirages. This is because the specific characteristic of the unsuitable mirage is not suitable for the form of water. For one should not think that what lacks the nature of water is suitable for the appearance of water.

The refutation begins with the words "vikalpa" and so forth. "Dependent on the object" means arising in conformity with the form of the object. He explains this very point with the words "for not," and so forth. The term *yathārtham* is an avyayībhāva compound meaning "not deviating from the nature of the thing. The particle *eva* (only/just) is placed out of its logical order. The meaning is: indeed, a cognizer does not arise at all in accordance with the nature of the object.

If it is asked, "How then is the arising of the cognition of water from mirages explained? he says: "When [the mirage] exists," and so forth. A delusion arises regarding the mirages within the visual consciousness and other cognitions; when that [delusion] exists, there occurs the delusion of water, which superimposes the form of what was previously experienced. Thus, because it arises through a succession [of causes], it is said to "arise from the mirage" (*marīcikodbhavā*). The term *yathāsvabhāvam* is an avyayībhāva compound as before. It has been stated that jars and the like are "non-water" because they lack the capacity to produce the delusion of water.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "by such an object called a mirage (*marīcikā*), which is capable of producing the delusion of water in one who is discerning—that is to say, by such an object—it is said to 'give rise to that' because it does not produce [the cognition] according to its own nature (*yathāsvabhāvam*). The meaning of the phrase "according to its own nature" is expressed by the words "imitating its own nature" (*svabhāvānukāra*) and so forth. It "imitates its own nature" (*svabhāvānukāra*) because it conforms to its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); [this occurs] by means of projecting—that is, by superimposing—its reflection upon the cognition.

Furthermore, he explains by what that [error] is directly produced, saying "But that," and so forth. "That" refers to the error of water; because of a lack of proficiency (*apāṭava*) regarding the characteristic—that is, the discernment by way of difference—of that which distinguishes a mirage from water, there is one's own latent predisposition (*vāsanā*). The awakening of that seed of the error of water, through its conformity [to conditions], produces [the error]. By what kind of factor? By one dependent upon a causal condition (*pratyaya*); the causal condition consists of the perception of the mirage and the recollection of the similarity between it and water. "Therefore" is the conclusion.

An entity distinct from those of a different class is the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular). That conceptual error (*vikalpavibhrama*) which has its origin solely in that [particular] is described as such; the analysis of the compound is "conceptualization itself is the error. It is not [due to] the perception of a universal (*sāmānya*) that is separate [from the particular], because that would entail the consequence of the cognition "it is here" [applying to the universal]. Nor is there recognition [of identity] due to the perception of a universal that is non-separate [from the particular]; this is how it connects with the subject at hand. The phrase "like the individual" means that since it does not persist in the same way as the individual—which is the very nature of the [supposed universal]—there is no such thing as a universal form at all.

"Of another" refers to the proponent of the universal (*sāmānyavādin*). "That" refers to the form of the universal. "From the solitary" means because it is independent of the individual (*vyakti*). The explanation begins with "For not," etc. To the question "Why does it not [cognize]? he says: "Eternal," etc. "Cognition of that alone" means the apprehension of the universal alone. He explains this with "If," etc. "Another" refers to that which has the form of the universal. "By this cognition" refers to that which has the universal as its objective support (*ālambana*).
"In that case" means when the individual is not apprehended; "of the related" means of that which possesses the universal, i.e., the possessor of the universal.

"Possession of that" (*tadvattā*) means possession of a universal (*sāmānyavattā*). If both the universal and its substratum were apprehended by that cognition, then the ascertainment of "possession of that"—which is preceded by the apprehension of both—would not occur. Consequently, how could there be linguistic usage or activity directed toward the individual based on the apprehension of the universal? It would be impossible.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "yadā" (when). "The two" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*). "This" refers to the universal of this particular. "And likewise" means when there is no apprehension of the relationship between the universal and that which possesses it. "By the apprehension of that" means by the apprehension of the universal. "In that which possesses it" means in that which possesses the universal. "Like another object": for at the time of apprehending a horse, there is no apprehension of the substance "cow" through the apprehension of the horse, provided it has not been grasped in its own form. "Assisted by a single entity" means assisted by the universal.

The phrase "it might be so" (*syād etat*) is itself an explanation [of the preceding]. "Of that" (*tasya*) refers to cognition. "There is one auxiliary cause" (*ekaṃ sahakāry asti*) means that the universal (*sāmānya*) serves as an auxiliary cause. "Then, accompanied by that" (*tatsahitāḥ*) means accompanied by the universal. And thus, because both the universal and the possessor of the universal (*tadvat*) are apprehended, the apprehension of the possessor of the universal is established through the apprehension of the universal; this is the intended meaning.

The teacher says: "That [word] *tat*. A single entity, which is the universal (*sāmānya*), removes—that is, eliminates—the multiplicity (*nānātva*) of these individuals. But why is the removal of their multiplicity desired? He says: "And because of multiplicity," and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "for" (*hi*). "In them" means in the individuals. He explains this with the words beginning with "Why? and so on. By that single universal, whatever multiplicity exists among the particulars is said to be the cause of those particulars' not being the cause of a single cognition. Because of their multiplicity, the individuals do not produce a single cognition.

Even if there were a connection with a single universal, since the particulars are diverse, they would not lose their distinctness; thus, as before, there would be no cognition of a uniform form, and consequently, no apprehension of the individuals.

"Even though it is manifold," refers to the form of the individual (vyakti). "One" refers to the universal (sāmānya). He explains this with the words beginning with "no" (na): if [the universal] were opposed to the non-production of distinctions, then even when the universal exists, it would not produce a single cognition that includes distinctions.

"By those" means by the individuals (*vyakti*). But [does this mean] only when all are absent? No; he says: "individually. For instance, in the absence of a *śāvaleyā* cow, the cognition of "cow" occurs in a *bāhuleyā*; likewise, in its absence, it occurs elsewhere. Thus, even when all individuals are individually absent, there is no capacity in those individuals toward that cognition—consisting of recognition—which is produced by that single universal (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, for this reason, there is no apprehension of those individuals by the cognition that consists of the knowledge of the universal.

He says that very thing with the words "How so? and so forth. In that case, regarding the cognition of a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*): "Because of its existence" means because of the existence of the cognition of a universal. By this, the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatirekābhāva*) is stated. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever occurs even in the absence of something else is not caused by that [other thing], just as a barley sprout, which occurs even in the absence of a rice seed, is not caused by it. And yet, the cognition of a "cow" occurs in each instance—such as in a *bāhuleya* cow—even in the absence of a *śāvaleyā* cow; thus, there is a contradiction with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha*). This is because being caused by that [specific individual] is pervaded by the absence of that [universal].

But he says that the universal (*sāmānya*) possesses the causal capacity there—starting with "asati" and so on. Because when the universal is absent, the cognition of a universal does not occur; by this, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated. And "otherwise"—that is, when the universal is present, the cognition of a universal occurs; by this, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated.

If it is maintained that only individuals accompanied by a universal possess the capacity for the cognition of a universal, then, by the reasoning already stated, the capacity belongs to the universal alone and not to the individuals.

The opponent says: "This is not a fault. [He explains: "Even upon the removal of one" means even when each individual [element] is removed. For instance, visual consciousness arises having the collection of blue and so forth as its object; and even when each individual blue element and the rest is removed, visual cognition still occurs with respect to the remaining aggregate of colors. It is not by this much that there is an incapacity of the blue and other elements in the aggregate; rather, they possess very well the capacity for the cognition of the aggregate. Thus, each of the blue and other elements [has the capacity] individually in the cognition of the aggregate.

Likewise here as well, even when each individual [particular] is removed from among the particulars, the cognition of the universal still occurs; therefore, by this much alone, it does not follow that the particulars are individually incapable at all times—this is the connection [of the argument]. Consequently, in the formal argument—"that which occurs even in the absence of X"—there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). The Teacher [Dharmakīrti] says "it is dissimilar" (*viṣama*); the meaning is that the example of blue and so forth, which is being adduced (*upanyāsa*), lacks similarity with the subject under discussion. "Not at all so for the particular" means that there is no capacity in the particulars, whether taken individually or collectively.

He explains this with the words "of blue and so forth," and so on. "Capability is observed even in each individually" means that just as blue and the other [colors] are distinct by way of their own forms (*svarūpa*), so too are the visual consciousnesses (*cakṣurvijñāna*) distinct, due to the difference in their respective aspects (*ākāra*). In that regard, the visual consciousness produced by a collection accompanied by blue is not the same as that which is produced by one lacking it; and that which is produced by one lacking it is indeed something else entirely.

Therefore, because consciousness colored by the form of a collection conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to each individual blue object and so forth, their individual capacity is understood; thus, it is not contradictory for there to be a capacity even in the collection. "In the same way" means like the blue objects and so forth. "Never" means neither individually nor collectively.

This is what he says: If the cognition of a cow produced by a universal conjoined with a *śāvaleya* cow were one thing, and that produced by a companion *bāhuleya* cow were another, then the capacity of individual individuals to produce a cognition through their own substrates would be perceived [as distinct]. However, there is only one single recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) across all individuals, because it has a single form everywhere. Furthermore, even in the absence of each individual, this [cognition] arises from the universal alone. Therefore, the individuals are simply incapable [of producing that cognition]; for this reason, they would not be apprehended by that cognition of the universal.
"Among those individuals, 'relative to any one'" means relative to some particular individual. "That," namely the universal, is "purely independent of individuals."

He explains [the passage] beginning with "atha" and so forth. A *kuvinda* is a weaver. Among many shuttles (*vema*), even in the absence of each individual shuttle, he produces a cloth by means of any one of them. Although there is thus a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding all [shuttles], nevertheless it cannot be said that the production of the cloth occurs from the weaver alone when he is devoid of the shuttle. This is because a weaver devoid of a shuttle does not produce a cloth, since a solitary [weaver] lacks the capacity to produce a cloth. And likewise, the universal (*sāmānya*) is not the cause of that cognition in its isolated state.

The Teacher says: "It is so. By stating that the universal is capable [of producing cognition] in dependence on any one of those individuals, he accepts that the universal is assisted by the individuals, because dependence is impossible for that which provides no assistance.

If this is so, how is it that those individuals do not assist in producing a single cognition? The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "eva" (indeed). How is it that they would not assist in producing a single cognition consisting of recognition? The meaning is that they certainly would assist in producing that very [cognition].

He explains by means of the words beginning with *bhinnānām*. [The verse states: "The performance of a single purpose by distinct [things] that possess different characteristics is not contradictory to a single purpose such as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like, even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*). This entire undertaking is for the sake of establishing the universal. Regarding the word *āsām* ("of these"): it refers to individual instances (*vyakti*). The sense is this: since no [instance] performs that cognition called "recognition" which has been performed by [another instance], why would any [instance] perform it? Therefore, what is the use here of this useless internal tumor (*antargaḍu*)—the so-called universal?
A "lump of flesh" refers to the mass of flesh situated between the forehead and the crown of the head; it is said to be "like that" because it is similarly useless. This is the meaning.

It might be thought: "Individuals possess a power to assist a single universal; therefore, they assist the universal directly, not the cognition. To this, he says: "Just as... and so forth. Let those [individuals] simply produce that single cognition which is generated by the universal. What is the use of an assistance to the universal that is fruitless? He thinks as follows: in the case of cognition, the individuals do not operate by way of superimposing their own forms, because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear in the cognition of the universal.
However, it is merely by way of predominance (*ādhipatya*). And that [predominance] is the same in the case of the universal as it is in the case of its cognition.
Furthermore, if the individuals (*vyakti*) benefit the universal, then this universal essence would become an effect of those individuals; for benefiting is nothing other than production.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "For not," and so forth. "Excellence" (*atiśaya*) means a distinction; because that is absent, [the universal] possesses a nature (*svabhāva*) that lacks excellence. Since no benefactor is present for the universal, even when a benefactor is present—as before—the connection is: "there is indeed no benefactor whatsoever. This is because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for in that case, everything would be a benefactor of everything. Therefore, one must admit that an excellence is produced in the beneficiary precisely through the act of benefiting.

And since that excellence (*atiśaya*) is of the very nature of the beneficiary (*upakārya*), its production is itself the act of benefiting. [The opponent might argue: "The excellence produced by the individuals is indeed something other than the universal (*sāmānya*), and not anything else. To this he says: "Something other," and so forth. What benefit is produced for that universal, which is the beneficiary, by that [excellence] which is a different entity? And what is the use of that excellence, which is a different entity, for that universal, by virtue of which that excellence would be related to the universal?

Because they perform an assistance that belongs to the universal, the individuals would also be benefactors. Since the universal is the locus of that assistance, the relationship between the two is characterized as that of the locus and the located; therefore, he says "of that," and so forth. This means: when that assistance has that [universal] as its locus—considering that the universal is the locus of it—or when that universal has that [assistance] as its locus—considering that the universal is the locus of that assistance.

It assists, thus it is an "assistant" (*upakāra*); because that [assistance] is absent, a universal (*sāmānya*) is "non-assisting. An "assistant" (*upakārī*) is that which possesses an assistance produced by a universal. By the negation of that, it is "non-assisting. The meaning is "that which is not assisted. This is expressed through the repetition of the same word (*tantra*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: what kind of relationship of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) could there be, respectively, between a non-assisting universal and an assistance that is itself non-assisted? Or else, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If there were no assistance [rendered], that consequence would apply everywhere regarding the relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). Alternatively, if assistance produced by the universal is admitted, then there is a restriction of that assistance to that very universal. If it is argued: "What other distinct individual (*vyakti*) could assist that universal by performing that assistance? It does not assist it at all," [the reply is: "[Of that which depends on it]" means [of the substratum] which depends on the individuals; that is, of the universal, because it is the substratum with respect to the assistance. "In its application" means in that assistance.

If utility is being postulated, since the universal is eternal and thus incapable of being assisted, what is this so-called "dependence" upon the individual? It is none at all. If one asks, "Then what is it that depends? he says: "Because its production [depends] on that," and so forth. That which has as its property or nature (*dharma*)—its very essence (*svabhāva*)—production from that which is to be depended upon, is "that which has production from that as its property. Because its nature is dependent due to a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), it is said to "depend" upon the benefactor; the word "it is said" (*nāma*) indicates common usage.

If it is argued that even a universal (*sāmānya*) which is of a nature not subject to origination (*anutpattidharmaka*) requires [other factors], he replies with the words "that to which no excellence can be imparted," and so forth. That is to say, it is such that no excellence (*ātmiyātiśaya*)—meaning something produced or brought about (*utpādya*)—can be imparted (*anādheya*) to its essence by those auxiliary factors; such is the nature of its own self. Furthermore, the compound *evambhūtātmiya* is itself a *bahuvrīhi*. Thus, it is contradictory to say that a category of entity (*padārtha*) characterized in this way both exists and yet depends upon others. This is because [dependence] is pervaded by the quality of having an excellence that is to be imparted, and the state of having no excellence to be imparted is the opposite of that. For dependence is necessarily concomitant with the possession of an excellence to be imparted, while the state of having no excellence to be imparted is the contradictory of that.

Whatever entity arises in dependence upon some locus, all of it arises precisely as something produced or as an effect. If it is argued that the locus performs an assistance that is not part of its own nature (*anātmabhūta*) for that which is supported by it, he replies with the words beginning "parabhāva" (the nature of another), and so forth. Because there is no assistance [rendered] to that which is assisted, since there is no assistance [rendered] to it; for when one thing is assisted, it is not called "assisted" by another. If that [locus] were its support while providing no assistance, then what kind of relationship between support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) could this be? All of this must be explained.

Nor is there the fault of redundancy; for previously it was stated by way of the relationship between benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) between the universal and its instances, whereas now it is stated with reference to the real (*vāstavika*) relation that pertains to all objects. Therefore, because it produces a different [conceptual] object, that which is regarded as the substratum (*āśraya*) is of no consequence. If it is argued that even such a thing is not a producer, he says: "Of that which is of no consequence," and so forth. Since this is so, in the production of a corresponding cognition—that is, in the production of a cognition that conforms [to the universal]—the causal efficacy (*tatkāryatā*) of this universal, namely its being produced by the manifestation (*vyakti*), is evident and necessary.

If, out of fear of the aforementioned defects, one were to admit that the universal alone—without depending on individuals—possesses the capacity to produce a cognition of concomitance (*anvayivijñāna*), then because the capacity [of the universal] to produce such a cognition would never be established at any time with respect to individuals, those individuals would be ungraspable. This is because that which is not a cause cannot be an object of cognition. As for the claim that [individuals are objects] "because they appear in cognition," there is no appearance of something incapable, such as a rabbit's horn, in a cognition of concomitance.

"But the individuals do appear; therefore, they too are capable [of producing the cognition]. [Response: The assistance toward the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyavijñāna*) which belongs to those individuals is unestablished; how then could there be an appearance of those individuals whose assistance is unestablished in the cognition of the universal? It is not at all. If it is asked, "How is the assistance itself unestablished? he says: "That very [assistance]," and so forth. "That" refers to the assistance. For when the universal is admitted, its alone is the capacity for that [cognition], not that of the individuals. As it has been said:
"Even without them, [the cognition] occurs with respect to the intellect produced individually," and so forth (1.105).

[Objection: "Let there be no assistance [rendered] by the individuals; why, then, do they not appear in the cognition of the universal? [The author] says: "Because," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgāt*): if that which provides no assistance were an object, then everything would be the object of every cognition. [Objection: "Let it not be the object; why, then, does it not appear? [The author] says: "Not that which is not an object," and so forth. "That which provides no assistance," and so forth. There is an alternative reading: *anupakārasya*.

In this context, it should be explained that "non-beneficial" (anupakāra) refers to that object from which no benefit for the effect of consciousness is derived. Regarding its not being an object, the term "and so forth" (ādi) includes past and future things, as well as the Primordial Matter (pradhāna), the Lord (īśvara), and other such entities postulated according to their respective scriptures. "Of non-existent things" (asatām) is the general reason [for their not being objects].

With the words "let them be," etc., he states that [the argument] proves what is already established: that those [cognitions] have past objects as their domain (*tadviṣayāṇi*). [The opponent asks: "If they are without an object (*nirviṣayatve*), how will they be included among those [past cognitions]?"—thus, because the appearance conforms to such meanings as these, he says: "Even though they are without an object," and so forth. "Not assisting that" means not assisting that object which was experienced and has passed away. Because it conforms only to a past object in an unclear form, there is no such thing as a "past" or similar [object] whose form it could conform to.

And that appearance is indeed identical with the nature of consciousness itself, because [the object] does not exist externally in its indistinct form. He states the reason for its conformity to that form: "by the experience of that form," and so forth. The meaning is this: whatever kind of experience of a present object has arisen, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by it gives rise to a cognition that arises in the form of the experienced object. [Objection: It is logical that there is an arising of an experience of an object of that form during the present state, since the object is being experienced then; but how is this possible in the future and other such times?

For there is no direct experience (*anubhava*) of that [external object] therein. Even in that case, the thought "there will be an object of such a nature" arises; the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsṛṣṭa*) resulting from such a word is itself an experience of that form because it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*). Thus, since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is produced by that [conceptualization], there is no fault.

In this same way, regarding the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of *pradhāna* and so forth, the arising of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the experience of conceptualizing the forms of words and their referents should be explained according to the scriptures. Thus, the argument previously stated—that because the past and so forth are not objects, an object must necessarily be something that provides assistance—is indeed absolute. Likewise, since individual instances (*vyakti*) do not appear in the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) because they provide no established assistance, there is no manifestation of them therein. Consequently, as for what was said—that "individual instances are capable [of appearing] in cognition because they manifest"—its lack of proof has been demonstrated.

Now, having accepted the [mere] appearance (*pratibhāsa*), he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) with the words beginning "existence and non-existence" (*bhāvābhāva*). The conformity to existence and non-existence of consciousness consists in its existence when the object exists and its non-existence when that [object] is absent. From this reason, the causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*) of the object in relation to consciousness is understood; however, it is not [understood] from the mere appearance. For, according to the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), even though there is no appearance of a universal (*sāmānya*) in conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*), its causal efficacy is admitted. He says exactly that with the words beginning "even by that which does not appear" (*apratibhāsināpi*).

Indeed, a universal does not appear apart from the individual. Even though conceptual cognition appears as a universal, it too has only the form of color, shape, and so forth. For even there, no other form of a universal is perceived distinct from the forms of color and the rest. Nor is a universal of the nature of color, shape, and so forth. Therefore, a universal does not appear according to the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*). Nevertheless, according to your own view, that which does not appear [as such] nonetheless exists.

[The term] *bhāva* [is used here] because of its capacity (*sāmarthya*) with respect to consciousness. It is called *bhāva* because it is that by which an effect is brought about (*bhāvyate*) or produced (*janyate*). And showing that even when there is an appearance, there is no such capacity, he says: "of those that appear," and so forth. They are called *viplava* because they deviate (*viplebante*) from being real entities (*vastutva*), that is, they depart from it; thus the analysis of the compound is "the hairs and so forth themselves are the *viplavas*. For these indeed appear in the vision of those suffering from ophthalmia and the like, yet they do not exist.

As before, the incapacity [of atoms] is expressed by the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) because of the etymological derivation of the word "existence" (*bhāva*). The meaning is that they lack the capacity for producing consciousness. Thus, even though there is indeed a capacity [for atoms to exist], since their manifestation is observed—that is, since they do appear—this [argument] is shown to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), namely, that "capacity exists. Therefore, [the verse asks]: "How could those [atoms] assist a single [atom], yet not produce a single cognition? (1.107)

Regarding what was stated there, he anticipates the opponent’s reply with the words beginning "abhinnapratibhāsā" (having an undifferentiated appearance). "Abhinnapratibhāsā" means having a single form. "Bhinneṣu svalakṣaṇeṣu" means among the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that are distinct. "Tadākāra" refers to the form of those particular characteristics; that cognition in which such a form is deposited or placed is described as such. And such a cognition, being one that has an undifferentiated appearance, would not exist if it were produced from particulars alone that possess different characteristics. Yet, it does have an undifferentiated appearance. Therefore, it is not produced from particulars alone that possess different characteristics, but rather from the category-entity (*sāmānyapadārtha*).

He replies with the words "No," and so forth. This explains as follows: if it is maintained that particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or their own forms are the producers of cognitions possessing universal forms, then this would be logical [only if one could answer] how a cognition with a non-differentiated appearance can arise regarding things that are different. But that is not the case, because there is no appearance of particular characteristics within cognitions that manifest universals. For, if one were to admit the appearance of particular characteristics in cognitions that apprehend universals, three alternatives would follow.

(1) By whichever form individual entities appear in perceptions of the eye and so forth, by that very same form they appear in universal-cognitions as well; (2) or else, whatever form appears in the cognition of a universal, that alone belongs to the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); (3) or rather, one must admit two forms for a single distinct entity: by one it appears in perceptions of the eye and so forth, and by the other in conceptual cognitions.

(1) Regarding the first position: just as in the case of the cognitions of the eye and so forth, there would be an absence of universal-cognitions (*sāmānyabuddhi*) even in the absence of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); yet this is not so. For those universal-cognitions exist even in the absence of that particular characteristic. He states the non-existence of the second position with the words "by another form" (*ākārāntara*), etc.: because it appears in its own cognition—the cognition of the eye and so forth—in a form other than the universal form, namely in an uncommon [form], the particularity (*vyakti*) of things is not merely the universal form.

(3) To refute the third position, he says: "Because of the impossibility of multiple forms. It is illogical for one thing to possess multiplicity, because oneness and multiplicity are contradictory. Furthermore, due to the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), if one were to imagine multiplicity in that which is one, then oneness would not exist anywhere; this is the meaning. Moreover, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear in a cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Since this is so, this cognition of a universal form does not grasp distinct objects; rather, having been impressed with the forms of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it appears as if it possesses a non-distinct form. Arising from that—that is, arising from distinct entities—it nevertheless occurs by its very nature as a mere error, relying upon the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by an experience that grasps particular characteristics. And indirectly, individual manifestations are said to be its cause.

If it is asked, "If the cognition of a universal does not manifest the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), how does it cause people to act toward that particular characteristic? he says: "Even though it does not manifest that [particular characteristic]," and so forth. Even though it does not manifest the particular characteristic, because of the error consisting in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the non-object as the object within its own manifestation, it causes people to engage in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); that is to say, it causes them to act by unifying the perceived and the conceptualized.

If the cognition of a universal has the form of a universal, then that [form] itself would be the ultimate universal; to this he says: "But that [form] in it," and so forth. That appearing form of a universal does not exist in external objects, because it is not perceived as distinct from them, and because, if it were non-distinct, it could not be concomitant [with all individuals], just like the individuals themselves.

[Objection: How then is there the appearance of a non-different form among individuals? [The author] says: "Apart from difference, they are non-different. Difference is *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others); that very thing is non-different with respect to each individual. For instance, just as one individual cow is excluded from what is not a cow, so too is another. Thus, in this manner, the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves—being excluded from those of a different class—are called "non-different" and "difference. Furthermore, this word *anyatra* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that resembles a case-ending; it has the same meaning as the word *anya*.

However, it does not end in the suffix *yat* [forming an adjective], because the sense of the locative case is not intended here. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: there is no form appearing as something distinct from the difference consisting of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in the manner described; rather, the difference itself, which consists of the specific characteristic, exists everywhere as non-distinct due to the exclusion of heterogeneous things (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtti*), because of the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*). And that very difference is the indirect cause of the determination of non-difference.

[Objection: But surely the cognition appears with an undifferentiated form; how then can it be said that [this form] does not exist in the objects? To this he says: "And that is formless" (*sa cārūpaḥ*). The word *ca* has the sense of "but" (*hi*) here. For that form appearing in conceptual construction is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because—as was just stated—it is impossible to establish it from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as being either identical to or different from [the object].

The cognition that apprehends that very form—the arising of a cognition with that form—is its "grasping" (grahaṇa) in that manner; thus, because it grasps a form that is not [actually] external, it is said to be "distorted," meaning it becomes erroneous, as was stated previously. This incapacity of conceptual cognitions has already been explained through their being produced from ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth. Having stated the refutation of the fault, he now says "Moreover... etc., in order to demonstrate that the same fault applies [to the opponent's view]. The opponent replies: "It is not equal. [He explains: "In that case"—that is, regarding distinct individuals—because the cognition arises from that very universal which possesses a similar form, the objection is not equal.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says, "But surely," and so forth. In that regard, among the individuals (*vyakti*), the appearance—that is, the form—of that existing universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived. Alternatively, the word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to conceptual (*vikalpikā*) and non-conceptual (*avikalpikā*) cognition. It might be argued: "In conceptual cognition, its appearance does exist. To this he says: "For that," and so forth. For that conceptual cognition is experienced (*vibhāvyate*) as possessing color and shape; it is perceived as having the very form of color and so on. If it is argued that the universal is precisely the form of color and so forth, he says: "And not," and so forth.

"Such as this" refers to the form of color and configuration; because color, configuration, and so forth are qualities (*guṇa*), and because a universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct from a quality. "Nor from that" means nor from color, configuration, and so forth.

Having thus refuted the distinct universal (*sāmānya*), and desiring now to refute the non-distinct one, he says: "The form" (*ākṛti*), etc. Similarity that constitutes the very essence of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the "form"; that itself is the universal. One who holds that [view] is a proponent of it; or, one whose habit is to speak of it is the Sāṃkhya. Because that universal is not different from the particular characteristic—just as [the universal] is not different from the particular characteristic—it does not subsist in other objects, namely in the second and subsequent individuals.

For this reason, that universal (*sāmānya*) is also produced as nothing other than the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, because of the cause of its difference [from the particular], a non-different appearance of what exists is not tenable among individuals—this is to be supplied [as the ellipsis].

Thus, having accepted the non-different appearance asserted by Uddyotakara and others, it has been stated that since neither a distinct nor a non-distinct universal is possible, this single-form appearance among individuals is merely an illusion (*bhrānti*).

(p.224) Now, [the author] says "Or rather, let it be... and so forth, because there is no single appearance among individuals. As for what was stated—that "cognition does not have a non-different appearance regarding distinct things"—let that be so; the meaning is that this is indeed accepted. For the appearance of cognitions, that is, of universal cognitions, is distinct. What is the reason? Because those individuals are apprehended as being "similar. He explains this with the words beginning with "not at all": in those universal cognitions, there is a single, non-different appearance. What is the reason? Because those individuals are apprehended as being "similar."

Now, one might object: "If there is a cognition of 'they are similar,' why is a single appearance not logically possible? To this he says: "For not... and so forth. What then? It would be as if one were thinking, "This very thing which was seen before is what is being seen now," rather than "This is similar to the former"; for the conventional usage of "similarity" is based upon a distinction [between two things]. As for the phrase "of the two," etc.: if only the universal (*sāmānya*) itself were grasped by those cognitions, then this fault would indeed arise.

However, both the universal and the particular are grasped by a single cognition of the universal; therefore, because both are apprehended, there is no fault. For it is precisely through that universal that the particulars, being conjoined with it, are grasped as "similar."

"Even so," says the Teacher. Even if the apprehension of a pair [of the particular and the universal] is postulated, it would have to be "that is here. That is to say, that universal which was previously seen in one individual would be seen here in another individual; thus it would be "the same" (samāna), but not "similar" (sāmāna), because the universal is absolutely distinct from the individuals. If it is argued that "that very thing"—namely, the cow-ness (*gotva*) and so forth, which is a separate entity—is the similarity (*sāmya*) of those individuals, by virtue of which they are called "similar" (*samāna*); [the response follows].

How, in what manner, could there be a similarity (*sāmya*) between one thing and another’s own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is distinct from it? The intention is that there is none whatsoever. For instance, a universal (*sāmānya*) might be postulated as the similarity of individuals (*vyakti*) on the grounds that it conforms to the form of the individuals; however, that is not the case, because the universal is absolutely distinct from the individuals. Nor could others be similar by means of this [universal], for similarity does not arise through conformity to the form of the individuals or the like, but rather through a connection with them—that is, through a connection with the individuals.

If it is argued that the universal belongs to individuals because it is a "universal," this is not so. Why? Because [the universal] is unconnected—that is to say, independent of the individuals and not assisted by them. If it were admitted that the universal possesses similarity through a relationship characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): even numbers, conjunctions, and effect-substances would possess the nature of a universal. Consequently, due to that connection, there would be a uniform appearance (*samānapratibhāsa*) with respect to the numbered objects and so forth.

"How so? and so forth asks the opponent. By the use of the term "similar" (*samāna*), a difference in appearance among individuals (*vyakti*) is established; however, this is contradictory. For if these individuals are indeed similar, how can they be apprehended only by a differentiated cognition? The meaning is that they would necessarily follow as being apprehended by a non-differentiated cognition as well. To explain: where there is some commonality and some particularity, it is logical to employ the term "similar"; otherwise, just as in the case of a jar and a cloth, there would be an appearance of non-difference, and not the notion that "they are similar."

He explains this with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*). By the phrase "in these individuals," he expresses the specific form; the words "a non-different appearance is established" must be supplied as an ellipsis.
And by this, the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) has been stated.

Thus, the collective meaning is that individual instances (*vyakti*) are perceived as identical because their common and uncommon forms are grasped. Now, does a single or multiple manifestation exist among these identical things, such that it can be said thus? It has been stated that if it were so, there would be the cognition "it is here. If it is argued that the manifestation as "identical" occurs because particulars possess a universal nature (*sāmānyātmakatva*), [we reply: but in the absence of a recurring manifestation (*anugata-pratibhāsa*), how can it be established that a universal exists?

Nor is it logical to postulate a universal on the grounds that its homogeneous form would otherwise be inexplicable; for it is from their own respective causes that some things arise as homogeneous and others as heterogeneous. Furthermore, it has already been stated that their homogeneity cannot be derived from a universal.
Therefore, as for what is said by Bhaṭṭa:
Furthermore, no one at all is able to cognize cows and the like— without distinction— as having the nature of an exclusion (apoha) whose similarity is unestablished.
Now, even if there were no similarity of form, if the conceptualization of exclusion (apoha) were possible,
why is this "exclusion of non-cow" not conceived for both a cow and a horse?
The difference from a brindled cow is the same for both a black cow and a horse;
no other universal is accepted [by you], so where could the application of "non-cow" (apoha) possibly occur?

Furthermore, without the recurrence of a single common property (*ekadharmānvaya*), it is impossible to determine even the things to be excluded, such as horses and so forth; thus, their exclusion (*apoha*) cannot be established.
(Ślokavārttika, p. 226)

[This objection] is refuted. Even without a universal (*sāmānya*), since cows and the like arise from their own causes as similar entities, even if one does not accept a "similarity" (*sārūpya*) that exists as a separate entity, they are certainly accepted as being "similar. And those horses and so forth by virtue of which they possess such a form are all negated without distinction as having the nature of a non-cow (*ago-rūpa*); thus, there is no loss [to our position].

The Teacher, however, wishing to demonstrate that although things indeed arise from their own causes as identical, there is nevertheless no cognition of them as "identical" by virtue of a universal (*sāmānya*), says: "No," and so forth. "In the perception of that" (*taddarśane*) means in the cognition that apprehends the individual (*vyakti*), or in the cognition of the universal. "Of the distinct and the non-distinct" (*bhinna-abhinnayoḥ*) refers to the particular (*viśeṣa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*). "Similarity consisting in having a single effect" (*ekakāryatā-sādṛśya*) means that similarity or equality is simply the state of having a single effect; it is by this alone that individuals are cognized as "identical. This is the meaning.

But it is not by means of an ultimate universal. Therefore, it is established that those things which possess similarity through having a single effect are the objects of exclusion (*apoha*), whereas those which do not have a single effect are what are excluded. And how it is that even things which are absolutely distinct perform a single effect has already been explained previously.

He asks: "Why are they not perceived as identical in a general sense? and replies with the words beginning "For not... (*na hi*). In the cognition of an object—that is, in the cognition of experience—there are two distinct aspects (*ākāra*) due to the conceptualization of two objects, namely, the conceptualization of the similar and the dissimilar. "The state of being an object of conceptualization" means the state of being an object for a conceptual construction that superimposes identity. "In that way" means by way of having a similar form. "By this conceptual cognition" refers to the aforementioned mental construction. The opponent objects with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*).

The portion of the verse beginning with "the cognition of those individuals is the effect, and that [cognition] differs" is recited in reference to the phrase "with respect to each object. This means "with respect to such a state. The commentary beginning with "tadvat" (like that) explains: "of the cognition which manifests those [universals], even though it also manifests the individuals"—that is, because of the difference between the individuals that possess those [universals]. How is it that individuals do not have a single effect? (110)

It might be argued: "Individuals do not have a single effect with respect to experiential cognition (*anubhavajñāna*), but rather with respect to that conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) which superimposes a single form; [the unity] is in relation to that. To this, he says: "That, indeed," and so forth. That is, experiential cognition is the effect of those individuals, whereas conceptual cognition is not, because the latter occurs even in the absence of the individuals. Furthermore, regarding that very conceptual cognition as it arises in such a way that it perceives the individuals as "similar" (*samāna*), what is the basis for this similarity among the individuals?

The phrase "removal of cold by cloth and so forth" includes such examples. The form *pratidravyam* is a feminine genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) derived from the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*). The meaning is that because there is a difference between each individual substance—that is, due to a difference in cause—it appears as distinct. The Teacher [Dharmakīrti] says "no. Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness—that is, a cognition of a single form regarding its own object—the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpikā dhīḥ*) appears as non-differentiating. By being the cause of a cognition whose form is determined as one—namely, by being the cause of a conceptual cognition (*adhyavasitai karūpāyā buddheḥ*)—the non-difference of the individuals appears.

This is what is meant: although the cognitions apprehending the individual forms of each [particular] are distinct, nevertheless their unity is determined through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). And by this similarity of having a single effect, the unity of the individuals is [established]. However, the unity of the experiential cognitions is not figuratively attributed to them on the basis of being the cause of a single reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); nor is the unity of the individuals figuratively attributed to them on the basis of being the cause of such experiential cognitions.

Because there is no possibility of being an object for a cognition of error, and because there is no metaphorical application of a metaphor, the meaning of the verse would not have been explained in accordance with its intended function. (111) Now, if the determination of identity among individuals occurs through similarity based on having a single effect, how then does the determination of identity among cognitions occur? For they lack a single effect. If it is argued that those [cognitions] produce the determination of identity by their very nature, then individuals will do the same; so what is the use of similarity based on a single effect?

True; this was stated according to the intention of the teacher Dignāga, so there is no fault. Therefore, unity is accepted due to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of unity, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For this reason, he says "it has been explained," and so forth. Because it was stated there [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*]: "All things participate in exclusion by their own nature" (PV 1.42). In that context—referring to distinct entities that are not conjoined—a cognition with a single form is nothing but an error, because it apprehends as that which it is not.

Now, it might be argued that without a universal (*sāmānya*), error itself would be impossible; therefore, he says: “But those...,” and so forth. Those objects which differentiate error—namely, the excluded particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—produce [cognitions] sequentially, not directly. “By their own nature” (*svabhāvataḥ*) means by their very essence (*prakṛtyā*). The word “and” (*ca*) serves to draw back the previously stated term “it has been explained. This too was explained in that very same context. The explanation of what was said regarding “sequentially” is: “they become the causes of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).”

Because it is the cause of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), experiential cognition (*anubhavajñāna*) is itself a conceptualization. The meaning is that they [the particulars] become the causes of that experiential cognition which is the cause of conceptualization. The sequence of the argument is as follows: those [particulars] lead to an experiential cognition of individuals, and that [cognition] is an error consisting of a single form. He states the meaning of the verse with the words "But this of them" (*sa tveṣām*), etc.: for all entities, difference is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). What is its nature? It is the distinction from what does not perform that function. That [distinction] is said to be non-different among them. Why? Because they produce a single effect corresponding to their own nature, such as cognition and so forth, or the sense organ, or the fetching of water and so forth.

Alternatively: [Objection] But surely, this non-differentiated form (*abhinna-ākāra*) belongs to cognition; how then can it belong to individual instances (*vyakti*)? To this he says: "But that form of these external [objects] is non-differentiated because it is perceived as such. [Question] From what does this perception arise? [Answer] Because it is produced by some single thing, such as a cognition. And that form is called "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), not a universal (*sāmānya*). What is the reason? Because it is the differentiation from the nature of what is not that [cause].

This is what is meant: in each individual instance, by the cognition "cow, cow," a nature that is indeed excluded from the nature of non-performers of that function is made the object; however, there is no universal (*sāmānya*) as a separate entity [apart from that nature], and thus it is called "difference" (*bheda*). This is the explanation of the second half of the verse. (111)

Now, one might ask: "How can there be oneness of cognition and so forth? To this he says: "That too," and so on. This is the explanation of the first half [of the verse]. The connection is as follows: "That too"—meaning the effect consisting of cognition and so forth—"appears as non-different. "By nature" means by its own essence (*svabhāva*). "Grasping at non-difference" means determining [the object] as non-different.

With the words "tathābhūta" and so forth, he states that even individual particulars (*vyakti*) are indirectly causes with respect to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): "that in which there exists the determination of non-difference, [namely] of that cognition and so forth. This means that because they are the causes—by way of being the basis—for the cognition of experience and for practical purposes such as fetching water, the individuals also produce a single conceptual cognition in succession; this is the connection. He asks, "Of what kind? and says: "having a blended form," and so forth. That by which a single form is blended—that is, superimposed—upon the individuals is "so characterized."

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: *svabhāvabheda* is a form excluded from others; that very thing is the "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) which exists non-figuratively (*anupacarita*). This is because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is derived through a succession [of causes] by way of the excluded particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). But has this point not already been stated immediately before in the passage beginning with "those objects of things which are distinct"?

(True. However, the meaning of the first [statement], namely that "they become causes of conceptual construction gradually," has been clarified by this. [An opponent might argue: "There will be a universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of a real entity that is a distinction among things having a single effect. To this, he says: "And that," and so forth. And that "state of having a single effect" is merely the nature (*svabhāva*) of exclusion—that is, the state of being differentiated from those things that do not have that effect; it is not a universal existing as a real entity. Why? Because no other [entity]—distinct from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), following after [it], and possessing positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—is observed apart from the individual manifestations (*vyakti*), and because of the refutation [of such an entity] stated previously.

He explains with the words beginning "na hi" (not indeed). [The universal] is "visible," meaning it meets the conditions for perception; "distinctly," meaning by way of being separate from individuals. Or, even if a universal exists, because it is eternal and thus incapable of having any quality added to it (*anādheyātiśayatvena*), how could it—being unattached to any particular individual (*vyaktyantara*)—be a cause of cognition? It certainly could not. The intended meaning is that its status as a cause of cognition is accepted only on the grounds that it is manifested by its substratum (*āśrayavyaṅgya*). This too should be connected with the phrase "this has also been stated," since this point was already mentioned previously.

Since such a universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist, it follows that "the convention (*saṃketa*) also," and so forth. The word "that" (*tat*) is connected with "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). "Cognition of that" (*tad-vit*) refers to the knowledge (*vit*) of this exclusion (*apoha*), which is superimposed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) as non-different from its own form (*svākāra*); "attainment preceded by that" is also [meant]. "Tad-vit" is thus the object; it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "the result is that very thing. The suffix *-in* in *samayasya* indicates possession, meaning "of the convention" (*saṃketasya*). The collective sense is: "for the sake of the comprehension of the external object as determined by conceptual thought."

Every undertaking is for the sake of a result; thus, although the root *vid* primarily means "to find" (*lābha*), it is necessarily implied [here] as well, since otherwise the making of a convention would be purposeless. Now, one might object that it should be a *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, *tad-vid-arthaḥ*—for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). However, because the possessive sense (*matvartha*) has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *taddhita* is not produced; this is what constitutes brevity. And so it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "A *bahuvrīhi* occurs instead of a *karmadhāraya," and so forth.

This is not a fault. This too has been stated there: "In some cases, the word *karmadhāraya* itself [serves] for the sake of all means (*sarvasādhana*) and so forth. And because it belongs to a class of words (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the term *āyantadvirathika* should be understood therein as signifying all such means and the like. (112)

The explanation beginning with “this which... is as follows: Mutual exclusion (*anyonya-viveka*) is the nature (*svabhāva*) of things that is differentiated from others. For the sake of cognizing and determining that [nature], a convention (*saṃketa*) is also established—even though it is applied to one’s own mental reflection (*svapratibhāsa*), which has the form of an external object superimposed upon it—because it is logically consistent. If one asks for what purpose it is established, he says: “not performing that [action],” and so forth. Its purpose is for the sake of activity through the exclusion of those things that do not perform the intended causal function (*arthakriyā*). The meaning is: "May there be no activity toward those things that do not perform that [function]."

Strengthening this very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he says "yadi" and so forth: if the meaning of that exclusion of others were not the convention, then [the word] would not produce that exclusion of others even at the time of linguistic usage, because it would not touch upon it.

Alternatively, if the meaning of "convention" is not the cognition of that [particular object], but rather the convention is for the purpose of cognizing a nature excluded from heterogeneous things, then—since that nature excluded from others is not touched by the word at the time of linguistic usage, let alone at the time of the convention, and is thus not made an object of it—one would not act by excluding other things.

This is what is meant: when an object is made the focus of a cognition by way of a positive formulation (*vidhirūpeṇa*) as excluded from others, then the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) is understood. This very point he states with the words "for not," and so forth. "Distinction" (*viveka*) means a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Of those which perform that [function]" means from those which do not perform it—that is, from those which do not produce that effect. For if a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) were established for the sake of cognizing that distinct intrinsic nature, then it would likewise be prompted by the word during practical usage (*vyavahāra*); and thus, one would proceed by avoiding other things. Therefore, even the linguistic convention is rightly restricted to that [distinct nature] alone.

But surely, since the cognition produced by a word grasps its own internal form by superimposing it as something external, it is false. Consequently, how can the word that produces it correspond to a real entity, and how can its object be the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? To this, he says:

"And that," and so forth. That conventional term (*śruti*) which exists for the purpose of apprehending the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—the connection is that it "produces a cognition. Of what kind [of cognition]? One that "does not perform the function" [of grasping the external object]. [This refers to] its own form, which is not external. "Performing the function" means performing a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by way of a similar form; "appearance" (*avabhāsa*) is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) as having a single external form. This is a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), and the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is added afterwards to indicate that this [determination] belongs to it. What is meant is this: it determines its own internal form—which is not external—as if it were external. By this, the fact that the term serves the purpose of [inducing] activity (*pravṛtti*) has been explained.

If it is asked, "How can that [conceptual cognition] arise without a real universal (*vastubhūtasāmānya*)," he says: "The thing," and so forth. That of which the mere differentiation of things—the mutual exclusion (*itaretarabheda*)—is the seed or cause through a continuous succession is described as such. Because it grasps the inclusive form and the excluded form as one, the verbal expression (*śruti*), although producing something unreal, is not non-concordant with the object. Why? Because it functions as a factor for the exclusion of what does not perform that function; because it serves as the cause for the exclusion of what is of a different class.

This is what is meant: if the word were to produce a cognition that determines a thing as excluded from others, then it would lead a person toward that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is excluded from others, and thus it would be non-contradictory. Furthermore, at the time of the convention, the basis for the word is indeed a nature that is distinct from others, because it was established there as such. Thus, because it is indirectly based on a real distinction between things, it is considered non-contradictory with respect to the object; for even at the time of practical usage, it brings about the attainment of precisely that thing which is excluded from others.

Now, one might object: "Since there is a determination of a real entity by way of a positive form, how can the scope of the word (*śruti*) be the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*"? To this he says: "Therefore," and so forth. Because the word has its basis in the differentiation of real entities through its being an auxiliary factor in the avoidance of that which does not perform that function, for that reason its scope is the exclusion of others. He states these same two points as: "by virtue of its being based on the agent of that [exclusion]. That is, by virtue of its being the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to that exclusion.

And the word's status as dependent [upon exclusion] arises from its being an instrument for the exclusion of what does not perform that function, by way of denoting its own referent; thus, the word functions as the agent with respect to that exclusion. Furthermore, because it operates at the time of conventional usage and at the time of the convention's formation by way of relying on a particular entity, the word's status as dependent upon that exclusion is established.

He states the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "eka" (one), etc.: [it is] that [cognition] which arises by superimposing—that is, by attributing—to objects a single form (*ākāra*) appearing as itself. And that appearance of itself, because it is a false manifestation, does not perform a function. Yet, [the cognition] determines that very [appearance], though it is such, as if it were performing a function. By this, the phrase "not performing a function," and so forth, is explained. The analysis of the compound is: "that cognition whose nature consists merely in the distinctness from the thing [itself], that is, merely the exclusion of others."

Even though the scripture produces a false cognition, why is it called a "false cognition"? To this he says: "It has a uniform determination," meaning it has a determination of a single form. This is because it functions as a factor for the exclusion of others—that is, by being the basis for a delimitation (*vyavaccheda*) through its functioning as a factor for the exclusion of anything other than the intended object. In the ultimate sense, that is, in reality, it is said not to be non-concordant with respect to those things that are distinct from it and do not share its causal efficacy.

For instance, because scriptural statements such as "impermanent" or "produced" are established through convention by taking up the exclusion of a real entity that is excluded from permanence and so forth, they likewise serve in practical discourse as causes for the attainment of such an entity by functioning as factors for the exclusion of other things. Therefore, since they are derived from the principle of seeing things as they truly are, even scripture possesses correspondence with reality.

Alternatively, when a verbal expression (*śruti*) has been conventionally established for the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of things as they truly are, it possesses non-deceptiveness (*avisamvāditva*) merely by virtue of the fact that its referent exists among real entities (*vastu*) in an ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). However, words do not necessarily possess a connection to real entities in the manner of smoke [indicating fire], because they are dependent solely upon the speaker’s intention.

Establishing non-contradiction itself, he says: "For instance," and so forth. Among those entities, that exclusion—that is, the differentiation—is real and true. Why? Because even if one accepts a universal in every respect, one must necessarily accept exclusion; otherwise, if there were no nature differentiated [from others], it would follow that the universal itself does not exist. This has already been stated.

If it is argued that [the universal] exists there even though it was mentioned in general terms, he says: "Not one," and so forth. The connection is as follows: a single category of the universal—whether distinct from the individual, as for the Vaiśeṣikas and others, or non-distinct, as for the Sāṃkhyas—does not exist in them. Why? Because it is impossible and untenable, since both the entirely distinct and the non-distinct [universal] are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The subverting valid cognition has been stated previously and will be stated [later].

If, however, even that which appears as a universal (*sāmānya*) is expressed by a word, then, when that universal—which does not exist in the thing—is introduced, i.e., made an object of the word; or if the introduction of that universal—which is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—into the external thing is admitted, the thing would become something utterly remote, like a message sent by a messenger. Why? Because [it would be remote] from both the word and the cognition, meaning from the word and from the cognition produced by it.

Or rather, it is because [the object] is cast far away and abandoned by both word and cognition. Why? Because it does not touch upon—that is, it does not apprehend—any other property of the thing, that is, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the actual nature of the thing, distinct from the universal (*sāmānya*) that is intended as the object of words and so forth. And since it does not apprehend the specific characteristic, yet determines it as non-different from its own form, for that very reason that hearing is said to have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object.

[Objection: Since there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the external object itself in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), how can it be said that [the word] has "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object? To this he says: "Of others," and so forth. The meaning is: because the word is applied—that is, because the convention (*saṃketa*) is established—among individual instances of the same class, by specifically taking up the distinction of exclusion among objects excluded from those of a different class, namely their nature as delimited by the exclusion of dissimilar things, and by relying on the mere form that is excluded from those of a different class. By this, it is explained that the word (*śruti*) is based upon the exclusion of others.

Because it functions by excluding other [referents], the status of the word as the agent with respect to the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) has been stated. (115) With the words "not a tree" (*avṛkṣa*), etc., he anticipates the objection of the opponent: For the proponent of the exclusion of others (*anyāpohavādin*), it is said that there is no apprehension of the referent "tree" (*vṛkṣārtha*) by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), nor is there apprehension of the referent "non-tree" (*avṛkṣārtha*). Rather, it is through mutual differentiation (*vyavaccheda*). In that regard, if the apprehension of the referent "tree" occurs by means of the exclusion of "non-trees," and if the apprehension of the referent of the word "tree" is admitted to be the apprehension of that very referent, then the apprehension of both "tree" and "non-tree" would be mutually dependent (*anyonyāśraya*).

For instance, when the meaning of "tree" is apprehended through the exclusion of the meaning of "non-tree," it is admitted that the apprehension of the tree is preceded by the apprehension of the non-tree; because it is impossible to exclude what has not been apprehended. Furthermore, since the apprehension of the non-tree also occurs through the exclusion of the meaning of "tree," there too the apprehension of the non-tree results in being preceded by the apprehension of the tree; because it is impossible to define the meaning of "non-tree" through its exclusion from the tree without first having apprehended the tree. Thus, between the tree and the non-tree, if there is no apprehension of either one—the tree or the non-tree—there is no apprehension of both.

Because there is a non-apprehension of both [the cow and the non-cow], for that reason some declare that the convention of a word regarding an object excluded from others is impossible. Thus Uddyotakara says: "As long as one does not comprehend the 'cow,' so long is comprehension of the 'non-cow' not possible; and as long as one does not comprehend the 'cow,' so long is there a lack of comprehension of both, such that there is no comprehension of the 'cow'.
Bhaṭṭa also states this very point:
"The non-cow must already be established in order to be excluded, and it consists of the negation of the cow."

In that case, it must be the boat itself that is to be mentioned, and not something else which is being negated. If [the boat] were of the nature of the exclusion of non-boats, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
If the cow is already established, then the application of exclusion for the sake of the object to be excluded is futile.
"But if the cow is not established when the non-cow is not established, then how can there be a cow even in the absence of that [non-cow]?
[Response:
"Therefore, a real entity (vastubhūta) as a universal (sāmānya) must be accepted; they maintain that the linguistic convention (saṃketa) regarding it is based solely on its positive form."

He explains this with the words beginning "yadi" (*if*). "Of that" refers to the tree characterized by the exclusion of non-trees. Thus far, he has stated that there is no apprehension of either the tree or the non-tree; he says this with the words beginning "avijñāta" (*unapprehended*). For a person by whom the tree is not apprehended, [there can be] "of that which consists in the exclusion of it"—that is, of that which consists in the exclusion of the tree—because it has not ascended into the mind. If both tree and non-tree were to ascend into the mind, then there could be a convention regarding the tree by way of the exclusion of the non-tree. But if they have not ascended into the mind, how can there be a convention regarding an object that is neither tree nor non-tree?

With the words "of these," etc., he states that this same fault applies equally to the opponent as well: the sense is that whatever solution he has, that shall be mine too. (116) He explains with the words "that which is one," etc.: when a convention (*saṃketa*) is being made by means of the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*), there are certain proponents who, accepting a single entity as a universal (*sāmānya*), raise the objection of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Against them, even in that case where a convention is being made regarding a real entity (*vastubhūta*) characterized as "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), there are two possible alternatives: is the non-tree excluded or not? (117)

If they are excluded, then those [non-trees] must be admitted as being known, because there can be no exclusion of what is unknown. And that knowledge is not possible regarding them. Thus he says: "How," and so forth. "How could they be known without the apprehension of the object 'tree'? This much is the portion of the verse. The word "prior" (*prāk*), however, is included by way of the *Miśraka* commentary. Without the apprehension of the object "tree"—that is, prior to the apprehension of the object "tree"—[the non-trees] are "non-trees. The meaning is: "How could they be known?"

However, those who read the word *prāk* (previously) in the verse should not read the word *artha* (object). For at the time of determining "non-tree," there is no apprehension of the object "tree," because the apprehension of "tree" is preceded by the apprehension of "non-tree. Nor is it logical to have an apprehension of the object "tree" without the determination of "tree," since that too is preceded by the apprehension of "tree. This is what [the author] says with the words "For not... and so forth. "Then" (*tadā*) refers to the time of the convention (*saṃketakāla*), [referring to] the cognizer for whom the convention is being made.
