He asks, "Why does he not know [them]? and replies with the words beginning "tad" (that), etc. It is because he has approached—that is, presented himself—with the desire for that very thing, namely the knowledge of what is a tree and what is not a tree; that is, with the desire for the convention (*saṃketa*), thinking: "How indeed shall I come to know the tree and the non-tree after the time of the convention? Alternatively, "because he has approached with the desire for that" means because he has proceeded with the desire for the convention. Therefore, at the time of the convention, there is no knowledge of the tree and the non-tree for the cognizer.

And since he does not know what a tree is, how could he understand the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣavyavaccheda*) in the context of linguistic convention? He certainly does not understand it. And when there is no understanding of the exclusion of non-trees, that which is other than the tree—namely, that which is not excluded from it—is not set aside; thus, the application of the convention is the placement [of the word] upon that object which is a tree, [an object] in which "that which is other than it" has not been set aside. The compound is formed by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the locative case. It is a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) meaning "that in which this [exclusion] exists by means of the word."

The suffix *ṇini* is used here because it is his nature (*śīla*) to designate that which is not excluded from others; that is to say, [the word] is applied by convention to an object whose form is completely obscured, such that it is not distinguished from non-trees.

There is another way [of explaining the compound]. "Exclusion of the other" (*tadanya-niveśa*) means the application (*niveśa*) of the word to that which is other than the tree. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "that which is not excluded" (*aparihṛta*) and "application to the other" (*tadanya-niveśa*). The phrase "of which word" refers to the word "tree," as before. Because the referent of the word "tree" is not excluded from non-trees, it follows that there would be an application of the word being designated [as a convention] even to non-trees, just as there is to the various individual trees; such is the meaning of the whole passage. (118)

Therefore, for men who are thus situated, at the time of linguistic usage, there would be no directed activity toward a specific object possessing branches and so forth by way of excluding that [object] or by way of excluding non-trees. Rather, there would be activity toward both trees and non-trees without distinction. How so? Like [activity toward] individual trees. For from the word "tree," when devoid of context and the like, there is no activity directed toward a specific tree such as the *khadira* by way of excluding other trees, because they were not differentiated at the time of the convention.

He explains with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*), etc. The phrase "at the time of convention" (*saṃketakāla*) is expressed by the word "convention" (*saṃketa*); "by way of exclusion from others" (*parārthavyavacchedena*) means by way of excluding the object "tree" from what is other than a tree, namely, non-trees. In the second interpretation, however, it should be explained as: "by way of non-exclusion [of the application] of the word 'tree' to that which is other, i.e., to a non-tree. The term "established" (*niveśita*) means "conventionalized. The explanation of the phrase "like a tree, by way of excluding that, i.e., by way of excluding non-trees" is "like the particularities of a *śiṃśapā* tree and so forth."

The compound *śiṃśapādayo bhedāḥ* is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), while the suffix *-vati* is used in the sense of the locative case. In the sūtra, however, *vṛkṣabhedāḥ* is a genitive compound. For the distinctions such as the *śiṃśapā* and so forth are indeed the distinctions of the tree; thus, this mode of application is entirely appropriate. Furthermore, just as the word "tree" does not apply to those [particulars] by way of mutual exclusion, so too has it been explained in the very analysis of the sūtra.

With the words beginning with "atha," the author anticipates the opponent's objection. Some read the two negations as "without prescribing and without negating another" (*avidhāyāniṣidhyānyat*). They explain this as: having designated the object in the conventional designation, one does not negate anything other than that. However, this appears to be incorrect, because it is impossible for a word to function apart from affirmation and negation. For by asserting the demonstration of one thing, affirmation is necessarily accepted. Consequently, the two terms "without prescribing" (*avidhāya*) and "having demonstrated" (*pradarśya*) would be contradictory.

Therefore, the negative particle (*nañ*) should be understood as applying only to the word "without enjoining" (*avidhāya*). The reading is: "having not enjoined, that is, having negated, another. This means: without having enjoined—that is, without having established—another object of convention by way of excluding what precedes it; in other words, without performing an injunction preceded by a negation, but having performed only the injunction itself. Therefore.

Having thus demonstrated that even in the case of the [term] "one" (*eka*), nothing is predicated through the exclusion of anything whatsoever, he thereby negates a predication that is preceded by the negation of another. However, a purely affirmative predication (*vidhi*) is indeed accepted. By the word "one," a universal (*sāmānya*) is meant; by this, he explains that because the convention (*saṃketa*) is established for the universal, it is effectively established for all individual instances (*vyakti*). (119)

"This is a tree" indicates the very nature of the convention (*saṃketa*). Whatever object is pointed out when a convention is made is understood even in practical usage (*vyavahāra*). For that reason, this aforementioned point is not a fault for the proponent of the universal as a real entity (*vastusāmānyavādin*). Likewise, "the object seen itself" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to which the convention was made; or "that which is related to it" refers to the substratum (*āśraya*) related to the universal.

Regarding the phrase "even there": even when a convention (*saṃketa*) is established by means of a mere affirmation alone, two alternatives arise for one establishing the convention "this is a tree": he might formulate it as "this is also a *taru* (tree)," or "this is indeed a *taru*. In the first case, since the state of being a *taru* is not excluded from anything else, there would be no necessary engagement in practical usage (*vyavahāra*); thus, that same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains. If, on the other hand, he formulates it as "this is indeed a *taru*," then that very exclusion of the non-*taru* (*ataruvyavaccheda*) is admitted.

Consequently, when one encounters [the object] at the time of convention, how could one distinguish between a tree and a non-tree? Thus, the same undesirable consequence remains. Therefore, he says: "The undesirable consequence does not cease. He explains this with the words beginning "one," namely: "This is a tree, and this very thing is a tree. "Gati" means a mode or manner. "Of those two" refers to both of these modes. "There is no fault," etc., says the opponent; for a perceived form has been experienced, and because that which is the opposite of it—being distinct from it—is easily known.

This very statement of apprehension (*grahaṇakavākya*) is explained by the passage beginning with "for one [thing]... (*ekaṃ hi*). For when a person perceives some single universal, such as "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), and then experiences—in another object that lacks that universal, namely its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—a cognition that distinguishes its form [from the former], having a form distinct from the form previously observed; and when, based on that experience, he forms the determination of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyaniścaya*), which is a determination of difference (*vailakṣaṇyaniścaya*) in the form "this is other than what was previously observed"; by this, the nature of the determination of dissimilarity has been stated. (120)

The operation called "discrimination" (*tadvivecana*)—which consists in the discrimination between an object previously seen and one not seen—establishes their distinctness. Since this discrimination is already established by the phrase "different from that" (*tatonyat*), the explicit mention of "discrimination" (*tadvivecana*) again is for the sake of clarity. This being the sequence, the cognizer, possessing a determination of dissimilarity according to experience, discriminates that object possessing branches and so forth—which possesses a specific universal—from other forms.

Placing that [tree] before him and pointing it out as "this very tree," he is instructed and made to grasp the convention (*saṃketa*). Even when he does not perceive that universal essence (*sāmānyātmāna*) which corresponds to the convention in another instance, he himself understands that very thing to be a non-tree, even without the operation of words. Thus, when the convention is established by taking up that universal essence—which is itself determined through discrimination from other forms—it becomes established for all individual instances of the same class, because the universal is present everywhere.

Furthermore, because of the restriction "this very [thing is a tree]," once the convention has been established, it is easy to recognize what is contrary to what has been seen; thus, the determination "it is not a tree" occurs with respect to anything other than that, and so the aforementioned fault does not apply.

If it is argued that the same applies to the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), he says: "This is not so," and so forth. Because the unique form (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) perceived at one time during the convention (*saṃketa*) does not follow along with—that is, is not concomitant with—any other individual instance; and therefore, there is no perception elsewhere of that particular distinction which was grasped as "this is a tree" at the time of the convention. In this regard, the reason is that when a perception arises which appears as distinct between the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) seen at the time of the convention and that subsequently seen, [it cannot be based on a single universal].

If the cognition [of "tree"] were produced based on individual trees, then that same cognition "this is a tree" would also occur with respect to another individual tree, even one distinct from the first. For instance, just as other objects such as jars are distinct from a particular tree seen at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*), so too is any other tree distinct from it. In that case, just as the cognition "this is a tree" does not occur with respect to jars and the like, it would likewise not occur with respect to the other tree; rather, the cognition would be "this is a non-tree"—this is the meaning.

"In that case, then," says the Teacher: "even there" means even when a convention is made regarding a generality in the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), this [objection] is equal; thus he provides a rebuttal to the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). This is what is meant: it has already been established that all things are distinct from their own causes. Therefore, trees and non-trees appear as distinct entities in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). Furthermore, the conceptual construction of a "tree" is said to occur among trees by way of a positive form (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*) alone, while the conceptual construction of a "non-tree" arises among non-trees through the negation of "tree. Thus, how can there be mutual dependence?

Now, even if the cognition of the conceptual construction of a tree occurs in a positive form, nevertheless, because it arises by way of the exclusion of non-trees and so forth, it depends upon the cognition of non-trees and the like; and thus, that very same fault of mutual dependence remains.

This is not the case. Since the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣa-vyāvṛtti*) is simply the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the tree and so forth, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a tree arises solely through the mediation of that [direct] experience, and does not depend upon the apprehension of non-trees; how, then, can there be mutual dependence? In that conceptual construction of a tree, the form of "tree" appears as undifferentiated across each individual instance, such as the *śiṃśapā* and others. And since that [form] is established prior to linguistic convention by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), because it is of the nature of cognition, it is precisely therein that the word is conventionally assigned. Therefore, as for what was stated by Bhaṭṭa:
Prior to linguistic convention, the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is not apprehended by the sense faculties;
nor is there a linguistic convention elsewhere—having seen what, then, would it be applied?

Because it is liberated through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there is no inference [of it] where [the object] exists; therefore, even the experience of its relationship is not possible. (Ślokavārttika, Anumāna, v. 113)

This is refuted. Why? Because the rebuttal of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) is equal [in both cases]. To explain this, he says: "Because," and so forth. "Recognition of a single form" (*ekākārapratyabhijñāna*) refers to a cognition that has a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*) as its designation (*tathākhyā*). By this, it is stated that even though the individuals (*vyakti*) are distinct, recognition of a single form superimposes unity upon them.

And thus, the seed for the claim that "wherever a convention is made regarding individuals that are [erroneously] superimposed with unity by conceptual cognition, it is made in all cases" has been explained. By the phrase "for in one [instance]," he states that the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) possesses a determinate form because its form is devoid of any reference to heterogeneous objects; the meaning is that it is established in that single reflective awareness-cognition which, through the exclusion of the forms of heterogeneous objects, occurs with respect to all members of the same class.

By this also, the seed for the differentiation between similar and dissimilar entities has been stated. For this very reason, he says: by the word "that" (*tat*), one reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is grasped; by the word "not-that" (*atad*), its opposite is grasped. "That and not-that" are *tadat* and *atad*. Their causes are *tadataddhetavaḥ*. He differentiates them.

It is by convention itself that [the mind] distinguishes those things which are the causes for the conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*) of forms such as "having a single branch" from those that are the opposite of them; this has already been explained in the passage: "The accomplishment of a single purpose, such as a single reflective awareness or a cognition of an object" (1.75). This is because both a universal (*sāmānya*) that is distinct [from the particular] and one that is non-distinct have already been refuted or will be refuted.

Entities are differentiated by their very nature and are distinct by their own essence; thus, through the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "cognition and so forth," it is meant that only certain [entities] perform functions such as fetching water, and not others. (121)

Because those [entities] possess by their very nature the character of producing that [effect] or not producing it, this cognizer, quite by himself and without the operation of words, distinguishes—having made a division—and understands those entities as being either causes of that [effect] or non-causes of that [effect]. Therefore, how can there be the fault of mutual dependence? For one who understands by himself the entities as being causes of that [effect] and non-causes of that [effect], the phrase "of that cognition" and so forth—which consists of the object-term (*karmapada*)—is dependent upon the verb "he would understand."

That cognition which, having distinguished the causes of that [object] from those that are not its causes, establishes it—such is that cognition. It arises from what appears as the cause of a conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanā*) that has been transformed by and mounted upon that [object].

Because of the connection with the word *iva* which is to be explained [later], it should be understood as "as if by way of being a cause"; however, those causes appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are not [real] causes, because they do not exist externally. It is merely said so because of the cognizer's determination (*adhyavasāya*) in that manner. The connection here is with the phrase "appearing as deficient in the form of a non-cause. And the application of the word *iva* is as before: [it means] "as if deficient in the form of those things which are not causes for the cognition that reflects upon them as having a single form."

The connection here is as follows: because of the unification of the perceived object and the conceptual construction, [the object] appears as if it were of one form with the external thing. This occurs even after the time of the convention itself, on the grounds that one would understand those entities as distinct from things that do not perform that function. "Utterance" refers to a word; it is applied—that is, conventionally designated—to that nature which is excluded from dissimilar classes and superimposed by conceptual construction as non-different from its own form. That exclusion is as previously described.

From that scripture, as one proceeds in practical usage (*vyavahāra*), one perceives through delusion a single entity; the meaning is that the cognition, perceiving the nature—which is excluded from those of a different class—as non-different from its own form, beholds it as if it were a single entity among individuals of the same class.

Consequently, the notion "tree" arises with respect to all things that are the causes for a single conceptual determination (*ekaparāmarśa*); therefore, what was stated—that if perception were the means of apprehension, this would not occur regarding another individual—is refuted.
Furthermore, as for what was said by Bhaṭṭa:
How indeed could horses and other such animals not be denotable by the word "cow"?
If you say that the word "cow" was not perceived there at the time of the convention,
then everything other than that single [referent] would be excluded by it.

"It would follow that [the exclusion] itself is what is to be excluded; thus, there is no such thing as a universal being denoted"—this too has been refuted. For when the word "cow" is conventionally established with respect to a single individual, its referent is followed through into other individuals, because of the cognition "this is that very same cow. Nevertheless...
(fn.1: Ślokavārtika).

With the words "of these," etc., he states the meaning of the *kārikā*: the connection is that [the conceptualization arises] because of the continuity (*anvaya*) of those objects—which are distinguished from heterogeneous things—that by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*) are the causes of such conceptualizations. "By nature" means by their own essence (*svabhāvena*), and not through a connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*). To the question, "Why then do they all not produce a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)?", he says: "by the power of conditions" (*pratyayavaśāt*); that is, experience-knowledge (*anubhavajñāna*) is the condition, and through its mediation, those [objects] generate the conceptualization.

Because there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—that is, a presence—of the causes of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) that consists in a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*) of such a nature; just as one particular tree is by its very nature a cause of such a conceptual cognition, so too are the second and subsequent ones. It is in this manner that there is positive concomitance, and not because there exists a single real entity (*vastu*) whose nature is a universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, for this reason of positive concomitance, [the things] are "fit for a single superimposition" by virtue of having a single effect; this is the completion of the sentence.

Regarding the phrase "of that seer" (*taddraṣṭuḥ*): it refers to one who perceives the performance of a single function among individuals—[perceptions] revolving in the intellect but not yet ascended [to the level of conceptualization]. Therefore, it ought to be "of that seer. If it is argued that this is incorrect because the genitive compound is prohibited by the rule *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16), we say no; for it is intended as a genitive of the remaining relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, since the word *draṣṭṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛn*, the prohibition of the genitive applies there by the rule *tṛn* (Pāṇini 2.2.15). Thus, the compound is formed with the word *tat* ending in the accusative case, according to the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

Others, however, on the basis of the instruction beginning with "that which causes it" (*tatprayojaka*), indicate that this is an exception (*anityatva*) to the prohibitive rule. In the same way, for other such instructions of this kind, similar defenses must be stated. "By being the cause of the knowledge of that" means by being the cause of that conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). "And by the exclusion of others" means by the exclusion of those things which are different from the causes of the recognition of a single form—that is, those things which are not causes of such conceptual cognitions. And [it is established] by the exclusion from those.

For even those things that are not as they appear do not serve as causes for conceptual construction, because they do not exist externally. For this very reason, their status as "conceptual constructions lacking the form of a cause" is also due to their non-existence as real entities (*avastusattva*). [The phrase] "as they are determined" refers to those things superimposed by way of exclusion from others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) because they are the causes of that cognition. By this, it is explained that [the term] "lacking the form of a cause" means [they are so called] because they appear to the intellect as being the cause.

By the phrase "those in which the distinction between external and internal is undivided," he explains the term "of a single form. The analysis of the compound is: "those in whom the distinction between external and internal is undivided. The meaning is: "grasped through the unification of the perceived object and the conceptual construction. The "understander" is the one for whom the convention is established. "In accordance with the understander" means: according to the kind of understanding he has at the time of the convention.

Those entities which lack the nature of non-causes, which produce a single effect, and which possess a single form—in which this word "tree" has been conventionally established—they alone are [the referents] of the cognition having the form "these are trees. Following that [convention], recollecting that [convention], and remaining within conceptual-cognitive awareness (*vikalpavijñāna*), one [perceives] those aforementioned entities as distinct from those things that are not the causes of that cognition and from their opposites.

Thinking, "How indeed might one understand [the meaning] even at the time of linguistic usage from hearing the word 'tree' [as in] 'these are trees'?"—with this intention it was said: "The maker of the convention applies [the term] to that intrinsic nature which is excluded from what does not possess that cause and has been made an object by conceptual thought. (123)

[Objection: But surely there is no persistence (*anugama*) at the time of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is excluded [from others], nor is there a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the universal form appearing in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), because it is non-different from its own cognition; nor is there a cognition by the listener of that which belongs to the speaker, or by the speaker of that which belongs to the listener, because as properties of distinct individuals they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). And since a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is not possible between the person to be instructed and the instructor unless [the object] is cognized equally by both, he says: "one's own and another's," and so forth.

Having shown that things, which are the objects of convention, possess a single appearance due to the cause of error characterized by the performance of a single function—despite the conceptual distinctions between the speaker himself and the listener to whom he speaks.

This is what is meant: just as one person with cataracts, having seen two moons, when instructing another person with cataracts, instructs them based on exactly what he himself has seen, and not on what the other has seen, because that is not perceptible to him; and yet it occurs to him: "This very thing has been communicated by me to the other. And the other person, perceiving the form of the two moons occurring within his own mental continuum, thinks: "That very thing which was communicated to me by the instructor has been understood by me."

In the same way, although there is a difference between the mental forms of the speaker and the listener—which are respectively determined as external objects—there is a convention established because of the determination of their unity, and at the time of linguistic usage, there is the cognition of that very [form] due to the determination of unity. The cognition, superimposing upon its own form that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which is excluded from others as if it were non-different from it, apprehends it; "of that" refers to the word. It appears as if grasping a single entity.
Therefore, as it was said by Bhaṭṭa:
Furthermore, the operation of words and logical marks is not devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Without these two, there can be no cognition of exclusion (*apoha*); nor is there positive concomitance in that which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*). Moreover, since exclusion itself is unestablished, where could its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) be stated?

"And in the absence of that [real universal], there would be no validity for those two [the word and the sign]. This is refuted; because even when one understands the relationship through a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) excluded from others, one indeed understands the relationship with other things of that same form as well, due to the determination of identity (*ekatvādhyavasāya*). Thus, how can faults such as the lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) be established? Furthermore, a distinction between "tree" and "non-tree" based on a real entity (*vastubhūta*) universal is not tenable. As he says: "But not again," and so forth.

There exists a single common entity (*sāmānya*) that is perceptible and meets the conditions for apprehension within those particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). For example, just as jars and other objects are distinct from various types of trees, so too are *dhava* trees and others distinct from one another. Even when these distinct things are perceived, there must be some commonality whose presence or absence allows one to distinguish between what is a tree and what is not a tree—such that it is said: "That in which this commonality is perceived is a tree; that in which it is not perceived is not a tree."

He states why it does not exist: "Of that," and so forth. Because a universal (*sāmānya*) that is distinct [from its particulars] is not perceived when there is a division [of the object] based on the appearance of branches and so on. Indeed, two appearances are not observed in trees and the like: one having the form of branches and so on, and another having the form of non-branches and so on. Nor can it be said that the universal appears as the very form of the branches and so on, because that [universal] would then possess the form of branches and so on. The phrase "like a staff-bearer by means of a staff" is a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Just as a staff is perceived through its distinction from what is not a staff, it is not so with the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, because the universal—which is not perceived as distinct from another [particular] possessing branches and the like—is not observed within the individuals (*vyakti*), how could there be the "observation" (*upalakṣaṇa*) of another by means of its own form when it is not itself apprehended? Observation is the perception of another through its own nature; and how could that occur for something that is not itself grasped?

However, for one who maintains that the universal is not a distinct entity from the particular, it is impossible to perceive elsewhere—in another individual—the form (*ākṛti*) of a tree seen in one individual, because that form is non-different from the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, regarding the phrase "that which possesses this or does not possess that": at the time of the convention, the form of a single tree observed is "that which possesses it" (*tadvān*); later, at the time of linguistic usage, a different tree being perceived is "that which does not possess it" (*atadvān*), as it lacks the previously observed form of the tree.

Since it follows logically that one of those two is a tree and the other is not a tree, there would be only a single individual [to which the term "tree" applies]; thus, only that which was seen at the time of the convention would be a tree, but not what is seen at the time of linguistic usage, because the form seen at the time of the convention is not observed elsewhere.

Those who maintain that the meaning of a word consists in the exclusion of other things (*anyāpoha*) have raised the objection that this definition lacks universal applicability (*avyāpitva*). Desiring to refute that, the author first presents a mere indication of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), beginning with the words "Let it be so," and so forth. He asks: Why is there no exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyavaccheda*) in that case? He replies: "For [there is] no 'non-cognizable' (*ajñeya*)," and so forth. From what [is it excluded]? From the non-cognizable. If one asks why the non-cognizable does not exist, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

The proponent of exclusion from others (*anyavyavacchedavādin*) must admit that the knowable is made an object by way of its distinction from the unknowable; otherwise, how could there be an exclusion of the knowable from the unknowable? For it is only when the knowable is made an object by way of its distinction from the unknowable that the latter, which is considered unknowable, becomes known as knowable. Indeed, an exclusion cannot be demonstrated from that which has not been made an object. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as "all," "collection," and "duality" are included.

As stated by Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara: "The claim that the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is incorrect, because it is not universally applicable. Where there is a duality of categories, there one is cognized through the negation of the other; for example, in the word 'cow,' the cow is cognized through the negation of the non-cow."

Furthermore, this [usage] does not apply to the word *sarva* (all). For there is nothing whatsoever that is "not-all" which could be excluded by the word *sarva*. If you think that a single thing or so—which is "not-all"—is excluded by the word *sarva*, then there follows the fault of the negation of its own meaning (*svārthāpavāda*). For if it were so, the word, functioning by excluding one or more things, would be meaningless; because the parts are negated, and since you do not admit a whole (*aṅgin*) distinct from its parts (*aṅga*), it would have no referent.

In this way, all words denoting a collection (*samudāya*), when functioning by way of negating a single part, would result in being meaningless because no collection distinct from its constituent parts (*samudāyin*) is admitted. Furthermore, since words such as "two" and so forth have conjunction (*samuccaya*) as their object, if one or more [parts] are negated, those being negated would not constitute a conjunction; thus, words such as "two" and so forth would be meaningless.

"This is not a fault," says the Teacher. For, having turned back from some [object] a cognition that possesses expectancy, a certain word is employed by a speaker for the sake of directing that cognition toward a specific object for a person who possesses expectancy. By the phrase "for the sake of directing toward something," positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated; by the phrase "having turned back from something," negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated.

What is the reason why a word is withdrawn from one thing and established in another? To this he says: "Because its object... and so forth. This is because the meaning of a word is determined. Otherwise, if no object were excluded by that word, the employment of the word would be useless. Since this is so, [it applies] to words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*)—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including terms like "all" (*sarva*) and "universe" (*viśva*). In what kind of cases? In those brought into common usage (*vyavahāra*).

Verbal usage is characterized by affirmation and negation; it concerns those things brought forward for that purpose, meaning those situated within common worldly practice. Among those factors of verbal usage, there is some object of exclusion (vyavacchedya) in whatever way. This is what is meant: since the object of a word is that toward which the word is directed (*yatparaḥ śabdaḥ sa śabdārthaḥ*), even an affirmative sentence has exclusion as its primary aim; therefore, exclusion is also called the "meaning of the word," and there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "For sound... He asks: why does every person, whether a worldly person or an investigator, not transcend [sound]? He replies: "Because of that," and so forth. The meaning is: because that sound has the fruit of engagement and withdrawal—that is, because its purpose is to cause one to withdraw from something and to engage in something else. Otherwise, the employment of words would be fruitless. He states this with the words "If," and so forth.

This speaker would not turn away from anything undesirable for someone regarding some object to be established, nor would he direct the mind toward anything desired; this is because, prior to the use of words, the object exists for the cognizer in a state of total confusion, and such a [confused] object is not apprehended as it truly is by means of the word. The meaning is that it is apprehended in some way or another, just as it happens to be.

In all conventional transactions (*vyavahāra*), one should not employ—that is, utter—any [specific] word. What is the reason? Because verbal convention is inseparable from restriction. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Just as," and so forth. When it is said, "Bring water here," the listener necessarily has an expectation regarding the specific instrument; and for the sake of restricting that, it is said, "with a jar."

The statement "This is not a jar" becomes fruitful by first denoting its own primary object and thereby implying the exclusion of other instruments; otherwise, even if the word "jar" were employed, one might bring water by means of the hollowed palms (*añjali*) or some other instrument in any manner whatsoever—meaning that the intended bringing of water could be either in small quantity or in large quantity.

If even the word "water," by excluding other actions, does not function to denote a specific action, then its employment would also be purposeless; thus he says, "In the same way," and so forth. There would be only the bare statement "bring"; what kind [of thing] would that be? It would be one in which no instrument or object is implied—that is, a statement consisting of only so much as "bring" in which neither an instrument (such as a pot) nor an object (such as water) is implied or relied upon. That is what is meant by "in that manner."

Likewise, regarding the activity "bring it here," a person who has become oriented toward that activity—if by the word "bring" one were not to exclude [the act of bringing] from other activities, then even the word "bring" would not need to be uttered.

(p.245) He says this very thing: "In this way, bringing [it]," and so forth; or "some other performance. This means something other than bringing. What? The performance of eating and so on. And as for "non-performance," if by that one intends the non-exertion of activity and the non-bringing, then one would not even say the verbal form "bring" (*ānaya*). The reading found in some manuscripts, "bringing or something else" (*nayanam anyad vā*), is more appropriate, because the word "bringing" (*ānayana*) was the subject under discussion.

Therefore, just as there is an exclusion for words such as "jar" when they are brought into conventional usage, so too there is an exclusion—namely, the "unknowable"—for words such as "knowable" when they are brought into conventional usage by some means of exclusion.

"Non-suspicion of another" (*ananyāśaṅkā*) means that "suspicion of another" (*anyāśaṅkā*) is the suspicion regarding [the object] being unknowable and so forth; the absence of that is "non-suspicion. The meaning is: when there is no suspicion that [the object] is unknowable and so forth. For instance, when there is the suspicion that "sound is unknowable in its form as impermanent and so forth," this [term] is employed: "it is knowable in the form of impermanence and so forth. In that case, precisely that unknowability which was suspected in the form of impermanence and so forth is excluded.

In this way, all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are [known] by the knowledge of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña-jñāna*). Here too, that very state of being unknowable which was suspected in relation to the knowledge of the Omniscient One is what is to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*). Likewise, someone says: "Since things that are indefinable (*nirupākhya*) do not exist, there is no operation of cognition toward them; therefore, they are unknowable. Here too, that superimposed state of being unknowable is precisely what is to be excluded, because even non-existence is made an object in the sense that "the non-existence of everything does not occur."

The same should be understood regarding the use of the word *jñeya* (knowable) elsewhere, as well as the word *prameya* (cognizable). Likewise, in the case of the statement "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary," some might imagine that momentariness applies only to certain things like lamps and not to everything; [the term "all"] excludes that [limited view] and establishes the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena. Similarly, when there is a doubt as to whether "someone has arrived" or "everyone has arrived," one says, "the entire village has arrived."

Thus, when the movement of a particular person is suspected, that very [movement] is what is excluded. Likewise, in the statement "the five groups of consciousness have a collective object," the fact of having a partial object is negated. In this way, regarding other terms such as "two" and so forth when brought into usage, the exclusion should be stated according to the context and as appropriate.

This is the collective meaning here: it is not said that a real entity (*vastubhūta*), which is apprehended by a distinct cognition as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), is established in two groups and then "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is expressed by the word. Rather, even though it is not so [real], the form (*ākāra*) that is superimposed (*āropita*) by the hearer as being such [a real entity] is also indeed that which is to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*) by the word.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "In that regard," and so forth. That which is the ground for doubt—that is, the object of doubt—for the dull-witted person who is to be instructed, that alone is what is to be excluded by words such as "the knowable" (*jñeya*) and so on. If it is argued that the listener does not have any doubt at all, he replies: "Or, one who has no doubt," and so forth. If he has no doubt whatsoever—meaning, if he possesses a certainty regarding things as they truly are—then why would he require instruction from another speaker? The intended meaning is: "He certainly would not."

The removal of expectation is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the listener; where that is absent in a statement, there is no such refinement of the listener. And how could a speaker who utters such a statement not be considered insane? Therefore, a speaker employs words precisely with the desire to produce a refinement in a listener who possesses expectation. For what reason? Because words have been established by convention solely for the sake of that refinement—that is, for the sake of the refinement of the listener.

Granted that for words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth—which are employed in sentences for the sake of linguistic usage—the exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) is indeed as previously stated; but how is it in the case of those words like "knowable" that are not employed in linguistic usage and exist in isolation? For in those cases, there is no occasion for doubt on the part of the cognizer. To this he says: "And those not employed in linguistic usage," and so forth. The meaning is that there is no expressive word that is not included within sentences.

Since a speaker seeking a result first employs [an utterance] such as "Devadatta, bring the cow" with the intention: "I shall communicate this object, connected with a specific action, to him by means of these words," there is therefore the denotation of word-meanings only as already connected with an action; but there is no subsequent connection of word-meanings that have already been denoted. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-occurrence of case-endings such as the accusative in "gām" and so forth. Therefore, words are employed only as they exist within a sentence.
He states that very point: "of that which is contained in a sentence," and so forth. The intended meaning is that it alone is the conveyer of the sense.

As for those words that are recited by grammarians in lists such as *sarva-viśva* and so forth, or which are refined through the analysis of stems and suffixes, as well as those treated by the etymologists (*niruktakāra*), these should be regarded as substitutes for oxen in a drawing (*rekhāgavaya*)—mere means for the comprehension of words found within actual sentences. They possess no worldly meaning whatsoever. Therefore, only words situated within sentences possess meaning; it is precisely regarding those situated therein that an investigation into their meaning is conducted. Thus he says: "But where, etc."

Regarding the word *eta* (these): when the investigation into the domain of linguistic usage (*prayoga*) proceeds, those words situated within a sentence are asserted to have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as their meaning, on the grounds that "that by which another is excluded" is [the meaning]. However, as for those words not situated in usage—such as *jñeya* (knowable) and so forth—since no referent is possible for them, there is no investigation at all; thus he says: "not having a specified usage," and so on. The compound *nirdiṣṭaprayoga* is a *karmadhāraya*, meaning "that which is both specified (*nirdiṣṭa* = *upātta*) and a usage (*prayoga*). Subsequently, with the negative particle *nañ*, it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of negation, according to the rule beginning with "the indeclinable *abhāva* [is compounded] with [a word ending in] *bhikṣu*" and so forth.

And thus, by the rule *saptamyāḥ tṛtīyā-saptamyor bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.4), there is the substitution of *am* [for the case-ending]. The meaning is that, in the absence of the employment of a [preceding] word (*upāttaprayoga*), the question is: "What is the meaning of the word *jñeya* alone, as introduced by the sentence? Others hold that this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). For the action of questioning (*praśnakriyā*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and adverbial modifiers are treated as objects (*karman*).

Furthermore, in this context, if it were a *karmadhāraya* compound, since its function would reside within its own constituent members (*svapadārthavṛttitvāt*), one must explain how the action of questioning is qualified by it.

Now, if it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the word *jñeya* has its application (*prayoga*) unspecified," even then the word is qualified, not the action. However, when the analysis is as follows—"that in which the question (*praśna*) has its application unspecified"—then, because of the qualification of the action, the locative case alone is appropriate due to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *praśna*: "the question in which the application is unspecified."

If one asks what the reason is for the fact that the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) alone does not have its own referent, he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). This means that from the word "knowable" alone, there is no comprehension of a real entity (*vastu*), because the word "knowable" is never employed in isolation within linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*), which has affirmation or negation as its result; how, then, could there be comprehension of a referent? Only when a discussion has begun in such a manner as, "Is that which is indicated by the word 'beginning' (*yadādi*) knowable in the form of being impermanent and so forth, or is it unknowable?"—is the word "knowable" employed in isolation.

Even then, whatever comprehension of meaning occurs—arising in dependence upon a word that lacks a formal status (*apada*) within the context—is produced from the sentence alone; for a word accompanied by other words constitutes a sentence. Therefore, there is no comprehension of the meaning of a word independent of other words, just as there is nothing expressible by the isolated words "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth, so too there is nothing expressible by isolated words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*).

But surely, in the context of the inquiry, "Shall I bring water in a jar or with my cupped hands?", when the word "with a jar" (*ghaṭena*) is employed, even for a listener who did not know the context, a cognition in the form of a jar certainly arises from hearing the mere word "with a jar. How then can it be said that there is no cognition from a word alone? To this he says: "Even that which... and so forth. That cognition in which the intended object is incomplete is "one in which that object is not fully realized" (*aparisamāptatadarthā*).

To the question, "In what sense is its meaning incomplete? he replies: "In accordance with observed usage. This refers to as many instances as there are in which the injunctions for actions such as bringing or taking away are operative. Since the use of the word "jar" has been observed in those instances, in accordance with that, there arises in the preceding sentences a cognition characterized by expectancy, such as: "Is this the intended meaning, or is it this other? Because of this state of expectancy, the appearance [of the object] as a form is incomplete in its meaning; it is merely a delusive error (*viplava-bhrānti*).

This explains that there is no comprehension of meaning from the mere hearing of isolated words; rather, when one hears an isolated word, the notion of comprehending meaning arises because the mind is presented with a similarity to a meaningful word previously perceived within sentences. Just as the comprehension of meaning from hearing isolated words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is known to be an error based on following previously observed usage, so it is with words such as "cognition" (*jñeya*). This occurs according to what has been seen and according to the observation of usage.

In as many sentences as the word *jñeya* (knowable) is observed to be employed, there is indeed a confusion in the comprehension of the meaning upon hearing the word *jñeya* alone, following that precedent. By this, he states that in every respect the words *ghaṭa* (pot), etc., are equivalent to the words *jñeya*, etc.—and as for what was also said: "The word 'existent' (*sat*), functioning by excluding [the numbers] one and so forth, would be meaningless because it negates a part [of the whole], and since a whole (*aṅgin*) distinct from its parts (*aṅga*) is not admitted."

That is incorrect, because the objects of cognitions such as "one" and so forth are distinct from the objects of cognitions such as "collection" and so forth, which appear differently. Furthermore, those entities in specific states that serve as the objects of cognitions like "collection" are precisely what are called the "possessors of parts" (*aṅgin*), since no other possessor of parts is established. Moreover, we accept that those very entities—which the opponent maintains initiate properties such as "collection"—are the objective supports (*ālambana*) of the cognition of a collection, insofar as they produce that cognition; there is no contradiction here.
Therefore, the negation of "one" and so forth with respect to all terms such as "collection," "duality," and the rest is indeed logically consistent.

"From that," and so forth. Since every sentence is restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*), the meaningfulness of words exists only within the context of a sentence; therefore, "in the employment of all words" is the conclusion. "Because of its fruitfulness" means because of the fruitfulness of that employment of words. Thus, when the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the denoted meaning of all words according to the aforementioned method, as stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara [in the *Ślokavārttika*].
And is this exclusion of others (anyāpoha) intended to be denotable or undenotable? If it is denotable, is it so by way of a positive form or by way of the negation of another?
If it were to be expressed as having the nature of an injunction, the extremist view would have to be abandoned;
for it has been described that in every case, the meaning of a word consists in the negation of other things.
If exclusion is expressed by means of the rejection of non-exclusion,
then for every such instance you would face an infinite regress.
Moreover, if you maintain that this "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is itself inexpressible,
then your statement that "a word effects the exclusion of others" is contradicted.
"For since the mere exclusion of others occurs only in those words with which the negative particle (*nañ*) is joined, whereas elsewhere its own nature alone is understood."
That is incorrect, because it is accepted that the positive injunction (*vidhi*), which is the literal meaning of the word, entails by implication the negation of other things.

If, then, the positive injunction alone is the word-meaning and the negation of others follows by implication, why did the Master Diṅnāga state: “Words express entities as qualified precisely by the exclusion of other objects” (*śabdorthāntaravyāvṛttiviśiṣṭān eva bhāvānāha*)? [124–25]

Since there is no contradiction, he says: "And the application," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that even in the case of a convention (*saṃketa*), a word functions by way of a positive form (*vidhi-rūpa*); how much more so, then, in actual usage (*vyavahāra*)? The meaning of "tree" is that which is distinguished from, or excluded from, non-trees such as pots and the like; the sense is "having abandoned what is not a tree. "Application" (*niveśana*) should be understood as the formulation of the convention for the word "tree."

By the phrase "by excluding that," it is stated that the word "tree" is not conventionally applied to what is non-tree. To the question, "Where, then, is its application? he says: "In the difference [of trees]; that is, the difference of the various trees from that which is their difference—namely, from the non-tree; it is the nature distinct from the non-tree. For just as one particular tree is distinct from that [non-tree], so too are all varieties of trees.

Then, through the increase of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that difference among them is superimposed as a unity upon all [individuals], whereby it appears in an identical form. Therefore, the word is applied to that difference—which appears in an identical form—by way of its non-existence within the distinct [particulars]. And the particle *ca* in the phrase "this very" (*sa cāyam*) has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). This very form appearing in conceptual construction is non-different from the external [object].

Alternatively, that very distinction from non-trees, characterized as an absence (*abhāva*), is what was taught by the Master Diṅnāga. To the question "How was it taught?", he says: "By means of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), some part of that real entity (*vastu*) is understood. We shall clarify the meaning of this in the commentary (*vṛtti*).

[Objection: Why is it that the portion of the real entity (*vastubhāga*) qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) is not apprehended in ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*)? [Response: He says: "Its nature (*rūpa*) is its own-being (*svabhāva*); there is nothing [of this sort] even for this differentiation. This is because this differentiation, which consists of exclusion (*nivṛttirūpa*), is non-existent, and because that which appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpapratibhāsin*) is a delusion of the intellect (*buddhivibhrama*).

If difference has no form whatsoever, how then is it said that words express entities as qualified by the exclusion of others? To this he says: "In the cognition of that," and so forth. When there is the cognition of that aforementioned nature of difference—which is excluded from what is of a different class—in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*) through words, it is precisely then that the exclusion of others is understood. (127)

For instance, when the word "tree" is uttered, the exclusion of non-trees is understood by implication. By this much alone, the state of being qualified by the exclusion of others is expressed; however, in the ultimate sense, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified. Thus he says: "Not," and so forth. Therein—meaning in the case of the word-referent as the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), or in the treatise of the Master (Dignāga)—some other person [objects]: "An object excluded from others is not understood as being qualified by some characteristic defined as the exclusion of others. Therefore, that which was stated by Bhaṭṭa: "And a unique particular (*asādhāraṇa-vastu*) is not understood as possessing exclusion (*apohavat*)."
Or how could a relationship between a real entity and a non-entity be conceived?
By its mere existence in its own nature, nothing can be a qualifier;
that by which the qualified object is colored through its own cognition is a qualifier.
Furthermore, from words such as "horse" and so forth, there does not arise a cognition of exclusion (apoha);
for in this context, a cognition of the qualified object is required, and that [cognition] does not occur when the qualifier is unknown.
Nor can one form produce a qualification for a cognition that is of a different nature;
and how could that be called a qualification when the cognition is of a different nature? Furthermore, if its form is cognizable through non-existence, the qualified object lacks substantial reality.
"The entity qualified by exclusion (apoha) cannot be the denotable object [of a word]," this [position] is refuted.
(Ślokavārttika, fn. 1*)
But how can a single word have two functions characterized by injunction and prohibition? He says:

Nor does a word perform two functions. It performs the pair consisting of the denotation of its own object and the exclusion of others. What is the reason? Because they are mutual non-existences (*anyonyābhāva*). The word *iti* indicates the reason. Since the meaning of "tree" is the absence of the exclusion of non-trees, and the meaning of "non-tree" is the absence of that [tree], by virtue of being mutual non-existences, the understanding of the exclusion of non-trees occurs as a matter of course through the very understanding of the meaning of "tree" from the word "tree. Thus, the word does not have two direct operations. Therefore: "If this word 'cow' is capable of excluding others..."
One must seek another term for the cognition of "cow" that occurs with respect to Janaka.

The objection—"Words do not have cognition as their fruit, nor can there be two fruits for a single [word]; how then, according to you, can the cognition of both negation and affirmation be the fruit of one [word]?"—is refuted. If the difference expressed by words were to persist everywhere, then that itself would become the ultimate universal (*sāmānya*); therefore, he says: "This" refers to the persisting difference which is the object of words; it is "formless," meaning devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Regarding that formless [difference], the seeing of it as having a form by the speaker and the listener through the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized—that is a "distortion of the intellect," meaning an error (*bhrānti*). This is the sense.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "being established" (*niveśyamāna*). The connection is as follows: because an object such as a tree is differentiated, it is established by excluding—that is, by setting aside—that [differentiation]. To the question "Where? he says: "Of those being differentiated," and so forth. This has its meaning analyzed in the commentary on the *kārikā*. The analysis of the compound is: "that which is implied by a word through the exclusion of other things. And this very differentiation, which appears in a uniform form, is what was indicated by the teacher Diṅnāga.

He asks, "How so? and says: "By the exclusion of other referents (*arthāntara-vyāvṛtti*), some part of that real entity (*vastu*) is understood. Likewise, [it is said] by such statements as: "In the same way, a word denotes entities precisely as qualified by the exclusion of other referents," and so forth. By the inclusion of the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi-grahaṇāt*), there is the inclusion of such passages as: "The auditory cognition (*śruti*), performing the exclusion of other referents of the word, expresses [its object]," and so on.

The passage beginning with "For that" (*sa hi*) is a justification of this very point. For that word "tree," while expressing the specific nature (*svabhāva*) of a tree as distinguished from non-trees, functions precisely by implying the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of other objects—that is, of objects that are not trees. What is the reason? [It is because] "the distinction residing in one [term]," and so forth. For just as the various types of trees, such as the *khadira* and others, are by their very nature distinct from non-trees, so too are non-trees distinct from trees; for distinction is a property that belongs to both sides.

In this context, regarding the word "tree," because the exclusion of what is other than that is inseparable from the injunction of a distinction—which, though distinct as it pertains to the object "tree" and residing within a single [cognition], appears in a single form; and because that exclusion of what is other than the object "tree"—namely, the non-tree—is inseparable from it. For in this way, the object "tree" would be expressed as having a form excluded from non-trees only if the cessation of the object "non-tree" were understood therein.

That very difference, which appears as a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) when [an object] is distinguished from another, is the distinct intrinsic nature (*bhinnasvabhāva*). By means of its exclusion—that is, by the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyāvṛtti*), which is understood through implication according to the aforementioned reasoning—it is said that "a portion of the real entity (*vastu*) has been apprehended. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "a portion of the real entity has been apprehended. The intended meaning is that because [the cognition] is brought about through the door of perceiving the excluded real entity, and because it is determined (*adhyavasāya*) as having the form of the real entity, it is said that "a portion of the real entity has been apprehended."

This is what is meant: a word expresses in verbal cognition that very form which appears in conceptual thought (*vikalpabuddhi*), which is excluded from those things that do not produce a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that [object], and upon which a unity is superimposed in relation to those things that do produce such a reflective awareness; this form has no distinction between external and internal, because it is precisely that which appears in verbal cognition.

And while establishing that [exclusion], one implies by implication the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*). It was with this intention that the Teacher stated: "By the exclusion of others, some part of that entity is understood. However, it is not the case that some part of an external entity is grasped by means of the exclusion of others—which constitutes the word-meaning and takes the form of a qualifier—because the exclusion of others itself does not exist [as a real entity]. Thus, it has been established that "by the exclusion of others, some part of that entity is understood."

Now, in order to justify the claim that [the author] speaks of entities as being qualified precisely by the exclusion of other words and objects, he says: "Because of the cognition of that," and so forth. Because of the cognition of that—that is, because of the cognition of the exclusion of others—it is a qualification (*upādhi*) of that [entity]; since it is a qualification of difference (*bheda*), that very [exclusion] is said to be "qualified by that difference" by the Teacher.

Alternatively: because that aforementioned distinction of entities (*vastubheda*) is understood—that is, apprehended—from the word, by virtue of being restricted, it possesses that as its qualification (*upādhi*). That exclusion of others (*tadanyanivṛtti*) is the qualification of that apprehension, since it is implied by the object; thus it is so described. To possess that [exclusion] as an inseparable concomitant is precisely what constitutes having it as a qualification. This is what is meant: that very distinction which is understood from the object through the exclusion of other objects—because it is inseparable from that—is said by the Teacher to be "apprehended" as qualified by the exclusion of others when it is understood from the word.

[Objection: Is it not the case that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from other objects is the basis for the application of words, such that external objects qualified by it—such as "cow" and so forth—are denoted by words like "cow"? [This cannot be], because it is not perceived. The phrase "like a staff" is an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Just as one is called "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) by way of a staff, it is not the case that one is called "possessor of exclusion" (*vyāvṛttimat*) by way of exclusion. Why is it that exclusion is not a separate entity? He says: "For of the two," and so forth.

Because when two things—a tree and a non-tree—are mutually distinguished, the distinction resides in both; that is to say, it resides in both the tree and the non-tree, because their intrinsic natures are differentiated as tree and non-tree. Therefore, even when a distinction residing in one [of the two] is expressed by a word—namely, the distinction residing in the tree relative to the non-tree, which is its differentiated intrinsic nature—even though that is what is expressed by the word, there occurs an implication of the other [the non-tree] as an inseparable concomitant.

In relation to a non-tree, there is an implication of the difference residing in the tree—which is characterized by the exclusion of the non-tree—and in relation to the tree, there is also an implication of the difference residing in the non-tree—which is characterized by the exclusion of the tree. The word *iti* signifies "because. Because of this reason, [the phrase] "it is said that [the tree] is qualified by that" should be supplied as an ellipsis, since they possess that as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). The phrase "not of those two" means that there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the difference residing in one [of the two] and the exclusion of the other.

But what is this distinction residing in a single [entity], and what is that exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*), by means of which there arises from a word the cognition of a distinction residing in a single [entity] that is inseparable from the exclusion of others? If this is asked:

It is said: First of all, that which is denoted by the word "tree" is the form possessing branches and so forth, which appears as a manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). Appearing as if it were a non-differentiated form across all trees, and as if distinct from those things that do not possess that form, it is "the exclusion residing in that [single object]," meaning its differentiated intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). In this same way, the "exclusion residing in a single [object]" should be understood for words such as "jar" and so forth. And while conveying that exclusion, the word causes the cessation of dissimilar things (*vijātīyanivṛtti*) to be understood through the sense characterized as a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); that is the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*).

Now, one might object: "If a portion of the real entity qualified by the exclusion of others is not apprehended, for what purpose was it stated that [the word] is 'qualified by the exclusion of others' and so forth? To this he replies: "In the expression of a single difference," and so on.

And this very distinction, which exists as a single entity yet is divided [into positive and negative aspects], is what is expressed by the word. The cognition of that [positive aspect] itself is the apprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). However, the apprehension of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) which follows from the meaning is the apprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Thus, through both positive and negative concomitance, the word becomes meaningful. Therefore, it should be understood that by the expression of positive and negative concomitance, there is a direct expression of the positive concomitance, whereas the expression of the negative concomitance occurs through the implication of the meaning.

Demonstrating that words serve as a constituent part of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) by means of that very injunction, the Master Dignāga said: "By the exclusion of that [other], a portion of the real object (*vastubhāga*) is understood. Likewise, he said "or qualified by that"—here, the word "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) expresses negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), while the phrase "portion of the real object" expresses positive concomitance (*anvaya*). By this, the following is also explained: the meaning is that a verbal cognition (*śruti*), while effecting the exclusion of other words, denotes its own referent.

In this context, that single part which has been explained as appearing to the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*) is itself the "own-object" (*svārtha*). "Exclusion of other objects" (*arthāntarāpoha*), characterized as a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), means "making that [exclusion]," which in effect means "implying it. If the application of words such as "tree" were preceded solely by the exclusion of others, then the explanation beginning with "by the instruction of positive concomitance and negative exclusion" would be redundant.
Therefore, the word-meaning is indeed a positive affirmation (*vidhi*).

"Because it is precisely for this reason that, when one particular [form] is expressed, there is an understanding of the exclusion of others by implication"—this is what "precisely for this reason" and so forth means. "Because its own object (*svārtha*) has the nature of a particular" means as follows: the object of the word *vṛkṣa* (tree), which consists of the form possessing branches and so on, appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*). That [object] has the nature of a particular because it is itself of a distinct nature, being excluded from the form of non-difference. Therefore, since the expression of the word's own object—which has the nature of a particular—necessarily results in an understanding of the exclusion of others, it is thus that the object "tree" is understood precisely as having the nature of being distinct from non-trees.

If it is argued that the exclusion of the tree occurs there by implication (*arthāt*), then the function of the word is merely the denotation of its own meaning (*svārthābhidhāna*); the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvarttana*) occurs through implication, and thus the word does not have two functions. [Objection: But surely, by an affirmative sentence (*vidhāyaka-vākya*), only a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is conveyed, and neither the affirmation nor the negation of anything else; likewise, by a negative sentence (*niṣedhaka*), only a mere negation is perceived, and neither the affirmation nor the negation of anything else. To this, he says:

"Indeed, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," and so forth. Positive concomitance is the prescription of a specific object, such as "cut the tree. In that case, the exclusion of non-trees is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Where that [negative concomitance] does not exist, that is precisely what is meant by "lacking negative concomitance. Such a positive concomitance does not exist for me; rather, every [positive concomitance] is necessarily accompanied by negative concomitance. Therefore, as it was stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: "He who does not accept that the meaning of a word has a positive form..."
"Nor could there be a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for that [exclusion], since the latter is preceded by the former"—this objection from the *Ślokavārttika* (p.

254) is refuted because it is [our] accepted position. The connection is as follows: "nor is there a lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), or a negative concomitance devoid of positive concomitance. In this context, the negation of a specific [attribute] is the negative concomitance; therein, by implication, there is positive concomitance regarding the remaining [attributes]. This very point is established by the passage beginning with "of a single positive concomitance" (*ekānvayasya*). For if there is a single positive concomitance, then in the absence of anything to be set aside—that is, in the absence of anything to be excluded—the formulation [of the rule] would be fruitless.

If, upon hearing the command "Cut down a tree," there were no exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of non-trees by implication, then the use of the word "tree" would be fruitless. Alternatively, when the listener has the inquiry, "Which tree shall I cut? Or another? the negation of others is indeed understood from the statement "Cut down a tree"; otherwise, the utterance would be useless in the absence of anything to be avoided.

Likewise, even when a listener who is free from desire is urged by the words "Cut down the tree," he acts only toward the tree and not elsewhere; for the speaker employs the word with the intention that "this person shall act toward the tree alone and not otherwise. And sound follows the speaker's intention. Therefore, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) devoid of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and likewise, there is no negative concomitance devoid of a single exclusion; that is to say, there is no negative concomitance devoid of a single negation.

Because when an object is made the subject of a prohibition by the word "somewhere," there is no basis for the injunction to be effective if the thing were not otherwise established. For instance, in the prohibition of drinking alcohol: if there were no occurrence of drinking even elsewhere than with regard to alcohol, then the specific prohibition of drinking within the entire scope of the prohibited domain would be purposeless.

In this regard, since the sentence has fulfilled its purpose by prohibiting the mere act of drinking *surā*, even though the drinking of water and so forth is not explicitly enjoined by the words, nevertheless, the drinking of anything other than *surā* would not be prevented; thus, the understanding of the connection [of the prohibition] follows from the sense (*arthāt*). Otherwise, the mention of *surā* would be meaningless.

Alternatively, when the question is asked whether liquor should be drunk like water and other such things or not, and it is replied that "liquor is not to be drunk," one understands from this very statement that "it is liquor [that is prohibited]. Thus, the drinking of water and so forth—which is not the subject under discussion—is not what is being negated. Therefore, in all cases, the meaning of a word consists solely of the form of either an injunction or a prohibition.

What, then, is the distinction between affirmative, prohibitive, and exclusionary (paryudāsa) statements? It is a great distinction. For an affirmative statement primarily expresses an injunction while implying the negation of others; a prohibitive statement primarily expresses a prohibition while implying the injunction of others. However, an exclusionary statement primarily expresses the injunction of something else preceded by a negation. Thus, there is indeed a difference.

Now, one might ask: "If the exclusion of others is understood through implication, why is it not accepted that this very [exclusion] is the ultimate reality of things, by which they are apprehended as qualified? Why, then, is it further explained that because it is an attribute (*upādhi*) residing in that [object], the object is apprehended as qualified by it? To this, he says: "And this," and so forth. That difference characterized by exclusion, which was intended by Master Diṅnāga as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), is this very form, which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

This is because it has no form that is either distinct or non-distinct [from the object]. If it is asked, "How then is there the cognition of the difference of things from those of a different class? he says: the mere perception—that is, the cognition—of that difference as having a form and as being connected to the entity is a misconception, an error (*viparyaya*, *bhrānti*). The word "mere" (*kevalam*) means independent of such an external [object] as it appears. This same explanation should be understood for the verse as well. (126–29)

Now, one might ask: if there is perception by way of possessing form (*rūpavattva*), how can this be a cognitive error? To this he says: "By that very [form]," and so forth. That perception of difference which occurs by way of possessing form—that is, by way of being related to an entity—is not ultimately real; it is not a substantial reality because it lacks existence. This "it" refers to difference, which is of the nature of a negation (*prasajya-rūpa*). "Otherwise," meaning if this were not accepted: for a negation (*vyāvṛtti*) that is related to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity cannot itself be a real entity. What is the reason? Because difference is determined as "this is different from that."

This is what is meant: if that [exclusion of non-trees] were a real entity (*vastu*), then its exclusion from non-trees would have to be either non-different or different [from the trees themselves]. If it were non-different, there could be no cognition of a distinction in the form "the tree is distinct from this non-tree," because the exclusion of non-trees is non-different from a single *palāśa* tree; consequently, the exclusion of non-trees would not apply to the *dhava* and other trees, since that exclusion—which has the same nature as that [single *palāśa*]—does not extend to them, just as it does not to the *palāśa*. Now, suppose it is different from the *palāśa*.

In that case as well, there would have to be an exclusion of the *palāśa* tree from the exclusion of non-trees; and since the *palāśa* is being excluded from the exclusion of non-trees, it would follow that the *palāśa* has the nature of a non-tree, just like a non-tree. Consequently, there could be no cognition of the distinction of this tree from that non-tree, yet such a distinction is indeed intended. Therefore, that exclusion is not a real entity (*vastu*). The phrase "the distinction of this from that" means by way of verbal expression (*uccāraṇa*); this is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the inclusion of cognition (*pratīti*) as well.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "rūpaṃ hi" (for form...). "Hi" means because. What is called "form" (*rūpa*)? It is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing. "Difference" (*bheda*) is exclusion from others (*anyavyāvṛtti*). If this were form, if it were the intrinsic nature; then "that" refers to the form consisting of exclusion from non-trees. "Having that form" (*tadrūpa*) means having the nature of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* tree which is excluded from those [others]. Or "not having that form" (*atadrūpa*) means being other than that. This is because a real entity (*vastu*) cannot transcend being either identical to or different from [something else].

With the words "tādrūpye" and so forth, he states the fault in the first position: if that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which constitutes the universal (*sāmānya*) by which all distinct trees are seen to be excluded from non-trees, is admitted to be identical with the *palāśa* tree—that is, not different from the *palāśa*—then, since that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* would be the exclusion itself, it follows that only the *palāśa* is distinct from non-trees, and no other [tree] such as the *dhava* and so on. Consequently, the *dhava* and others would not be distinguished from non-trees. He asks, "For what reason? and replies with "na hi" and so forth.
For the exclusion from non-trees is the very nature of the *palāśa* tree; and that nature cannot belong to another, such as the *dhava* tree.
