The presentation of the second position begins with the words "na tad eva" and so forth. It is not that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* tree itself which is the nature (*rūpa*) of that difference; for "nature" (*rūpa*) is its intrinsic being (*svabhāva*), and this difference is held to be that [nature]. Therefore, it would have to be something entirely other than the *palāśa*, having the form of exclusion from the *palāśa*. Or else, the nature of the difference would be something entirely other. And because of that otherness, the entity consisting of the *palāśa* would be excluded from that form of exclusion from non-trees. For that reason.

If [the particular] were merely the exclusion of "non-tree," then there would be no distinction between that *palāśa* and [other things] such as heat (*ūṣman*). For whatever entity there is, from which a distinction arises—that is, from which something is excluded—that very thing becomes [that exclusion]. [In this case,] it would be the exclusion of "non-tree. Since the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* is excluded from the exclusion of "non-tree"—which consists in the cessation of "non-tree"—it would either become a non-tree itself, or like a non-tree. Or, even if there were no identity between tree and non-tree, still, the claim that "this is its distinction" would not hold.

Furthermore, if this exclusion from non-trees (*avṛkṣa-bheda*) were something other than the *palāśa* tree itself, then it would not be the case that "this exclusion from non-trees is related to this *palāśa*. The passage beginning with "for not" (*na hi*) and so forth is the justification for this. An exclusion that is a distinct entity and independent becomes related to another thing only when it takes the form of a property (*dharma*). Or, if such a relationship is admitted, then a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must be accepted as the basis for that connection; for between two distinct things, a relationship is impossible without causality.

In that regard, that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛttimat*) is the cause, and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is the effect. Thus, the nature of the reason (*hetu*) is indeed a distinct entity produced by that; it is called "differentiation" (*bheda*) because it is produced by that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which possesses exclusion. Since this is merely a name given to another category of object (*padārtha*), there would be no distinction between this so-called "differentiation"—the effect—and other effects of causes. Consequently, all effects of causes would be exclusions or differentiations. But this is not the case.
Therefore, let there be no designation of "differentiation" for anything else that is intended to be a differentiation.

Now, if it is not maintained that the effect is the difference, but rather that the difference is the effect, even then he says: "And if a difference is admitted to be a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then this difference, despite its being possessed of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), must itself have a difference [from the object]. Otherwise, the difference would not be a distinct entity at all. Consequently, since the difference of the *palāśa* tree from non-trees has a difference from the *palāśa* tree, that difference—being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of difference—is the difference from the *palāśa*."

That distinction for which a specific limiting condition (*upādhi*) exists is a "distinction conditioned by that"; because of that state, this distinction of the *palāśa* tree from what is not a tree would not be a distinction [of the *palāśa* itself]. It would be like another substance (*dravyāntara*). For just as another substance, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), is not a distinction of the *palāśa*—because the distinction from what is not a jar is a limiting condition for that [jar]—so it is here. The intended meaning is that [the distinction] is independent (*svatantra*).

Now, one might object: "Even if difference is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of difference, why does the difference not belong to the *palāśa* tree? To this he says: "For not... and so forth. Because of the specific designation "this [difference] is from that," namely, "this" refers to the difference from a non-tree; "from that" refers to the non-tree. The word "of this" must be supplied. Thus, because of this specific designation—namely, "this difference of this *palāśa* is from this non-tree"—and because it is designated in a manner dependent on another, it is established that difference is a property belonging to the *palāśa*.

Furthermore, a designation based on dependence is established only when there is non-difference [of the property] from that which possesses it, by way of excluding other differences; it is not so, however, if difference were a separate entity (*arthāntara*). For if difference were a separate entity, then—because it would be a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of difference—the difference would not belong to the *palāśa* tree itself, as in the case of a jar. Consequently, a specific designation such as "the difference of this from that" would be impossible. Thus, according to the position of absolute distinction (*vyatireka*), even the difference of the difference from the non-tree must itself possess form; therefore, that too would have to exist as distinct from its own substratum.

And thus, since all differences, by virtue of having a distinct nature, possess difference as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), they themselves do not constitute a difference in form; consequently, no difference whatsoever would exist.

This is precisely what [the author] says with the words "And therefore," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of an adjunct": if there were an absence of an adjunct—which is a property (*dharma*) characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—then because everything would be a subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of possessing its own distinct intrinsic nature, difference itself would be non-existent, since difference consists in the nature of a subject.

As for the one who thinks: "If exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were to possess a form (*rūpa*), then the fault inherent in the positions of identity or difference would apply; however, since it is formless (*nīrūpa*), and by means of it entities are apprehended as qualified," that is incorrect. [For it has been said: "It is precisely through the comprehension of that [exclusion] that the exclusion of others is understood from words."

This is because it contradicts the text [of the *Pramāṇavārttika*]: "Nothing superior is perceived there by anyone" (PV 1.128). Furthermore, existence is incompatible with that which lacks form (*nīrūpa*), like the horn of a rabbit. Precisely because it lacks form, perception does not apprehend it, nor does inference, due to the absence of a necessary connection (*sambandha*).

Nor can that [nature] be postulated on the grounds that its restricted form would otherwise be inexplicable, precisely because there is no relation [between them]; for it has already been stated in the passage beginning with "all entities participate in exclusion by their own nature" (1.42) that things arise from their own causes as having restricted forms.

Nor can that [exclusion] be a qualifier if it is not itself apprehended; for as long as the staff is not perceived, there is no perception of "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Nor does it reside anywhere, because it lacks form (*nīrūpatva*). Furthermore, that which is unrelated cannot be a qualifier. Nor does the word "tree" apply to trees and so forth preceded by the apprehension of the exclusion of others, because it has already been stated that such [exclusion] is not perceived. This is because exclusion, being formless, is not apprehended, and because a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) cannot function with respect to what is unperceived.

How is it that sound has sound as its object? Therefore, through the medium of experience, there arises the ascertainment: "This is a tree, not a non-tree. Thus, the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is conceptually constructed by means of a conceptual cognition of negation (*pratiṣedhavikalpa*). Furthermore, when a word is applied to a tree or the like according to convention, it implies the exclusion of others; the meaning is that it brings about a conceptual cognition of the exclusion of others. It is said that, by means of this exclusion of others, a portion of the real entity (*vastubhāga*) qualified [by that exclusion] is understood.

If exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are not accepted as being external entities that constitute universals (*sāmānya*), nor is the universal imagined by others [such as the Vaiśeṣikas] accepted, then it follows that an external entity itself must be the denotable object. And since there is a fault in that position, he asks: "How then? This refers to the indication by means of a word; it is also an illustration for its establishment by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*). For that very undivided, partless entity, which is distinct from one thing, is likewise distinct from another.

For instance, by that very nature through which sound is not different from the unproduced (*akṛtaka*), it is likewise [not different] from the corporeal and the impermanent, because it is partless (*anaṃśa*). And when a single, distinct nature—which is differentiated from the unproduced—is indicated by the word "produced" for a partless entity, and when it is established by a logical mark (*liṅga*), then all distinctions are understood; thus, the nature that is differentiated from everything is apprehended. In that case, regarding a partless entity, how could other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as words not be redundant?
If [the meaning] were enjoined by a single word, other words would be rendered useless; if it were established by a single indicative mark, other means of valid cognition would be rendered useless.

He refutes [this] with the words "Because... and so forth. This objection has already been refuted previously by the passage beginning, "Therefore, whatever distinction is perceived by means of a particular property" (1.44). However, it is introduced again for the purpose of providing further explanation. "The superimposition of another form upon objects is the 'fusion' (*śleṣa*) of the object. And that [superimposition] is manifold due to the difference in cognition. In that context—referring to the subject (*dharmin*) appearing in cognition—they are to be described as being distinct from the external [object], because it is precisely that mental form (*buddhyākāra*), which is superimposed as something external, that is denotable by words.

Furthermore, neither the external object nor the mental form alone is denotable by a word, because they are particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). In that case, with respect to the substratum (*dharmin*), a single sound operates through the exclusion of the connection with other objects by means of the cognition of its own referent in a positive form (*vidhirūpa*). (130)

And the *liṅga* (logical mark) functions in the exclusion [of other meanings] through the connection of a single referent. In that regard, the point is that the efficacy of other means of knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*) lies in the exclusion of superimpositions by way of denoting its own object. However, there is no external thing as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from cognition, nor is there any external thing as a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) distinct from the particular characteristic that could be expressed; for if such a thing were denoted, there would be comprehension of the entire nature of reality.

“By the power of the thing” means by the force of the real object (*vastu*). And because a word effects an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) by way of its own denotation, for that reason, while effecting each respective exclusion, the word has manifold results and yet has a single substratum. How so? By determining (*adhyavasāya*) what is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*). The meaning is that even though it does not perform causal efficiency itself, it superimposes its own appearance as being the performer of causal efficiency and as having the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-rūpatva*). “In that very [place]” means in the manifestation of cognition (*buddhi-pratibhāsa*) which has been superimposed as something external.
What is it that occurs? Through various causes of error, it appears as if its form were mixed with [other qualities].

(131) When it appears as if its form were mixed with aspects such as permanence due to causes of error—such as the arising of similar subsequent moments—those words like "impermanent" function to exclude whichever superimposition corresponds to the convention; for how could there be a convention regarding one's own appearance? They operate to exclude each respective counter-correlate. Explaining exactly in accordance with the convention, he says: "And not," and so forth. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *hi* (for).

Since the operation [of a word] proceeds according to its conventional designation (*saṃketa*), one word does not effect the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) that is to be accomplished by another word. What is the reason? Because of the restriction of the convention. This is because the form of the cognition (*buddhyākāra*) is established as a verbal designation within an undifferentiated external form for the sake of each individual exclusion. The meaning is that even at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it causes that very same exclusion to be understood by way of denoting its own object. The mention of "word" (*śabda*) is merely illustrative; it should be understood that the same applies to the logical mark (*liṅga*) as well.

[Objection: Since the object of a word has the form of an external thing superimposed upon it, and since that [word] apprehends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in its entirety through another [conceptual] characteristic, how is it that other words are not rendered useless? To this he says, "And not," and so forth. The word "ca" (and) functions as a restrictive particle. There is no entity whatsoever that is "severed"—that is, distinct from a portion of cognition—such as a *svalakṣaṇa*, or a *sāmānyalakṣaṇa* separate from the *svalakṣaṇa*, or that which is characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which could be projected or grasped by a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*).

If [a thing] were apprehended through the power of the object itself by virtue of its verbal designation, then because the object is partless (*niraṃśatva*), there would be a complete apprehension of it in every respect; for properties (*dharma*) are not distinct from it. Even if they were distinct, since it has been stated that there is a complete apprehension in the passage beginning with, "Even if the adjuncts (*upādhi*) are distinct, [there is apprehension] of the self which is non-different from the capacities that are the factors contributing to the assistance of the various adjuncts" (1.54), why would a thing be indicated by words as something fragmented? To this, he says: "Of words," and so forth.

This is what is meant: since words determine as external that which is actually a non-external form of cognition, they appear, for that reason, as if they were apprehenders of discrete objects. "The error of cognition" (*buddhiviplava*) refers to the grasping of the form of cognition as having an external nature; this is because words have that [form] as their object. If it is asked, "Even when there is an error of cognition, how is there comprehension of the entire range of denotable objects through the power of the real entity?"—the author says: "And in that case," etc. "In that case" means in the absence of a real entity due to the error of cognition;
[comprehension occurs] because of the absence of the power of a real entity [to act upon such an error].

Although the form of cognition is a real entity because it is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of knowledge, nevertheless, when it is superimposed by words or conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) as non-different from the external object, it is indeed not a real entity. Therefore, neither word nor conceptual construction has the specific characteristic as its object, because there is no apprehension, even in the slightest degree, of either the external thing or the form of cognition as they truly are.

If all words have as their object only the distortion of the intellect (*buddhiviplava*), how can there be non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) for words such as "produced" (*kṛtaka*) or "impermanent" (*anitya*) with respect to a real entity (*vastu*) that is not of that nature? To this he says: "In that manner," and so forth. The meaning is: by way of the experience of an object that is distinct from each respective [opposite], such as the unproduced (*akṛtaka*) or the permanent (*nitya*). This is to be connected with the phrase "this conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*). Of what nature is it? It is "various and one," and so forth. "Various and one" (*nānaika*) means both various (*nānā*) and one (*eka*). That [pair] and the property (*dharma*) form a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Then, there is a three-membered *dvandva* compound consisting of the words "difference" (*bheda*), "non-difference" (*abheda*), and "words" (*śabda*). It is these very appearances—namely, difference and non-difference regarding various properties—that manifest in the intellect; they are "distortions" (*viplava*) because they are erroneous. "Following that" means proceeding with that mental form. For this reason, when there is a connection between that linguistic convention and its object—meaning, when there is an indirect causal connection with such a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—there is no deviation from it; that is, there is no deviation from the real entity (*vastu*).

For just as words with forms such as "produced" are erroneous, so too the ultimate existence of things in the form of being "produced" and so forth must be understood as non-deviation in this respect.

He says this very thing with the words "from that too," and so forth. From that—i.e., from the word which is the object of a cognitive distortion, from the linguistic convention characterized as inference for others, which is "vitatha" (unreal), meaning erroneous—at the end of the activity, i.e., upon the completion of the activity, [the cognition occurs] regarding an entity that is exactly of such a nature, namely having the form of being produced and so on, and not having the form of being unproduced and so on. By this, the nature of non-deviation is stated. This is because of the correspondence with knowledge, that is, because of the arising of a cognition that grasps the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or because of the correspondence of the word or the cognition itself.

He states that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established only when the meaning of a word is this very exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and not in a real entity (*vastu*)—beginning with the words "not, however, distinct," and so forth. "Distinct forms" refers to universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so on, which serve as the grounds for the application of words. Because the cognitions and words that apprehend them have a single real entity as their object, there is the connection [expressed as]: "the word has a single substratum. For if a cognition of distinct forms were to proceed having a single real entity as its object, then, following that [cognition], the word would likewise be so.

And thus, it would follow that a word with multiple effects has a single substratum, which constitutes grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); yet this is not the case, because it involves a contradiction. To explain: for the words "blue" and "lotus," the referent must be either a single entity or multiple entities. In the first case, since the partless entity would be denoted in its entirety by a single word alone, a second word would have no application; or, if it were to apply, it would be a synonym, and thus there would be no plurality of effects. In the second case, there is no single substratum, because—like the words "pot" and "cloth"—the objects are distinct.

Now, it might be thought: the word "blue" denotes a substance qualified by the quality of blueness; the word "lotus" also denotes that very same substance qualified by the universal of lotus-ness. Therefore, because the qualifiers are distinct, the words have different results, yet because the qualified object is non-distinct, they share a single substratum.

That too is incorrect. Because a substance qualified by the quality of blue, when denoted by the word "blue," is denoted in its entirety, since it is partless. Consequently, what other nature of the substance—distinct from its being qualified by the universal *utpala*—remains that could be denoted by the word "lotus"? Thus, they would simply be synonyms. If, on the other hand, there were a distinction in the qualified substance due to the difference in qualifiers, then they could not share a single substratum. [The author] states "as has been described," etc., to show that this fault applies only to the proponent of Apoha.
That verbal object whose basis is a mental appearance is described as such.

Demonstrating how there is no fault, he says: "Exclusion," and so forth. A single word, "blue," while indicating one exclusion—the blue nature excluded from non-blue—functions without rejecting another exclusion—the lotus nature excluded from non-lotus; that is to say, it does not negate it. (132)

The word *sa* (that) refers to a nature excluded from non-lotuses. Being pervaded, encompassed, and implied by that word *nīla* (blue), it appears as a single unity in the intellect when the word *utpala* (lotus) is employed. This is because a single substratum (*dharmin*), endowed with the two properties of being blue and being a lotus—which are brought about by two exclusions (*vyavaccheda*)—appears in conceptual cognition. And when this is the case, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in accordance with the intellect.

This is what is meant: by the employment of the word "blue," the subject appearing in cognition manifests as having the very form of blue; therein, by implication, that which is non-blue is excluded, but its nature is not excluded from being a non-lotus. Likewise, by the employment of the word "lotus," it is cognized as having the form of a lotus, whereby that which is non-lotus is excluded, but its nature is not excluded from being non-blue.

However, when two words are employed, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) arises that manifests a single substratum (*ekadharmī*) possessing the two properties of "blue" and "lotus"; therefore, since the word has a single basis despite having multiple fruits [of denotation], there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in accordance with that cognition.

Therefore, what Uddyotakara says—namely, "For one for whom the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it must be explained how the exclusions of 'non-blue' and 'non-lotus' can be co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*). But for one [like us] for whom the meaning of a word is that which is being positively enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*), a substance qualified by a genus and a quality is denoted by the words 'blue' and 'lotus,' and the genus and the quality reside in the substance; it is not, however, the exclusions of non-blue and non-lotus. Consequently, there is no such thing as a co-referential meaning"—is refuted, because we accept that the meaning of a word is that which is being positively enjoined. (133)

Furthermore, when it is admitted that a word effects the exclusion of superimpositions (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*) by means of denoting its own object, or rather, when it effects exclusion—that is, when it takes as its object an excluded nature (*vyavacchinna-svabhāva*)—there would necessarily be some slight contact, characterized by attainment, with a real property (*vastu-dharma*), that is, a real nature (*vastu-svabhāva*) which is differentiated from what is of a different class (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtta*). What is the reason? Because that which is determined (*adhyavasīyamāna*) as "it is true" (*satyam*) is indeed an existing, excluded nature.

In that regard, if one accepts that words denote a single entity (*vastu*) by treating it as a real thing (*vastu*), then because the universal (*sāmānya*), which is a property of the entity, would itself lack the status of a real thing, how [could this be]? If you ask why, [the text says] "in the cognition" and so forth. This means that because there is no perception of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility, it is non-existent. Since there is thus a fault in taking the word-meaning to be a real thing, for that reason the Teacher Diṅnāga stated that words and cognitions have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their object—that is, they have as their object the appearance within conceptual cognition. What kind of cognitions are these? The meaning is that they are conceptual cognitions whose domain is the universal.

This is a qualification of cognitions alone, and not of words, because those [words] deviate from their general object. What is the reason? Because these words and conceptual constructions (vikalpa) can occur with respect to a real entity (vastu).

He explains [the passage] beginning with "yadi hi" (if, indeed). If only the thing-in-itself (*vastu*) were made the object, it would be apprehended, but it would not be determined (*adhyavasīyeta*) as having a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*). This aforementioned consequence—that all objects would be cognized in every respect due to the causal capacity of the thing-in-itself—is what is meant by "this. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the absence of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), the non-operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), and so forth. The author is the Master Dignāga. The two words "these" (*etāv*) refer to the terms for "cognition" (*buddhi*). That which is excluded by another is called the "aspect of conceptual construction" (*vikalpākāra*); [the compound] refers to those two [terms] which have that [aspect] as their object.

If a single object were to be made the object of cognitions having distinct forms, and likewise expressed by words, then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because two words with different results would apply to one and the same substance; however, this is not possible. For instance, would that universal denoted by those words be non-different or different from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? Regarding the first position:
since the nature of the object is unitary, from where could there arise a cognition with distinct forms—the aspects of universal and particular—that possess different forms? (136)

Furthermore, since the universal is not distinct from its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when a particular consisting of a *śābaleya* cow is excluded from a particular consisting of a *bāhuleya* cow, and the "cow-ness" (*gotva*) consisting of the *śābaleya* follows after the *bāhuleya*, it follows that for a single entity, both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would occur with respect to the same locus. And this is untenable; thus he says: "positive and negative concomitance," and so forth. That is to say, those two positive and negative concomitances which have a single object as their domain—that is, their scope—are described in that way.

He explains this with the words beginning "That [entity] is one," and so forth. Precisely because it is one, it is partless, since a single thing lacks parts. An "aspect" (*ākāra*) is that which is formed; it is the appearance in cognition. Its "differentiation" is the differentiation based upon it, namely, the multiplicity of the real entity (*vastu*). If it were apprehended by cognitions possessing different aspects, it would be differentiated. But this is not the case, because such [multiple aspects] do not exist for the real entity. If it is argued that, because a real entity consists of both the universal and the particular, even a single entity can be apprehended by cognitions possessing different aspects, he says: "Even as its own nature," and so forth.

Because that which has the nature of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) shares a single fate (*ekayogakṣema*) with it; that is, because it shares a single fate with the specific characteristic, it is non-different from it in exactly that same way. "That" refers to the reason why this [phenomenon of] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth would not occur—this is the connection. What is the reason? Because they would have distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), meaning they would exclude each other's referents through mutual exclusion. This is because it is impossible for two words to function when they have a single object and are based upon a single substance.

He explains the portion of the verse beginning with *anvaya* by means of the passage beginning with *na ca*. When the single essence of a thing (*vastvātmā*)—the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is also the universal (*sāmānya*), then, because the particular of a brindled cow (*śāvaleyasvalakṣaṇa*) consists of the universal "cowness" (*gotvasāmānya*), its occurrence (*vṛtti*) would be in that very [brindled cow]; yet, because it consists of the particular, its non-occurrence (*avṛtti*) would likewise be in that very same [brindled cow] at that time. That [simultaneous occurrence and non-occurrence] is illogical, because it involves a contradiction (*vyāghāta*) and is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhitatva*). Since it is non-different from the particular, the universal does not exist elsewhere at all.

If it is argued that "therefore, there is neither occurrence nor non-occurrence for a single [entity] in one place," he replies with the words beginning "And not... and "Of the universal...". The intended meaning is: "Therefore, there is neither occurrence nor non-occurrence for a single [entity]."

"No," says the Teacher, because there is no difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) according to the systems of the Sāṃkhyas and others. The passage beginning with "that" (*tat*) and so forth is a justification of this very point: for that entity, being of a single form and a single nature, must either be a universal or a particular. Since the particular is not distinct from the universal, it would be the universal alone; or else, since the universal is not distinct from the particular, it would be the particular alone. But a single thing cannot possess two forms.

For if there were no difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*), this distinction between "universal" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*) would not exist; or, if such a distinction did exist, there could be no non-distinction (*avyatireka*) between the universal and the particular, as was stated previously. Therefore, "that" means this very nature of the entity (*vastv-ātmā*). "Indivisible" (*avibhāga*) means partless (*anaṃśa*). If it were exclusively a universal, then it would follow after—that is, it would enter into—other individuals. If, on the other hand, its nature were exclusively that of a particular, then it would not follow after them at all. The point is that two contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single thing. He says exactly that with the words "not again," and so forth.

"Even he" refers to the Vaiśeṣika and others. He asserts that the universal (*sāmānya*), which is the denotation of a word, is indeed distinct from the substance (*dravya*). [The author replies: If a difference between the individual (*vyakti*) and the universals were admitted, then linguistic usages based on non-difference—such as the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth—would be without a basis. "According to their respective [objects]" (*yathāsvam*): this is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*). For instance, words such as "blue lotus" denote their respective blue lotuses and other such entities as universals that are mutually distinct.

Even when the word "blue" is held to denote the quality of blueness, there is still the denotation of distinct objects. [The compound] *ekārthā buddhiḥ* is a *karmadhāraya*, meaning "a cognition whose object—the referent—is a single property-possessor (*dharmin*)," with the masculine form applied according to grammatical rule (*pumvadbhāva*). How could these [words] be the basis or cause of such a cognition? And consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); this is the intended meaning.

If words such as "blue lotus" were to produce a cognition whose object is a single substratum qualified by two qualifiers, then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the communication of a single referent; however, that is not the case. The universal (*sāmānya*) is a different entity from the individual (*vyakti*); and for those [words] denoting it [the universal], there is no implication (*ākṣepa*) of the particulars contained within it. Implication is a function that occurs without abandoning [the primary object]; this is not so here. Why? Because of the absence of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*). When the word "tree" denotes only "treeness," [it has no further expectancy].

In that case, since the word [‘tree’] would be devoid of any qualification, it would be complete in itself by that much alone; how then could it imply [the specific terms] such as ‘dhava’? And if they are not implied, how could *dhava* and the others be the particulars (*bheda*) of the referent of the word ‘tree’? Furthermore, since they would not be its particulars, how could there be the relationship of qualifier and qualified in the expression “a *śiṃśapā* is a tree”? To this he says: “How,” and so forth. If it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because the substance is denoted as qualified by the universal, we say no, for the answer has already been stated.

Even when a substance qualified by its attributes is denoted, because the entire [object] is understood from a single word through the inherent power of the thing (*vastu-sāmarthya*), another word does not apply to it; and if it were to apply, they would not be synonyms. Thus, for one who maintains that the meaning of a word is the real entity (*vastu-śabdārthavādin*), the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth cannot arise in any way.

It has been stated that even a universal (*sāmānya*) is not possible for them. For instance, when the universal is non-different from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), then, like the particular itself, it does not follow through other individuals and thus is not a universal. Even if it were different, how could one thing be the universal of another? This would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as was stated previously. (137) However, for the proponent of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), this is not a fault; thus he says: "In all cases," and so forth. "These faults" refers to the absence of a universal and its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and so on. "For just as," and so forth.

A single cow-individual, such as a *śāvaleyas*, is distinct from that nature which is non-cow; likewise, another individual, such as a *bāhuleyas*, is also distinct. Therefore, the nature excluded from heterogeneous things is identical everywhere. Thus, because the nature—which is distinguished from heterogeneous things—is superimposed by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) everywhere without distinction upon its own form, there is no fault regarding its being a universal (*sāmānya*). As for the remaining point—that there would be an absence of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth—this has already been stated [in the verse] beginning with: "It functions without rejecting the one, while indicating a distinction" (1.133).

Thus, having first established that a single entity—which is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) excluded from heterogeneous things and superimposed by the intellect as non-different from its own form—is the denotation of a word; [the author] now states "Moreover," etc., to show that even without a non-different form, a single word is applied to entities that have a single effect. The phrase "in order to indicate their common effect" (*tatkāryaparicodane*) means either for the purpose of indicating the state of having a single effect, or for the purpose of indicating those entities that have a single effect. Regarding those diverse entities that have a single effect—even though they lack a single [intrinsic] existence—there is one common term (*samā ekā śrutiḥ*).

It has been established and designated by the Buddhas, who are experts in conventional usage. The meaning is that a single term is applied to things that perform the same function, based on that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) which consists in their being distinct from those things that do not perform that function—that is, based on their exclusion from what is of a different class.

(138) Now, if there is no application of words to a universal (*sāmānya*), then the application of words must pertain to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), since nothing else exists. Yet, the particular is not denotable by words.

This is not so. For the communicator, intending to establish a convention by means of a single effect, first takes as his object entities existing across the three times; he then establishes the convention upon those very entities for the purpose of communication at the time of linguistic usage. At that time, the state of being an effect is what is enjoined. Thus, the meaning is that a single word is not applied as a convention to them [the individual causes] individually. This is for the sake of perceiving the entire collection of causes simultaneously—that is, all at once. "Even without," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: even though there is no distinct universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by having a single effect—namely, that commonality of form belonging to those [faculties] such as the eye; if it is argued that "existence" (*sattā*) itself is their universal, we say no, because since that [existence] is undifferentiated, it would follow that visual consciousness would arise at all times and in all places. "Without a non-distinct object" means without a real entity (*vastubhūta*) that serves as a universal. "In many" refers to the various individuals such as the *śābaleya* cow and others. "Of them" refers to those specific individuals like the *śābaleya*.

If there were a universal (*sāmānya*) belonging to them, then, because the word would be applied to that universal, it would be applied to every particular (*bheda*). However, without a single universal, the application of a single word to many [particulars] is not logical. Consequently, when that word is being conventionally established (*saṃketyamāna*), it would be established as referring to only one particular. And thus, because a word whose application has been fixed to one particular does not produce a corresponding cognition regarding another distinct particular, [it could not apply to all].

In that case, a second individual cow would not be understood from that word as "cow," because the universal—which serves as the basis for proximity—would be absent there. If it is argued that even in the absence of a conformity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānugama*), a cognition established in a *śābaleya* (spotted) cow will produce a cognition in a *bāhuleya* (black) cow despite the lack of proximity, he replies: "And in the case of what is not proximate," etc. This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); that is, from the word "cow," there would be a cognition even of a horse. Thus far, it has been stated that without a single universal, the application of a single word to many individuals is impossible.

Having granted the futility [of the opponent's position], he says: "And in those cases," etc. For instance, a single word is applied to many things either to convey a single object that exists in multiple instances, or to convey those very distinct entities without confusion. Regarding these, he states the absence of the first case: "because there is no application to a single object. If the application of a word were restricted to a single object, then it would follow that it conveys a single object. He states the absence of the second case with the words: "distinct," etc.

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the cognitions of the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) and other such [individuals], which possess distinct natures and are unmixed. Regarding the phrase "separately" (*pṛthak*): it means in each individual particular. When the application—that is, the convention—of a single word has been made, later at the time of linguistic usage, because there is no discernment of the distinction between those things that were enjoined for the sake of non-confused cognition as they were enjoined, the application of the word to them is not fruitful. For in this way, the application of words separately to each of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) becomes fruitful.

The intention is this: if one were to hold that individual particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) are understood without confusion from that word, and since the application of a single word is indeed made toward many [particulars], there must therefore exist a real entity (*vastubhūta*) in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*).

The Teacher says, "Of that too": the first alternative is that a word should be applied by the world simply on the grounds that a single entity, namely the universal (*sāmānya*), exists, even in the absence of any other purpose. He states the second [alternative] with the words "that" (*tad*) and so forth. "That" refers to the universal; "by the power of the entity itself" means without depending on human activity. It causes one single term to resound or arise. However, neither of these two [alternatives] exists at all, because there is an absence of application without a purpose and without human activity.

He says "by some purpose" and so forth, [asking] "what then?"—[meaning] that from these words, in worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), one might understand an object as being either its own means of accomplishment or not its own means of accomplishment, because it is a cognition. By this, he states the absence of the first alternative; by the word "are designated," he states the absence of the second. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "they are designated—that is, they are conventionally established (*saṃketyante*)—by those desiring to engage in worldly usage. In this principle, multiple causes would be employed—that is, they would operate—in a single effect. That [effect] is "multiple. Why? Precisely because it arises from a collection of causes.

In this regard, those who wish to engage in linguistic practice concerning this effect must necessarily rely upon a single term to express it—even though its causes are many—by taking recourse to the unity of the effect characterized by the exclusion of what is not that effect. He states the fault in expressing it through multiple terms with the words "of that," and so forth. "Separately" means by distinct words. And this has been stated while accepting the application of words to specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*).

He says "nor indeed... and so forth, because this very thing is not possible. "Of this entity" means of the particular (svalakṣaṇa). "A nature not shared by others" means that which is not shared by others; the meaning is "the unique particular. "Nor of this" refers to the application of multiple words.

And this is a sequential elaboration of the statement "because the capacity of the word 'cow' would be futile. If one asks why it is futile, he says: "Only," and so forth. By this [word], for the agent in this particular task, the purpose is merely that the meanings—the things that serve as causes—should be prompted. However, whether those things serving as causes are prompted by a single word or by many is a matter of the speaker's freedom regarding the prompting.

Since this is so, therefore this single word (*śruti*), proceeding by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*abhiprāya*) toward many objects to be expressed, does not deserve censure. If it is argued that "it is impossible to apply a single word to many [objects]," he says: "And this is not... and so forth. This refers to this single word. The analysis of the compound is: "that for which application is impossible. Why is its application not impossible? He says: "Because it is dependent upon desire (*icchā*). That which is dependent is what makes application impossible [for others].

"For even in one case," and so forth. For instance, in that case, regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) imagined by others, the application of a single word does not occur through the actual state of things; rather, it occurs by virtue of the speaker's intention. Thus, if the speaker’s intention were not present, how could this single word apply even to a single object? The intended meaning is: "It certainly would not. Therefore, in applying [the word] even to a single object, intention alone is the cause.

It is not the power of the object [that determines this]; for even when there are many [objects], there is no contradiction whatsoever. Thus he says: "Or in the case of desire," and so forth. Even when there is a desire to apply [a single term] to only one [of many], if that [desire] is postulated as the cause, then this single word—[the objection being] "because of the absence of a purpose," and so on—is not [justified]. For applying a single word to many [objects] without a single underlying entity is not fruitful. This was stated previously. He asks: "What was stated? and answers: "In the case of distinct [things]," and so forth.

When there are distinct particulars such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) and others, there is a cognition from the single word "cow" by way of differentiation from those things that do not serve its purpose—that is, by way of differentiation from horses and the like, for whom the function or purpose to be accomplished by those cow-particulars, such as carrying or milking, does not exist. But why is it not asserted that this oneness is indeed a real entity? To this he says: "Nor, however, is there a single denotation for distinct things because of the oneness of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor because of the oneness of a real universal (*sāmānya*); for it is impossible for that [universal] to be either distinct from or non-distinct from [the individuals]. (139)

Granted that the universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct [from its particulars], even so, it remains established within those individual natures (*svabhāva*) as something unmixed. He says this very thing with the words "according to their own" (*yathāsvam*), and so forth. Since the natures of things are established according to their respective characteristics, how could a single word—having a single cause and based on a universal—apply to distinct things through a mutual blending of their forms? The intended meaning is: it certainly could not. For one thing does not become identical to another by virtue of being associated with something else. And this has already been stated previously in the context of verse 1.42: "All entities, by their own nature, are established in their own respective natures."

But for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), this is not a fault; thus he says: "The non-connection with what is not that," and so forth. Since the exclusion from those things that do not have that purpose is not contradictory even among distinct things, that very exclusion from what does not have that purpose constitutes the non-difference of those things that do have that purpose, because such exclusion exists everywhere. Let this be the cause of the non-difference of words. And since a real, ontological universal (*sāmānya*) cannot in any way be established.

As for what was stated—that these types of cattle are distinct, having as their purpose the functions of carrying loads and yielding milk—that means they are indeed described as being distinct from horses and other animals that do not have those purposes.

Furthermore, their status as performing those functions does not exist apart from their distinction from others; rather, it amounts to saying that their very nature is simply the exclusion of others. By this, the portion of the verse beginning with "their status as performing those functions" (*tatkāryatāpi*) has been explained. (140–141)

With the words "Just as," etc., he explains [the verse] starting from "In the case of the eye, etc., just as visual consciousness has a single result," and so forth. The phrase "in the contact of self, sense-faculties, mind, and object" is stated according to the conventions of others (the Naiyāyikas). The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom visual consciousness is the single effect. That visual consciousness is the effect; those things ending with the woman are its effects. The "commonality" of these is their capacity to produce that single effect without distinction; the "instruction" (codanā) regarding that is its manifestation.

When that [possibility] exists, he asks: "By what occasion, however, does the possibility of an inquiry arise? The meaning is: when there is a question regarding the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) without qualification, such as "From where does the cognition of form (*rūpavijñāna*) arise? For the sake of brevity in conventional usage, and for the purpose of conveying many things by means of a single word, the connection is as follows: one should establish the linguistic convention (*śruti*) that the cause of the cognition of form is the collection of the eye and so forth, [referring to it] as either *saraḥ* or *śaraḥ*.

With the words "api nāma" and so forth, he explains precisely the economy of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra-lāghava*). Regarding "the causes of that"—namely, the causes of visual consciousness—"and not here," meaning not in the eye and so forth; [there is no] such a universal (*sāmānya*) belonging to the eye and so forth by which, through a recurring form, they produce a single visual consciousness. If it is argued that "existence" (*sattā*) exists [as that universal], then, because that [existence] is without distinction everywhere, there would have to be visual consciousness and so forth everywhere.

Nor does existence (*sattā*) differ due to the difference of its relata, because, being eternal, it cannot have any excellence (*atiśaya*) added to it. Rather, entities such as the eye and so forth are distinct from those things that do not serve that purpose—that is, from those which do not produce the cognition of form—precisely because they have the single effect of producing the cognition of form and because they exist for that purpose. Thus, their "difference" is simply their exclusion from those that do not have that effect. There is no actual non-difference among these [individual] eyes and so forth, because the exclusion from those with other effects is common to all of them.

Just as there is no difference among the eyes and so forth because they are all equal in their exclusion of what does not produce that effect; and just as, even in the absence of a single universal among the eye, visible form, and so on, a single word is applied to indicate their single effect—so too with "all things of this kind" and so forth. Words such as "collection," "continuum," and "particular state" are denoters of a collection, a continuum, and a particular state respectively. Regarding that, with reference to the word denoting a collection, he says: "Those which are combined," and so forth.

All those [factors] such as form, taste, smell, and so forth, which perform some single effect such as the fetching of water; because there is no distinction among those forms and so on in their status as causes toward that effect—since all of them have a single effect—it is said that there is no distinction by virtue of that single effect. However, this is not because there is no distinction in their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

When it is merely necessary to demonstrate their capacity to perform a single function, a specific injunction is pointless. Considering that an injunction by means of a word differentiated by form and so forth would be fruitless, this world—namely, the user of language—employs a single word, "jar," for all of them simultaneously in order to enjoin them toward a certain task, such as holding water, since they are identical in their functions regarding specific qualities like form and so on. (143)

If it is asked, "But since form and the other [sensory objects] are indeed distinct, how can they be perceived as non-different from the single word 'jar'? he says: "They too," and so forth. Although there is no difference in their distinction from form—which is of the same class—and from others such as taste, [they are so perceived] because they constitute a factor for that purpose; that is, because they constitute a factor for the specific effect of fetching water and so on. They are distinguished from "others than those"—that is, from things like cloth which are incapable of performing that function. Thus, their very distinction [from others] constitutes their non-distinction [from one another].
Therefore, due to this non-distinction, all forms and the rest are perceived without distinction—that is, by way of the universal alone—from the single word "jar."

If the pot is merely the form and other qualities themselves, and not a substance distinct from them, then how is there a distinction expressed as "the form and other qualities of the pot"? To this he says: "In that regard," and so forth. Even regarding the distinction expressed as "the form and other qualities of the pot," its meaning is this: that the form and other qualities have the nature of the pot, and do not have the nature of a cloth or other things.

He explains this very point with the words beginning "of water" (*udaka*) and so forth. The specific quality (*viśeṣa*) of bringing water is that it cannot be accomplished by anything other than a jar. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other effects to be accomplished by a jar are also included. The compound is formed according to the rule of splitting the *yoga* (*yogavibhāga*): "the locative [case] is used for that which is capable toward that effect. This is the meaning here: the words "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth denote form and the rest non-specifically as being endowed with the capacity for whatever effect is to be accomplished by form.

The word "jar," however, by virtue of its connection with a specific causal capacity, denotes specific forms and other qualities as distinct even from the natures of cloth and so forth; thus, through the operation of two words—the expression "the jar's" and "forms and so forth"—there arises a cognition in the form of a universal and its particulars, whereby the relationship between universal and particular and the notion of their distinction are employed.

He says this with the words "etad eva sāmānya... and so forth: "The accomplishment (*siddhi*) of that [effect], which is the accomplishment of a common effect (*sāmānyakārya*)—namely, that which is to be established by the mere form (*rūpa*) and so on—is by means of its own nature (*ātmanā*) as something well-known (*prasiddhena*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) here denotes a characteristic state (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*), or it denotes the cause (*hetu*). By such a form or by such a cause, being well-known through the words 'form' (*rūpa*) and so on acting as instruments (*karaṇa*), they accomplish a specific effect (*viśiṣṭaṃ kāryaṃ*)—that which is to be accomplished by a jar (*ghaṭasādhya*), namely, the fetching of water and so forth. It is called 'accomplishment' (*sādhana*) because it is that by which something is accomplished."
That which has such a designation or name is "thus"; they are distinguished by that. Thus, it is said that "those" refer precisely to form and the other [sensory objects].

Furthermore, in this case—whether regarding the collection of form and so forth, or regarding the conventional usage "this is a jar"—there is no substance distinct from form and so forth that possesses the characteristics as previously described. This refers to such a "whole" (*avayavin*) as being distinct from form and so forth. For others maintain that the whole meets the conditions for perception, based on the statement: "The substance is visible and tangible. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that such a [whole], which is accepted as meeting the conditions for perception, is not perceived apart from form and so forth.
Just as it will be demonstrated in the second chapter that atoms alone, even without a whole (avayavin), are the objects of direct perception; so too [is this case].

If [it is argued]: "If the jar is merely the collection of form and so forth, then how is there the singular number in the expression 'the jar' when there are many [factors]? [The author] replies: "The singular number," and so on. Just as a single word is used for many things to indicate a single capacity (*eka-śakti*), so too is the singular number. It is for the purpose of indicating that capacity of those [factors], such as form and so forth, which exists toward a single effect, namely the fetching of water. The meaning is that the singular number is used by superimposing unity upon them by virtue of their performing a single function; however, a single [inherent] capacity does not exist among them.

[This refers to] that which does not depend on an external object, which consists of a single word, and is dependent upon convention (*saṃketa*). And this has been established by [the verse beginning] "For those whose words are under the power of real entities" (1.66). With reference to words that denote a continuum (*santāna*), he says "in the same way," and so forth. "Cause and effect" (*hetuphale*) means cause and result. Their "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) is their state of being based on a single continuum through the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*). "Those who have become" (*bhūtāḥ*) means those who have attained it; the verb *bhū* is transitive when it signifies the act of attaining.

The term *sādhanam kṛta* is a *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* compound. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom a specific cause-and-effect has become (*bhūta*) or been accomplished (*niṣpanna*). The word *bhūta* is placed at the end [of the compound] because it belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class beginning with *āhitāgni*. "Accomplishing some one thing" means as follows: for example, the sprout, stalk, leaf, and so forth, accomplish a single fruit; and they are themselves accomplished by a single [cause], namely, the seed which serves as their material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, those sprouts and so forth do not consist of a single moment; this is for the purpose of showing that they are perceived simultaneously.

Because of this similarity—either through having a single effect or a single cause—the terms *vrīhi* (rice) and so forth, which denote a continuum (*santāna*), were established as conventions at the time of the convention itself. Subsequently, at the time of linguistic usage, they are employed for the sake of brevity in communication; for if there is a desire to know the continuity [of the entity] without [noting its] distinctions, the employment of multiple words based on the distinctions of seed, sprout, and so forth would be futile. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), terms such as *manuṣya* (human) are also included, since these too denote a continuity that is differentiated by stages such as infancy, childhood, and so on.

[Objection: But surely words such as *vrīhi* (rice) are also indeed collective terms (*samudāya-śabda*), since they denote a collection of [qualities] such as color and so forth. [Reply: True; however, it is stated thus because they denote a continuum of results that are specific causes and effects. Likewise, a collective term becomes a generic term (*jāti-śabda*) in relation to multiple collections, and the same applies to a term for a state (*avasthā-śabda*). There is no fault, for a particular word is designated as such simply by the intention to express a specific meaning. And this is just as the colors and other qualities of a jar are referred to as "the jar," where the use of the singular number is explained by a specific basis.

Likewise, one should not view the term "rice" as being in the singular when referring to the color-forms (*rūpa*) and so forth of that rice; for this very reason, he says: "or it should be stated as before. With reference to words denoting states (*avasthā*), he says: "even those which," and so forth. "Even those blue atoms and so forth" refers to blue, yellow, and the rest, whether "separately"—meaning independent of one another—or "collectively"—meaning joined with one another. "In some instance" means either in visual consciousness, or in a specific location, or for the sake of conveying [the object] all at once by preventing its production elsewhere.

For the purpose of determining many things from a single word: therein, those which are employed in visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) and which express specific states are called "visible" (sanidarśana). Those which obstruct the arising of another in their own location are called "resistant" (sapratigha). Now, one might ask: since blue, yellow, and so forth are absolutely distinct, how can they be expressed by the single term "visible" and the like? To this, he says:

"By way of the generality of difference from others than those. The very difference from others—that is, from those that are non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*) and non-obstructive (*apratigha*)—is their generality, because all of them are excluded from that [difference]. For that reason, it might be argued: "Words such as 'demonstrable' (*sanidarśana*) are also merely collective terms (*samudāya-śabda*), because they denote a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*). This is not so; for even a single atom is denoted by words such as 'obstructive' (*sapratigha*).

Having explained the application of words by way of their effect (*kārya*), he now explains it by way of their cause (*kāraṇa*): "Just as color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest have a single effect, so too is there a designation for that effect. This means: when there is a designation for that capacity of color-form and the rest which has a single effect—such as the holding of water—it is a designation for a single capacity. [This occurs] through words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), distinguished from other things such as jars; by the use of the word "etc. (*ādi*), rice (*brīhi*) and so forth are included. It is understood from the context that they are "designated by convention" (*kṛtasamaya*)."

Likewise, with respect to the cause as well, there is a manifold meaning; by means of a single word, that which has been conventionally established is made known—this is the connection [of the sentence] through a shift in the expression, for the sake of linguistic usage alone, with brevity as the purpose. For example, all offspring of a brindled cow (*śabalā*) are denoted by the term *śābaleya* because they share a single cause, and the offspring of a speckled cow (*bahulā*) are denoted by the term *bāhuleya*.

Whatever sound is produced by human effort as its cause is all said to be "immediately following effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*) because it is generated from an identical cause. "Effort" (*prayatna*) is the volition (*cetana*) expressed as "I shall do. That which exists immediately after it, without any interval, is [the object]; the suffix *cha* is applied here because [the root] *grah* belongs to the class of roots beginning with *ākṛtigaṇa*. The inclusion of the word "place" (*deśa*) is not recorded there [in the rule]. The suffix *kan* is added to it for the sake of its own meaning (*svārthika*). And this has been stated with reference to a specific type of cause.

Relying on the mere fact of having a cause, he says: "or produced" (*kṛtaka*). This is because the term "produced" is applied to everything that arises dependent upon causes, including that which follows immediately after effort and all other such things.
Thus far, it has been stated by way of affirmation (*vidhi*).

He states it by way of negation, beginning with "likewise" (*tathā*) and so forth. By the negation of that visual cognition which is the effect of such [objects] as blue and so on—which are visible—sound is "non-visual. It is not the case that visual cognition is incapable; rather, it is expressed generally by the term "non-visual" through such negation. Likewise, the term "impermanent" (*anitya*), when established by the exclusion of the permanent (*nitya*), is also established precisely by the negation of its [the permanent's] effect.

For in this way, others always desire an entity to be eternal; however, such an entity—being neither that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) nor the means of proof (*sādhana*)—does not enter the path of conventional discourse. Therefore, one must accept both the proven and the means of proof. By negating an eternal effect, [the term] "impermanent" [is established]. Furthermore, the word "self" (*ātman*) is sometimes employed to indicate something independent with respect to a certain effect; thus, the word "non-self" (*anātman*) would function by excluding what is not that effect.

Having thus expressed [the point] by way of negating the effect, he speaks by way of negating the cause, beginning with "that" (*tad*) and so forth. The connection is as follows: by negating that which is the cause of this world—which is [otherwise considered] possessed of a master and non-empty—it is proclaimed for the sake of conventional usage that this world, consisting of sound and the rest, is without a master and empty. For indeed, it is maintained by others that [the world] is "possessed of a master" when it is presided over by an independent self (*ātman*) or similar entity.

In this way, even that which is not empty is [said to be] presided over precisely because it is presided over by such [a cause]; and being presided over means the appropriation of that which is to be presided over, for otherwise the state of being a presider would be impossible. Therefore, for others, words such as "having an owner" function by way of a cause. Among entities that perish moment by moment and are dependent solely upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no permanent presiding agent whose dependence causes the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) to proceed.

Therefore, [the states of] having a master and being empty are established by the negation of the causes as previously stated. "In the same way, others too" means that [states such as] suffering, non-emptiness, being without a protector, and being without refuge are also [established]. "According to what is appropriate" means that some are established by the negation of the effect and some by the negation of the cause. This is because, by negating the effects such as suffering and non-emptiness, [the states of] happiness, emptiness, and so forth are established through their nature as having the effect of being non-adverse.

And because everything conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is subject to transformation and is thus adverse [to one's aims], it is "without protector" (*anātha*) and "without refuge" (*apratisharaṇa*). This is because, by negating the effect, there is an absence of an independent protector and so forth. Thus, in this way, the fourfold application of words has been explained by way of affirmation and negation regarding cause and effect.

If it is asked, "But since there is no such thing as 'non-empty' or 'non-eternal' to be excluded, how can words such as 'empty' and so forth express the exclusion of others? he replies: "In whatever manner stated. This means that according to whichever conceptualization based on a philosophical tenet (siddhānta) one adopts, one fashions a desired form for things such as the "empty" or the "eternal"; having conceptually constructed that form and projected it onto the mind, the designation "empty" and so forth is made by way of excluding it—that is, by excluding the forms of "non-empty" and so forth imagined by others.

He asks "Why? and says: "Because of the intellect," and so forth. "The effort of the intellect" is the volition (*saṃkalpa*) [thinking], "I shall superimpose this object. Likewise, that word which possesses such a confusion of everything—that state of being so—is what is meant. By the inclusion of the term "all," he says this: even in the case where there is a real entity... [etc.]

This is what is meant: the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity is neither enjoined nor negated by words in its own form. Rather, the entire conventional practice of affirmation and negation is manifested solely through the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Consequently, in the case of words such as "impermanent," there is no counter-entity such as "permanent" to be excluded; thus, the objection regarding the absence of a counter-entity (*apratipakṣadoṣa*) is merely its presentation or raising [of that point].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author refers to] the objection that there is a fault of non-refutation even when negating [the self] with the statement "there is no self," and so forth; these are the writhings and outpourings—meaning, the incoherent ravings—of the dull-witted such as Uddyotakara and others. For one whose cognition is governed by logic would not bring forward what is incoherent. Therefore, the meaning is that those objections regarding faults are to be disregarded and do not deserve serious attention.

"Then," and so forth, says the opponent. The word *api* (even/also) is displaced [in the compound]. Because of the occurrence (*vṛtti*) of a single entity—a universal—even though it is one, there are multiple distinct individuals (*vyaktibheda*). "A single hearing" (*ekaśruti*) means a single sound; that [single hearing] belongs to this plurality, thus it is "possessing a single hearing. The meaning is: "if it were denotable by a single word. He thinks: "There is no distinction whatsoever, whether [the word is one] because of having a single effect, or because there is a single word for many, or because of a single universal. For this very reason, he explains: "Not only," and so forth.

The very distinction of those [things] from others that do not produce that effect is precisely the non-difference among all those things that do produce that effect; therefore, they are denoted by a single word. Furthermore, what contradiction would there be if many objects were denoted by a single word even through the occurrence of a single universal—that is, by the subsistence of one commonality? Likewise, there is no contradiction in the application of a single word to many things on the basis of their having a single effect, just as there is none when it is based on a real entity (vastubhūta) such as a universal. Thus, the point is that the postulation of a real universal is indeed logical.

The Teacher says: "It has been stated. That universal, which is [supposed to be] a real entity, is intended to be perceived by way of its form (*rūpa*). Since it is intended to be perceived, the state of being perceivable is intended as the instrument (*karaṇa*); thus, the compound is formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. The meaning of the sentence is that the universal does not exist, because it is not perceived apart from the individual (*vyakti*), despite having reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

Or, if non-apprehensibility is accepted, then designations, recognition, and so forth—which are based on the perception of that [universal]—would not occur; that is to say, they would not be based on the perception of a universal. This is how the connection with the word "it has been said" (*uktam*) is to be understood. "Designation" (*vyapadeśa*) is the application of a single term to many things; "recognition" (*pratyabhijñāna*) is a cognition of an identical form. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such points as: "the application [of a word] to individuals would not be based on a universal," and so on.

For a designation and recognition based on perception cannot be applied elsewhere with respect to something that is not itself perceived. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "they would not exist," etc., other previously mentioned faults are also included. For things that are distinct from one another cannot be said to possess those [qualities] if they do not actually have them; likewise, the universal (*jāti*) is not employed for tasks such as carrying or milking, and so on. By this, he states: there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the conceptualization of a universal.

Therefore, designations and the like cannot be based upon that [universal]. However, since there is no contradiction when there is a single effect, it is logical that designations, recognition, and so forth are produced by that very [single effect]. He states another refutation as well: "Moreover" (*api ca*), etc. One who maintains that the universal is a real entity must admit that its occurrence resides in its own single substratum. For it is not logical that something which does not reside in its substratum could be the cause of designations and the like. Furthermore, this occurrence of the universal in its own substratum must either be its being contained (*ādheyatā*) or...

Because it persists by virtue of that [power]. Manifestation (*vyakti*) would be either perception through the power of the substratum (*āśraya*), or it would be its occurrence (*vṛtti*). Neither of these two is tenable in the case of that universal. (144–45)

He explains this with the words "that which is this," and so forth. That which is called "one"—a real entity that is a universal (*sāmānya*) existing in multiple substrates—brings about a single verbal expression (*śruti*). Having raised the question, "What is this mode of existence (*vṛtti*) of that universal in its own substrates? he himself states two alternatives: "being contained" (*ādheyatā*), and so forth. Alternatively, the word "what" (*kim*) is used in the sense of negation; the meaning is: "What is this mode of existence? None at all. For instance, the mode of existence [of a universal] in its own substrates would have to be either being contained (*ādheyatā*), or...

Just as jujube fruits reside in a vessel as their support, so too the manifestation (*vyakti*) must reside in the locus of that universal (*sāmānya*), because the universal is made manifest by those loci. In this regard, if "residing" is intended to mean being contained (*ādheyatā*), then the manifestations must be accepted as its supports. However, since the universal is admitted to be eternal, it cannot be contained prior to the arising of the manifestations; therefore, because an eternal entity cannot be assisted by its supports, the manifestations—despite being considered supports—are not actually the support [of the universal].

He explains by means of the words "nityaṃ hi" and so forth. Now, if permanence is not accepted, then even in the case of impermanence—because of the arising of one after another, that is, the arising of this or that [individual]—the universal would be manifold; and because of its manifoldness, just as there is difference among individuals, it would be impossible for a single cognition to arise with respect to that universal. This is because a single cognition would be impossible. This connects with the statement, "A permanent universal is accepted. Furthermore, what could a substratum do to serve as the support for a permanent universal? The intention is that it could not do anything at all.

It is not an *ādhāra* (substratum) because of providing assistance; rather, it is so called because that universal (*sāmānya*) is inherent (*samavāya*) in that locus (*āśraya*). As Uddyotakara says: "How, then, does 'cowness' (*gotva*) operate among cows? By way of the relationship between the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). But what is this relationship between locus and located? It is inherence (*samavāya*). In that [relationship], cowness is that which possesses occurrence (*vṛttimat*); occurrence is inherence, because it is the cause of the cognition 'here' (*ihapratyaya*). Anticipating the objection that inherence is impossible if there is no relationship of assisted and assister (*upakāryopakāraka*), he says: "What is this... and so forth.

The opponent says: "Not separate," and so forth. Those that are established as being in non-different locations are "inseparably established" (*apṛthaksiddha*). The relationship between support and supported among these is inherence (*samavāya*).

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says "that," and so forth: we do not conceive of this very status of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) for a substratum that provides no assistance. Why? Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If the status of being a substratum were accepted for that which provides no assistance, then everything would be the substratum of everything. If it is argued: "It does not happen [that everything is the substratum of everything] because everything is perceived as not inhering (*asamaveta*) in everything," [we reply: even in the absence of assistance, just like "cowness" (*gotva*), everything would indeed inhere in everything; thus, there would be no perception [of a specific thing] from a single [substratum]. This is precisely what is being challenged.

Now, this relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*) is distinct from the relation of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) and so forth. And since that [inherence] does not exist everywhere, how could there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? It is replied: True; however, inherence occurs only for that which is inherent in something else. And being inherent in that [substratum] consists in dependence upon it. Furthermore, for a distinct entity, dependence upon that [substratum] is nothing other than its arising from it. Therefore, in the case of the cognition "here" (*iha*), the basis is precisely arising in a state of being situated above one another, and not inherence; thus, the argument based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted. [Otherwise,] if [the cognition "here"] were to occur even when there is no state of being situated above one another...
Nor does inherence exist for those things that are not already inherent, because if it did, it would follow that everything would be inherent in everything.
