Summarizing, he says: "Therefore," and so forth. *Inherence* (*samavāya*) belongs to two things that are not established separately, such as between the produced and the producer substances; *conjunction* (*saṃyoga*) belongs to things that are established separately, such as fire and smoke; *inherence in a single object* (*ekārthasamavāya*) is, for example, the inherence of color and taste in a single substance. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the relation of "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamaveta*) is included. The compound "real relations of things" (*vastubhūtāḥ sambandhāḥ*) is either a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) or a genitive determinative compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

The inclusion of the term "entity" (*vastu*) is for the purpose of excluding what is constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*). They do not differ from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), nor do they exist otherwise. Proving this very point, he says: "mutually," and so forth. Because there is no dependence—due to the lack of obstruction among things that mutually assist one another, or among those that do not assist one another, such as those considered to be the substratum—and because there is no connection for that which is unobstructed, all connections between entities do not differ from the causal relation; this is the connection with the subject at hand.

But surely, if assistance is provided by means of the substratum, there can be no mutual relationship of helper and helped between the two things supported; so for what purpose is the phrase "or from another" introduced?

This is true; however, even if there is no direct mutual assistance between them, the proposal is made that one might nevertheless postulate a connection through a mediated succession (*pāram paryeṇa*) by virtue of their dependence upon a single cause. If it is argued that a relationship of mutual assistance is not at all accepted between things inhering in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*), he replies with the words "even if," and so forth. For, in the absence of such assistance from that single substratum, the aforementioned logical fault would necessarily follow.

The fault has already been stated [by the opponent] as being due to the fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, since there is necessarily a mutual benefit between two things inherent in the same substrate (*ekārthasamavāyin*) by virtue of their own substrate, the proponent explains—having connected the second inherent thing through that very means of "self-benefit" (i.e., the benefit to itself produced by its own substrate)—that the two inherent things are "connected. Thus he says: "the two inherent things are related."

This is what is meant: just as for another [school], there is a connection between two things inhering in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*) even though they are not mutually connected, by virtue of their inherence in that single object; so too for us, there is a connection between those two by virtue of having a single effect (*ekakāryatva*). Since this is so, therefore even in that case of inherence in the same object, the connection with the substratum (*āśraya*) is produced solely by the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); it is precisely through that causal relation which exists with the substratum that the connection is projected. For the status of being a substratum (*ādhāra*) and so forth occurs only by way of assistance (*upakāra*).

Therefore, this substratum, such as a brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*), does not assist the universal by means of its own nature; thus, to call it the "substratum" of the independent universal is a borrowed ornament (*yācitakamaṇḍana*). An ornament (*maṇḍana*) is a decoration, so called because one is decorated by it. This forms a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word "borrowed": an ornament that is borrowed from another, which does not exist in the self of a poor man. In the same way, the status of being a substratum for the universal belongs to the substratum of the universal only in relation to something else.

Alternatively, [the compound] is an instrumental tatpuruṣa expressing a state (*bhāvasādhana*). Just as there is an act of adorning with borrowed ornaments, so too the designation of a substratum for that which relies upon a universal occurs through a state of being a support requested from another, and not by way of actual reality, because there is no benefit [to the universal] from that [substratum].

The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. For a bowl is not the producer of jujube fruits, since they are produced solely from their own causes. Consequently, he considers the statement—"In all cases, relations between entities do not differ from the relation of cause and effect"—to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding a jujube fruit (*badara*) or the like that is in the process of moving—that is, having the nature of migrating to another location—its production in that specific place occurs in the very same location where its preceding material cause (*upādāna*), characterized as a jujube fruit, was situated and connected with the bowl (*kuṇḍa*); this is because it does not move elsewhere. This is the capacity [of the support] belonging to the bowl and other such things considered to be supports, with respect to the jujube fruits and others considered to be supported.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with *prakṛtyaiva*. That which is "unequal in space" (*asamānadeśa*) by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), that is, by its own essence (*svabhāvenaiva*), is described as such. Even though it depends on the word *prakṛti*, it forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound because it is expressive [of its meaning]. Furthermore, the term *tathābhūta-tat-kārya* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is such and is an effect. And the "effect" (*kārya*) is precisely the jujube fruit (*badara*) and so forth, as comprised within successive moments. The production (*utpādana*) of that [effect] is the property (*dharma*), that is, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*), of the heavy substance—the jujube fruit and so forth—as comprised within the preceding moment.

The state of producing an effect in the same location is caused by the support (*ādhāra*). The meaning is that the capacity to produce [an effect] in a location identical to one's own is produced by the support. Since this is so, therefore, the bowl (*kuṇḍa*) is the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) for that preceding moment which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the effect, namely the jujube fruit (*badara*); because it produces the effect of the jujube fruit in that very location of the material cause-moment, the bowl is called the "support."

By this, it is stated that there is no relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) between the bowl and the jujube fruits, both of which depend upon a single complex of causes (*sāmagrī*). Otherwise, if the aforementioned assistance were not rendered by the bowl to the jujube fruits, there would be no such designation as "the jujube fruits are here in the bowl. For a designation restricted to a specific locus is impossible without a cause. This designation—"the jujube fruits are here in the bowl"—is produced by the assistance rendered by the locus; rather, it is produced by the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the bowl and the jujube fruits.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) asks, "How then," and so forth. The intention of the questioner is this: you maintain that conjunction and the like are postulated [as causes] only when there is momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). If, however, the non-momentariness of entities is admitted, then the very production of conjunction and the like would not occur; such is the meaning. Furthermore, the intention is that even the designation "the conjunction of the bowl and the jujube fruit" lacks a basis for its application, because there is an absence of the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakatva*) between those two.

"By those two," and so forth, says the opponent. Because conjunction is produced by those two—the bowl and the jujube fruit—conjunction is held to belong to them. Since the production of conjunction occurs by both [factors], its inherence (*samavāya*) is in both places. Having considered what was stated by the opponent, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "That," and so forth. Why does that conjunction not inhere, or why is it not produced, in one place alone—either in the bowl or in the jujube fruit?

When one asks by means of a bowl (*kuṇḍa*) or a jujube fruit (*badara*), this is the intended meaning: if those two things called the bowl and the jujube fruit are each individually capable of producing a conjunction or of attaining the state of being a substratum, then why do they depend upon one another? If it is argued that "those two have separate purposes and are only capable when joined with each other," he says: "That," and so forth.

The point is this: that entity consisting of the bowl and the jujube fruit, which is individually incapable, remains just as incapable even when joined together, because it is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*). However, momentary things, though individually incapable, become capable when combined after having acquired specific qualities through auxiliary causes; thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, since the entity called the "bowl and jujube" does not provide any assistance toward conjunction, it cannot possess conjunction as its property.

The opponent says: "Of the conjoined," and so forth. Because of the assistance rendered by each to the other—namely, because of the assistance to the pit (*kuṇḍa*) from whatever constitutes the nature of the jujube fruit (*badara*), or because of the assistance to the jujube fruit from whatever is other than that, namely the pit—the capacity for the production of conjunction between the pit and the jujube fruit, or for the attainment of the state of being a substratum, does not belong to the two individually. Rather, it belongs to them when they are together.

The teacher asks: "What is this assistance? [He means: What is this assistance between the jujube fruits (*badara*) and the bowl (*kuṇḍa*), which stand in the relationship of non-produced and producer? There is none at all. If one asks, "How is it that they are precisely non-produced and non-producers? he says: "Because of their own nature," and so forth. The point is that since the nature of the jujube fruit is established from its own cause alone, it is not an effect; therefore, the jujube fruits have no status as produced, nor does the bowl have the status of a producer. For the opponent does not maintain that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the jujube fruits and the like arises from the bowl and the like.

Because they are produced from their own causes alone. It is not that the form of the jujube fruit (*badara*) is produced by the bowl (*kuṇḍa*); rather, it is a form other than that [of the bowl]. Therefore, he says: "by another form," and so forth. Therein, "there" refers to the substrate (*ādheya*). For if one thing were produced, another thing would not be assisted. By the phrase "for both purposes," [it is meant] through the production of its own nature and the nature of another. According to the method just mentioned, that which does not provide assistance—such as the bowl—is ineffective (*akiñcitkara*).

And this has already been mostly stated. The word *prāya* signifies abundance. That which is stated for the most part is *uktaprāya*. Because the group beginning with *rājadanta* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), there is the posterior placement of the word *prāya*. And this meaning has been explained in detail in such passages as: "And their function is attained when they assist in the act of production" (1.108). Others say that the word *prāya* has the sense of similarity; thus, *uktaprāya* means similar to what has been stated.

The meaning is that this assistance rendered by the receptacle, such as a bowl, to the contained object is equal to the assistance to the nature of the universal provided by its substrate, as previously described. The conclusion is given with the words "all indeed," and so forth: the connection is that all real relations are established on the basis of the cause known as the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). If it is argued that there would be no distinction among them, he says: "of the producer alone," and so forth.

Or rather, they are established through a distinction—that is, a differentiation—from the relationship of cause and effect. To explain how there is this distinction, he says: "Of the producer alone," and so forth. The meaning is: by virtue of that specific assistance which the effect receives from the cause. For instance, in the case of jujube fruits (*badara*) and the like, which possess the property of spreading out, there exists a relationship of support and supported (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) through the utility consisting in their being produced in the location of their own material causes (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, because the lamp produces a nature capable of generating cognition, there is between the jar, the lamp, and so forth, a relationship characterized as that of the manifested and the manifestor; in this same way, the relationship should be stated accordingly for other cases as well.

Now, [it may be argued] that by the statement "all relations are indeed relations between real entities" and so forth, a relation characterized as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not included within the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), because this [conjunction] exists only for things that arise at the same time. Furthermore, if one holds the position of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇika*), the production of conjunction is not logical; however, in the case of momentary things, it will be possible. Moreover, no difference in their own nature is perceived between the states of being conjoined and not conjoined in the cases of a bowl and a jujube fruit. Therefore, even in the case of non-momentary things, conjunction certainly exists, because it is perceived.

As Uddyotakara says: "If conjunction were not a distinct entity (arthāntara), then since the field, seed, water, and so forth would be indistinguishable [from one another], they would always produce effects such as sprouts; yet this is not the case. Therefore, because the effect is not produced at all times, the field and other factors depend upon another cause for the production of the sprout. Just as the causal complex consisting of the lump of clay and so forth depends upon the potter and others for the making of a jar, that which is independent of the field and other factors is established as conjunction."

Furthermore, this conjunction, because it is perceived as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*) between two substances, is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddha*) as being a distinct entity from them. For instance, when someone is told by another, "Bring those two substances that are conjoined," he brings only those two substances in which he perceives the conjunction; he does not bring the mere substance.

Furthermore, for a person standing at a great distance, this cognition—which perceives even a forest with gaps as being continuous—arises as a false cognition (*mithyābuddhi*). A false cognition never arises without the experience of a primary object (*mukhyapadārtha*); for instance, one who has never experienced the sight of a cow does not have the delusion that a *gavaya* is a cow. Therefore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) must necessarily be accepted as the primary [basis].

Likewise, by this prohibitive statement "Caitra is not wearing earrings," it is not the earring that is prohibited, because it exists elsewhere, such as in another location. Therefore, what is prohibited is Caitra’s conjunction with the earring. Similarly, by the affirmative statement "Caitra is wearing earrings" as well, neither Caitra nor the earring is being affirmed, since both are already established. By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is the conjunction that is affirmed. Therefore, conjunction certainly exists. (Nyāyavārttika, fn. 1)

To this it is replied: (1) Just as it is accepted that the auditory organ and other sense faculties initiate conjunction by attaining a specific state, why is it not likewise accepted that they initiate an effect even without conjunction? Otherwise, they would always be initiating conjunction. (2) Furthermore, when a substance in conjunction is apprehended in its own form by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), a third conjunction does not appear [to consciousness].

(3) Furthermore, in a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), no conjunction other than the word "conjunction" appears as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) apart from the two substances that are conjoined. (4) Nor can conjunction be postulated on the grounds that the cognition of being conjoined would otherwise be inexplicable; for it is precisely the two entities existing in a state of immediate proximity (*nirantara-avasthā*) once they have arisen that serve as the cause for the cognition of being conjoined.

Furthermore, as long as those two are accepted as being the objects of the cognition "conjoined" by virtue of producing conjunction in that state, why are they not accepted as the causes of the cognition "conjoined" and its objects even in the absence of conjunction? Why resort to such indirectness? Nor is the cognition appearing as continuous with respect to a forest that has gaps preceded by the experience of primary entities, because it is non-metaphorical due to being the object of a non-erroneous cognition.

(6) Likewise, in cases such as "Caitra is not wearing earrings," it is neither the earring related to Caitra that is negated nor affirmed; rather, it is the conjunction [that is negated]. Therefore, the cognition that "these two are conjoined" arises only with respect to two things dependent upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*), just as in the case of a bowl and a date fruit. Consequently, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also included within the very relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). It is merely by excluding other differences that there arises the cognition "these two are conjoined" or "of these two there is conjunction," but not by virtue of a conjunction existing as a real entity (*vastubhūta*). And since there is no real relationship apart from the relation of cause and effect, [conjunction is not a separate category].

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadayam" (then this, etc.): the connection is that for things such as jujube fruits (*badara*), the very power of production (*jananaśakti*) is the substratum (*ādhāra*) of the bowl (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth. If it is argued that the substratum of the universal (*sāmānya*) may likewise be the substratum by means of the power of production alone, he says: "no," and so forth. "When there is the power of production" (*sati jananaśaktiḥ*); "here" (*atra*) refers to the universal.

He explains this with the words beginning "na hi" (for not). "Arising in the very location of its own material cause" is the specific mode of arising; that which has this as its characteristic is the state of being a substratum (*ādhārabhāva*). [The phrase] "because it is unproduced" means that because the universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal, it is unproduced. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of that": even in the absence of a substratum, since the universal remains, the persistence of the universal does not depend upon a substratum.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "atha" and so forth. "Of that" means of the universal (*sāmānya*). "Even in its absence" means even in the absence of the individual (*vyakti*); that is, because the universal persists in a location devoid of individuals. For if the universal did not exist in a location devoid of individuals, then when a new individual arises there, it could not have a connection with the universal. Indeed, it cannot come from elsewhere because it is inactive (*niṣkriyatva*). Nor can an individual situated in a different location be the substratum (*ādhāra*) of that universal, because they occupy different locations.

If it is argued that because the universal is one, there can be no existence in different locations, then it follows that all individuals possessing a single genus would occupy the same location; nor could all [individuals] possess that genus. If it is asked how a single entity can be situated in different locations, let this be another fault of yours.

With the words "having the nature of falling," etc., he states the reason for accumulation; the word *hi* has the sense of *ca* (and). The word *api* is intended to indicate an admission (*abhyupagama*). Even if this mode [of action] were admitted, it could not be established in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*), because a universal does not have the nature of falling; it is for this purpose that the statement is introduced. However, it is not possible for that which is not a producer to be a sustainer. For this very reason, he says: "In this case too," and so forth.

Even here, if one who speaks according to reason (*nyāyavādī*) were not to inquire into the prevention of falling when a "supporter" (*sthāpaka*) is postulated on the grounds that it prevents falling, then even a non-producer (*ajanaka*) might be considered a supporter. This is the underlying intention: [that such a claim would hold] merely in accordance with one's own system (*svasamaya*). However, even in this case, the following critical inquiry (*paryanuyoga*) is possible: Is the prevention of falling produced by the supporter identical to the supported object, or is it a separate entity (*arthāntara*) from it, or is it the mere absence of falling?

It is not, first of all, identical [to the support], because its own nature is admitted to be produced from something else; nor is it a different entity. Thus he says: "If a difference in entity were admitted, then the utility of this support would consist in providing a connection (*pratibandha*) for that which has become a different entity. What, then, is the connection—the obstruction—of a falling jujube fruit or the like? None at all. And consequently, even a jujube fruit situated in a bowl or similar vessel would surely fall; such is the sense."

If it is argued that the non-falling of the jujube fruit (*badara*) and so forth is brought about by a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) produced by the support, namely, the prevention of falling, he replies: "Even if there is no falling due to prevention," and so on. When a distinct entity called "prevention" is accepted as the cause for the non-falling of the jujube fruit and so forth, the same objection applies. Is this non-falling produced by the entity called "prevention" something identical to the nature of the jujube fruit, or is it a distinct entity? If it were a distinct entity, then the utility of this "prevention" would reside in that very [distinct entity] alone; all of this is equal to what was stated immediately above.

If it is argued that the non-falling of the jujube fruit and so forth is also brought about by that very object called "non-falling," then the same objection applies there as well; thus he says: "And there would be an infinite regress."

The presentation of the third position begins with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth. How, or by whom, could that absence of falling (*pātābhāva*) be produced? By no one at all; the point is that absence is not an effect (*akāryatvāt*). If it is asked how there can then be the designation "he produces an absence," he says: "An absence" and so forth. In the designation "he produces an absence," no such thing as an absence is intended to be an effect. Why? He says: "Of that" and so forth.
The intention is that because that [absence] would be an effect, it would necessarily be a positive entity (*bhāva*).

If it is argued: "Just as a cloth does not have the nature of a jar because it is an effect like a jar, so too non-existence will not have the nature of non-existence because it is an effect like an entity," [we reply: No. For even a jar and the like possess the nature of an entity precisely because they have the property of coming into being (*bhavana*). If it is argued that since non-existence is not [an entity] that exists, how could it not have the nature of an entity? [We reply: No, because non-existence does not appear [as an object]. If it is argued that it does not have the nature of an entity because it appears as having the nature of non-existence, [we reply: No, because there is no appearance of non-existence.

It has been stated that because non-existences are perceived as mutually distinct—as in "the absence of a jar" and "the absence of a cloth"—there is a difference between the cloth and so forth, and not because non-existences appear as a single unity. Since this is so, the expression "he produces non-existence" (abhāvaṃ karoti) is an instruction for the negation of that action which belongs to an existent entity (bhāva).

For this very reason, he clarifies: "it does not produce an entity," meaning that whatever is the meaning of this statement, that same [meaning] applies to the statement "it produces non-existence. And "likewise" means that since the prevention of falling is merely a non-entity, it is not something produced. "This" refers to the bowl or similar vessel. "By that cause" refers to the jujube fruit or similar object; it is obstructed by some support such as a bowl. If it were not prevented from falling, it would never remain stationary; the meaning is that it would fall at all times.

The conclusion is stated with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth. By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that even by this designation "the supported," what is meant is the production of an effect—comprised within a subsequent moment—in the same location as its cause, which is comprised within a preceding moment, for things that are momentary. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that this mode [of support] is also impossible in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*), this was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's view]: that even that which does not produce [an effect] may be called a "supporter" (*sthāpaka*) because it prevents falling.

To demonstrate that very impossibility, he says: "Let it be so," and so forth. Let there be, for falling objects such as jujube fruits, a prevention of that [falling], namely a prevention of falling, which consists in their having a nature of non-arising. Because of performing that—that is, because of performing the prevention of falling—how could a substratum be a sustainer by producing a "stasis" (sthiti) characterized by what for a moving substance, i.e., for that which possesses activity, whereas a universal, moreover, being incorporeal, is inactive?

For a universal has no "falling" by which its connection [with its substratum] could constitute its stability. Rather, the stability of that universal is said to be simply its non-deviation from its own nature (*svarūpa*). And that non-deviation from its own nature does not depend on a substratum, because the universal is eternal. Even granting [for the sake of argument] that it does depend, it is stated: even that stability of the universal depending on a substratum is indeed illogical, when one analyzes whether that stability is different or non-different from the universal—that is, when the investigation into its being other or not other is carried out.

He explains with the words “let it be so,” and so forth. “Dependent on the substratum” (*āśrayahetukā*) means reliant upon the substratum. “It” refers to persistence (*sthiti*). That substratum produces that very persistence as something distinct from itself, not the universal (*sāmānya*). Since that persistence is tied to the universal, the universal is indeed benefited through this connection; therefore, he says “and that,” and so forth. “That” refers to the persistence which has become a separate entity. For there is no cause whatsoever for its connection to the universal; [the question] “what is accomplished by the substratum for the universal? is to be supplied.

If it is argued that a causal connection (*pratibandha*) is indeed admitted for the persistence (*sthiti*) of the universal (*sāmānya*), he replies: “And if there is a causal connection,” and so forth. That is, if a causal connection is admitted, and if there is the production of persistence—meaning that the persistence produced by the substratum (*āśraya*) is itself made to persist by the universal—then that persistence produced by the substratum would be connected to the universal. In that case as well, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) applies regarding the production of the persistence of that persistence.

That which is performed as a general maintenance for the maintenance that is bound to its basis must either be identical with or distinct from the maintenance whose cause is the basis. If it were identical, since that [maintenance] would already have been performed by the basis itself, how could it be performed generally? And if it were distinct, then that very same maintenance being performed generally—what would be performed generally for the first maintenance produced by the basis? Or, if a second maintenance is performed generally...

That [subsistence] is bound to the subsistence produced by the substratum. Then it must be stated: what is that binding? Since another third subsistence would arise from the subsistence produced by the substratum—which itself is produced by the general property—this leads to the same consequence, and thus there would be an infinite regress.

Therefore, because there would be an infinite regress, and because the assistance rendered by the universal toward the subsistence produced by the substratum cannot be determined, there is no cognition that "this subsistence produced by the substratum belongs to this universal. As for the point under discussion—that production constitutes the connection—it is not the case that another subsistence is produced by the universal for the subsistence already produced by the substratum; rather, it is that very first subsistence which is produced.

In that case, let the universal alone be capable of effecting its own persistence; what is the use of a substratum such as a *śāvaleyā* (a brindled cow), which would be required for the sake of maintaining it? For dependence upon that which provides no assistance is not logical. Thus, "dependence" indeed means a connection (*pratibandha*). When one says "there is dependence of this [entity] upon this thing," that dependence is a connection with the object of dependence, meaning its being contingent upon that. And since such a connection is impossible for that which is eternal and incapable of having any excellence added to it, the universal exists alone.

The sense is this: since one would have to produce its persistence, there can be no substratum that serves as the cause of that persistence; therefore, the claim that the substratum is the support of the universal because it effects its persistence is untenable. Thus, regarding the aforementioned analysis of difference and non-difference, the position of difference has first been set aside.

Relying on the second position, he says: "In the absence of difference," and so forth. If it is accepted that [the individual] exists without being distinct from the universal (*sāmānya*), then the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the universal would be the form of its existence. And since that nature of the universal exists eternally, the existence of this universal is not brought about by any substratum (*āśraya*). Because it is thus, [he says] "therefore," and so forth. The conclusion is expressed by "that," and so forth; "that" means "therefore," and "of this" refers to the universal.

Thus, regarding the two positions stated—namely, that "subsistence" (*vṛtti*), "being supported" (*ādheyatā*), or "manifestation" (*vyakti*) [is the relation]—the refutation of the first has been completed.

2—Relying on the second position, he says: "Now, however," and so forth. "Of the unmanifest" means of that which is not yet revealed. Regarding "manifestation": since cognition is not the cause [of the object's manifestation], the manifestation of that [object] by means of its substratum—that is precisely what would constitute the existence (*vṛtti*) of the universal (*sāmānya*) in that substratum. (146–47)

"No," says the Teacher. The production of cognition with respect to its own object, the self, is the capacity [of that object] therein; this capacity is common [to all objects], and for that purpose, it conforms to others. That which depends on other causes and is perceived as being manifested—let that be the case. And that which is the cause of this capacity to generate cognition of its own object, such as a lamp and so forth, is indeed a *kāraka* (productive cause) of the manifested object, precisely because it brings about the production of a jar or the like, which was previously incapable but subsequently becomes capable of generating cognition.

If, however, a jar or similar object were already capable of producing a cognition of its own form even prior to the proximity of a lamp or other such factors, then, since this jar and so forth would have been capable from the very beginning, its dependence on them—namely, its dependence on the lamp—would be pointless. This is because a universal is eternal and thus unchangeable. The meaning of "that" is as follows: why is it that the aforementioned characteristic of being manifested does not arise at all from the substratum (*āśraya*) which possesses the universal? As for the term "another," it refers to that which is called a "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*) when it produces only a state of being that is distinct from its own continuum.

What is it that, being real, is capable of producing a cognition of its own object, depending upon a homogeneous material cause—that is, depending upon a preceding moment included within its own continuum? For example, a light is an illuminator because, while depending upon a preceding moment of a jar or similar object situated in darkness, it produces a subsequent moment of the jar that is capable of generating a cognition.

If it is argued that, since the jar is an effect of the lamp, there would also be an increase of the jar upon the increase of the lamp, we say: no. For the difference in the effect arises from a difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), not from a difference in the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*). And since the lamp and so forth are merely auxiliary causes for the jar, which is the manifested object (*vyaṅgya*), how could there be the consequence that the jar possesses largeness and so on? Alternatively, this objection applies equally even if manifestation itself were being produced; therefore, this [argument] is trivial.

Furthermore, a moment similar to the moment of the manifested [sound] does not arise from a lump of clay, but rather from something such as a lamp; how then could there be the production of such [a sound] from something of a different nature? And regarding the term "independent" (*anapekṣa*): for example, an impact produces a sound that is capable of generating a cognition of its own object while depending on a homogeneous material cause (*upādāna*). For prior to the impact, the sound does not exist, such that the sound would have to depend on a homogeneous [cause]. Indeed, it has been stated thus because others maintain that sound is also something to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*).

If, then, the manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*) is indeed the same as the producing agent (*kāraka*), what then is the distinction between the causes that are producers and those that are manifesters? To this he says: "In another case," and so forth. The meaning is: in something other than the manifesting agent, which is intended to be a producer. The capacity to generate cognition is not implied for the produced effect. For an effect is not produced by a producer—such as a seed or the like—merely as something capable of generating a consciousness of its own object. Therefore, being a producer consists merely in the act of generation, whereas being a manifester is defined by the specific quality of producing an effect capable of generating a consciousness of its own object. (147–48)

If it is argued that although the manifested object acquires the capacity to produce a cognition from the manifesting agent, it is nevertheless not produced [by it], the author replies with the words "yadi hi" and so forth. "Yataḥ" means from the manifesting agent. "Sa cet" refers to the manifested object. "Tasya" refers to the manifesting agent; that capacity already exists in this manifested object even prior to the proximity of the manifesting agent, because that capacity is of the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the manifested object. Just as the manifested object exists even prior [to manifestation], so too does the capacity that constitutes its nature exist.

That which depends upon it is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*). If it is argued that the manifestor produces a capacity (*yogyatā*) that is distinct from the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), he says "the other," and so forth. "In this" refers to the capacity. That very [capacity] is what is produced. "From that" means from the manifestor; there would be the consequence of its being permanent, just like the object itself. What was stated—namely, "if it were something else, the substratum would produce that very thing," and so forth—that would also apply here. "It" refers to the manifested.

Nor is [the cause] something other than the manifested (vyaṅgya); for since nothing at all is produced in the manifested when that [cause] acts, it is not required [by it]. By this, its status as a benefactor (upakāritva) is stated. Therefore, the denial of that [status] on the grounds of its being "inefficacious" (akiṃcitkaratva) is contradictory.

Regarding what was stated—that the producer itself is the manifester—he points out its fallibility with the words "that very thing" (*tat tu*) and so forth: for smoke is not the producer of fire, yet because it is an effect, it is its manifester; by the word "etcetera," [he includes] light and so forth as the manifester of water. He refutes this with the words "True" (*satyam*) and so forth: fire does not, however, depend upon the mark (*liṅga*) of smoke to produce a cognition of itself in its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why? Because such fire, which is intended as the object of inference, is not a direct producer [of that cognition].

Otherwise, because it would have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire as its form, there would be no distinction from the manifestation [of perception]. By the words "only," etc., he demonstrates that the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) alone is its direct producer. The cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the material cause; it is not by the force of the object—that is, by the force of the specific characteristic of fire. Why? Because even when that fire is absent, the cognition of fire occurs due to its existence in the past. How so? He says: "by way of a succession," and so forth.

"Following the mark" (*liṅgānusārī*) refers to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that recollects the mark; by means of this. For instance, when a certain person has seen smoke in a particular place, and subsequently, while both the smoke and the fire are present, a conceptual construction recollecting the smoke arises there in some way, then—following the recollection of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—the thought occurs: "There was smoke here, therefore there was also fire here. Thus, through this sequence, the cognition of fire indeed arises from the smoke produced by fire.

With the words "nor indeed" (*nāpi*) and so forth, he applies what was stated previously to this very point: inferential cognition manifests in a general form (*sāmānyākāra*), and it does not have a proximate object as its domain. For it is possible even when the object has perished or has not yet arisen; and even when the object is present, it has already been explained previously—starting with the passage "for conceptual constructions do not operate exactly according to the way things are"—that its production does not occur by the power of the object.

And because there is no prescription of existence or non-existence, it will be established in the third chapter by means of [the arguments] beginning with "by capacity," "by appearance," and so forth. "By direct utility" means by the capacity to produce a cognition that conforms to its own form (*svarūpa*). "Therein" refers to the production of the cognition of its own object. "Another" refers to [an object] such as a lamp. "From that" refers to the dependence upon the lamp and so forth.

This is what is meant: not every manifestor is called a producer; rather, it is only that which renders assistance to another thing that produces a cognition having its own form. Therefore, there is no deviation [in the definition]. A universal (*sāmānya*) is also accepted as being manifested because it depends upon a basis for the production of a cognition having its own form. Consequently, by means of that basis, its own nature must be obtained as something capable of being perceived. However, this acquisition of its own nature is not possible for a universal from anything whatsoever, because it is accepted as being eternal. "That" refers to the universal.

The opponent says, "Not so," and so forth. The connection is: "We speak of the manifestation of the inherence in its own substratum. If it is asked how inherence in its own substratum can be a manifestation, he replies with the words beginning "svāśraya" (its own substratum). "Tat" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*). "Anyatra" means in its own substratum.

The Teacher says: "This has already been stated," because it was said in the passage beginning, "We do not conceive of this very thing—being a substratum for that which provides no assistance. For one who asserts that [the universal] is the cause of cognition when it is inherent in its own substratum, whether in itself or elsewhere, accepts that the category of the universal is the cause of cognition in dependence upon its inherence in its own substratum. Consequently, by means of that inherence in its own substratum, the universal would be produced in the cognized object.

What is the reason? Because that cause—the nature which is the cause of cognition—exists prior to its inherence in its own substratum; and because, once there is inherence in its own substratum, that nature which is the cause of cognition exists subsequently due to that very inherence in its own substratum. If it is argued that this [reason] is unestablished because a universal has the nature of producing cognition eternally, he says: "Eternally," and so forth.

The phrase "the existence of its own nature" means that even prior to its inherence in its own substratum (*svāśraya*), from the universal (*sāmānya*) alone—namely, from that which has the nature of producing cognition—even in a location devoid of manifestation, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the arising of a cognition having the form of the universal.

"No," says the opponent. Manifestation (*vyakti*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the universal; "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) is the imparting of capacity (*yogyatādhāna*). For that reason, [manifestation] is not the manifester (*vyañjikā*) of the universal, such that the universal would be produced by it. Rather, what is meant is that it is the manifester through the refinement of that which grasps it—that is, through the refinement of that which perceives the universal. This is the context.

The teacher begins with the words "And whoever... and so forth. The phrase "like collyrium and the like" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Just as the refinement of the sense organ is appropriate from the side of collyrium and the like, it is not so from the side of manifestation (*vyakti*). Why? Because this is a locative dual ending referring to the two times—existence and non-existence—of the manifestation that is intended to be the manifester of cognition, which is to say, of knowledge.

He explains [the verse] with the words "saṃskṛtam" and so forth. An organ that has been refined by means of collyrium and other such substances attains a certain excellence (*atiśaya*) as its own nature. "In perception" (*pratipattau*) means for the sake of the cause of perception; that is to say, for the purpose of producing a distinguished cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*). The locative case here is according to the rule *nimittāt karmasaṃyoge*. If one asks, "Why is this so?", he says: "clearly" (*spaṣṭa*) and so forth. The connection is made by changing the case-ending of the word "perception" (*pratipatteḥ*).

For instance, a sense faculty impaired by cataracts or similar conditions produces an indistinct cognition; that very same faculty, when refined by collyrium or other means, is perceived clearly. Thus, the refined sense faculty attains a superior capacity for the sake of comprehension.

Now, if there were no difference in cognition arising from [the application of] collyrium and the like, then—since those things which do not produce it (collyrium, etc. do not produce a difference in cognition—they would not be its refiners (*saṃskāraka*), because they do not refine the sense faculty. Just as there is no refinement of the sense faculty from collyrium and the like, so too there is none from manifestation. What is the reason? It is because of the phrase "at the times of its presence and absence," and so forth.

For instance, at a time when the manifesting cow-individual is absent, the visual consciousness that arises with respect to a tree or the like is exactly the same even when that cow-individual is absent. If, during the period of its absence, a previously unclear cognition had arisen regarding trees and so forth, and it were subsequently understood that this was due to a sensory refinement (*indriyasaṃskāra*) produced by the cow-individual; [then it would follow that the cow-individual exists].

If it is argued that even when there is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of one object, there is no difference in the cognition of another object, and therefore that [refinement of the sense organ] is also not logical—the author says: "The object," and so forth. Whatever refinement there may be of an object such as odor by some means, even though there is no distinction in the sense organ itself regarding the cognition of other objects, nevertheless, it would be beneficial because it provides a distinction to that cognition which apprehends the refined object, by imparting a specific quality to it.
The connection is that the refinement of the sense organ itself would not be beneficial.

This is what is meant: objects are indeed restricted; they serve as the means for producing a cognition that possesses only their own form, not one endowed with another form. Therefore, because the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of an object is restricted, it does not contradict [the principle] by producing a distinct apprehension only of its own object. The sense faculty, however, is an equal means of production regarding all the various objects it perceives; consequently, its refinement would result in a differentiator of the apprehension across all those objects it perceives.

It is not the case that the individuality of the particular (*vyakti*) itself deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the sense organ for the sake of producing a cognition with a clear form regarding every visible object perceivable by that organ. Rather, if it is argued that the individuality of the particular is beneficial because it bestows the power of vision upon the sense organ toward the universal (*sāmānya*), which was previously invisible prior to the arising of the particular—then, precisely from the perception of that which is beyond the senses, the latent impression of the sense organ is clearly understood.

That which was previously incapable due to the absence of a particular individual, but later becomes capable upon the presence of that [individual], demonstrates a distinction between individuals—an object called "universal" (*sāmānya*) that is beyond the senses. How then could it not be a differentiator in every case of cognition? The meaning is that it is indeed a differentiator.

This is what is meant: even in the case of a visible object that is initially unclear, an embellishment of the sense organ—such as that produced by medicinal ointment—is observed to differentiate the cognition regarding every object graspable by that sense organ, by bestowing the capacity to perceive it with a clear form. How much more so, then, [should this apply] to one who reveals a supersensible object; for in that case, he would likewise reveal other supersensible things, such as atoms. This is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that a particular individual (vyakti-bheda) effects a refinement of the sense faculty for the very purpose of perceiving the universal, and therefore there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga), the author replies with the words beginning "In one," etc. If a restriction regarding the refinement of the sense faculty is accepted when a single universal is to be perceived, then the refinement of the sense faculty would not be the revealer of other universals—such as existence (sattā), substantiality (dravyatva), and so forth—which are inherent in that very same particular individual, such as a brindled cow (śābaleya). Yet, such revelation is indeed desired.

If it is argued that the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is for the sake of perceiving all universals (*sāmānya*) inherent in the individual (*vyakti*), and not for the sake of a single one alone, he says: "And by the individual," and so forth. "In the perception of those" means in the perception of those universals inherent in the individual. "Manifested by that" means manifested by that individual. And it is observed that when a mere substance is seen from a distance, even though there is certainty regarding "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and "object-ness" (*arthatva*), there is no certainty regarding "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like.

If it is argued that "the differentiation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) is not intended for the perception of that in which there is no certainty," he replies: "Or, there would be certainty of one [thing] alone"—the connection being that this would not be the case. The word "one" (*eka*) has the sense of "other"; thus, there would be no certainty even of another thing intended as certain, such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth. What is the reason? Because that individual manifestation (*vyakti*) is non-differentiated, there is no distinction among those universals (*sāmānya*) inherent in its own nature. For that manifestation is not proximate to some and not to others.

Therefore, it has been explained that the refinement of the sense organ by means of an individual instance is not tenable, whether that instance is determined as being universal or as belonging to nothing at all.

Now, even granting [the opponent's position], it is said: "From the manifestation," and so forth. Since, according to both positions, the universal has the nature of producing cognition by virtue of the manifestation, it follows that because of its departure from that nature of producing cognition, it is not logical for that which is capable to depend upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). That universal whose auxiliary cause is the conditioned sense faculty is described as such; the state of being that is what is meant [by the compound].
Because the universal is eternal and thus incapable of having any excellence added to it, what is this so-called "auxiliary purpose"? None at all.

By the words "impermanent" (*anityā hi*) and so forth, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): because of the acquisition of a distinct self from the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*). "That" refers to the auxiliary cause. Why? Because that self which is the producer of these momentary things did not exist prior to the presence of the auxiliary cause; it exists at that very time when the auxiliary cause is present. This is on the grounds that [the effect] arises from the auxiliary cause. "Of these" refers to the momentary things.

Now, one might object: even for momentary things, how can there be a dependence on auxiliary causes for the attainment of a specific nature? For those that arise simultaneously cannot be related as benefactor and beneficiary to one another; and furthermore, for that moment which is being born, there is no dependence on auxiliaries during either its state of existence or its state of non-existence.

It has been said that it is illogical for one who is beneficial to be dependent; however, this is not a fault. This is stated with reference to existence (*sattā*). Therefore, he says: "Their very state of being produced is their mutual dependence. [The phrase] "without reaching another" refers to a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). "That nature" means a capable nature. For that universal (*sāmānya*) alone, which is devoid of cooperative causes—if it previously lacked the nature of producing cognition, how could that [nature] ever come to be? The word "not" (*na hi*) connects [to this]. The implication is: because it is eternal (*nityatvāt*).

Furthermore, since the opponent has accepted that the sense faculty is refined by the individual instance (*vyakti*)—on the grounds that when the refinement of the universal occurs through the individual instance, the universal would be produced by it—he says "the individual instance," etc., [to show] that even so, the consequence of being produced by the individual instance remains. If it is admitted that the universal is the cause of cognition when it acts as a cooperative factor for the sense faculty refined by the individual instance, then because the sense faculty is the effect of the individual instance, the universal would be said to be the indirect effect of the individual instance. (149–50)

Granted that the individual (*vyakti*) may indeed be the manifestor (*vyañjikā*) of the universal (*sāmānya*), it is nonetheless not logical for it to possess the universal (*jātimattva*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth. If it is maintained that the particular individual (*vyaktibheda*), which is the manifestor of universals—that is, of generalities—possesses the universal; then a lamp or similar object, which illuminates [the universal] such as "cowness" (*gotva*), would, by virtue of being its manifestor, necessarily possess that "cowness" and other such universals, just like a brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*). The meaning is that it would become a substratum (*ādhāra*) of cowness.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "For that which... Even lamps and the like possess the quality of being causes for the cognition of universals such as "cowness" when these are to be manifested. If one asks how this is so, he says: "Light," etc. Since light possesses causality with respect to cognition, [it follows] "therefore"—that is, because of its being a cause of cognition. "Lamps and the like"—by the word "etcetera," the refinement of the sense faculties and so forth are included, since these too are causes of cognition.

If it is argued that the manifestation of the universal occurs as something distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), whereas this is not the case with a lamp or similar objects, he replies: "Not indeed," and so forth. Apart from being the cause of cognition, there is no other manifestation of the universal from the individual whatsoever. For if the individual were to produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the universal that a lamp or the like does not, then there would be a distinction; but such is not the case, because it is impossible to produce an excellence in an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The meaning is that this is because the universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal. Regarding the phrase "inherence" (*samavāya*), etc.: the cowness (*gotva*) inheres in the individual (*vyakti*), but not in things such as lamps. This is because it has been stated [elsewhere] what kind of inherence exists between that which is neither produced nor productive—namely, the universal.

Let it be granted that there is inherence; nevertheless, for this universal (*sāmānya*), there arises only its inherence with the individual (*vyakti*), and no other distinct quality characterized by the production of cognition. "As before" means that even after the inherence with the individual, just as prior to it, if there is still no distinct quality in the universal despite its inherence with the individual, [the opponent might argue]: "Nevertheless, by the very power of inherence, it produces a cognition whose object is itself. To this, he says: "Inherence alone," and so forth.

If it is accepted that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the cause of cognition, then for whatever is inherent (*samaveta*) in its own substratum, there would follow the consequence that even things other than the universal—such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth—which are inherent in atoms, would also become perceptible; for inherence (*samavāya*), being a single entity, is without distinction everywhere.

For just as *samavāya* alone reveals the universal even though it is beyond the senses, why should it not likewise reveal color and other qualities that reside within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? And since this fault exists in the position of *samavāya*, therefore, in the case of the universal, the very fact of being a cause of cognition constitutes its manifesting nature (*vyañjakatva*) with respect to the individual (*vyakti*). Since such a manifesting nature is common to lamps and so forth as well, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows, namely that [the lamp] would be the possessor of "cowness" and so on. (150–51)

Therefore, there is no inherence (*nādheyatā*) of the universal in its own substratum, nor is manifestation by the substratum the occurrence of the universal in its own substratum. Consequently, because it does not occur [therein], the universal cannot be the cause of a single-form cognition regarding the difference between various individuals. For it is not logical that something which does not exist in a particular place should be the cause of a cognition therein by means of its own occurrence.

For this very reason—namely, because a single universal does not reside in multiple [particulars]—if for those disputants the genus (*jāti*) is either different from or non-different from the individual (*vyakti*), then [it would follow that it is perceived] in individuals that have arisen previously, or are now arising, or are seen later. The word *tu* (but/then) is to be understood after the word *vidyate* (exists), serving the purpose of restriction. For this reason he says: "It exists indeed," and so forth. That is to say, for those for whom the genus is a real entity (*vastusatī*), [it would be perceived] by means of its own cognition when it is present in itself.

The phrase "in another [instance]" refers to producing a cognition regarding a different individual. What kind of cognition does it produce? One that conforms to its own nature and is followed by a single form. Wherever it produces such a cognition, it requires a relation; for without a relation, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of producing a cognition with its own form [even in unrelated things]. (vv. 151–52)

The phrase "And that" refers to the connection of a universal (*sāmānya*) which exists—that is, is present—with another individual (*vyakti*). This [connection] is impossible under both the view that [the universal] is identical [to the individual] and the view that it is different. Why? Because it is impossible for a distinction between individuals—whether it be an entity distinct from the object or not distinct—to be observed in one place while existing in another, namely, in a different individual. The passage beginning with "For that... establishes this very point: for that cognition, which grasps what is real and grasps a real universal, would have to occur as a single [undifferentiated] occurrence.

In one particular individual instance, having arisen, that [universal] would "leap over" or go to another individual instance; that is to say, it would grasp even the other individual instance by way of its universal form. If some real entity in the form of a universal were perceived in one particular individual instance, then it might leap over to another—namely, to that other individual instance where it ought to be perceived. And such a perception elsewhere is not possible for a universal that exists as a real entity; this is the connection [of the argument].

What is the reason? Because if one accepts that [the universal] is distinct from its substratum (*āśraya*), there would be no continuity (*anvaya*). For that which is not distinct from one thing—that is, which has it as its very essence—cannot be continuous with another. Furthermore, even if the universal were distinct from its substratum, it could not reside in the individual (*vyakti*), because the status of being a substratum has already been refuted by the preceding argument that negates the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*).

If, because an extrinsic universal lacks a connection [to individuals], it does not produce a cognition of its own form in another individual, then this is equally true for the very first individual; why, then, is it said "in previously unperceived individuals" rather than simply "in individuals"? Furthermore, one must also say that it is because what is seen in one place cannot possibly be seen elsewhere, since even in a single case, seeing is impossible without a connection despite the difference between individuals. This is true; however, this was stated as a concession [for the sake of argument], so there is no fault.

As for the one who thinks: "In the positions of identity or difference, the perception of something other than the universal is impossible; however, for us, the universal is indeed both different and non-different. For it is said:
'A universal cannot exist without particularity, like the horn of a hare;
it possesses oneness in some respect and multiplicity in another.'"
"And when a variegated object appears simultaneously,
then all distinctions such as difference and non-difference and so forth simply vanish.
(Ślokavārttika, Ākṛti 10)
To refute that, he says: "For its own nature," and so forth. The connection is that [an entity] does not transcend being either identical to or different from its own nature.

Now, one might object: "Even though there is no difference in terms of place, time, or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), a distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is nonetheless accepted through their forms of being inclusive (*anugata*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*). To this he replies: "Because an inclusive form—that is, an intrinsic nature that is not of that [particular] kind, which has an exclusive form as its intrinsic nature—does not transcend otherness. The meaning is that the universal, which is inclusive in form and distinct from the exclusive forms of the particulars, must necessarily be something other [than them]. It is indeed otherness that constitutes its not being of that nature; how so? To this he says: "This very... and so forth.

"That which is not that" means "that which does not have that form. This alone is the definition of otherness; this is the meaning. [The suffix] *-vat* is used in the sense of the genitive case, as in *ākārāntaravat*. For instance, the otherness of suffering from pleasure is established by taking suffering to be of a non-pleasurable nature. By this much, the pervasion of the definition of otherness—namely, being of a different nature—is stated. And since this definition of otherness is without distinction, it applies even to the intended universal (*sāmānya*).

By this, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been stated. The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: Whatever, while being a real entity (*vastu*), does not have that [other] nature, is necessarily different from it; for example, suffering is different from pleasure. And since the universal (*sāmānya*) is accepted as having the nature of non-manifestation while being a real entity, it is different because it lacks that [particular’s] nature. Since the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of its difference is what is to be proven, this is a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*). Thus, first, it has been established that if the universal lacks that nature, it must be different. Now, if difference is not accepted, then it would follow that it is identical to it; thus he says: "And that... and so forth.

If that [universal] were other than the individual, then it would be nothing but the form of the individual itself; for if it were not that (i.e., if it were not of the nature of the individual), there would follow the consequence of its being distinct, just like any other entity. This has been stated immediately prior. [Objection: Let the universal be distinct; nevertheless, it will still follow after another individual. To this he says: "Nor can one... and so forth. For that which has the nature of a single individual cannot have an entry into or a following after (*anvāveśa* = *anugama*) by another individual—that is to say, it cannot possess the nature of another individual. Why? Because if it were perceived as such, it would follow that it is not distinct from that other individual.

If the universal, which consists of the *śābaleya* (the brindled cow), were identical with the essence of the *bāhuleya* (the black cow), then the *bāhuleya*, being born as nothing other than the *śābaleya* due to its non-difference from the universal consisting of the *śābaleya*, would be just like the *śābaleya*. How, then, could it be a distinct individual? Therefore, [the cognition] is "concomitant" (*anvayinī*), meaning it follows along, from that universal which is non-different from the individual; nor is it the case—this being the subject at hand—that the cognition is concomitant from a universal that is different [from the individual].

Why? Because that universal (*sāmānya*), being distinct [from the particular], has no basis in any particular instance and thus does not function there; for without a relation, its functioning is impossible. Furthermore, because the relations of the manifested and the manifestor, as well as the relation of container and contained, have been refuted by such statements as, "Functioning, being contained, and manifestation—these are not applicable to it. If it is argued that there must then be some other relation between the universal and its possessor, he says: "Of another also," and so forth.

The ablative case in "vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāvādeḥ" (from the relationship of the manifested and the manifestor, etc. is used; by the word "etc.," the relationship of locus and located is included. This is because, other than these two types of relationships previously refuted, there exists no other relationship whatsoever for a universal with respect to manifestation. What is the reason? Because it is eternal, the universal cannot be assisted by any particular instance of manifestation, and thus there is no connection [between them]. For it has been stated that there is no relationship for that which lacks a connection. By this, the portion of the verse beginning with "anyattve 'pāśrayāt" (if it were different, [there would be] no dependence) is explained. (152–53)

If it is argued that even a universal (*sāmānya*) lacking a real connection produces a cognition that conforms to its own nature among individuals, he says: "Because of the connection," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "it has no connection" (*na asya sambandho 'sti*). The meaning is that there would be a cognition of everything everywhere. "Therefore" (*tat*); "this one" (*ayam*) refers to the proponent of the universal (*sāmānyavādī*). By means of the cause, which is the perception of a single universal.

When one seeks the occurrence of this [universal] in another individual instance—distinct from a single brindled cow—in relation to that universal which is intended as a real entity (vastu) because of its occurrence in other instances, the options of its being either identical to or different from the individual are not traversed, since there is no other possible mode of existence for a real entity. Thus, the aforementioned fault applies; therefore, it is correct to say that the following cognition arises from a universal that is a real entity.

Since this is so, therefore this cognition—which has a single form and a single aspect regarding objects that are mutually distinct—is indeed an error (*bhrānti*), because it functions by superimposing non-difference upon things that are different. From what, then, does it arise? He says: "By conceptualization," and so forth. It arises from that latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) which, by its very nature, produces such a conceptualization through the experience of objects excluded from those of a different class; this has already been stated previously, as he says: "The difference between entities," and so forth.

The distinction of entities from those that do not produce their effects; and the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of such [entities], as well as its *prakṛti*—that is, its inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and its substratum—has been established previously. In that context, the distinction between entities was presented as a cause through a mediated succession, while the latent impression and the *prakṛti* were presented as the two immediate causes. [Objection: "If only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the denotation of words, then how is it so now... and so forth.

The terms "effect" [applied to] Pradhāna, Īśvara, and so forth mean that the world is the effect of Pradhāna and the effect of Īśvara; by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of such terms as "the transformation of Śabdabrahman" is intended.

Regarding internal and external entities: those whose distinctions (*bheda*) do not consist of that [Pradhāna]—that is, whose distinctions do not consist of the effects of Pradhāna and so forth—are described as such. Even if their distinction were from the effects of Pradhāna, it would then follow that their distinction consists of the effects of Pradhāna and so forth; and that very thing is the non-distinction (*abheda*) of all things. By means of that non-distinction, which is without a cause, they would exist everywhere. But that [non-distinction] does not exist for entities according to the view of the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), because [entities] consist of effects other than those of Pradhāna and so forth.

And therefore, how could they function without distinction toward things that are so constituted? The intention is that they certainly do not. Consequently, the point is that the determination of exclusion (*apoha*) would be non-pervasive. He refutes this with the words "They too," and so forth. The connection is as follows: those words for the effects of *pradhāna* and so on also function with respect to an object appearing in conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*). To the question "How? he says: "By convention," and so forth. With respect to a thing being such [as it appears], there is a convention by the force of desire, such as "the world is the effect of *pradhāna*."

Because the continuum of consciousness has been refined by the successive transformation of moments through that latent power (*vāsanā-śakti*) deposited therein, it perceives all external and internal objects; thus, even though those distinctions exist within the perceptions and experiences, it disregards the distinction inherent in the thing itself as a primary effect.

Even if there is indeed a perception of things that are non-primary effects by means of the property of the real entity (*vastudharma*), the meaning is nevertheless "without depending on the intrinsic nature of the real entity" (*vastusvabhāva*). This is because of such a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*); that is, due to the conceptual determination of entities as primary effects according to convention, even though they are non-primary effects. Consciousness (*caitanya*) is imagined by the Sāṃkhya as having the status of a primary effect through an imagination of what is not so; [the phrase] "due to the exclusion of that" refers to the object appearing in the conceptual cognition [that thinks]: "there is an absence of primary effects."

The meaning is that this very [cognition] is "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) by way of the exclusion of heterogeneous things. To the question "Of what nature are those words?", he says: "upādāna... and so forth. That which has its origin—its arising—from the strength of the appropriation, namely the firmness of the latent impression (vāsanā) which is the cause of conceptual construction (vikalpa), from that [strength] they have arisen.

This is what is meant: even if there is indeed no such real distinction among things, nevertheless, exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—which is merely superimposed by conceptual construction—is the basis for the application of words; therefore, it does not suffer from the fault of being non-pervasive. If it is asked: "Why is a universal (*sāmānya*), which is a real entity, not accepted as the basis for the application of words like 'effect of *pradhāna*' etc., since they apply without distinction to those entities? he replies: "For not... and so forth. The point is that in those [entities] which are superimposed as being effects of *pradhāna*, there is an absence of a universal because the individual instances (*vyakti*) do not exist, since they are not actually effects of *pradhāna*.

But for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), there is no fault; thus he says, "In that way," and so forth. The meaning is: by means of the conceptualization of being an effect of the *pradhāna* and so on. The "difference" (*bheda*)—that is, the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)—of that which is other than those, namely what is not an effect of the *pradhāna* and so on, would occur for cognizers due to the force of their determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding entities that have been superimposed as being effects of the *pradhāna* and so on. If it is asked: "Why is there not a universal (*sāmānya*) that serves as the cause for a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) among [individuals] such as the *śābaleya* cow, precisely due to that determination, that is, due to the determination of the cognizer?"

This is not the case. For even by that proponent of a universal (*sāmānyavādin*) who postulates a universal, the exclusion from heterogeneous things (*vijātīyabheda*) among those such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) must necessarily be admitted as an inseparable concomitant; otherwise, the [universal] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth would remain unestablished. That very exclusion is capable of fulfilling the function of a universal, characterized by the application of a single term and the like. Thus, the postulation of a universal is purposeless.

This is what is being said: Just as even with respect to entities that are effects of the Pradhāna, the words "effect of the Pradhāna" and so forth, as well as the cognitions thereof, occur in a single uniform manner even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*); likewise, why is it not accepted that in the case of cows and so forth, the words "cow" and so forth, and the cognitions thereof, occur in a single uniform manner? What is the use of a real, imagined universal? Moreover, even by others [such as the Naiyāyikas], the occurrence of non-different designations and cognitions with respect to many universals is observed even in the absence of a [higher-order] universal.
As it was stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara:

"Therefore, the word for a universal, such as 'existence' (sattā) and so forth, is based either on the occurrence of a single [entity] among diverse things, or on the production of a single cognition. — *Ślokavārttika*, Ākṛtivāda 24.

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as the word "universal" (*sāmānya*) and the cognition thereof apply to [categories] such as "existence" (*sattva*) and "substantiality" (*dravyatva*), each of which is the locus of multiple things, even in the absence of a [higher-order] universal; and just as the state of being the locus of multiple things—which is not itself a universal—is not the same in existence as it is in substantiality and so forth, because of the statement that "universals are devoid of universals"; nor does the application of those two [the word and the cognition] occur merely by way of metaphorical designation, because they are grasped by a non-erroneous cognition.

Therefore, just as their occurrence in [the properties of] existence and so forth takes place without a universal, so too [it occurs] among [individuals] such as the *śābaleya* without a universal. The meaning is: why is the occurrence of identical designations and cognitions—not accepted—such that the *śābaleya* is excluded from non-cows, the *bāhuleya* is excluded from non-cows, and the *khaṇḍa* is excluded from non-cows?

It might be argued: "In all cases, the cognition of a universal is indeed accepted as being without an object; however, were there no universal, there would be no non-discrepancy [of that cognition] in any instance. To this, he says: "If," and so forth. The word "if" is intended to indicate a hypothetical admission. If it is admitted that this [cognition] is entirely without an object in all instances—[that is,] when things exist (*satsu*), meaning when things exist as excluded from what is not-cow (*ago-vyāvṛtta*); and when things do not exist (*asatsu*), meaning when things do not exist in reality (*paramārthataḥ*) as effects of [causes such as] Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) or God (*īśvara*).

This conceptual cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) is not meaningful [as a perception of reality], because that undifferentiated form which is superimposed by it does not exist externally; and since it thus grasps what is unreal, it is nothing but a distortion (*viplava*), that is, an error (*bhrānti*). Therefore, one need not pay any heed to defining the object of this conceptual cognition, which is itself devoid of an object. If all conceptual cognition of a universal is erroneous, how then is there correspondence with a real entity (*vastu-saṃvāda*) through inference? To this he says: "In some cases," and so forth.
