In some cases, there is non-contradiction for this cognition with respect to an object, because it is connected to cause and effect as previously described; and this has already been explained by the passage beginning, "Where there is a connection with the real entity, as in the aforementioned inference" (1.83). There is no contradiction of the inferential conceptualization with the real entity, because such a thing—which possesses a non-different form and is apprehended by inference—is present and included within the real entity. "Like perception" serves as an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

What is the reason? [It is] because [the cognition] occurs even when things are not as they appear; that is, even when the object has passed away, [the cognition] arises through a succession following the mark (*liṅga*). Alternatively, "even when things are not as they appear" means that even with respect to an object devoid of a universal (*sāmānya*), there occurs a cognition possessing a non-differentiated form. This is what we shall explain. And it has already been explained previously in the passage: "Capacity [is established] because [cognition] conforms to the presence and absence [of the object]."

If a universal cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*) apprehends distinct entities as non-distinct by superimposing upon them its own form (*svākāra*), thereby perceiving them as positive entities (*vidhirūpa*), how can it be said that its object is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? To this, he says: "By the power of seeing distinct objects," and so forth. This means: by the force of the perception of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīya*). The word "because of its arising" (*utpatter*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].

The inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) functions even in the absence of a real entity, as in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like. This is because, among those distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of existence; that is, due to the determination of one's own form (*svarūpa*) as non-different from its own aspect (*svākāra*). The meaning is that activity proceeds by unifying the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized object (*vikalpya*).

Because cognition arises through the power of perceiving distinct objects, and once arisen, it apprehends those very same distinct objects as being non-different from its own form; therefore, "having difference as its object" means "having distinct objects as its object. It is indeed logical that conceptual constructions such as impermanence and so forth—which come about by way of the perception of an object—have difference as their object, since they arise through the power of perceiving an object. However, this is not the case where there is no such distinct object, as in the case of conceptual constructions such as permanence and so forth.

And regarding conceptual constructions such as "the horn of a hare" and so forth, if it is asked how these can have difference as their object, he says: "In that way, existence," and so on. Just as cognitions of impermanence and so forth—arisen by the force of an experience that grasps the intrinsic nature of distinct entities—function by determining their own internal reflections as being distinct entities, and thus have difference as their object.

Thus, when there is such a conceptualization of an entity (*bhāva-kalpanā*), that is, when there is the conceptualization of determining a distinct external entity within one's own manifestation, and while there is a distinct object—namely, in the case of non-existent things such as eternal *pradhāna*, effects, and so forth, as well as rabbit horns and the like—the conceptualizations of "eternal *pradhāna* and its effects" or "rabbit horns" possess a distinct object. Consequently, they remain restricted solely to the difference between individuals (*vyakti-bheda*) residing within their own substratum, and not in a place devoid of individuals. As the Bhaṭṭa has said:
"Since a universal (*sāmānya*) is perceived only in individual bodies (*piṇḍa*) and not in between."
For no one indeed accepts that which is called a "universal" (sāmānya) as being like space (ākāśa).
Since it is observed to be inherent in each individual [particular], it will not cease [to exist].
And this being so, there will be no multiplicity for a single cognition.

"Just as a single individual, though perceived again and again even at different times, appears as if it were non-different [from itself], so too is the universal (*jāti*), although it resides in different substrata, [perceived as] non-different. (Ślokavārttika, Vana° 33)

Uddyotakara also says: "By whom is the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) of the universal (*jāti*) accepted, such that there would be 'cowness' (*gotva*) even in a lump of clay or a clay cow? Rather, it is called 'omnipresent' because its occurrence exists everywhere within its own domain. What, then, is the specific domain of cowness? It is wherever cowness exists. And where does cowness exist? Wherever there occurs a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) caused by cowness."

But where does "cowness" (*gotva*) produce a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*), such that it would be its means of proof? Furthermore, what is the purpose of proving "cowness" if it is eternal? [The opponent replies: "It is that by which it is manifested. [The author asks: Is the manifestation of "cowness" something distinct from the hump and other [physical features]? No; for "cowness" is not a separate entity from the individual bodies (*piṇḍa*), because it is not perceived in the intervals between those bodies. To this, the Buddhist who speaks thus should be questioned regarding the "intervals between the bodies": What is this "interval between the bodies"?

Is it space, or rather non-existence, or perhaps a distinct substance? If it were space, then "cowness" would not reside therein, for space is not perceived as a cow. By this, [the cases of] non-existence and a distinct substance are also explained.
(Nyāyavārttika, fn. 2)

Furthermore, because specific cognitions are not accidental: this cognition, which arises as distinct from the cognition of the individual object (*piṇḍa*), must arise from another cause. Indeed, it is observed that cognitions occurring in distinction from the individual object arise from another cause, just as the cognition of "blue" in relation to leather, cloth, or woolen blankets; and that other cause is the universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, the universal is omnipresent in all individuals, because it exists even in places devoid of the individual.

"And there is no cognition of the universal therein, because of the absence of the individual that manifests it. And only that individual in which the universal is perceived is capable of manifesting the universal; this is understood through the principle of the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of the universal, and not others.
Thus says Bhaṭṭa.
Alternatively, even though [the universal] is omnipresent, its manifestation occurs in accordance with its capacity (*śakti*).
Capacity is to be inferred from its effect, and manifestation has perception as its cause.
Therefore, only in that place where the capable manifestation is perceived does [the universal reside].
And for that very reason, this [capacity] is not perceived in all individuals;
for even though they are distinct, some possess the capacity while others are incapable.
Furthermore, there can never be any questioning regarding the power of a real entity.
"Fire burns, but space does not; who here is to be questioned about this? (Ślokavārttika, Akṛtivāda, 25–29).

In that regard, between those two positions, if [the universal] resides only in its own substrate, then how could there be a possibility of it existing in those subsequently produced jars and so forth—which are located in a different place from the jar produced later in a location devoid of "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) and the like? Such is the intended meaning: there would be no possibility at all. There might be a possibility if that universal were to move from that prior substance to the substance being produced later.

And since that [universal] does not exist, he says: "Because," and so forth. "That" refers to the universal. "From the previous substance" means from that in which it was previously inherent; the substance about to arise—that is, desiring to arise—such as a prior jar or the like, does not go [to the new location]. Because the universal is formless, it is devoid of motion. If it is argued that even without moving from the previous substance, there will be a connection with a different location, just as a reflection appears in a mirror, he replies: "For not," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: for a "being" (bhāva) called a "universal" (*sāmānya*), which resides in a substance at a different location from the substance about to arise—that is, a being that does not move from its previous substrate, nor pervades the interval between those two, nor pervades the interval between the two [substances] produced earlier and later—it is certainly not logical for there to be a conjunction with a substance located in a place different from its own substrate. For how could one who asserts that there is a conjunction of a reflection with a mirror in a different location not be considered insane?
Through the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), an erroneous cognition arises there, appearing as a reflection in a mirror that follows the contours of the object. As it has been said:
"In objects such as the surface of a diamond or a mirror, which possess contrary transformations, there is no possibility for entities whose nature is that of mountains and the like."

Even for those who maintain that there is the arising of a distinct entity (*bhāvāntara*) therein, it is not connected with the original form (*bimba*); thus, this [position] is trivial. Prior to the substance that is about to arise, the universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist in that location where it is about to arise, because it is not admitted to be so in a location devoid of the individual (*vyakti*). Subsequently, once the individual has arisen, that universal exists, because an individual devoid of the universal is not admitted. Nor did it arise in that location together with the individual, because it is eternal.

Nor is the production of the universal identical to the production of the individual, because they are distinct; or, if they were non-distinct, there would be no relationship of general and particular between them. Furthermore, this is a presentation by way of a conclusion of that which was previously stated: "it does not come from any prior particular individual, nor does it go [anywhere]."

In as many ways as the existence of a universal in another individual is possible, those very ways are not accepted while the universal itself is nevertheless asserted therein; this is a contradiction. And because it is difficult for the wise to endure, it is a "burden. For this very reason he says: "Who is this," and so forth. For how could a wise person tolerate what is illogical? An insentient being, however, being incapable of investigating what is logical or illogical due to its lack of knowledge, might even tolerate it—as it is said elsewhere: "due to dullness."

But surely, even when a universal arises in a substance that is about to arise, its state of inherence must be understood through perception alone; and since that perception of inherence in the individual exists even when the universal has not yet arisen, what is the purpose of its arising? Furthermore, if the nature of the universal is held to be inherent in the individual, then—since it is perceived as having been inherent in a previous substance and as remaining there without moving, while simultaneously being perceived as inherent in the substance about to arise—how can the objection beginning with "how does it not go" be raised? [The answer is: because this is precisely what is accepted.

True. This objection—namely, "it appears"—would apply to one who does not accept the appearance of a universal (*sāmānya*). But how could this be an objection for one who considers the appearance of a universal to be unreal (*alīka*)? Furthermore, the Master has demonstrated through such passages as "the substance that is about to arise does not go there, nor was it there, nor has it arisen," that even in the absence of a universal, a cognition appearing as a universal arises. Moreover, truth does not follow merely from appearing;
otherwise, it would entail the consequence that even things like a double moon would be real.

Nor is sublation by perception the only form of sublation, for sublation by inference is also a form of sublation. If that [substance] were to possess parts (*sāṃśavat*), then it would have to pervade—by one part—the substance that previously resided in a different locus and is about to arise in another part; or else, it would have to abandon its previous locus entirely, being itself partless. He states that this [partless] substance also does not exist with the words beginning "And not" (*na ca*). The phrase "the previous locus" refers to a portion of the Sūtra. He clarifies this with the *Miśraka* commentary as "a location different from the location where it was about to arise. And the phrase "of those two" refers to the two substances, the former and the latter, which have arisen.

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "divided" (*bhinnā*). "It would become twofold" means either by way of having a nature consisting of various parts, or by abandoning its former substratum. First, he states the first position with the words beginning "various" (*nānā*). And this is stated for the purpose of refuting the opponent; it has not been asserted that a single entity consists of multiple parts. [The phrase] "due to the connection with those called 'parts' which are mutually distinct from one another" means due to the connection with those two parts located in different places.

For light, because it possesses parts, is connected with a pot by one part and with other objects such as pots by another; likewise, a rope, a bamboo pole, and so forth, are also connected with their own respective relata.

The passage beginning with "na hi" is a justification for this very point. Now, if it is maintained that a universal exists in many [individuals] because it possesses parts, even so, how could one [entity] exist in many? For [it is argued that] the parts of the universal exist [therein]. And as for those parts of the universal which exist in each individual object, are they of the nature of the universal or not? If they are indeed of the nature of the universal, it follows that [the universal] exists in only one [individual].

Furthermore, it is not logical to say that a single universal exists in multiple locations. If, on the other hand, those [particulars] do not have the nature of a universal, then how can it be said that a universal exists in many places? Moreover, if a universal were to exist in one part by means of another part, there would be an infinite regress. And it is not possible for a single entity to exist in many places without possessing parts.

Furthermore, because it is complete within each individual object (*piṇḍa*) and lacks parts, a partless universal cannot be non-common (*asādhāraṇa*), like the individual objects themselves. Why? Because that partless universal has a nature consisting of a connection with one substance; since there is no second nature apart from that, and because that universal, being of a single nature, consists in its form of connection with what exists in that location—namely, because it has the form of being connected to the substance of the jar existing in the previous location [before] the jar about to be produced.

There is no simultaneous connection with a substance located in a different place. "Otherwise" means that if [the universal] were of the nature of a relation with a substance in the location where it is about to arise, such a relation would be impossible; for it could not be related to that previous substance. Therefore, a universal whose nature is restricted to a single individual has no connection at that very same time with a substance in a different location.

Alternatively, regarding the relation [of the universal]: since the universal has a nature determined by its connection with a previous individual, it would remain in that previous individual; yet at that very same time, it would not remain there due to its connection with an individual in a different location. This is a contradiction, as he states in the verse beginning with "of a single located thing" (*ekasyādheyasya*). In this context, "remaining" refers to remaining in the previous individual. For you yourself have admitted that at that very same time it exists in another individual; and because it is impossible for a single entity to be connected elsewhere without abandoning the previous individual. In that regard, "there" means in the previous individual.

"It is improper to say that there is no locus for that universal by means of that very nature which was restricted to the previous individual. Why? Because of the verse beginning with *tatsthitā* [and so forth]. For it is a contradiction for a single universal to simultaneously possess two natures—being both situated and not situated—in that very same individual."

(305) Now, just as the occurrence [of a word] in many [objects] is accepted as being twofold—namely, that it occurs in one by the abandonment of others, and likewise that it occurs in many through successive parts because this is observed—so too, since it is observed that a universal exists in another at the very same time and in the very same form in which it existed in one, why is that third mode of occurrence not also accepted? As it was said by Bhaṭṭa:
"For there is no restrictive rule that the function [of a word] must be of only two kinds; for since it is observed to be even threefold, it could just as well be twofold. (Ślokavārttika, fn. 1)

Uddyotakara also says: "The universal *gotva* is neither a whole (*avayavin*) nor a collection (*samudāya*); therefore, the terms 'entirety' and 'part' do not apply to it. Since these two terms do not apply to it, the question—whether the universal *gotva* exists in its entirety or by way of a part—is not logical. How, then, does the universal *gotva* exist in cows? By way of the relationship between locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). What, then, is this relationship of locus and located? It is inherence (*samavāya*). In that [relationship], the universal *gotva* is that which possesses existence."

Inherence (*samavāya*) is the mode of existence (*vṛtti*) here, because it is the cause of the cognition [of "herein"]. Therefore, in all cases—both in the prior substance and in the substance about to arise—inherence alone is the mode of existence. Consequently, how can it be said: "This is untenable because there is a contradiction between the stationary and non-stationary natures in a single locus"?
(Nyāyavārttika, fn. 2).

He says this very thing with the words "everywhere," and so forth. "Everywhere" means in the previously manifested [substance] and in the substance about to arise. Even when it exists at all times, including during the production of the substance about to arise, it does not abandon the substance. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the nature of being stationary and the nature of being non-stationary in a single locus, because of the absence of the nature of being stationary. That is incorrect.

For inherence in one [individual] is not itself inherence in another individual, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the latter appearing there [in the former]. Therefore, inherence in one and inherence in another are indeed mutually distinct. Furthermore, if that [inherence] were non-different from the universal due to its inhering in one, then—just as there is no persistence [of the universal] in other instances—it would follow that the universal would also lack persistence elsewhere. Alternatively, the power of the universal to produce a cognition through its connection with a single individual, time, and so forth, does not exist by virtue of its connection with another individual and so forth.

Therefore, in one individual there is the power of the universal to produce cognition, while in another there is a power that is opposed to the production of cognition. And since power is non-different from that which possesses it, and because a real entity is defined by its powers, it follows that whatever is a single entity must reside in only one [individual]. This establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, if the universal is a single entity, how could it reside in another [individual] as well? If it is argued that this is because it appears as such [in others], we say no.

For it is the appearance of one thing that sublates the non-appearance of another, not the non-entity, because even that [non-entity] appears. However, it has been stated that for this [entity], the appearance of a real entity is the sublater; yet no pervasive real entity exists. For this very reason, there is no sublation of the thesis by perception, since the cognition of a universal is merely a semblance of perception.

If it is argued that there would be a circularity—since as long as this [perception] lacks validity, inference does not function, and as long as inference does not function, this is not a pseudo-perception—[we reply]: no. For inference proceeds by means of the mere doubt regarding the reality of the object as it appears.

Nor does an inference that serves as a cause for its invalidity operate; rather, it is caused by a mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with its own probandum. Therefore, it is the sublater of the cognition of a universal. Consequently, in ultimate reality, there is no single entity that exists at one time in multiple locations. For if it were so situated, there would be a direct contradiction between its being present and its being absent. The Teacher, however, having provisionally accepted the fault, says: "Having that nature," and so forth.

That cognition which has the perception of a universal nature as its basis would, in every case, manifest in all aspects even with respect to a substance belonging to a different genus. And this being so, one would perceive even a cow as a horse, and so forth. Why is this? He says: the analysis of the compound is "that whose essence (*ātman*) resides in the horse is the 'substanceness' (*dravyatva*). Because it conveys the meaning, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed even with a term in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Alternatively, it is a compound formed by the rule "a word ending in a kṛt-affix [denoting an agent] is compounded with a word denoting the object" (*sādhana-kṛtā saha*), resulting in "residing in the horse" (*aśve sthitaḥ*). Subsequently, a two-membered *bahuvrīhi* is formed with the word *ātman*.

This is because of the determination [of the object] through the apprehension of its own nature (*svabhāva*) and through the apprehension of the substancehood (*dravyatva*) inherent in the horse, as in the determination "the cow is a substance. [Objection: It might be argued that the cognition "it is a substance" does not arise from the apprehension of substancehood as inherent in the horse; rather, it arises from the apprehension of substancehood in general. To this, he says: "And of that," and so forth. This is because, apart from the fact of being inherent in the horse—which is a single, unperceived, and unapprehended state of substancehood—there exists no other form characterized by such inherence in the horse.

Therefore, one who perceives a cow as qualified by "substanceness" (dravyatva) which is inherent in the horse would perceive it as "horse. But for one who perceives the cow as something distinct from the horse and qualified by the universal "substanceness," he would necessarily perceive it as "horse. Thus ends the summary. A partless universal is not simultaneously deposited in multiple locations—that is, in things such as jars and the like; it does not undergo the state of being a substrate. By this much, the statement "nor is it possessed of parts" has been explained.

He explains the phrase "it does not abandon its former substratum" with the words beginning with "former. Furthermore, the abandonment of the former substratum by the universal is not accepted [by the opponent]. With the words "elsewhere," he mocks [the opponent's position] as being highly illogical: that a substance whose birth occurs in a place other than its former substratum—while the universal remains without moving from its own former location—should subsist in that [new] place. (154–56)

If it is argued that the universal, though not moving from the location of its previous manifestation, pervades a substance in another location, he says: "Where," and so forth. In whichever location that entity existing at a later time resides, the universal is not connected with that location, because it is admitted [by the opponent] to be omnipresent within all its own manifestations.

He mocks [the opponent] by way of another argument, saying, "This is truly a great marvel," because it transgresses logic: that something which does not exist in a particular place should subsequently pervade that very location and a future entity. For one who follows logic cannot possibly conclude that what does not exist in a certain place can pervade that place. (157)

Desiring also to refute the conceptualization of its being omnipresent, he says: "Of which," and so forth. For that proponent of an omnipresent universal (*sāmānya*), if the genus (*jāti*) is omnipresent, then by means of its manifestation—that is, its becoming manifest—in a single instance such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), that genus would be manifested—that is, made evident—everywhere, even in places devoid of instances, and even in the diversity of instances belonging to other classes, because of its non-difference, that is, its oneness; thus it would be perceived everywhere, even in places devoid of instances.

This is what is meant: although there is an absence of a manifesting individual instance (svavyakti) both in a location devoid of individuals and in an individual of a different class, nevertheless, because the universal (jāti) exists therein in a form manifested by its own individual instance, it would be perceived; otherwise, it would follow that it possesses a plurality of natures, whereas it is intended to be of a single nature. This is the sense.

It has already been refuted in this context—that is, in the passage beginning with "The occurrence [of a universal] consists in being supported or being manifested; this is not tenable in that case" (1.146)—that a permanent universal can never be manifested, because no excellence can be imparted to it. Therefore, that universal is eternally independent of any external embellishment and incapable of having any excellence added to it. If, by its very nature, it were capable of producing its own cognition, then it would be perceived at all times, both before and after its manifestation. On the other hand, if it were not so capable, then it would never be perceived at any time.

What is the reason? Because [the universal] would persist in both that nature which is capable of producing cognition and its opposite; the meaning is that it would remain of one and the same form at all times. [If one argues: "It is incapable when the individual is absent, but becomes capable when that [individual] is present," [we reply: therefore, there is neither constant perception nor constant non-perception of the genus (*jāti*). To this he says: "In its own nature," and so forth. The point is that, because it is eternal, no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be imparted to it. (157–58)

If the universal (*jāti*) does not exist [independently], then why is it said that "it is manifested in one place by means of the individual (*vyakti*) itself," and so forth? To this he says: "Even granting... and so on. Even though the universal is all-pervading (*vyāpin*), it is manifested in one substrate because there is no difference [in the universal] due to its unity; thus, it is indeed manifested—that is, revealed—everywhere, even in places devoid of individuals and among heterogeneous (*vijātīya*) individual differences. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even in places devoid of individuals," it is implied that it is also [manifested] among heterogeneous individual differences. Furthermore, that universal does not depend upon an individual.

The manifesting individual would not need to be depended upon; the sense is that the individual lacks the capacity to manifest the universal (*jāti*). For if it were to depend upon the manifesting individual, then in the absence of the cognition of the manifester, there would be no cognition of the manifested; for indeed, when a lamp or the like is not perceived, there is no perception of a jar or the like. Likewise here, in the absence of the perception of the individual, there would be no perception of the universal. Furthermore, why is the reversal of the roles of the manifested and the manifester—where the universal and its possessor [the individual] are treated as such—accepted?

For it is a rule that cognition does not operate upon a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without first apprehending its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); thus, the apprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*) must necessarily be accepted as occurring first, and through that [universal], the apprehension of the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, to maintain that the universal—which is intended to be the manifested (*vyaṅgya*)—is cognized even without the apprehension of the individual which manifests it (*vyañjikā*) is a contradiction.

He explains [the verse] with the words "yo hi" and so forth. Its own substratum (*svāśraya*) is that wherein the universal (*sāmānya*) is inherent; the sense faculty that perceives the universal and its conjunction—dependence upon these two constitutes what is meant by the phrase "that universal whose cognition depends on them. Regions devoid of a substratum are those occupied by individuals of a different class, and those devoid of any individual are empty spaces. In these, [the universal] is not perceived because of the absence of the aforementioned conjunction. This applies even for one who speaks in such a manner.

In some cases, when an individual is perceived, the contact between the substratum and the sense organ—which exists everywhere—is indeed an auxiliary factor for the universal (*jāti*). Therefore, due to that cause, namely the contact between the substratum and the sense organ, one who perceives that [individual] would perceive the universal as it truly is—pervading all locations—even within a particular individual. If it is argued that "the nature of the universal is visible only where the manifesting individual is present, and not elsewhere," he replies with the words "Not indeed" (*na hi*), etc. [The word] "in that" (*tasyām*) refers to the universal.

When a particular individual is perceived, the phrase "belonging to that" refers to its connection with the universal; for it is contradictory for one and the same thing to be both seen and unseen. Thus, having first accepted that the individual is the manifester [of the universal], the meaning conveyed by the word has been explained.

Now, in order to explain the passage beginning with “it does not depend on the individual” (*adhunā na sā vyaktyapekṣiṇī*), he says: “because it is manifested by the individual” (*vyaktivyaṅgyatvāt*), and so forth. Furthermore, its falsity has already been established by what was just stated. For it is impossible for one and the same thing to be both seen and unseen; therefore, this is merely a restatement of the opponent’s own position, presented while closing one’s eyes like an elephant, for the sake of pointing out a different fault. The term “of such a kind” (*tathābhūtasya*) refers to that which is logical (*nyāyyasya*). “Therein” (*tatra*) means in the case of the universal and its locus (*jāti-tadvati*). This is because there is an absence of a logical relationship between the manifestor and the manifested (*vyañjaka-vyaṅgya-bhāva*).

What is the reason? "In its own [empty] place," and so forth. For, in a location devoid of its own nature, a lamp or similar object is placed; [it illuminates] its own manifestation, such as a jar or the like. It is not thus that the manifestor (*vyañjikā*) manifests the universal (*sāmānya*) according to the logic already stated. What is the reason? Because of the opposite. For the opponent maintains that the universal is apprehended first even without having apprehended the individual (*vyakti*), since they admit that the apprehension of the individual occurs precisely through the gateway of the apprehension of the universal. And because the manifested is apprehended even when the manifestor is not cognized, the individual transgresses the properties of a manifestor.

He states this very point with the words "For how... and so forth. The connection is as follows: "That" refers to the individual (vyakti), and it would be the manifester (vyañjikā) of the universal (sāmānya). "By means of the cognition of that" means by the power of the perception of the universal. When the perception of the individual is admitted, it follows—this is the ellipsis—that both that individual and the universal would be manifested (vyaṅgya). The phrase "like a jar by a lamp" is a compound formed either through the separation of the rule *tṛtīyā* [Pāṇini 2.1.30] or through the rule *sup-supā* [Pāṇini 2.1.4].

Just as a jar is manifested by a lamp, so too is the individual (vyakti) manifested by the universal (sāmānya); this is the meaning of "attainment" (prāpti). For without the cognition of that—that is, without the cognition of the universal—the individual would be invisible in form. Others, however, say: in the phrase "and thus it follows that it [the individual] is what is manifested," the word "and" (ca) includes the idea that the universal is the manifestor. Therefore, the suffix -vat should be understood as derived from a copulative compound (dvandva), meaning "similar to both the lamp and the jar."

Because the rule regarding initial placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is subject to exceptions, the word *ghaṭa* is not placed first. Like a lamp, the universal (*sāmānya*) is the manifestor; and like a jar, the individual (*vyakti*) is what is manifested. "It follows" (*prasajyate*)—this is the meaning of the sentence. By this [phrase], he refers to the proponent of the universal. Having observed what effect would be impossible without a universal? "In this way" (*evam*) means by the method of statement. "Great effort" (*bahvāyāsaḥ*): because it cannot be accomplished, it is a cause of great suffering. (158–59)

"Mutually," and so forth, refers to the opponent. Because the reason is characterized by difference and the like, it applies to negative (vyatirekin) [inferences] that lack positive concomitance (ananvayin). The mention of "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is merely an illustration for a single-form cognition; the same applies to the word. This is because [such a cognition or word] would be impossible without a universal (*sāmānya*); thus, the connection is that the theory of the universal has been resorted to.

"How so? asks the Teacher. This was said in response to those who do not accept that words such as "cook" (*pācaka*) are based on action (*kriyā*). Without an undifferentiated object called a "universal" (*sāmānya*), how could a single word be expressive with respect to "cooks" and the like? By the mention of "expressive" (*vācaka*), the recurring cognition (*pratyaya-anvayin*) is indeed already included, because a word does not function without it. For this very reason, he states in the commentary: "there is a recurrence of the word and the cognition."

Uddyotakara also [argued]: "The recurring cognition regarding cows and the like arises from a cause distinct from the individual bodies and so forth, because specific cognitions are not accidental, just like the cognition of blue and so forth. That which is the cause is the universal (*sāmānya*). Having thus established the proof for the existence of the universal, he himself raised a doubt:

Now, you might think: "Just as words such as 'cook' are recurring [general terms] yet there is no universal called 'cook-ness'—for if it existed, it would have been manifested at the very moment the person was born—so too are there recurring cognitions with respect to cows and the like. This is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason. The meaning of the reason—"because specific cognitions are not without cause"—is that a cognition distinct from the cognition of the individual body arises from another cause.

Furthermore, it is not the case that every cognition of conformity arises from a universal alone. This being so, when one says that the primary instrument of the act of cooking is denoted by the word "cook" (*pācaka*), and that this primacy exists even in other cooks—thus avoiding the fault [of over-extension]—Uddyotakara has effectively admitted that words such as "cook" function even without a universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*). With this intention, the Teacher also said, "How... and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not logical that words such as "cook" (*pācaka*) should apply on the basis of the primary factor in the act of cooking. For if that were the cause [of the designation], there would be a recurring term "primary" (*pradhāna*), and not the word "cook. Therefore, he says: "For not... and so forth. "In them" means in those such as cooks. "Other" means distinct from the substance (*dravya*). Thus, there would be a single undifferentiated [property] among all capacities by which those various individuals, such as cooks, though being distinct, would be cognized as such—that is, as non-different—by means of a cognition.

This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication); thus they would be designated accordingly: in the case of cooks, [the action] characterized by placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth; in the case of readers, that which consists of recitation; and likewise for others as appropriate. If it is argued that there exists a cause such as a single suffix (*pratyaya*) and so forth for the action, then "that" (*sa*) refers to the recurring element (*anvayī*). The mention of the "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is merely an *upalakṣaṇa*, and the same applies to the word (*śabda*). Or else, by "another," he means the cause of the action, such as effort (*prayatna*) and so forth. He supports this very point with the words "distinct" (*bhinnam*) and so forth. "That" (*tad*) is used in the sense of introducing an external object.

Or it should be connected as "that action" (*tatkarma*), because the action that brings about maturation is distinct. By means of which transgression those individuals [are affected] in such a way, by virtue of being the cause for a non-differentiated cognition.

True; there is no fault whatsoever. However, it is because those individuals possess a single form (*ekarūpa*). For instance, a substance (*dravya*) has a single form because it is partless (*anaṃśatva*). If this very [single form] is the basis for the non-differentiated cognition, and not some other distinct property (*dharmāntara*) separate from it, then the cognition of distinction—such as "the cook's quality of being a cook" (*pācakatva*)—would not occur. Indeed, it is not logical for that very [substance] to be distinct from itself.

The form of that unmanifest is "its form" (*tadākāra*). That which is different from it is "the form of non-difference" (*abhedākāra*). That which possesses a particularity (*viśeṣa*) of that [form] is "possessing the particularity of the form of non-identity with it. The meaning is: possessing a form other than the form of substance (*dravya*).

This is what is meant: the cognition "this is a substance" arises from substances alone; however, the cognition of a "cook" or the cognition of a "negation" [arises] in a completely different manner. If that [latter cognition] were caused by the substance alone, then it would be indistinguishable from the cognition of the mere substance. Now, for what purpose are both stated as "possessing a specific form"? One should have said simply "not having that form," or simply "possessing a specific form."

It is said: when it is stated that [the cognition] has a non-differentiated form (*abhedākāra*), one might argue that even the cognition of negation—namely, "there is an absence of substance"—could be designated as not having that [non-differentiated] form; however, this [negation] is not accepted by the opponent as being based on another real entity (*vastvantara*), because only cognitions of specific qualities (*viśeṣapratyaya*) are held to be based on a distinct property (*dharmāntara*). Furthermore, if only the apprehension of a specific [quality] were performed, the cognition of Caitra would possess a specific character in relation to Maitra, and would not be "not having that form," since the very substance is what is communicated by the designation "Caitra" and so forth.

However, from the acceptance of both [positions], this meaning follows: that cognition, while lacking a substantial form, possesses particularity due to its contact with a real entity. Therefore, in that case, there need not be another cause distinct from the substance.

The Teacher says: "It has been stated. The connection is as follows: it has been stated how there is a distinction, such as "the cowness of a cow" or "the cook-ness of a cook," and likewise how the aforementioned particular cognitions [arise]. To the question "How has it been stated?", he replies: "According to their respective [objects]," and so forth. "Exclusion of other objects" (*arthāntaraviveka*) means the delimitation (*vyavaccheda*) from other objects. "According to their respective [objects]" (*yathāsvam*) means that from whichever exclusion belongs to whichever word according to its convention, from that [exclusion it arises]; this is the meaning.

For instance, the word "cook" (*pācaka*) denotes a substratum (*dharmin*), as it expresses that which is excluded from non-cooks while not excluding other distinctions. The word "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*), however, expresses that very same excluded entity while excluding other distinctions; thus, it denotes a property (*dharma*). Consequently, through the conceptual construction of a distinction between property and substratum, the ablative case of separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) is employed, as in the expression "the cook-ness of the cook."

In this way, since the word "substance" (*dravya*) is also conventionally established (*saṃketita*) with respect to a nature that excludes non-substances (*adravyavyavacchinna-svabhāva*), a cognition arises that conforms to it—that is, a cognition that follows the exclusion of non-substances and thus imitates the exclusion of non-substances. From the word "cook," however, a cognition arises that imitates only the exclusion of non-cooks; therefore, according to the exclusion [intended], a cognition characterized by a specific distinction is not contradictory even in a single case, following the convention. And this has been established in the discussion beginning with "the rejection or non-rejection of other distinctions."

The conclusion is stated with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth. Just as there is a difference among individuals, so too, because of the difference among actions, the connection is that action is not the cause of this cognition of non-difference regarding the "cook" (*pācaka*) and so on. Among those actions of the cooks known as "cooking," the universal (*jāti*) of "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) which inheres (*samaveta*) in those actions is itself the cause of the cognition of non-difference regarding the cook. [The author] refutes this with the words "No" (*na*) and so forth. It is understood from the context that the universal is not the cause.

What is the reason? Because it depends upon action (*karman*). Since it is inherent (*samaveta*) in action, action is a distinct entity from substance (*dravya*); [the universal] resides in that which is related to it. "A distinct entity" refers to the substance. "Like cowness (*gotva*)" is the illustration. For cowness is not related to Śābaleya and other individual cows; rather, it is the cause for the cognition of "cow" in various horse-classes such as Karka and others. The universal of action (*karmajāti*), called "cooking," is inherent in the actions known as "cooking. And those actions are not themselves what are called "cooking. The mention of "word" (*śabda*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Likewise, they are distinguished by the cognition "cook. The substance that is the locus of that action called "cooking" is denoted by the word "cook. And yet, the universal of action does not inhere in that substance.

Thus far, it has been explained how the word and cognition "cook," which have a substance as their object, function as causes for cognition by relying on the connection of the universal of action with a distinct entity. (159–60)

Now he states [the same point] by another method, beginning with "of that" (*tasya*), etc. "Another scriptural mention" (*śrutyantaram*) refers to a scriptural mention other than the word "cook" (*pācaka*). The use of the term "scriptural mention" (*śruti*) is merely illustrative, because it serves as the cause for other cognitions as well. He specifies this "other scriptural mention" with "cooking," etc. The word "from that" (*tataḥ*) means from the class of action (*karmajāti*); the intention is that [the class of action] is the cause of both the denotation and the cognition whose object is the action.

It might be thought: "The universal of action (*karmajāti*) does not produce the cognition of a 'cook,' but rather it is the action itself [that produces it] by virtue of its being the substratum for that universal of action. To this, he says: "Of that," and so forth. "Of that" refers to the non-differentiated cognition of a cook and the like. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has action as its cause. It has already been stated that "action is not the cause of this [cognition], because of the difference [between individuals], just like the individual [substance]," and so on.
But was it not said that even though action is distinct [from the person], it is the cause of a non-differentiated cognition by virtue of its being the substratum for the universal?

This has been stated, but it is incorrect. For even if there were a connection with a genus (*jāti*), the action would likewise remain distinct. With the words "Furthermore," etc., he states the reason for this accumulation: if that cognition of non-difference such as "cook" and so forth were admitted to have its cause in the action, then once the action had ceased, one could not call a person a "cook. Yet, [the term] is used on the basis of mere capacity (*yogyatā*). Therefore, this designation is not caused by an action that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because past karma also exists, he says: "Precisely because of its cooking," and so forth. If the past were to exist, it would be perceived just like the present; yet it is maintained that karma has attained the conditions for perception.

It might be thought: "The universal of action (*karmajāti*) inheres in the action, and the action also inheres in the substance; therefore, through a connection with that which is connected, the universal of action is the cause of the cognition 'cook' which has the substance as its object. To this he says: "Precisely for that reason," and so forth. "Precisely for that reason" means that because the action has perished, there is no direct connection between the universal and the action.

Nor is the universal (*sāmānya*) the cause of the designation and cognition of "cook" and so forth through an indirect connection by way of the action, because there is no connection with that [action] as a cause. If it is argued that even something unrelated can be a cause, he says: "No," and so on. "Unreasonable" means unrelated. The mention of "word" is an illustration; the meaning is that an unrelated universal is not the cause of cognition or the word. Why? Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even "cowness" (*gotva*) would then be the cause of the cognition of a horse. (160–61)

He explains [the passage] beginning with "For when it has perished" (*vinaṣṭe hi*) and so forth. Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*)—namely, the universal of action (*karma-sāmānya*)—is not inherent (*samaveta*) in the action, because that [action] no longer exists. Precisely because of the absence of the action, it is not even inherently present in the agent, such as a cook (*pācaka*), even through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*). Consequently, this universal has no connection whatsoever with the substance, whether through direct or indirect relation (*sambaddha-sambandha*). He anticipates another position with the words "therefore, past" (*tasmād atīta*) and so forth: "past" refers to that which has perished; "future" refers to that action which is yet to come.

"Of those two" refers to word and cognition. "Even an action that is past, future, or non-existent serves as the cause for cognition and designation"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. Why? Because of the phrase "of those two," etc. "Of those two" means of cognition and designation. He explains by means of the words "exists," etc. That by which a thing is "designated" (*upākhyāyate*)—that is, made manifest—is "designation" (*upākhyā*), namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*). That from which this [capacity] has departed is called "non-existent" (*asat*). Since the non-existent is devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency, how could such a thing be the cause of word and cognition? This is the meaning.

Now, if the status of being a cause is admitted even for that which is non-existent, then it would follow that it is actually existent and not non-existent. Why is this so? He says: "Because of the effect," and so forth. The word *lakṣaṇa* expresses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "That" means therefore. The past is that whose form has ceased; the future is that whose form has not yet been attained. Furthermore, the proponent of universals does not accept that anything other than the action—such as the individual instance (*vyakti*) and so on—is the cause for cognition and verbal designation.
[As it is said: "The individual instance is the substance which is the locus of the action."

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of convention and its maturation is intended. "Those two" refers to the word and the cognition. And thus, since the words "cook" and so forth, which follow [the individual], would lack a causal basis (*animittatva*), the existence of a universal (*jāti*) is not established. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that there would be either constant existence or non-existence of the word and the cognition. Why is the universal not established? He says: "Of that," and so forth. Because that universal is accepted as the cause for a non-distinct cognition and verbal designation. And this is just as in the case of the object "cook" and so forth.

Since those two [the universal and the particular] function in the same way with respect to cows and so forth as they do in the case of the "signless" (animitta), on what basis could a genus (jāti) be postulated?

With the words "power" (*śakti*) and so forth, he raises another alternative position: [it is argued that] power belongs to the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of the action. The mention of "sound" (*śabda*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); thus, power is also the cause for the cognition of "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth. He refutes this with the words "no" (*na*) and so forth: the power of "cook" and so forth is not the cause for the word "cook" and so forth. Why? Because since power is not distinct from the substance, it does not persist [throughout the series], just like the substance itself; and it is not admitted that a non-persistent object can serve as the cause for a persistent cognition or verbal designation.

Or, if it were admitted [that power is distinct], it would follow that the postulation of a "universal" (*jāti*) is without foundation. If it is argued that "power is indeed distinct," he replies with the words "for not," and so forth. For power is certainly not something other than the substance; if it were, then because that single power is employed in purposeful activities such as cooking, it would follow as a consequence that the substance—the substratum of the power—is useless as a cause. Its utility lies in that power which brings about the cooking and so forth.
Even so, the substance would be useful for the cooking and so forth through an indirect succession; this is the intended meaning.

"Why? and so forth says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). There is no purpose whatsoever in a capacity (*śakti*) that is a distinct entity. For instance, regarding the first capacity which brings about cooking and the like, there is a substance (*dravya*) by means of which that capacity is employed. If that capacity were also admitted to be distinct [from the substance], then, in order for the substance to be employed toward the capacity that effects cooking and so on, one would have to admit another distinct capacity separate from the substance; this would lead to an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*).

The meaning is this: even for that power (*śakti*) which is to be employed, another distinct power would have to be postulated, and for that one as well another, leading to an infinite regress. Therefore, it must be stated that without a separate power, the substance itself is what is employed in the first power that brings about cooking and so forth. And thus, if the employment of the substance in the power is accepted, why is it not accepted that the substance itself is employed in the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by cooking and the like? What is the use of postulating a purposeless power in the interval between the substance and its causal efficiency?

Since this is so, therefore by the phrase "the capacity for causal efficiency such as cooking," it is precisely the substance (*dravya*) that is being denoted. Of what nature is it? It is that which has "that effect"—namely, cooking and so forth—as its effect. And having considered that this substance does not persist through other individuals (*vyaktyantara*), there would consequently be no recurring (*anvayin*) word or cognition such as "cook, cook" based on that substance. The mention of the "word" (*śabda*) is, however, merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). (161–62)

If it is argued that in substances such as cooks there exists a universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*), which serves as the basis for the corresponding word and cognition, he replies with the verse beginning "the universal," etc. The meaning is this: if a universal such as "cook-ness" is accepted, then it would have to inhere in the substance at the very moment of the substance's production—even prior to the state of possessing the capacity to perform the act of cooking. And if that were so, even a child born on that very day would become an object of the cognition and designation "cook. This is the intended point.

If it were not [manifest] previously, then it would not be manifest later either, because there is no difference in that substance. Indeed, qualities such as being a cook exist at all times in the substance; however, because they were unmanifest previously, they were not the cause for words and cognitions. Therefore, he says: "manifest. The meaning is that it must have been manifest even previously, like existence (*sattā*) and so forth. Just as existence, substantiality (*dravyatva*), and the like, persist as long as the substance exists;
and with respect to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the substance was already situated in a suitable location even previously.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "athāpi" (now, moreover) and so forth. Because the inherence of that—inherence of the universal (*sāmānya-samavāya*)—in the real object which is the locus of the universal is non-occasional, that is, because it exists at all times. Strengthening this very point, he says: "For as many... and so forth. "In the object," meaning in the locus of the universal. Those universals possess the property of inherence, meaning they are capable of being related. "The arising" (*utpāda*) of this object; [the universals] "inhere together" (*samavayanti*) with that. The connection is made by changing the case-ending in the phrase "in this locus of the universal."

The meaning is that it is related with the substance at the very same time as its arising; such is the convention (*samaya*), the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the proponents of the universal (*sāmānyavādin*). As Uddyotakara said: "Prior to [the connection with] cowness (*gotva*), this is neither a cow nor a non-cow. What is the reason? Because those two qualifying cognitions (*viśeṣaṇapratyaya*) would not exist in the absence [of the universal]; and qualifying cognitions do not occur without a relation to a qualified object (*viśeṣya*); yet prior to the connection with cowness, the entity does not exist."

And that which does not exist cannot be designated as either "cow" or "non-cow. At the very moment an object arises, it is simultaneously connected with "cowness. Likewise, there is no connection with existence for that which already exists, nor for that which does not exist; rather, at the very moment the object [arises], it is connected with existence.
(Nyāyavārttika, fn. 1)

Now, if one disregards the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and instead postulates that the universal (*sāmānya*) comes into existence later, then upon that transgression—that is, the transgression of the established doctrine—the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of that universal would not possess inherence (*samavāya*) with it even subsequently, because there is no difference [in its nature] even then. Therefore, there would be no inherence with that universal.

Just as even for that which has the single nature of being a fruit, redness does not exist previously but exists later, so too is the case with the generality of "cook-ness" and so forth in relation to a person. To this he says: "Because of the deficiency in the nature connected to that," etc. This means because of the deficiency in the nature connected to the generality of "cook-ness" and so forth. "That" refers to the inherence of the generality. "Of that" refers to the person. For indeed, for one who remains in an unimpaired nature, there could not be a lack of connection to that [generality].

Furthermore, it is difficult to follow and hard to understand how a substance that exists at that very same time with a nature devoid of universal inherence (*sāmānyasamavāya*) and qualities (*guṇa*) should subsequently possess universal inherence. If the fruit, such as a mango, possesses a single, identical nature both before and after [the action], the same objection applies there as well. [The opponent might argue: "At that time, the substance is indeed connected to the universal; however, it is the universal that manifests [itself] by depending on the assistance of an action. (162–63)

And since that [manifesting agent] does not exist prior [to the action], there is no manifestation of the universal beforehand; therefore, he says: "due to the assistance of the action," and so forth. Action is characterized by cooking and the like. When its being a manifestor of the universal is accepted as being dependent upon the assistance produced by that [action], then—because that substance is non-momentary and thus unchanging—it has no dependence upon a cooperative cause.

If it were to undergo modification, then that substance would necessarily be momentary. And because it is momentary—perishing immediately after its arising—how could there be any action by which the action might serve as a manifestor of the universal (*jāti*) by depending upon that assistance? He explains this with the words beginning "by the assistance of the action" (*karmopakāra*). Action (*karman*) is an operation characterized by placing [the pot] on the stove and so forth. "Assistance produced by that" means the excellence (*atiśaya*); depending upon that, for something of a stable nature—which does not deviate from its prior nature and does not assume another nature due to the absence of excellence—what dependence could there be on an action that produces no distinction? None at all.

Alternatively, if an excellence produced by an action is admitted to belong to a substance, then because that action which imparts the excellence is momentary, another excellence—which constitutes the very nature of that substance being assisted—must likewise arise.

If the excellence produced by an action were not an inherent property (*svabhāva*) of the substance, then that substance would not be benefited at all by the production of something else [namely, the excellence]. Therefore, since a distinct excellence arises as an inherent property in each moment corresponding to each moment of action, that substance—such as Devadatta and so forth—would also be momentary (*kṣaṇika*). "From that" means because of its momentariness. An action characterized by cooking is performed upon a person who perishes in his own place of origin—that is, who perishes in the very location where he arose.
That which depends [on action] would be dependent on that action as the manifestor of the substance-universal, such as "cook" and so forth.

If it is asked: "But since the momentariness of a substance is established by way of the first and subsequent moments of action, how can there be momentariness in the absence of action?"—it is not so; for the meaning is that there is no other action to manifest the universal for those moments produced in connection with a [prior] action.
Therefore, it is established that there is no such thing as a real, ontological universal. (163–64)
The opponent asks, "How then? and so forth.

The proponent of the established doctrine replies, "Just as... and so forth. Just as in the case of cooks and the like, there is no universal such as "cook-ness" and yet the inclusive cognition and term apply to them, so too in other cases they will function even without a universal.

"Similarly," and so forth, says the opponent. [The question is: "How can there be the application of co-referential cognition and terms (*anvayi-jñāna-śabda*) to those [such as] cooks and the like, in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*)? Therefore, it was considered immediately thereafter that because co-referential cognition and terms apply even to cooks and the like, there must exist a universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) in them. However, such a universal as "cook-ness" and so forth is not possible in those cases.

If there is no recurring form (*anvayi-rūpa*), then how could those verbal cognitions now be without a cause? [The opponent asks: "No," and so forth—the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) replies. There certainly is a cause for those two; what is intended by the opponent is merely rejected. He says this very thing: "What then? and so forth. Those two do not have a real entity (*vastubhūta*) as their cause—that is, an external universal (*bāhya-tattva*). What then is their cause? To this he says: "According to their respective [objects]" (*yathāsvam*), and so forth.

Whichever awakening of one's own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) occurs, from that arises a corresponding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). From the arising of that conceptual construction, words come into being according to the conceptual construction. However, there is no real existence of an entity (*vastu-sattā*) for either the conceptual construction or its designation. This has already been largely explained as being based upon the existence of a recurring referent (*anvayi-padārtha*). And this must necessarily be accepted.

For instance, due to the force of their respective latent predispositions for synthesis (*samavāya-vāsanā*), by relying on their own philosophical tenets and in accordance with the latent predispositions of their cognition, they superimpose mutually contradictory forms through the penetration of conflicting natures. Thus, regarding all distinct entities, there occurs a continuity of both cognition and expression—such as "the world is the effect of Pradhāna," "the effect of Īśvara," "uncaused," or "mere conventional appearance"—even when viewing various different objects that are mutually distinct.

"And not there" refers to objects conceptualized through mutually contradictory forms, such as being the effect of *pradhāna* and so forth. "Based on that" means based on those [forms] for both word and cognition. Why does it not exist? He says: "Because of mutual contradiction," and so forth. The opponent says: "By way of non-restriction," and so forth. [Otherwise] every cognition and every designation would apply to everything. Proving this very point, he says: "For it is not without a cause," and so forth.

[Objection: But has not the lack of a cause for those two [conceptualizations] already been refuted by the statement beginning with "because conceptualization arises from the awakening of its respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*)"? Thus, this objection is without foundation. [Reply: The following is intended: An internal cause alone is accepted for those two; and since that cause lacks any proximity or distance [from anything], it would follow that it is the cause of all conceptualizations everywhere. For in the phrase "it does not exist without a cause," it should be understood that it is "causeless" because of the absence of an external cause.

"Not in the case of a non-existent cause," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). This means they do not arise when the cause is indistinct. For this very reason he says: "Because they have specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as their cause. The meaning of the whole passage is this: a latent impression that has arrived by way of seeing things as they truly are produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines its object as having that very nature; it does not do so in all cases. "Of such a kind" refers to the form possessing positive concomitance (*anvayi-rūpa*). And even in the absence of such an external cause possessing positive concomitance, it is not the case that there should be no conceptual construction; indeed, there must be one.

He establishes this very point with the words beginning "asleep" (*supta*) and so forth. Among the objects perceived respectively by one who is asleep and by one suffering from cataracts—namely, cows and the like, and hairs, flies, and the like—and among non-existent things such as a rabbit's horn and the like, there is the *saṃsthāna-vāsanā* (the latent impression of configuration). There is the *saṃketa-vāsanā* (the latent impression of convention) according to one’s own established tenets, [projected] by its power onto specific forms such as the "Primal Matter" (*pradhāna*) or "Effect" (*kārya*). Likewise, because of the arising of conceptualization—that is, the arising of a recurring conceptualization.

For in these aforementioned [examples], there exists no external, recurring form, because those perceived in dreams and by those with ophthalmia are non-existent. Their non-existence will be demonstrated in the third chapter (3.85). As for that which is superimposed by way of philosophical tenets, its non-existence has already been established by the statement beginning with "of two mutually contradictory [things] occurring simultaneously in one place," and so forth.

And those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of yours arise even in the absence of real entities, as in the case of things perceived in dreams and the like; thus, although objects may appear in all forms everywhere, they are in fact strictly determinate. He states the cause for this restriction with the words "only by way of distinction," etc. "Of those perceived in that very way" means of those perceived by way of distinction. This is because they are conceptualized only by way of distinction. First, in the state of sleep or ophthalmia, there is a perception by way of distinction of objects established within erroneous cognition.

Even for those things superimposed by various philosophical systems (*siddhānta*) at the time of hearing their respective systems—such as [the concepts in] "the horn of a hare" and so forth—at the time of learning the linguistic usage [of such terms], [these are established] because the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of linguistic usage is beginningless. And it has been said in this regard, etc., in the passage:
"The means of accomplishing a single object, such as the cognition of an object through a single unifying reflective awareness" (1.75).

Moreover, just as *dhava*, *khadira*, and other trees are mutually distinct, so too are cows and the like. Since the distinction is equal in both cases, when asked why "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) subsists only in the *dhava* and others and not in cows and the like, the opponent must simply say this: it is merely the inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*) of the *dhava* and others by which they alone are proximate to treeness, while cows and the like are not.

In that case, let that very power of being (*bhāva-śakti*)—by which proximity (*pratyāsatti*), characterized as the capacity of being, a universal (*jāti*) extends over and pervades a certain mass of objects intended as its own substratum—be the basis for the word and cognition that follow it. What is the use of postulating a "universal" (*sāmānya*), by means of which it is said:
"For the arising of cognitions is not held to occur without an object"?
"Because they desire the universal to be distinct from the particular, that [universal] is therefore constant;
for if those [particulars] were produced without it, they would be false in the absence of an object.
However, in this case, the existence of the universal without the other [the particular] does not incur any fault."

That is rejected. For the opponent is not being forced to accept that "just as the occurrence of a universal among certain things is desired without a [higher-order] universal, so too should the cognition of a universal be desired without a universal"—an admission by which the opponent's reply could be: "In that case, those cognitions, having arisen without it, would be false."

The intended meaning here is this: let that very proximity by which a universal functions among certain entities—even in the absence of a real universal, as in the case of another—be the cause for erroneous cognitions of concomitance and for verbal designations; what is the use of a universal? Thus, there is no fault.
Therefore, it is established that because exclusion alone is determined to be one, there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among entities, and not of anything else. (164–65)

On this point, the Sāṃkhya says: "Not cessation," and so forth. "The continuity of entities" (*bhāvānvaya*) refers to the uniformity (*ekarūpatva*) of entities. "The other" refers to that which is substantially real. [If this were not the case], the effect produced by one seed would not belong to another, such as the earth. Why? Because of the absolute difference between those two: the seed and the earth. (165–66)

He explains [the verse] with the words "If these," and so forth. "Of these" refers to entities (*bhāva*), just as from a single seed there arises one effect called a sprout. He establishes that very point with the words "For he who," and so forth. For that which is the nature of that seed to produce a sprout does not belong to another thing, such as the earth. That which is superimposed by the intellect and characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not a producer. Why? Because exclusion, which is characterized by the differentiation from others, lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).

Therefore, only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the seed is the producer; and that which has the nature of being a producer is alone the real entity (*vastu*). And since it is "that which produces," it is the specific characteristic that produces the sprout. [The phrase] "elsewhere" refers to earth and so forth. [If it were otherwise,] earth and so forth, which are other [than the seed], would produce the sprout. Regarding the words "for he... and so on: the word "for" (*hi*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*). "Of that" means of the seed. "Of another" means of earth and so forth. That [other thing], such as earth, would—by virtue of that production of the sprout—be non-different from the seed-nature, and thus non-different from that seed.

Thus, there is a continuity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānvaya*). Therefore, it has been incorrectly stated that "some things, despite a difference in their intrinsic natures, produce a single effect by virtue of their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), like the sense faculties and so forth. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) replies with the words beginning "If... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "even in one [of them]": that undifferentiated self (*ātman*) by which the collection of causes is held to possess the capacity for production—that self exists even in one among those causes. On the grounds that the effect is produced by that single [self], the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) would be rendered useless.
Objection: Even for the proponent of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), since all [causes] possess the capacity to produce at the final stage, other causes would be redundant.

Response: This is not so. It is only when those momentary factors are combined that they possess such a capacity, because their presence is dependent upon causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). For the opponent, however, who maintains the doctrine of permanence, that nature exists at all times; thus, other causes would indeed be useless. Therefore it was said: "It exists even in one [cause]"—the meaning being that it exists even in a state where other causes are deficient.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "yadi" (*if*). If a plurality of things (*padārtha*) were the producer (*kāraka*, i.e., generator) of a single effect because they possess a single nature, then that undifferentiated productive nature of those things regarded as causes would exist even when only one cause is present. Consequently, since the cause would be unimpaired in every state, even a single thing situated anywhere at all would be a producer. (166–67)

Strengthening this very point, he says: "Because," and so forth. Even when a single [cause] such as a seed is present, its non-differentiated capacity to produce that effect does not depart. The particularities (*viśeṣa*)—that is, the distinct individual instances—are what depart. For there is no difference in that non-differentiated nature of producing the effect, whether it resides in the seed or in other things such as the earth. Why? Because if there were a difference, the non-difference would be lost. For that non-differentiated nature, which is intended to be the producer, exists even in the seed alone.

Even when that [nature] persists, there is no loss—that is, destruction—of its undifferentiated form which is considered to be the producer [of effects], because the triad of qualities (*traiguṇya*) exists everywhere, at all times, and in its entirety. However, as for those particularities (*viśeṣa*), which are distinctions of state, there may be their loss, since there is no rule that they must necessarily coexist.

This has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. Otherwise, how could there be the disappearance even of those specific features (*viśeṣa*) that are distinct from the various states of a permanent entity? And since they are not productive, why are these specific features not accepted? To this he says: "Of the auxiliary causes," and so forth. Therefore, because the producer remains in its own nature even when a single factor such as a seed is present, the non-enduring specific feature would have to produce the effect even when only one [factor]—such as the seed—is present.

And yet, the production of the effect does not occur; therefore, even though the universal remains present among the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), if one particular (*viśeṣa*) is absent, the result is not produced. Thus, the arising of that [effect]—the arising of the product—proceeds from the particulars, not from the universal. What is that effect? It is the sprout and so forth. Of what nature is it? "Multiple," and so on. This means it is common to multiple auxiliaries, i.e., produced by multiple auxiliaries. "Even upon the absence of one particular" means even upon the absence of any one of the distinct types of auxiliaries. By this, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

By means of the words "again," etc., [the author] explains the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Therefore, the positive and negative concomitances of the effect pertain only to the specific instances (*viśeṣa*), and not to the universal (*sāmānya*). He says this [in response]: "But [if it were] non-deficient" (*nanv avikala*). Even when a single specific instance is present and the undifferentiated form is non-deficient, that effect does not arise. He analyzes this very point with the words "For the effect," etc. Arising from something is "existence" (*bhāva*); that itself is the property (*dharma*). That which possesses this is "that-which-has-existence-as-its-property" (*tadbhāvadharmi*).

Sometimes, when [the effect] does not arise, it is due to the deficiency of that which is considered its producer; nor is there a deficiency among the auxiliary causes for a non-different form that is intended to be the producer. Even when one [auxiliary] is present, there may still be a deficiency. When that universal form is complete, the fact that the effect does not arise indicates the non-productive nature of that universal. (167–68)

Now, it might be argued: "Is it not the case that it is not the universal (*sāmānya*) alone that is held to be the producer—such that there would be the aforementioned fault—but rather it is said that [the entity] is a producer by virtue of its manifold nature? To this, he says: "That totality," and so forth.
