And those particularities (*viśeṣa*) through whose completeness or deficiency the effect exists or does not exist—it is from those very particularities that the production of the effect occurs. "When that [is present]" means when the particularity capable of functioning as a cause is present, for the effect that comes into being. "From something other than that" refers to [the universal].

If [the cause were] a generality distinct from the particular, there would be the over-extension that everything would be the cause of everything. Since this is so, therefore only particulars are producers; the generality is not a producer. Consequently, because they are not producers, those very particulars are the real entity (*vastu*); the meaning is that they are ultimately existent (*paramārthasat*). What is the reason? Because an ultimately existent thing means that which exists in the ultimate sense. That alone is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*).

He explains this with the words "For this very [reason]," and so forth. The definition of a real entity (*vastu*) is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogyatā*); conversely, the definition of a non-entity (*avastu*) is its incapacity for such efficiency. The connection [of the text] is: "We shall explain [this]"—namely, by the passage beginning, "That which is capable of causal efficiency is here ultimately real" (PV 3.3). No object that is capable of all causal efficiency exists as a particular (*viśeṣa*), because a particular does not follow after other individuals. That which does follow [others] is of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, no effect is possible from that which is of the nature of a universal.

The conclusion is stated with the words *tasmāt* and so forth. "Because of the unfitness for causal efficiency" (*anarthakriyāyogyatvāt*) means because of the lack of fitness for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). "Precisely from that" (*tata eva*) means precisely from the particularity (*viśeṣa*), since it is from that [particularity] that the production of that [causal efficiency] arises. Thus, the non-productivity of that which is imagined by others has been established. (268–69) Now, in order to refute what was stated by the opponent—"The effect of one would not belong to another because of absolute difference"—he restates that very objection with the words *svabhāvānanvayāt tarhi* and so forth.

This has already been refuted previously by the passage beginning with, “In the alleviation of fever and so forth, some [cause] acts either together or individually” (1.76, p. 324). Nevertheless, this is introduced again for the sake of providing further explanation. If one considers that the nature which produces a seed or the like does not exist in another, such as the earth, then the latter would be a non-producer acting as a cooperative cause.

Furthermore, if it were admitted that a nature distinct from the productive nature could be productive, then, since there is no difference in their being distinct, even barley seeds and the like would become producers of the rice sprout.

He refutes this with the words "This is not so," and so forth. Although there is an absolute difference between the earth and other factors on one hand, and the barley seed and others on the other, yet some factor such as the earth is the cause of the rice sprout, while another such as the barley seed is not. The word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of completing the verse, or it has the sense of the particle *eva* (only/exclusively). What is the reason? This is the nature of things (*svabhāva*): if all things were to differ from that very nature which is the productive essence of a single entity, they would all equally follow as being producers [of that effect], because there is no distinction in their difference; or else, nothing at all would be a producer.

This objection might be raised: if these [causes], being distinct from a single productive self, were not possible to have a distinction characterized by a restriction regarding the production of that effect and not another, then it would indeed be possible; however, such a distinction is impossible. Therefore, because of the impossibility of such a distinction.

Even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities, due to some specific excellence of nature characterized by a restriction to a particular effect, a certain thing such as the earth is the producer of a rice sprout, while another such as a barley seed is not. Why is it that this excellence of nature for producing a rice sprout belongs to that auxiliary cause, the earth and so forth, and not to the other, the barley seed? If one asks, "From what does this very distinction arise? he says: "For not... and so forth.

One does not deserve to be questioned as to why fire burns and hot water does not burn, provided that it is hot, because this is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It would, however, be appropriate to ask only this: "From what cause does this possess the aforementioned nature? For there must necessarily be a cause for a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because if it were causeless, being independent [of causes], there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [such a nature] being restricted to specific places and so forth, resulting in the consequence that it would exist everywhere, at all times, and in its entirety.

Therefore, it is said that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this [effect], which is considered to have causes and so forth, arises from its own cause. Furthermore, the fact that this own cause possesses the nature of producing that [effect]—namely, the nature of producing an intrinsic nature of a cause of such a kind—arises from another of its own causes; thus, the succession of causes is beginningless.

For there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the distinction of causes for entities that are distinct. He states this very point with the words "distinct," and so forth. "From their own nature" means from the established state of things. However, he states that there is a subverting proof in the case of identity with the words "But [if there were] non-difference," and so forth. The meaning is that because they would be mutually non-different, upon the destruction of one, there would be the simultaneous destruction of all; and upon the arising of one, there would be the arising of all.

He explains [the argument] with the words "due to non-difference" (*abhedāt*) and so forth. Because the entire aggregate of all things (*viśvasya sarvasya padārtharāśeḥ*) is non-different by its very nature (*svabhāvena*), there would be no production and so forth through such a division as "the production of one and the non-production of another," "the persistence of one and the cessation of another," and so on. The phrase "like its own self" (*svātmavat*) means that just as for a single particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*), there is no production and so forth through division, so it is here. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [cases such as] "the apprehension of one and the non-apprehension of another" are included.

In the Sūtra, however, the mention of destruction and arising is for the sake of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is because non-difference is ascertained through that very illustration, such as the arising of a division and so forth. Otherwise, by what would difference and non-difference be characterized? "Even of that which has a single form" means even of that which has an identical form. "Distinction" (*vyatireka*) is division, the state of having a separate arising and so forth; that is the definition of difference. "Non-distinction" (*avyatireka*) is non-division, the absence of having a separate arising and so forth; that is the definition of non-difference.

Even though there is the possession of distinctions such as arising and so forth, why is there difference? He says: "Because of the contradiction between two contradictory [factors]," and so on. Because there is a contradiction within a single self when two contradictory factors—such as arising and non-arising—are simultaneous. It is not that objects possess only non-difference; rather, difference also exists. As it has been said:
"For every thing is differentiated by its own form, but not from one another;
and their mutual differentiation is in relation to their own specific nature (*svarūpa*)."

For that reason, [if it is argued]: "It is not so; there is no consequence of simultaneous arising and so forth," he says: "No," etc., which is the explanation of this very point. We certainly do not assert non-distinction—that is, non-difference—in every respect, such that there would be simultaneous destruction, arising, and so on.

However, regarding this distinction between the external and the internal, there is no separate essence characterized by specific states such as a jar or the like that is distinct from [the three qualities]; rather, it is none other than the nature of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). This is because the state of being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, the state of being a real entity (*vastu*), the state of being a substance (*dravya*), and the state of being existence (*sattā*) are found to persist everywhere. Therefore, the meaning is this: although there is no mutual difference between the state and that which possesses the state, there is indeed a mutual difference among the states themselves. Thus, it is due to the aforementioned difference characterized by states and so forth. (169–70)

In that case, since the universal is eternal, its presence is everywhere; however, it is accepted that particulars are subject to destruction. Consequently, when one particular perishes, that which remains as the universal essence cannot be a possibility for that [perished] particular. Due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, there would necessarily be a difference between the universal and the particular.

Otherwise, if it were admitted that possibility (*sthāna*) and impossibility (*asthāna*) have a single substratum, then even two contradictory properties would be accepted as residing in one and the same self; yet what other property could there be to differentiate them? None at all. Indeed, two contradictory properties are not accepted in a single locus, because they are distinct due to the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*).

For indeed, particularities (*viśe�sha*) are distinguished in every respect through their distinct arising and so forth, whereas the universal (*sāmānya*), due to the absence of distinct arising and so forth, is undifferentiated everywhere; therefore, he says "in all aspects," etc. This is because one accepts that the objects—particularity and universal—are respectively differentiated and undifferentiated in all their aspects. The phrase "merely a name" means that the designation "the particular and the universal are distinct" would be a mere verbal expression and not a reality, or else it would be a different name applied after having accepted a difference in the object itself, and so forth.

"Tad" means "therefore. These entities—whether particulars (*viśeṣa*) or universals (*sāmānya*)—are indeed mutually distinct. Of what nature? They are "not sharing a common fate" (*naikayogakṣema*), meaning they are superposed with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsita*). For this reason, there would be no cognition of a universal and its particulars; the meaning is that there would be no cognition connecting the universal and the particular to one another. And because of the absence of such a cognition, even linguistic designation (*vyapadeśa*) is refuted, since that [designation] is based upon cognition. Therefore: "There would always be a mutual dependence between the universal and the particular."

"But the universal belongs to the particulars, and they [the particulars] belong to it" (Ākṛti 9)—this is refuted. "That" means for that reason. This universal is a different entity from the particulars; it is not dependent upon the particulars. Why? Because that universal is not produced by those particulars.

The second point: This entity, which consists of particularity (*bheda*), is a different object from the universal (*sāmānya*), because it does not depend upon that universal—that is, because it is not produced by it—and because a permanent thing lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, it is not fit to be designated as "this universal belongs to this particular," nor as "this particular belongs to this universal."

This same undesirable consequence applies even if the universal is defined as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*): namely, that when one [individual] perishes, its nature remains, and so forth. For instance, when a *dhava* or a *khadira* tree perishes, the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtti*) certainly persists in other trees.

He refutes [the objection] with the words "No," and so forth. Here, the meaning is as follows: exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is twofold. One is the external [exclusion], which is superimposed by conceptual cognition through its own form and differentiated; it is that which is made an object by verbal expression. Precisely because this alone possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it is the object of purposeful activity (*pravṛttiviṣaya*), since mere appearance in cognition lacks causal efficiency. The other is that which is understood from the [external] object as the mere negation of others (*anyanivṛttimātra*). (170–71)

And as for this [objection] that mere exclusion of others is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), this is not a valid objection; or rather, the meaning is that because that which is intended by the Teacher is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is non-existent. Thus he says: "Because cessation is devoid of intrinsic nature, there is no conceptualization of 'possible' or 'impossible'."

When a particular (*viśeṣa*) perishes, does the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) remain, or does it cease? This conceptualization of its persistence or non-persistence is appropriate [only for a real entity]. "Of that" refers to the exclusion of others. [The properties] are connected to its own nature and do not follow the thing itself. One might then argue: "In that case, the conceptualization of the persistence or departure from its own form will apply to that universal (*sāmānya*) which is superimposed by conceptual cognition. To this he says: "And it is a cognitive distortion," and so forth.

That general form which appears as non-different from multiple objects is a distortion (*upaplava*) of the cognition of the universal; therefore, it too does not exist externally at all. Precisely because it is thus a distortion, for that reason the cognition of the universal is "not subject to refutation" (*adūṣaṇā*). The analysis of the compound is: "there is no refutation as previously stated in this [cognition]."

This conceptual cognition with a single form is without an object. If it is asked how this is so—since false cognition must have a false object—the author says: "Because," and so forth. Because it has a single form despite [the presence of] many things, there is neither existence nor non-existence of its object—that is, the universal which is the object of the conceptual cognition. Why? Because that object of false cognition does not exist. (171–72)

Having removed the charge of parity of fault (*samānadoṣatā*), he speaks—beginning with the words "But as for that" (*yat punar*)—in order to resolve the objection raised by means of another method: "For that which produces it" (*tajjanako hi*) refers to the nature (*svabhāva*) of that rice seed which is the producer of that rice sprout. And as for that form of the rice seed which is the producer of the rice sprout, how could earth and the other [elements], being distinct from that productive form, be producers? The word *tatra* is used as an introductory particle; or rather, the objection is answered therein.

We do not say that earth and other factors lack the nature that produces that [sprout], namely, the nature that produces the sprout from a rice seed. Rather, we say that the nature which is the producer of one rice seed does not belong to another factor such as earth. This is because entities do not share a mutual continuity (*ananvaya*). The phrase "another too" refers to earth and so forth. "Not by way of another's form" means not by way of the form of the rice seed. What is the reason? Because it is not that [rice seed]; that is to say, because it is not its nature.

And he says that there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in this regard: "Those [elements], earth and so forth, according to their respective [natures]" (*te pṛthivyādayo yathāsvam*). Since they are distinct from one another by virtue of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet produce a single effect by their very nature (*svabhāvena*), what contradiction is there? None at all, because of the absence of a subverting proof. However, it is not contradictory for earth and the other elements—which are devoid of the form of a rice seed that is considered the producer of a rice sprout—to have the rice sprout as their effect; therefore, he says: "of a single form," and so forth.

That nature which is the producer of a single grain of rice, if the earth and other factors were devoid of it, they would not possess the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of that rice seed and so forth. It is not the case that they do not produce that effect; rather, they certainly produce that effect. The analysis of the compound is: "that [rice] sprout is the effect of this [earth, etc.]. If, however, the capacity to produce the sprout belonged to the seed alone, then there would be a contradiction; but that is not the case. He says this with the words "by that very [nature]," and so on: by the rice seed itself, that effect called the sprout is produced. Furthermore, with the words "api ca" (moreover), he recalls what was stated previously.

"Because in the absence of even one [factor], the fruit does not arise; therefore, its production results from specific [causes]. By the force of this valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it was stated previously that [the other factors] do not produce the specific [result]. "By that nature" means by that generative form. That generative form which belongs to one thing, such as the seed, does not belong to another, such as the earth and so forth. "Not to that extent" means that the earth and so forth are not non-generative merely because they lack the specific form of the rice seed. "Even though there is no difference," etc., means that even among those differences, there is also a non-difference.

He explains this with the words beginning "It might be so," and so forth. By that general form (*sāmānyarūpa*), those particulars (*viśeṣa*) are non-productive. What is the reason? Because that general form, being eternal, does not perish. And this was stated previously in the verse beginning: "That nature does not depart [from the particular], for it is undifferentiated; indeed, the particulars are subject to departure" (1.167). (172–73)

Having established difference through the superimposition of contradictory properties with the verse beginning, “Destruction and origination would occur simultaneously” (1.170), [the author] says “Furthermore,” etc., in order to establish it also by means of a difference in manifestation (*pratibhāsa*). What kind of difference in manifestation is it? It is “not shared by others” (*ananyabhāk*), meaning it is distinct for each individual instance. By the word “also” (*api*), the difference in origination and so forth is also included as a differentiator; this is merely being added to what was stated previously.

Furthermore, the Vedāntin says: "The apprehension of difference is indeed caused by the apprehension of non-existence, and non-existence is not graspable by perception. Therefore, by perception only pure existence (*sattāmātra*) is grasped, not difference. As it has been said: "Perception arising with respect to a cow or a horse does not distinguish [between them]."

Therefore, he says: "This is not," and so forth. "Of that" refers to the proponent of non-difference (*abheda*). "Difference in the appearance of cognition" means a difference in the form of cognition. "And the attribution of contradictory properties" refers to [properties] such as arising and perishing separately. If that difference in appearance and so forth were admitted while maintaining the non-difference of entities, there would be no difference anywhere; yet difference is perceived by the world. And thus, if there were non-difference, this distinction of appearance and so forth—such as "this is an appearance"—would be like a single self.

Just as there is no difference in appearance and so forth within a single nature of pleasure, likewise this distinction between the external and the internal is merely a particularity that is mutually distinct. Of what nature is it? It is "one whose appearance and so forth are different" (*bhinnapratibhāsādi*). The analysis of the compound is: "that for which the appearance and so forth are different."

If it is argued that because a thing consisting of two aspects is apprehended by non-conceptual cognition, there is no difference [between the two], he says: "And not here," etc. "Here" means among these differences. "The other" refers to the second [aspect]. "By whose power" means by the power of the non-different appearance. Therefore, there is only distinction—that is, difference—and not non-difference. That very distinction is the real entity (*vastu*).
As for those other general properties (*sāmānyadharma*), such as "being an entity" (*vastutva*) and so forth, they are merely conceptualized exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) of that very [entity]. (173–74)

"‘That is the effect,’ and so forth. Because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the general term ‘effect’ (*kārya*), it is neuter; otherwise, since a specific [subject] was introduced, it would have been ‘that’ (*saḥ*). That very thing which has been described as both the effect and the cause in its specific form is called the ‘particular characteristic’ (*svalakṣaṇa*). ‘Having as their fruit the abandonment or attainment of that’: those activities whose fruit is, respectively, the abandonment or the attainment of that very particular—whether it be something to be rejected or something to be accepted—are thus described. And that [particular] is precisely the specific entity that performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).”
"Of that very [particular]" means that the difference of a particular from another dissimilar thing is a mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); it is not some real entity called a "universal. (174–75)

For if it were [present], being characterized by the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), it would be perceived as distinct from the particular (*bheda*). For indeed, since that universal (*sāmānya*) exists as an object and as a real entity (*vastu*), it is not logical for its form—being visible—to remain unperceived; that is, for its own nature (*svarūpa*) not to be grasped. Why? Because the cognition of difference regarding particulars is produced by the perception of that [universal]; for that which is not itself apprehended cannot be a cause for knowledge of another.

Thus, having first refuted the appearance-based (*prātibhāsika*) universal according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and others, he says "Moreover," etc., in order to refute the previously mentioned inferential [universal] according to the Sāṃkhya view. Just as for the Sāṃkhya, despite the lack of distinction in difference, not everything is the means of accomplishing everything; so too for the Buddhist, despite the lack of distinction in difference, not everything is the means of accomplishing everything. To which objection, then, does this resolution apply? He says: "As was stated," etc.

"Because of having a nature that produces that" means that earth and the other [elements] are distinct from the nature that produces a rice sprout. "Of this" refers to the sprout. Or, if one were to admit its status as a producer, then because there is no difference in their distinctness (*bheda*), everything would be a producer. To this objection, the answer has already been stated; however, this second point is now being stated. He asks, "What has been said [before]? and replies with the words beginning with "If. [The objection is: "There would be no distinction characterized by being a producer or a non-producer of a specific effect"—this is the objection that might arise.

He states the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathā*): "In the same way, even though there is distinction, it will be that not everything is the producer of everything"—this is the connection [of the words]. "By way of the nature of things" (*vastudharmatayā*) means by the power of the thing itself (*vastuśaktyā*). However, if non-difference among entities (*bhāvānām abhede*) is admitted, then for that [non-difference] which is accepted as being undifferentiated everywhere, both activity and non-activity in a single instance would be contradictory. (176–77)

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "merely through differentiation" (*bhedamātra*). The "cause" (*hetu*) is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*); the "conditions" (*pratyaya*) are the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been determined—that is, rendered capable of producing a specific effect—by their own causes and conditions, are so described. Because of that state [of being so determined], nothing else [could produce it]. Thus, those things considered non-producers would not be producers. Why? Because they lack that intrinsic nature; that is, because they lack the intrinsic nature of producing that particular effect. "Of that" refers to the single [nature of] the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).

In that case, it would follow that there is only one single effect; and "in that way" means by that very same undifferentiated mode. Nevertheless, when a rice seed produces a rice sprout, at that very same time, a barley seed does not produce a rice sprout. Furthermore, that which is the nature of the rice seed is the very same as that of the barley seed; thus, it would entail both activity and non-activity for a single entity in one and the same respect. Even though there is a distinction in the three constituents (*traiguṇya*) due to their respective arrangements as a rice seed and so forth, if you claim that activity belongs to something because of that distinction—

"If difference were the cause of non-action, then auxiliary causes would not act, because they too are mutually distinct. He explains this with the words beginning with "no," etc. [The question is: "Do all the forms of cognition belong to that single entity? The meaning is: "Certainly not," because [cognition] is based upon difference; the sense is that this refers to a successive occurrence (*paryāya*).

He explains [the passage] beginning with "atha" and so forth. Because all distinct entities (*bheda*) are employed in every effect either alternatively or sequentially; and this was stated when the view held that it is the distinct entities themselves—presided over by the power of *pradhāna*—that act as the agents of effects through successive transformations (*pariṇāma*). However, when the view is that the power of *pradhāna* itself is employed in purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) through successive forms of transformation, then this is said: "or of the power," and so forth.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: because of the utility of that [nature] which is characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), which resides therein, which was previously established as the object intended to be the agent (*kartṛ*), and which subsequently transforms into another form—that is, the form intended to be the factor of action (*kāraka*)—there is no such thing as a non-agent at all. "Bheda" means manifoldness; that *paryāya* (successive state) for which this is the substratum is described as such. How could there not be [transformation] for a single, undifferentiated entity? The meaning is that it is not logical for a single *śāli* seed to transform into the form of a barley seed and so forth.
By this, the phrase "how could that very entity [transform]" has been explained. (177–78)

Regarding what was said, "or from the power," he replies: "or transformation. How can there be a transformation—or the attainment of another state—of a power that is non-distinct [from its substrate], that is, a power that is undifferentiated? If it is maintained that the attainment of other states is indeed identical with the triadic nature (traiguṇya) itself, then how can any distinction whatsoever be admitted for the Pradhāna? For in that case, the unity of the Pradhāna would be lost.

Having thus refuted the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*), he now speaks—beginning with "Furthermore," and so forth—in order to refute the general property (*sāmānya*) as conceived by the Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsaka, Naiyāyika, and others, whether it be accepted as (1) non-different [from the individual], (2) both different and non-different, (3) different, (4) vertically pervasive (*ūrdhvavṛtti*) because it persists through all successive states, or (5) horizontally pervasive (*tiryagvṛtti*) because it persists through all individual manifestations.

Therefore, even the Digambara who maintains this view holds that there is no single universal (*sāmānya*) admitted in things such as jars and cloths because they are absolutely distinct; rather, it is this very substance (*dravya*), which undergoes transformation through successive states designated as "modes" (*paryāya*), that is called a "universal" because it persists through all those modes.

For instance, when a gold pot is broken and a crown is produced, that very same substance of gold, having perished in the form of a pot, arises in the form of a crown while persisting through its own nature as gold; thus, it is "transformative" (*pariṇāmin*) with respect to its successive states. This is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*). Precisely because it is transformative, there is no difference between the state and that which possesses the state; otherwise, if the state were different from that which possesses the state, transformation would be impossible.

When the substance gold is destroyed in the form of a jar, one who desires a crown experiences sorrow; when it arises in the form of a crown, the seeker of the object experiences joy; and when there is neither destruction nor arising in its state as gold, the seeker of gold maintains equanimity. Therefore, that which is characterized by simultaneous arising, passing away, and persistence is the definition of a real entity (*vastu*). As it has been said: "Seeking a jar, a crown, and gold, people undergo sorrow, joy, and equanimity, respectively, based on destruction, arising, and stability—each with its cause."

There is no sorrow without destruction, no happiness without arising, and no equanimity without stability; therefore, every entity possesses these three natures. One who observes a vow of milk does not eat curd, nor does one who observes a vow of curd drink milk.
"Therefore, because it does not possess the nature of a universal, the entity is threefold in essence:

it does not arise nor does it perish in its aspect as a universal, due to its persistence; yet it perishes and arises through its specific [particular] aspect, for its arising and so forth exist together with that particular in one and the same locus."

This [position] should also be understood as already refuted here. If one were to admit a real entity (*vastu*) that possesses both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), then absolute non-difference and difference would result. Because the universal—characterized by the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and so forth—is not distinct from the particulars such as pots and cloths, the universal would also consist of the particulars; thus, there would be absolute difference [of the universal from the particulars], since the universal [as something separate] would be non-existent. Alternatively, because the particulars are not manifested apart from the universal, they would be identical with it; thus, there would be absolute difference [of the particulars from the universal], since the particulars [as something separate] would be non-existent. In short, there would be no single entity that consists of both difference and the universal.

Now, if it is maintained that there is some kind of difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), to this he replies with the words "mutually," and so forth. If there were some kind of mutual or reciprocal difference between the universal and the particular, whose natures are respectively similar and dissimilar, then by that [difference] there would be only a difference between the two, like a jar and a cloth. Yet no universal is perceived as a separate entity (*arthāntara*). Therefore, no single object exists that consists of both the universal and the particular.

Even for the Digambara, if that [gold] is admitted to exist in the object, there would have to be either absolute difference or non-difference. When there is non-difference of the universal "gold-ness" from the various states such as the jar and so forth, then there would be absolute and total difference between the jar, the crown, and the like, because of the absence of the universal "gold-ness. Alternatively, if there is non-difference of the various states such as the jar and the crown from the universal "gold-ness," then there would be absolute non-difference—a state of absolute oneness—such that there would be nothing but the form of gold; this is the meaning.

Now, even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between the state and that which possesses the state, a distinction is nevertheless maintained on the basis of a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). For instance, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the universal "gold-ness" is perceived as persisting through all states, whereas the essential nature of the states such as "jar" is perceived as distinct. Therefore, since there is indeed a distinction between the state and that which possesses the state due to this difference in defining characteristics, [the opponent] says: "Mutually," and so forth.

If there is a difference between the two—the one whose nature is similar and the one whose nature is dissimilar—referring respectively to the state and that which possesses it, then there would be a mutual difference between them; that is, an absolute difference from one another, because those whose forms are respectively inclusive and exclusive do not coalesce with each other. Nor is there any other intrinsic nature by which their non-difference might exist, since a substratum (*dharmin*) consisting of infinite properties (*anantadharma-ātmaka*) is not perceived. The connection [in the verse] is "if entities (*bhāvāḥ*) are different. [They might be non-different] through a non-distinct self, such as that called *pradhāna* (the primordial matter), or some other.

By virtue of being "real entities" (*vastutva*) or by way of being "gold," those very particulars such as pots would possess that [universal], meaning they would have an undifferentiated nature. That which has as its essence (*ātman*)—its form (*rūpa*)—an undifferentiated nature not distinct from those primary principles (*pradhāna*, etc. is "that which has an essence with an undifferentiated nature" (*tadabhinnasvabhāvātmā*). Because of that state [of having such an essence], how could there be any mutual difference even among the particulars? There would be none at all. By this, absolute non-difference is explained.

Now, that single, common self of that particularity characterized as a jar and so forth does not exist; for a particularity, by virtue of its form as a jar and so forth, possesses a manifold nature. This being the case, it is not logical that even that category of generality—such as the "three qualities" (traiguṇya) and so on—should likewise exist as a common self through that very nature of particularity. The meaning is that because the generality is non-different from the particularity, commonality cannot be attained. By this, absolute difference is also explained.

"In the case of such a state" means if the nature of the primary cause (*pradhāna*) and so forth is accepted as being of a general character, then the essence of the primary cause and so forth would not possess those properties—that is, it would not possess the property of differentiation. The meaning is that it would not be possessed of that [property] known as "state," which is non-different from it; in other words, there would be a mutual difference between the state and that which possesses the state. Establishing this very point, he says: "For this... and so forth. The connection is: "It is not logical for this single intrinsic nature to possess both activity and cessation. "Abiding" (*sthāna*) refers to activity (*pravṛtti*).

"Disappearance" means cessation. For instance, while the power of the primary cause remains—given that the substance of gold and so forth persists—cessation is not admitted as long as there is persistence. By this, the argument that "there is a mutual difference between those two," and so forth, is explained.

With the words "no" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's objection: "It is not that there is absolute non-difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*); rather, if there were even a difference between those two—the particular and the universal—[it would be untenable]. He explains this with the words "for not," and so forth. The connection is as follows: in any given substance, there is no absolute difference or non-difference between the universal and the particular. Why? Because [they are] established through such distinctions as "the universal is the capacity [of gold], namely gold-ness and substanceness, while the particulars are the jars and so forth. This is because they are established by way of such a differentiation.

The Master says: "By which [nature]. This means that by whichever nature—characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*) and characterized by inclusion (*anugata*)—the distinction between those two, difference and generality, is established as "this is the difference" and "this is the generality," if the difference between generality and particularity exists by that very nature, then it exists absolutely. (179)

He explains by means of the words beginning with *yadi*. "That nature" (*yam ātmānam*) refers to both the inclusive (*anugata*) and the exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*). The connection is: "if there is a difference between the universal and the particular by way of that nature. Clarifying this very point, he says: "Because," and so forth. "Those two natures" (*tau ātmānau*) which establish the distinction refer to those two, namely the universal and the particular. "Their own natures" (*svātmanau*) means they are their essential nature (*svabhāva*). If those two natures—the inclusive and the exclusive—are distinct (*vyatirekiṇau*), meaning mutually excluded (*parasparavyāvṛttai*), then there is indeed distinction; that is, there is difference. What is the reason? Because of the difference in their essential natures. (179–80)

It might be thought: "Since it is precisely the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that establishes the distinction between the state and the entity possessing the state, it is the *svabhāva* that differs, not the entity (*bhāva*). To this he says, "For the intrinsic nature," and so forth. The meaning is that the intrinsic nature itself is the entity. And "in that case" means: when there is an absolute difference between the particular (*bheda*) and the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular would be devoid of any universal.

And the connection is that the universal would be devoid of distinctions; that is to say, because of the absence of a relation, the universal would not possess distinctions, nor would the particulars possess the universal—just as, for example, there is no mutual possession of those qualities among particulars such as jars due to the absence of a relation between them. (181)

He states the meaning with the words beginning “And if there were a difference,” etc.: because there is no relationship between the particular (*bheda*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) due to their being neither produced nor producing, yet they are perceived as related, it was stated [in the verse] that this is an error, namely in the passage “there would not be the cognition of the universal and the particular” (1.171). (180–81) (p. 336) Having thus refuted, by means of a common refutation, the doctrine of the vertical universal (*ūrdhvasāmānyavāda*) favored by the Digambaras and others, as well as the doctrine of the horizontal universal (*tiryaksāmānyavāda*) favored by the Sāṃkhyas and others, he says “Moreover,” etc., in order to refute specifically the proponents of the horizontal universal.

This is what is meant: for one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), there is no purpose whatsoever in investigating whether a universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct or non-distinct, because it is devoid of purposeful action. Rather, this person proceeds by taking as an object that very nature which is capable of purposeful action; desiring the fruit to be accomplished by that [nature], he acts out of a longing for the fruit to be achieved through that nature. It is with respect to that basis—the distinction or non-distinction residing in that which is capable of purposeful action—that these two are investigated.

Furthermore, for that [particular] which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is indeed an absolute difference from its own nature—that is, from its own form. And by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is indeed a state of generality (*sāmānyatā*) through a form excluded from those of a different class, insofar as it has the nature of a determined unity. To this extent, the investigation into difference and non-difference for one who seeks causal efficiency is concluded. Therefore, what is the point of investigating the difference or non-difference of a universal—which performs causal efficiency—relative to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? (181–82) But surely, for a person seeking causal efficiency, what is the purpose of a commonality even by way of exclusion, since it is devoid of causal efficiency?

True. It is precisely the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves that are called "universals" (*sāmānya*) by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). There is no fault here, because [the word] functions through the determination of oneness (*ekatvādhyavasāya*) with respect to them, so that [the listener] may act accordingly. Now, one might argue: "Since the particular characteristic itself follows after other particular characteristics, what is the use of this imagined exclusion? To this he says: "Because of the mutual difference between particular characteristics. If the form of a jar were present in a cloth, then one seeking to fetch water would also act toward the cloth. He states this with the words "action and so forth" (*pravṛttyādi*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the implication of the undesirable consequence of having identical arising, cessation, and so on.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "all indeed" (*sarva eva*). The meaning is that the particular (*viśeṣa*) alone—namely, that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*), which is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and which constitutes the very essence—is what is intended. With reference to what kind of entity (*bhava*) does [the word] function? For it is that very particular which performs causal efficiency. "In that way" means by means of words such as "cow" and so forth. For one who seeks causal efficiency employs a word with the intention of conveying the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), having unified the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpya*). The cognizer likewise understands it in exactly that same way.

Therefore, this was stated with respect to the operation of words based on the determinations (*adhyavasāya*) of speakers; however, since there is no appearance of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) within verbal cognition, the particular is said to be inexpressible, and thus there is no fault.

"But substance and so forth do not [occur] there" means that when cows and such are enjoined by words such as "cow," why is this? Because they—substance-ness and so forth—are designated separately from those cows and such by their respective terms, as in "the substance that is a cow" and so on. If one asks, "How then are existence, substance-ness, and so forth understood when the word 'cow' and the like are employed? he says: "Of the object," etc. Because of the non-deviation of the object—the cow and such—from that [existence, substance-ness, etc.], there would be a cognition of the universals from that object.

However, a word denoting a particular does not function with respect to a universal. This has been thoroughly examined by the teacher Diṅnāga in the *Sāmānyaparīkṣā* and other works, showing that words denoting particulars do not have their application in a universal. Here it is objected: With which kind of universal, then, is there non-deviation from the particular? First, that which is imagined by others simply does not exist. Furthermore, that which is characterized as the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), being a mere negation (*prasajya-mātra*), also does not exist. Nor is there non-deviation between the appearance in conceptual cognition and an external object, because the former is independent [of the latter].

It is said: the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, when excluded from those of its own class, is the "particular" (*viśeṣa*); that very same thing, when taken with respect to its exclusion from other classes through a difference in perspective, is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*). Therefore, because the universal and the particular are in reality one, there is no deviation between them, just as there is none between "being produced" and "impermanence. However, due to a difference in the operation of words, it is merely said that in some cases the comprehension is verbal (*śābdī*) and in others it is objective (*ārthī*). "Therefore" (*tad*) means for this reason, this person [acts].

The object presented by words such as "cow"—that is, the object brought near by words such as "cow" which serves as the basis for causal efficiency—is that which possesses a dual-aspect cognition through the introduction of another object, namely the universal (*sāmānya*), in the form of both the particular and the universal. Its "self" (*ātman*) is its own nature (*svabhāva*). This very nature, which is unique and not shared with anything else, is what is denoted by the word; this is the connection with what will be stated hereafter.

Having set before him and taken as his objective an object characterized by a dewlap and so forth, one who desires a specific purposeful action speaks of that very thing—beginning with "just as," and so on. The meaning of the sentence is to be established as follows: just as one who desires the carrying of a load or the body [of a beast] proceeds with reference to a cow; whereas one who desires an object possible in something other than a cow does not proceed with reference to a cow, but rather to a horse, which is possible in something other than a cow. To the question "What is that which is possible in another? he says: "Just as entering a battle," and so forth.

"According to their respective [denotata]" (*yathāsvam*) means that for each [object], there is a specific word that expresses it. It is not the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth. The connection with the word "indicated" (*codita*) is made by changing the gender [of the pronoun]. That is, by the indication [of cows and so forth]—that is, by the indication through words such as "cow" and so forth, of cows and so forth. "At that time" (*tadā*) refers to the time of activity on the part of one who seeks a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). The connection with the phrase "because the universal such as substantiality is not intended to be attained" is made by changing the case ending [of the noun].

But why is it not intended that the universal such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) be denoted by words such as "cow"? To this he says: "Because of the inclusion of cows and so forth," meaning that in common worldly usage, the word "cow" and the like has been conventionally established (*saṃketita*) for the cow and so forth. If it is argued that the universal such as "substance-ness" is denoted by the mention of the cow and so forth because it has the nature of the cow and so forth, he replies: "And of those which have become its very self. This means that since the universals such as "substance-ness" have the nature of the cow and so forth, they are [included] therein—that is, within that particular instance of a cow—by reason of their non-deviation from the cognition of the cow and so forth.

Because it possesses neither form [of universal nor particular], that is to say, because it lacks the nature of both universal and particular; and for that reason, only the particular (*viśeṣa*) is what is being questioned. He states this very point with the words "that very," and so forth: "A person seeking causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) interrogates that very entity, which is not shared by anything else, by means of modes of difference and non-difference. Even for the proponent of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the non-difference characterized by the exclusion [of others]—such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so on—is accepted as residing in the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, since absolute difference among particulars is contradictory, he says "of that," and so forth.

When the difference of that object which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is established by its very nature, then the non-difference of this particular, characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth, does not at all contradict it; for that [non-difference] is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*). Therefore, difference is ultimate (*pāramārthika*). Thus, the unity of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is imagined, and in this manner, difference and non-difference are indistinguishable for us. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In all cases," and so forth. The connection is as follows: there is difference by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from those of its own class and from other classes, because a universal characterized by exclusion is admitted.

If it is argued that non-difference does not exist by way of a universal in the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), but rather by way of a real entity (*vastubhūta*) itself, he says: “of that which has become its own nature,” and so forth. This means that if there is non-difference from the individuals by way of a real universal, then—as was stated previously—because particulars are not distinct from the universal, there would be a unity of the particulars; or else, like the particulars themselves, the universal would also be manifold. It is not being said here that the unity of particulars is established through the medium of a universal.

But he says—"by its own self," and so forth—to show that the very particularity [itself] constitutes the non-difference: "If there were non-difference of cows, horses, and so on, by their own particular forms, then a person desiring that purposeful action characterized by carrying, milking, and the like, for which that cow-substance is the basis—[would act] equally," meaning with the same determination toward both, since the state of being a cow has been ascertained in both, namely, in the cow and in the horse.

For even a single object, such as a cow, which is intended to be a cause, performs that purposeful action—consisting of the nature of carrying, milking, and so forth—precisely because it possesses that nature, that is, because its very nature is to perform that specific purposeful action. Since another entity, such as a horse, other than that cow-substance, would likewise possess the same nature of performing those actions of carrying and milking, why does that horse not also perform the purposeful action accomplished by the cow? (182–83)

"By this very [means]" refers to the proof of the difference between all things. The *kṣapaṇakas* are shameless, being devoid of modesty due to their nakedness. Because improper speech is contemptible, he says "something" (*kim api*)—namely, that which is indecent and vulgar. As for what they prattle—that everything has the nature of everything, yet everything does not have the nature of everything—that too is refuted because of the possibility of absolute [difference]. This is because there exists only one extreme, namely the mode of absolute difference. (183–84)

[Objection: Is it not the case that for the Digambaras, everything is of the nature of everything, and thus [the view] that "everything is not of the nature of everything" is not their doctrine? For what purpose, then, is this stated by the Teacher?

[Reply: True; however, according to their actual doctrine, it has already been refuted previously by [the verse] beginning with, "Then absolute difference and non-difference would both result" (1.178).

As for what was stated previously: just as the universal "gold-ness" (*suvarṇatva-sāmānya*) is postulated because of the existence of a persisting cognition of "gold" in things such as bracelets and armlets, why is a single universal "substance-ness" (*dravyatva-sāmānya*) not likewise accepted because of the existence of a persisting cognition of "substance" in things such as pots and cloths? That it is not so accepted is intended to show that even though a non-differentiated cognition exists, one should not postulate a universal in the case of bracelets, armlets, and so forth. This is the purport of that statement.

It may be that a camel is curd, because of its identity [with it] in terms of its nature as a substance (*dravya*) and so forth. It may not be curd, because the state of being a camel is distinct from the state of being curd. The explanation of the term *aślīla* as "inappropriate" is incorrect; for that [explanation] is improper. The sense is that it is "vulgar" (*grāmya*) due to its unsuitability for learned people, since *aślīla* is a synonym for *grāmya*. "Neither to be rejected nor to be accepted" means neither to be abandoned nor to be grasped. Why? Because there is no final determination (*apariniṣṭhāna*).

For if something were determined as a means to happiness and another as a means to suffering, then they would respectively be to be abandoned or accepted. But that is not the case, because everything possesses the nature of everything else—and yet it is not the case that everything possesses the nature of everything else. For this very reason, it is confused, since it is impossible to grasp even a single distinct nature.

This is what is meant: when there is no difference between the state (*avasthā*) and that which possesses the state (*avasthātadvat*) in every respect, yet there is mutual difference due to their states, then this fault arises; thus he says, "or else other than that" (*tadanye vā*). This means: either in the case of a mutual connection with that very difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*), or because a substance whose intrinsic nature is curd and so forth would follow through identity (*tādātmya*) in things such as camels.

Everything possesses a dual nature. The mention of "both" is intended to indicate multiplicity; for when that [multiplicity] exists, its specific distinction is established—such as "a camel is a camel and not curd," and "curd is curd and not a camel"—thereby precluding such [confusion]. Why would a person commanded, "Eat the curd," not run toward a camel to eat it? Furthermore, since a camel is also a substance (*dravya*) non-different from curd, it too would be curd. Nor can it be said that it is "only this" [and nothing else], for the extremist view (*ekāntavāda*) that "a camel is only a camel" is rejected.

If [the substance] were that very same thing, then just as curd would be a camel, so too would curd be a camel; for curd is related to the camel through identity by virtue of the property of substantiality (*dravyatva*), which is non-different from the camel. Nor is it the case that it is *only* that, such that curd is simply curd, whereby another thing, such as a camel, would also be curd. By this, the fact that everything possesses both forms is explained.

He explains "because of the exclusion of its particularity" with the words "of these two," and so forth. In either case, there would be a particularity [confusion] between curd and camel: either the absence of the form of curd would belong to the camel, or the form of the camel—which is impossible for curd—would be restricted to the very nature of the camel. The same should be said regarding curd as well.

First, the impossibility of the former [the universal] is stated by the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth. Thus, the connection is as follows: there is no distinction whatsoever between two things, such as curd and a camel. Regarding the phrase "even of one," this refers to either the curd or the camel; [it means] because of the absence of that form—namely, the absence of the form of the camel and the absence of the form of the curd.

He states the absence of a second mode as well: "of its own nature" (*svarūpasya*), etc. This refers to the absence of either the nature of a camel—which does not become curd—or the nature of curd—which does not belong to a camel. Because there is an absence of that which is restricted to its own [specific] nature—that is, restricted to the nature of a camel and restricted to the nature of curd—[the following would follow]: suppose there were some excellence (*atiśaya*) between curd and camel, by virtue of which excellence a person, when commanded "Eat the curd," would act with discrimination; that is, he would proceed toward the curd alone, avoiding the camel.

This is what is meant: just as the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) of curd and a camel are mutually distinct, so too, if a difference between substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) is admitted on the basis of a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*), then that very excellence of form (*rūpātiśaya*) which constitutes the curd does not exist elsewhere in the camel. Nor does "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) appear as something distinct from the curd and the like. By this means, every entity is neither [of the two], being devoid of both generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*); it is merely "the other" (*param kevalam*). Unity (*ekatva*), however, is a conceptual construction (*kalpita*).

"Of these two" refers to the curd and the camel. "Thus commanded" means commanded [with the words] "Eat the curd. Curd is a modification of milk; it does not exist elsewhere, namely, in the camel. That very excellence belongs to the curd. Of what nature is it? It is the object of the activity of one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). It is the object of the activity of that person who seeks the purposeful action to be accomplished by the curd. What is the reason? [It is because] "that result," and so forth. The result to be accomplished by the curd is itself distinguished from others, and thus it is a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*).

The nature of that [substance] as a cause is characterized by its state as a material cause (*upādāna*); this refers to the very thing which, being considered as curd, possesses such a nature. And "of such a kind" refers to the aforementioned nature of curd. "Elsewhere" means on a camel. Why? Because one who desires curd does not engage with that camel. (185–86)

"Being the self of all" means being of a single nature. "Distinct" refers to two things with fixed meanings: cognition and verbal expression; that is, knowledge and sound. Because of their absence—that is, because of the absence of distinct cognitions and words—there is the impossibility of a doctrine of synthesis (*saṃhāra*) regarding distinctions, which is to say, a doctrine of unification. This refers to the synthesis or designation of two things perceived or heard as distinct as being one, such as saying, "The camel is curd," and so forth.

He explains [the verse] with the words "so 'yam" and so forth. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: not perceiving even in some instance—whether in curd or in a camel—a single, determinate form, how could one designate objects by means of cognition? He asks, "By what kind of cognition? and replies with the words "unmixed," etc. An object in which another form is mixed is described as such; that cognition which possesses this [object] is "possessing a mixed other-form. This means, in effect, that it must be one that grasps distinct objects. Or else, how could one express [them]?

It has been stated that [the object] is denoted by a sound through a convention fixed for each respective object. To the question, "Why should one not be convinced [of this]? he says: "Because there is no differentiation among entities. Thus, the doctrine of their synthesis—that is, the doctrine of the synthesis of distinctions—would not exist; such as the [absurd] claim that "it might be a camel" or "it might be curd," and so forth.

Furthermore, if one were to first apprehend the curd and the camel as unmixed and then combine them—thinking "it may be a camel" and "it may be curd"—even then, because the cognition associated with a single form (whether by way of the form of the camel or the form of the curd) apprehends an unmixed aspect in a particular camel or a particular portion of curd, the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those two, the curd and the camel, is produced solely by the difference in their manifestation (*pratibhāsa*). Regarding the phrase "one or many," etc.: the object of the determination of multiplicity is the difference in manifestation.

The phrase "the single establishment of the difference in appearance" is to be applied [here]. Furthermore, yogurt and a camel have distinct appearances as their objects; and this being so, a single entity is neither the camel nor the yogurt, nor does it possess the nature of both—this is the analysis of the compound *tadubhayarūpa* (having the form of both), meaning a form consisting of both yogurt and camel. Thus, the doctrine of "maybe" (*syādvāda*) would be nothing but a false doctrine. Regarding the "characteristic of difference": this refers to the moment of exclusion (*vyāvṛttikṣaṇa*). Particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves, which are excluded from those of a different class, are called "universals. "By nature" means by their own essence (*svabhāva*). From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand that they share a single result, such as the fetching of water and so forth.

With the words "Let it be so," and so forth, the Teacher anticipates the opponent's objection: "The differentiation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities—that is, of things—is not at all an exclusion from others within their own nature. In that case, regarding those things which are devoid of any designation (*nirupākhyeṣu*), how can words have as their object the differentiation of intrinsic nature, which is to say, they have as their object exclusion?"

One might object: "Since there is no application of words at all to things that lack any defining characteristic (*nirupākhya*), for what purpose is this doubt raised? To refute this, the Teacher says: "There must necessarily be an application of words to them. Regarding this, the commentators explain that the challenger (*codaka*) asserts: "It is not possible for one who maintains the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) to say that there is no application of words to things lacking defining characteristics; therefore, there must necessarily be an application of words to them."

By this sequence, the negation of place and time is indeed performed with respect to all entities. Likewise, the non-expression of the nature of the relation has been stated. Thus, as for the passage beginning, "Furthermore, since there is no employment of meaningless words when that object is negated, and since a negative particle (*nañ*) without an object is not employed," and so forth—the text to be cited hereafter—would, from the perspective of the opponent, be non-expressive.

Therefore, the Teacher himself establishes the application of words to things that lack any defining characteristic (*nirupākhya*) through the passage beginning with, "In those [things], there must necessarily be the application of words," and so forth. Why? Because if things lacking any defining characteristic were not established in any way whatsoever as objects of cognition or verbal expression, then in all cases—whether regarding the affirmation or the negation of an object—it would be impossible [to speak of them]. If, however, there were cognition and verbal designation of the negation of some non-existent form in a certain instance, then, by the exclusion of that negated form, there could be an affirmation of the object.

"Likewise" refers to affirmation and negation (*vidhi-pratiṣedha*). That conventional usage which has affirmation and negation—namely, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—as its basis is described as "thus. He states that very nature of conventional usage with the words "heat," and so forth. "Fire has heat as its intrinsic nature" is a conventional usage based on positive concomitance; "it is not non-hot" is one based on negative concomitance. By the word "also" (*api*), he indicates that even this most well-known worldly convention would not exist: for the determination of "heat" occurs through the exclusion of "non-heat."

And since that non-hot [entity], characterized by the absence of heat, is established in some way, how could "hot" be established through its exclusion? To this he says: "By another intrinsic nature," and so forth. The absence of heat itself is "another" (different) from the intrinsic nature of heat; because it consists in the negation of that [heat], it is called "another intrinsic nature. For this very reason, the statement "of that which is non-existent" is appropriate.

Now, a specific nature cannot be established as the object of conceptual cognition or of a word in any way whatsoever, because it is not distinct from other natures. Since nothing that is not hot is perceived—and thus not ascertained—the nature of fire, which is defined by the exclusion of that [non-hot], is likewise unperceived and unascertained. As it is with the nature of fire, so it is with every entity. Consequently, the world would be utterly deluded, its form remaining unascertained.

It might be argued as follows: "In that case, there is no negation of something non-existent regarding fire and so forth, such that one would be compelled to maintain that activity must necessarily occur even toward a non-entity. Rather, it is a real entity indeed—namely, the thing called 'touch' which is not hot—that is being negated as being a different thing from fire."

"How so? asks the Teacher. "Because of the statement 'it is existent,' existence is intended; because of the statement 'it is negated,' non-existence [is intended]. And how can there be that which is called both existent and non-existent? The opponent replies with the words beginning with "no": "In that regard, by the statement 'heat does not exist in fire,' we mean that everywhere heat is non-existent. For if this were said, having first asserted existence and then subsequently negating existence everywhere, one would be asserting both existence and non-existence in a single place."

We say only this: that there is no non-hotness in that fire. Therefore, the absence [of something] elsewhere than where it exists is not contradictory. And he says that this very thing is "place" (*deśa*): "it is not here" is the negation of place; "it is not now" is the negation of time; "it is not in this manner" is the negation of the property (*dharma*). [The negation of] the substratum (*dharmin*)—why? Because if that [property] is negated, the substratum is negated; for, since its object is the substratum, the word would lack an object and thus could not function.

Furthermore, since the word *dharma* does not apply [to non-existence], the object (*viṣaya*) of that negative particle (*nañ*) would remain unspecified; and because such a [negation] is never employed, the object of the negation must necessarily be presented by words such as "this" (*idam*), in the form "this is not here. Otherwise, it would not be known what the object of this negation is. All of this has been set forth as the opinion of Uddyotakara and others.

"The same [applies] there as well," says the Teacher (Ācārya). "There too," says the Teacher. By the negation of place, time, and property (*dharma*) in the passage beginning with "there too," there is a negation of place and so forth because they exist. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), time is included. The plural number is used because of the distinction between individual instances. "Of the object" (*arthasya*) means of the property (*dharma*); it is because it exists in some cases. However, the term "object" (*artha*) does not refer to the substratum (*dharmin*), because even the opponent does not accept the negation of the substratum. It might be argued: "Neither is the negation of place and so forth being made, nor is there a negation of heat; rather, what is negated is the connection of fire with that which is non-hot."

"But not so," says the Teacher [Dharmakīrti]. "Even in the negation of that" means even in the negation of the relation; the fault is the same because the relation, like the property (*dharma*), is not negated. He proves this very point with the words "even when it exists," and so forth. When a relation does not exist, there is no application of the word; for, by the word "etcetera," it is implied that the negative particle (*nañ*) is not employed when its object is not specified. Alternatively, the fault is the same. How? It should be explained thus: since you yourself negate that negation which occurs regarding something non-existent, [the fault remains].

How is there a negation? He says: "It exists," and so forth. This refers to the negation of the relation of this [entity] which is non-existent. "In that same way" means like the relation; there is a negation of the substratum (*dharmin*) as well.
"No," and so forth, is the opponent's reply: "By the very words 'the relation does not exist,' there is indeed no negation of the relation."

This is what is meant: just as there is no denotation of the relation itself by its own word in its essential form, so too it is in the case of negation. He states this very point: "What then? When there is a statement of negation such as 'there is no jar here' [in this place], or 'not now' [at this time], the cognition arises that 'this jar has no relation with this place,' or 'it does not exist at this time. Likewise, when it is stated, 'the jar does not exist in this manner,' the cognition arises that 'the jar does not possess this attribute (*dharma*). This occurs when such a cognition is present."

"Even so," says the Teacher. By the words "not now" and so forth, how is the relation negated? It is until the cognition arises that for this person there is neither a relation nor a property. When there is the negation "not here" or "not now," the cognition is that the relation does not exist. When there is the negation "not thus," the cognition is that the property does not exist.

[Objection: Is not the negation of a property (*dharma*) also simply the negation of a relation? For [the property] is the negation of the relation between the property and the substratum (*dharmin*). [Response: True. However, because relations are distinguished as being characterized by either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), they are stated separately as "relation" or "property. Furthermore, if this notion "it has no relation" exists in some way, then the existence of a relation and so forth would be possible; why then [is it said] "in the case of absences," etc.? The word *tathā* implies the meaning of the word *yathā*, because of the constant connection between the pronouns *yat* and *tat*.

Just as there is an absence of the cognition "it does not exist" when [the locus] and other factors are present—because the cognition of non-existence is contradictory to what is present—so it is with respect to absences themselves. This is because we do not admit the occurrence of the cognition "it does not exist" in the case of a non-existent thing. Therefore, the cognition "this is not here," and so forth, does not arise from the perception of the absence of a relation; for if that [cognition of the absence of a relation] were absent—that is, if there were no perception of the absence of a relation—it would not occur. Alternatively, "that" refers to the perception of the absence of a relation, and "its absence" refers to the absence of that relation.

Or, regarding its non-existence—that is, the non-existence of the relation—if such a cognition of the non-existence of the relation exists for a person, then for that person who possesses such a cognition, by whom can the word whose object is the non-existence of the relation and which is produced from the cognition of that non-existence be prevented? If it is argued that "the non-existence of the relation is the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), but not of words," he says: "For that very thing," and so forth. That which is not the object of mental deliberations (*vitarka*) is precisely that which is not the object of words.

The meaning is that the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is necessarily the object of language. And if these [concepts] have proceeded, they are *vitarkas* (initial thoughts). But surely, regarding blue and so forth situated in front of one, there is a conceptual construction such as "this is blue"; its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and yet the particular characteristic is not denotable by language. To this he says: "For not... and so forth. "The inexpressible object" refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Because conceptual construction is the topic at hand, conceptual cognitions are understood [by the term "they"]. "They strive" means they take it as their objective support (*ālambante*). Even though the particular characteristic is present, the conceptual cognition always possesses only a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*).

However, this misconception of the dull-witted—that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the cause of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—arises from the false impression that conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions occur simultaneously. This has already been examined by the author of the treatise in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

Now, if it is argued that because [the relation] is made an object by a conceptual cognition, its non-existence must be stated, then in that case, the relation itself would also have to be stated, since it too is made an object by a conceptual cognition. If you accept this, then one might ask: how is it that the Teacher Diṅnāga stated that the relation is inexpressible? To this, he says: "Of the relation," and so forth.

"By its own form" means by way of a relation (*sambandharūpeṇa*). A relation is characterized by mutual dependence between two related entities; thus, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a relation is a mere state of being (*bhāvamātra*), not a substantial entity (*adravyabhūta*). There is no word that denotes it by that very form. For the word "relation" (*sambandha*) must be regarded as its denoter, and when that word is employed, it implies [the question] "of which two? (*kayor iti*).

In that context, when it is stated "the relation between the king and the man," the relation is the cause of the distinction expressed by the phrase "of the king and the man. At that time, that relation is perceived in the form of a relatum. Thus it is said: "by means of the designation as a relatum," and so forth. When there is the expression "the relation between the king and the man," because the relation—extracted from its specific forms—is presented to the intellect as a relatum by means of the two, the king and the man, who are mutually dependent.

"Unperceived according to its intended meaning": although the relationship characterized by mutual dependence—as in "the king's man"—is desired to be known in that form, it is not perceived as such. Therefore, even though this relationship is being perceived, because it is [only] the form of the relata themselves according to the aforementioned rule, it is not denoted by the word "relationship."

Therefore, the objection does not apply to the relation in the same way it applies to non-existence (*abhāva*). The meaning is this: just as the absence of a relation is said to be made an object of cognition by the mind, it is not so said to be denotable with respect to the relation itself. For the absence of a relation is made an object of cognition by the mind in its own form, and it is likewise expressed by the word in that very way. But a relation is not grasped in its own form, nor is it denoted [as such]; for it is only when it has assumed the form of the related entities that it is made an object of cognition and denoted. Thus he says:
Since the relation is not an existent entity, its form is not perceived;
nor can the relation ever be denoted by its own intrinsic nature.

Therefore, it is established that the object of conceptual construction must necessarily be expressible. Consequently, if there is the notion that "there is no relation," then the word arising from that [notion] would indeed function; and thus, it follows that the word has non-existence as its object. Now, if one does not accept that the relation is made the object of the cognition "it does not exist" for fear of this fault, then in the case of "there is no jar here," what is being negated? It cannot be the place and so forth, because those exist; nor can it be the relation, because its absence is not perceived. Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Furthermore, regarding one who asserts that non-existence (*abhāva*) is the denotable object, this proponent of the expression of non-existence, while responding—that is, rejecting—the claim by saying "non-existence is not expressible," how could he respond if he were himself not speaking? For it is not possible for one who utters the word "non-existence" to establish the expressibility of non-existence.
