Now, if he accepts the verbal expression of non-existence, then, given that such an expression of non-existence is admitted, how can non-existence be unspoken? It is indeed spoken.

If it is argued that "non-existence is not expressible" because it is expressed by that very word "non-existence," and that the negation is made by restating what others claim regarding the expressibility of non-existence—namely, that "non-existence is not expressible, therefore there is no fault"—[we reply: ... [The argument continues as follows: ... [This is] not so, because the expression of that [non-existence] occurs through the very word "non-existence. Furthermore, if one were to negate the expressibility of non-existence by restating what another says about its expressibility, [one might say], "Non-existence is not expressible; therefore, there is no fault. But this is not correct. Why? Because even by the word "non-existence," that [non-existence] is indeed expressed. If it were not expressed by that word, then the word "non-existence" would be meaningless, like the word "hare's horn. Therefore, since it is expressed by that very word, the fault remains. Thus, the statement "non-existence is not expressible" is itself an expression of non-existence. Consequently, the opponent’s position is untenable. Therefore, the objection raised against us does not apply. This concludes the explanation of the refutation of the view that non-existence is not expressible. Now, the refutation of the view that non-existence is expressible will be stated. What is that? It is as follows: [The opponent claims: "Non-existence is expressible, because it is the object of the cognition 'this is non-existent'. To this we reply: No, because it is not perceived. That is to say, non-existence is not perceived, because it is devoid of color and shape (*varṇasaṃsthāna*). Since it is not perceived, it cannot be the object of a cognition. For it is observed that only that which is perceived can be the object of a cognition, such as color and the like. However, non-existence is not perceived. Therefore, it cannot be the object of a cognition. Furthermore, since it is not perceived, it is not established as an entity. And since it is not established as an entity, it cannot be the object of a cognition. Moreover, if non-existence were an entity, it would follow that it is expressible. But it is not an entity. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a positive entity (*bhāva*), because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a positive entity. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is characterized by existence (*sattvalakṣaṇa*), because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not characterized by existence. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is produced by causes, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not produced by causes. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is subject to destruction, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not subject to destruction. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a cause of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a cause of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a support for cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a support for cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a means of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a means of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a result of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a result of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a locus of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a locus of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a property of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a property of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a universal (*sāmānya*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a universal of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a particular (*viśeṣa*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a particular of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a relation (*sambandha*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a relation of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a collection (*samūha*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a collection of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a sequence (*krama*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a sequence of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a simultaneity of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a modification (*vikāra*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a modification of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a transformation of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a part (*avayava*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a part of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a whole (*avayavin*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a whole of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a quality (*guṇa*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a quality of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is an action (*karman*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not an action of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is an instrument (*karaṇa*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not an instrument of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is an agent (*kartṛ*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not an agent of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not an experiencer of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a knower (*jñātṛ*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a knower of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a means of knowledge of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not an object of knowledge of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it is a doubt (*saṃśaya*) of cognition, because it is the object of a cognition. But it is not a doubt of cognition. Therefore, it is not expressible. Furthermore, if non-existence were expressible, it would follow that it

Now, even in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), why should non-existence (*abhāva*) not be something that can be expressed, such that this [objection] is raised? Therefore, it is precisely the intended non-existence that is expressible. If it is argued that its own nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist at all, and thus because of its non-existence there is no expression of non-existence, he replies: "But if [it is said] 'only non-existence' and so forth. By the word "therefore" (*tena*), he means by the non-existence of non-existence. Now, if non-existence itself is non-existent, how can there be the statement "that very thing is non-existent"?

The very word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) would not be employed [if it meant] that "there is no non-existence. And why would it not be so? Because non-existence itself is not admitted. For "non-existence" is its denotation, and that is not admitted. If you argue that there is a negation of a non-existence imagined by another, then at least a word whose object is non-existence is accepted. Therefore, by one who in some way initiates the conventional usage of non-existence, cognitions and words whose objects are non-existence must necessarily be admitted.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that since an object is negated, the word denoting that object cannot be employed, and therefore the negative particle (*nañ*) is used without an objective referent—the answer to this will be given by the passage beginning with:
“...established by conceptual construction arising from the impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless [time]” (1.207).

The word “therefore” (*tasmāt*) serves as a conclusion. By this much of the text, the Master has established the point he previously stated: that words must necessarily function with respect to those [objects].

On this point, an opponent says: "If words also exist for non-entities (*abhāva*), then how could there be a distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) among those non-entities to serve as the cause for the application of words? Otherwise, how could words that express non-entities have exclusion (*apoha*) as their object? To this, the Teacher replies with the words beginning "In that case also" (*tatrāpi*). Because of the absence of form—meaning because of the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) in a non-entity—words that denote form and grasp an intrinsic nature are simply not to be suspected [of applying there]. For it is already established that those words have non-entities as their objects, being the expressers of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), that is, other-exclusion (*anyāpoha*).

This is what is meant: since words whose objects are absences do not grasp the essential nature of an existent entity, their object is exclusion (*apoha*); likewise, even those words whose objects are existents, because they do not grasp the essential nature of an existent entity, have exclusion alone as their object. The only difference is that some words are said to have existents as their objects due to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an existent, while others are said to have absences as their objects due to the determination of an absence.

A doubt might arise as to what the denotable form of those words whose operation or function pertains to a real entity (*vastu*) is: is it apprehended as a positive form (*vidhi-rūpa*), or is it determined as a particularity (*bheda*) consisting of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtta-svabhāva*)? However, since non-existence (*abhāva*) is characterized by distinction (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*), why should it be made the cause for a form that is the very nature of a real entity—a form which, in its presence, would indeed involve non-existence through the existence of that [other] form?

The state of that form is "tadbhāva"; that entity whose characteristic is precisely that state is so described. This alone is the primary distinction (*viveka*), which is other-exclusion (*anyāpoha*). However, another [exclusion], characterized by the absence of all entities, is metaphorically called "exclusion" because it is the cause for the exclusion of the objects of words such as "cow. Of that distinction, the term "manifesting its state as such" means expressing the nature of the distinction. The connection is as follows: conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) have the distinction as their object—that is, they have other-exclusion as their object—and thus they are said to have the distinction as their object.

Those are the words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). A single entity (*vastu*), which serves as the basis for exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), is the point of reliance (*pratiśaraṇa*) and the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for those words and conceptual constructions; thus they are so described. For instance, that very same thing which is the substratum for the word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and its conceptual construction—by way of excluding what is unproduced—is also the substratum for the words "impermanent," "selfless," and so forth, and their respective conceptual constructions. Even though they are of such a nature, the connection is that they nonetheless have distinct objects. Why? "According to their own [respective domains]," and so on.

That from which a distinction is established is its limit (*avadhi*). For example, "non-produced" is the limit of the exclusion termed "produced"; likewise, "permanent" is the limit of the exclusion characterized by "impermanence," and so forth. The distinctions among those respective limits are the differences constructed—that is, fashioned—by those limits; these are the mutual particularities (*viśeṣa*) that distinguish impermanence and the other properties for those who discern them.

When those properties (*dharmin*) appear as if divided by those distinctions (*bheda*) within the conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), because those words are brought forth in their respective isolates (*viveka*) or differences (*bheda*), and because they are joined respectively as the designator (*vācaka*) and the designatum (*grāhaka*).

But surely there is no difference in their limits between the produced (*kṛtaka*) and the impermanent (*anityatva*), because that which is unproduced (*akṛtaka*) is of the nature of the eternal (*nitya*). Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) would be merely a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*). This is not a fault. Why? Because even for the prior non-existence (*prāgbhāva*), which is unproduced, there is impermanence; and even for the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), which is produced, there is permanence. Thus, there is indeed a difference in their limits.

Alternatively, just as the term "produced" (kṛtaka) excludes the superimposition that "sound is not produced by a cause," and the term "impermanent" (anitya) is used to exclude the superimposition of persistence in the second and subsequent moments, so too there is a difference in their limits. Thus, by means of this aforementioned difference in exclusion (vyāvṛtti), even though in a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu) the essential nature itself constitutes both the probandum and the probans, there is no conjoining or identity between the probandum and the probans.

And therefore, he says "that is not so" to show that the fault previously mentioned—that if *svabhāva* were the probandum, the reason would be a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*)—does not apply. "That" (*tat*) means "for that reason. The connection is: "And this is *svabhāva*. *Svabhāva* refers to a property (*dharma*) that is non-distinct [from the subject]. That may be existence (*sattva*) or something else. Even though existence exists and "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) exists in things that exist, nevertheless, when one intends to express merely that "this *svabhāva* is produced by causes," the "produced" (*kṛtaka*) is called the reason.

But this is not the case when one intends to express capacity, as in the case of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. When one intends to express merely that "capacity exists," existence (*sattva*) is stated as the reason; however, when one intends to express that it is produced by a cause, [existence alone is not sufficient]. (187–88)

Therefore, what was said—that existence is found in what is produced and there is no deviation from its impermanence—why then is it qualified by a distinction of conditions (*upādhi*)? That is refuted, because in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, efficacy (*sāmarthya*) is not intended [as the meaning]. When stated as a reason (*hetu*), it is being expressed. "Dependent on a distinction of conditions" means dependent on a distinction of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). "Or alone" means independent of conditions. It is stated for the purpose of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*).

When impermanence is to be proven, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) depends on a distinction of conditions (*upādhibheda*), whereas "existence" (*sattva*) does not. By the words "depends," etc., [the author] states that "being produced" depends on a distinction of conditions: the very capacity to produce what is intended by another as a non-cause is the operation (*vyāpāra*). Dependence is precisely the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). That entity which depends upon the operation of another as the cause for the production of its own nature is "produced."

Because the suffix *kan* is prescribed [by Pāṇini] in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), this word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) is a proper name. For this very reason, although this term "produced" expresses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it implies an intrinsic nature that has another adventitious condition (*upādhi*) as its absolute qualifier. By the phrase "by this"—that is, by the demonstration that "being produced" depends upon a distinction in adventitious conditions—it is shown that the diversity of causes (*pratyaya*) is the means of differentiation; that which has the habit of being differentiated by that [diversity] is so described, and its state of being such is its "reality" (*tattva*). Thus, sound is differentiated by the diversity of its causes, such as the effort [to produce it], and by the word "etcetera," properties such as "occurring immediately after volitional effort" are explained.

The conclusion is stated with the words "In this way," and so forth. In certain applications, [the reason] is independent of any distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*). For this very reason, he says: "When the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply 'impermanent' in a general sense, as in the case of existence (*sattva*). By including that property which is its own nature (*svabhāva*), it is stated in the present context that "in some cases, the reason is an essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*)," as in that same instance where "origination" (*utpatti*) is the reason when "impermanence" is the probandum. Furthermore, origination is not something other than origination itself, because if it were, then since a non-existent thing is unproduced, it would follow that there is an absence of origination.

The meaning is that [the property] is merely imagined as a distinct entity by way of being a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), because it arises from that; thus, "because it possesses origination" (*utpattimatvāt*) is the sense. This nature (*svabhāva*) should be understood as depending solely upon an adventitious condition (*upādhi*). In the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is essentially identical with the subject itself, being devoid of an adventitious condition that is extrinsic (*parabhūta*); this much is the distinction. "By this direction" means by the method of distinguishing between reasons that depend on or do not depend on adventitious conditions. (189)

If "existence" (*sattva*)—meaning that which is called a "sentient being"—is the reason (*hetu*), then how is it that the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth is not established? If, on the other hand, existence in general were to be the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Therefore, a specific kind of existence must be the probandum; and if that specific kind is the probandum, because the particularity does not follow through (*ananvaya*), the example would be devoid of the probandum. Consequently, existence is not established [as the probandum]. In that case, since the particularity also does not follow through in the reason (*hetu*), the example would likewise be devoid of the means of proof (*sādhana*). Thus he says: "For there is no following through," and so forth.

The reason for the particulars—that is, the specific instances—is contradicted and thus defective with respect to both the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*); this means [it is defective] in the case of the probans and the probandum, and "elsewhere" refers to [the case of] non-selfhood (*anātmatva*) and so forth. "That" refers to existence (*sattva*). The word *kila* indicates that it is being established as a matter of mere assertion (*anabhimata-artha*). (189–90)

By means of the formulation beginning with "Pradhāna exists," [the Sāṃkhya] attempts to specify [the subject] through its connection with the definition of Pradhāna; yet, a specific particular (*viśeṣa*) cannot be established because it lacks logical concomitance (*anvaya*). As the Master Dignāga said: "When it is stated by the Sāṃkhya that 'by the proposition "Pradhāna exists," the very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of Pradhāna is being proven,' this is contradicted and rendered faulty because of ignorance regarding the object of inference as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). For inference has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, whereas the particular characteristic is not its object. Thus it is refuted.

Rather, [it is so] because the same fault applies even to the reason (*hetu*). He states this very point: "For the reason," and so forth. That which lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is "non-concomitant" (*ananvaya*); it is not a constituent part of the proof for establishing the probandum. Why? Because of the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason. Existence (*bhāva*), that is, being (*sattā*), is the qualification (*upādāna*) of the subject (*dharmin*) alone. Precisely because it is restricted to that alone, when the subject is established in its general form, nothing at all would be proven for the Sāṃkhya.

Because the definition consisting of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth is unestablished; and such [a thing] is not prohibited. "Such" means merely a generality (*sāmānyamātra*). By this, he states that [the argument] would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). (190–91)

He explains [the point] with the words "not in every respect" (*na sarvathā*), and so forth. "In the proof of existence" (*sattāsādhane*) means in the establishment of existence (*sattāsiddhau*). "A qualifier of the mere entity" (*bhāvamātraviśeṣaṇa*) means a qualifier of existence alone (*sattāmātraviśeṣaṇaḥ*). The analysis of the compound is: "that whose specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is not specified. "Not here" (*neha*) refers to the proof of the mere thing (*vastumātrasādhane*). This is a negation of the proof of existence. However, that proponent (*vādī*) does so without taking into account—that is, without touching upon—any particular distinction or specific property (*viśeṣa*) of this subject (*dharmin*), such as its permanence (*nityatva*) and so forth. "By him" (*anena*) refers to the proponent.

"Apāttabheda" means that the distinction is not included [in the subject]. In this case, where the property to be proven (*sādhya*)—consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), being eternal, and so forth—is not included as a distinction within the subject (*dharmin*) such as *pradhāna* and the like, the reason (*hetu*) would be "non-concomitant" (*ananvaya*). It is called "non-concomitant" because there is no concomitance (*anvaya*) of this [reason] with the specific qualification of the property to be proven in the example. Since this is so, by that [reason], a distinction would be established within existence (*sattā*) itself as the property to be proven.

However, others first explain the latter half beginning with "in existence" (*sattāyām*) and its subsequent application to the property (*dharma*) and so forth, and only later explain the first half beginning with "the distinction is not included."

He explains [the verse] with the words "For that... and so forth. It is "one" because there is no differentiation within the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). It is "eternal" because it lacks destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*). It consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion because its essence is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). "Or else, another" refers to that which is endowed with agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth. "In any way whatsoever" means characterized by all or some of the aforementioned properties.

“Of that nature” means having a nature characterized by the aforementioned qualifications. And that subject (*dharmin*) does not thus conform to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by way of such a qualified nature, because a subject possessing such a nature is unestablished in the example. “Not by that which is established” means not by mere existence (*sattāmātra*), because there is no dispute regarding mere existence. (191–92) The opponent objects with “But surely,” and so forth. “Such a consequence” refers to what was stated regarding existence through the alternative of general or particular [nature]. As it has been said: “There is an absence of conformity to particulars when the general is established as the probandum.”

Because even in those cases where fire and so forth are the probanda (*sādhya*), there is no dispute regarding the existence of fire per se, since the mere presence of fire is already established. Nor does that established fact serve any purpose, because it is not a factor for initiating action (*pravṛtti*). For it is fire as qualified by a specific location and so forth that is a factor for action, not fire in general. If it is argued that "then that [qualified fire] alone is the probandum," he says: "That which has a qualified locus—wherein fire and so forth are being proved—is the qualification of that fire and so forth; this is what is meant by 'having a qualified locus as its qualification' (*viśiṣṭādhāraviśeṣaṇa*). Of that which is intended as the probandum, there is non-establishment (*asiddhi*) due to the lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*) in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)."

"No," says the Teacher. "Indeed, that locus, even when apprehended as a qualifier, does not qualify that fire such that there would be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*). What is the reason? 'Because of its non-connection,' and so forth. This is because [the fire] is qualified by the exclusion of that non-connection of the property (*dharma*) with that subject (*dharmin*) which was suspected. And this has been stated under the definition of the 'property of the subject' (*pakṣadharma*) in [verse 1.3], and will be stated in the fourth chapter (4.149)."

But surely, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), fire as excluded from non-connection with the specific location is unestablished. Or, if it were established, what would be the purpose of following the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? How so? Because it is unestablished: for one who realizes the pervasion—"wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—fire as excluded from non-connection with the intended location is indeed already implied by way of generality. It is only now that the following of the positive concomitance is desired for the sake of a specific cognition, namely, "in this particular place there is fire."

"Therefore" (*tasmāt*) is the conclusion. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the location and so forth. "By the exclusion of non-connection with that" (*tadayogavyavacchedena*) means that by excluding the non-connection of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) with that locus (*dharmin*), such as the location, one proves the generality of mere fire; thus, there is no fault of lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the exclusion of non-connection with the location is itself unestablished. If it is argued that in a locus such as *pradhāna*, the mere existence is to be proven by the exclusion of non-connection, he says: "Not so," and so forth.

"In some cases" refers to a subject (*dharmin*) such as *pradhāna* and so forth. Why? Because the very object denoted by words like *pradhāna*, characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so on, simply does not exist. That existence (*sattā*) is indeed without qualification, because there is no substratum (*ādhāra*) that could serve as a qualifier.

"How so? and so forth asks the opponent. That subject (*dharmin*) must also be known; once known, it must be expressed by a word; and having been expressed, it must be ascertained through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, since it is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and so on, that [subject] is indeed established. It is upon that [subject] that existence (*sattā*)—the universal (*sāmānya*)—is being proved. In that case, let the establishment of the Primal Principle (*pradhāna*) occur merely by the fact that "there exists an object of knowledge without qualification. For the meaning of "object of knowledge" and so forth would then be the primary meaning of the word in the form of a mere referent, rather than [the Primal Principle] endowed with attributes such as eternity and the like.

If it is argued that "the *pradhāna* is first established, and other properties will be established by other means of valid cognition," he replies: "Even so, what would be established by [the property of] being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and so forth? There would be no establishment of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *pradhāna* as intended, because this [property of being an object of knowledge] consists in the nature of a word-meaning (*śabdārtha*). He then says: "In the case of the inference of fire, however, only 'fire' in general would be established, and thus it would not be something to be proven (*asādhya*). But in another case, that very thing—the particular locus determined by the generality of fire—is unestablished; therefore, it is proven that it was not established previously."

[Objection: But even there [in the case of the universal], it is said to be "devoid of non-connection with that. The meaning is as follows: "non-connection with that" (*tadayoga*) refers to the absence of connection with that particular location; "devoid of that" (*viraha*) means having a connection with that location. That universal which possesses this [property] is described in that way. Therefore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not established.

He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (na). Indeed, no one who knows the principles of logic establishes a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a fire-generality (*agni-sāmānya*) that is connected to such a specific location. Therefore, when demonstrating [the argument] to an opponent, one must show that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire—that is, inseparable from fire—in the form: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire."

That smoke, having been established as pervaded by fire alone through the demonstration of a universal concomitance (*sarvopasaṃhāravyāpti*)—to which he assents with "so it is"—produces the cognition of fire precisely in that place where it is perceived in its own form within the subject (*dharmin*). In this case, since the inferendum is understood through the force of this [perception], there is no purpose whatsoever in stating the probandum (*sādhya*); for the probandum is established even without it. He says exactly this in the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*).

In that case, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is observed in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), the intended probandum (*sādhya*) is established merely through the declaration of the [invariable] relation. Furthermore, since there is no formal statement of the probandum as a composite of property and subject (*dharmadharmisamudāya*), and since it is not so stated, how could there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) in that which is qualified by it? There would be none; for thus there would be the fallacy of non-concomitance (*ananvayadoṣa*). Therefore, this smoke, being established as invariably connected (*avinābhāvitayā*) with fire, by its very capacity (*sāmarthyāt*) excludes the possibility of its non-connection with that specific location.

Therefore, it is said that the collection [of the locus and the property] is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). For if there were no fire there, smoke would not exist at all; this is the logical capacity (*sāmarthya*). However, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) should be shown by the property to be proven alone, and not by the collection of the property to be proven and its locus, because such a collection is unestablished in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and because there is no purpose in demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a collection. For this very reason, he says: "But not for this [reason], in that manner"—meaning that the positive concomitance is not preceded by the presentation of the locus as qualified [by the property].

What is the reason? Because at this time, when the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is being demonstrated, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not a constituent part [of the proof]. Or, if one were to require that the positive concomitance be preceded by the indication of the probandum, then no one would ever remove the thesis-statement (*pratijñā-vākya*) from the syllogistic argument (*sādhana-vākya*).

Therefore, it is established that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must be stated precisely by demonstrating the subject (*pakṣa*). Thus, the Master Dignāga said: "The non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the logical mark—such as smoke and so forth—from the property to be proven must be shown elsewhere, in a general case, and not merely in the locus (*dharmimātra*). And when the logical mark, whose non-deviation has been ascertained, is well-known in that [general] locus of the property to be proven, it will cause one to understand the locus of the property to be proven as being conjoined with that pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*)."

The conclusion is stated with the words "Therefore," and so forth: Just as the proof for fire is faultless because it involves the apprehension of specific [instances], the proof for existence (*sattā*) is not faultless, because the specific [instances] are unestablished. Thus, because it would result in proving what is already established and because of the lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the existence of *pradhāna* and the like is not to be proven.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that all means of proof (*sādhana*) are not specified here [in the definition of the thesis], he says: "unexamined" (*aparāmṛṣṭa*), and so forth (PV 1.192a). "Unexamined" means unappropriated; that is, in a mere entity (*vastumātra*), which is a mere existence (*sattāmātra*). When a proof is formulated with respect to that, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not violated. Of what? Of the probandum (*sādhya*) that pervades that alone—that is, that pervades mere existence. Explaining this very point, he says: "in a probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) that pervades the mere entity."

Furthermore, when existence (*sattva*) is established by not grasping at specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), there is no contradiction with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). The meaning is that the example is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnya*). For "therein" refers to the proof of existence. Why? Because even though it relies on mere existence—meaning, even when relying on mere existence as the reason—it does not, however, fail to rely on the specificities of existence when existence is the property to be proven. Why? Because it would be futile. (192–93) ad PV 1.193

To point out another fault when "existence" (sattā) is the property to be proven (sādhya), he says: "Moreover" (api ca). Since the substratum (dharmin), such as primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth, is unestablished (asiddha), the reason (hetu) is unestablished because the property of existence does not reside therein. Furthermore, a property that depends on both existence and non-existence is inconclusive (anaikāntika) and deviates when existence is the property to be proven. Even a property that belongs to non-existence is contradictory (viruddha) when existence is the property to be proven, because it proves the very opposite of existence.

Whatever reason (*hetu*) may be adduced for the sake of proving that existence of *pradhāna* and so forth which is the probandum (*sādhya*), all such reasons fail to transcend the three logical fallacies (*doṣatraya*). How can that existence be proven? For here, having admitted the established nature of the reason, the contradictions and inconclusiveness have been stated; these two [fallacies] are impossible if the reason itself is unestablished (*asiddha*).

[Objection: But surely, even when the existence of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) and so forth is the probandum (*sādhya*), the fault of the reason (*hetu*) being unestablished (*asiddha*) and other such defects are equally applicable; how, then, can its existence be established? [Response: This is not a fault. Whatever is taught is preceded by knowledge of that very thing, just as is the case with anything else. And the Four Noble Truths are taught. Therefore, they too must be preceded by knowledge. He who possesses that knowledge is accepted by us as the Omniscient One. Thus, there is no harm whatsoever. The phrase "its cause" (*taddhetu*) refers to the cause of its existence.

The term *trayī* does not exclude the various types of defects belonging to the class of defects consisting of three parts. He states this [in the verse] beginning with "unestablished" (*asiddham*). Regarding "contradiction" (*virodham*), he means the state of being contradictory (*viruddhatā*). In that case, how could a reason (*hetu*) which is a property of an existent (*bhāvadharma*) be established for something whose existence is unestablished?

It might be argued: "A property of an existent is established in relation to *pradhāna* and so forth, but the existent itself is not. To this he says: "For whoever," and so on. For how could a proponent who accepts a reason that is a property of an existent such as *pradhāna* not accept that *pradhāna* and so forth exist as an existent? Therefore, the property is indeed a property of an existent.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is it said that a property (*dharma*) belongs to an entity (*bhāva*)? he replies: "By some point of view," namely, by means of the definition that excludes other distinctions; thus, a property is indicated from the subject (*dharmin*) as if it were distinct or as if it had a separate form. For example, when it is said, "this has the quality of being produced" (*kṛtakatvam asya*), it is the entity itself, excluded from what is unproduced, that is expressed. It is not that a different property is denoted by the word "property," while something else entirely is denoted by the word "subject. Thus he says: "For not... and so forth.

For when a person, independent of the exclusion of other [properties], desires to know the exclusion of sound from one thing alone—namely, from that which is unproduced—it is said that "sound possesses the property of being produced" (*kṛtakatvam asti*). When, however, desiring the exclusion of others, he seeks to know the exclusion of sound from one thing alone—namely, from that which is unproduced—it is said that "sound is produced" (*kṛtakaḥ śabdaḥ*). And this has already been stated previously by the passage beginning with "the rejection or non-rejection of other distinctions," and so forth.

Now, however, one might say that the reason (*hetu*) is a property (*dharma*) common to both existence and non-existence. But how can a single property belong to both existence and non-existence? For a property is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and how could that which is the intrinsic nature of an existent be the intrinsic nature of a non-existent? To this he replies: "not dependent," and so forth. This is because there is no contradiction even in the case of non-existence for that which is imagined as a property—namely, a mere exclusion (*vyatireka-mātra*) consisting of a simple negation—which does not depend on any real entity.

He explains how there can be mere exclusion (*vyatireka*) alone: "by way of non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). A positive injunction (*vidhi*) subordinate to a negation is a presuppositional negation (*paryudāsa*), and that is not intended here. For example, [the statement] "it is not corporeal" implies incorporeality, which is merely the cessation of corporeality; this would apply whether the entity is a positive thing like consciousness (*vijñāna*), or even an indefinable state (*nirupākhyam*), or a non-entity (*abhāva*).

The opponent says in response: "Because that which is indefinable (*nirupākhya*) lacks existence, it cannot be the object of negation. Only that which possesses the capacities of being a substratum and so forth could be the object of something; however, how could that which is indefinable and devoid of all capacities be an object? Now, since its status as an object of negation has been refuted, could it be the object of an affirmation (*vidhi*)? If you say that even that—its being an object of affirmation—is not possible for the indefinable..."

How, then, is non-existence not the object of negation? For it is precisely by the negation of being an object of affirmation that it becomes an object of negation. What is the reason? Because negation has the nature of the cessation of affirmation. Therefore, how could this aforementioned mere non-exclusion (*avyavacchedamātra*), which is possible in both existence and non-existence, appropriate to itself the status of being a prover when existence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*)? Of what kind is this prover-status? It is as follows: "in the case of the dissimilar instance," and so forth.

If the reason (*hetu*) were to occur in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), there would be a suspicion regarding it; and even if that suspicion were excluded, [the reason] would not be established. Furthermore, since there is no exclusion of the mere property common to both [sides] from the dissimilar instance, how could it appropriate for itself the status of being a prover (*gamaka*)? And that proponent [would do so] either by his own words or by the words of another.

One who asserts that the reason which establishes existence possesses both properties (ubhayadharmatā)—namely, that this reason possessing both properties occurs elsewhere than in the existent thing to be proven, even in what is non-existent—is indeed not insane? For he claims that when existence is the probandum, this very [reason] is the basis for non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), which is the ground for its being a prover (*gamaka*); how then could he not be deranged?

However, for this proponent who asserts that a cause which is a non-existent property (*abhāvadharma*) exists [in the effect], there would be a contradiction, because he is proving non-existence (*asattva*), which is the opposite of existence (*sattva*). What, then, is the property of this very non-existence? He says: "Exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*). Of what kind? It is that which pervades mere existence and is characterized by causal capacity; its exclusion necessarily belongs to non-existence alone. However, the exclusion of properties such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) does not belong to it, because those possess the nature of both [existence and non-existence].

Why is it contradictory? He says: because that exclusion of objects which is pervaded by mere existence is absent in some cases where existence is present, yet present in all cases where existence is absent; thus, there is contradiction. Therefore, this property—though of three kinds, being related to existence, non-existence, or both—is stated as the definition of a reason for proving existence [only] when it is connected with existence. And there is no other possibility or another mode apart from these three types of properties; therefore, existence is not proven [by such a reason].

Regarding its being a means of proof (*sādhana*) or a logical mark (*liṅga*), this existence (*sattā*)—because it has not been presented with specific qualifications in a general sense—is not unestablished (*asiddhi*) when the subject (*dharmin*) is one whose existence is already established. This applies when what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is a property of the real entity (*vastudharma*) such as impermanence and so forth; specifically, when that [property] pervades only that [subject].

And if the pervasion of the logical mark by that property to be proven is ascertained in some way—either through the method of agreement (*anvaya*) or through the method of difference (*vyatireka*)—then there is neither contradiction nor deviation; that is, the reason is neither contradictory (*viruddha*) nor inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, this [reason] does not fall under the definition of an unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory, or inconclusive reason.

However, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mark (*liṅga*) by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is uncertain, or when its subsistence in the subject (*dharmisamāśraya*)—that is, its status as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—is uncertain, then that reason which is intended to be a prover because it is certain in its nature, namely, certain in its three-fold nature (*trairūpya*), is not a prover at all. For this very reason, it must be stated that the essential nature of the reason (*hetusvabhāva*) is that which is pervaded by its own property—that is, by the form of the probandum—and is established, meaning ascertained, in the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmi*). Strengthening this point, he says: "For not... and so forth.

When, while illuminating jars and other objects by virtue of its luminosity and radiance, it occasionally comes to reside within the interior of a jar or the like, then—provided that its own nature is not perceived but its radiance is perceived—it does not indeed perform its own causal function, which is characterized by the illumination of the jar and so forth.

Having explained the nature of the indicator (*gamaka*), he now states the nature of the indicated (*gamya*): "of that, the pervader" (PV 1.194b). That which is the indicator is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) nature; the nature that is its pervader (*vyāpaka*), when ascertained, is the indicated (*gamya*).

He explains [the passage] beginning with "its property" (*taddharma*). A property of the subject (*dharmī*) is what is to be understood. Of what kind is that [property], which is intended as the prover, determined to be the pervader (*vyāpaka*)? But how is it determined to be the pervader? He says: "Precisely from the determination of that property," that is, precisely from the determination of the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*). By this much, the essential nature of the object to be understood and the means of understanding has been shown.

He also states the essential nature of that which is to be excluded (*nivartya*) and that which excludes (*nivartaka*), beginning with the words “of that” (*tasya*) and so forth. “This” refers to the pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*). When it [the pervader] itself ceases, it is the excluder of that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*). (PV I.194cd)

He explains [the passage] beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth. The connection is as follows: this pervading property (*vyāpako dharmaḥ*), while itself ceasing, is the "remover" (*nivartaka*) of that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*). What is the reason? Because it is only in this way that this property to be proven (*sādhyo dharmaḥ*) is established as its pervader, provided that the pervaded does not exist in the absence of this pervader.

The word *tad* is used here to introduce the statement. By this—through the demonstration of the relationship between the follower (*anuvarttin*) and the followed (*anuvarttaka*), as well as the relationship between the thing to be removed (*nivartya*) and the remover (*nivarttaka*)—it should be understood that the definition of the indicator (*gamaka-lakṣaṇa*), characterized by the capacity to prove the probandum (*sādhyasādhakatva-lakṣaṇa*), has been stated for both types of formal argument (*sādhana-prayoga*): namely, that which possesses similarity (*sādharmyavat*) and that which possesses dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat*). He explains this with the words "For it is of two kinds," and so forth. As some say—the Naiyāyikas—only the argument possessing similarity is positive (*anvayin*), and only the argument possessing dissimilarity is negative (*vyatirekin*).

[Objection: "In the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*), there is the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*); likewise, in the formulation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), there is the property of being a feature of the subject and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Thus, the logical mark (*liṅga*) would result in having only two forms. To this he replies: "Of these two," and so forth. Of these two—the reasons characterized by both positive and negative concomitance—there is in reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), no difference whatsoever, because both possess both positive and negative concomitance, except for a difference in their formal connection (*saṃyoga*).

Therefore, it is merely the mode of formulation that differs—whether positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are demonstrated at one time through the application of similarity (*sādharmya*) or at another through the application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—but the meaning does not differ. What is the reason? Because even when formulated by way of similarity, the exclusion of the reason from the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*) follows by implication (*arthāt*), through its inherent capacity; this is its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). He states that very capacity with the words beginning "asati" [in the verse]. "In that" refers to the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmye*).

For in this way, the reason would be concomitant with the probandum if it did not exist in the absence of the probandum. Likewise, "in the case of dissimilarity" refers to the formulation of dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya*). "In that" refers to positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For if there were a positive concomitance of the reason with the probandum, then the reason would cease upon the cessation of the probandum; and we shall explain this in the discussion on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). (PV 1.195 and PVSV)

PVSV 97,20: Regarding impermanence, just as the effect is [present] only in that which is impermanent, so too is the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). This is an example of the positive concomitance (*anvayin*). Alternatively, "or what is not an effect is indestructible" is an example of the negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*). By this, the meaning is as follows: in that which is indestructible—that is, in the absence of destruction—the state of being produced does not exist. (PV I 195ab)

He states that very point with the words "by this," and so forth. "Of these two" refers to the positive and negative [reasons]. By stating the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*) in the form "whatever [is produced]," the exclusion of "producedness" from eternal things is effectively stated; thus, there is the cognition of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). "And sound is produced" is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). To the question "Why is the subject (*pakṣa*) not explicitly mentioned? he replies with the words "of the produced," and so forth.

When "the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is stated by means of sound as being pervaded by "impermanence," then, by necessity, it brings its own pervader (*vyāpaka*) into proximity; thus, by the very force of this [logical implication], it follows that "sound is impermanent. Therefore, [the author says] "not necessarily," and so forth. "Here" refers to the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*). He states the formulation possessing dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the words "even in the case of negative concomitance" (*vyatireke 'pi*), and so forth. This is an explanation of the statement "or that which is not an effect is not perishable. Here too, there is no explicit statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*).

Because, when the absence of that [impermanence]—that is, when there is an absence of impermanence—is established by means of a reason consisting in the ascertained nature of being produced and the nature of impermanence, and when the existence of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) in sound is declared—that is, when its presence is stated—then, by implication, since "being produced" exists in sound as something whose very essence is impermanent, it is established that "sound is impermanent," just as in the previous case of the application of similarity (sādharmya-prayoga).

Now, one might object: "In this application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been stated. To this he says: "But as for positive concomitance," and so forth. The impossibility of dissimilarity without positive concomitance is an implication (*arthāpatti*). What is the reason? "For not," and so forth. Because it is not logical that there should be a cessation [of the reason] upon the cessation of impermanence—that is, when impermanence is absent—for that which is restricted to what is not of that nature and is unconnected to the essence of impermanence.

Since this is so, therefore, having established by means of valid cognition the restriction of the reason to the probandum through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), the cessation of the reason must be stated for the sake of the ignorant person by means of the cessation of the probandum.

Therefore, what was said—that if the restriction has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is the use of a fruitless statement of exclusion; or how could one not understand the restriction [itself], rather than the absence [of the object] upon the absence [of the means of cognition]—is refuted.

Others, however, explain it differently: having established [the rule] from the word and its meaning through an implied statement (*ākṣepavacana*), this is the meaning: having established the restriction (*niyama*) and having implied the restriction by implication, the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) must be stated. Exclusion must be stated by such a statement; the statement of exclusion implies the restriction by the force of the context (*sāmarthya*). For this very reason, he says: "And that," etc. "That" refers to the exclusion which implies the restriction, which is established for the sake of the other person.

If it is manifested by such a statement, then it implies—by the force of the expression and by implication—the restriction of its own nature, that is, the restriction of the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*). For this reason, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established.

"How so? and so forth is the opponent's question. "Now" means: given the acceptance that a reason is a prover only when the relationship of pervader and pervaded has been ascertained. By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it to be understood—that is, ascertained—that "whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent," such that you may say: "Sound is produced and impermanent; whatever is produced is impermanent"? Being thus questioned, he says "Because... and so forth, in order to demonstrate the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the scope of the pervasion.

PVSV 98,6: Because destruction—which is characterized by the property of cessation—is necessarily concomitant with its own nature (*svarūpa*), that is, with its mere essence; or else, "being" (*bhāva*) means "that from which something comes to be," thus "own being" (*svabhāva*) means "its own cause. Therefore, the concomitance of destruction—that is, its presence in the entity—arises from that very [cause]. Consequently, what is produced is impermanent. Why is this so? Because it lacks a separate cause. Since there is no cause of destruction other than the cause that produces it, its concomitance follows from its own nature.

This, then, is the collective meaning here: immediately following the operation of the hammer, two things are perceived—the cessation of the jar and the potsherd. Furthermore, these two are perceived as having the nature of destruction. Regarding this, he will state that because the cessation of the jar is formless, it cannot be an effect; thus, its perception as an effect is merely an illusion. Or, if it were an effect, it would not have the nature of the cessation of the jar, because it would be produced through its connection with the jar.

Furthermore, there would be no cognition [of the jar] as having the nature of destruction because the jar still exists. Even in the case of the potsherd, although it is the effect of the mallet, it does not have the nature of destruction because the jar has not ceased to exist; as he will state later, "how then could there be a cognition of this [potsherd] as having the nature of destruction? Thus, how could there be a cognition of it as being of the nature of destruction?

But if destruction were causeless, then even as the jar is naturally ceasing, the hammer and other auxiliary factors would act as its producers of shards; since the jar ceases immediately after the operation of the hammer and the shard comes into existence, it is indeed appropriate for those of dull intellect to conclude that these two constitute destruction and that destruction is thus caused.

Because the continuum is interrupted immediately after the operation of the hammer. Therefore, how can it be argued that those who assert the acceptance of causeless destruction are contradicted by perception? He states this very point with the words "For not... and so forth. Those produced things for which destruction is observed as they perish—while perishing—that is, while having the nature of being perishable, do they depend on a cause other than the producer of their own nature? Why? Because those things which are perishable by nature possess the property of cessation from their very own causes.
And since entities are independent with respect to their perishable nature, therefore whatever is produced is perishable by its very own nature.

(195–96) (p. 361) He says "sāpekṣāṇām" and so forth [to address the objection]: "If destruction were caused, then it would not be necessarily occurring. For [the word] "hi" means "because"; because entities that are dependent do not have necessary occurrence, therefore an entity that is independent regarding destruction has a perishable nature. For if there were dependence on a cause, then among things such as jars, some might even be eternal—namely, those for whom the cause of destruction is not present.

If it is argued that because causes of destruction are so numerous, there is nowhere an absence of them, he replies with the words "by which," and so forth. The connection is as follows: "of that cause" means that even for those very causes of destruction, there is not necessarily a presence [at all times]. Why? Because their presence is dependent upon their own conditions (*svapratyaya*), that is, because their presence depends upon their own causes. Furthermore, causes do not exist everywhere up to the point of the cause of destruction. Consequently, due to the non-presence of the cause of destruction, something might indeed not perish.

Even when the cause of destruction is present, destruction is not certain; for causes do not necessarily possess their effects—that is, they do not necessarily possess the effect called "destruction. Why? Because there may be an absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), a deficiency, or an obstruction caused by the encounter with a contrary factor. By this, it is stated that for that which is dependent [on other factors], there is no necessary occurrence, and thus it is subject to deviation. (195–96)

Regarding those causes that are adduced as the marks (*liṅga*) for the destruction of all things that have destruction as their cause: why? Because the effect is not established; that is, because there is no necessity in the production of the effect characterized by destruction. For those who maintain that destruction has a cause—those who assert that destruction possesses a cause—[it is argued]: since destruction is causeless, therefore, whatever entity is produced (*kṛtaka*) is independent with respect to its own being—that is, with respect to its perishable nature—and is thus determined to be that state; it is fixed in its nature of having the property of ceasing.

He states the example: "Asambhava... and so forth. That causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) is one in which an obstruction (*pratibandha*) is impossible. "Complete" (*sakala*) means it is fully endowed with auxiliary conditions (*sahakāripratyaya*) and the transformation of the continuum (*santānapariṇāma*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is independent of the existence of something else is necessarily restricted to its absence. For example, a causal complex that has no possible obstruction is [independent] regarding the production of its effect. And a produced entity (*kṛtako bhāvaḥ*) is independent of destruction; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). (196–97)

With the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely), he raises the objection of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). He states—beginning with "bhūmi" (the soil)—that even for certain causes that are independent with respect to a particular effect, its occurrence is not necessarily certain; for that [soil] is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) required for the production of the effect, and since the sprout does not arise at times when there is an obstruction, even though that complex is absent. And this has been stated assuming the unity of the continuum (*santāna*).

He refutes this with the words beginning "no," and so forth. In that regard, within the aforementioned causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the continuum, characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-antara-utpatti*); [the opponent's argument fails] because [destruction] depends upon that [complex]. Therefore, the reason "because of independence" does not apply in that case. To the objection that even for a produced thing (*kṛtaka*) there is a dependence on a later time (*kāla-antara*) regarding its destruction, and thus the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "It is not so," and so forth. He will explain that for a produced entity, there is no dependence whatsoever on a later time for its destruction.

It might be argued: "Since the earth, seeds, and so forth possess a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*), why should they depend upon a transformation of their continuum? Therefore, the reason is indeed inconclusive. To this he says: "In that case also," and so forth.

This is what is meant: the earth, seed, and so forth do not possess a single, unchanging nature, for if they did, it would follow that the effect would be produced even before [the final moment], just as it is later. Rather, they are distinct through successive transformations (*pariṇāma*). In this context—that is, within that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) which is differentiated by the transformation of the continuum—the final complex, being unmediated by any other characteristic in the production of the effect, is indeed productive of the fruit. Therefore, on what grounds could there be any inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in the reason?

It might be argued: "Even though the preceding causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is productive, it is not determinate. To this he says: "That very [complex]"—meaning that among those [predecessors], the final complex alone is the cause of the sprout, and no other. Why, then, do those seeking a sprout take up the preceding complex? To this he says: "But others," and so forth. The "prior transformation" refers to a specific prior state; it is for that very purpose—that is, for the sake of the final complex capable of producing the sprout—that [the complex] is taken up by those who seek it, and it is determined as being of the nature of a causal complex.

It might be argued: "An obstruction to even the final causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is possible; therefore, because there is no certainty regarding the production of the effect, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*. To this he says, "And not," and so forth. [The phrase] "in that [final complex] when the effect is to be produced" refers to the final moment (*antye kṣaṇe*). Regarding the "occurrence in one place": if there were the arising of a modification (*vikāra*), that final moment would lose its singularity, because the preceding [moment] would have ceased and a second moment called "modification" would arise. Consequently, it would not be the final [moment].

Now, if it is not admitted that this final [moment] deviates from its nature as a producer, then—for that which has not deviated from its own nature as a producer—there is no deficiency regarding the production of that [effect], because an obstructing cause, by not acting as an obstruction, does not effect any impairment toward the production of the result.

Again, he anticipates the charge of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*): "The barley seeds and so forth are not dependent [on other conditions]—with respect to what?—with respect to the effect to be produced, namely, the rice sprout. Why? Because the conditions for its production are sometimes present even in that case, such as the barley seed itself. [The opponent argues: "Even though they are independent, they do not produce a rice sprout; therefore, the reason is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."

"How so? asks the proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntavādī*). The meaning is that they are indeed dependent. "Of these" refers to barley seeds and the like; the connection is that they lack that very nature which produces a rice sprout—that is, the nature of producing a rice sprout. "Dependent upon that nature" means dependent upon the nature of producing a rice sprout.

"And when, and how, could there be independence? For in that case," the opponent argues, "it would mean that among certain produced things, whether they exist or not, that very nature which is perishable does not exist. Therefore, because they depend on that nature—namely, dependence on a perishable nature—they are not perishable; thus, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*)."

He begins to refute this with the words "the rice seed," etc. By the word "etc.," barley seeds and others are included. "That nature" refers to the nature of producing or not producing an effect other than the one intended, by virtue of its own cause. That which is a barley seed or the like is not the cause of that [rice]; the meaning is that it is not the cause of whatever has the rice seed as its cause. "It has a different nature" means it has a nature that does not produce a rice sprout.

But would it not then follow that something could both lack the cause for a certain effect and yet possess its nature? To this he says: "and having a restricted capacity," and so forth. That which has a restricted—that is, specifically determined—capacity is thus described; such is the cause, possessing by its very nature the character of producing rice or barley seeds. It is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) precisely as a distinct essential nature (*svarūpa*).

It might be argued: "The difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities is not produced by causes; rather, the very nature of one thing is such, while that of another is different. To this, he says: "And not," and so forth. "Arising without cause" (*ākasmika*) means being causeless. For that which is independent and lacks a cause, there would be no restriction regarding the production of a rice sprout from a rice seed as its specific nature, with respect to any particular place, at any particular time, or in any particular substance.

However, because there would be no dependence [on anything else], everything would exist at all times and in all places. Therefore, it is understood that a restriction which occurs in dependence on place and so forth must have a cause. Just as there is a restriction of nature (*svabhāva-niyama*) in the case of rice seeds and the like, so too here in the case of produced things (*kṛtaka*) or existent things (*sat*), a cause for this restriction must be stated—by virtue of which restrictive cause some produced or existent things are born with a perishable nature, while others are not.

It might be argued: "Even if a determining cause cannot be shown, it is nevertheless conceivable. To this he says: "And in this world, there is no determining cause for a perishable nature; that is to say, it is not even conceivable. For the destruction of all things that possess birth is established through observation. That is to say, destruction has no fixed cause."

If the destruction of all living beings is established [independently], then the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this, he says: "That which has birth," and so forth. The opponent thinks: "Destruction is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of those things that have birth, not of those that lack birth; it does not belong to space (*ākāśa*) and the like, even though they exist. The Teacher says: "Indeed, there is no birth... For the nature of an entity does not arise by virtue of its birth. Therefore, birth is not the cause of destruction. Nor is there existence in space and the like; thus he says: "And not," and so forth.

There is no restriction of intrinsic nature—that is, no restriction of essential character—for that which is causeless, such as space and so forth, because for what lacks a cause, there can be no restriction regarding place, time, or inherent disposition. Furthermore, since the destruction of all living beings is established and the non-existence of space and so forth is proven, there is therefore no differentiation of intrinsic nature among produced things or existing entities based on whether a cause produces something perishable or imperishable. Because that [cause] does not exist, and thus there is an absence of differentiation in causes, there is no differentiation between the perishable and the imperishable for the effect—whether it be produced or existent—just as in the case of seeds and other factors that do not possess a common causal basis.

This very independence of destruction with respect to any given entity at any given time is incompatible with that which is the existence of the entity; [this independence] brings about the absence of that [existence], and by its own nature—that is, by its very being—it establishes the non-existence of destruction at any place and at any time. The meaning is that it establishes the existence [of the entity] everywhere and at all times. What is the reason? "For whoever... and so forth. "Dependent on that time and substance" means:
whatever time it occurs in, or whatever substance it occurs in, it depends upon that time and that substance; thus, as was stated previously, it would not be independent at all.

Is it not the case that destruction is independent because it does not depend on a cause of destruction, and not because it is independent of time and so forth? If so, how can it be said that "destruction would not be independent, as it depends upon that [specific] time and substance"? Furthermore, if destruction were independent of time, there would be no destruction even in the second moment, since it would depend on that [specific] time. And if it were independent of substance, of what indeed would there be destruction?

He thinks as follows: because of the statement that "for that which has arisen, destruction occurs without dependence on anything else" (*jātasya tadbhāve ’nyānapekṣaṇāt*), destruction occurs in the very second moment and not in any other moment. If it happens thus for everything that has arisen and not for a specific substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*), then, since there is no dependence on a substance, of what indeed would destruction occur?

This is refuted. If destruction were to occur at a later time and in a specific substance, then that later time and that specific substance would themselves have to be the causes of destruction, because destruction exists only when they exist. Therefore, if it were dependent on that time and substance, it could not be said to be independent. Thus it is stated.

"In that case," says the opponent. "No," says the Master. Because it arises from that very cause of existence which is its being—namely, because that which has a perishable nature arises [from that]. He clarifies this very point: for there is the arising of only such a thing, i.e., only that which has a perishable nature, for one who attains existence—that is, for one who becomes existent. If it is argued that the arising, or production, of an existent entity does not necessarily come from some cause;

For some indeed think that even though things exist, they do not arise like space and so forth; thus, [existence] is considered to be "accidental," meaning causeless. This existence would never cease for any object, at any time, or in any substance.
But surely, if the existence of jars and the like is restricted by their own causes, how can there be the consequence of the existence of space and so forth?

True; however, the meaning of the statement "it would not cease for anything" is as follows: some say that there is no entity whose intrinsic nature this [space] and so forth would not possess, for otherwise it would follow that it is composed of everything. This is incorrect. For if the form of a jar or the like were present in space, it would be causeless, since it would exist even without a lump of clay and so forth. Therefore, this existence of space and so forth does not belong to anything such as a self at any time or in any place;
the meaning is that it would not be restricted by place, time, or substance.

Strengthening this very point, he says: "For that," and so forth. For that entity—something would adhere to, or depend upon, that in which something such as its production is bound or contingent. And it would not adhere to that in which it is not bound. If this existence (*sattā*) were non-contingent with respect to anything, it would not be restricted with regard to substance or time. Consequently, there would be no such distinctions as: "this existence belongs to space, not to the self or the mind," or "the existence of the self does not belong to time," and so on. And since this is so, this existence is not accidental even in those things regarded as eternal.

If the arising of that which is perishable occurs solely from the cause of its existence (*sattāhetu*), how is it now said that destruction is causeless? [The opponent] states this contradiction; [the author] replies with the words beginning "of that which is born" (*jātasya*). Of that which is born—that is, produced—if there were no state of perishability (*vinaśvaratā*) in its being, then because nothing other than the producing cause would be required, destruction is said to be causeless. And it was stated previously in this regard: that what is called "destruction" is not something distinct from the entity itself, but rather the entity itself is indeed the destruction.

But surely, destruction is non-existence through annihilation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); how then can it have the nature of an entity? To this he says: "For that very [entity]," and so forth. Because it has arisen as something enduring for only a single moment due to its own cause, therefore destruction is said to be the entity itself. That which has the habit of remaining for only that one moment which is the time of the entity's existence is thus described. It does not, however, remain for even a moment after having arisen; for we shall explain later that if it were to remain, it would not cease.

If destruction is a state that lasts for only a single moment, why is it not determined to be such even before the interruption of the continuum? And because it is not so determined, one might think the thing is non-momentary. To this he says: "That [destruction] is its... and so forth. They determine that lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) in this jar and so forth only after [the end of] *saṃsāra*, due to the persistence of ignorance, at the time when the continuum is interrupted; they do not determine it previously, at the time of its existence. Even though there is seeing—meaning, even though the perishable nature is being seen—there is no conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) at the time of seeing.

This is because, due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the arising of a subsequent similar [moment], there is an absence of clarity in perception. And since the determination of the nature of destruction occurs at the time when the continuum is interrupted, it is by virtue of that—that is, by virtue of that determination—that the nature of destruction of the entity is established as having precisely that temporal condition (*upādhi*), namely, the time at which the determination of the nature of destruction occurs.
