He states the example with the words "in the case of transformation," and so forth.

Just as a poisonous substance, even when held in the hand, is not recognized as poison by ignorant persons because of their delusion until later it is identified as such upon seeing the effects produced by the poison, such as the flow of saliva and so forth; this much alone constitutes the illustration. It is not, however, an illustration in the sense that the power to kill was grasped earlier and only later identified. Therefore, the connection is: "this destruction is like that.
Since there is no cause for destruction apart from the existence of the entity itself, it is said to be "pervasive of existence" (*sattāvyāpī*), meaning it pervades all that exists.

"How so? and so forth is the opponent’s question. "And because of incapacity" is the reply. "Because of that cause" means because of the cause of destruction; the word "and" implies also because of being a non-agent (*akārakatva*). Explaining this very point, he says: "Of one who produces non-existence," meaning because of the negation of agency (*kārakatva*) in an action that is intended to be the producer of non-existence. That which is intended to be the producer of a non-entity becomes precisely a non-agent. To demonstrate its incapacity, he says: "For when [the entity] is established," and so forth.

Does the cause of destruction produce a destruction that is non-different from the entity, or one that is different from it? First, the initial position is not tenable; for once an entity is established, a causal agent cannot produce that entity simply because it is already established. Nor is the second position tenable, because the production of something else does nothing to that entity, since its state remains unchanged. Regarding the phrase "of the nature of that or not that," etc.: since destruction—whether of the nature of the entity or other than it—is produced by a cause, the cause of destruction performs no function [with respect to the entity]; therefore, it is established that it is not required, as it lacks efficacy.

But how is there a negation of activity? He says: Proponents of a caused destruction maintain that "destruction" is the non-existence (*abhāva*) of an entity (*bhāva*) and thus possesses a cause. We, however, have stated that destruction is the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity itself. Therefore, since this cause of destruction brings about destruction—that is, it brings about non-existence—it follows [that it acts]. Now, if this were the case, and if something called "non-existence" were an effect possessing an intrinsic nature, then, because it would be an effect like a sprout and so forth, it would be an entity itself and not a non-entity.

Now, just as a jar is to be produced in the form of a jar and a cloth is to be produced in the form of a cloth, but a jar does not become a cloth simply because it is a product; likewise, an entity (*bhāva*) would have to be produced in the form of an entity, and a non-entity (*abhāva*) would also have to be produced in the form of a non-entity, rather than [the non-entity] becoming an entity itself. That is incorrect. For an entity is that which "comes to be," and a non-entity is that which "does not come to be. Thus, a non-entity is the opposite of an entity. Furthermore, its nature as a non-entity is not established by its appearing in that form, but rather by its being the absence of an entity.

It is precisely this that is being questioned: if [non-existence] were of the nature of existence, it would lack the form of non-existence and thus could not even appear. Furthermore, there is no appearance of non-existences as having mutually distinct forms; and since non-existence is devoid of form and thus lacks causal efficacy (*akāryatva*), the meaning of the statement "one produces non-existence" would be "one does not produce existence. Consequently, the negation of an action would be effected by this cause of destruction. Nevertheless, even if an action is negated, this cause of destruction remains ineffective.

How is it that a thing does not depend on anything else for its destruction? Thus, it is established that a thing is independent with respect to its own destruction. But one might ask: even if destruction is causeless, how can a thing be independent with respect to its non-existence? For its very nature is such that it ceases upon encountering an opposing factor—just as the stream of other things [ceases] upon meeting a hammer or the like. Therefore, since it does not cease when an opposing factor is absent, just as before, how can there be momentariness?

That is incorrect. For if the nature of a thing consists in its dependence upon a contradictory [factor], and if that [nature] did not exist previously, then because there would be a difference between its prior and subsequent forms, it would necessarily be non-eternal. Alternatively, if that nature exists even previously, then its cessation should have occurred even before. Or, if it does not cease at that time because the contradictory factor is absent, then how can it have a nature that depends upon a contradictory factor? [It can only do so] when the contradictory factor is actually present; the nature of depending upon a contradictory factor exists only then, and not at other times.

If that which is contradictory does not assist the entity, how can it depend upon it? Or, if there is assistance, then even in the presence of the contradictory, the other entity would arise; thus, the preceding entity would be seen in its former state, because it has not ceased due to the absence of the presence of the contradictory. If, on the other hand, it does cease, then the cessation of the entity is not dependent upon the contradictory. And if it does not destroy the entity, how can it be contradictory?

Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), existence does not cease upon the presence of an opposing factor; rather, it simply fails to arise. For instance, a jar, while undergoing cessation, depends on auxiliary causes such as a mallet to become a producer of shards, thereby ceasing to initiate similar moments. Thus, there is a non-arising of the continuum, but the flow does not cease by depending on an opposing factor.

And since a thing that is about to arise through a continuum does not arise from that continuum when an opposing factor is present, for this very reason, the determination of "destruction with a cause" by those of dull intellect, as well as the determination of "opposition" in the case of a hammer and so forth, is entirely consistent. Therefore, precisely because it is independent, wherever destruction is observed by you to occur, it occurs there solely by its own nature.

Now, even if destruction were causeless, it would only be causeless at the very moment when the destruction of a jar or the like is perceived, and not prior to that, because it is not perceived then. [Objection: Since a jar or the like arises with the property of lasting for only a single moment, its destruction must exist even before [that moment]. [Reply: But just as there is no arising from its own causes with the property of lasting for only a single moment, so too there could be an arising with the property of lasting for many moments; for causal complexes are seen to possess diverse potencies.

In this regard, one might think that there could be something which produces an imperishable nature; to this he says: "From this," and so forth. And from this [cause], which exists as mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even when [the effect] is not perceived elsewhere due to spatial or other obstructions, destruction occurs by its very nature even previously, because of the presence of the contradictory factor when it is thus perceived.

He thinks as follows: For those things whose destruction is observed, if their destruction did not occur at every moment, then the very perception of destruction would not be possible. To explain: if an entity were to persist in the second moment, it would have to persist forever, because its nature would be to endure for two moments even in that second moment. And in that case, it would have to persist for another two moments.

Furthermore, because its nature would be to persist for two moments, it would necessarily remain in the subsequent moment as well; this should be understood for each successive moment, such that the entity would endure as long as saṃsāra lasts.

Now, if at the first moment the nature of an entity were to endure for two moments, then at the second moment that nature would endure for only one moment. Even so, because of the difference between these two natures, there would be momentariness. But this is not the case; for even if that were so, since the entity at the first moment possesses a nature that persists for multiple moments, it would follow that it is non-momentary, which—as has already been stated—would entail its remaining [in existence] as long as saṃsāra lasts.

If it is argued: "But even in the second moment, although the entity does not persist into subsequent moments, since it persists in the first moment as well—due to the non-difference of its form—it certainly possesses a duration of two moments."

No. For it is the very nature of an entity that it remains in one moment and will remain in another moment. If that same nature persists in the second moment, then it would likewise remain in one moment and persist in another; this should be understood for each subsequent moment as well, and thus there would be no destruction of the entity. Yet destruction is observed. Therefore, because destruction cannot otherwise be accounted for, one infers momentary destruction.
In that case, how can there be an inference of momentary destruction regarding produced things that are not perceived, since destruction itself is not observed?

This is not a fault, because if that very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) which exists in their first moment also exists in the second and subsequent moments, then there is indeed "coming into being after having not existed" (*abhūtvā-bhavanam*), just as in the first moment. Alternatively, if in the first moment there is only its birth (*janman*) and not its duration (*sthiti*), and in the second moment there is only its duration and not its birth—even so, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would still follow, because there is no difference between birth and the thing born, nor between duration and the thing enduring. Furthermore, duration without birth in the second moment is not logical.

If there is birth, then there is no persistence, because that [persistence] occurs in the second and subsequent moments. If it were likewise in the second moment and so on, then in every case there would be only origination and not persistence; thus, there is momentariness. Furthermore, since the connection with successive times—which is distinct from one another—is non-different from the produced entity, there is indeed momentariness.

He states the meaning of the verse with the words "so 'yam" and so forth: "this" refers to destruction. "In some [place], such as a jar, when a mallet or similar object is present" means likewise in other cases as well—that is, even prior to the presence of the mallet. The same applies even when there is an intervention by space and so forth. (198–99)

Concluding the point previously set forth—that "therein, two [types of evidence] are proofs of an existent"—he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). For this reason, whatever inference has an existent as its object is of only two kinds, by means of the two marks (*liṅga*) consisting of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*). Why? Because only those two, effect and essential nature, have a necessary connection (*sambandhaniyama*) with the [probandum's] own nature, as stated in the *Svabhāvahetu* section. The analysis of the compound is as follows: that inference for which the effect is the mark; likewise, that for which the essential nature is the mark.

In the case of "pervasion according to its own [nature] regarding the probandum," the cause is the pervader of the effect as the probandum; likewise, for an essential nature (*svabhāva*), the essential nature itself is the pervader and the probandum. When that is the probandum, it is because of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between those two very signs—the effect and the essential nature—with the possessor of the sign (*liṅgin*). (198–99)

With reference to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), he says: "Because of activity," and so forth. Because activity—characterized by the certainty of existence and by verbal usage—is preceded by cognition and preceded by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). When there is no apprehension of its existence—that is, when that entity which is the object of activity is not apprehended through either perception or inference—a prudent person should not engage [with it]. By this much alone, the status of non-apprehension as a means of valid knowledge is stated, even in the case of one whose object is invisible.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "But the third reason is said to be that which makes non-apprehension known. The phrase "without distinction" means setting aside the qualification "having a perceptible object," [it applies] generally when some object is to be proven. He demonstrates that very same object with the words beginning with "ascertainment of existence" (*sanniścaya*). An ascertainment of existence is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "it exists" which follows upon a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). The verbal expression "it exists" (*sac-chabda*) is precisely the sound that follows upon that [conceptualization]. Likewise, the practical application "it exists" is the conventional usage of existence (*sad-vyavahāra*).
For in their negation, [non-apprehension] is of every kind—both having a perceptible object and having an imperceptible object.

[Objection: But surely it was stated in the *kārikā* that there is "activity" (*pravṛtti*); how then is it explained in the *vṛtti* as "ascertainment of existence," and so forth? [Response: He says: "Because of the ascertainment of existence," and so on. Since linguistic conventions (*śabdavyavahāra*) proceed from the ascertainment of things that exist—that is, of those which are present—therefore, those three, namely the ascertainment of existence and linguistic conventions, are called "activity. This is because they are factors of activity (*pravṛttyaṅga*), meaning they serve as the cause for a person’s engagement. Consequently, there is no contradiction between the *sūtra* and the *vṛtti*.

Furthermore, what is the reason that the conventional usage of "existent" ceases when perception ceases? For it was stated previously that non-perception itself, in both its forms and without distinction, constitutes non-existence. And that non-existence is spoken of in terms of the cognizer’s perspective when there is a superior non-perception; for the cognizer determines that "it does not exist" because it is not being perceived, not by virtue of the object itself. For instance, regarding a remote object, both its existence and non-existence remain doubtful.

Therefore, that remote object is indeed non-existent for this person’s cognition as long as there is no cognition of it here. Why? Because even though that remote object exists, it does not produce its own objective form [in cognition] due to being unperceived; since it does not produce an objective form for this person, even if it exists, it is as good as non-existent. In reality, however, that which is not perceived is neither existent nor non-existent. Why? Because even among existing things, since perception sometimes fails due to remoteness of nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, there is no certainty of non-existence.

In some cases there is the exclusion of existence, because this non-perception is equal even with respect to non-existent things. "That" means "therefore"; the connection is that "this existence" [is excluded]. Of what nature is it? It is characterized by non-perception and remote in terms of place and so forth, because for the cognizer there is an absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since it has ceased due to the absence of perception and inference, what does it do by virtue of the object? It turns back the linguistic conventions (*śabda-vyavahāra*) caused by itself. Others read "characterized by perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇam*); the meaning is that existence itself is figuratively termed "perception," and such existence has ceased.

For that very reason, this non-apprehension—of what? Of those things that have reached the conditions for apprehension—is of the nature of non-existence even in reality; [the word] "even" implies that it is so also by virtue of the cognizer. What is the reason? Because it is unfit for engagement and because it is fit for the conventional usage of "non-existent. This non-apprehension also possesses equal authority (*prāmāṇya*) insofar as it negates the conventional usage of "existent" regarding this object. In this context, [it concerns] the negation of the conventional usage of "existent."

This non-apprehension, which consists in the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, also has the ascertainment of non-existence as its result. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose result is the ascertainment of non-existence. (200–201)

He explains [this] with the words "in the case of non-existence," and so forth. Even in the case of non-existence—that is, even when there is no certainty—there is certainly no possibility that an entity capable of being perceived would not be perceived while existing and while all other causes of perception are present. However, the aforementioned non-perception of a remote object does not prove non-existence. For instance, non-perception is characterized by the cessation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*).

In this regard, the scope of the treatise (*śāstra*) is limited to this specific section; therefore, many objects that are irrelevant, not necessarily implied, and remote by nature and so forth, are not the subject matter of the treatise—this is what is meant. Furthermore, they are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as he says they are "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*). Nor are they objects of inference (*anumāna*), because they are "without a mark" (*aliṅga*). They are "without a mark" because no inferential sign (*liṅga*) exists for them. How can there be a non-existence of those supersensible objects on the basis of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which is characterized by the cessation of the three means of valid cognition? It is certainly not so. (200–201)

The proponent says, "this very [scripture]... regarding all objects—those remote in space, time, and nature—by the cessation of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is, by the cessation of perception, inference, and scripture. "Of that" refers to the scripture; for it proceeds toward an object that is not useful for human goals (*puruṣārtha*) only when there is no application of it [as a source of knowledge]. This is because, as stated in the passage beginning with "for the scripture," if the scripture were to proceed by relying on an object not useful for human goals, it would result in the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) for the scripture, which would otherwise be mere incoherent chatter (*abaddhapralāpa*) consisting of unrelated speech.

It might be argued that all objects are useful for the purposes of the person (*puruṣārtha*). To this he says: "In that context," and so forth. "In that context" means in the introduction to the investigation of the purposes of the person. "Fixed for each individual" means fixed for every person. By this, he states that because persons are infinite, the mental fluctuations (*cetovṛtti*) are also infinite—the analysis of the compound being: "those whose nature it is to arise from indeterminate causes. By this, even in the case of a single person, there is multiplicity due to the diversity of causes.

Such mental states (*cetovṛtti*) need not necessarily be described in their entirety at every step, because that would be impossible. Alternatively, specific substances (*dravyaviśeṣa*) separated by time and space, or those not conducive to human goals (*puruṣārtha*), need not necessarily be described; therefore, the treatise does not take them as its subject matter. Those mental states and those specific [substances] are referred to in the masculine gender (*puṃliṅga*) by using the pronoun *tān*, applying the rule "the masculine remains when combined with the feminine" (*pumān striyā*).
(Pāṇini 1.2.67)

Nor are they objects of direct perception; thus he says, "And not," and so forth. Likewise, regarding things that are remote—meaning remote in terms of space and so on—there is no capacity to produce cognition because of the absence of their own power, that is, the absence of their presence in their own form (*svarūpa*). By this, the term "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*) is explained.

He says that even inference does not have those things as its objects, beginning with "And that necessarily," etc. "Of these" refers to those separated by space and so forth. "By which" refers to the perception of an effect. "Nor these" refers to those that are remote. "All" includes even the non-perception of the unobservable. "Of the certainty of cessation" means of the certainty of non-existence. "Since this is so, therefore" means for that reason. "This"—namely, the non-perception of the unobservable—does not have the result of a certainty of existence; that is, it is not the cause for the conventional usage of "existent."

Nor does it have the result of a certainty regarding non-existence, because of doubt. For this reason, non-apprehension would lack the status of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*), since the results of means of valid cognition consist in determination—that is, they have certainty as their result. For even perception, though a means of valid cognition, brings about certainty only with respect to those aspects among all possible aspects that it determines.

One might object: "Could this not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the prohibition of activity? To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. "In this way" refers to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Regarding the phrase "cognition free from doubt" (*niḥśaṅkaparicchedam*), the analysis of the compound is: that cognition whose determination (*pariccheda*) is free from doubt. The meaning is that when there is doubt, the mind does not produce a certainty such as, "One must certainly not act. This is because even from doubt, activity sometimes occurs in people such as farmers.

If one asks, "In that case, how is its validity established as having activity as its result? he says: "In that state, that... and so forth. In that way—that is, by that nature—this [non-apprehension] called non-perception is faultless and without defect as a cause for non-activity, provided that someone were to engage in conventional practice preceded by certainty; that is, they would initiate such practices as those concerning existence based on valid cognition.

By this means, this non-perception of the unobservable is said to have non-engagement as its result; that is, it is said to have as its result the negation of certain conventional practices regarding existence and so forth. However, since conventional practices regarding existence and so forth that are merely doubtful are not negated, human engagement may still occur.

"Arising from a specific excellence of the mark" (*liṅgātiśayabhāvinī*) means: the mark (*liṅga*) is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); its excellence (*atiśaya*) is its specific quality (*viśeṣa*), namely, the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehensibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*). That [non-apprehension] in which this state (*bhāva*)—its actual existence (*sadbhāva*)—resides is so described. The meaning is that it possesses a specific mark (*liṅgaviśeṣavatī*). In other words, it is the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehensibility. He explains this with the words beginning with "here" (*atretyādi*). "Here" refers to the ascertainment of absence (*nivṛttiniścaye*). "As previously exemplified" refers to [the verse]:
"A certain [non-apprehension], depending on a distinction of causes, has the cognition of non-existence as its result," and so forth.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)—that should not be understood without qualification; rather, it refers to [non-apprehension] such as that of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth. [In this context,] "intrinsic nature" refers to that which is remote in terms of place and so on, and "indicative mark" (*liṅga*) refers to a signifier. "Non-cognition" refers to the lack of knowledge regarding these two. "The principle here has been illustrated as pertaining to the non-cognition of intrinsic nature and of the signifier; when non-existence is to be proven, there is no validity [to mere non-apprehension]. (1.203) The non-cognition of intrinsic nature is the cessation of perception (*pratyakṣa-nivṛtti*); the non-cognition of the signifier is the cessation of inference (*anumāna-nivṛtti*). The overall meaning is that this principle has been illustrated with respect to the cessation of both perception and inference when their objects are invisible (*adṛśya-viṣaya*).

He explains [the passage] beginning with *yasya* (of which). "Of whomsoever"—that is, of any [being] such as a *piśāca*—*saḥ* refers to that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "By the mere non-apprehension of that" means by the mere non-apprehension of its object, in the form of the cessation of perception, [one concludes] "it does not exist. As was stated previously: "Because even existing things are sometimes not apprehended," and so forth. By this, the ignorance of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvājñāna*) has been explained.

He says "yopi... and so forth in order to explain the non-cognition of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The gloss of the term "of the indicator" is "of the mark" (*liṅga*). An object that is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is rejected; for example, "there is no dispassionate [person]," and so forth. Likewise, due to the absence of an indicator, i.e., a mark, either a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is rejected. Therefore, a particularity is rejected, not the mere locus (*dharmimātra*); for example, "there is no [act of] giving," and so forth. "Giving" (*dāna*), "violence" (*hiṃsā*), and "hostility" (*virotiḥ*) form a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The volitions (*cetanāḥ*) have these as their objects.

The meaning is: [the intention] of giving and the intention of abstaining from violence. (p. 375) By means of being a cause for prosperity—that is, by means of being a cause for results such as heaven—it is not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of these intentions that is denied here, because they are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). Rather, it is said that their specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), namely the state of being a cause for prosperity, does not exist.

[Objection: Since intentions are directly perceived, their status as causes for prosperity must also be part of their very essence; therefore, how can there be an error regarding that which is directly perceived? And so forth.

The connection is that even regarding an object that is directly perceived, one who is mistaken might even deny it. To the question "In what way is he mistaken?", he says: "Because they have that result," and so forth. Those specific volitions (*cetanā*) which are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and have been observed to lack that result—that is, to lack the result of spiritual elevation (*abhyudaya*)—are the basis for the analogy. He asks how there is indeed this similarity, and replies: "Because there is no immediate succession of the result. This refers to those other volitions that lack that result, as well as those that do have that result; in both cases, the immediate succession of that result is not observed.

"Not for that long" means that the absence of the result is not established merely by the non-perception of its immediate succession. Why? Because of the observation of results that are separated [from their causes]—as expressed in the phrase "of those that are separated," and so forth. This is because results are seen to occur at a later time, characterized by a successive transformation of states following from the cause. It is like the toxic reaction of a rat or a mad dog infected with the *ālarka* virus; for that does not manifest at the very moment the poison enters the body, but rather arises upon the presence of a specific time acting as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*).
It is not, however, produced by some other distinct cause; it is just like that.

It might be argued: "Since the transformation caused by the poison of rats and the like is observed after a lapse of time, its existence is indeed logical; however, the fruit of giving and so forth is never observed at any time, so how can its existence be established? To this he says: "That," and so on. "The existence of that" means that there is no contradiction in the existence of those two things—the fruit of giving and other such things, and supersensible entities. In this regard, mere non-perception is not a proof against the existence of the fruit of giving or of supersensible states.

The opponent argues: "If there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), there is no rejection [of existence]; however, what proof is there for the existence of an entity? There is no proof at all; therefore, a determination of its reality is not tenable."

"Therefore," says the Teacher: "Since there is an absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses, doubt is appropriate for a discerning person. Or rather, when something cannot be rejected and no proving means of valid cognition for it appears, such a possibility is reasonable: 'Perhaps at some time a proving means of valid cognition for this might appear to someone possessed of insight. Therefore, because of doubt regarding the object or doubt regarding the means of valid cognition, there is no rejection."

Others, however, explain that because there is an absence of both proving and refuting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding whether a detached mind is a cause for [attaining] excellence, there is indeed doubt; thus, they state that there is no denial that a detached mind might be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for omniscience, and that this means of valid cognition will be explained in the second chapter.

This is because an effect can arise even from something obstructed. Therefore, although the sequence of the text here is "among the supersensible (*atīndriya*), of certain objects and intrinsic natures," nevertheless, the connection is made according to what is appropriate.

For certain intrinsic natures, such as the cause of prosperity and so forth, there may be a lack of proof for the indicator (*jñāpaka*). How so? Due to the absence of clarity in perception; that is, because the experience of those objects lacks the capacity to produce a determination of their nature exactly as it was apprehended—this being the case for certain objects such as states of detachment of mind and the like. This is because the effect characterized by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), which serves as the indicator for that [nature], is absent.

He asks why there is an absence of such an effect and says: "Of the causes," and so forth. There is no rule that an effect which necessarily makes itself known through its causes must be produced as something perceivable by all persons. However, others explain it differently: for certain natures that are proponents of the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and for objects such as the dispassionate mind and so forth, there would be a non-establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes them known—that is, that determines them. Why? Because of the absence of clarity in perception (*darśana-pāṭava*).

This is what is meant: perception itself is the indicator of some object, yet because it lacks clarity, it does not produce a determination of all its aspects. Furthermore, since there is no necessity for causes to produce their effects, one does not perceive the immediate effect [of perception]. Thus, even by way of its effect, its status as a cause of spiritual elevation (*abhyudaya*) cannot be denied. Likewise, because the perception of supersensible objects—which is characterized as mental cognition (*manovijñāna*)—lacks clarity, it is not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For there is no determination of these [causes] by means of their effects, because there is no necessity for causes to produce an effect. Indeed, there is no rule that an effect must necessarily be produced in another continuum as a signifier of its own cause. Therefore, neither perception nor inference applies to them.

"It is not certain" means that the non-existence [of those things] is not established merely by the absence of the aforementioned indicators; for there is the non-existence of supersensible objects. This is because even some objects that have not been perceived through perception or inference may later, in due course or sequence, be apprehended through perception or inference when they are revealed—such as objects situated behind a wall or in a crevice. Thus, in the case of remote objects, the non-perception of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is not a proof of non-existence, nor is the non-perception of their effect (*kāryānupalambha*).

"But even in that case, the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalambha*) is a means of proving non-existence," he says with the words "But regarding the effect" (*kārye tu*), etc. Regarding the effect, however—even when it is remote in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth—the non-cognition of the causal agent (*kāraka*), which is the non-perception of the cause, is indeed a means of proving non-existence. He explains this with the words "intrinsic nature," etc.: when the non-existence of an intrinsic nature whose object is remote is to be proven, only the non-perception of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is said to be not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); but the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalambha*), on the other hand, is certainly a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a remote object, the non-perception of the cause itself cannot be ascertained; how then could it establish the absence of the effect? [Response: True. This much can be said: in a case where no cause is specified, the effect necessarily does not exist. It is for this slight reason that it is introduced here. For this very reason, he says in general: "For it is not the case," and so forth.

The opponent [objects] with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely): because smoke is observed in places such as dwellings even when fire has perished, there is thus a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since an effect is seen even when its cause is absent. [The author replies: By this statement—"when the cause is absent, the effect would not exist"—we do not mean that the effect exists at the same time as the cause’s duration, nor that the existence of the effect lasts as long as the existence of the cause; for if we did, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) expressed by "even when the fire has perished," etc., would follow. Rather, what is stated by this sentence? He says: "The cause has been produced," and so forth.

Thus far, it has been stated on the assumption that [the effect] is stable. However, if [the cause] is momentary, once the cause has perished, there is no possibility at all for the effect to remain; so how could there be any suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? For instance, a moment of smoke produced by fire has no existence whatsoever once that fire has perished, because it perishes due to its momentariness. And as for the smoke that remains subsequently, that is caused solely by [that] smoke and not by fire. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "And not in that way," and so forth.

"Likewise, it persists" means that even when the initial cause has perished, it continues to exist for a period of time. "Having that as its material cause" means having the previously ceased cause as its material cause. To the question, "How then is it said that even subsequent smoke has fire as its cause? he says: "By way of succession," and so forth. First, fire alone produces the initial moment of smoke; that moment of smoke produces another, and that another—thus by way of succession. Clarifying this very point, he says: "Because of the assistance rendered to the continuum. Because it first generates the series (*prabandha*), it is designated as the cause of that [subsequent] effect.

Therefore, when there is such a designation for a cause that its effect exists even subsequently, if the non-existence of this cause is somehow established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is determined that the fruit of that cause—that is, the effect of that cause—does not exist. And this has been stated with the intention of establishing the non-existence of a subject that has been specifically indicated; however, regarding a subject that has not been so indicated, this is not a [valid] means of cognition, because its result depends upon a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

"Of its own nature," and so forth. "Of the object" refers to the pervader; when its non-existence is to be proven in the subject (*liṅgin*)—which is not distinct from its own nature—both the non-perception of the own nature and the non-perception of the pervader are the means of proving non-existence. This is the context under discussion. (203–4)

He explains [the passage] beginning with "the absence of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvābhāva*) and so forth. The term "some" (*kaścit*) refers to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). If the pervading intrinsic nature were established as existing for this pervaded [subject], even while it is not being perceived, then that would constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the non-perception of the cause or the pervader would be a valid means of knowledge only if their absence—the absence of those two, namely the cause and the pervader—were cognized by some reason known as the "non-perception of intrinsic nature."

He states the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "yadi" (*if*): the connection is that "if the non-existence of this causal factor (*kāraka*) were established," and likewise the non-existence of the pervading nature (*svabhāva*). This is due to some indicative reason (*gamaka*), namely, the non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānupalambha*). Thus, this causal factor or pervader, being non-existent, does not establish itself; consequently, it respectively excludes the effect (*kārya*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*). For if their absence is not established—that is, if the absence of the causal factor and the pervader is not established—there remains doubt regarding the effect and the pervaded which are to be excluded. (204–5)

If it is argued that when the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to be proven, its non-apprehension alone is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then how is the non-existence of an entity such as a jar established through its own non-apprehension?

He states the reply: "Of the perceptible," and so forth. The meaning is that non-apprehension (*svabhāvānupalambha*) has been stated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to a remote object, but not with respect to a perceptible object. "Of the perceptible" refers to an entity whose nature and other qualities are not remote; when such an entity exists but is not apprehended, the absence of the existence of that entity is cognized. When? When there is no possibility of causes for the non-perception [of the object]. That is, when there is no deficiency in the other causal factors; the meaning is: when all the other conditions for apprehension (*upalambhapratyaya*) are complete.

The commentary begins with "bhāvo hi" and so forth. If an entity (*bhāva*) were remote from its own nature (*svabhāva*) and other such factors, it would be perceived by its respective grasper; that is to say, whatever is the grasper of a given thing—namely, the sense faculty—it would necessarily perceive that entity, provided it is as described. This applies when there are no obstructions to perception, such as physical barriers and the like—the word "and the like" (*ādi*) including deficiencies or impediments—and when the conditions for perception (*upalambha-pratyaya*) are present. (205–6)

Thus, that which is not perceived as it actually exists is determined to be non-existent. What is the reason? Because for such a thing—one that exists and has reached the conditions for perception—there is no deviation from being perceived. This very reason that was stated previously regarding the determination of the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a perceptible object, beginning with "the non-seeing of the perceptible," is to be understood here as well. In what respect is it the probandum (*sādhya*)? It is when the probandum is the absence of both the cause and the pervader.

"And of that which is contradictory," and so forth. When there is the perception of something that is contradictory to that by means of whose absence the probandum is established, there would be the ascertainment of non-existence—that is, of the absence of the object to be negated. For what reason? Because when a contradictory entity exists—that is, when it is present—there is a sublation of its existence; because there is a sublation of the existence of that which is intended to be negated.

The passage beginning with "yo hi" is an explanation. To the question "Why does it not remain [stable]?", he says "tad" and so forth. This means that because those two contradictory [causes] possess as their substratum (*āśraya*) a mutual deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in their respective material causes (*upādāna*); for example, the material cause of cold is the substratum for the deficiency of the material cause of heat, and vice versa. For that reason, there is a contradiction in the simultaneous commencement of two contradictories in a single location. Thus, when one of those two contradictories exists, the non-existence of the other is understood.

As was stated previously regarding the divisions of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*): "There is no cold touch here because of fire," and so forth. Although the term "non-apprehension" is not explicitly heard here, nevertheless, this logical mark (*liṅga*) called the "contradictory nature" (*svabhāvaviruddha*) is not stated as something distinct from non-apprehension. What is the reason? Because the cognition of contradiction arises from that very same non-perception (*anupalambha*), and it has been stated that the proof of absence (*abhāva*) results from contradiction.

"Let it be granted that the cognition of an entity arises from such a non-perception of the perceptible; however, how is that [non-perception] an inference?"—the sense being that it is not an inference at all, but rather a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
"How could it not be [an inference]? asks the Teacher.

"Because it requires an example," says the opponent, "for inference possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and thus depends upon an example. He states this very dependence on an example with the words "For it is not... (*na hi*); "in this" refers to non-perception.

The Teacher asks: "What [is the reason] not? The opponent replies with the words "That," and so forth. That [refers to] things such as a sky-flower. How, and by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is it to be understood that they are non-existent, such that this would be the case? [Otherwise] there would be no example. If it is argued that the non-existence of a sky-flower and the like is to be understood from the very mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), then [the Teacher asks]: "In that case"—that is, regarding the sky-flower and so on—how can there be an establishment of non-existence that lacks an example, being devoid of an example? Or, if there were an example, there would be the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because one would have to posit yet another [mark of non-apprehension] for that [example] as well.

And thus, if there were an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the object to be proven (*sādhya*) would not be established; furthermore, since there is the fault of infinite regress regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the proof of the existence of an indefinable non-existence (*nirupākhyābhāva*) is unique in that it requires no example. Likewise in other cases—as in the formal argument, "There is no jar here, because it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception" and so forth—non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is not an inference (*anumāna*), because it does not depend upon an example.

The Master [Dharmakīrti] says, "Even though he hears... This has been stated more than once: that in the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), it is not non-existence itself that is proven, but rather the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence. Even though he hears this, Deva—the favorite of fools—is not clever enough to comprehend it, such that he raises the objection that the [reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) even when the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) exists. He begins to show the very example with the words, "For the cause," and so forth.

The non-apprehension of what is apprehensible is the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), which is the sign or cause of the conventional designations of non-existence. By its own presence—that is, by its own proximity—it establishes these very conventional designations of non-existence, which have non-apprehension as their own sign or nature. This being so, it serves as the example in all cases. Of what kind is it? It is one whose presence is capable [of producing its effect] through the totality of its own causes.

The "assemblage of its own causes" refers to that [collection] in which there is a suitable proximity for the sprout and so forth; such is what is meant by that term. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever has its complete and unimpeded causal conditions present must necessarily exist therein, such as the sprout and so forth. And since the status of being a cause for the conventional designation of "non-existent"—in the case of things that have reached the conditions for perception yet are not perceived—is indeed present [in the assemblage], this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Why is it that here only the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) is being proven, and not non-existence itself? To this he says: "Non-existence," and so forth. Here, in the case of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), non-perception itself is existence, as was stated previously. Therefore, non-existence is not what is being proven. Since it is precisely the conventional usage of non-existence that is being proven here, this non-perception is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*); such is the connection.

The non-perception of the cause leads to the inference of the conventional designation of the absence of the effect; that which has this very [non-perception] as its characteristic is indicated here as a bahuvrīhi compound in a general sense, and subsequently the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied. Furthermore, when the effect is inferred from a complete cause, it is an inference of capacity (*yogyatā*), and thus it is included within the *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason); we shall explain this in the fourth chapter.

"Let there be an example in the case of the non-perception of the perceptible; but how can there be one in the case of the non-perception of the imperceptible? To this he says: "By the word *sat*," etc. When the negation of the conventional usage of "existent" (*sadvyavahāra*) is to be proven regarding objects remote in space and so forth by means of the cessation of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇanivṛtti*), the absence of the effect is proven from the absence of the cause. Therefore, in this context, the example is not merely that which is devoid of any designation (*nirupākhyam*); rather, sprouts and the like—which are absent due to the deficiency of their causes or conditions—are also examples.

The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: that which has deficient causes does not come into being, just as a sprout [does not arise] from a seed lacking its [necessary] conditions. And since the causal conditions for the conventional usage of "existent" are unperceived in the case of the non-perception of the invisible, this is a non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).

Furthermore, as for what was said—"How is that which is non-existent and indefinable (*nirupākhya*) to be understood?"—even in that case, regarding the example of the indefinable, this very activity characterized by the conventional usage of "ignorance" is negated; however, it is not through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) that non-existence is established. What is the reason? [It is] because of the phrase "non-apprehension," and so forth. Non-apprehension is, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), simply the apprehension of a rabbit [as distinct from] horns and the like, which are non-existent.
That very thing is the characteristic of the non-existence of a rabbit's horn, and thus it is already established.

It might be argued: if non-existence is established as the object in the case of the non-perception of the unobservable, then the conventional usage of "non-existent" based on that [non-perception] is already established; so what is the use of that conventional usage of "non-existent"? Furthermore, since even in the case of the non-perception of the unobservable, the non-occurrence of the conventional usage [of "existent"] is already established due to the absence of the grounds for such usage, what is the point of establishing the negation of the conventional usage of "existent"?

Likewise, there is no purpose whatsoever in using an example characterized by the demonstration of a previously established object for the sake of non-apprehension; therefore, he says "so this," and so forth, meaning that this is being established for the sake of the deluded person. [This is done] while not acting contrary to the engagement in the conventional usage of "non-existent" by accepting non-apprehension of the perceptible as the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent"; and while not acting contrary to the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" by accepting both the absence of that [object] in the case of the non-apprehension of the imperceptible and the absence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which is the cause for the conventional usage of "existent."

It is established that [the convention] is applied according to what has been accepted. By means of the reason of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), you have elsewhere employed the conventional designation of "non-existent" (*asadvyavahāra*); that same reason exists here as well. Therefore, it is established: "Therefore, employ the conventional designation of non-existence. Likewise, by means of the reason of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), you have elsewhere employed the conventional designation of "existent" (*sadvyavahāra*); that same reason does not exist here in that which is indefinable (*anirupākhyā*). Therefore, it is established: "Therefore, do not employ the conventional designation of existence. Just as in the case of the indefinable?

Just as in the case of a rabbit’s horn and the like, the conventional usage of "non-existent" occurs because of the non-perception of something perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), so too does it occur here.

Or else: just as there is the cognition of a sprout and so forth when its causes are present, so too is there the conventional usage of "existent. And just as the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" occurs in the case of the indefinable (*nirupākhya*) due to the absence of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), or as there is the cessation of an effect when its cause is deficient, in the same way it is established that there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" regarding remote objects.

First of all, how and by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this very absence of apprehension, termed "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*), established? It is not by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that is contradictory to having non-existence as its object. Nor is it by inference (*anumāna*), because the latter is preceded by perception. Furthermore, the non-apprehension of the location (*pradeśa*) associated with the object cannot establish its absence, because absence, being formless (*nīrūpa*), cannot possess the nature of a related term (*sambandhin*). Moreover, if the location itself is not apprehended, the property (*dharma*) [of non-apprehension] cannot be established, and thus the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Therefore, Uddyotakara and others maintain that non-apprehension does not possess the status of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*).

To this, he says: "We shall explain this later: since there is no perception of that which distinguishes it, there is likewise non-perception of that [object]; therefore, this non-perception is established by perception itself. Furthermore, regarding what was said—"What is the use of showing an example in the case of non-perception?"—he says: "In other cases as well," and so forth.

Even in an inference that establishes a positive proof, why must the person to be convinced—who accepts the probans, such as "being produced," as being pervaded by the probandum-property which is the pervader—be made to understand it through an example? What is the reason? Because the probandum-property, which pervades, is established simply from the statement of the reason (*hetu*) which is pervaded by its respective probandum; for one who possesses certain knowledge of the relationship characterized by [invariable] concomitance, the purpose [of the example] is merely for the sake of recollection regarding that which is confused.

This [point] generates a recollection for the deluded person regarding this non-apprehension by means of an illustration. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "so 'yam" and so forth. The phrase "in other cases as well" refers to [non-existent things] such as a rabbit’s horn. Now, regarding that formal argument stated by the teachers beginning with Dignāga—namely, "the *pradhāna* and so forth do not exist because they are not apprehended"—the Teacher asks: "And how could it not be [the case]?"

The objector speaks according to his own intention, beginning with "tadartha" and so forth: when there is a negation of that object—that is, the primary object—there is no employment of the designation that expresses the substratum (dharmin) such as "primordial matter" (pradhāna), for there is no employment of a signifier (vācaka) without its signified (vācya). And when words such as "primordial matter" are not employed, then only the word expressing the negation remains, namely, "they do not exist."

Furthermore, since there is no mention of that which is to be negated, the negation would be devoid of an object; consequently, the word expressing the negation itself could not be employed. Thus, because neither of the two terms of the proposition—namely, "pradhāna" and so forth, nor "do not exist"—would be employed, one could not determine where or what is being proven. Therefore, the application of the means of proof (the reason) through non-perception would be futile. Moreover, since the *pradhāna* and other such entities, which constitute the subject (*pakṣa*), do not exist, the reason could not be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

Alternatively, there is a mutual contradiction between the two terms of the proposition; for, by the employment of the phrase "the primal matter and so forth," their presence is indicated, whereas by the subsequent statement "they do not exist," their absence is indicated. And these two—presence and absence—are mutually contradictory when occurring simultaneously in one and the same place. (206–7)

"This is not a fault" is the rebuttal. Because the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) is established and situated within a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has arisen from beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and because it relies upon existence, non-existence, or both, it is a threefold property (*dharma*). Regarding that verbal object, "that which has no real entity as its material cause" (*bhāvānupādāna*) is the probandum (*sādhya*). "Of this" (*asya*) refers to the locus (*dharmin*)—primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth—which exists only as a mental construct.

"So be it. Non-perception here refers to the non-perception [of the object] as having external *pradhāna* and so forth as its material cause (*upādāna*). Rather, perception itself—[understood] as having mental impressions (*vāsanā*) as its material cause—is what constitutes "non-perception" in this context. It is not the non-existence of that very subject (*dharmin*) established by conceptual construction that is being proven. Why? Because of the employment of terms such as "*pradhāna*" and so on. For if that were negated, there would be no employment of words at all, since they would lack an objective referent (*viṣaya*).

He explains this with the words beginning "niveditam" (it has been stated). For if the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were the denotable object, then upon the negation of the particular characteristic, because the referent of the word would be negated, there would be no employment of the word that expresses it. However, it has already been stated that these words do not have the particular characteristic as their object; rather, they appropriate as their own object that thing which appears in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose origin or production is from beginningless mental impressions (*anādivāsanā*).

Why is it that [words] take as their object only that thing which is the domain of conceptual construction? He says: "Because they share the conceptual construction of the speaker. This means they share the conceptual construction of a general form (*sāmānyākāra*) based on existence, non-existence, or both. He states the reason: "Just as," and so forth. It refers to the object as it appears. Because words are employed with the intention of communicating without overstepping the appearing object, they therefore take as their objects only those things that appear within conceptual construction.

Likewise, the connection is that [words] also possess those conceptual constructions of the listener. What is the reason? Because they generate conceptual constructions having the form of those [objects]. And because they generate conceptual constructions of a general form based on existence, non-existence, or both, words take as their objects only those things that appear within conceptual construction.

It might be argued: "Even if that is so, words nonetheless have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, because they bring about the cognition of the particular characteristic. To this he says: "And not... and so forth. The material cause (*upādāna*) and the effect (*kārya*) are themselves the conditions (*pratyaya*, i.e., cognitions). That form which does not appear therein cannot be determined to have that [particular characteristic] as its object. In this context, the "material cause condition" is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the speaker consisting of the desire to communicate, because it is the cause of the word. The "effect condition" is the conceptual construction of the hearer arising from the word.
For that which does not appear in the cognition of a word is not the meaning of the word; and the particular (svalakṣaṇa) does not appear therein, because it is devoid of a clear form.

[Objection: But how can it have non-existence as its basis, given that [if it were] produced by an object, it would follow that it is non-conceptual? And how can it have non-existence as its basis, since non-existence is not a cause? And how can it have both as its basis, since that would entail the consequence of being causeless? To this he says: "But that... and so forth. A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the form of existent, non-existent, or both; it is produced from the impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by cognitions of the existent, non-existent, or both. That which has its origin—its arising—from that is so described. For this reason, it is said to have the properties of existence, non-existence, and both.

He states the second reason, beginning with "tad" and so forth: "The determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that aspect which appears in that very conceptual construction as being of the nature of existence, non-existence, or both; and by virtue of that [determination], it is said to have the properties of existence, non-existence, or both. (209)

This is what is meant: a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) is said to be that which arises from impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by a cognition of existence (*sat-pratyaya*) and which appears as if it were a determination of the form "existent. This should be understood to apply likewise to properties of non-existence and both [existence and non-existence], because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "existent" and so forth are beginningless precisely because they arise from impressions deposited by preceding cognitions of "existent" and so on. Therefore, they are not produced by an entity or the like. Furthermore, the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) is of three kinds.

Therefore, in this case, persons who are established upon the subject (*dharmin*) which is the referent of the word, and who stand as the basis for the dispute, deliberate upon the existence or non-existence of the *pradhāna* and so forth. To explain how they deliberate, he says: "Does this object, which appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) when the word 'pradhāna' is uttered, have as its basis an external *pradhāna*, or not?"

When that appearance of conceptual construction (vikalpa-pratibhāsa), such as [the notion of] primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth, is the subject (dharmin) to be proven as not having an external entity as its material cause, that very appearance of conceptual construction is the object that cannot be denied; for, being of the nature of cognition, it is personally experienced and is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).

But is it not the case that the very object apprehended by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it is determined (*adhyavasāya*) as having the form of a particular characteristic? And therefore, since [the object] is established by perception, Pradhāna and so forth, as well as the word, would have the particular characteristic as their object. To this he says: "And not that very [object]," and so on. It cannot be said that the very object appearing in conceptual construction is an external particular characteristic. Why? Because even when the particular characteristic has not been reached—that is, when it has not arisen—or when it has ceased, that appearance in conceptual construction does not disappear.

Furthermore, regarding an object such as a jar, there are mutually contradictory aspects such as permanence and impermanence. Since those who possess the habit of adhering to these—the cognitions of other schools—possess the appearance of an object, that very object is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); this is the connection with the subject at hand. (209–10)

To summarize this very point, he says: "The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); that which has its occurrence (*pravṛtti*) located in a single place within that [reality] is its state of being suchness (*tattva*). When that exists, the occurrence of words would be without a basis—that is, devoid of a basis in the ultimate reality—regarding objects distinguished by different philosophical systems, or regarding past and unborn things; that is, there would be no occurrence of words with respect to past and future objects. Likewise, there would be no falsity—that is, no untruthfulness—of any speech whatsoever."

Thus, for the reason stated above, this statement—“it is held to have as its object an entity appearing in conceptual construction” (vv. 210–11)—means that [the cognition] has as its object an entity appearing in conceptual construction regarding a Buddhist entity.

“Of that” refers to the appearance in conceptual construction regarding *pradhāna* and so forth. When it is to be proven that [this appearance] does not have as its material cause (*upādāna*) an external *pradhāna* or similar form as it is imagined—that is, as it is intended—then, since there is a non-perception [of it] as having the intended form as its material cause, the meaning is that the probans is neither unestablished nor a non-property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).

Furthermore, regarding this application [of the argument], it is not the case that "this very word" and so forth [is the object]. What is negated is the object appearing in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises from the word. Why? Because the word is employed in order to present that object appearing in the conceptual construction to the mind of the listener. In its absence—that is, in the absence of the object appearing in the conceptual construction—there would be no application of the word, because such an application would be untenable.

Furthermore, if the negation of the word and its object is what is being proven, then, when that negation of the word and its object is the probandum, the locus (*dharmin*) characterized as the word and its object—which serves as the substratum for that property to be proven, namely non-existence—is itself refuted. Consequently, the aggregate consisting of both the locus and the property would not constitute the probandum; moreover, the property to be proven alone would already be established, since mere non-existence is established somewhere or other.

The passage beginning with "yadi" is an explanation. "Tat" means "therefore"; this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is independent of that exclusion or qualification by the locus (*ādhāra*), namely, its non-existence. For this reason, it should certainly not be introduced at the time of debate. (211–12) "By the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence" means that the real entity itself is investigated through the distinction between the theses of existence and non-existence by discerning persons who do not deny the referent of words and who seek causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This is because the arising of the result is tied to this real entity. (212–13)

Even if this is so, why should the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) not be investigated? To this he says: "The referent," and so forth. What is the use of investigations—namely, investigations into existence or non-existence—of a word-referent that is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), for those who do not seek it but rather seek causal efficiency? He provides an illustration with the words: "Of a eunuch," and so forth. What is the use of an examination regarding the beauty or ugliness of the form of one devoid of masculinity, for a lustful woman desiring sexual union? (213–14)

The passage beginning with "na hi" is an explanation. For a word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), whether it exists or not, does not obstruct—that is, cause one to turn away from—any human goal (*puruṣārtha*), nor does it establish or accomplish one, as the case may be. What is the reason? Because a person adheres to—that is, determines—that word-meaning as being external according to their own attachment (*abhiniveśa*), yet it lacks existence (*asattva*) in that manner, meaning it is non-existent; or alternatively, because it is not desired in accordance with reality (*yathātattva*).

Because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as it truly is, or the specific characteristic of the cognition itself, remains as it is and is not made an object by a word; for this very reason, when a person engages in the investigation of what exists and what does not exist, he always disregards the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*), and without depending on the appearance of conceptual construction, he takes only the real thing (*vastu*) as his basis and makes it his object—that real thing in which this human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is bound up. "In fire" means in the specific characteristic of fire. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), burning, cooking, and so forth are meant.

It might be argued: "An object of this kind is established even by the meaning of a word. To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. "In this case" refers to [the case of] warding off cold and the like. Why? Because even when there is the attainment of the experience of that [word-meaning], that is, even when there is the attainment of the experience of that word-meaning, there is an absence of that—namely, an absence of the remedy for cold and so forth. Therefore, this person is one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Therefore, it is not proper for one who has directed his inquiry toward a word-meaning that is incapable of performing that causal function to apply his attention to it. For a woman desiring sexual union does not fix her attention on examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch who is incapable of engaging in intercourse.
[The author] asks in order to refute the objections stated by Uddyotakara and others: "As for what was said by the Master Dignāga, beginning with 'of the imagined,' etc., what is its meaning?"

He states the answer: "The object of a word," and so forth. Because it is the object of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), the "object of a word" refers to the referent of words such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter). It is "conceptualized" (*kalpita*) in that it relies upon an external reality characterized as *pradhāna*. Therefore, the "non-establishment"—that is, the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)—of this object of words such as *pradhāna* is stated by the Master Dignāga, the proponent of logic (*nyāyavādin*), as the logical reason (*liṅga*) when proving the property of not being based on an existent entity (*bhāvānupādānatva*).

Therefore, what has been stated by Uddyotakara and others—namely, "If the *pradhāna* is conceived as existing by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can its non-perception be understood as its property? Or, if the *pradhāna* is conceived as non-existent, even so, how can its non-perception be its property, given its non-existence?"—is refuted. This is because that which is conceived is merely the object of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), which is the referent of words; it is not an external *pradhāna* conceived as existing by means of a valid cognition.

"The meaning of 'of that'—namely, of the referent of the word *pradhāna*—is the non-perception of a basis in an external *pradhāna*-entity; this is the intention of the teacher Dignāga. (214–15) The opponent says, "As for what was stated," and so forth. The "three means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatraya*) are characterized by perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*). "In the absence of other means of valid cognition" means in the absence of perception and inference; [this refers to] the absence of those things remote in space and so forth. "Of those two" means of perception and inference. "It does not encompass anything" means it takes everything as its object. "The absence of that" is the absence of scripture.

"The [objection] has been stated here," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). This is because [the objection] does not pertain to the context, as it is useless for the introduction of the inquiry into the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). This is because it was stated in the intervening passage (1.201): "Many matters are unrelated to the scope of the treatise (*śāstra*).
And this was stated while provisionally accepting the authority of scripture (*āgama*) regarding external [objects].

Now he states that external objects do not possess validity at all, beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth. Because there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*), that is, no inseparable connection, between words and real entities (*vastu*), namely particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), no establishment of an object (*arthasiddhi*)—that is, no determination of an external thing—follows from those words. For they [words] merely indicate the intention (*abhiprāya*) of the speaker.

Even though the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) arises from the intention to speak of a "jar" (*ghaṭa*), nevertheless, because it arises directly from the impact of the vocal organs and other such factors, there is no lack of a cause, and thus no deviation [from the rule]. Furthermore, for one who perceives the word "jar" as being produced by the intention to speak of a jar, the inference of the intention to speak of a cloth from the word "cloth" occurs; and such perception by people through context and so forth certainly exists. Therefore, in the inference of the intention to speak, there is indeed no deviation.

"According to the state of being" (*yathābhāvam*) means according to its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). "From which" (*yataḥ*) refers to the fact that because [words] function according to the state of being, the nature of the object—the intrinsic essence of the object—would be determined from words. "Those" (*te hi*) refers to words. They are so called because they operate through the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). "Inseparable from that" (*tatrāntarīyakāḥ*) means inseparable from that intention to speak. That very intention to speak does not exist without the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, there is indeed no deviation of words from the object; thus he says: "And not," and so forth.

Those whose nature is to exist in accordance with reality and in accordance with the state of things are so described. [The author] says that for one whose defects are exhausted and who is compassionate, all [cognitions] exist in accordance with reality: "If it is argued that even a word not connected to an object will convey its meaning," he replies: "And not," and so forth. This refers to a word whose essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not connected to that particular object; it is another [object] to which it is not connected.

If the word has no authority regarding external objects, then how is it that [it is said]: "Because of the commonality of non-contradiction with the speech of a reliable person (*āptavāda*). Whatever is the speech of a reliable person, that is non-contradictory, such as 'all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary,' and so forth. And this [scriptural statement] is the speech of a reliable person even regarding an object that is completely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). Therefore, this too is non-contradictory. Thus, because of the commonality of non-contradiction with the speech of a reliable person—that is, because of its non-contradictoriness—it is an inference (*anumāna*); in this way, the teacher Dignāga stated that scripture (*āgama*) possesses the nature of inference with respect to external objects.

"How is that so?"—with these words, he states the contradiction with what has been accepted. He refutes this with the passage beginning "This is not," and so forth. This explains as follows: the Teacher, when describing the intrinsic validity (*bhāvika-prāmāṇya*) [of scripture], did not state that scripture possesses the nature of inference; rather, he spoke with regard to human activity, because this person, desiring to act, is unable to remain without relying on the validity of scripture. What is the reason?

The connection should be understood as appropriate to each case: "of some [actions], the fruit of which is either perceptible or imperceptible, [there is engagement or withdrawal]. For it is heard that there is great benefit from the withdrawal from objects of consciousness such as violence, since their fruit is heaven and the like; and it is heard that there is great sin from engagement in specific types of consciousness such as violence, since their fruit is hell and the like. Furthermore, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here that functions by the power of the thing itself (*vastubalapravṛtta*), by virtue of which one might proceed by another means of knowledge without depending on scripture (*āgama*).

Nor is there any subverting factor by virtue of which [the person] would desist. He states the very absence of a subverting factor: "In the existence of that," meaning that when the desired or undesired result exists through the aforementioned engagement and withdrawal, no contradiction is observed; and furthermore, this person wishes to engage by the force of scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, since one must engage [in action], it is better to engage after thus examining the scripture. Thus, the Teacher asserts the validity of the scripture through its examination. (215–16)

Nor is every treatise subject to critical examination; rather, it is that treatise which—beginning with the words "but that" (tac ca)—is coherent due to the mutual relationship of its topics, and which possesses a compatible means for achieving [its goal], meaning a treatise in which the method for accomplishing the result is feasible. This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of "coherent" and "possessing a compatible means. Even if it is such a work, only if it expresses human goals (*puruṣārtha*) is the statement subject to examination. Therefore, any other statement whose nature differs from what has been described is not subject to examination.

He explains by means of the words "connection" (*sambandha*) and so forth.
