The connection between sentences is their mutual assistance through their synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*)—that is, their convergence—within a single object characterized by what is to be enjoined or prohibited, by way of a relationship of principal and subordinate. He asks, "Of which [sentences] would there be no such assistance? and answers with the example beginning "Ten pomegranates," etc.: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a bowl, a goat-skin, minced meat"—such are the sentences. For there is no synthesis of these into a single object, because they lack mutual connection.

The term *ananyathā* (not otherwise) refers to the fault of the speaker or author of the treatise, namely their lack of coherence or their propounding of what is incoherent; this would bring to light the defect of being an incoherent speaker. *Aśakyopāyāni* means those whose fruits have infinite [consequences] but whose means are impossible to perform. Those treatises which possess such fruits are what is meant. A person seeking the fruit would not care to investigate them. This is an explanation by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*) to the phrase "having suitable means" (*anuguṇopāyam*). Those treatises whose fruit is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) are so described. Others than those are those whose fruits are not the human goal; and one would not care to investigate them either.

An example of [an action] whose fruit has an impossible means is "poison," and so forth. For it is said that his poison is pacified if he is adorned with a jewel situated on the ear of the Naga king Takṣaka; however, this is something that cannot be accomplished. An example of [an action] whose fruit is not a human goal is "like the examination of a crow's teeth."

By the opposite of these—namely, by the reverse of those three qualities previously mentioned—it is like a summary. By this, the phrase "connected" is explained; and by the phrase "feasible means," [it is explained as] "concordant means. "Elsewhere" means in that which is devoid of the triad beginning with connection. "Of attention alone" refers to earnest application (*ādara*). "That"—meaning the treatise endowed with the three aforementioned qualities—is not subject to contradiction when it undergoes examination. A person proceeding toward such a non-contradictory treatise is truly distinguished. (PVSV 1.215)

What, then, is the non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) of this treatise? He says: "By perception," and so forth. The first meaning [of the word *pratyakṣa*] is that which denotes a thing (*vastu*); the second is that which denotes an object (*viṣaya*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: the non-contradiction of this treatise is its non-sublation (*abādhana*)—respectively by perception and by inference—of both seen and unseen things, which are the objects of perception and inference, [inference] being of two kinds: that proceeding from the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta*) and that relying on scripture (*āgama-āśrita*). (216–17)

He explains by means of the words beginning with "pratyakṣa. In the treatise, the "being such" (tathābhāva) of those objects that are considered or accepted as being perceptible—that is, their state of being perception—is their non-sublation by perception.

With the words "Just as," etc., he shows that in his own established system, the object intended by direct perception is comprised within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). By the term "blue and so forth" (*nīlādi*), he refers to the five objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest; by this, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is stated. "Pleasure and pain" (*sukhaduḥkhe*) refers to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). "The discernment of signs" (*nimittopalakṣaṇa*)—where "sign" (*nimitta*) means the characteristics of woman, man, and so forth—is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*). By the mention of "attachment and so forth" (*rāgādi*), the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is indicated; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hatred, delusion, and the rest are included.

By the term "intellect" (*buddhi*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is meant. The compound consists of a copulative (*dvandva*) of "blue and so forth," "pleasure and pain," "the apprehension of signs," "attachment and so forth," and "intellect. Thus, according to the treatise, those things considered to be perceptible are indeed perceptible: because blue and so forth are perceptible by visual consciousness and the like, and because pleasure and so forth are perceptible by self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

The non-perceptibility of objects that are not intended to be such [i.e., not perceived] and those intended to be imperceptible is connected with the subject under discussion, namely, "ascertainment by means of perception. The word "as" serves to indicate the object [of comparison]. The non-perceptibility of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth—those things whose nature it is to be arranged in the form of sound and so on—is stated because pleasure, pain, and delusion, which have the nature of sound and so forth, are not apprehended through perception;
this is said in order to refute the Sāṃkhya view.

In order to refute the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, he says: substance is of two kinds: substance without constituent parts (*adravya-dravya*), such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth; and substance with multiple constituent parts (*aneka-dravya-dravya*), such as a composite substance (*avayavin*). Action (*karman*) consists of throwing upward and so forth. Generality (*sāmānya*) consists of existence (*sattā*), cowness (*gotva*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [qualities such as] disjunction (*vibhāga*) and others are included.

For there is no perceptibility of anything other than the five [sense-cognitions] with respect to objects such as blue; this is because nothing is perceived apart from them. Inference that functions by the force of facts (*vastubala-pravṛtta*) is inference that does not depend on scripture (*anāgama-apekṣā-anumāna*). Regarding those things intended as its objects, their being otherwise—that is, their not being objects of inference—is not sublated by inference. Furthermore, there are the four noble truths, which will be explained later. Regarding those things that are not inferable, their not being inferable is not sublated by inference.

As in the case of the self and so forth—the word "and so forth" including [the concepts of] *pradhāna*, the Lord (*īśvara*), and others—there is indeed no mark (*liṅga*) by which these could be objects of inference. This too he will demonstrate later. When the two types of objects have been purified, and regarding an object of scripture that is absolutely beyond perception, one directs inquiry toward it despite contradictions between earlier and later [statements], then even inference is dependent upon scripture. "Non-sublation" (*abādhana*) is the term under discussion.

To explain what this non-contradiction is like, he says: having accepted as unrighteousness that which consists of passion and so forth—that is, the nature of passion, hatred, and delusion—and having accepted as unrighteousness the physical and vocal actions produced by them, namely those originated by passion and so forth; for the sake of abandoning that, i.e., for the removal of that unrighteousness, [he speaks of] bathing, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and so on. There is no such instruction as "the destruction of evil occurs through bathing at sacred fords," or "the destruction of evil occurs for one who offers ghee and other substances into the fire for a specific purpose," and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), fasting and so forth are included. For instance, bathing and the like do not remove sin, because there is no contradiction [between them] and passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which are the causes of sin. This aforementioned [rejection] consists in the sublation of the entire range of objects—which can be determined and ascertained through both types of inference and through direct perception—by means of the non-contradiction of the authoritative word (*āptavāda*). This is due to its general similarity [to other cases]: just as the authoritative word is non-contradictory regarding an object that can be determined, so too is it non-contradictory regarding an utterly imperceptible object, precisely because it is the word of an authority (*āptavāda*).

Therefore, the teacher Dignāga has declared that the cognition arising from a mark characterized by reliability is inferential. This applies even to an object that is beyond the senses—that is, even within the scope of this treatise regarding objects that are extremely remote. And this [inferential nature] is stated as the only recourse, because activity toward an extremely remote object is impossible through any other means. For if activity does occur, it is better to have proceeded in this manner.

The passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) is an explanation. It refers to that scripture (*āgama*) whose nature as inference was pointed out by the master Dignāga. "Of this" (*asya*) refers to what has been examined by us through the [passage] beginning with "a means consistent [with reality]" (*anuguṇopāya*), due to its connection [to the context]. For this very reason he says: "of such a kind" (*evaṃbhūtasya*), meaning "endowed with qualities such as connection" (*sambandhādiguṇayuktasya*). Because there is a commonality of non-contradiction (*avisamvāda-sāmānya*)—that is, because of the cause of being non-contradictory—with respect to that object which is accessible through perception and inference, [this applies] to the domain of objects accessible through perception, inference, and scripture, where deviation has been observed and [therefore] refuted.

From the statement of a reliable person (*āptavāda*), the non-contradiction of a cognition that has not yet arisen—that is, of the practice [based on it]—is inferred. Why? Because it is based upon that; for its being based upon the statement of a reliable person is established through the instruction of the lineage of teachers. This is like the case of another practice: as in the case of a practice regarding an object entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*) that is other than the objects of perception and inference.

Therefore, regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), the cognition based on the aforementioned authoritative testimony—which, although it arises from words and is produced by words—is not like other verbal cognitions in that it merely communicates an intention. This is because the particle *eva* (merely/only) is placed out of its logical position [to negate the mere communication of intention]. Just as another verbal cognition communicates only an intention, this cognition does not communicate an intention alone.

What then? It is because there is no contradiction with the object—which is desired and not accessible through perception or inference—by means of the reasoning just stated, that even inference [is considered valid] for a person desiring action, due to the force of his intention. In reality, however, it is not an inference, because there is no relationship between words and their objects. The word "even" (api) is used for the purpose of clarifying this very point. (PVSV 1.217)

Demonstrating the non-contradiction of the words of an authoritative person (*āptavāda*) by way of another method, he says: "Alternatively," and so forth. That which is to be abandoned (*heya*) is all suffering (*duḥkha*). That which is to be adopted (*upādeya*) is the abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*), namely, *nirvāṇa*. The reality (*tattva*) of these two—their non-erroneous nature—is that which exists together with its means (*upāya*), pertaining to the truth of suffering and the truth of cessation. Regarding that reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, there is its means: the means for what is to be abandoned is the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*); the means for what is to be adopted is the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).

Because this reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—along with its means—has been shown by the Blessed One and is established through certainty by means of a cognition arising from the power of the object itself; there is no contradiction in the Blessed One’s word regarding the primary subject matter characterized by the four truths. The subject matter characterized by the four truths is primary because the attainment of nirvāṇa occurs through its realization. Therefore, it is due to the non-contradiction regarding this primary subject matter.

Knowledge arising from the word of the Blessed One is an inference even with respect to an object that is extremely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*) for another person. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*), in reference to the preceding type [of inference].

The means for those two—the things to be abandoned (*heya*) and the things to be adopted (*upādeya*)—are the "means for them. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "the thing to be abandoned," "the thing to be adopted," and "the means for them. The non-erroneousness of those [teachings] taught by him—that is, taught by that authoritative person (*āpta*)—is their non-falsity or non-contradiction when examined through inference, as in the case of the four noble truths beginning with suffering, as discussed in the second chapter. This is according to the method of investigation that will be explained below.

"Of this"—that is, of that which was previously indicated by the Blessed One and is now analyzed, namely, that which is characterized by the four truths. Of what nature is it? "That which serves as a means for the human goal. The human goal is *nirvāṇa*; "serving as a means" (*upayoga*) therein means being its cause; that which possesses this is so described. For this very reason, because it is non-deceptive regarding even other objects that are accessible through perception, inference, or scripture—objects for which application and cultivation are appropriate—the acceptance of its suchness is the acceptance of its non-deceptiveness; it does not lead to deception, nor does it become a source of contradiction.

What is the reason? Because there is no contradiction; because it is not sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and because, regarding the primary object characterized by the four truths, the speaker’s utterance of falsehood—which would otherwise be purposeless in the third instance where he does not deceive the person—is fruitless.

If it is argued that such a statement might occasionally occur there even due to ignorance, he says: "That," and so forth. "In both ways" means by the manner indicated in the two verses. The connection is: "This very nature of scripture as inference has been described as a last resort. It should be understood that it is called "inference" because it is a cause of inference. When action proceeds from scripture, it is better to proceed from a scripture that is thus logical rather than from one that is deceptive regarding an object accessible through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Indeed, even with the aforementioned method, knowledge based on scripture (*āgama*) is not an infallible or faultless inference. Why? Because it has been explained that words do not possess an invariable concomitance (*anāntarīyakatva*) with objects, and thus they are unreliable; as stated in the passage beginning, "Because words lack an invariable concomitance with real entities" (1.213). Other disputants might claim that one should rely upon a person whose excellences consist in having exhausted all defects and so forth, and that whatever statement proceeds from such a person is true to the facts. However, [this view is rejected].

Knowledge that perceives things exactly as they are and as they exist—namely, according to their true nature—is "knowledge of reality" (*yathārthadarśana*). Compassion, detachment, and so forth, which have this knowledge of reality as their beginning, constitute "the qualities beginning with the knowledge of reality. A person endowed with these very qualities is an *āpta* (a reliable authority). Because he imparts [teachings], his word is "authoritative speech" (*āptavacana*). Others hold that the non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) of scripture consists in this. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says, "This is accepted," and so forth. This matter just mentioned is indeed accepted by us; however, while it may be possible to know the excellence of a person through such characteristics as [his] vision and so forth, it is not possible to determine the specific limits of a person's [excellence].

He explains [the passage] beginning with "all indeed" (*sarva eva*). Every person who acts with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārī*) investigates and examines whether something is based on scripture (*āgama*) or not. Desiring to engage by means of scripture, he abandons what is not scriptural; he does not do so out of mere addiction or attachment. He states that even this desire to engage is not for its own sake, etc., saying "apināma" (perhaps/how might it be) in the sense of "how indeed. Thus, having understood from this scripture the object to be practiced—that which is to be directly realized—and having engaged [in it], he thinks: "May I be successful, may I possess the fruit (*phala*)."

A person seeking [truth] is able to see that which is certain regarding an object cognizable through perception and inference; its non-contradiction consists in its being ascertained by means of perception and inference. That very cognition is the basis [of trust], and by means of it, one may proceed even toward other objects not accessible through perception and inference. Why? Because worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) is for the most part (*prāyas*) of such a nature. Thus, proceeding toward another [object] by seeing non-contradiction in one part is what is meant; "for the most part" means predominantly, referring to that worldly convention.

Furthermore, if activity is admitted on the grounds of an examination of persons, then no activity at all would occur. Why? Because for such a person—one endowed with qualities such as the vision of reality—there would be no activity due to a lack of desire [to speak]. This is connected [in the text] by the phrase "not from a lack of desire. Therefore, the meaning is this: it is not the case that there would be no activity simply because there is no desire to speak untruthfully among persons endowed with qualities such as the vision of reality.

What is the reason? Because such persons—who possess qualities such as the vision of things as they truly are—speak non-erroneously, since they illuminate objects exactly as they exist. But what is the reason that such a person cannot be known? He says: "For instance," and so forth. Others maintain that it is difficult to understand whether this very person possesses such defects or not; or whether he possesses such defects, or rather is free from them—that is, his freedom from other defects is likewise difficult to discern. The term *nirdoṣatā* (freedom from defects) is used with the singular number and feminine gender in reference to this [difficulty].

With reference to the phrase "other faults," however, a grammatical modification must be made by changing [the gender and number] to the masculine plural, as in "are difficult to understand. Why? Because they are difficult to understand and difficult to attain, due to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determine the virtues and faults of others.

He explains this with the words beginning "from the mental" (*caitasebhyaḥ*). Those persons whose activity—characterized by bodily and vocal action—is correct or false are referred to as such. Mental (*caitasāḥ*) qualities and defects are those which exist in the mind. From mental qualities, such as causes like compassion, dispassion, and awakening, arise correct activities, that is, activities in accordance with reality. From mental defects, such as attachment and so forth, arise false activities, that is, contrary activities.

And those [qualities and faults]—namely, the mental qualities and defects of oneself and others—are beyond the senses because they are properties of the mind; therefore, they are not accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor are they accessible through inference (*anumāna*), precisely because they are beyond the senses and thus the evidence of their essential nature (*svabhāva-liṅga*) is unestablished. Rather, they are to be inferred by means of the evidence of an effect (*kārya-liṅga*), namely, that bodily and vocal action which originates—that is, arises—from one’s own qualities and defects. Yet even that does not exist, because conventional behavior (*vyavahāra*), characterized by bodily and vocal actions, is for the most part—or in the majority of cases—[merely conventional].

Considering that "intellect comes first," it is possible to act otherwise through deliberate reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*). For instance, those who possess passion (*sarāga*) display themselves as if they were free from passion (*vītarāga*), and those free from passion appear as if they possessed passion. What is the reason? Because linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) function according to human will; the analysis of the compound is: those whose functioning or activity proceeds by means of human will.

Even if worldly conventions (*vyavahāra*) proceed according to human will, why then are they not established otherwise? To this he says: "And because of those men... Since men possess diverse intentions—that is, diverse purposes—conventions proceed according to their own whims. Consequently, there is no definitive determination (*vivekaniścaya*) regarding conventions that arise from either virtues or faults. Therefore, because this inferring person does not ascertain [the truth] due to the corruption of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and the deviation of the mark, how could he—being one whose faults have not been eliminated—accept the author of scripture?
The conclusion must be: certainly not.

"Now, what [is the reason]? and so forth. Is there no such person who is faultless—that is, free from defects such as passion? Demonstrating that there is one, he says: "Of all," and so forth. Those passions and other afflictions which undergo diminution (*nirhrāsa*)—that is, decrease—when their counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) is present, and which undergo intensification (*atiśaya*)—that is, increase—when their counteragent is not present, are said to "rely on diminution and intensification" (*nirhrātiśayāśrita*). This is because they are all factors to be abandoned (*vipakṣa*).

Furthermore, that very thing which undergoes decrease or increase through the presence or absence of its opposite is the adversary (*vipakṣa*) of those [defilements], being their subduer; thus, it "possesses an adversary" (*savi-pakṣa*). The state of being such is "adversariality" (*tattva*); therefore, it means "because of that subduing power. And because of the cultivation—meaning the repeated, uninterrupted production—of that subduer by which the defilements possess an adversary, that which is the state of becoming one's own nature (*sātmībhāva*), that is its firmness or identification (*tadaurjitya-tanmayatā*).

Therefore, through the internalization of the antidote, the outflows—namely passion, aggression, and so forth—would be exhausted or destroyed within a certain continuum where the counteragent to the defects has been internalized. Furthermore, he will demonstrate that the antidote to the defects is the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*). Consequently, it is not that such a person is not accepted; rather, we simply say that such a person, whose outflows are exhausted, is difficult to know.

The passage beginning with "for the defects" (*doṣo hi*) and so forth is an explanation. For the defects are passion (*rāga*) and the rest. Of what nature are they? They possess the properties of diminution and excess; being of the nature of decrease and increase, they establish—that is, they lead one to understand—the increase and decrease of the subjugation caused by the counteragent, where "subjugation" refers to the suppression or eclipsing [of the defects] by that counteragent.

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: those things characterized by diminution (*nirhrāsadharmāṇaḥ*) establish the increase of the subjugation of their opposites (*vipakṣa*), because defects are diminished through the increase in the subjugation of the counteracting factors (*bādhaka*). Those characterized by excellence (*atiśayadharmāṇaḥ*) establish the decrease in the subjugation of the counteracting factors, because they possess the quality of excellence due to the weakness of the subjugation of the counteracting factors. This is like a flame and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of cold and hot touch is intended.

Just as flames and the like—possessing the qualities of diminution and excellence respectively when there is an increase or decrease of the counteracting factor such as water—establish the increase of the subjugation of water and so forth, so it is in this case.

But surely, attachment and the like are dependent upon external objects, and external things are always present; so how can there be an eradication of attachment and the rest? To this he says: "For those... and so forth. The word *hi* has the sense of "because. The analysis of the compound is as follows: those [afflictions] such as attachment have their origin (*prabhava*)—that is, their production—from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is characterized by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).

For indeed, even when external objects exist, passion and the like do not arise without improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*); yet, when that [attention] is present, they arise even in the absence of an object. Thus, passion and the like originate from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, even though the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) characterized as previously described exists, [passion and so forth] diminish—that is, they undergo decrease—through the cultivation of a certain mental quality characterized by the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*). This locative case is used here in the sense of disregard.

This is what is meant: although there is no permanent eradication of the cause of the defects at all times—because the counteragent lacks absolute proficiency—nevertheless, due to the practice of the counteragent, the defects become increasingly attenuated as they are diminished by the appropriation [of the mind] whose power has been weakened; this explains the reason. But when proficiency arises in that mental quality as described, because it reaches the ultimate limit of the excellence of cultivation, then, upon that proficiency...

When that quality of the mind (*manoguṇa*) reaches proficiency, there is "concomitance" (*anvaya*), meaning that from this [proficiency] faults arise because the seed of the afflictions (*kleśabīja*) follows along. That destruction in which concomitance has departed is "destruction without concomitance" (*niranvayavināśa*). Those faults whose nature is such destruction are "possessing the nature of destruction without concomitance. The meaning is that they possess the nature of being destroyed together with their latencies (*vāsanā*). It is like a flame and so forth; just as flames and the like, when there is an increase of their opposites such as water, possess the nature of absolute destruction, so too is it in this case.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever things are subject to diminution through the application of a particular factor possess the nature of being destroyed without remainder once that factor reaches its ultimate increase, due to its overwhelming power. For example, flames and the like [are destroyed] when their increase is overwhelmed by water. Defects (*doṣa*), which are by nature subject to diminution through the application of the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), [are likewise destroyed]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Since this is so, for that reason, it might be that someone is indeed faultless. [The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. The particle *yāvatā* functions here in the sense of *yadā* ("when"). "As in the case of the arising of the antidote for one whose nature is faulty" means: for a person whose nature is faulty, the arising of the antidote—the arising of the vision of selflessness—[occurs]. Thus, even though the vision of selflessness, which is the antidote to faults, has become his very nature (*sātmatva*), nevertheless, according to conditions—that is, according to the presence of causes—the arising of faults may also occur.

"This is not so," says the Master. It is "free from affliction" (*nirupadrava*) because it is devoid of all the calamities of saṃsāra. It is "of true meaning" (*bhūtārtha*) because its object or domain is the reality that is the opposite of what is unreal—the specific characteristics such as impermanence and so forth. And precisely because it grasps the true meaning, the path is the very nature of the mind.

It is a *karmadhāraya* compound containing within it another *karmadhāraya*: "that which is free from affliction (*nirupadrava*) and is the true object (*bhūtārtha*)" is "the true object free from affliction"; and "that which is such (*tathābhūta*) and is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)" is "the intrinsic nature that is such. When, through the repeated cultivation of the true object free from affliction as being the true object, it has reached the state of becoming one's own nature (*sātmībhāva*), there is no longer any subversion by the defects—the opposites of the mind’s intrinsic nature—which are characterized by affliction, are not the true object, and lack intrinsic nature, being distinct from the three aforementioned [virtues].

The meaning is that once the path has become naturalized (*sātmībhūta*), faults no longer arise. What is the reason? [It is] "even when there is effort," and so forth. This is what is being said: for one in whom the path has become naturalized, it is simply not possible for faults to arise.

Nevertheless, it is said even while granting [the opponent's position]: because the intellect has a partiality for that [path], when effort is exerted toward producing faults, it does not do so regarding that fault-antidote, the virtuous path of selflessness. This is because of its partiality for that [path] due to great respect. The meaning is that, having turned back the effort toward producing faults, one applies effort precisely toward the antidote to faults through partiality for virtues.

First, he explains the term *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature): "Indeed, intrinsic nature—characterized by the vision of selflessness—is not something that can be removed by a person established in its opposite [the view of self] without effort, just like the aversion of a Vedic scholar who has become a Kāpālika. Just as the aversion present in the state of a Vedic scholar cannot be removed without exertion when that same person becomes a Kāpālika, so it is in this case.

Furthermore, an effort made to turn away from the intrinsic nature of the path would be undertaken by perceiving the virtues of that which is to be attained—the intrinsic nature of passion and so forth—and by perceiving the defects of that which is to be turned away from—the intrinsic nature of insight (*vipaśyanā*). And that perception of defects cannot arise in a person whose very self is the opposite side [of passion] or whose self is the antidote to those defects; likewise, that perception of virtues cannot arise in one whose self is the opposite side regarding the defects.

Why, then, is it not possible to perceive faults in the antidote? He says: "Of that," and so forth. This is because that antidote is free from affliction (*nirupadravatva*). For there are three kinds of affliction, due to the absence of which the path is free from affliction. To explain: first, the cause of mental obstruction is the affliction of the faults (*doṣa*), by which the mind is obstructed and does not engage in the perception of reality. Second, the affliction of suffering and dejection is the cause of physical and mental pain.
Third, because contaminated pleasure is not peaceful, there is a sense of distaste and agitation toward its enjoyment.

Regarding that, he states the absence of the first calamity with the words "due to the abandonment of all defects" (*sarvadoṣahāneḥ*). This means because of the abandonment—that is, the disappearance—of every defect such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth. He states the absence of the second [calamity] with the words beginning "obsessions" (*paryavasthāna*): obsession (*paryavasthāna*) and birth (*janma*) constitute "obsession-and-birth. Because of the separation from the suffering that is bound to those two: the suffering characterized by the burning of body and mind at the time of the arising of passion and so forth is bound to obsession; whereas the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and so forth is bound to birth.

He speaks of the absence of the third calamity, beginning with "tranquility" (*praśama*) and so forth. Tranquility is *nirvāṇa*, characterized by the absence of passion (*rāga*) and the like. The "savor" (*rasa*) is the tasting of that untainted (*anāsrava*) bliss within it; [the calamity is absent] because there is no revulsion toward that savor, and because it does not cause one to turn away from it. Furthermore, passion and the like have non-existent objects as their domain (*abhūtārtha*); the connection is that they would simply not exist.

If it is not a real object, how then does its arising occur? He says: "It exists through the power of grasping" (*upādānabalabhāvī*), meaning it exists through the power of the latencies of false conceptualization (*vitathavikalpavāsanā*). Thus, because the continuum of consciousness—which is the substratum for the seeds of passion and so forth—is based on perverted grasping, [the antidote] characterized by the reversal of passion and so forth would not exist, nor would it arise. However, it is not the case that it would not be a real object with a non-perverted domain; rather, it certainly would be so.

What is the reason? Because [the cognition] proceeds by the power of the object (*vastubalapravṛtti*); that is, it arises through the efficacy of the object as it actually exists. Even for one who remains habituated to defects, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which grasp the aspects of reality such as impermanence and so forth, bring about the path of the antidote (*pratipakṣamārga*). (222–23)

How much more so for one who is established in insight (*vipaśyanā*)! For defects such as passion and the like are unreal objects; they arise with respect to objects superimposed as "self" and "mine. Therefore, they cannot apply to that which expresses the state of being naturalized (*sātmya*), which is the true nature (*bhūtārtha*) that serves as their antidote. Since this is so, there is no further arising of defects for those whose defects have been abandoned.

Even when there is an effort to produce faults, because the intellect has a natural partiality toward virtues as its cause, one applies effort precisely toward the antidotes to passion and the other defilements; that is, one exerts effort [in this way]. For whom? For one who possesses discernment, who investigates by means of reasoning, and who remains even while established in a state of habituation to faults. Specifically, with excellence, one who is of uncorrupted nature and established in the nature of the antidote applies effort specifically toward virtues.

What, then, is the source—the cause of origination—of these faults? It is so called because they originate and arise from it. By the cultivation of the antidote to that cause of the faults, they are abandoned.

He states the reply: "Of all," and so forth. The origin—that is, the arising—of the various classes of faults, the types of defects, is from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), that is, from the persistent attachment to a self and what belongs to a self.

But surely, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are said in the scriptures to have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause; so how is there no contradiction? He says: "That ignorance" means that very view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is ignorance. Therefore, there is no contradiction. By what sequence, then, do the faults arise from the view of a self-identity? He says: "In that regard," and so forth. In that regard, with respect to an object clung to as "self" and "mine," there is attachment to it—namely, attachment to self and mine. From that attachment to self and mine, there arises aversion and the rest; such is the sequence.

He explains this with the words beginning "na hi" [not indeed]. "Not I" is the negation of the aspect of a self (*ātman*); "not mine" is the negation of the aspect of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*). For a person who perceives neither by way of the aspect of non-self nor by way of the aspect of what belongs to a self, there is no attachment toward any object without grasping. "Without grasping" means: without the apprehension that conceives of something as "self" or "mine," or as being a benefactor; without that, there is no affection for any object. Furthermore, for one who is without passion—that is, devoid of affection for self, what belongs to self, and so forth—there is no aversion anywhere, because aversion cannot exist without prior endearment (*anunaya*).

What is the reason? [It is] because of the self and what belongs to the self (*ātmātmīya*), and so forth. In the case of one who does not obstruct or act contrary to the self and what belongs to the self—that is, in the category of the neutral—there is an absence of that [hatred], because hatred is absent there. And in the case of one who obstructs or resists [the self and its belongings]: obstruction is the suffering caused to that which is grasped as "self" or "belonging to the self"; in one who resists that, who acts to prevent it—that is, in the category of friends—there is an absence of that [hatred], because hatred is absent there. However, [hatred arises] through opposition to that which has become the object of attachment for the self and what belongs to the self.

Hatred exists only toward that which remains adverse. Therefore, there is no hatred without the affection for self and what belongs to the self (*ātma-ātmīya-sneha*). The conclusion is stated with the words "therefore" and so forth; since this is so, "those two" refers to the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) and the grasping at what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-graha*). These two are connected to the phrase "they produce affection," with the verbal form adjusted accordingly. And that affection produces—that is, generates—hatred and the other afflictions.

To the question, "What then is the cause of those two—the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) and the grasping at what belongs to a self (*ātmīyagraha*)? he says: "Of a similar kind," and so forth. That very view of a self is of a similar kind; its cultivation (*abhyāsa*) is its repeated arising from beginningless time. Its latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is not [something separate]. From that [cultivation] arises the view of a self, which produces the grasping at what belongs to a self. Therefore, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are born from the view of a real body (*satkāyadarśana*). Furthermore, in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), that very view of a real body is called ignorance (*avidyā*), which is non-knowledge (*ajñāna*).

For this very reason—that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is itself ignorance (*avidyā*)—delusion (*moha*) is declared in another Sūtra to be the source, the primary cause, of the defects such as passion and the rest: "All afflictions have ignorance as their cause. Yet, in other Sūtras, the view of a self-identity is stated to be the source of the defects. Why? Because when that is abandoned—that is, when the view of a self-identity is abandoned—there is the abandonment of the defects. The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have said that delusion is the source of the defects, the cause of the defects.

Why? Because faults do not arise in one who is undeluded and free from ignorance. Furthermore, they state that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the cause of faults in another context. This causal status of delusion (*moha*) and the view of a self-identity would hold true when referring to the primary cause (*pradhāna-hetu*), but not when referring to a mere cause (*hetu-mātra*). What is the reason? Because it is contradictory for those faults which arise from a complex of multiple factors—such as the sense faculties, their objects, and improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*)—to arise from a single factor, namely delusion or the view of a self-identity.

Therefore, it should be understood that although other causes are possible, the causality of delusion (*moha*) and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is stated by taking their predominance [as the criterion],
according to the words of the Buddha.

If delusion (*moha*) were one thing and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) another, and if both were predominant, then it would not be the case that there is a singular designation for each of these two—namely, that in some instances only delusion is mentioned, while in others only the view of a self-identity is mentioned; [otherwise] such a distinction would not be fitting and would only reveal the speaker's lack of skill. However, when there is no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [the two are not distinct].

In that case, there is no contradiction regarding the primacy [of the view of self-identity], because both the term "delusion" (*moha*) and the term "view of self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are synonyms for the same entity, used as alternative designations. Furthermore, the primacy of the view of self-identity is due to its being the basis of the [other] defects, just as it is the basis of the [defilements]. This has already been established immediately above and will be demonstrated in the second chapter.

And when that view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned, it is preeminent by virtue of the abandonment of the faults. Since this is so, birth arises from that view of a self-existent body; therefore, the antidote to that view of a self-existent body is the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadṛṣṭi*), and through its cultivation, [the faults] are abandoned. That person whose faults are exhausted is difficult to follow and difficult to understand—that is, one must rely on the instruction of that person whose faults are exhausted, following whose instruction this seeker of liberation would practice. One should carry out the meaning taught by him. ||o|| (25)

[Let it not be that] a statement based on a person or caused by a person is the *āgama*. What is the reason? Because, according to the principle just stated, the author of the *āgama* is difficult to connect with and difficult to understand.

The faults, such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which are the causes of the falsity—that is, the deceptive nature—of words and utterances; this genitive case here is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). "Resorting" (*āśrayaṇa*) means a resort (*āśraya*). The compound is "the resort of the person" (*puruṣasyāśraya*). Furthermore, the genitive case after the word *puruṣa* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Nor is there a restrictive rule stating that when both [agent and object] are possible, the genitive must be used only for the object; for there is an optionality provided by the rule "the remaining cases are optional" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*). Therefore, the meaning is: "because it is appropriated by a person through the faults which are the causes of falsity. Alternatively, the genitive in *doṣāṇām* is used in the sense of the object: "because the faults are resorted to and appropriated by the person."

Some Mīmāṃsakas declare that the Vedic word is non-human (apauruṣeya) and possesses true meaning because of the absence of defects, which are the cause of falsity. This is what is meant: the threefold lack of authority—characterized by falsity, ignorance, and doubt—is simply not present in the case of [the Veda]. For words have a twofold nature: that established by nature (*nisargasiddha*) and that adventitious (*aupādhika*). Among these, that which consists in the capacity to convey things as they truly are is established by nature; conversely, the capacity to convey things incorrectly is adventitious, because such a nature depends upon a person. Thus it is said:
It has been established that the arising of defects in words depends upon the speaker.

Their absence in certain cases occurs because the speaker is possessed of excellence; for it is impossible for those [defects] which have been removed by his excellences to be transferred to the word. (ŚV, Codanā 62)

"Or rather, due to the absence of a speaker, there would be no defects, as they would lack a substratum" (ŚV, Codanā 63). Therefore, when the person [as author] is excluded from the Veda, falsity is also excluded. Nor is there invalidity characterized by untruth, because the meaning is understood from the Veda; nor is there invalidity characterized by doubt, because when the meaning is understood from the Veda, no doubt appears. Thus he says:
"Thus, for such a Veda which produces knowledge,
both its contrary nature and doubt regarding it have been refuted by the Bhāṣya" (Ślokavārttika, Codanā 99).

Since the three grounds for invalidity have been excluded, and since the Veda possesses an intrinsic nature characterized by the communication of its meaning as established by its very origin, its validity is therefore inherent (*svataḥ*) because it conveys meaning. Furthermore, since in the case of ordinary speech the defect of a speaker—characterized by contradiction or a defective cause—is possible, whereas in the Veda, with the absence of a person, defects are absent, its validity is inherent. Because the two factors that invalidate validity—the cognition of contradiction and the cognition of a defective cause—are excluded, there is no suspicion of invalidity.
Thus he says:
In that regard, the exclusion of [the charge of] sublation is easier in the case of the Veda because of the absence of a speaker;
therefore, the lack of authority in the Veda does not even admit of suspicion. As for authority in human [utterances], it arises from the existence of other means of valid cognition. (68)

But in its absence, that [Vedic injunction] would be corrupted, whereas the Vedic [injunction] is never so corrupted. Therefore, the non-concordance of the injunctions with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitutes their very authority; otherwise, they would be mere restatements (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, when one establishes through inference that the meaning of the Vedic injunction is otherwise than it appears,
how can the cognition arising from that very [inference] be prevented?
If you argue that there is no sublation because that [Vedic cognition] is false, then you have fallen into a circular argument.
"For you, there is nothing other than inference and so forth that makes another understand [the Veda].

(90) And it is not the case that because the meaning of the Veda is not grasped by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is non-existent, like taste and so forth. Now, since taste and the like are grasped by a subsequent cognition of taste, the validity of the preceding cognition of taste will likewise apply to the meaning of the Veda. Thus he says:
"Or rather, the non-existence of an object because it is not grasped by others would not follow, as in the case of taste and so forth."
"If the cognition of the object occurs through that very [Veda], then such a cognition shall arise for me as well.
If you say, 'This is unestablished for me' once the understanding has arisen from the Veda, it is not proper for one who speaks the truth to say so out of mere malice. (91, 92)

With the words "Certainly not" (*na khalu*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the verse. "All" refers to both that which is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) and that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). "Possibility of deception" (*sambhāvyavipralambha*) means that deception—that is, contradiction—is possible or conceivable therein. However, it is only that which is of human origin where deception is possible, because the faults (*doṣa*)—the causes of contradiction—which are the causes of deception, reside in persons. (227)

Furthermore, some maintain that whatever is of human origin is of true meaning; because the Vedas lack the presence of persons who are causes of falsehood, they establish the absence of the effect, which is falsehood—thus, that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) is of true meaning.
Against those Mīmāṃsakas who argue in this way, others speak as follows, speaking through the mouth of another:

The author of the treatise himself says: "Those qualities which are the causes of the truthfulness of words depend upon a person; therefore, in the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) utterances, since the person is absent, the quality that is the cause of truthfulness is also absent, and consequently, the effect—truthfulness—is also absent. Thus, why should a non-human utterance not be false?"

This is what is meant: since truthfulness and falsity in respect of a word depend upon the person [who utters it], if it is claimed that truthfulness occurs when the person is absent, why is falsity not likewise claimed? However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since both truthfulness and falsity cease upon the absence of a person, they become purposeless; thus, invalidity is characterized precisely by non-origination. Therefore:
"If this [invalidity] is unestablished for me because [the Veda] produces no cognition, it is not right for one who speaks the truth to assert it merely out of malice. (vv. 92, 93)

[The view that] the Veda [is the source] is refuted, because no cognition of an object arises from it by its own nature. Furthermore, since phonemes—whether individually or collectively—are non-expressive, and the Veda consists of the form of phonemes, how could there be knowledge of an object from it?
Now, it may be argued that even for one who has grasped the convention [of meaning], a doubt is observed when a sentence is uttered: "What object was expressed by this?"

Its lack of authority would be characterized by doubt, because the capacity to manifest both a desired and an undesired object is possible [in either case]. Furthermore, if this capacity belongs to it by its very nature, what is the use of convention (*saṃketa*)? If it is argued that—just as a lamp, though capable of illuminating an object, requires the eye, so too a word requires convention—this is not so. For in the case of the lamp and the eye, since they lack the power to illuminate an object when each is absent individually, it is logical that they depend upon one another. It is not so, however, with the capacity of the word and the convention.

Since the cognition of an object arises solely through convention (*saṃketa*), a word is therefore not inherently capable of conveying an object; thus, its lack of validity is characterized by non-origination (*anutpatti*). (3) But surely, in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the fact that the Agnihotra and so forth are the means for achieving heaven and so forth is indeed understood. How, then, can there be a lack of validity characterized by non-origination?

This is true; however, it is simply that cognition contradicts non-cognition, but it does not contradict falsity, because that [falsity] is also cognized. Therefore, by means of these [Vedic] statements, the doubt as to whether the *agnihotra* and so forth are shown to be non-means for achieving heaven while being presented as means, or whether they are indeed means, is not at all removed. This is because there is an absence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and because there is no contradiction between the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda and its having false content. Furthermore, it is observed that even things which are not of human origin can be causes of erroneous cognition.

For example, moonlight and the like serve as causes for the cognition of yellow in white cloth and such; therefore, since the falsity of the meaning of the Vedic injunction is established through inference, how can there be sublation by that cognition? As for cognitions of taste and so forth, because their validity is first ascertained precisely through the non-contradiction of their effects—such as satiety—at other times, however, it is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*) through repeated practice and the like; thus, how could there be an intrinsic ascertainment of validity even at other times?

Therefore, just as intuition (*pratibhā*) and the like do not possess the status of a means of valid cognition due to their independence, even though a cognition occurs, let it be seen that the same applies to the Veda as well.

(4) Furthermore, the knowledge of the meaning of an injunction (*codanā*) is false because it consists in the apprehension of what is non-existent. For it is held that the Veda has authority regarding an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*); and such an object is precisely that which is to be performed. Since that [object] exists as something yet to come into being, it does not exist at the time when the knowledge of the injunction arises. Therefore, how could the knowledge of the injunction not be false, given that its object is non-existent?

Furthermore, since it has already been established that all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have non-real things as their objects, by that very fact the knowledge derived from Vedic injunctions (*codanājñāna*) is also necessarily false. Moreover, the phonemes and words in both common usage (*loka*) and the Veda (*veda*) are identical; only a difference in sentence construction is admitted. In common usage, the meaning of words is determined by convention (*saṃketa*). And since the meaning of Vedic words is the same as that of worldly words, the relationship between the word and its meaning is purely human in origin.

Furthermore, since the understanding of the meaning of Vedic sentences occurs by means of worldly objects, this [Vedic sentence] is indeed of human origin, just like a worldly sentence. And since words in the world have multiple meanings, the possibility of a Vedic sentence also having multiple meanings remains; thus, the doubt regarding a contrary meaning does not cease, and so the Veda possesses the characteristic of doubt as its lack of authority (*apramāṇya*).

With the words "Just as" (*yathā*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the verse. "Overcome by passion and so forth" means possessed of passion and the like. "Compassion" (*dayā*) is that very [compassion] which has become one's own nature (*sātmībhūta*); it is *dharmatā*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), wisdom, faith, and the rest are included; one is "endowed with" these. Therefore, just as the falsity of a statement depends upon its reliance on a person, so too does its truthfulness. "He" refers to the person. He removes even that truthfulness, not merely the falsity. Thus, when the person is removed, and consequently the two properties of truthfulness and falsity are removed, the Veda would be rendered purposeless.

Now, if it is maintained that there is truthfulness of meaning even when the person has ceased to exist, then there would either be a reversal of truthfulness of meaning or it would be falsity of meaning.

(5) It might be thought: "The meaningfulness of words does not depend upon a person, but rather arises from their very nature (*svabhāva*. To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. [Words are] meaningful by nature, that is, by their own essence (*prakṛti*). What is the reason? Because of convention (*samaya*), that is, through agreement (*saṃketa*). For it is from those words that the manifestation of meaning—that is, the cognition of the object—occurs, just as in the case of bodily gestures and signs. Bodily gestures include hand movements, winking of the eyes, and so on. Just as in those cases there is a comprehension of meaning in some instances due to convention, so it is here.

If, on the other hand, words were by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*) revealers of meaning, they would not depend upon convention (*saṃketa*). Therefore, words do not possess an inherent capacity to reveal meaning; rather, their capacity consists precisely in their functioning in accordance with convention, which is non-opposition to it. What is the reason? Because at the time of the convention—the time of making the agreement—words are introduced at will according to the desire of the one who establishes that convention to employ them.

If, on the other hand, words were established by nature or established by their own essence (*svabhāva*) with respect to some object, then it would be impossible to convey meaning through convention according to one's desire regarding those [words] established by nature, because that would depend upon human will.

Therefore, words are meaningless by themselves; being thus meaningless, they become meaningful through human refinement—that is, through human convention (*puruṣasaṃketa*). Now, if it is maintained that they possess meaning in dependence upon human refinement so that they may not be meaningless, then they would necessarily be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). This is because the very fact that these words are refined by him—the fact that they are refined by a person—is their state of being of human origin; it does not consist in their production from a person.

What is the reason? Precisely because of that convention established by the person (*puruṣasamaya*), there is a deception or contradiction regarding the object. It is not from the mere production [of the word] by the person that there is deception. For even though a word is produced by a person, it is "conformed" (*samita*) otherwise—that is, it is designated (*saṃketita*) in accordance with the actual state of things (*yathābhāvam*)—and thus, by not contradicting the true nature of the object, it is not obstructive or deceptive. Just as that which is "other than that"—namely, the qualities of a person other than the word, such as the opening and closing of the eyes—which, though in themselves purposeless, are conformed by the person to the actual state of things and are not deceptive; so it is with the word.

Summing up, he says: "Therefore" (*tad*). Therefore, this person, upon ceasing, also causes to cease that manifestation of the object—that is, the cognition of the object—whose occurrence or arising was based on his own established convention. "Therefore" (*tad*) means for that reason. Why? Because by its cessation—that is, by the cessation of that person—how could there be truthfulness of meaning? On the contrary, there would be only meaninglessness. By this, it is refuted what is said by others regarding the proof [of the Veda's authority] at the two limits of the past and the future.
Having refuted that [position], the proponents of the Vedas have accomplished their purpose.
The former limit of the Veda is characterized by its being composed by a person;
the latter consists in its destruction. For the absence of these two is what constitutes eternity. (Ślokavārttika, fn. 1)
That [position] is refuted because, even if the Veda were non-human in origin and eternal, it would be purposeless and thus fail to achieve its intended goal.

(6) Alternatively, if "human authorship" (*pauruṣeyatā*) refers only to the act of production itself—not to the communication of a convention or the establishment of a linguistic sign—then the idea is that the Veda is authoritative precisely because it is non-human in origin.

Even so, when the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of words is accepted, the convention (*saṃketa*)—which serves as the cause for making the meaning known and the cause for manifesting the meaning—is dependent upon persons and conforms to the will of persons; it does not necessarily function in accordance with the actual state of things. Therefore, because the convention conforms to the will of persons, the possibility of falsity exists.

(7) The explanation beginning with "What [is the reason]? is as follows: "Of this"—that is, of the Veda—"since" (*yataḥ*) there is a comprehension of meaning, i.e., the manifestation of an object, from a convention (*samaya*), that convention would be human-made; therefore, it might even be false or unreal, because of its independence [from external reality]. Consequently, for that heaven which has morality (*śīla*) as its means or cause—that very heaven characterized by the summit of Mount Sumeru—the statement regarding it in the Veda would not be overturned by another convention.

One might represent the contrary meaning by stating that "heaven is unsurpassed pleasure," and one might likewise produce a contrary result through means such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice; for this reason, since there is the possibility of revealing something that is not in accordance with reality, that very same defect which was stated regarding human [compositions] applies here: "In the case of human [works], deception is possible due to the defects of the person. (228)

(8) But surely the relationship between word and meaning is indeed non-human (apauruṣeya). For instance, just as the elders of the present day teach the relationship between word and meaning as it has already been established from before, so too did the elders of each preceding generation; thus, because it is beginningless, the relationship is indeed non-human. As it has been said: "Apart from the beginninglessness of words and meanings, there is no other cause for the beginninglessness of their relationship; therefore, in the Veda, no beginning of the relationship is found."1
fn. 1: *Ślokavārttika*:

"And that relationship is established by three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, when a certain elder has employed a word for the sake of another person's comprehension of an object, another observer standing nearby perceives both the speaker and the signified object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, he understands the listener’s state of comprehension by means of his subsequent activity. And, through the fact that the comprehension of the object would otherwise be inexplicable, he understands the power of signifier and signified residing in the word and its meaning. Thus, the relationship is indeed established by three means of valid cognition. As it has been said:"
In this case, one perceives the words and the objects denoted by elders through direct perception,
and the listener’s comprehension through inference from their behavior.

"And by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), based on the impossibility of [the effect] otherwise, they understand that the capacity of the intellect resides in the *dhātṛ* (the creator), and that this [creator] is established by the authority of the relationship."

Regarding this, he says: "If the relationship were non-human-made," and so forth. If the relationship between word and meaning is accepted as being non-human-made (*apauruṣeya*), there would be cognition—that is, the comprehension of the meaning—even for one who lacks *saṃvit*. *Saṃvit* is the knowledge of the convention (*saṃketa*). For one in whom that does not exist, [there would still be comprehension]. Those whose relationships are "not produced by humans" (*akāryaḥ puruṣaiḥ*)—that is, not generated by men—are such [relationships]. Those words, with respect to their meanings (*artheṣu vācyeṣu*), [would function] because they manifest the objects exactly as they are, even by humans.

They are not made to be causes of false cognition; rather, they are simply mistaken due to their own nature. Because there is no such error, there is no fault characterized by inconsistency. Now, if the relationship [between word and meaning] is non-human (apauruṣeya), what is the purpose of a convention (*saṃketa*)? For that relationship between word and meaning, if it is the cause for the comprehension of the meaning and that relationship is non-human, then a person understanding the meaning from the word—since the relationship is established by nature (*nisargasiddha*)—would not depend upon a convention.

Like a lamp and so forth, [the word] depends upon convention (*saṃketa*); therefore, there is no non-human (*apauruṣeya*) relation between words and their objects, unlike royal insignia and the like. It might be thought: "The relation is indeed non-human, but it is independent of convention and serves as the basis for cognition. To this he says: How can something that is not a basis for cognition—or rather, how can it be the very basis for the cognition of an object—be a relation? It is not at all. For a relation is postulated because the cognition [of the object] would otherwise be impossible. In the absence of cognition, how can there be a relation? Furthermore: "Since a relation is a means of making known (*jñāpaka*), it depends upon its own cognition."
Therefore, although it exists, that manifester of all unmanifested things is not apprehended by those who have previously employed it; thus,
the relationship is established, and in this way, the relationship and so forth do not exist [as independent entities]."

To this he replies with the words beginning "saṃketa" (convention), etc. When that relation is manifested by convention, the postulation of a relation other than convention is ineffective—that is, fruitless.

This is what is meant: since the cognition of an object arises when there is a convention and does not arise when there is none, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), convention alone is the cause of the cognition of the object; so what is the use of another relation?

He explains by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*). [The relation] is the cause for the cognition of an object that has not been manifested or revealed. The connection is with the word "this" (*enam*); the connection is with the phrase "then that" (*sa tarhi*). Since the communication of meaning is established through convention (*saṃketa*) alone, why is this relation—which has the nature of being present—maintained without cause, that is, fruitlessly?

(10) He states the very futility [of the relation] with the words beginning with “nanu” and so forth. [The relation] is merely this much: that the production of a cognition—that is, the arising of understanding—regarding the meaning to be expressed is brought about by convention (*samaya*). Thus, the relation is fruitless. Convention is not capable regarding what is unfit. What then? Only in that word which is understood by the speaker as being capable because the comprehension of the meaning would otherwise be impossible, is convention effective. If it is argued that fitness (*yogyatā*) is the relation, then it has been said: “Power (*śakti*) alone is indeed the relation, and no difference in it is perceived.”

"For since that [relation] is to be inferred from its effect, it follows the distinctions of those [two]. (Saṃbandhaparīkṣā 28). Here he says: "Then what," and so forth. He thinks as follows: A single power does not reside in both word and object; rather, the expressive power resides in the word, while the expressed power residing in the object is quite different. But when the relation is the power of the word, then it follows that the relation itself becomes the related entity. Therefore, he asks: "Or rather, let the word itself be the relation."
But surely, capacity (*yogyatā*) is one thing and the word is another; how then can the word be the relation? To this he says:

because the form of the word which is capable with respect to the communication of meaning is its capacity. It is like the capacity for cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇayogyatā*). "Capacity for cause and effect" means the capacity for producing an effect. Just as [this capacity] is identical with the nature of the cause, so too is it here. If that capacity were something other than the word, then one would have to state the relation between the word and the capacity—otherwise, it could not be established that "this is the capacity of the word."

If it is argued that there is an assistance of the word toward that fitness (*yogyatā*) which is a distinct entity—meaning that an assistance is produced for the fitness by the word—the implication is that fitness is called "verbal" because it is produced by the word. This is not so; there is no assistance of the word toward fitness. Why? Because fitness, being eternal, is devoid of any excellence (*niratiśayatvāt*). Or, if it is further argued that an assistance entirely distinct from fitness itself is produced by the word...

In that case, it must be stated what the relationship is between the word and its capacity for producing an auxiliary effect (*upakāra*). If one argues that yet another auxiliary effect is produced in that [first] auxiliary effect through its capacity, then—by the same reasoning already stated—one would have to postulate further and further auxiliary effects; this leads to the fallacy of infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, since no auxiliary effect is established due to this infinite regress, the very relationship of the word with its capacity remains unestablished.

Furthermore, a word that assists a capacity distinct from itself assists it by its own nature alone, not by the nature of another; otherwise, it would follow that the word itself is non-assisting. Therefore, since the capacity is inherent (*svataḥ*) and the word is capable by its own nature, why is it not accepted that the meaning itself is the very essence of the word, being fit to generate cognition? What is the point of an indirect process? Consequently, capacity is neither the relation nor the cause of the cognition of the meaning, because the cognition of the meaning arises precisely from inherence (*samavāya*).

In that case, how can the convention (*samaya*) of a Buddhist be the relationship between word and meaning? And why would it not [be such]? Because it resides in persons. This convention consists in [the cognition]: "This is the designator of this object. And that resides in persons, not in the word and the object. Furthermore, a property belonging to one thing cannot be the property of another, just as the property of a horse is not the property of a cow.

(1) But the Teacher says—"No," and so forth—to show that there is not only no convention (*samaya*) nor a relation (*sambandha*), but furthermore, no other real relation exists. For instance, the relation between entities would have to be either a fusion of their forms (*rūpaśleṣa*), or dependence (*pāratantrya*), or mutual expectancy (*parasparāpekṣaṇa*). Among these, for things that are unmixed and mutually distinct, there can be no relation characterized by a fusion of forms, because that would entail their non-difference and result in their becoming one.

Likewise, for established (*siddha*) or perfected forms, there is no relation characterized by dependence (*pāratantrya*), because dependence is impossible in that which is already established. He states that there is also no relation characterized by mutual dependence, saying: "And because of non-dependence," since that which is established is independent of everything. (2) [Objection: If, then, there is no relation between word and object, how is there the cognition of the object from the word? And how is verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) included within inference (*anumāna*)? Or, if that were so, what would be the purpose of the linguistic convention (*samaya*)?

He says: "The specific object," and so forth. The specific object is that which has been taken as the domain by the intention to communicate. The striving for that is the desire to communicate. Speech, impelled—that is, produced—by that [desire], indicates or reveals the object that appears as its own cause. The cause of speech is the intention to communicate. Of what does it indicate that which reveals it? It indicates it for one who knows, "This is from that."

Therefore, for one who knows that this speech has arisen from the intention to communicate, there exists a relationship characterized by the producer-and-produced (*janyajanaka*) nature between the intention—defined as the mental state of cognition—and the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*). Consequently, comprehension [of the meaning] arises from the word through inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); that is, the comprehension of the object arises from the sentence by virtue of that producer-and-produced relationship.

Therefore, that which was stated—namely, "Even if the cognition of an object from a word is an inference, the cognition of an object from a sentence is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) because the relationship [between the parts] is not grasped, and in this case, inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is of no use"—is refuted; for without inseparable connection, the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) cannot exist. Furthermore, as for what was asked—"How is there a comprehension of an object from a word? And how is verbal cognition included within inference?"—that has been answered.

kha. Now he states the purpose of *samaya* (convention): “The exposition of that,” and so forth. *Samaya* is the exposition of that [invariable concomitance] (*avinābhāva*); it is so called because it is by means of this [convention] that [the concomitance] is expounded. “From that” means from the convention; it refers to the establishment—that is, the cognition—of the characteristic of invariable concomitance, which is the member for establishing the object of the signifier. The designation “relation” is applied to the convention figuratively, because it expounds the relation; however, the convention itself is not the primary relation. Therefore, as it has been said:
“Is the convention [established] for every individual person, or indeed for every single utterance?”
The claim that "it is created at the beginning of the world, or once by some single agent" has been refuted. [Ga:

But surely, if the cognition of an object from a word occurs through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), then the word’s communication of its meaning would not be by way of denotation (*vācakatva*), just as smoke communicates fire. And if it is said that the relationship between word and meaning is called "convention" (*samaya*) because they express their existence through convention rather than [invariable concomitance], then there would also have to be a convention between fire and smoke.

This is not a fault, because: when one intends to communicate a meaning and employs a word—superimposing upon it the status of being denotable for that meaning and the status of being denotative for the word itself—even if no convention has been previously established—the word arises precisely in its form as a denotator. [Objection: But surely, with the intention of communicating a meaning, only phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced, and phonemes are not accepted as being denotators. So how can it be said that "the word, which is the denotator, arises from the intention"? [Response: This is not so. For the following reason: when a person intends to communicate a specific meaning, they first reflect, "I shall communicate this meaning by means of a word even though no convention has been made. Having thus superimposed the state of being denotable upon the meaning and the state of being denotative upon the word, they employ the word. At that time, the word indeed arises in its very nature as a denotator. Therefore, the statement that "the word, which is the denotator, arises from the intention" is entirely consistent. Furthermore, since the phonemes are not perceived individually, they cannot be the producers of the cognition of the meaning. Nor can they be the producers of the cognition of the word, because the word is not something distinct from the phonemes. Consequently, it must be admitted that the word, which is the denotator, arises from the intention. Thus, the objection is refuted.

True. However, because the speaker and the listener have the conceit (*abhimāna*) that the phonemes themselves are the signifiers, it is said that the signifier alone arises. Therefore, the convention (*samaya*)—which is the communication of this very relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*), characterized by inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) as the relation between word and object (*śabdārthasambandha*)—is called "convention" for the sake of the ignorant. But not every communication of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is a convention; thus, the relationship in the case of smoke and so forth is not called a convention.

Although there is a difference in the relationship between word and meaning between the time of the convention and the time of usage, nevertheless, people proceed by determining them as one due to their similarity. For this very reason, the speaker conveys that very same relationship between word and meaning which was previously apprehended, and the listener apprehends it as such. Therefore, it is said:
Furthermore, that relationship would have to be either distinct for each instance or else a single unity.

If it were a single unity, it could not be produced; if it were distinct, there would be a cognition of its difference. (Saṃbandhaparīkṣā 14) Due to the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, linguistic usage is not impaired.
For the relationship [of the word] is one thing for the speaker in his own cognition, while it is another for the listener.
What kind of relationship does the speaker establish for the listener?
Indeed, that which was previously perceived by him, he cannot produce for the listener.

As for the claim that "whatever new [relation] one might create, it too has never been observed to be a signifier," that is refuted; for in all cases, people proceed by determining the identity of the various relations between the signified and the signifier, even though they are distinct. Nor is there any beginninglessness to these relations, because recognition is not a valid means of knowledge. (229)

Or, let there be a connection between word and meaning that is indeed distinct from the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and is eternal. If, by virtue of that connection, words (*girāṃ śabdānām*) were restricted to a single meaning, then there would be no further comprehension (*gati*) of another meaning through convention (*samaya*), because that word would not have been restricted to it.
