Why? Because it is not logical for there to be cognition of an object that is not connected by that connection which is restricted to a single meaning. Why? Because it would follow that such a connection would be rendered futile (*vaiphalyaprasaṅga*). [Objection: "There is simply no cognition of it."
He says: "And it is observed," and so forth. A lamp is an illuminator because its convention (*samaya*) is established by the power of human intention.

Regarding the passage beginning with "aneka" (many): if it is admitted that a word has a connection with many objects, and the maker of the convention brings about its manifestation through a restriction to a single object, then he does so only for the intended object and not for another, contradictory one; thus there would be no such restriction, and consequently, the possibility of a contradictory manifestation arises. It is possible that even a contradictory meaning might be manifested instead of the desired one.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth: "If there were a restriction to a single meaning, then the observation of the expression of multiple meanings through the force of convention would be contradicted. Therefore, in order that this observed fact not be contradicted, all words are denoters of every object."

With the words "tathā" and so forth, there is the demonstration of a contradictory instance. Just as it is accepted that all [words] are denoters of everything, so too must this necessarily be accepted: that not every object is the producer of every effect, because this is established by logic (*nyāya*). And he states that logic: "because of confusion (*saṃkara*)," meaning because the relation of cause and effect is restricted (*pratiniyata*).

In this regard, given this principle, there is a specific and distinct entity that serves as the means (*sādhana*) or cause for a desired object to be established (*sādhya*), such as heaven and so forth. With respect to that [object] which has become the domain [of the word], what kind of word [is involved]? It is one that is "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), etc.—meaning common by virtue of being the designator (*vācaka*) of all possible *sādhyas* or effects, each according to its own respective means or causes. Why is it that the author of the convention (*samayakāra*) brings about the manifestation of that common word only in its intended individuality—that is, its manifestation specifically in the object intended as having that particular *sādhya* as its object? [The answer follows: Because...

This is what is meant: there is indeed a doubt as to whether the very same object that, by the nature of things, is a means to heaven, has been expressed therein by the author of the convention through words such as *agnihotra*, or whether, due to intellectual dullness, it has been expressed as something else entirely that is contrary to being a means to heaven.

The word "it" (sa) is unrestricted in its denotation with respect to everything; it attains restriction in a particular instance through a person—that is, through human convention. And that person might establish a convention even for something that is not [logically] incompatible. In such a case, not only would there be the possibility of a contradictory manifestation, but even this postulation of the Veda’s authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*), which is desired by you, would become purposeless. The phrase "api nāma" means "how indeed"; "unmixed" (*asaṃkīrṇa*) means not conjoined with what is undesired.

Thinking, "I shall know the very object intended from words that are not of human origin," the cause of confusion—the intermingling of the desired and the undesired—is excluded from Vedic words by being attributed to persons. Such being the case, those words which are considered to be of human origin, when employed by persons for some intended meaning, become confused through the possibility of expressing what is undesired.

Even those words considered to be non-human (apauruṣeya), being common to all possible meanings, have been restricted by those persons to a specific meaning according to their own whim through convention (*samaya*). What is the reason? Because those persons lack knowledge of the true nature of reality (*tattva*). If it is argued that Vedic words are restricted to their intended meanings by their very nature (*prakṛti*) or essence (*svabhāva*), and therefore the fault of being produced by human refinement does not apply—then, if this were so, they would not require instruction for the manifestation of their meaning; yet they do require it.

Because there is no cognition of an object from them by virtue of their own nature. Moreover, if they were restricted to specific objects by their very essence, then once they had been combined for a certain object at some time, they could never again manifest another object through a different convention. Yet they do manifest [other objects]. Therefore, they are not restricted to a single object by nature. And if there were restriction to a single object by way of intrinsic nature...

Furthermore, there would be no diversity of interpretation among commentators regarding Vedic sentences, nor any difference between successive explanations, because [the meaning] would be restricted to a single sense. Yet such diversity does exist. Therefore, unlike human utterances, Vedic words are not restricted to a single meaning.

Sixth. Now, it might be argued that their teaching refers only to a fixed meaning; therefore, he says: "The teaching... and so forth. In a Vedic sentence where there is a conceptualization of various possible meanings due to different interpretations—that is, in a Vedic sentence characterized by such possible alternatives—the teaching of the commentators lacks correspondence with what is intended. This is because there is no restriction [on its meaning], such that one could say, "This is its meaning," or "That is another. For this reason, authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) is indeed useless. Even if one were to postulate it, suspicion of error would not be eliminated.

Furthermore, for one who maintains that there is a relationship between word and object, the reason [for this] must be stated, because the establishment of a relationship [requires a basis]. For whom? For those words and objects that are distinct—that is, mutually different. (1) First of all, the relationship between word and object cannot be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*). This is because external objects such as jars and cloths are not the form or the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the word. For if jars and so forth were of the nature of the word, they would be non-existent.

Nor is the word the form of objects; for if it were the form of the object, it would follow that the form of the word itself would be lost, whereby there could be an inseparable connection (*anantarīyakatā*) through identity of essence. That is, there would be an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitā*). This applies even when there is a distinction in formal arrangement—that is, even when there is a distinction between the probandum and the probans based on a distinction in exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). What is this like? It is like "producedness" and "impermanence. Just as there is an inseparable connection between producedness and impermanence despite a distinction in their exclusions, because they share a single essence, so it is here.

(2) He states that there is also no connection characterized by "origination from that" [tadutpatti], beginning with the words "nor even," and so forth. This is what he means: for a connection between words, if it were to exist as characterized by origination from that, would it be with an object established in the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), or with an external object?

(a) First, the first position is not tenable. This is because these Vedic sounds are not accepted as being born from the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). The analysis of the compound is "those whose birth is from the desire to speak. This is because their eternity is admitted. Alternatively, being unborn or unproduced, they cannot be manifested by the desire to speak either, for that would entail the loss of their eternity; as was stated previously, things that are manifested are produced. (b) Nor is the second position tenable, as he says: "They are not dependent on objects" (*nārthāyattāḥ*). Nor are they dependent on external objects, precisely because of their eternity.

Others, however, compose and explain this as a single passage: "Since [Vedic words] are neither produced by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) nor manifested by it, they are therefore not dependent on meaning—that is, they are not tied to an external object—in either case. And because they are not dependent on meaning, for that reason—meaning, 'now,' in the absence of a connection—how could those words establish the concomitance, i.e., the existence, of that object? They could not establish it at all."

Of what nature is it? It is to be established by a specific restriction (*pratiniyama*) regarding that external object. That is, it is to be established by means of that specific restriction of words based on identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*) with respect to that external object; for there is no restriction [of words] when there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*) with an external object. (232)

3. He summarizes the very point already stated in a verse, beginning with "by being incapable of being modified by humans" (*asaṃskāryatayā*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in every way": if words were neither produced nor conventionally established by persons with a specific intention toward a meaning, then, by reason of their being incapable of being modified by persons, Vedic words would be devoid of meaning. This is because the truth or falsity of the meaning of words is dependent upon the modification by persons; therefore, in the absence of that [modification], they would necessarily be meaningless.

(2) Furthermore, if one were to resort to the refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) in order to avoid the charge of pointlessness (*nirarthatā*), there would also be the consequence of falsity (*mithyārthatā*); this would thus be like the "primary elephant bath. For an elephant, having bathed to remove mud, again covers itself with mud. Since there is no other possible state for a real entity (*vastu*)—it must be either eternal or non-eternal—(3) its activity could either be subject to the will of the person, meaning it would arise by the power of the person's desire like contraction and so forth, or it would be without activity; however, its activity does not occur by the will of the person.

Like a sprout and so forth. In that regard, under the view that [words] are impermanent and dependent upon persons, there would be a change according to place and so on; by the word "and so on" (*ādi*), time and state are included. The phrase "according to the intention of persons" means that a person would not be able to communicate by means of a particular word in the manner they intended to convey it; such is the connection [of the argument].

What is the reason? Even when there is a desire to communicate a meaning, because a word is independent [of human will], it is impossible for a person to ever apply it [in a specific way]; this is the meaning. It is like mountains and so forth. Just as mountains and the like, being independent of persons, cannot be applied at will even when there is a desire [to do so], so it is here. Furthermore, we observe that communication according to one's intention occurs through the shifting of place and other factors. Therefore, the relationship [between word and meaning] is not dependent upon persons.

If the relationship were not dependent on a person, then this very same fault just mentioned would apply even if the relationship were impermanent. Why? Because it is impossible for that relationship, having a stable nature, to undergo change through the shifting of place and so forth; otherwise, such a thing would be impossible, just like space. 4. ka. Now, [if it is argued that] the word is related to all objects—regarding that, he says: "The same," and so forth.

Even if it were assumed that the connection [of a word] with all objects exists simultaneously at one and the same time, since there would be no restrictive factor regarding the specific object intended, the cognition of a particular intended object could not arise from a word that is common to all objects. Therefore, one must admit that even a word connected with multiple objects attains restriction to the intended object through the mental refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person; and in that case, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before follows.

This is what was stated in the passage beginning with: “When there is a connection with multiple meanings, and the possibility of contradictory manifestations” (1.231). Thus far, the defect has been stated regarding the relation’s lack of dependence on a person, whether that relation is eternal or non-eternal. Furthermore, if the relation were to function according to human will, it would be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*); and on this basis, there arises the suspicion of deception, since one must admit that the person is the cause of contradiction.

kha. Furthermore, with the words "api ca" and so forth, he states another refutation regarding that very point: "The object of words is indeed twofold: the universal (*jāti*) directly, and the individual (*vyakti*) indicated by it. (1) Regarding that, if [the word] has a connection with the individual, he says: because the meanings—the objects to be expressed—which are the correlates of the relation, are impermanent; when they perish, the relation which depends upon them also perishes, and thus the relation possesses no permanence. It is called "dependent on another" (*parāśraya*) because its support (*āśraya*) is another, namely, the correlate.

If there were no necessary connection between a relation and its relata, those two relata could not possess the status of being related. For one thing cannot be possessed of another unless it is connected to it, just as a cow is not possessed of a horse [because they lack such a connection]. Furthermore, that substratum would be impermanent because objects are impermanent; upon the departure—that is, the destruction—of the substratum, the relation which depends upon it would also depart, just as light perishes when the lamp that supports it perishes.

Otherwise, if it were maintained that even when the substratum (*āśraya*) perishes, the dependent (*āśrita*) does not perish, then the relation would not be dependent upon that which is intended to be its substratum. Therefore, because the relation perishes along with the destruction of its substratum, relations are not eternal. Furthermore, the meaning of "substratum" must be stated: in what sense are the two relata the "substratum" of that relation? The meaning of "substratum" must be explained; for the meaning of "substratum" is the sense of providing assistance (*upakāra*).

And that [relation] does not exist here. What is the reason? Because a permanent relation cannot be assisted, since it is incapable of having any excellence added to it; and that which is intended to be the locus, if it does not provide assistance, would not be a locus. [Objection: This might be so if the individual were the object of expression, for then the fault just mentioned would occur. However, since it is the eternal universal (*jāti*) that is the object of expression, there is no fault; for there is no fault of impermanence regarding the relation due to the departure of the relata. [Reply: No, etc., is the response. Because there is no purpose in expressing that [universal], this has already been thoroughly examined in the investigation of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) [in verse 3.55].

"A person acts only after having recognized things capable of purposeful action"—in this context, because a universal (*jāti*) is impossible in every instance of denotation, the communication of a universal is untenable. For example, among those words denoting individuals that are arbitrary—where "arbitrary" (*yādṛcchika*) refers to those words such as "Devadatta" and the like, which are used by the speaker's whim (*yadṛcchā*) without any external cause, and which denote specific individuals—(234) [the universal cannot be the object].

5. According to the view of some, there is a fourfold application of words: genus-words (*jātiśabda*), quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), action-words (*kriyāśabda*), and arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*). According to their opinion, this has been stated. Now, if even a word such as "Devadatta" is intended to denote a genus through its various states, then, since a genus would be admitted to be denoted at all times, it would be impossible for the word to apply to a specific individual intended in a particular instance—by excluding other particulars and abandoning other individuals—and therefore it does not denote a genus.

And when the owner of the cows says, "Bring the cow," the activity directed toward bringing a specific cow occurs by way of excluding cows belonging to other owners; and this would only be possible if, through context and so forth, the word *go* were to function as a term for a particular [individual]. Furthermore, there would not even be a comprehension of the sentence-meaning, such as "the bringing of a cow," because the object of the word *go* would not be established. Therefore, the universal (*jāti*) is not what is enjoined in all cases. For this reason, a real relationship between words whose bases (*prakṛti*) are distinct is not tenable.

Therefore, regarding those [reasons] characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*), the very fact that the existence and non-existence of the intended effect—namely, an entity possessing both presence and absence—occur through the medium of the existence and non-existence of the intended cause, is itself the relationship; that is to say, the relationship between things that are not distinct is precisely the relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*).

For this reason, therefore, the relationship between words—which are of the nature of effects—and their objects—which serve as the causes—must be established and fixed by persons through the intellect (*buddhi*) and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is because a word is employed when an object exists and is not employed when it does not. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that the relationship between word and object is established by the intellect, based upon the presence or absence of the word corresponding to the presence or absence of the object.

6. He explains this very point with the words "those two alone," and so forth. Relying upon the presence and absence of the object by way of the word, the word and the object—though by their own nature unmixed and unrelated—appear to a person as mixed and related; they appear in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). Why? Due to the cultivation of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra-bhāvanā*), that is, due to the habituation to linguistic usage from beginningless time. For this reason, the conjunction—the relation—between things and words is a human product (*pauruṣeya*), because it is established through the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of linguistic usage.

7. There is this further fault in accepting a relation that exists as a real entity (vastubhūta); thus he says, "Furthermore," and so forth. Because the substratum intended as the signified has perished, even though the relation itself has not perished, that verbal relation intended as its signifier would no longer exist—since it would be the case that "this [relation] does not belong to this"—and due to that absence of relation, it could not again be connected with a new signified object. Consequently, all things that arise as they arise would be unexpressible, because they would lack a relation.

Why [is there no relation] for those very things that are unrelated? Because no relation is established. For whatever things arise, no relation is established among them prior to their arising, since it is impossible for a relation—which by nature resides in two things—to exist in the absence of its relata. Regarding the phrase "in that case also," etc.: even in that case, when the arising of a relation with those objects is postulated for each object as it arises, a change in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of words is not logical.

That connection which subsequently arises with an object did not previously exist because of the absence of that connection; yet it exists later. Thus, there would be a change in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of words. And that is not tenable, given their permanence (*nityatva*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth, the explanation is as follows: when a previously existing relation has perished, the word for which that relation was destroyed suffers a deficiency—that is, a lack of relation—when another object subsequently arises. To prevent the subsequent objects from becoming unexpressible [by the word], one might argue that every object, as it arises, possesses a relation even if that relation has not yet been grasped. Even so, although the relation has arisen, it would not belong to the word; the word would not possess that relation by virtue of it.

What is the reason? Because it is impossible for that sound, whose nature was previously unrelated, to possess that [new] state through a relation produced later; nor is it possible for it to possess a nature related to that relation. When? Without a reversal of its own nature—that is, without abandoning its prior unrelated nature. He states another fault as well: because a relation that arises simultaneously with the object and is established from something other than the sound cannot be based upon that sound, since the sound provides no assistance [to the relation]; thus, it is simply impossible for that [relation] to exist [in the sound]. (234)

Now, if that relationship is postulated as being a cooperative cause for the production of that sound—meaning it acts as a cooperative cause with respect to its arising—it would follow that the sound, being already capable, must produce [the relationship] at all times; it would follow that the relationship is generated at every moment. Why? Because it would not depend on a cooperative cause. Furthermore, this independence is due to the fact that a permanent sound cannot be assisted by cooperative causes. Alternatively, if the sound were incapable [of producing it], it could only produce it by depending on a cooperative cause.

In that case, even if there was an incapacity to produce a prior relation, there would likewise be an incapacity later on, even at the time when the object is present. Why? Because the previous nature of incapacity has not been abandoned. This objection applies to a relation that is considered to be a real entity (*vastubhūta*); it does not apply to a relation manifested by conceptual construction (*buddhisandarśita*).

The explanation begins with "For not... and so forth. Their mutual dependence—that is, the dependence of those entities upon one another due to some cause imagined by the intellect—is a relationship characterized by that [dependence], which appears through human mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This is because it has the nature of appearing to the conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) of a person who possesses the habituation of such mental cultivation. Furthermore, this relationship, being of human origin, does not depend on the actual connection between the entities themselves.

The "conjunction of entities" (*bhāvaśleṣa*) is their mixing; it does not exist [as a real entity], because all entities abide in their own respective natures due to the difference in their intrinsic natures (*prakṛtibheda*). Rather, this person—without altering his own eternal nature, and without discarding one stable related nature while assuming another related nature—[acts] from some cause, because the existence of something is observed when that [other thing] exists, or because of the maturation of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for such conventional usage within.

Thinking, "I shall myself conceive this connection here and thus bring it about," they too would become such through the repeated practice of human activity; that is, they would possess connections fashioned by persons. Yet, by that much, they do not lose their previously established nature of being unrelated.

This is what is meant: the relation conceptualized by the intellect—that is, the relation postulated by you—is not contradicted even in the case of those [entities] you consider to be eternal. Therefore, it is logical to rely upon that very [conceptual relation] rather than a real one. As for the objection previously stated—that the relation is impermanent because the relation, being dependent, perishes when its substratum perishes—if it is argued in response to this refutation that the relation does not perish even when the substratum perishes because it is eternal, just like a universal (*jāti*), [then we reply as follows].

"Just as [there is] no destruction of a universal (*jāti*) despite the destruction of its substratum because the universal is eternal, so too [there is none] of the relation. (235) Regarding this, he says: "Even in the case of universals and the like—which are eternal and yet regarded as having a substratum—is there no capacity of the substratum at all, such that this [substratum] is accepted as being of no benefit? It is 'heard,' etc., which is the explanation. By the word 'heard,' he indicates that this is merely a conventional renown devoid of any real entity. [The phrase] 'dependent on the individual' [means]: we do not perceive any capacity of the substratum, nor any assistance produced by the substratum, in the case of eternal universals and the like, by virtue of which that which is intended as the substratum would truly be a substratum."

What is the reason? Because there is no cause for that which has an established nature (*siddhasvabhāva*). Furthermore, a substratum (*āśraya*) that is not an agent is independent. (236) If it is argued that from the substratum arises the manifestation (*vyakti*)—that is, the manifestation in the form of a capacity (*yogyatā*)—of both the birth and the relation [to the universal], and that this very [manifestation] is the "substratum of the category" (*padārthāśraya*) by virtue of being an assistance (*upakāra*) produced by the substratum; [we reply:]...

He states the reply: "By knowledge," and so forth. From the connection with auxiliary causes—such as lamps and the like, which are the causes for the production of cognition—and from their being situated in a suitable location, there arises in jars and other manifested objects that very capacity to produce a cognition corresponding to themselves by virtue of their fitness for such production; this alone is accepted as "manifestation" (*vyakti*) by those who know logic and understand the principles of reason. However, in the case of universals (*jāti*) and the rest, which are manifested and are unchanging due to their eternity, there is no differentiation [in them] arising from the manifestor.

Regarding the non-arising of the capacity to produce cognition: what is the purpose, what is the benefit, and from where [does it come] for those universals (*jāti*) and so forth by means of their own manifestors (*vyañjaka*)? None at all. For it is precisely because of this that those universals and so forth are considered to be manifested by those manifestors. (237)

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "sahakāriṇaḥ" (from the auxiliary causes). From what kind of auxiliary causes—such as a lamp—is [the manifestation]? From those that depend upon a material cause (*upādāna*). [The jar, etc.,] which was previously incapable of producing cognition, is the material cause; for the jar, characterized by its capacity, depends upon the jar [as its own substrate]. Manifestation (*abhivyakti*) for jars and the like is simply the production of another moment that is capable of generating cognition of its own object.

Otherwise, if jars and other objects did not acquire the capacity to produce cognition from the proximity of a lamp and so forth, then it would follow that cognition would arise in jars and other objects even without depending on that assistance—the assistance provided by the lamp.
(fn. 1: In the margin. 2: "tadapekṣatvāt" is missing.)

Now, if it is maintained that a lamp or the like bestows capacity upon a manifestable object that was previously incapable, then, because the lamp or the like—which produces that capacity—is a producer (*janaka*) of the jar and so forth, what is the reason? It is because that capacity has the nature of that [jar], for it does not have the nature of something unmanifestable. Upon the production of that [capacity], the jar itself would be produced.

Now, lest this fault should arise, it might be maintained that the capacity produced by a lamp or similar causes is a different entity from the manifested object. But if such a difference between the capacity and the object is admitted, it follows that entities such as jars would receive no assistance from lamps and the like; for when something is done to one thing, another is not thereby assisted, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Furthermore, if the capacity produced by a lamp or similar factor were a distinct entity from the pot and so forth, then because the production of the cognition of the pot and such would depend on that [external] capacity, the pot and so forth—which do not produce a cognition of themselves—would necessarily never be perceived. Yet, the perception of pots and such is indeed admitted. Moreover, in that case, it would follow that their perception would not depend on light; the meaning is that it would follow that the perception of pots and such occurs even without depending on light.

If it is asked how it is that [the manifestation] is independent of light, he says "independent," and so forth (p. 424). This independence from light that has been attributed to jars and the like follows from the fact that there is no benefit to their own nature; for no benefit whatsoever accrues to the nature of the jar and so on through lamps and the like, because those [lamps] produce a capacity that is distinct [from the jar's nature]. Therefore, these [objects] are manifested insofar as they depend upon another, such as a lamp, for the production of the cognition of their own objects.

The word "tataḥ" means that they accept from the other [the lamp] an excellence of nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*), which is its own form (*svarūpa*) capable of generating cognition. For that reason, those things considered to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*), such as the lamp and so forth, are indeed produced (*janya*) by it. If they are produced, why are they designated as "manifested"? To this he says: "Because of the acquisition of the form of the object of knowledge," and so on. Because of the acquisition—that is, the obtaining—from the manifesting agent, such as the lamp, of the form of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-rūpa*), which is the form of the apprehended (*grāhya-rūpa*), cognition necessarily arises with respect to that object. Therefore, it is by virtue of cognition [that they are called manifested].

By the term "kāryātiśaya" (the excellence of the effect). An effect whose cognition has not been grasped is the "excellence of the effect"; by the word "vyaṅgya" (manifested), which denotes that excellence, [the author] intends to distinguish it from those effects whose cognitions have already been grasped. When something necessarily involves a cognition that has been taken up, even though it is produced (*janya*), it is called "manifested" (*vyaṅgya*). On the other hand, that which is not of such a nature is called merely an "effect" (*kārya*). It is for the sake of establishing this distinction that "manifested things" (*vyaṅgya*) are explained; it is not the case, however, that this applies to universals (*jāti*), relations (*sambandha*), and so forth.

"Birth and relation" (jāti-sambandha) are those which have these as their beginning; by the word "beginning," other things also considered eternal that are dependent [upon a substratum] are included. Since they cannot be assisted in any way by that which is considered their substratum, it follows that they cannot be manifested by that which provides no assistance—this is the connection [of the argument].

And in order to show that a relation is not established by three means of valid cognition, he says: "If the relation were a real entity (*vastu*), then because the relation is distinct from the two related terms, a third entity called 'relation' would come into being. And if that [third entity] were to meet the conditions for perception, then there would be a diversity of cognition based upon three objects. Furthermore, this relation between word and meaning, if it were a real entity, could not—by necessity—transcend or bypass both difference and non-difference from the word and the meaning."

If it is argued that there will be a mode distinct from both difference and non-difference, he says: "For form... Since form is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing, it has been stated previously—in the passage beginning, "Because for a form that has not become [something else], there is no deviation from its otherness" (p. 425)—that the very non-reality of that intrinsic nature, its being not that [nature], is precisely what constitutes otherness.

And this relation, being sensory—that is, in the cognition which has the relation as its objective support—is [perceived] through the exclusion of what is other than it. How could that [relation] be "excluded from others" if it does not appear in the form of an entity distinct from that related thing? How could it have a nature excluded from others?

What is the reason? It is because there is no distinction—that is, no difference—from the object that is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, regarding the non-perception of those two—namely, the non-distinction from the perceptible and the non-perception themselves—they respectively depend upon the opposite of distinction and existence. The "opposite of distinction" is the absence of distinction; its basis is the non-distinction from the perceptible. The "opposite of existence" is non-existence; its basis is the non-perception of the perceptible. Therefore, the meaning is this: whatever is not perceived as distinct from something else is not other than that. Whatever is perceptible yet is not perceived is, in short, non-existent. (fn. 2: *te ced*)

"Otherwise" means: if it is admitted that the object is distinct from its cognition, yet there is no distinction between them despite their being distinct, and if—while the object is not perceived—a distinction and existence are nevertheless postulated for it, then there follows the undesirable consequence that the established status of that [distinction] and the absence of non-distinction would both cease to exist. For instance, the non-perception of the non-distinction from the perceptible is the cause of this established status; if those two—the distinction and the absence of non-distinction—are not accepted as the means of establishing it, then that established status is destroyed.

If it is argued that because the relation is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), even though it does not appear in the cognition as distinct [from its relata], the aforementioned fault does not apply—just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth; that is to say, just as the sense organs such as the eye do not appear in the cognition as distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and the like, yet they exist as separate entities, so too will the relation exist. [fn. 3: *prāpya*] Having reached.

The Teacher says: "No; the relation is not supersensible. For it would follow that there could be no comprehension of the object from a relation that is supersensible. What is the reason? Because that which is unestablished—that is, not ascertained in its own form—is not a communicator [of meaning]. Indeed, it is not logical for there to be a cognition of something X by means of something Y when the relation between X and Y has not been apprehended.

Now, [the opponent] says that the sense organ itself makes the object known even without the relation being known—namely, "by mere proximity," and so forth. If it were admitted that the relation makes the object known by its mere proximity—that is, by its mere existence—then even those who are unacquainted with the relationship between word and meaning would have the cognition: "This is the designator of this object."

It might be thought: "The perception of the relation through its distinction [from its relata] certainly exists; however, that does not arise from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but rather from inference (*anumāna*). To this, he says: "There is no comprehension of the relation through inference. Why? Because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). For there is no logical mark whatsoever that establishes the relation. Furthermore, the cognition of the object (*arthapratīti*) is not a logical mark, because an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished. Indeed, nowhere in an example is the cognition of the object, which is the effect of the relation, ever apprehended.

What is the reason? Because even in that case, when [the example] is adduced as an illustration, it depends upon a proof on account of the fact that the relationship is beyond the reach of the senses; yet no such proof exists, because the example itself remains unestablished in that instance.

If it is argued that this lack of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntarahitatva*) is the same when an inference is being made to establish the existence of the sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth, which are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), we reply: it is not the same. Why? Because those sense organs and so forth are inferred through other means. No specific form of the sense organs, which are not themselves perceived, is established as "this" (i.e., in its own nature), by which the fault would be equal. Rather, cognition—which is the effect—is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) to possess positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with certain factors such as light and the like.

Just as in states such as the eyes being closed there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and in states such as the eyes being opened there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*); so too, knowledge of such a nature is an effect that does not arise from those [tanmātras] alone. That it is seen not to occur even when those [tanmātras] are present establishes its non-origination from those tanmātras alone, and establishes its dependence on something distinct from them—just as one establishes dependence on a cause distinct from the proximate causes.
fn. 1: B. *kāryatanmātrā°* (effect-tanmātra)

"There must be some other cause. From that, by means of the aforementioned logical connection (*anvaya*), the sense organs are established through their effects. Here, sprouts and the like—which cannot arise in the absence of other causes—are the illustrative examples. However, there is no inference of a relation distinct from its effect, as in the case of the eye and so forth, because it is an inference of a specific [relation]. For indeed, whatever inference establishes that "the relation exists" is an inference of that very particular [relation]. fn. 2: B. *°ktānnyāyāt* |

And that is incorrect. Why? Because, while that very relationship remains unestablished, there is an absence of the cognition of its effect—that is, the effect of the relationship itself. If it is argued that "the word and the object are the logical mark (*liṅga*)," he replies with the words "for not," and so on. For in that case, neither the form of the word nor the object is the logical mark for that specific relationship. What is the reason? Because both the word and the object are capable [of being related] everywhere.

Because every word is capable of being expressive of every object, and every object is capable of being denoted by every word; and because the cause for the cognition of a specific object is a specific relation, and that relation—which is the basis for the cognition of a specific object—is not conveyed by an indefinite word and object; or, if it were conveyed, then from the cognition of every relation there would follow the comprehension of every object. But this is not the case. Therefore, this relation is not cognized through an indefinite word and object.

fn. 3:B. Because every object is capable of being denoted by every word—[this phrase was added]—if a specific relation between words and objects were established along with the general relation itself, then there would be a cognition of that specific relation in some cases. For, in the absence of a specific qualification of the relation, such a cognition of a specific relation is not tenable when the general relation of words [to their objects] has not been established.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that the cognition of a specific relation arises from a word even without a [pre-existing] relation, or if such a cognition of a relation is desired to be without a cause, then why is it not also accepted that the communication of meaning by words is likewise without a cause—just as there is a fixed rule for the cognition of that [relation], so too there would be a fixed rule for the cognition of the specific relation?

The indicative mark (*liṅga*)—which is the very nature of the word’s meaning—is similar and equal in all relations. Consequently, if the word were not qualified [by convention], it would bring about a relation with everything; thus, there would be a cognition of every object without distinction. Furthermore, for every person—whether they have grasped the linguistic convention (*samaya*) or have not grasped it—there would be a cognition of all objects. Therefore, since the cognition of an object occurs through the establishment of the relation by the aforementioned logic, no person would require the instruction of tradition (*saṃpradāya*) for the cognition of an object.
fn. 1:B. Like that which is restricted to the cognition of its specific [object]. 2:B. The relation is the same. 3:B. *ca* — added.

If it is argued that it is not the word alone that possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the establishment of the relation, but rather the word together with the traditional transmission (*saṃpradāya*), then what is the use of this succession? Is the word a logical mark because of the tradition, from that the cognition of the relation, and from that the communication of the object—what is the use of this succession?

Why does that very same word, being a mere entity devoid of any real relation and dependent upon tradition, not itself produce the cognition of meaning—such that another relation would have to be postulated?

For this very reason, the postulation of a relation called *śakti* (power) on the grounds that the cognition of meaning cannot otherwise be accounted for is also refuted; because even without such a power, the cognition of meaning is possible through the force of convention (*saṃketa*) alone. Therefore, the claim that "the relation is established by three means of knowledge" is discarded.
[This is] because [the relation] exists [only as a convention].

And that word is observed to be employed by persons with a specific intention—that is, with the intention of conveying a particular meaning—at the time of convention; it is not observed otherwise. That is to say, it is not observed when employed contrary to the intended meaning. By this, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) have been stated. (238)

Thus, through the aforementioned observation and non-observation, it produces the cognition of that object, just like smoke and so forth. This very relationship between word and meaning, known as "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), is indicated by the terms "observation" and "non-observation. Nor do we perceive any capacity for another, ontologically real relationship to produce this cognition here, apart from the aforementioned inseparable connection. Furthermore, we perceive no means of establishing, nor any cause for the establishment, of such a relationship.

Having thus stated the fault in accepting a distinction between the relation and its two relata, he states the fault even in the case of accepting their non-distinction with the words "Now," and so forth. "From those two" means from the two relata; when there is no distinction between the relation and the two relata, then those two—the relata themselves—are merely the word and the object, and there is no such thing as a "relation. If it is argued that the relation will then exist as something neither identical to nor different [from them], he says: "Not from this," and so forth. There is no other ontological possibility for a real entity than these two alternatives: identity or difference.

The explanation begins with "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth. "Difference in form" (*rūpabheda*) means difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). This is because another determination—that is, the determination of a different intrinsic nature—is based upon that [difference]. As for that which is not of a different form, but rather is intended as having that very form—the entity called "relation" (*sambandha*) which is the very nature of the related things—that must be precisely those [related things] themselves; it would be nothing other than the intrinsic nature of the related things. If this is so, how is there the cognition "the relation between these two"? To this he says: "But the distinction of properties (*dharmabheda*) would be merely conceptualized (*parikalpita*)."

By means of the previously mentioned sequence—established through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and based on the distinction between exclusions—that distinction of exclusions is not contradictory even in a single [entity], as it is produced by conceptual construction (*kalpanākṛta*). However, a real distinction (*vastubheda*) is not non-contradictory in one place; rather, it is indeed contradictory. Because multiplicity is impossible for a single [entity] in an ultimate sense, there is no other way for a real entity (*vastu*) than difference and non-difference.
[fn. 1: B. *vacanam*]

(p.429) How could there be [such a relation] for that entity? Because it is characterized by form (*rūpa*) and characterized by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And because this form does not transcend conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since it does not transcend the conceptual constructions of difference and non-difference; for the nature of the entity, which is the very essence of the word’s referent, is distinct [from the word]. It has been stated previously that the connection characterized by the fusion of forms is not real, but is produced solely by conceptual construction.

"Due to a person's habitual practice of conventional usage, even though those two [word and meaning] are not actually mixed, they appear as if mixed; based on that, the determination of their relationship [is established]," and so forth. For a relationship characterized by *śleṣa*—defined as the mutual intermingling of two related things—is not possible in the case of objects that are unjoined or unmixed. He states, beginning with "nor indeed," that for words and meanings, the relationship is a third entity entirely different from the *śleṣa* of their forms. (239)

Since that which is established as a separate entity is independent [of others], how could it be dependent upon a relation? Furthermore, a relation is held to be dependent upon a relation because it resides in two things (*dviṣṭhatvāt*). Nor is it logical for a relation to be a separate entity, because a relation consists in the nature of mutual contact (*paraśleṣarūpatvāt*); thus he says: "How could a substance or a distinct category be the relation of another related thing?
By this, both points desired by the opponent—that a relation, while being a separate entity, is dependent upon the related things and consists in the nature of mutual contact—are refuted.

If it is indeed a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), why is it not dependent on another? To this he says: "For not," and so forth. For that which is already established does not depend on another, because that which is fully accomplished has no further expectations. Since it is independent, it cannot have a connection with anything else. Nor is it logical for a connection to be a distinct entity; for "substance" (*dravya*) is said to be an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and it is spoken of as a distinct category of object (*padārthāntara*). How then could it be a conjunction of two related things belonging to the nature of another?

It could not exist at all; nor does it serve as a cause for conjunction. Why? Because the nature of two related entities is not made "conjoined" by the existence of a third, distinct nature. For a thing that is unjoined—that is, unrelated—cannot become conjoined by means of something called a "relation" which is itself unrelated. If it is argued that it becomes conjoined by means of something already conjoined:

This is not so. Why? Because that very thing called a "relation" cannot be established as a conjunction (*śleṣa*) with those two related entities (*sambandhin*). [The opponent argues: "That relation, once produced, would join those two related entities. To this [the author replies] with the words "If this... and so forth. If the two related entities were joined by a third, distinct entity, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); everything would be joined by some third entity, because there is no distinction [between them]. For there is no difference whatsoever in the fact that both the thing intended to be a relation and any other thing are connected with another distinct entity. (240)

Furthermore: since those phonemes (*varṇa*) which are real are [only] substantially real, they are therefore meaningless; consequently, they are not denoters (*vācaka*), and thus the operation of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakasambandha*) does not occur therein. If it is argued that because words (*pada*) and so forth possess meaning, the operation of the relationship will occur there, he says: "The word and so forth—by the word 'and so forth' (*ādiśabda*), the sentence (*vākya*) is included—is merely imagined (*parikalpita*); it would be the denoter. And since that imagined word or sentence is a non-entity (*avastu*) whose nature is non-substantial, how could there be the operation of a relationship characterized as the signified and the signifier, which is itself a real entity with a substantial nature? It could not occur at all.

The phrase "for it is the designator" (*vācako hi*) and so forth is an explanation. For the designator must possess that [meaning] by means of the factor of expression, namely the cause of utterance known as the "relation. Even though the phonemes (*varṇa*) exist—that is, they are present—they are not designators because each one individually does not convey a meaning, due to the absence of simultaneity (*sāhitya*). Furthermore, because no comprehension of meaning is observed from phonemes uttered by various speakers [at different times], they are not designators.

"Therefore" (*tat*) means that the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) does not exist among those phonemes (*varṇa*). If that relationship were to reside in them—that is, if the relationship were to reside in those expressive phonemes—then it would follow that the relationship's status as an auxiliary to expressiveness (*vācakatvāṅgatva*) would be lost. If it is argued: "The phonemes themselves, when employed by a single speaker in a specific order (*krama-viśeṣa*), that is, in a specific sequence (*ānupūrvī-viśeṣa*), are the signifiers; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply," it has been said:
"In whatever number, of whatever nature, and whichever [phonemes] are involved in the communication of a particular meaning..."
"The phonemes, whose capacities are well-known, are likewise the means of comprehension. (Sphoṭasiddhi 69).
This very point is clarified [by the following]:
"But with respect to the communication of meaning, those [phonemes], being subordinate..."
The sequence [of words] in a literary composition is also intended to have a single author and so forth.
And when a sequence exists based on the identity of the author, the regulating factor for one who employs it is that observation of the sequence previously seen among the elders. (Sphoṭasiddhi 71)

"Just as things that have been observed to possess causal capacity simultaneously are not at all capable [of acting] sequentially, so too things that are capable sequentially would not be able to act simultaneously. (Sphoṭasiddhi 73) fn.1:
B reads *sāmarthyā naiva*.
Furthermore, regarding the communication of meaning:
"There is always an inevitable proximity of something [to the word]; yet, by that much alone, others do not cease to be factors simply because they are remote. (Sphoṭasiddhi 83)
Just as the visarga has no capacity when there is an intervention,
so too other [sounds] have no capacity when there is immediate succession.
(Sphoṭasiddhi 85) And it is not the case that where each individually lacks capacity, all together lack capacity.

"The parts of a chariot (*rathāṅga*) are seen to be capable of being used for carrying [loads] and so forth. (Sphoṭasiddhi 86) [The opponent objects: "In all cases, there is a lack of capacity" [to denote meaning]. [The author] states the refutation with the words beginning with "no" (*na*): This is not so, because the sequence (*krama*) must be either non-different from the phonemes (*varṇa*) or different from them. Regarding the first position—that the sequence is non-different from the phonemes—it follows that because the sequence is non-different from them, it lacks the quality of differentiation (*abhedakatva*), that is, it lacks the quality of distinction (*aviśeṣakatva*). For that which is non-different from something cannot be a differentiator of the nature of that thing. Consequently, [this applies] to the sequence consisting of phonemes (*varṇātmaka*) which possesses that form.

In the word *rasa*, whatever form exists, then in the case of the other sequence *sā* as well, the comprehension of the meaning would be identical, because there is no difference [in the phonemes], just as in the case of the individual letters (*varṇa*). And... (fn. 4:B).

If it is then argued that the sequence is distinct from the phonemes, he says: "Even its being a different entity [is not]. This is because the sequence's status as a different entity from the phonemes will be refuted later. For a sequence is not possible for phonemes produced simultaneously, since such a thing is never perceived. Nor is there a sequence existing as a separate entity for phonemes produced non-simultaneously, because the very nature of non-simultaneous production *is* the form of the sequence. Indeed, when people in the world speak of a sequence, they are speaking precisely of non-simultaneous production.

Therefore, sequence (*krama*) is simply non-simultaneous production. Nor is sequence [a property] of two things produced non-simultaneously, because when one is perceived, the sequence is not perceived; nor is it a property of both, since both do not exist at the same time, and how can there be a property of what does not exist? Therefore, he will state that sequence is said to be the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the prior and posterior entities. And even if sequence consists of a prior and posterior form, syllables nevertheless do not become the cause for the comprehension of meaning through sequence.

Because each [phoneme] individually does not convey the meaning; because there is no simultaneity [among them]; and because it is impossible for those occurring in a fixed sequence to act together simultaneously. [Objection: It might be argued that just as a seed, though not a producer of a sprout when alone, becomes a producer when in proximity to auxiliary factors due to its specific state, so too the phonemes, though individually incapable, become causes for the cognition of meaning when distinguished by a particular sequence (*ānupūrvī*).

That is incorrect. For what difference is there between the utterance of the final phoneme when it is accompanied by other phonemes and when it is uttered alone, such that there would be the presence or absence of the cognition of meaning based on that? [Objection: But surely this very fact—that it is accompanied or unaccompanied—is the difference. [Response: True; however, their "conjunction" (sāhitya) pertains only to the performance of an effect. And they do not exert their causal activity toward the cognition of meaning while they are existing, because each is individually incapable, nor at the time of any other phoneme, because they are non-existent then.
"In that case, this is the distinction: that the perception of the preceding letters has occurred in some instances and not in others.

This also is not tenable; for the perception of the preceding letters, even if it has occurred, cannot affect the final letter because it is non-existent [at that time]. Furthermore, when letters are individually incapable of producing an effect, they remain equally incapable even when combined, just as blind people are unable to see the sun.

By this, the argument beginning with "where there is no capacity individually" and so forth is refuted. For it is only when a specific transformation has occurred in the parts of a chariot that they possess the capacity for carrying loads and such in their state of conjunction; otherwise, as with individual parts, there would be no capacity even in conjunction. Furthermore, there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect among the phonemes by which the preceding phonemes could be capable of the indirect cognition of meaning.

Nor can it be argued that the preceding phonemes possess efficacy through a causal chain because the final phoneme—accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those preceding phonemes—is the cause of the cognition of the meaning. For the impression deposited by the experience of the phonemes serves as the cause for the recollection of those very phonemes, not of the meaning; indeed, an impression deposited by the experience of a cow does not produce a recollection of a horse. Furthermore, the status of being the cause [of the meaning] cannot be established merely because the cognition of the meaning is observed when there is the perception of the final phoneme accompanied by the impressions deposited by the preceding phonemes.

Because there is no cognition of an object in the absence of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). And since convention has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, not the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phoneme, how could phonemes be expressive through a particular sequence? Furthermore, if a single phoneme by itself does not convey an object, it would not do so even when accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), because no difference [in its nature] has arisen. Therefore, how can it be said that one phoneme is capable of conveying an object directly while another is capable only indirectly? As for what is also said:
"Thus, whether they exist simultaneously or are grasped in succession..."
"Therefore, that [simultaneous presence] would be our eternal cause with respect to the cognition of meaning.
(Śloka-vārttika,

Sphoṭa 108) In this way, because the phonemes perceived in succession are eternal and all-pervading, their simultaneous existence in the locus of space is precisely the cause for the comprehension of meaning.

That is incorrect. For it is the word-meaning as it is being perceived that conveys [the cognition], not mere proximity, because that would entail the consequence of conveying the meaning of all words. Furthermore, simultaneity is not perceived among things produced by a single agent, nor is it logical for them to possess eternality and omnipresence, as he will state later; thus, this argument is unsubstantial. As for what is also said:
"Or else, regarding those [words] previously known in sequence through perception, that which is subsequent..."
The cognition of all phonemes is the cause for the cognition of their meaning.
And in that cognition, the simultaneity of the phonemes is perceived; however,
that [simultaneity] need not necessarily exist as something established by direct perception.

The answer "that which is subsequent" refers to a cognition whose object is the entire sequence of phonemes through the reflection upon what precedes and follows; it is the cause for the comprehension of that meaning. The phrase "it would be so" means that the communication of the meaning would occur, or rather, that the communication of the meaning would occur even by another simultaneous cognition.

This too is incorrect, for sequence is dependent upon the speaker, whereas simultaneity is not. Since the cognition of meaning arises from phonemes that exist in a state produced by a speaker, there could be no cognition of meaning through simultaneity. Furthermore, if there were a simultaneous apprehension of phonemes that possess a temporal sequence, it would result in the fallacy of error; nor indeed does simultaneity exist among them, because [otherwise] their permanence would be untenable. "And some say that this cognition is of a variegated nature, having both existent and non-existent phonemes as its object, by which the final phoneme is grasped in each word. (Sphoṭasiddhi 11)

Some say that the cognition by which the final phoneme of each word (*pratipada*) is grasped has the nature of both recollection and direct perception (*smaraṇapratyakṣarūpa*), because its object consists of both proximate and non-proximate phonemes.

That too is incorrect; for it is a contradiction for a single cognition to have the dual nature of being both perceptual and non-perceptual. Nor is direct perception alone capable of having both existent and non-existent phonemes as its object, because that would contradict its nature as having absence as its object. Nor does it have the nature of recollection, because it is not accepted that recollection has a proximate object. For this very reason, the cognition grasping a word or the like would have to have a conceptualized (*kalpita*) object.

Others, however, maintain that when the final phoneme is cognized, the recollection—induced by the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience of the preceding phonemes—is what conveys the meaning across all the phonemes. As it has been said:

"When the final phoneme is cognized, others declare that a simultaneous recollection, produced by all the latent impressions, occurs with respect to all [the phonemes]. If it is asked how there can be a simultaneous recollection of things experienced sequentially, he replies:
"And in this way, for all such objects, there is mental [recollection] for all proponents [of verbal cognition]."
A collective cognition (*samuccaya-jñāna*) is desired [to account for the perception of a word] even though there are successive cognitions [of the individual phonemes].
Therefore, although there is first a cognition of the phonemes by the ear and the mind in succession,
subsequently a simultaneous recollection (*smaraṇa*) occurs.

"Therefore, the linguistic units (*varṇa*) mounted upon that [sphoṭa] are not far from the comprehension of meaning; for that reason, the cognition of meaning from the word is so designated by worldly people. (Ślokavārttika, Sphoṭavāda 102)

This too is incorrect. For [words] convey meaning only when employed by a single agent, and thus they convey meaning only as they exist sequentially. Furthermore, simultaneity is not apprehended among the phonemes that are objects of memory, because they are remembered precisely according to a fixed order. Nor is there a grasping of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phonemes through memory, because, unlike perception, there is no clear manifestation. Moreover, it is impossible for a single [cognition] to possess multiple forms, both clear and unclear.

Because letters, whose nature is not clearly perceived, are apprehended through mere recollection in a form identical to their own internal images as being non-different from external letters, it is said that external letters alone possess the capacity to signify. Furthermore, regarding those letters which are not external, we maintain that words and so forth are merely conceptual constructs based on the determination of external letters within them.

Thus, in the Mīmāṃsaka position, once the signifying capacity of letters is refuted, words and so forth are likewise refuted, because there exists no word or such entity apart from the letters. As it has been said:
"Indeed, no word exists other than the letters."
And there is nothing whatsoever distinct from letters and words.

Now, in order to refute the Grammarians' position that words and so forth exist apart from the phonemes (*varṇa*), he says: "That is non-existent" (*tadasat*). The word "that" (*tat*) is used for the purpose of introduction, or in the sense of "therefore. If the phonemes were not expressive, then something like a word (*pada*) would have to be the expresser; yet such a thing as a word does not exist at all. Why? Because there is a contradiction regarding whether that word is distinct or non-distinct from the phonemes. If it were distinct, it would be perceived separately, provided it were perceptible. Even if it were imperceptible, it would lack expressiveness, because that which is not apprehended cannot function as a signifier. If, on the other hand, it were non-distinct, it would follow—just like the phonemes themselves—that it lacks expressiveness.

Therefore, for this reason: auditory consciousness—which is more acute than the specific sensory consciousnesses that apprehend individual phonemes in succession—is followed by it; that is, it arrives by way of the experience of that [auditory consciousness]. That conceptual cognition whose material cause (*upādāna*) is the homogeneous latent predisposition (*sabhāgavāsanā*), which consists of the capacity for a similar conceptualization, is described as such. This conceptual cognition has the homogeneous latent predisposition as its material cause, and its "delusion of appearance" (*pratibhāsavibhrama*)—the very error of appearance—is the word and the sentence, which appear as a single unit but are in fact false.

This is what is meant: the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising subsequent to the experience of sequentially occurring phonemes determines those phonemes as having a single nature in the form of words and so forth; thus, the conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) of words and the like is purely false. [Objection:

Since the phonemes themselves are experienced as distinct, how can a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) arise that manifests as a single word or the like? [Response: It does indeed arise; therefore, there must be an experience of a single word and so forth among the phonemes.

This is not a fault. For at the time of establishing the convention, the communicator indicates to the other person—precisely that sequence of phonemes which has already been apprehended as having the form of a single word or the like—saying, "This is this word," and so forth. And at that time, a cognition arises in the other person as well, which superimposes the status of a single word upon that sequence of phonemes.

And for that person whose mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has been instilled by the experience of a single form superimposed upon those [sounds] beginning with the first syllable, there arises at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)—upon hearing the sequence of phonemes—a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a single form, such as "this is one word" or "this is one sentence. In this way, for each preceding listener, there occurs a cognition through the superimposition of unity upon the sequences of phonemes received from each preceding speaker; thus, the linguistic usage of words and so forth is beginningless (*anādi*).

Therefore it is said: "The delusion of conceptual appearance, which arises from beginningless homogeneous impressions (*sabhāgavāsanā*), wherein word and sentence appear as a single [entity], is indeed false. This falsity [is established] because distinct phonemes appear in the memory-cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*) in the form of a single word or the like; and because it is impossible for that much [of an entity] to exist, given the contradiction between being both one and many. Now, one might argue: "If the word and so forth were indeed a single entity perceivable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could it be false?"

That is correct. For a word or the like is not a single [unit]. What is the reason? Because it is impossible for it to be grasped sequentially by a cognition that apprehends the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*). For if it were a single entity, it would be grasped all at once by a single cognition; however, a word or the like is not grasped by a single cognition alone. Thus he says: "Not by one," and so forth. That word or the like is not to be grasped by a single cognition. What is the reason? Because words and sentences are grasped according to the sequence of phonemes—that is, through the succession of phonemes.

[The opponent argues: "In that case, a word would consist of a single phoneme (*varṇa*) and would be graspable by a single cognition. To this, he says: "A single phoneme," and so forth. Even at the time of the production of a single phoneme, it is not a single phoneme because it is traversed by multiple cognitions. For instance, when "bhāg" is uttered, the vowel-less *ga* is perceived for the duration of half a mora (*mātrā*), whereas the *ga* with its vowel is perceived for the duration of one full mora. Thus, how can there exist a word consisting of a single phonemic form that could be graspable by a single cognition? Therefore, as it has been said: "One grasps the word in its entirety; even with the slightest effort, the mind perceives the sound that has been uttered."
Or else, one does not perceive the color at all clearly and in its entirety;
nor are the parts of a color ever perceived separately anywhere. (Śloka-vārttika, Sphoṭa 10–11)

That which has been set aside by the aforementioned reasoning—namely, that a phoneme possesses parts—and that there can be no apprehension of successive phonemic parts by a single cognition, because cognitions are momentary.

It might be argued: "The duration of time required for the completion of the phonemes is a single moment (*kṣaṇa*); therefore, the apprehension of the word will occur by means of a single cognition. To this he says: "Of the moment," and so forth. A moment is of such a duration that a single atom (*paramāṇu*) passes over another atom; for a moment is precisely that length of time. Time devoid of further division is logically possible only as the time taken for the passing of a single atom. This is because if one were to accept a moment as being longer than the aforementioned time, [it would no longer be indivisible].

Because it is impossible for a moment (*kṣaṇa*) that possesses divisions and is itself divisible to reach the end of time; therefore, even a single, most subtle phoneme (*varṇa*) is produced over multiple moments. What is the reason? [It is] "aneka... and so forth. A *nimeṣa* (the blink of an eye) in which there is a displacement—that is, a transgression—of many atoms is a *nimeṣa* involving many atoms. Because of its equality in duration with that, even the final, most subtle phoneme, such as the letter 'A', is completed. Therefore, a word whose form consists of a single phoneme is not graspable by a single cognition.

Nor is a single word, consisting of multiple components, graspable by memory. Why? Because memory follows the manner of experience. Just as the experience of the phonemes occurs in a specific sequence, so too does the memory; thus, memory also exists at that same time. This is because its temporal sequence is identical to the sequence of the experience.

This was stated with reference to another type of activity; however, in an activity characterized by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), although there occurs a simultaneous recollection (*smaraṇa*) of phonemes that were experienced sequentially, nevertheless, because no distinction is perceived between the sequence of experience and the sequence of recollection, a single word or the like does not [arise].

Therefore, this is the meaning: the distinction or difference between the sequence of phonemes that appears in experience and the sequence of phonemes that appears in recollection is not perceived; hence, how can it be said that a single word or the like is grasped by a single cognition?

Nor is it even multiple, such as a series of syllables and so forth. What is the reason? Because cognition appears without differentiation. Since the cognition that takes the form of a word or a sentence appears as non-different—that is, as a unity—when a word or a sentence is uttered, people have the thought, "This is one word" or "This is one sentence. Therefore, it is said:
"Due to rapidity and the smallness of the interval, that [cognition] might indeed occur regarding the word 'go'..."

The claim that "in words such as *devadatta*, a clear distinction is perceived" (*Sphoṭasiddhi* 121) is refuted; for it is only after the experience of the individual phonemes that a cognition arises which superimposes a single word, and because the multiplicity of those [phonemes]—that is, the multiplicity of the word and so forth—will be negated later on.

(p.437) Nor is it exclusively manifold, such as a word (*pada*) and so forth. "That" means for that reason: because it appears as both one and many, and because oneness and manifoldness are contradictory and thus incompatible, the word and so forth are not a real entity (*vastu*). Alternatively, the meaning is that those words and so forth are not real entities because they lack the compatibility of being either one or many. What is the reason? Because that real entity cannot transcend these two alternatives. For a real entity must be either of a single nature or of a manifold nature at any given time; it cannot possess both natures simultaneously due to contradiction.

Furthermore, the opponent maintains that the relation (*sambandha*) is a real entity (*vastu*); how then could it have that [relation] as its locus? It would have to have unreal words and sentences as its locus. This is the analysis of the compound: "that word and sentence are the locus of this. What is the reason? Because, due to their non-existence, words and so forth cannot serve as a locus. Thus, in the absence of a locus to be relied upon, the relation would be ungrounded. And being ungrounded, the relation would not be a relation at all, because it lacks dependence upon related terms (*sambandhin*).

Since this is so, therefore the relationship between word and meaning is not innate or non-human-made (*apauruṣeya*); rather, the relationship is indeed human-made (*pauruṣeya*). Why? Because sound—whether produced from the physical movement and so forth that constitute the application of the speaker’s intention, namely the intention to communicate a meaning, as stated according to our own view; or whether it is manifested [from that movement], as stated according to the view of others—is non-deviant with respect to that [meaning].

Since it is non-deviant in the communication of meaning, the relationship of this word is its being an effect of the intention to communicate that meaning; for the word is employed with the intention of communicating meaning. And whether that [intention] results in the production or the manifestation of the word, it is the basis for the non-deviance regarding the communication of meaning—the cause of that non-deviance—and it is human, produced by a person. Thus, the relationship between word and meaning is indeed human-made.

And by that means—that is, by way of the aforementioned relationship—there is no restriction regarding the communication of meaning by words; thus, even if words were not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), that very same deception or inconsistency would persist. The point is that, consequently, the postulation of their non-human origin is entirely futile. (241–242) Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the Vedic sentences are of non-human origin on the basis of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the non-recollection of any authors or composers of the Veda. The particle *kila* is used here to indicate that this [position] is incorrect.

The explanation begins with the words "yāpi" and so forth. [It is argued that] the author of many things is not remembered, yet those things are not for that reason uncreated, such as, for example, old wells and the like. In this way, this "authorlessness" (*apauruṣeyatā*) is illogical due to the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason. Jaimini describes it [as authorlessness] based on the non-remembrance of an author of Vedic sentences. He says: "There are speakers of such a thing even today. What is there to say here? It is simply a pervasive darkness; fie upon it!

For instance, when Jaimini asserts that [the Veda] is not of human origin because its author is not remembered, our minds are moved by both wonder and compassion, wondering how such a lapse in wisdom could have occurred even for him—that is, "with wonder and compassion. It is "with wonder" because even one so learned can exhibit such a play of ignorance; it is "with compassion" because sentient beings are tormented by the tight bonds of ignorance.

In this regard, others who follow contemporary views, such as Kumārila and his followers—who consider themselves investigators—repeat this very thing: "The world has been ruthlessly and mercilessly assailed by that darkness which is so described; fie upon that all-pervading darkness! Here, the expression of reproach (*dhig*) is appropriate for ignorance alone, not for the living being. For what fault is there in the living being, even one who speaks thus, who is deceived regarding the desire for welfare—that is, deceived by the wish to attain what is beneficial—and who is thus deluded?
However, this is merely a fault of ignorance. What, then, is the lapse in wisdom of one who speaks thus?
For this proof is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). (242)

Regarding that, he says "tathā hi" and so forth with reference to the unestablished [reason]. The Buddhists remember the authors of the Veda, such as Aṣṭaka and others; by the word "others," [he refers to] Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, and so forth.
