The Vaiśeṣikas, such as the followers of Kaṇāda, remember Hiraṇyagarbha, Brahmā, as the author of the Veda. Consequently, the non-remembrance of an author is unestablished. And for those Buddhists, that doctrine of remembering the author of the Veda is a false doctrine. If it is argued that this is because of the means of proof [for the author], [the response follows].

What other human-authored word is there now besides the Veda? The meaning is that none whatsoever is human-authored. "In this way" refers to the falsity of the tradition of remembering an author. Clarifying this very point, he says: "In the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth," etc. In works such as the *Kumārasambhava*, since Kālidāsa and others designate themselves or another as the author or composer, they would thus be refuted; they would be rejected. (p. 469)

[The opponent says: "Your statement is false; you are not the authors [of these works]. To this, [the proponent replies: "In that case, there is a contradiction with what has been accepted regarding the authorship of the *Kumārasambhava* and other such texts. [The opponent objects: "If it is argued that the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth are accepted as being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), then how can there be a contradiction? [The proponent replies: "Is it not the case that this very non-remembrance of an author is the very basis for accepting them as non-human (*apauruṣeya*)? That [non-remembrance] exists in the case of the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth according to the reasoning already stated. Therefore, how is it that the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth are desired by you to be of human origin? By what means, then, could there be a contradiction?"

Now, even though the logical principle (*nyāya*) is the same, if it is maintained that there is a sublation of one's own accepted position (*abhyupetabādhana*) when refuting an author in works such as the *Kumārasambhava*, then this very sublation of what has been accepted applies equally to the opponent—the proponent of the Veda—as well, when refuting an author regarding the Vedic sentences. For that proponent of the Veda accepts the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas; therefore, since non-human origin is accepted, there is no fault even in refuting an author.

If it is argued that there is no fault of contradicting what has been accepted (*abhyupetabādhā*), [we reply: from where could this proponent of the Veda have derived such an acceptance? Prior to the investigation into the grounds for accepting the scripture, this very position—that "the Veda is not of human origin"—was an acceptance devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇikā*, i.e., lacking proof). For instance, when the non-human origin of the Veda was accepted, the non-remembrance of an author was stated as the proof; yet, the fault already mentioned immediately follows regarding that point. Thus, this accepted position is without a basis in valid cognition.

Now, if the proponent of the Veda (vedavādī) has accepted the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then why is this Mīmāṃsaka—who grasps things without reason—still dependent upon a means of valid cognition as a proof for certain matters, such as whether something is human or non-human in origin? By stating "that which [is the consideration of] human or non-human origin," he brings himself into the position of one who must present proofs for establishing human or non-human origin. For if one who grasps things without reason were to proceed in that same manner in all cases, why would he trouble himself by introducing means of valid cognition in some instances? This is the collective meaning.

Therefore, since the Vedavādin accepts the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the infinite Veda as his reason, even when he refutes the author of the Veda, there is no contradiction with what he has not accepted (*anabhyupetabādha*), provided that such a contradiction is not desired. Consequently, for anyone other than that Mīmāṃsaka—specifically for one who desires the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth to be authorless—even when he refutes their author, the presence of a contradiction with what he has not accepted is equal; thus, this is not a valid reproach. The meaning is that in that case, the reproach consisting of "a contradiction with what has been accepted" (*abhyupetabādha*) does not exist.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "one who perceives no distinction" (*anatiśayadarśin*): the connection is as follows: "one who perceives no distinction" refers to the Mīmāṃsaka who, while observing the proofs for the non-human origin of sentences—such as "because there is no recollection of an author of such types"—applies them to sentences intended by both human and non-human origins. For instance, just as there is a lack of recollection of an author for many human compositions, so too, in the case of Vedic sentences, the Mīmāṃsaka is one who observes no distinction (*anatiśayadarśī*)—that is, one who sees no difference—in the proof consisting of the non-recollection of an author and so forth.

Alternatively, "effects" refers to the properties of words produced by human effort—such as their conformity to the presence and absence of persons—and so forth. Since he perceives no distinction or superiority in these effects of words within worldly and Vedic sentences alike, yet accepts a specific superiority characterized by non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) in some Vedic word but not in others, there is no means of proof for such an acceptance; thus, the conduct of this proponent of the Veda is either irrational or based on a lack of conviction.

Thus, according to the method described, the reason "because the author is not remembered" is unestablished (*asiddha*). He also states its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) with the words "And they are seen," etc. *Sampradāya* means a tradition of instruction. Those words such as "Vaiśravaṇa at every banyan tree" for which there is an interrupted tradition of practice and an interrupted tradition of human authorship are so designated. By this, he expresses the state of having an unremembered author; [these words] are both produced (*kṛtaka*) and of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).

Therefore, since the non-remembrance of the author also occurs in the case of human speech, this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). [The word] "those" (*tān*) refers to those whose tradition of performance has been interrupted. [The word] "produced" (*kṛtakān*) refers to words. [The opponent claims: "Diligent persons perceive that these were produced by such-and-such a person. This is not so. What is the reason? Because there is no rule regarding the remembrance of an author even when one is diligent. It is not necessarily the case that a diligent person perceives the author; thus, there is only doubt.

Furthermore, even in other cases where words are claimed to be non-human (apauruṣeya), no author is perceived; thus, there is no certainty from any means of valid cognition regarding the perception or non-perception of an author for these [Vedic] words. For, on the one hand, there is no certainty through any authority that an author of this non-human work is indeed perceived; rather, it is based on the instruction of others—an unreliable and invalid source. And because such an instruction is untrustworthy and lacks validity, it is incapable of providing certainty regarding whether an author is perceived or not.

The claim that "the absence of an author for the Vedic sentences is determined because no one is observed to say, 'I have composed these Vedic sentences,'" is also not tenable. This is because we observe people who deny even words they themselves have composed; having composed words themselves, they are seen to repudiate them by saying, "These were not composed by me. In such cases, it is impossible to reach a definitive conclusion or certainty as to whether these [words] were composed by this person or by another. (242) Thus, having refuted the reason "because the author is not remembered," there is yet another proof.

He introduces [the argument] in order to refute it: "The entire study of the Veda is preceded by study under a teacher, because it is designated as 'Vedic study,' just like the study [of the Veda] at present" (verse 1). Regarding the phrase "just like," etc.: just as this contemporary student of the Veda is not capable of speaking or studying this sequence of Vedic phonemes—the sequence of letters and words—without having heard it from another.

Likewise, any other person who is considered the author of the Veda would also require instruction from another, and that person likewise from another; thus, because of this beginninglessness, its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) is established. To this, someone might say: "The same answer applies to such an arguer as was stated regarding the point that 'the author is not remembered'. [To this we reply: Even if non-human origin were established in the manner just described, would it then follow that every human sentence is also non-human?

This is because the study of any other instance of the *Kumārasambhava* is also established as being beginningless by virtue of its being preceded by prior study. If it is argued that establishing this [beginninglessness] results in the contradiction of one's own accepted tenets (*abhyupetabādha*), we reply: surely all of this—including the statement "this very [fact] is a constituent of the accepted tenet" (*abhyupagamāṅga*)—must be stated. It is precisely for the sake of summarizing this that the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) has been employed. (242–243) fn. 1: Ślokavārttika, Vākya, 366.

Demonstrating the very same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says: "For instance," and so forth. Or, another work composed by a person, such as the *Kumārasambhava* and others, [is cited]. "Apart from tradition" means without the instruction of others; no such work has ever been seen to have been uttered by other individuals. For that reason—since that too is a work other than the Veda—why is it not likewise inferred to be authorless (*apauruṣeya*)?

He explains with the words beginning "not indeed" (*na khalu*). Indeed, there is no other ground for establishing the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) [of the Veda] than the inability of people today to recite it without instruction; for it is not the case that one is able to recite this [Veda] without the instruction of another. Thus, the non-human origin of the Vedic sentences is intended [as a proof]. And that inability to recite without instruction is the same in other cases as well—those accepted as being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*)—composed by some single person for another student. (p. 442)

Regarding the phrase “following that” (*tadanusāriṇā*): that which follows [the argument] as a proof for non-authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) because of the inability to recite the instruction [of the Veda] implies that every word—whether worldly or Vedic—is likewise to be inferred as having an author. Or rather, no [Vedic word] is [different], because there is no distinction [between them]. This is because that worldly sentence is not established as being thus, i.e., as non-authored (*apauruṣeya*), and so forth. By the word “etc. (*ādi*), the contradiction with what is accepted (*abhyupetabādha*) is included. Regarding that, it was stated immediately after: “Because the desired [conclusion] depends on that, because it depends on the proof of non-authorship,” and so on. (243–244) fn. 2: *sādhanatvāt* etc.

Moreover: Whatever belongs to a certain class and is of the same genus as a particular substance—because it has been established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that it arises from that cause—it is understood that another thing, even if its cause is unobserved, does not arise from that [same] cause provided it is not distinguished by belonging to that same class. How so? Like fire and wood. Just as one fire is observed to arise from fuel and the like, so too another fire of an identical nature—even if its cause is unobserved—is understood to have that very same cause.
By this, he states the sublation of the thesis (*pratijñābādha*) by inference (*anumāna*) in the proof of the Veda’s lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*).
fn. 3: B. *°torbhavatī°*

He explains by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*). [The term] "causeless" (*ahetuka*) does not apply because a cause is not observed; for even those things whose causes are unobserved—this is the analysis of the compound meaning "those for whom no cause is seen"—even such entities, while existing, experience non-difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) with other things whose causes are observed, and thus they are of a similar form. By the phrase "of such a kind," those things possessing identical causes are inferred. This is the collective meaning here: by means of worldly speech, Vedic speech as well would either have a person as its cause, just like worldly speech, or else nothing at all [would be caused].

Now, even if the nature of the cause—that is, the causal essence—is absent, if it is nevertheless maintained by the proponent of Vedic speech that its form remains unceased—a form identical to the term "human cause"—then there is a transgression of the property of an effect. For this is the property of an effect: that it ceases when its cause ceases. But if, despite the cessation of the person, a human form were to exist within the Vedic [words], then the property of an effect would have been overstepped by that [proposition].

Consequently, because there would be a deviation from the properties of what is produced by an agent (*kāryadharma*), no speech whatsoever could originate from a person; thus, no worldly word could be designated as such on the grounds of its being of human origin. Alternatively, a specific characteristic of human compositions must be shown that distinguishes them from the Vedic, such that this specific characteristic would follow upon the cause called "the person. By means of such a distinction, the desired non-human origin of the Veda and the undesired [human origin] of the worldly would not be subject to the reversal of what was intended.

Accordingly, there would be either human authorship or lack of human authorship [respectively]. However, it has been stated that there is no difference whatsoever in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of worldly and Vedic [utterances];
therefore, [the distinction you propose] could not exist.

Furthermore, even when the nature of the cause known as "person" (puruṣa) ceases, there is no cessation [of the Vedic sentences], because the genitive and locative cases are non-different—just as one says "the branch in the tree" or "the branch of the tree. If it is accepted that Vedic sentences are identical in form to human sentences due to their lack of distinction, then that difference between those [Vedic] sentences and worldly sentences—a distinction created by a person—would be accidental, meaning it would be without a cause; for that distinction would exist in the Vedic sentences even in the absence of a person.

And thus, it would not cease anywhere, such as in space and so forth. Nor is this the case; therefore, that which has a certain nature produced from something—this is the analysis of the compound *yasmājjanma yasya* ("that from which the birth of which [occurs]")—is seen, even when its cause is unobserved, as being non-distinct (*avibhajyamāna*) elsewhere. That is to say, while not being separated from the observed effect that serves as its cause, it attains the status of being that effect. Being so, it does not, by its own nature (*svātmanā*), transcend the status of being that effect in its own form (*svena rūpeṇa*). What is it like? Like fire and fuel (*agnīndhanavat*). Fire and fuel together constitute "fire-and-fuel" (*agnīndhana*); it is like that, similar to that.

Just as fire, even when its cause is not perceived, does not transcend the state of being an effect of fuel because it is experienced as non-different from the fire whose cause—fuel—is perceived, so too is it here. (244–245) In this context, while this principle is established, those reasons that are elaborated and set forth at length to prove the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) for both worldly and Vedic sentences, without demonstrating the difference between them, are as follows: "Because there is no recollection of an author," and so forth.
The study of the Veda is preceded by the study under a teacher,
because it is designated as the "study of the Veda," just like the study [of the Veda] nowadays. (Vākya° 366) The past and future times are devoid of an author of the Veda.
Because it is time; just as, for example, present time is perceived.
It should be understood that Brahmā and others are not the authors of the Vedas, because of reasons such as their being human beings, just like ordinary men. (Ślokavārttika, *Autpattikasūtra* 109)

All those reasons are fallacious, being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because of the observation of a commonality of effect; for a commonality identical to that found in words produced by human effort is observed in Vedic words as well.
[Question: What is the reason? [Answer: He says "just as," etc., to explain why they are inconclusive.

Or rather, regarding the phrase "in that case": in the formal argument, "Whatever study of the Veda is such, it is preceded by a prior study of the Veda," one does not demonstrate a distinction—that is, one does not show the difference from a person devoid of the capacity for Vedic action. Now, by merely showing the general nature of the effect characterized as "Vedic study"—namely, that "the present study of the Veda is preceded by a prior study of the Veda, and so too was it at other times"—all such types of reasons are elaborated; yet all of them are fallacious (*vyabhicārin*).

Just as even a fire produced by a traveler, because its cause is unperceived, is preceded by another flame and not preceded by the friction of wood—why? Because it is like a traveler’s fire; what is it like? It is like a fire that is seen to arise from another flame.

"How so? and so forth. This is because, by relying on the capacity for arising from a flame—meaning, by relying on the capacity for arising from the proximity of a flame—the friction of the fire-sticks used by a traveler is rejected as being the cause of the fire. What is the reason? For if this fire could exist without a flame, then it would also exist "here," meaning even at the location of the traveler's fire which was preceded by a flame, it would exist even in the absence of a flame. In that case, an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) is asserted regarding this proof.

How [could there be] a contradiction between the production of a flame and its production from something else? That is, the production from the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇi*)—since these two productions belong to the same generality of fire (*agni-sāmānya*), they are mutually neither sublated nor sublaters. For what contradiction is there here in that there might be fire which is not preceded by another flame? This being so, the nature of fire as originating from a flame would exist otherwise as well; it could also arise from the friction of fire-sticks.

Thus, because two things possessing such characteristics—one arising from a flame and the other not—can both occur in a single object, namely fire in general, it is suspected that there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [The suspicion is: "That fire of a traveler, or something else such as Vedic study, might be restricted to one [category]—that is, the fire of a traveler would necessarily be preceded by a flame, while Vedic study would necessarily be preceded by Vedic study; this would not be the case. For it is possible that there could be Vedic study that is not preceded by Vedic study, and likewise a fire of a traveler that is not preceded by a flame, since there is no contradiction [between these possibilities].
fn. 1:B. "It might be" (syāt). *araṇi*°. 2:B. abandoned (*tyaktaḥ*). 3:B. the study of the Vedas and so forth (*vedādhyayanādiḥ*).

One might object: "Since that which arises from a flame is not the same as that which arises from the friction of fire-sticks, how is there no contradiction? To this he says: "That too," and so forth. That [fire]—which possesses two mutually exclusive and contradictory properties characterized by arising from a flame and arising from the friction of fire-sticks—is said to be non-contradictory with respect to the general category of "substance" (*vastusāmānya*). It is not said to be non-contradictory with respect to a specific instance of fire (*vahniviśeṣa*) that is distinguished by its particular state, whether it be produced from a flame or produced from the friction of fire-sticks.

But this is precisely the opposite. Why? Because for a partless self (*ātman*), whose nature is indivisible, there is a contradiction between being that [cause] and not being that [cause]. For in the case of the arising of a flame, its being preceded by a flame and its not being preceded by one are contradictory; and in the case of the arising from fire-drills, its being preceded by the drills and its not being preceded by them are contradictory. Even though there is a commonality in the fire of travelers, both [possibilities] are contradictory, as he says: "And not," etc.

Regarding the relationship of sublation and sublated between two fires produced from flames—one produced from the friction of kindling wood and the other a common traveler’s fire—the reason is this: for that common traveler’s fire, there is no non-connection with its arising from a flame, meaning it does not exist apart from the production of a flame. This means that while it exists even through the friction of kindling wood, it is apart from the production of a flame. However, such [fire] is one produced from a flame; not every fire is so without distinction.

What is the reason? Because, in the case of fire—which is differentiated by its various causes—it is impossible to deny a specific distinction, namely, the exclusion of the particularity produced by the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇi*). For there exists a particularity produced by the fire-sticks in that fire, and there is no rule that such fire must remain in that same state; there is no necessity regarding the state characterized by being produced from a flame. [fn. 4:B. *rūpaṃ* for *vanhe*; 5:B. *agnisāmānya* added; 6:B. *raṇi* for *araṇi*; 7:B. Therefore, he says:]

8:B. Existence. 9:B. Flame—omitted. 10:B. "That which is impossible, because of its absence, even from the friction of fire-sticks"—added. 11:B. "Even one who has seen such a thing, another [fire] produced from a flame"—added.
As for what was also said: "If the first fire of a traveler could exist without a flame, it would also exist elsewhere, even in a place devoid of flames."

To this it is replied: It is indeed possible. If that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by the friction of fire-sticks, by which that traveler’s fire comes into being, were present; or if, having demonstrated the possibility of that causal complex, one were to state that in its absence there is an absence of fire; or if, in a place where the aforementioned causal complex is possible, one were to point out a flame—then indeed fire would necessarily be preceded by a flame. But this is not the case. Therefore, since not every traveler’s fire is preceded by a flame, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Reply: In another case, even in a place devoid of flames, there certainly exists the fire of a traveler.

Therefore, the fact that the study of one person who lacks the power of performing the Vedic rites is preceded by another—that is, preceded by a teacher—is not observed as being true for all cases, including that of Hiraṇyagarbha and others; thus, it does not prove that every instance of study is necessarily preceded by another. Why? Because there is no possibility of a study occurring otherwise, namely, without being preceded by another; the meaning is that a study composed by oneself would be impossible.

Because the capacity for composing the Vedas is possible for those such as Hiraṇyagarbha; whereas for one who is currently devoid of such capacity—namely, a person like us who is unable to compose the Veda on his own—the phrase "devoid of the intuition regarding that activity" means being devoid of the intellect capable of producing the Veda. On the grounds that the study of such a person must likewise be preceded by another instance of study.

"Of such a kind" refers precisely to that which is devoid of the capacity for cognition or action; thus, the statement must be understood as preceded by another study, and not without qualification. However, since study may occur through one's own effort—given the possibility of human excellence—and thus possesses the potential for distinction, the claim that "all study whatsoever is preceded by another study" does not sustain its shadow [i.e., it fails], because the pervasion is unestablished and the argument is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). This is because it fails to prove the intended probandum.

"How so? and so forth asks the opponent. How is it possible for those outside the Veda to study [the scripture] after having composed it themselves? "Yāvatā" means "when. Even for those persons who are considered to be the authors of the Veda, there is an incapacity for the composition of the Veda because they are human beings, etc., just like contemporary persons.

To this, the Master replies: "In this case as well. That is, even in this application [of the argument], there is no observation of any contradiction between the capacity for composing the Veda and the person; that is, between the capacity to compose the Veda and the person [Brahmā and others]. Therefore, the fact of being a person, stated as a reason in the case of Brahmā and others, does not remove their capacity to compose the Veda, because it is not contradictory. Consequently, this is not an "application of non-contradictory proof" (*aviruddha-vidhi*). An application of non-perception (*anupalabdhi-prayoga*) in which there is a proof of something non-contradictory is of such a nature that it is not a means of valid cognition (*agamaka*).

He asks, "How is there an absence of contradiction? and replies with the words beginning "For not... [na hi...]. Regarding Brahman and other such beings who are beyond the senses and entirely imperceptible, there is no perception of a contradiction characterized by non-coexistence with the capacity for composing the Veda; this is precisely because they are beyond the senses. Nor is there a perception of a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion, because capacity and incapacity, as well as being a person and not being a person, are mutually contradictory.

The argument is not: "That person who is a human being is incapable of composing the Veda, just like a person of the present day"—for this formulation differs from the previous formulation, namely: "Whatever study of the Veda there is, it is preceded by [prior] study of the Veda, just like the study of the Veda by people of the present day. Therefore, the intention is that the inclusion of both [premises] is indeed redundant. Furthermore, as for what is said: "If persons of the past were capable of composing and then studying the Veda themselves, then persons of the present day would also be so."

To this it is replied: This [argument] which was just stated would hold true if there were no distinction among persons. However, that absence of distinction among persons is difficult to establish and its proof is impossible, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) [to the contrary]. Therefore, even in the proof [stated as]: "Where one person lacks capacity, all persons lack capacity, because they are persons (*puruṣatvāt*)," the logical mark (*liṅga*), namely "personhood," is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*), just like "being a student" and so forth mentioned previously. What is the reason?

Even in the case of works such as the *Mahābhārata*, which are accepted as being of human origin, although contemporary persons lack the capacity [to compose them], the power of some extraordinary person such as Vyāsa is nonetheless established.

Therefore, for one who discriminates causes—thereby removing the operation of the palate and other organs as the cause of Vedic utterances—one must demonstrate a difference in nature (*svabhāvabheda*) among words, whether worldly or Vedic, with respect to their objects. Of what kind are these? They are those produced from that and not produced from that; that is, among those whose causes are the palate and so forth, and those whose causes are not such. One must demonstrate this diversity of nature: that the nature of those caused by the palate and so forth is of one kind, while the nature of those not caused by them is of another kind. Thus, the plurality of natures must be shown.

By means of which [distinction] does the state of being produced from that or not produced from that arise through differentiation? In the absence of that—namely, the absence of a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—everything would be of that same nature. Consequently, every word would either be human-made (*pauruṣeya*) or else no worldly word at all would exist.

Now, one might argue: "There certainly is a difference in intrinsic nature between those two. To this he says: "And here," etc. Here, in this world, we do not perceive any difference in intrinsic nature between worldly and Vedic sentences.

In the absence of that difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) between those two types of sentences—worldly and Vedic—since one observes only their commonality, namely the identical form characterized by the sequence of phonemes, a person who, while discerning some property of a single sentence (whether worldly or Vedic) and attempting to establish its status as either human-authored (*pauruṣeya*) or authorless (*apauruṣeya*) through such a distinction, is addressed with the charge of "speaking with fallibility" (*vyabhicāravāda*). That is to say, he is so called because he is a person whose speech is suspected of being fallacious. By whom is this charge made?

By that [scripture] which possesses that very nature—by that general characteristic consisting of the arrangement of phonemes and words found in both worldly and Vedic sentences—one who asserts the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda, which possesses properties equal to those of human speech, is shown to be fallacious; such is the meaning. Now, the opponent thinks: "Surely there exists a distinction between the Veda and non-Veda characterized by identity and difference, namely the definition of 'Veda' and 'non-Veda. Therefore, due to this distinction, worldly and Vedic speech will respectively possess the properties of being authored and being authorless."

The Teacher says: "True. But surely such a distinction between those two [the worldly and the Vedic] establishes their being human-authored and not human-authored, because this distinction exists not only between these two—the worldly and the Vedic—but rather also between the *Ḍiṇḍika Purāṇa* and other Purāṇas. There is such a distinction even between the Purāṇa composed by the *Ḍiṇḍikas*, who were naked teachers (*nagnācāryas*), and other Purāṇas.

Nor does a difference in names—a distinction of terminology devised by convention to illuminate the differences in its own internal systems for the sake of its own usage—contradict the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda merely on that account. What is the reason? Because otherwise, the same consequence of non-human origin would apply to other Purāṇas as well, since a difference in names exists among the Purāṇas other than the *Ḍiṇḍika*.

If, however, men were unable to produce such an arrangement of phonemes and words as is seen in Vedic sentences, or if one who has not established a linguistic convention could distinguish—merely upon hearing—an arrangement of phonemes and words that has been produced or completed, thinking, "This was preceded by a person," then it would be evident that the Veda is authorless (*apauruṣeya*). Since he does not distinguish that arrangement, how could the Veda be authorless?

The opponent begins with "nanu" and so forth. We shall examine later that even mantras are indeed composed by persons. Furthermore, what is called a "mantra" is not something entirely distinct; rather, it is as follows: truth (*satya*) is the description of things as they actually are; austerity (*tapas*) is the subduing of the senses and the mind; those persons who possess the power (*prabhāva*)—namely, the capacity such as paralyzing poison and so on—derived from these two are [called] such [mantras].

For those men possessed of the power of truth and austerity, that very [power] which accomplishes their desired object is the mantra. That definition of a mantra is indeed observed even today among certain persons. What is the reason? Because we observe the capacity for paralyzing poison, fire, and so forth, as well as the impairment of their efficacy, through the power of one's own truthful resolve (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).

Likewise, even today, certain Śabaras who abide by their own observances are indeed able to compose mantras due to a specific cause—the possession of the power to remove poison and so forth. This refers to those outside the Vedic tradition (*avaidika*), that is, others besides the Vedas, such as the Buddhists and others; by the word "and others" (*ādi*), the ritual manuals of mantras (*mantrakalpa*) of the Ārhats, Gāruḍas, Māheśvaras, and so forth are included. This is because we observe both mantras and ritual manuals of mantras. Mantras are the syllables of knowledge (*vidyākṣara*); the instructional teachings on the methods for accomplishing them are the ritual manuals of mantras (*mantrakalpa*).
And because those ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*) of the Buddhists and others are "human-made"— that is, produced by persons—
therefore there is no difference in nature between the worldly [texts] and the Vedic ones.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth, the opponent [argues]: Even in that case—namely, even when the ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*) of the Buddhists and others are assumed to be authorless (*apauruṣeya*)—how could every sentence that is authorless be non-false? Rather, it might even have a false meaning. He makes this very point with the words "tathā hi" and so forth. In the Buddhist ritual manual, things such as sexual intercourse and the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*), as well as falsehood and so forth (indicated by the word "etc."), are described as causes for the lack of prosperity (*anabhyudaya*) and causes of suffering.

In other non-Buddhist mantra-calculation systems (*mantrakalpa*), however, those very same acts such as *kiṃsā* and so forth are described as causes for worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). If all mantra-calculation systems were indeed of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*), then how could these two mutually contradictory statements be true within a single non-human source?

It might be argued: "In the Buddhist ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*), is there some entirely different and unestablished meaning for words such as *kiṃsā* that is not contradicted by the Vedic ritual manuals? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth. That is to say, when another meaning is postulated in the Buddhist ritual manuals that differs from the well-established meaning.

Since the postulation of a different meaning is equally applicable elsewhere—in non-Buddhist Vedic mantra-rituals—there would be no determination of meaning because such alternative meanings can be postulated for all mantra-rituals. Consequently, there would be no comprehension or performance of the meaning established by them in any case. Thus, due to the lack of certainty regarding the meaning and the resulting absence of performance, even a sentence that is not of human origin (apauruṣeya) would be useless with respect to human goals.

If it is argued that Buddhist and other [non-Vedic] mantras do not possess the nature of mantras at all, he says: "Regarding the non-mantra-status of Buddhist and other [mantras]. Therefore, even elsewhere—in Vedic mantras other than those Buddhist and other mantras—one must undergo the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (*kośapāna*) in order to establish their status as mantras; for there is no such thing as a specific individual instance [that would serve as a definitive criterion]. Furthermore, this claim that Buddhist and other [mantras] are not mantras contradicts what is observed. For indeed, even among Buddhists, mantras are seen being employed by those performing acts involving poison and the like, such as the administration of poisonous rites.

Therefore, in that regard, the claim that the Buddhist and other mantra-collections lack the status of *mantra* is also refuted; for even Vedic statements are established as *mantras* by virtue of their efficacy in performing rites such as the neutralization of poison. Nor is it logical to conclude that a Vedic sentence is non-human (apauruṣeya) merely because it possesses excellence over worldly speech due to its connection with powers such as the immobilization of poison.

For instance, a *mudrā* is a particular arrangement of the fingers of the hand; a *maṇḍala* is a specific configuration of deities and so forth; and *dhyāna* is the contemplation of the forms of deities and so forth. By means of these—which are non-syllabic and lack the nature of sound—actions characterized by the removal of poison and the like are performed. Yet, it is not logical that those *mudrās*, *maṇḍalas*, and *dhyānas* should be non-human (apauruṣeya). It might be argued: "The capacity for action belongs to men only in respect of the *mudrās* and so forth, but not in respect of mantras consisting of sequences of phonemes."

That is not so. Because, given that those [actions] such as sealing and so forth are possible, what obstacle would there be for men who possess truthfulness and the like in the composition of syllables? Since there is no distinction [between them], nothing whatsoever is impossible for these men to perform. What obstacle would there be for men, since there is no distinction? Therefore, nothing is impossible for these men to do, by virtue of which one might perceive some excellence produced by a person and thereby postulate a difference in nature between worldly and Vedic [words].

If both the Buddhist and non-Buddhist ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*) were of human origin and derived from truth—meaning they arose from a person who speaks unerringly—then how is it logical that these very same Buddhist and non-Buddhist ritual manuals, which are mutually contradictory, should both be derived from truth? For in one [the Buddhist], acts such as violence are shown to be causes for the absence of prosperity (*anabhyudaya*), while in the other, they are shown to be causes for prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

He refutes this with the words beginning with "no," and so forth: "Indeed, it is not the case that in all instances those two types of mantra and ritual procedure (*mantrakalpa*) originate from truth (*satya*), such that this contradiction would arise. Rather, those two types of mantra and ritual procedure are also characterized by the promise (*pratijñā*) of a person endowed with power (*prabhāva*). A mantra and ritual procedure are also of the nature of a promise made by a powerful person, such as: 'I shall accomplish for that person who practices this arrangement of syllables and words and performs its prescribed method the purpose exactly as promised.'"

Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that even one who speaks otherwise might perform mantra-rituals endowed with power (*prabhāva*). He [the opponent] asks: "Since truth (*satya*) is absent, from where does that power come? He replies: That power may also arise from specific attainments (*gati*) and accomplishments (*siddhi*). Through merit (*puṇya*), such a specific attainment is acquired; it is a specific accomplishment of mantra, embraced by deities and the like, by which such power comes to be.

If mantras were of human origin, then why would not all men—being human—be creators of mantras? Yet they do not create them. Therefore, the intention [of the opponent] is that even those men who are desired [as potential authors] did not compose the mantras.

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies with the words "That," and so forth: "Because of the deficiency in those mantras of the means for their performance—namely truth, asceticism, power, and so on—not all men are creators of mantras.
However, if men were endowed with such causes of mantras as truth, asceticism, and the like, then they would certainly produce mantras."

Furthermore, since one might argue that a person creates poetry because they possess the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) for its production, then by virtue of the commonality of being human, every person—even one devoid of such creative intuition—should be a creator of poetry. Alternatively, if [the lack of intuition] prevents someone from creating it, then no one else should be able to do so either, just like a person incapable of composing poetry. This is an unprecedented argument; the meaning is that it is inconclusive (*vyabhicāriṇī*).

The opponent says: "Truth" and so forth. Persons who are deficient in the means for the performance of mantra-rites do not perform those mantras. However, we do not perceive such completeness of the means for mantra-rites—namely truth and the rest—in any person whatsoever, because all persons possess identical characteristics.

"It has been stated," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). To this objection, the following answer has been stated. What was stated? "There is no such thing as a mantra," and so forth. The term "vacana" (speech) and "samaya" (convention) form a *dvandva* compound. Because speech accomplishes the desired objects for persons possessing truthfulness and other virtues, and likewise because of the convention characterized by the pledges (*pratijñā*) of persons endowed with truthfulness and the like, there is nothing else whatsoever called a "mantra. Furthermore, those means for accomplishing mantra-rites—characterized by specific [powers] such as truthfulness, austerity, movement, and supernatural success (*siddhi*)—are observed only in certain individuals.

It might be argued as follows: whatever person is devoid of the means for performing mantra-rites, such as a common street-pedestrian, and this person intended as a "mantra-maker" is also a person; therefore, all persons are devoid of those means for performing mantra-rites. Since there is no contradiction between being a person and the possibility of possessing those means for performing mantra-rites, there is no definitive conclusion—that is, no certainty.

If it is argued that the determination of the self’s nature occurs precisely because the nature of the means for accomplishing mantra-rites is not perceived, he says: “And not,” and so forth. This means that regarding those things whose nature transcends the senses (*atikṣasvabhāveṣu*), that is, those which are absolutely beyond perception; non-perception is not a cause for determining their non-existence. If it is argued that because the means for accomplishing mantra-rites—such as memory and so on—are not perceived within oneself, their absence is determined elsewhere as well, he says: “And not,” and so forth. Memory (*smṛti*) refers to the recollection of past lives and the like.

The awakening to the minds of others is *mati*; the vision of the true nature of things regarding those not previously seen is *prativedha*; truthfulness is the state of speaking without deviation; and power is sovereign influence. These are the causes of the mantras, and they exist in all [beings]. They exist within the mental continua of all persons; therefore, one should not reject them elsewhere simply because they have not been perceived within oneself.

Now he states that mindfulness and the other qualities occur only in certain individuals—beginning with the words "the means for those" (*tatsādhanam*). The "means" (*sādhana*) for those aforementioned qualities such as mindfulness is their cause of production; the "transmission" (*saṃpradāya*) of that is its instruction. Its "distinction" (*bheda*) or particularity is that it occurs only in a certain scripture (*āgama*), not everywhere. Similarly, the means for achieving other qualities would also exist; they would occur only in certain individuals. "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is synonymous with "means" (*sādhana*).

The other qualities in the form of memory and so forth, which are the effects of the causes such as memory, and their means of accomplishment—that is, their production—would occur only in a particular person through the practice of the causes of memory and so forth. If it is asked, "If memory and so forth were a means [of perceiving another], why is it not seen?", he says: "Nor even... and so on. Even though it exists—that is, is present—the mental quality residing in another continuum cannot be perceived by a person who is merely a witness.

For this very reason, there is no denial or rejection of the mental quality (*manoguṇa*) belonging to another continuum (*santānāntara*), which is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). Nor is there any subverting proof (*bādhaka*) that could obstruct the arising of a mental quality intended to arise in persons, such that one could conclude that no one possesses a mental quality superior to other qualities. If it is argued that the property of "being a person" (*puruṣatva*) and so forth is itself the subverting proof, we say no. Why? Because that quality, which belongs to another continuum and is the object of negation, is not perceived by mere persons.

Because the relationship of sublated and sublater is not established by means of properties such as "being a human being," there is no rejection [of the opponent's position] on the grounds that it is not a sublater.

By this aforementioned [argument], the negation of all cognition of every object is refuted. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the refutations of those who claim to be free from passion (*vītarāga*) and so forth are described as having been answered.

Just as there is no refutation of omniscience and such qualities by means of the mark of being a speaker and so forth, so too in that case, the logical principle is appropriate for the refutation of freedom from passion and so forth: "A person of such a kind is not endowed with qualities such as freedom from passion. Of what sort is he? He is one for whom there exists no tradition of the means for achieving those [qualities]; that is, the analysis of the compound is: "one whose tradition of the means for achieving those—namely, the tradition of the means for achieving freedom from passion and so forth—is non-existent."

The meaning is that the logical principle is this: one who lacks the means of proof, such as the demonstration of being free from passion (*vītarāga*), cannot indeed be [established as] free from passion and so forth. Nor is it correct to say, "That which is not of that nature is not a perceived indicator. It is also improper to state that one whose indicator—such as freedom from passion—is unperceived, yet is the indicator itself, becomes by mere observation something "not of that nature," meaning its nature is devoid of qualities such as freedom from passion. For it is not logically tenable that the non-existence of the indicated object follows merely from the non-perception of the indicator. Why is that?

For even among certain things that exist, it is possible for an effect that serves as a mark [of their existence] not to be produced; and even if such an effect were produced by those supersensible entities, it would still be impossible to perceive—due to the remoteness of their nature—that "this is their effect. Therefore, it remains established that the certainty that the deficiency of mantras, rituals, or means belongs to one person applies equally to everyone is impossible.

Since this is so, therefore, if one were to prove that "study is preceded by another study, just like other studies," the reason (*liṅga*) "because it is a study" would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). This is because in the case of the study of the *Bhārata* and similar works, there exists the quality of being a study of something of human origin.

There is no fault because of the qualification by "Veda. The intention is that while mere study may deviate [from being preceded by another study], study qualified by "Veda" does not. But what [is this distinction]? This is the question posed by the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*). What excellence does the study of the Veda possess such that it could not be studied otherwise—that is, by one who has composed it himself? There is no excellence at all. Therefore, since there is no contradiction in the possibility that there might be study of the Veda without it being preceded by [another] study, that same deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains.

For the qualification of "being a Veda" is not incompatible with the counter-example (vipakṣa), namely, "not being preceded by another recitation. Therefore, it does not exclude the reason from that counter-example. Why? Because there is no contradiction between "being a Veda" and "not being preceded by another recitation," since [the former] is indeed studied [in this way]. This has already been answered: because the same consequence would apply to the study of the *Mahābhārata* as well; for even that is studied nowadays only through the instruction of others.

The study of that [Veda] as well, being preceded by another study, would—like the Veda itself—be authorless (*apauruṣeya*), according to what you accept. If it is argued that "the study of the Veda is necessarily preceded by the study of the Veda because no author is observed," this too has already been refuted and rejected previously. For we do see cases where the tradition of practice has been interrupted, as shown by the argument beginning with "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and so forth. Furthermore, since mere non-observation does not establish non-existence, there is indeed a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason "because it is the study of the Veda."

Therefore, the qualification "being a Veda" does not possess any excellence for the reason of study; it does not confer any distinction, because it does not exclude [the reason] from the counter-example due to the absence of contradiction with the counter-example. Even though it is employed, the qualification is equivalent to being unemployed.

Furthermore, even if the reason is qualified by the Veda—namely, that "whatever study of the Veda there is, all of that is preceded by another study"—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established. This is because, in the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) for the contrary case, it cannot be proven that every study of the Veda is of such a nature [as being preceded by another], and thus its being preceded by another study remains unestablished.

Just as it is observed that for one who is unable to perform the study themselves, there is another cause for that study—namely, the study performed by another—it would follow that [the study] is necessarily preceded by another's study. For one who is unable to study having performed it themselves, whatever study they do undertake is observed to have a specific result characterized by proficiency and so forth; this is caused by that [other person], meaning it is caused by a study preceded by another. By the abandonment of that [specificity], that is, by the abandonment of the observed distinction in the study which has proficiency and so forth as its result, or rather, by the fact that it is caused by that, meaning it is caused by [their own] capacity.

When a specific instance has been observed and understood—namely, that one who has personally performed the act characterized by Vedic study later abandons that specific instance and thereby grasps the general property of "Vedic study"—then to claim that all Vedic study, whether by a capable person or an incapable one, must be preceded by another instance of Vedic study because it possesses the general property of being Vedic study, is nothing but fallacious. How so? It is like the proof of fire; for example, [the fallacy of] "being a white substance" when attempting to prove the existence of fire.

The meaning is as follows: just as when smoke produced by fire is observed to have a specific shade of pale-yellow (*pāṇḍu*), the general property of being a pale substance (*pāṇḍudravyasāmānya*)—if taken while discarding that specific shade—becomes deviant (*vyabhicārin*) regarding the proof of fire; so it is with this. By this demonstration of deviance just mentioned, [the arguments concerning] speech and so forth are refuted. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities such as being a human being (*puruṣatva*) are included. Just as these too are deviant: in what respect? In proving passion and the like; that is, in the establishment of passion and so forth. For if one discards the specific kind of speech observed to be produced by passion and the like, the general property of being a speaker (*vaktṛtvasāmānya*) is deviant.

Even granting that it might be so, he says: "In any case, by proceeding in this manner, the beginninglessness of the Veda would be established; that is, its mere lack of a beginning would be established. However, its non-dependence on a person [would not follow], and thus its authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) would not be established."

Now, if you maintain that it is "not of human origin" (*apauruṣeya*) merely because of its lack of a human author, then other worldly conventions would also be non-human by virtue of their beginningless continuity. For it is indeed a person who, having inferred for himself or devised [the convention], learns it; or else, having heard it from another, learns it. These sounds do not themselves resound or manifest their own nature while those persons have their organs unengaged and their palates and so forth inactive. If they were to resound by themselves, on account of that self-resounding, they might be considered non-human.

However, because these Vedic words are articulated through human activity, they possess the very same quality of being human-authored (*pauruṣeya*) as worldly sentences. Even if they were not human-authored—if their non-human authorship were possible—that would only be so if there were a beginning of humans. Furthermore, even if study were beginningless, it would still not be established that the study of the first person was preceded by another study; for what reason? Because there would be no other person to teach him.

The first student of that Veda, being the first to study it, would himself have inferred and studied the Veda; thus, he alone would be the author of the Veda. Therefore, this worldly practice characterized by the study of the Veda—where one person, having studied from one source, teaches another, and that person likewise teaches yet another—is an endless human activity proceeding from successive prior observations. Consequently, it would follow that this practice was composed by humans and is not indeed *apauruṣeya* (of non-human origin). How so? Like the play of children with dolls and dust.

Just as the sand-palace games of children are beginningless because they proceed from prior observation, so too is human activity; by the word "beginningless," activities such as eating and so forth are included.

"Because of beginninglessness," and so forth. If it is accepted that the Veda is authorless (*apauruṣeya*) because it is beginningless, then the same status—namely, being authorless like the Veda—would apply to the practices of barbarians (*mleccha*) and others, such as the marriage of one's mother and so on, which have come down through the lineage of their own families, since they too are beginningless. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the beginningless practices of Aryans are included. Likewise, even the words of nihilists (*nāstika*), which proceed from the denial of dharma, adharma, and the next world, would have that same status; that is, they would be authorless because they are beginningless.

He explains how their beginninglessness is established: "Because of the continuity of prior formative impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*)," meaning that they proceed as a continuum by the power of preceding formative impressions. The linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) of barbarians (*mleccha*) are beginningless. He asks, "What, then, are these? and answers: "The practice of certain barbarians is that when the father has died, the son must perform the marriage of his mother. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such practices as the killing of the elderly for the sake of liberating them from *saṃsāra*, and so forth.

He states what is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*): "the festival of Madana," and so forth. On the thirteenth day of the month of Madana, there is the festival of Madana. Here too, by the word "etcetera," festivals such as the celebration of a son's birth and others are also meant, which are beginningless. And there are the words of the nihilists, the Lokāyatikas. Of what nature are they? They are "denials of the unprecedented, the next world, and so forth. They are denials—that is, refutations—of the unprecedented, namely *dharma* and *adharma*, as well as of the next world. These too are beginningless; this is the connection [with the previous statement], with the gender being modified. (248)

Furthermore, as to how the linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) of barbarians (*mleccha*) and others are beginningless, he says: "For not... and so forth. Regarding the expression "those conventions and those nihilistic utterances," there is a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the neuter gender according to the rule: *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.69). Thus, the meaning is this: contemporary people whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have not been instilled by others and whose intellects are untrained do not initiate those conventions or those nihilistic utterances;
rather, it is only those whose intellects have been trained [who do so]. Since they too were taught by others, and those by yet others, the beginninglessness is established.
Fn. 1:

Even for those who compose something unprecedented, such as poetry and the like, their activity proceeds only through linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by others; thus, even the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) created by them is beginningless. Stating this, [the author] says: "By one's own intuition," and so forth. For even those persons who have composed a convention (*samaya*) characterized by poetry and the like through their own intuition—that is, through their own intellect—the entire meaning, whether taken collectively or individually, is exactly as it was heard from another. Regarding that [meaning], the "synthesis" (*saṃhāra*) of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) means their gathering together in one place, which is to say, their categorization.

Because one composes works such as books by proceeding in that very same manner; even a work fashioned from one's own intuition is, in reality, preceded by another. To the question, "How then can it be called 'one's own creation'? he says: the connection is that such poetry and the like are said to be "not preceded by another. It is called "done by oneself" by someone [only] because some collection of meanings has come from a certain teacher. This is because there is no single teacher who possesses [the knowledge] in its entirety through a continuous tradition.

Thus, even a treatise composed by one’s own intuition is, in the ultimate sense, preceded by others; how much more so, then, those activities that proceed according to what has been observed? Those whose engagement and withdrawal proceed exactly as they have been observed from others are described in that way. These are activities that are either correct or false. Those worldly practices whose conduct (*ācāra*) is both correct and false are described in that way. Among them, correct activities include [virtuous acts such as] honoring one's father and so forth; false activities include those associated with sensual desire and so forth. And these are clearly preceded by others.

Here, he raises the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "Now, etc. (p. 458). Those belonging to the first eon are the *ādikalpika*s; among them, linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) are held to be unobserved. For they did not perceive linguistic conventions from predecessors, precisely because they are the very first.

He refutes this with the words "of those as well," and so forth. Even for those men of the first eon (*ādikalpika*), whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) were established by others—namely, impressions established through the linguistic conventions they had previously observed during the succession of their former births—their subsequent activity proceeds from awakening [of those impressions] according to conditions, that is, according to the presence of auxiliary causes. Thus, even they do not have a lack of prior [causes]. If it is argued: "Let it be that because of beginninglessness, all linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) of barbarians (*mleccha*) and others are authorless (*apauruṣeya*)," [we reply: even if the authorlessness of all conventions were established merely by such beginninglessness, what benefit would there be?

Not at all. For instance, while it may be granted that being non-human (apauruṣeya) is intended to mean being non-contradictory, such non-human status also exists for certain worldly conventions that are nevertheless contradictory. Thus, non-human status is not a prover of truthfulness because it is fallible; so what is the use of postulating this non-human status?

Now, if the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedic sentences themselves is asserted, then even though the Vedic sentences are indeed authorless, there remains doubt once again regarding the objects expressed by them; that is to say, even after postulating their authorlessness, doubt is still reached. What is the reason? Because different interpretations of the meaning of the Vedas—the various alternatives for explaining the Vedic sense—are seen according to the difference between teachers. He explains this with the words beginning with "If... (*yadi*).

Even if the Vedic statement were not of human origin, if it were to produce in each case a specific intuition of its own meaning—namely, a cognitive engagement directed toward the object expressed by the Veda—then, due to the absence of any superimposition of a contrary meaning, there would be confidence, and the person would attain that confidence. But that is not the case; because [the intuition occurs] "according to one's whim" through either superimposition or denial, which means by the addition of extra words or the omission of other words.

Those who practice contrary scriptures are called *naiyāyikas*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the Vaiyākaraṇas and others is intended. They are seen to "tear apart" (*viśasantaḥ*) Vedic sentences, making them have various [contradictory] meanings. And it is not the case that those mutually contradictory meanings, brought about by their different interpretations, do not at all cohere with those Vedic sentences; rather, they do indeed occur—this is the meaning. What is the reason? Because the application of a word toward an object, which functions as its denotation, depends primarily upon convention (*samaya*).

Because [words] are bound to conventions (*saṃketa*), even for a single sentence, since there is the possibility of conceptualizing multiple meanings according to the agreement [of usage], there is indeed doubt. Furthermore, because Vedic sentences are explained by following the rules of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), and because those [roots and suffixes] have fixed meanings, the claim that "there is no possibility of conceptualizing multiple meanings in Vedic sentences" is also false. Why? Because it is possible for roots and suffixes to be listed with multiple meanings; for even a single root is recorded in many senses.
Likewise, the cognition as well remains in that very state; thus, there is doubt because the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the object varies according to one's intention.

It might be argued: "Since the meaning of the Veda is explained by relying on conventional usage (*ruḍhi*), there is no doubt even though roots and suffixes are listed with multiple meanings. This too is incorrect. Why? Because conventional usage itself is not accepted as being absolutely self-evident. Why is that? Because of the abundance of words that are not conventionally established (*arūḍha*). Those very words that are not established in common worldly usage are seen in great abundance in the Veda, such as *jarbhurāṇa* and others. Therefore, in those cases, no determination can be reached based on conventional usage.

In that regard, because the determination of the meaning of those [Vedic passages]—that is, the meaning which has not been established by the words themselves—depends upon the instruction of a person who explains them, and because both that instruction and the instruction of a person follow their own whims (*tadicchānuvṛtti*) rather than following the [objective] state of things (*puruṣecchānanuvṛtti*), there can be no certain determination regarding the meanings of Vedic sentences. (249) Furthermore, this proponent of the non-human origin of the Vedas must establish either the non-human origin of the phonemes (*varṇa*) or that of the sentence (*vākya*). By the very same alternative applied to the sentence, the case of the word (*pada*) should also be understood.

(1) With reference to the conceptualization of phonemes (*varṇa-vikalpa*), he says: "In that regard," and so forth. "Because they are not distinct from others" means because the Vedic phonemes are not distinct from worldly phonemes. What would be the result of proving that phonemes are not of human origin? None at all.

He explains this with the words beginning with "na hi" (for not). For it is not the case that the phonemes (*varṇa*) of worldly and Vedic sentences are different. What then? Just as the Vedic *a*-sounds and so forth are non-distinct, so too are the worldly ones, because they are recognized as being identical. Even though there is such recognition, if one were to maintain a difference between the Vedic phonemes and the worldly ones, then even if such a difference exists—

Consequently, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the oneness of Vedic phonemes such as 'a' and so forth—which [you claim] exists at every utterance—would result in being unestablished. Why? Because of the lack of distinction in recognition. That is to say, since the recognition observed when there is a difference between worldly and Vedic phonemes is no different in the case of Vedic phonemes, how can the oneness of Vedic phonemes be established based on a recognition that deviates from oneness? This is the meaning. Furthermore, Vedic phonemes are not established because their difference [from worldly ones] is not perceived; for no difference between the worldly and the Vedic is perceived.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of Vedic phonemes, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is indeed a valid means of knowledge because they are identical, whereas elsewhere it is invalid due to being an error caused by similarity; to this he says: "Because it would follow that there is no cognition [of momentariness] through recognition. If it were invalid elsewhere, then it would follow that even in the case of jars and so forth, there would be no cognition of their momentariness through recognition, precisely because they are different. Furthermore, this is because you Mīmāṃsakas do not admit any difference between worldly and Vedic phonemes.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that these phonemes are established as being non-human (apauruṣeya), then since those phonemes are identical everywhere—both in common worldly usage and in the Veda—what kind of class of phonemes has this Mīmāṃsaka, by thus proving their non-human origin, either set aside or abandoned that might be human?

Thus, even if worldly and Vedic phonemes were of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*), all verbal usage—whether worldly or Vedic—would be non-human; yet not all would be non-erroneous, nor would all have true meaning, because even in the case of non-human origin, the possibility of erroneous meaning exists. For this reason, the labor expended in postulating non-human origin is futile.

(2) With the words "Now," etc., the second position is presented. Alternatively, if it is maintained that the sentence is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), that is incorrect. For indeed, the sentence does not exist as something distinct from the phonemes. What is the reason? Because that which is perceptible is not perceived.

He explains with the words "For indeed," and so forth: "For we do not perceive, in the case of words and sentences such as 'Devadatta'—that is, in the words 'Devadatta' and in sentences—any manifestation of the word or sentence consisting of other phonemes apart from the manifestation of the phonemes beginning with the letter *da*. It is like the manifestation of a second phoneme; just as when the letter *da* is manifesting, a second phoneme does not manifest at that same time, in the same way, the word or sentence does not manifest."

Furthermore, it is not possible to determine that something which does not appear as an object of apprehension in cognition exists as a graspable entity, even if it meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). Likewise, it is not possible to determine whether [the universal] is other than the phonemes (*varṇa*) or not; this is the connection [of the sentence]. Since existence has been negated, otherness is also necessarily negated. Nevertheless, both are mentioned in order to demonstrate absolute non-existence, just like another form (*ākārāntara*). For example, when one form is appearing, there is no other visible form that does not appear therein; it is just like that.

"Impossible in others," and so forth: [this means] impossible in other phonemes (*varṇa*). If it is argued that the effect characterized by the communication of meaning is the indicator of a word or sentence distinct from the phonemes—since, for instance, a lack of comprehension is observed in the case of words and sentences such as "Devadatta," and this [lack of comprehension] cannot arise from the phonemes because they are individually meaningless, and because there is an absence of totality since other phonemes do not exist at the time of a single phoneme; therefore, one concludes that there exists that word or sentence from which this comprehension of meaning arises.

He replies with the words beginning "It might be" (*syāt*). It might be that the word and so forth are something other than the phonemes, if—despite the presence of those phonemes—the effect characterized by the cognition of that meaning were not to occur. This would be the case if the cognition of the meaning did not arise from as many phonemes as have been conventionally designated for the purpose of conveying that meaning; however, it certainly does arise. As it has been said: "But there is no other way [for the cognition] to be impossible regarding the understanding of the meaning. Therefore, that which arises immediately after [the phonemes] must be its cause. (Sphuṭārthā 95)

"It does not exist," and so forth, says the opponent. There is no cognition of meaning from the phonemes (*varṇa*). Why? Because even though those phonemes are without distinction, a cognition of meaning is impossible in other words and sentences. For if the cognition of meaning were to arise from the phonemes, then the very same cognition of meaning that occurs in the word *sara* would also occur in *rasa*, since the phonemes are identical in both cases. This should be understood to apply similarly to sentences containing similar phonemes. Yet such [a cognition] does not occur.
Therefore, there is no effect characterized by the cognition of meaning arising from the phonemes.

He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth: because the non-distinction of those phonemes (*varṇa*) in different sentences is not established. For it is thus: those phonemes which exist in one sentence are not the very same ones in other sentences, because phonemes arise as distinct in every sentence due to the difference in human effort. If it is argued that the non-distinction—that is, the identity—of phonemes in every sentence is established on account of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "this is that very same phoneme," [the response follows].

This is not so. Why? Because that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is fallible. For it is observed that in the case of hair that has been cut and grown back again, even though it is different, there arises a recognition in one who is deceived by the apprehension of similarity. Furthermore, the apprehension of similarity is the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of what is similar, not the apprehension of "something similar to another. Moreover, because recognition lacks a logical mark (*aliṅga*), it cannot serve as an example due to its lack of demonstrative evidence.

For there exists no single, recognized example established for both the proponent and the opponent. Nor is it possible for there to be a perceptual recognition at every step that grasps the identity of a phoneme; this is because its connection with a previous time is not apprehended due to its being non-present at the present moment. If it were apprehended, there would have to be a clear manifestation, as in the case of auditory cognition; yet such is not the case. Therefore, [the cognition] does not grasp the phoneme as belonging to a previous time.

Since that which is being perceived belongs to the present time, how can a nature that is connected with the present time be connected with a previous time? Because the previous and subsequent times are mutually contradictory, how can it be said that reality is grasped by perception? Furthermore, perception is held to have a proximate object; yet proximity is not possible for a phoneme because it possesses parts. Moreover, at the time of the final part of the phoneme, the preceding parts of the phoneme do not exist.
Therefore, it is impossible for there to be a perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that apprehends the identity of phonemes (*varṇa*) in each individual word.
Consequently, it is established that the phonemes are indeed distinct in every sentence; their distinction is what brings about the cognition of the distinct meanings.

But was it not said that phonemes (*varṇa*) are devoid of meaning? How then can it be said that the difference in meaning arises from the very difference among them? True. While phonemes in their actual state are indeed devoid of meaning, those phonemes which are the objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—being of the nature of universals (*sāmānya*) and distinct in every sentence—are accepted as the expressive agents (*vācaka*), with the particularities of the phonemes' own specific characters (*svalakṣaṇa*) superimposed upon them through differentiation. Therefore, it is said that the difference in the cognition of meaning arises from the difference among the phonemes themselves. However, if this difference in the cognition of meaning were not accepted as resulting from the difference among the phonemes...

However, even though there is no difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), because the sentence—which is distinct from them—is different, there is a difference in the comprehension of meaning. That very thing would be the difference in the effect; and that comprehension of meaning would arise from the sentence. And that sentence is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because it does not appear in sensory cognition apart from the phonemes. Thus, how could this [comprehension] come from the sentence? It would not be that comprehension, because the relationship [between the sentence and its meaning] has not been apprehended.

It might be argued: "Even though that sentence is imperceptible, it produces cognition by its mere presence, just like a sense faculty; and the postulation of the sentence follows from the fact that cognition would otherwise be inexplicable. To this, he says:

If it is admitted that a sentence produces cognition by its mere presence, then even a person who is unlearned—that is, one who has not mastered linguistic conventions—should derive a cognition of meaning from the sentence, just as one does from the sense organs and so forth. Yet this does not occur. Therefore, since the cognition of meaning arises from the phonemes solely through the force of convention, how can a sentence be postulated on the grounds of its being otherwise inexplicable? Consequently, there is no such thing as a "sentence" distinct from the phonemes for which non-human authorship could be proven.

In the absence of that [sentence], and consequently in the absence of the sentence itself, only the phonemes (*varṇa*) remain. And since these are indistinguishable everywhere, they must be proven to be non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*) in order to establish the non-human origin of the Vedas. This would entail proving the non-human origin even of worldly phonemes whose forms are no different from those [Vedic ones]. In this regard, concerning the first position—the position that seeks to prove the non-human origin of phonemes—it has already been stated: "This effort is useless. (249–250) Furthermore, etc.: if the sentence is conceived as consisting of multiple parts, and if those parts are individually and separately devoid of meaning...

He explains this with the words beginning with "tepī" (those too). If the many constituent parts (*avayava*) of that sentence were individually devoid of meaning by their very nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*), then the sentence as well—which consists of a collection of multiple parts—would likewise be devoid of meaning. Consequently, in a collection of parts that is of such a nature (i.e., non-meaningful) and thus lacks the form of an expressive entity, there would be an "identity" (*tādrūpya*) with the form of an expressive sentence; that is to say, meaningfulness would be merely imagined or superimposed (*kalpita-samāropita*), just as in the case of a [superimposed] lion and so forth.

Just as in metaphorical designations such as "the boy is a lion," where the nature of a lion is superimposed upon those who are not actually lions, such as boys; so it is here. He explains this with the words "possessing meaning" (*arthavān*) and so forth: the self (*ātman*) is indeed possessed of meaning; the sentence is a nature that is expressive (*vācaka*).
