Yet, the parts (*avayava*) of that sentence are themselves devoid of meaning. If that self of the sentence were to possess meaning while its parts themselves remain meaningless, it would be a construction superimposed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*), just as the state of being a lion is [superimposed] upon boys. For this reason, that expressive self, because it is fashioned by conceptualization, is merely human (*pauruṣeya*). (251)

Now, if it is held that the parts of a sentence must each be meaningful with respect to the sentence-meaning so that this fault does not arise, then, since each part is meaningful, there is the false assumption of multiplicity; for if even a single part has a completed meaning, it is illogical for the sentence to depend on other parts. Furthermore, by the cognition of a single part—that is, upon the apprehension of even one part of the sentence—the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would occur.

Now, it might be argued: even through the cognition of a single constituent part, or by way of a general sense, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning indeed occurs. As Bhartṛhari says: "All words possess individual meaning-possessingness because the complete meaning is fully realized in each word. Thus, whatever first word is employed, while it grasps the form and meaning of all [the others], the subsequent words are understood as being based on restriction and restatement. If this is so, why is it said that the postulation of multiplicity is useless?
This is not a fault, because this is stated with reference to a specific intended meaning:
"Even though each [word] possesses its own meaning, there is a false conceptualization of multiplicity;
and through the comprehension of a single constituent part, the understanding of the sentence-meaning occurs."

Nor is it appropriate for the individual components of a sentence to possess meaning or efficacy such that one part denotes a specific *kāraka* (grammatical participant) while another denotes a specific action (*kriyā*), because each component must be meaningful. This is because it is impossible to denote a specific *kāraka* that is not connected to a specific action; however, if one were to denote it as already connected to that action, the fault of falsely postulating multiplicity (*mithyānekatvakalpanā*) and so forth remains exactly as before.

He explains [the passage] with the words "parisamāptārtha" and so forth. That linguistic form whose meaning is complete is "tathā" (of such a nature). And since those parts contained within the sentence are of that kind, they are "parisamāptārtharūpāḥ" (having the nature of complete meanings) individually, each one separately. For this reason, it follows that those individual parts would each be a sentence. And thus, a sentence would not consist of multiple parts; the meaning is that a single sentence could not be composed of many parts.

If each individual component were meaningful on its own, then through the comprehension of a single component, the entire meaning of the sentence would be comprehended; consequently, the listener would have no need for further components. Furthermore, there would be no delay. The meaning is that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would not require the passage of time. Why is this so? Because that sentence-meaning, being partless (*niṣkala*) and indivisible (*nirvibhāga*), is comprehended in a single moment.
How is this so? Because that sentence-meaning is apprehended in its entirety within the arising of a single cognition.

Others, however, explain it otherwise: if the meaning were understood through the cognition of a single part, there would be no lapse of time for that part [to be perceived]. Why? Because that part, being partless in nature, is cognized in a single moment. What is the reason? Because when a single cognition arises, that partless part is apprehended in its entirety. "Otherwise" means: if the grasping of everything did not occur in a single moment of cognition, then there would be a contradiction regarding the oneness of the natures of the apprehended and the unapprehended; for it is impossible for two contradictory things to be one. (252)

Now, if it is maintained that there is a single hearing [of the injunction] so that this fault may not occur, then, when a single hearing of all the constituent parts is postulated, the lapse of time [required for their performance] would be untenable. (252)

He explains by means of the words "mā bhūt" and so forth. Since the meaning of the sentence would be established from a single constituent part alone—without waiting for the other parts—and since the determination of the sentence-meaning would thus result in the loss of the sentence's possession of multiple constituents, it is maintained that all the constituents of the sentence must be heard simultaneously. Even then, a lapse of time is not at all logical. Why? Because all the constituents would be heard at the very same time as the cognition of a single constituent; yet, hearing is observed to occur sequentially.

Furthermore, if the parts were heard sequentially, since each part possesses its own distinct meaning, the meaning of that [part] would be established from a single part alone; consequently, the meaning of the sentence would be established, rendering the other parts redundant. This has been stated immediately prior. Showing another fault regarding the simultaneous hearing of all parts, he says: "If the simultaneous apprehension of all parts upon their being heard at once is admitted, then even when combined, the meaningfulness of those parts—which have not been observed to possess the capacity to denote their respective meanings individually—cannot be established."

It might be argued: "Since the meaning is perceived and the cognition of the object arises when the parts are combined, each part must possess the capacity to generate the cognition of the object even when separate; therefore, this is not a fault.

That is not so. Why? Because that nature which consists in the communication of the meaning—which does not exist in those parts individually when they are separate—cannot possibly exist when they are combined.

The form of the individual parts taken separately is entirely different from the form they possess when combined, which is capable of conveying meaning; therefore, he says: "And because no other entity arises. This means that no other entity—a form capable of [conveying meaning]—arises from the preceding form which was incapable of such function, because phonemes are eternal. This is the intended sense.

The proponent of impermanence asks: "Is this fault not applicable here as well? He replies with the words "In the production of sound," and so forth. For the proponent of the production of sound, this aforementioned fault does not exist at all. Why? Because for that proponent, even those [phonemes] which are individually incapable become, through a specific assistance produced by human effort, possessed of an excellence characterized by the capacity to convey meaning when in a combined state; thus they are employed in the specific effect characterized by the cognition of meaning.

For the proponent of eternalism (*nityavādin*), however, since each individual constituent part is capable [of conveying meaning], the postulation of any other constituent part would be useless, because the comprehension of the meaning could arise from even a single constituent part.
Thus, the defect has been stated regarding the position that a sentence possesses constituent parts.

Furthermore, suppose the sentence were indeed a single, partless entity. Even if the oneness of the sentence is accepted, since it is indivisible and without parts, a sequential apprehension—that is, an apprehension occurring in succession—is impossible; because such sequential apprehension is impossible, a distinction in time is not tenable. For it is not logical for a single thing to be cognized sequentially. Why? Because there is no difference between what has been grasped and what has not been grasped.

For there is no other nature of that [sentence] apart from its apprehended nature which could be apprehended sequentially. If it is argued that the apprehension of the sentence occurs non-sequentially, he says: "And [it is] by sequence," and so forth. What is the reason? Because the time of usage for the entire sentence—the time of hearing for the speaker and the time of recollection for the listener—is completed through a succession of many moments of eye-blinking (*animeṣa*).
That in which there are many moments is "many-moment-eye-blinking" (*anekakṣaṇanimeṣa*); because of its production through that succession, that is, through its serial order (*paripāṭi*).

If it is argued that there is a sequential apprehension of the phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the sentence is apprehended without sequence, he replies with the words beginning "varṇa" and so forth. This is because the nature of the word does not appear as something untouched by the forms of the phonemes—that is, as something distinct from the forms of the phonemes—appearing instead in a single momentary cognition. Why is this so? Because the sentence is perceived precisely through the sequence of the phonemes; that is, the sentence is perceived only by means of the sequence of the phonemes.

Indeed, no manifestation of sequence other than that produced by the phonemes occurs in auditory cognition apart from the manifestation of the phonemes themselves. For this reason as well, there is no manifestation of a sentence devoid of sequence; because, according to your view, even though those phonemes are indistinguishable, the perception of the sentence—which is differentiated by the sequence of phonemes—is sequential rather than simultaneous, precisely because it is produced by the order of the phonemes. This would not be the case if it did not depend on the assistance provided by the sequence of the phonemes.

If a sentence were not dependent upon the assistance provided by the sequential order of its phonemes, then any kind of sentence whatsoever would be understood even when those phonemes are employed in some arbitrary manner or in a different order—for instance, when "rasosti" is uttered, one would understand "saro 'sti. Furthermore, because it would not depend on the assistance of the phonemes, a sentence might be understood even without the phonemes. Yet, the understanding of a sentence does not occur independently of the assistance of the phonemes. What is the reason for this?

Because it is impossible for these phonemes, which possess a sequence, to assist this sentence [if it were unitary], an assistance characterized by sequence must be performed by those [phonemes] that possess sequence; consequently, the assisted entity would also have to possess sequence. Yet this is not what is accepted.

If it is argued that the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves, even without sequence, will serve to assist the sentence, he says: "And [the claim] that by non-sequence," and so forth. This is because it is impossible to utter or pronounce phonemes without a sequence. Furthermore, since there is no other mode besides assistance provided through either sequence or non-sequence, and because there is no other alternative, it is established that phonemes do not assist the sentence. Indeed, phonemes do not exist within the sentence; nor is the sentence composed of phonemes.

Rather, the sentence is a single linguistic form (*śabdarūpa*) which is a distinct entity from the phonemes (*varṇa*). The manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), possessing a sequence, manifest it through a specific order and not through a disordered one. As it has been said:
"Just as there is a fixed sequence in the transformation of milk and seeds, so too is the sequence among cognitions fixed for those who perceive [it]. (1)

fn. 1: Kumārila states that there is no fault [in this view] because [the sentence] is employed in whatever manner [it may be]. Due to the sequence of its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), even though that single sentence is unitary, it appears as if possessing a sequence by virtue of the sequence of its manifestations. Because the sounds (*varṇa*) in their form as noise (*nāda*) are perceived without distinction from the nature of the *sphoṭa*, they appear to a person as if divided into phonemes; yet in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is devoid of both sequence and the division into phonemes. As it has been said:
"Because sound is produced sequentially, it is neither prior nor posterior;
though itself non-sequential, it arises as if possessed of differentiation through its sequential form."

"Therefore, in the case of phonemes, sentences, words, and so forth, which exist at non-distinct times, the nature of the word and its duration is differentiated by the diversity of the sounds (*nāda*). (Kumārila, ŚV, *Śabdanityatā-adhikaraṇa*, v. 1)

To this he replies with the words "possessing a sequence," and so forth. He thinks as follows: Is manifestation of the nature of a definite determination (*avadhāraṇa*), or is it of the nature of non-determination? If it is of the nature of definite determination, then the manifestation of a sentence—which is itself without sequence—produced by a manifestor possessing a sequence, is rejected. Why? Because there is a contradiction between the two forms—the manifested and the unmanifested, or the determined and the undetermined—within a single entity.

For there is no other unascertained form distinct from the ascertained form belonging to a single [word], by which it might be manifested later. Therefore, the claim that "because what was manifested by the first phoneme is not ascertained, the function of the other phonemes is for the sake of ascertainment" is refuted; for the manifestation in the form of ascertainment has already been accomplished by the very first phoneme. He will state the answer regarding a manifestation in the form of non-ascertainment later, beginning with the words "by all the phonemes together," etc.

Now, it might be argued: "The sentence appears as something entirely distinct from the phonemes, and not as merged with the sounds (*dhvani*). As it has been said by some: "Sound (*dhvani*) is imperceptible; it has been postulated by others as something independent."

To this, he says: "A sentence without parts," and so forth. This means that if one were to accept a sentence in which there are no existing constituent parts (*bhāga*) consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), then for a person who hears it incompletely—that is, for a listener who hears the entire sequence of phonemes only in fragments—the comprehension or hearing of the sentence would never be complete. Why? Because there is no single sentence apart from the phonemes, and thus there is an absence of parts.

Furthermore, in the world, upon hearing a few syllables, there arises the cognition of having heard a preceding portion of the sentence; for it is accepted that a sentence consists of parts composed of syllables. Thus, when a few syllables are heard, the hearing of a preceding portion of the sentence is intended.

That is incorrect. Since a sentence is a single unit, if its initial portion were heard, then there would be hearing of the whole; that is, the sentence would be heard in its entirety because it is not distinct from its initial portion. On the other hand, if there is no hearing of the whole, then there would be no hearing of anything at all; for even the initial portion would not be heard, as it is not distinct from the sentence. Therefore, what Maṇḍana says—“And due to the similarity of the manifestors, there is the misconception of grasping the essence of the sentence [in each part]; thus there is neither non-hearing nor hearing of the whole”—is untenable.

That is rejected; for at the time of perceiving the portions of all or some of the phonemes, the partless sentence is not heard. Indeed, there can be no similarity between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), because they are dissimilar by virtue of being composed of phonemes or not being composed of phonemes. Therefore, the claim that there is a misconception regarding the apprehension of the nature of phonemes within the sentence is merely trivial.

Others, however, explain it differently: "Now, even though it is illogical for a sentence that is partless (*akrama*) to conform to sequential manifestors due to the absence of a relationship between the benefactor and the benefited, it is nevertheless admitted; and consequently, there would be no hearing of the whole [sentence]. To this, he says: "The whole," and so forth. Even for a listener who hears [the parts] in fragments, there would be a hearing of the entire partless sentence. If that is not accepted, then there would be no hearing of the partless sentence for any person at all; even for one who has heard all the phonemes (*varṇa*), there would be no hearing of the partless sentence.

Even in the final stage, because the phonemes are not heard simultaneously and only a portion [of the word] is heard, it might be argued: "Just as a verse, when manifested once, is not grasped, but becomes capable of being grasped when manifested at another time, and is finally grasped through repeated manifestation; so too, a sentence, though not manifested by the preceding sounds, is not yet grasped. However, through the impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the manifestations of each preceding part of the sentence—which serve as causal conditions for the grasping of the sentence—the sentence is grasped at the time of hearing the final phoneme."

Therefore, it is indeed logical that a sentence which is inherently without sequence is manifested by means of the phonemes in their sequential order. As it has been said: "Just as an *anuvāka* or a verse attains mastery through repetition, yet that is not called a repetition of the text itself."
When the word is manifested by sounds that are themselves inexpressible yet conducive to apprehension, its own form is then determined.
"In the intellect, whose seed has been sown by the sounds and whose maturation has been brought to completion, the word is apprehended together with the final sound. (Kumārila)

He says this very thing with the words beginning "samasta" (all): that cognition which possesses the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by all the phonemes—either collectively or individually—preceded by the manifestation of the sentence, is such [a cognition]. The notion that the determination of the partless sentence occurs through that final cognition, which possesses the impressions of all the phonemes and has the final phoneme as its object, is also false. Why? Because that sentence does not touch upon the nature of phonemes.

The meaning of the verse is that because nothing devoid of phonemes (*varṇa*), form, and contact is ever perceived by anyone’s auditory cognition at any time, there is no appearance of such a thing upon the utterance of each individual phoneme; yet, there is an appearance of the utterance [of the sentence as a whole]. Now, it might be argued: "The sentence is indeed of the nature of phonemes, and therefore it is exclusively an object of sensory cognition. To this he says: Since phonemes are not perceived simultaneously but are perceived only in succession, how could there be such a thing as a "sentence"—which is supposedly grasped by a single cognition—possessing a sequence? It cannot exist.

Now, it might be argued: "After the cognition of the final phoneme, there indeed exists the apprehension of a partless sentence by means of mental cognition. To this he says: "And not," etc. After the cognition of the final phoneme, we do not perceive any essence of sound that is distinct from the phonemes—meaning something incomplete, undivided, and partless.

Nor does this speaker himself perceive the nature of the word as it has been described; for even then, while apprehending the sentence, he apprehends only the sequence of phonemes as having an external form, and he does not apprehend a partless sentence distinct from the phonemes. This speaker merely possesses a desire for excellence—the hope for a favorable result—thinking, "If only this word, having reached its conclusion as spoken by me, were to appear in the final cognition, it would be well for me."

By that [ignorance], one of deluded intellect "dreams" (*svapnāyate*). Even while not actually sleeping, he behaves as if his self were situated within a dream. Regarding the rule *adhikaraṇāc ca* ("and from a word denoting a locus"), it should be stated that the suffix *kyac* applies even after a word ending in the locative case. Some say that this is also recorded as a rule for the application of *kyac*. Others, however, say: [he is] "one who dreams" (*svapnavān*) through the metaphorical transfer of identity (*abhedopacāra*). Alternatively, because the possessive suffix is prescribed by the inclusion of the *ārśa-ādi* group, he is expressed by the word "dream" (*svapna*). Thus, the suffix *kyac* is applied based on the comparison with the agent himself: "he acts as if asleep," which is to say, "he dreams. By this, he mocks [the opponent].

fn. 1: Restored. If it is argued that the word and the sentence are grasped without sequence by means of recollective cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*), he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. For even in the case of words and sentences being recollected, the phonemes (*varṇa*) which are the constituents of those words and sentences do not establish their distinction from one another within a single, non-sequential cognition, unless there is a specific sequence; for they are not manifested [as distinct] in such a way. Rather, just as the sequence of experience, recollection also occurs only in a sequence—this is the meaning.

If, however, in a single, non-sequential final cognition the phonemes of words and sentences were perceived without a specific sequence, then—since there would be no priority or posteriority within that non-sequential cognition—the phonemes would be perceived all at once. Consequently, there would be no distinction or difference among those various words and sentences, nor among the various word-forms and sentence-forms, as produced by the appearance of the sequence of phonemes.

The meaning is that the mutual distinction between words and sentences arises precisely from the appearance of a specific sequence of phonemes; in the absence of that [sequence], such a distinction would not exist.

Nor is there a non-sequential [word], and so forth. That form of speech in which no sequence of phonemes exists is a "non-sequential" form of speech; we do not perceive any such form of speech as distinct from the phonemes themselves, because it has been stated that nothing whatsoever is apprehended that does not partake of the nature of the phonemes.

The theory of the *jāti-sphoṭa* (the universal-sound), however, is refuted precisely because of the non-existence of universals (*jāti*). Even if such a universal were to exist, it could not consist of the form of a word (*śabda-rūpa*) in the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa-krama*). That form of the word would have to be either impermanent or permanent, for there is no other possibility for a real entity (*vastu*). If it were impermanent, then, being produced by human effort, how could it not be a human composition (*pauruṣeya*)? It would necessarily be a human composition. For whatever is impermanent must be born, and thus it must arise from some cause of its own.

For thus, if the occurrence of sound were admitted to be accidental—that is, devoid of a cause—there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth; by the word "and so forth," it is stated that there would be no restriction regarding time or substance.

And that sentence is observed to arise from those persons whose organs are impelled by human effort and are free from defect; however, it does not arise otherwise when there is no desire to speak differently or when there is a defect in the organs. It is not [observed] otherwise because the causal property—characterized by positive and negative concomitance with human activity—is seen in relation to the sentence. Therefore, human activity alone is the cause of the sentence; for this reason, the sentence is also of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). (253)

Now, if that sentence were eternal, then, its eternality being admitted, there would be constant perception of the sentence. What is the reason? Because for that which is eternal, an obscuration is impossible; that is, because of the absence of any obscuration.

Now, the explanation begins with the words "atha" and so forth. Suppose that this nature of sound, consisting of sentences, were eternal and possessed of a perceptible nature. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose nature is perceptible. Since that perceptible nature of that sentence would never depart from it nor diminish, it would consequently be perceived eternally. For if it were thus eternal, it could not fall away from any capacity whatsoever, even from the capacity characterized by the production of cognition.

What is the reason? Because that capacity to produce cognition is of the very nature of the word, being the eternal essence of sound. Nor is the capacity to produce cognition from the word a separate entity, because the existence of such a separate entity was already refuted previously in the passage beginning with "because it would follow that it [the capacity] would not assist the existent."

If it is argued that [the eternal word] is not perceived because of being obstructed by dense air, he says: "Nor... and so forth. For that external object, which is of a perceptible nature and visible, some kind of obstruction to its perception is possible. However, regarding the establishment of such an obstruction, there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even if an obstruction were to exist, it would be impossible for it to suppress the capacity [of the word] to produce cognition, because it could not deprive the essence of that [word]—which is the eternal nature of sound—of its integrity. Thus, it is impossible for it to obstruct the power [of the word] to generate knowledge.

For in that case, what is considered an "obscuration" does not produce any excellence (*atiśaya*) within the nature of the sound; thus, it is called "non-productive. And what object that is non-productive could be an obscuration of anything, or an impediment to knowledge, or otherwise a cause of harm? This has been thoroughly examined; this has been essentially analyzed previously. The opponent, asserting that even something non-productive is seen to function as an obscuration, says: "Walls and so forth," etc.

What excellence do walls and such produce in jars and the like, or what excellence of capacity do they destroy, by virtue of which they are considered "obstructions"? Therefore, the intention is that just as those things are considered obstructions for jars and so forth without producing any excellence [in them], so too there will be some obstruction for the eternal word as well.

He refutes [the objection] with the words "We do not say," and so forth. We do not say that those walls and such things "surpass" some jar or other—that is, they produce a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How, then, are they called "obstructions"? He says: "But rather, not all... and so forth. Not every moment of a jar is a cause for the sensory cognition of every person; rather, it is the object, the sense faculty, and light when they are mutually conjoined.

They are the causes of consciousness because they produce distinct, successive moments through mutual differentiation. Why is this? Because that which cannot be assisted by others—that is, that to which no excellence can be imparted by others—is incapable of being independent of them. Furthermore, that which cannot have excellence imparted to it by others must either possess a potent nature (*śaktasvabhāva*) or a non-potent nature (*aśaktasvabhāva*). In that regard, it has already been stated previously that for that which possesses a potent nature, there would be the constant production of effects, whereas for that which possesses a non-potent nature, there would be no production at all. And these [causes] are the objects, the sense faculties, and so forth.

When those [senses] are not obstructed by an opposing medium such as a wall, they are mutually supportive. What is the reason? It is because of the phrase "lack of obstruction," and so forth. That location for which no obstruction exists is a "location without obstruction"; its fitness or capacity consists in being a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). This is because, through that cooperation, there arises a mutual excellence (*atiśaya*) among those [factors] such as the objects and so forth. However, when there is an obstruction caused by a wall or the like, this is no longer the case for those [senses], such as the eye and so forth.

Because of the absence of the cause characterized by spatial proximity and suitability—due to the non-arising of another capable moment—the cognition of a jar or similar object does not arise. Since, in this way, there is no persistence of a single nature at all times among momentary things, the previously arisen and capable moment of the sense organ and so forth ceases by its own inherent nature.

Furthermore, when there is an intervening obstacle such as a wall, a subsequent moment capable of arising—though it was previously ready to do so—fails to arise due to the absence of the aforementioned causes; thus, there is a deficiency in the causes of cognition. It is on account of this deficiency of causes that walls and the like are called "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*) with respect to the non-arising of cognition regarding jars and other objects concealed by them. It is not, however, because they actually prevent a jar or the like from being capable of producing consciousness prior to their concealment.

What is the reason? Because that [entity], such as a jar, which remains in its functional nature (*yogyasvabhāva*), does not deviate from its nature even when in proximity to a wall or other obstacles; for that which is capable remains indeed capable. It is impossible to effect any alteration in it. Thus, regarding momentary entities, even though an obstruction does not produce any excellence (*atiśaya*) according to the aforementioned method, it is nonetheless called an "obstruction."

He says "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth to show that obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) occurs precisely through the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*). Even though things such as pots, which are momentary, can mutually assist one another—even assistance provided by a wall and the like—there is no dispute regarding assistance produced by a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). However, an obscuration does not exist at a distance from the sense faculty and its object. Therefore, he asks: how does it assist the sense faculty and the object? He replies: "because of its inconceivability" (*acintyatvāt*) and so forth.

It is not possible to conceive in this way how an obstruction situated in a distant place could assist the object. For even by means of a magnet situated at a distance, iron is attracted. A "cause" (*hetu*) is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), while a "condition" (*pratyaya*) is the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); because the efficacy of these two is inconceivable for one who is not all-knowing—that is, for one who lacks omniscience—therefore, by that reason, an obstruction situated between the sense faculty and its object might indeed surpass [the reach of] both the sense faculty and the object.

In what manner? By the degree of deficiency in the production of cognition. The word "api" (also/even) is used in the sense of possibility, implying that this matter is possible because there is no subverting evidence against it.

[Objection: But surely, by the presence of an obstruction, that substance is rendered incapable of producing cognition in the second and subsequent moments; it is not [rendered so] at the very moment of contact, because [at that time] there is no impairment. Consequently, in the first moment, even when the obstruction is present, that substance should be visible, since the capacity for generating cognition has not been obstructed.

This is not a fault. For that which is observed to be the producer of an obscuring moment is also observed to be the producer of the very same [obscured] moment when it is incapable, as in the case of the second and subsequent moments. Therefore, at the beginning as well, the producer of the obscuring moment would produce the obscured moment as something incapable. For this very reason it is said: "Because the capacity of causes and conditions is inconceivable. Consequently, how could there be perception of the substance in the first moment when an obscuration is present?

And this meaning has been demonstrated regarding the apprehension of degrees of intensity: at first, a deficiency is produced in the object even by that which acts as an obscuring cause; then, in the second and subsequent moments, that obscuration produces an excellence [in the object].

It might be argued: "The capacity of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) to produce a deficiency [in a sense-faculty] must be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); yet such concomitance does not exist. To this he says: "By means of the difference in obscurations," and so forth. This refers to the various types of intervention (*vyavadhāna*), such as rags, cloth, or walls, in the case of sound and the rest—namely, sound, odor, and touch. The mention of "hearing" (*śruti*) is intended as an illustration; by it, one understands that the capacity of an obscuration is perceived in the dullness or clarity of hearing, seeing, and so on.

Otherwise, if no distinction were produced by the obscuration, then that proximity of the obscuration—which would be ineffective—would be equivalent to non-proximity. Consequently, the attribution "this is the obscuration of this sound," whether as a summary or a relation, would be merely a construction of conceptual thought and not based on reality.

If it is argued that [the object] will be the basis for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) as superimposed by conceptual construction (vikalpa), he says: "And not," and so forth. Causal efficiencies do not follow along with superimposition—that is, they do not have as their basis objects superimposed by conceptual construction—because they have real entities (vastu) as their basis. For a young boy is not employed or appointed to perform cooking merely because of the metaphorical designation (upacāra) "the boy is fire" based on the metaphorical application of "burning. Since this is so, therefore, even when conceptual construction exists, things (bhāva) do not turn away from being what they are.

Those whose transformation (*parāvṛtti*) is brought about by that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) are such [as described]. Due to the absence of that [construction], their functions (*vṛtti*) would not be directed toward that [object], but rather they would function solely according to their own nature (*yathāsvabhāva*). The analysis of the compound is: "those whose functioning is according to their own nature. (p. 475) "Therefore" (*tad*) means for that reason. If no specific quality (*viśeṣa*) were imparted by the obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), then even when an obscuration is present, the sense organs and so forth would still cause cognition to be known—that is, they would simply generate cognition. But this is not the case. Therefore, it is understood that the sense organs and so forth possess a specific quality and a specific mode of arising (*janmaviśeṣa*) imparted by that obscuration.
Indeed, for eternal sounds, there is neither the loss nor the production of any excellence, even when a particular obstruction exists.

The word *tad* means "therefore. If those eternal sounds have the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of producing cognition, they would produce all cognitions of their own objects for every person at all times simultaneously. On the other hand, if their inherent nature were not to produce cognition, then they would never produce any cognition for any person; this is an absolute certainty. If it is argued that even though the sound is eternal, it is not heard at all times because of the deficiency of some auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*), [the response follows].

He explains [the objection] with the words "It might be so," and so forth: "However, for the comprehension of some of these eternal words, there exists a specific auxiliary cause for comprehension that is restricted; for some word, some particular object is fixed by its very nature as an auxiliary. It is due to this—produced by that auxiliary—that these words are heard at certain times and in certain places. (254)

"Granted," and so forth, says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). "Granted, in this way" is the meaning. Let there be the waiting for another auxiliary cause; that is not being prevented. However, the restriction is contradicted. The sound remains with its very same prior nature. This restriction—that [the sound] persists—would not exist because of the necessity of depending upon an auxiliary factor.

He explains this very point with the words "Indeed, we do not [deny] auxiliaries," and so forth. We certainly do not reject the auxiliaries of causes; rather, causes indeed depend upon auxiliaries—of what nature? Upon that which assists their state, namely, that which assists the state consisting of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) for producing the intended effect. What is the reason? Because the excellence (*atiśaya*) obtained from those auxiliaries is employed—that is, functions—in the production of the effect to be generated.

Likewise, if even a Vedic word, depending upon some auxiliary cause, were to produce an effect in the form of a cognition having itself as its object, let it do so—what is there to prevent it? It would simply not be the case that it remains fixed in its previous nature, being restricted to that very prior nature. Why? Because that prior nature has been abandoned, and because, through dependence on an auxiliary cause, a different and previously non-existent nature is acquired.
Because dependence is illogical in the absence of the attainment of some excellence; for it has been stated previously that "it does not depend on anything else."

Now, if the word receives an assistance (*upakāra*) from its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) that is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then, since that assistance is also a distinct entity, the absence of a relationship—such as "this is the assistance of that"—has already been stated. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the following is also implied: if another assistance produced by the word is postulated for the sake of establishing a relationship with the assistance produced by the auxiliaries, then there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because yet another would be required there, and so on. Furthermore, it follows that the word itself would become unknowable (*ajñeya*).

What is the reason? Because cognition arises from an assistance produced by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) that is distinct from [the object] itself. Since this is so, therefore: this sound does not depend on the sense organ called the ear, nor on the contact between the sense organ and the object, nor on itself. And this has been stated in order to refute the views of others. "And other [factors]" refers to effort and so forth. Of what nature are they? They are the basis for the arising of cognition; that is, they are auxiliaries for the arising of cognition and are required for the production of their own cognition. What is the reason? Because nothing is of use there to the eternal sound.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "api ca" and so forth: if [sound] were non-pervasive, then those sounds would not be perceived in all locations. For how could a person situated in a place devoid of that sound perceive a sound existing in another location? If it is argued that there is no such fault under the view that perception occurs without contact (*aprāptagrahaṇapakṣa*), [the response is: since the sound is grasped by the auditory faculty even without reaching the location of the ear, then one situated in a place devoid of sound would also grasp the sound; therefore, the fault of its non-perception everywhere does not arise.

This is not so. What is the reason? Even in that case, according to the position that [the sense organ] grasps what it has not reached, the grasping of a sound that is obstructed is not possible. What is the reason? Because the sense organ depends on the degree of proximity of that sound as it remains within its suitable range. How is this so? Like a magnet and the like. Just as a magnet, although it attracts without reaching its object, does not attract iron situated in an unsuitable location, so it is here. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), [other examples] such as a venomous snake causing harm to a lamp or similar objects are included.

"Otherwise" means that if the sense faculty, which perceives the sound, did not depend on its being situated in a suitable location, then there would be no distinction between clear and unclear cognitions based on the varying degrees of the sound's proximity to a suitable location. Yet such a distinction does exist; therefore, there is a dependence upon a suitable location.

Even if sound were perceived while remaining in a suitable location and without reaching [the sense organ], there would be no distinction between clear and unclear manifestations; to this he says: "And if the condition for perception—characterized by the activity of the palate and so forth—were present, sounds would be perceived equally in all locations, whether near or far. But this is not the case; therefore, they are not non-pervasive. However, the Buddhists do not maintain that sound is perceived by the sense organ without having reached the location of the sense organ; how then could there be a distinction between clear and unclear hearing? As it has been said: "For those according to whom this sound is perceived by the ear without even reaching it..."
Their non-attainment is equal in the case of objects that are distant, obstructed, and so forth.
"In that case, the apprehension and non-apprehension of objects situated far and near would be identical;
there would be no sequence [of perception], nor would the occurrence of degrees such as intense or faint be possible. — Kumārila.

He thinks as follows: This fault applies only to one for whom all cognitions—whether their appearances are clear or unclear—are non-erroneous; it does not apply to the Buddhist, because he accepts that a cognition with an unclear appearance is erroneous. Furthermore, since sound is perceived as it arrives through successive productions in different locations, its sequence is apprehended; and because sound is produced in the region of the ear as either intense or weak, the occurrence of intensity, weakness, and so forth is possible, so there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

It might be argued: just as a form is perceived at a distance when it is mixed with dust, mist, and so forth, but is perceived clearly nearby because of the absence of those [obscuring factors], so too sound is perceived clearly or unclearly according to the distinction of being distant or near.

That is incorrect. For, regarding the apprehension of the mixture of form (*rūpa*) with dust, mist, and so forth: if there is first a separate apprehension of each of those two, then the appearance of the form would be the same for two persons situated at a distance and nearby, because it would be apprehended in its actual, inherent nature. Alternatively, if there is an apprehension of them as one—that is, an apprehension of their being mixed—how could the cognition have an unclear appearance? Furthermore, since distinct things are apprehended as one, how can there be an appearance of a single form in multiple aspects?
As it has been said:
Since the substrata of cognitions are distinct for each [cognition] regarding that single object,
how can it possess a form that appears with diverse aspects? Indeed,
words do not pervade space and time.
"Since the eternity and omnipresence of sound are established by auditory recognition,
who could determine its opposite?"
The claim that [the object] is distinct due to a difference in location is inferential in nature; however, the perceptual cognition that "it is that very same [object]" sublates it.
This is just as in the world, where one who travels through various distinct locations in succession [is still recognized as the same person].
Just as Devadatta is not divided, so too the word is not divided.

fn. 1: Kumārila. 2: Ibid. "Therefore, sounds are all-pervasive. To this he replies: "If those sounds were all-pervasive, there would be the simultaneous perception of all sounds by all persons. For it is not the case that any sound does not exist in some place; rather, every sound exists everywhere because of its all-pervasiveness. For this reason, all sounds would be perceived simultaneously, and they would be perceived by persons situated in all locations. What is the cause? Because persons possess functional sense organs."

Because the object, characterized as sound, being eternal, is always present everywhere due to its pervasiveness; and because, precisely due to its eternity, it is incapable of having any excellence added to it, and because of its continuity. Regarding the phrase "of the refined" (*saṃskṛtasya*) and so forth: the genitive case is used either in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, the meaning is this: if it is accepted that sound—which has been refined by air struck by effort—is perceived by a sense faculty that has likewise been refined, then the aforementioned fault does not occur. To this, he replies: "Who is the refiner of sound, which is subject to modification? None at all."

He explains this with the words "It might be so," and so forth: Although sound exists at all times, not every sound is perceived by every person. What is the reason? Because a manifested sound is perceived only by a sense faculty that has been manifested by air struck by effort. In that regard, between those two [theories], there is first of all no perception of a manifested sound. What is the reason? Because it is impossible for sound—which is incapable of undergoing modification—to be associated with a manifestation (*saṃskāra*).
However, because the sense organ is impermanent, there may be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of it by means of a specific quality to be produced through air impelled by effort. As it has been said:
"The air within the body, undoubtedly impelled by effort, moves forth; having reached the space of the ear, it bestows power upon the auditory faculty" (Ślokavārttika, Śabdanityatā 122–124).

The capacity of the sense organ is postulated because the perception of sound and form would otherwise be impossible; furthermore, this capacity is held to be of the nature of a *saṃskāra* (a latent impression or refinement).
To this, he replies: "Even that refined sense organ would hear every sound without exception.

He explains this with the words beginning with "therein" (*tatra*). If it is assumed that the apprehension of sound occurs only through a refined sense organ, such that a person with an unrefined organ does not perceive it, then the previous undesirable consequence—that one for whom the refinement of the organ has been performed would hear all sounds simultaneously—remains unrefuted.

Now, it might be argued: just as the postulation of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ is based on the fact that the cognition of sound would otherwise be impossible, so too the postulation of a specific refinement is based on the fact that the cognition of a specific sound would otherwise be impossible. As it has been said:
"In the same way, its particularity [the particularity of the cognition] arises from a specific hearing.

Therefore, because the sense organ is distinct for each respective object due to the difference in refinements, there is a restriction to a single object; that is, if there is the apprehension of only one sound. (258)

This being so, how could there not be auditory perception of a tumultuous sound (*kalakala*), which consists of a collection of many words and is composed of a multitude of diverse sounds? Yet, such perception is indeed observed.

He explains by means of the words "athāpi" and so forth: "The refinements (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ are restricted (*pratiniyata*) to specific sounds; in that case, when there is such a restriction of refinement, a sense organ refined by a particular [refinement] would be the perceiver of only a certain sound, and thus there would be no simultaneous hearing of all sounds. In this way, if the restriction of the hearing of sounds by the sense organs is accepted as being due to a specific refinement, there would be no hearing of a "cacophony" (*kalakala*), which is a conglomeration of many sounds.

For a single sound is not what is called "cacophony" (*kalakala*). Why? Because in cacophony, sounds of different natures—such as those of flutes, drums, the recitation of poetry, and songs—are heard simultaneously. Nor is there non-differentiation even when there is the apprehension of different natures, because the establishment of difference is based upon the distinction of natures. [Objection: But when many sounds are heard, since that hearing of many sounds would otherwise be impossible, one must postulate multiple refinements (*saṃskāra*) of the sense faculty; therefore, the hearing of many sounds is entirely uncontradicted.

He thinks as follows: If those impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are produced by winds impelled by effort were non-different from the sense faculty (*indriya*), then how could there be a multiplicity of impressions? For the sense faculty is a single entity. If, on the other hand, they are different, then how is the sense faculty "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)? Furthermore, the relationship expressed as "its impressions" would not be established. Moreover, how could those [impressions] which come into being once [the faculty] has already been produced have that same nature? For they would involve the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*).

Therefore, it is a mere trifle to claim that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cannot be both distinct and non-distinct. It is not the case that multiple sounds are perceived simultaneously in a cacophony; rather, each individual sound is heard only in succession. Furthermore, those auditory cognitions are of rapid occurrence. If it is argued that, because of this rapid occurrence, there is the illusion of simultaneous hearing even though they are being apprehended in succession—

In that case, because the constituent parts of those *gamakas*—which are specific variations of notes within the stream of notes such as the *vaṃśa*—would also be withdrawn and unified due to their rapid occurrence, the cognition would become confused; it would not possess the sequential order of the unmixed parts of the *gamakas*. And a prohibition against this will be stated here in the third chapter, beginning with the words: "If there were the utterance of two short [syllables]," and so forth (3.493).

Since this is so, because the capacity for the apprehension of a single word is restricted, a cacophony—which by its nature consists of multiple words and possesses a manifold essence—is not heard by the sense organ; yet it is indeed heard. Therefore, it is not a refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*), but rather the production of sound by means of the palate and other organs. Thus, as many sounds as are produced, just so many are heard; hence there is the perception of a cacophony. If [it is argued that] only the resonances (*dhvani*) are heard therein and not the expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*).

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). In a cacophony (*kalakala*), expressive phonemes, words, and sentences are not heard. What is the reason? Because there, only non-expressive sounds (*dhvani*) are heard. If it is asked, "Even if the capacity for a single [expressive] function is restricted, how can there be a simultaneous hearing of even those sounds? he says: "And regarding the expressive word," and so forth. We maintain that the sense faculty has a restricted capacity only with respect to the expressive word, but not with respect to non-expressive sounds.

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "In that regard" (*tatra*). For it is specifically the sounds (*dhvani*) themselves, in the form of distinct phonemes (*varṇa*), that are the expressive agents. To claim that there exists a separate entity called "word-form" (*śabdarūpa*) distinct from them which expresses meaning—this is something to be believed with great difficulty, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its existence. What is the reason?

For we do not perceive the non-expressive sound (*dhvani*) and the expressive word (*śabda*) as having distinct forms—that is, as being of a nature different from the sounds themselves. Rather, at the time of hearing the sequence of phonemes one by one, we determine that there is only a single essence of the word, characterized by that sequence of phonemes. Therefore, how could we—while determining and discerning the essence of the word as distinct from the sounds—[claim it is otherwise]?

How can we, based on deliberate effort and prior determination, bring forth a form of sound (*śabdarūpa*) that is distinct from the articulated sounds (*dhvani*) and lacks any basis? Therefore, it is the specific articulated sound itself that exists in the form of *a*, *kā*, and so forth, which is designated as "phoneme" (*varṇa*). The analysis of the compound is: that whose designation is "phoneme" (*varṇa*), etc. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), words (*pada*), sentences (*vākya*), and so forth are encompassed.

Moreover, if in a tumultuous noise the sounds are heard but not as expressive words (*vācaka*), then how can that which is expressive be [perceived] when one man speaks while many speakers remain silent, and other sounds are present? How can that single person's speech be heard as expressive?

Now, it might be argued that the sound (*dhvani*) is also perceived at that time; therefore, he says: "The sound is not distinct from this expressive [word-form], because it is not heard separately from that expressive form. If it is argued that it is indeed heard apart from the sounds (*dhvani*), he replies: "For in a matter of direct perception, the instruction of another is not more authoritative, such that one who does not hear it for himself through his own discernment would nevertheless understand the hearing of a separate sound merely on the basis of your word."

Therefore, while other speakers remain silent, this listener hears only the sound of a single speaker—sound that is entirely distinct from other sounds—and realizes the incapacity of the conditions for perceiving it, namely the completeness of the vocal organs and so forth belonging to the speakers who are the conditions for perceiving sound. In what respect? In the production of something other than that; that is, in the production of a sound different from the one being heard.

What is the reason? If those conditions for perceiving it were capable of producing something else, then the nature of sound produced by those conditions for perceiving it would be perceived; yet it is not perceived.

Now, it might be argued that those [causes] in a clamor (*kalakala*) are the initiators of sound (*dhvani*). To this he says: "having that nature," and so forth. If the conditions for the perception of sound have as their very nature the production of sound devoid of resonance (*dhvani*), then even when many people are speaking in a clamor, how could they produce resonance—a different effect—while abandoning their own effect, which is sound? They certainly would not produce it. For it is not logical that there should be a difference in the effect when there is no difference in the cause.

In that very same cause, a distinction in the effect characterized as "word" (*śabda*) and "sound" (*dhvani*) is not tenable. Why? Because it was stated previously that for a distinction in the effect to exist without depending on a distinction in the cause would entail the consequence of its being causeless. Therefore, in a cacophony (*kalakala*), only the expressive words (*vācaka*) are heard, not the sounds (*dhvani*). [Objection: But if it is admitted that in a cacophony there are only expressive words, how is it then that those at a distance hear only the sound (*dhvani*), while those nearby hear both the expressive words and the sounds?

True. Those very same articulators produced by effort, through their mutual friction, initiate the *dhvani*s; therefore, in a tumultuous noise (*kalakala*), for some there is the perception of mere *dhvani*, while for others there is the perception of both—thus there is no fault.
As for what was also said: that even for one standing nearby, in a tumultuous noise, only *dhvani*s are heard and not the expressive words (*vācaka*).

That too is incorrect, because it is not the case that the expressive word is not heard amidst a cacophony; rather, it is indeed heard. What is the reason? Because the divisions of words and sentences are perceived. Furthermore, how could there be a perception of distinct sounds if the sense organ were restricted to a single power? [If it were so], there would be no apprehension of multiple sounds at all.

He explains this with the words beginning with "tāni" (those). Although those sense faculties possess specific capacities, they hear various sounds simultaneously. Of what kind? "Fixed for each respective sound" (*pratiśabdaniyatān*); that is, fixed as manifestors for each individual sound. But it is not the case that they do not hear sounds simultaneously; so what aversion or disinclination (*nirveda-vaimukhya*) could these sense faculties have toward sounds such that they would not hear them? Nor can it be said that the power of an entity is simply like this, because at times even many expressive sounds are heard. (260)

The opponent says: "As has been stated," and so forth. That which was stated by the Buddhist—that sounds (*dhvani*) are not established as distinct from the phonemes, words, and sentences that are the expressive agents—is not so. How are they not established? They are indeed established. For what reason? Because the comprehension of meaning arises from speech; for when a word is uttered, there is the understanding of the expressed meaning. And this comprehension of meaning is not possible from phonemes alone. For what reason? Because the comprehension of meaning does not arise from a mere fragment of sound that manifests a single phoneme.

Even a single phoneme (*varṇa*) is generally meaningless, let alone a minute portion of sound (*dhvani*) which serves as its manifestor. If it is argued that [phonemes] in conjunction are expressive, he replies: "And it does not join with another. That minute portion of sound, because of its momentariness, does not "join"—that is, it does not coalesce—with another portion of sound occurring at a subsequent time. Therefore, this comprehension of meaning belongs to that expressive unit in which the words and sentences exist in their entirety and completeness.

Therefore, [the property] to be proven is not possible in sounds (*dhvani*). In what kind of sounds? In those whose parts (*bhāga*) are "uncompounded" (*asamasta*), that is, unconnected; because each produced part of the sound is momentary, a second part of the sound does not persist. Thus, by the fact that the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be impossible, the non-sequential existence of the word-form is established. That which has non-sequential existence as its nature is "thus" (*tathā*); that is to say, it is partless (*nirvibhāga*).
Furthermore, sound (*dhvani*) is sequential and possesses divisions, being distinct from the signifier (*vācaka*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which has sequential parts."

He refutes this with the words "That is not so," and so forth. This which has just been stated is not possible. Why? Because sound (*śabda*) as a sequence is distinct from those phonemes (*varṇa*) that possess a sequence; for it has already been refuted previously by such statements as: "In words and sentences such as 'Devadatta,' we do not perceive any manifestation other than the manifestation of the letter *da* and so forth."

Furthermore, if it is postulated that the nature of the word is non-sequential because the cognition of meaning is impossible when the sounds are incomplete, then such a postulation leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, in the case of actions of the hands and so forth which indicate going, coming, and the like according to convention, since those constituent parts are momentary, there is no connection or integration of a subsequent part of the action with a preceding part; and because the meaning is not cognized from a single part alone.

Furthermore, because one does not understand the intended meaning—characterized by going, coming, and so forth—from even a single small portion of the action (*karmabhāga*), [the action] must be distinct from those portions; that is, other than the constituent parts of the action. This is like hand gestures and the like used according to convention; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), nodding the head and so forth are included when there is comprehension of the meaning. In these cases, one would have to admit a whole consisting of all the forms of the action as the cause for the comprehension of the meaning, just as in the case of sound. This is like the postulation of a sound-entity distinct from the audible vibrations (*dhvani*).

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Maṇḍana: "When those learned in the three Vedas accept that objects such as hand-gestures consist of generalities and particularities denotable by words such as 'upward movement' (*utkṣepaṇatva*), then what is this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*)? That one must accept a single substratum of action (*karmātmā*).
(Sphoṭasiddhi 33, pp. 253–54).

That is incorrect; for if a single action in the form of upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) were established, and likewise if subsequent and preceding [motions] were also established, then the universal of "upward-motion-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva-sāmānya*) would reside in each of those many instances of upward motion. But that very thing is not established, because there is no continuity (*ananvaya*) among the prior and posterior parts of the action. And in the absence of particulars, there can be no existence of a universal.

Nor is there a cognition of each part of an action as having the form of upward-thrusting (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth; rather, it is [cognized] as having the form of those parts themselves. How, then, could a universal of "upward-thrusting-ness" be admitted in those parts? Or, if it were admitted, then even from a single part of an action, there would be the comprehension of an object characterized by "going" (*gamana*) and so on, because of the presence of the universal that denotes that object—thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Just as there is no self of action distinct from the parts of the action, so too there is no self of sound distinct from the parts of the sound. If one asks, "How then is there the cognition of meaning? he says: "Only those occurring in succession," and so forth. "Yathāsvam" means that which is the respective instrument, such as the palate and so on; its "application" (*prayoga*) is its activity. From that [activity] arise the distinct parts of the phonemes, or the parts of the action, according to the application of their respective instruments.

The phrase "because they arise sequentially due to the application of karma" should also be connected here. It is logical that those aforementioned parts of phonemes or parts of actions, having sequentially become objects of conceptualization following the sequence of successive experiences and cognitions, produce the comprehension of meaning precisely according to convention; for [any other way] would be devoid of reason.

Furthermore, he states another defect: by whatever defects—such as the fact that each preceding portion of the sound (*dhvani*) is not connected with each succeeding portion of the sound—and so forth, acting as causes, those sounds are accepted by the Grammarians and others as being non-expressive (*avācaka*). [This is] observed. If the expressive element (*vācaka*), though distinct from the sounds, is manifested by those sounds occurring in a sequence, why would those defects inherent in the sounds not exist for it? They certainly do exist.

Now, it may be argued that according to the reasoning previously stated, neither individual nor collective *dhvani*s (sounds) are the conveyors of meaning; rather, they are held to be the manifesters of the signifier (*vācaka*) individually. Since the signifier manifested by a single *dhvani* is not definitively grasped, its definitive apprehension occurs through the awakening of the varying degrees of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by other successive manifestations. Thus, even though the signifier is manifested by the *dhvani*s, how can those defects [of the sounds] affect it? As Maṇḍana has said: "For the proponents of *sphoṭa*, neither a sentence nor a word consists of multiple parts."
"For even in the case of identity, the sequential manifestation of that which is undivided has been shown.

This is incorrect. For manifestation is indeed cognition (*jñāna*); and you do not admit that cognition occurs without the accompaniment of sound. Therefore, "manifestation" is said to be nothing other than ascertainment (*niścaya*). And there is no ascertainment of the expressive word immediately after the first sound. As for the claim that it "appears," how then can that be its manifestation?
Consequently, it is established that just as sounds—whether individually or collectively—are incapable of conveying the meaning, so too are they incapable of manifesting the expressive word.

The explanation beginning with "krama" [is as follows]: it is claimed that the non-sequential essence of the word (*śabdātmā*), which is the signifier (*vācaka*), expresses its meaning when manifested—that is, revealed—by sequential parts of sound (*dhvani*). It does not do so by mere proximity alone. (261)

Furthermore, those sounds do not manifest that essence of sound—which is distinct from the sounds themselves—all at once. What is the reason? Because those constituent parts of the sounds occur sequentially. Nor does a single constituent part of the sound manifest or determine the word. What is the reason? Because it would follow that the other constituent parts of the sound intended to be manifestors would be rendered useless. For this reason as well, a single constituent part of the sound is not the manifestor of the entire word: because at the time of a single phonemic constituent, the complete expressive form of the word is not perceived.

"Therefore" (*tad*) means for this reason: this essence of sound (*śabdātmā*), because it is manifested sequentially by parts of sound (*dhvanibhāga*) that occur in succession, is such that its complete perception (*sakalopalambha*) is not joined together—that is, it is not synthesized. How could such an essence of sound accomplish its own denotable object (*svābhidheya*), which has the characteristic of illumination and is to be established by the completeness of perception? It could not accomplish it at all. Why is this? Like the sounds themselves (*dhvanivat*).
Just as, according to your view, the parts of sound would not illuminate the object because they are not joined together by preceding and succeeding moments, so too [the essence of sound] would not.

With the words "Who indeed," etc., he supports this very point: regarding objects that are to be established through perception, what distinction could there be between existence and non-existence when there is an absolute non-perception? There is none at all. For just as momentary parts of sound are incapable [of producing an effect] because they do not exist at the time of the subsequent parts and thus lack complete perception, in exactly the same way, even if the nature of sound were non-sequential, it would still be entirely incapable if its complete perception were not admitted. And yet, this nature of sound does not exist.

Being independent of perception, it accomplishes the cognition of the object by its mere presence. Why? Because it does not depend on that [perception]. And this manifestation occurs sequentially for both the existent and the non-existent: for the existent, which is the nature of the word, and for the non-existent, which is the portion of the sound. Since it occurs sequentially, it is of equal utility; that is, it has an equal result. Thus, regarding the effect characterized by the cognition of the object—which cannot be accomplished by the sounds because it is impossible for them to accomplish—therein also it is likewise [ineffective].

Even if the nature of the word (*śabdātman*) is manifested by sounds (*dhvani*), it remains impossible to establish [its eternity] in that way. Therefore, enough with this imagined "word" distinct from sound. Consequently, there is no authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) in the phonemes (*varṇa*), nor even in the sentence (*vākya*). This is the conclusion. If it is argued: "The sentence is not something distinct from the phonemes; rather, the sentence is the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*), and that [sequence] is authorless."
That is not so. Why? Because there is no difference from the sequence of the phonemes (*varṇa*).

A sentence that is a form of speech distinct from the phonemes is not at all non-human (*apauruṣeya*). What then? For us Mīmāṃsakas, a sentence is characterized by the sequential order of the phonemes. If it is argued that this [sentence] is to be proven as non-human;

No, because there is no difference [between the letters] and their sequence. This sequence is not a distinct entity from the letters. Why? Because if such a sequence were admitted as being perceptible—that is, as having reached the conditions for perception—it would follow that its difference from the letters would be perceived as a separate entity; yet it is not so perceived. Thus, since its non-existence is established, one must state a "non-perception of the essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Alternatively, if the sequence is imperceptible, then even regarding that imperceptible sequence—

Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of not apprehending the meaning in its proper sequence. Furthermore, perception cannot be the apprehender of a sequence that is perceptible, precisely because [such a sequence] is not itself perceptible. Nor can it be apprehended by inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Moreover, if a sequence distinct from the phonemes does not exist, then there would be only the phonemes themselves without distinction everywhere—in both worldly and Vedic sentences—and thus the same undesirable consequence as previously stated would apply, namely: "What would be purified by this? and so forth. Now, it might be argued: "The sequence of phonemes is merely a property (*dharma*) and not a separate entity; therefore, there is no fault. As it has been said:
"This [sequence] is merely a property (*dharma*) of those [phonemes]; it is not held to be a separate entity.
It is by being known in sequence that the phonemes become the means of cognition.
Furthermore, the sequence itself is not something produced, because it is grasped as something already established."

Indeed, no speaker adopts a sequence independently; rather, he intends to express it exactly as it has been stated by others. And since others do likewise, this [sequence] is beginningless, like a relationship. (VP 1.24)
Regarding the claim that the sequence of phonemes—which has come down through the observation of elders from generation to generation—is necessarily non-human (apauruṣeya), [Kumārila] says here:
"And there is no fixed arrangement of them"; that is, those phonemes do not possess a fixed order. Why? Because from a fixed [order], another different order would be contradictory.

He explains this with the words beginning "yadi" (if). If the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*) were produced, and if those phonemes were not many and of the same kind—by which [means] the Vedic phonemes would have a fixed order, whereas other worldly ones could be reversed at will; for the analysis of the compound is: "those whose application is a reversal according to one's desire," meaning their use in a different order. What then? In the three worlds, there is only one form of the letter *a*, and likewise of the letter *ga*. As it has been said: "Even though there is a difference in place, time, and the speakers, it does not possess difference."
"Since the recognition [of the letters] is perfectly clear there, [they must be eternal].

And when this is so, if the sequence of the letters were fixed, the word would always be "agni" and never "gagana. What is the reason? Because the prior-posterior relationship between the letter *a* and the letter *ga* is fixed. The meaning is that the letter *a* is fixed as being only before the letter *ga*, and the letter *ga* is fixed as being only after the letter *a*. In the case of "gagana," the letter *a* would have to come after the letter *ga*; thus, no other sequence would be possible.

Strengthening this very point, he says: "Even of produced things," and so forth. Let alone the consideration regarding unproduced things, for which any alteration whatsoever cannot be brought about; even in the case of produced entities, what is the transformation of causes? It is the attainment of successive states. From that arises the necessity: the existence of the effect immediately following the cause. Those things in which this [necessity] exists are described as such.

Even for these, it is impossible to effect a reversal of their sequence, just as in the case of the seed, the sprout, and so forth—where from the seed comes the sprout, and from the sprout the stalk, in which flowers and the rest arise, and not otherwise. Likewise, there is a fixed sequence for the seasons, the years, and so on; that is, for the seasons characterized by winter and the others, and for the years such as the Śaukra and Bārhaspatya, and by the word "and so on," for the planets, constellations, and the like. How much more so, then, for the phonemes (*varṇa*), which are uncreated and whose nature consists of an immovable state?

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "those unconditioned things whose nature consists of states such as the unchanging sequence. How are they established? By a fixed sequence. For it is impossible for there to be a change of state without abandoning the previous state, and it is impossible for them to abide by a different sequence. Alternatively, if the abandonment of the previous state were admitted for phonemes, it would follow that they are subject to destruction.

Furthermore, even for phonemes (*varṇa*), a reversal of sequence cannot occur without the abandonment of their prior state; this is especially true in the case of an eternal sequential order (*ānupūrvī*). Thus, this difference in sequence could only exist if there were a difference in the phonemes themselves at each word—assuming that even though the phonemes are eternal, they are distinct in every word—or because new phonemes arise at each word, resulting in a plurality of phonemes; from that, the difference in sequence might arise. However, neither of these two possibilities is acceptable to the Mīmāṃsakas, because they hold that phonemes are both unitary and eternal. (262)

Moreover, with the words "api ca" and so forth, he states another refutation: How could there be an absence of sequence—which is produced by space and time—in phonemes? Because they are described as being all-pervading and eternal. As it has been said: "Furthermore, the eternity of sound is established by auditory recognition, and its omnipresence is likewise established; who then could determine the contrary? (1)

fn. 1: Kumārila [states]: "Because letters are described as being all-pervading like space, there is no sequence produced by place. Because letters are eternal, there is no sequence produced by time. He explains this with the words "And that... and so forth: "And this sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) of letters would have to be either produced by place—such as in a row of ants and the like situated by excluding one another's places—or it would have to be a sequential order produced by time, such as in the case of seeds, sprouts, and so forth, where when there is the seed there is not the sprout, and when there is the sprout there are not the leaves and so on. Thus, this sequential order is of two kinds."

Spatial sequence does not apply to phonemes. Why? Because of their omnipresence and permanence. In that regard, spatial sequence cannot possibly belong to phonemes. This is because spatial priority and posteriority consist in the existence of entities by way of excluding one another’s locations. Such a priority and posteriority is not possible for phonemes. What is the reason? Because, due to their omnipresence, every phoneme occupies the same location as every other phoneme, just like wind and sunlight.

This is a worldly example. He states the scriptural [example]: "like the self and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), space and other such things are included. Likewise, a sequence produced by time is not possible for phonemes. Why? Because "succession in time" (*kālapaurvāparya*) consists in their occurrence at different times, one after another. Why is this so? [He says: "at which time," and so forth. Since at the time when one [phoneme] is absent, the other exists, that succession in time is also not possible for eternal phonemes.

Because every phoneme exists at all times, and there is no other way to understand the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) than as a succession produced by space and time. Therefore, how could the sequence of phonemes—which you seek to establish as being non-human (*apauruṣeya*)—be a sentence?
Furthermore, a sequence among phonemes that arise simultaneously cannot be produced by sound (*dhvani*), for that would entail their impermanence. As it has been said:
"Because it is an effect of impermanent sounds, sequence is therefore perishable."
"And its dependence on a person would arise through the power of his [the speaker's] intention to speak.

(Kumārila). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: because phonemes are all-pervading (*vyāpin*), they possess simultaneity; thus, sequence is contradictory to their pervasiveness, and pervasiveness is contradictory to sequence.
