If sequence is admitted for phonemes, then the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that grasps their pervasiveness must be erroneous. And so, since phonemes would be distinct due to differences in location, time, and speaker, they would be produced effects (*kārya*); how then could sequence be beginningless?
Therefore, as it is said:
"Nor is the sequence something produced, because it is adopted from what was previously established;
for no speaker adopts a sequence through his own independent will."

"Since he intends to speak [the word] exactly as it was uttered by others, and since another person likewise [speaks it], therefore this [word] possesses a relation [of identity],"—this is refuted. For when there is a sequence, the recognition of the identity of the phonemes lacks validity, because phonemes are produced effects and the sequence is not a separate entity from them. Furthermore, the sequence is not a property (*dharma*) of the things possessing the sequence (*dharmi*); for if it were, the sequence would appear as distinct in auditory cognition due to the distinction between a property and its substratum. Yet, such is not the case.

Therefore, entities arise only non-simultaneously; this is "sequence. Consequently, because there is a difference in the production of phonemes, there is also a difference in their sequence. The recognition that "this is the very same sequence perceived before" is based on similarity. It is not the case that recognition is based on similarity, nor will it be demonstrated that recognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). So how can it be said that sequence is non-human (*apauruṣeya*) due to its beginninglessness? (263)

Now, if the proponent of the Veda should desire that this fault not arise by asserting that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are impermanent and non-pervasive, then the fault regarding their impermanence and non-pervasiveness has already been stated previously.

He explains [the passage] beginning with *atha* and so forth: "Let this fault of the absence of a sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvyabhāva*) not occur," thus the proponent of the Veda would accept that phonemes are both impermanent and non-pervasive (*avyāpin*). Thinking that "this" [sequence] is produced by time due to their impermanence, and produced by space due to their non-pervasiveness, those two positions—impermanence and non-pervasiveness—have already been refuted previously by such passages as: "How could that which is impermanent and produced through effort not be of human origin? (PV 1.247), and by "there would be no perception anywhere" (PV 1.250), etc., respectively; therefore, [the opponent's argument] is not a valid rebuttal. (264)

The manifestation (*vyakti*) of phonemes—that is, their becoming manifest—even its sequence, does not constitute a sentence. The meaning is that when the action resides in the object (*karmasthā kriyā*), then neither the manifestation of phonemes nor the sequence of those objects of manifestation constitutes a sentence. Why? Because eternal manifestation has been refuted.

He explains [the objection] with the words beginning "no," and so forth. It is not the sequence of the forms of the phonemes—that is, the sequence of their intrinsic natures—that constitutes the sentence, for if it were so, this fault would arise. What then? It is the sequence of their manifestation. That sequence belonging to the manifestation of the forms of the phonemes—which is characterized by being manifest—is the sentence. Showing that very point, he says "no," and so forth. That manifestation [occurs] according to the conditions for the manifestation of its own respective phonemes.

The claim that "the sequence of those manifested phonemes is the sentence—since the operations of the palate and other articulators, which are the conditions for the manifestation of each phoneme, occur in succession, the sequence of those [phonemes] thus possessing succession is their *ānupūrvī*"—is also false. Why? Because that manifestation has already been refuted in the section concerning the manifestation of universals (*sāmānya*) among eternal things. Recalling that very point, he says: "Because they are effects," and so forth. [This refers to] the direct imposition of the capacity for production by means of the manifesting agent.

It has already been explained that for things such as jars, which are incapable of producing cognition, manifestation is nothing other than a specific effect. Furthermore, because those phonemes are perceived precisely through the operation of the vocal organs—the palate and so forth—that very cause establishes the status of those phonemes as effects. This is because:

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Whatever form is perceived from a particular source, the world designates that form as being an effect [of that source]. Regarding the phrase "from whatever it is perceived," the word *yat* refers to that which has been indicated; "the perception of that" (*tadupalabdhi*) means relying on a perception that is necessarily concomitant (*nāntarīyika*) with it. The particle *eva* is placed out of its logical order [to mean "necessarily"]. That aforementioned perception also exists in the case of phonemes (*varṇa*), because the perception of a phoneme is necessarily concomitant with the perception of the operation of effort (*prayatna*).

And that perception [of being an effect] occurs even in other things well-known as effects; its basis is the basis for the designation of "being an effect. There is no distinction greater than this. Therefore, since the grounds for accepting "being an effect" are equal, why are phonemes not considered effects?

"No," and so forth, says the opponent. "This [establishment of causality] does not have perception as its basis. Rather, the establishment of causality has as its basis the fact that the perception of one thing is invariably concomitant with the perception of another. What then? It is that which occurs only when [the other] exists; that is, 'only when X exists does Y occur. In this way, the establishment of causality has existence (*sattā*) as its basis. Furthermore, it is held that for phonemes, existence arises from their instruments, but [in the case of cognition], it is only perception that arises."

"That is existence," says the Teacher. That this designation of "being an effect" applies only to that which is the substratum of existence is untrue. From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that existence established, by virtue of which it could establish this state of being an effect? For when this existence is not established, it does not occur in this way: "When this exists, that comes to be. Therefore, the establishment of existence is the means of proving that [state of being an effect]; it is the means of proving that state of being an effect. That establishment is indeed apprehension (*upalabdhi*), because establishment has the nature of cognition (*jñāna*).

Consequently, it is established that whatever is perceived only when something else exists is the effect of that thing; and since this is equally the case with phonemes, how could phonemes not be effects?

The opponent says: "True," and so forth. It is true that if the existence (*sattā*) of that sound were not established through the operation of the palate and other articulators, then its status as an effect of that operation would follow from the perception of the sound occurring solely through such activity. However, its existence is indeed established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, in a person who has previously heard the word "cow" (*gośabda*), upon hearing the word "cow" at another time, there arises a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) grasping its identity: "This is that very same word 'cow'. Such grasping of identity would not be possible otherwise.

If it were the case that the sound did not exist in the interval between the times of hearing the preceding and succeeding [sounds], then by means of *arthāpatti* (presumption), the existence of the prior sound would indeed be established. However, this establishment is not a proof of its being an effect (*kāryatā*) based on a prior establishment; rather, that establishment of existence is the cause for the conceptualization of its being an effect, which is itself preceded by an establishment. Just as a jar, which was previously non-existent, is established only after the activity of the potter and other factors.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says "nanu" and so forth. He explains this: first of all, it will be demonstrated that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, how can its existence be established? Let us grant for the moment that the existence of the word prior [to its utterance] is established; nevertheless, the nature of the word remains unestablished. To ask what that nature is, he says: "that which is of such a kind," and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: it refers to one for whom moral discipline (*śīla*) has been employed through an intervention by such a cognition in which the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound appears. For if such a form were already established previously, then there would be a constant perception of sound.
If it is argued that the aforementioned form of sound is indeed already established, but due to the deficiency of another auxiliary cause, it was not employed as a cause for auditory consciousness—

If this is so, then that state which is subsequently employed in its own cognition when the auxiliary causes are present, and that state prior to the effort which was not yet employed, are mutually contradictory. How, then, can there be non-difference between these two contradictory states—the employed and the un-employed? On the contrary, there is indeed difference. Consequently, because of this plurality, such a nature of the sound would be something produced; thus, the sound would necessarily be an effect.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "That excellence which occurs is not the very nature (*ātman*) of the word, but rather a distinct entity (*arthāntara*); therefore, this [word] remains entirely unaltered from its prior nature. To this, he says:

Nor is there a difference between the state of being a non-agent and the state of being an agent characterized by an excellence (*atiśaya*) that does not touch upon the nature of the sound; that is to say, it is not distinct from the nature of the sound. For if it were distinct, then since the utility of that very excellence would be established in the cognition of the sound, its status as the cause would be established, which would result in the absurdity that the sound itself is not the cause. To explain: it is logical that only that in whose presence the probandum is established is what is useful for that probandum, and nothing else.

Excellence is employed for cognition, whereas the word is employed for excellence directly; thus, by way of a traditional sequence, the word is indeed employed for cognition as well. Therefore, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with *tadatiśaya* and so forth: even if one assumes that a word (*śabda*) is employed for the sake of an excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in that [object], it follows that [the word] would be like that [excellence]. That is, it follows that it would be like a cognition (*jñāna*). Just as when a cognition is to be produced, a word is not employed for an excellence that exists as a separate entity, so too, when an excellence is to be produced, another excellence existing as a separate entity must be postulated. In that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the excellence must be non-different from the word; and because it is non-different [from the word], [it is established].

Therefore, it certainly excels other things—which possess the nature of sound—in producing cognition of its own object, by virtue of a difference in its essential form (*svarūpa*). [The compound] *avyavahitasāmarthyopayogāvasthābheda* is analyzed as follows: "a difference in state (*avasthābheda*) in which there is an application of unimpeded capacity (*avyavahitasāmarthyopayoga*).

Now, it might be argued: "A state that produces cognition does not arise at all because [the sound] is eternal; rather, this [sound] produces cognition in dependence upon the palate and other [articulatory organs]."

Therefore, he says: "Of that which possesses no excellence," and so forth. Since this [sound] has no excellence produced by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), the dependence upon such auxiliaries—which was previously refuted for that which lacks excellence—is already discarded. Furthermore, since that sound, as the nature of the producer, is established solely through the operation of its cause, it possesses properties identical to all effects. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has properties identical to all effects. If the manifestation of such a sound, which possesses properties identical to all effects, were intended, then everything, including sprouts and the like, would become manifest.

Or rather, there is nothing at all to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*). Even the word would have to be an effect (*kārya*), because there is no distinction [between it and other effects]. For instance: an object is considered a "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*) when, by means of its own cognition acting as an instrument, it becomes the cause for the cognition of another thing. When? At the time when the object has already been established. That is, if this manifested object has already acquired its existence through a cause—just as a lamp is a manifestor that causes the cognition of a jar already produced by a potter and so forth. Or otherwise, if the manifested object were previously unestablished, then what would be the distinction between this manifestor and a causal factor (*kāraka*)?

He explains [the passage] beginning with "one's own cognition" (*svapratipatti*). One's own cognition itself is the door, the means; by that instrument, it is established in the world that the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is the cause for the cognition of another thing, such as a jar. If that [manifested object] were the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), it would have to be already established prior to the operation of the manifestor.

[Objection: But does not a lamp and so forth also produce a momentary state of a jar that was previously unestablished, yet capable of being perceived? Why, then, is it said that "if it were already established beforehand"?

Therefore, he says: "Of the same kind," and so forth. The preceding moment of the jar or other object, which is capable of being perceived, is of the same kind as its material cause; because that [cause] is not established prior to the operation of the manifesting agent, it is said, "if it were established beforehand. It is not said to be established because that very excellence (*atiśaya*), which is the cause of cognition and is obtained from the manifesting agent, is established beforehand. What is the reason? Because that aforementioned excellence has as its condition the totality of causes (*sāmagrī*).

The analysis of the compound is: that [collection] whose condition (*pratyaya*) is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of manifestors. Furthermore, those which bring about the perception of something previously unestablished through their own activity are indeed *kārakas* (producers). What is it like? Just as a potter and others are with respect to a jar and so forth; likewise, the causes for the perception of sound are equal to potters and the like. Thus, sound too is an effect, just like a jar and other such things.

But surely, when a sound heard at one time is heard again at another time, its identity—that "this is that very same [sound]"—is perceived through perceptual recognition (*pratyakṣa-pratyabhijñā*). And since this apprehension of identity would otherwise be impossible, it is certain that the sound exists prior to the activity of the palate and other articulatory organs. Thus, how could the palate and so forth be perceivers of something already established? Therefore, it is logical that they are merely manifestors (*vyañjaka*).

The [opponent] thinks as follows: in the first moment there is the apprehension of the sound; in the second moment there is the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the previously apprehended sound; then, in the next moment, there is the recollection of the sound; and then, in the fourth moment, when that [sound] has vanished, how could the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) "this is that same pot-sound" be perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), since its object is no longer present?

Nor is recognition of the phoneme possible for a person whose prior latent impressions have already been awakened, because it has been stated that a phoneme possesses parts; furthermore, at the time of the final part of the phoneme, the preceding parts of the phoneme no longer exist, and thus even the final phoneme itself is not present.

For this very reason, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of recognizing words and sentences is also impossible, because words and the like are aggregates of phonemes (*varṇa*), and at the time of the final phoneme, the preceding phonemes no longer exist; furthermore, direct perception is held to have only present objects as its domain. Therefore, direct perception cannot possibly grasp the identity (*tattva*) of phonemes, words, or sentences. For this same reason, it was not even proposed by the Teacher (*ācārya*).

Or, let us grant that there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding them as being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); nevertheless, it is not logical to postulate the existence of sound prior to the operation of the palate and other organs on the grounds that its apprehension as such [i.e., as identical] would otherwise be impossible. For the apprehension of it as such is possible even through the apprehension of another similar instance; thus, if you argue that the apprehension of another similar instance is itself unestablished because it is not pervasive (*avyāpin*), [we reply: no.

But surely even oneness is not established. If it is argued that it is established by the apprehension of identity (*tattva*), we say no; for since the apprehension of identity is observed even in the case of distinct hairs that have been cut off and grown back, there is only doubt [regarding oneness] from this. How, then, can the prior existence [of the object] be postulated through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*)?

Now, sound is eternal because it is recognized [as the same]. For if it were non-eternal, there would be no recognition at all due to its multiplicity. Likewise: that which is employed for the sake of another must exist prior to its employment, as in the case of an axe or similar tools used for cutting; and sound is indeed employed for the purpose of communicating to others. Therefore, it too must certainly exist beforehand.

Therefore, he says: "Recognition," and so forth. Even those [reasons] that establish the eternal existence of sound do not fulfill the definition of a valid logical reason (*hetu*). For instance, recognition is observed even in the case of impermanent things such as a lamp. Therefore, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Likewise, it is seen in the application of action, which is momentary; thus, the reason "because it is being employed" is also strictly inconclusive.

Whatever mark (*liṅga*) may be adduced to prove the oneness of the word—namely, that the subsequent cognition of the phoneme *a* occurring later has the same object as the preceding one; that is, it has the same object as the prior cognition of the phoneme *a*.

By this, it is thought that the permanence [of sounds] is established through the proof of the oneness of words. "The cognition of the letter *a*" is the reason (*hetu*). "Like that" refers to the cognition of the previous form of the letter *a*, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the cognition that in the states of fast, medium, and slow [utterance], the phoneme *ga* and others are one and the same; that is, "this very phoneme *ga* and others is distinguished by the differences of fast and so forth. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is a cognition of the letter *a* has as its object something non-different from the cognition of the previous form of the letter *a*.

For example, there is the cognition of the letter *a* previously, and the subsequent cognition of the letter *a* is also a cognition of the letter *a*; thus, this is a pseudo-reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetupratirūpaka*). Furthermore, that proof is incapable of establishing the non-difference between the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the preceding and succeeding instances of the letter *a*. For instance, this reason—"because it is a cognition of the letter *a*"—must be stated either specifically, as "because it has the form of the previous cognition of the letter *a*," or generally, as "because it is merely a cognition of the letter *a*. In the first case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

What is the reason? Because its being of that nature is unestablished, and because its being a cognition of a prior form is unestablished. Or rather, [if one argues] specifically that the reason is "because it consists of the cognition of a subsequent form," even that is not a proof. What is the reason? Because its being of that nature is unestablished—that is, because its being of the nature of the probandum is unestablished. The meaning is that there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.

Now, if the logical mark (*liṅga*) is stated in a general sense, there is no contradiction even in its having a different object; for what contradiction is there in there being a cognition of the letter *a* that has an object different from the object of the cognition of the prior form?

Others, however, explain that just as there is a commonality consisting in the cognition of the letter *a* in those two cognitions, so too the state of having the letter *a* as their object is not contradictory.

Furthermore, regarding two cognitions directed toward the same object—that is, two cognitions occurring at earlier and later times which have as their object a single form established previously—their relation of priority and posteriority is contradicted by their being prior and subsequent. Why? Because the effect arises or does not arise according to the sequence of the cause being present or absent. And if the cause were present [for both], those two would exist simultaneously. If, even when the cause is present, only the former cognition of the form arises and not the latter—

In that case, even subsequently, it would not exist. Why? Because, even when the causes for the cognition of the preceding and succeeding [forms] are present, the specific subsequent cognition of the later form has not arisen, and thus it does not have those as its cause. The meaning is that the cause of the cognition of the preceding form is not its cause. Therefore, the two cognitions occurring in succession possess entirely distinct causes; the analysis of the compound is: "those two whose entire cause is distinct. It might be thought: "The single sound itself is the sole cause of those two cognitions of the forms; however, the order of their arising is due to the sequence in which the auxiliary conditions (sahakārin) are present."

Therefore, he says: "In that regard," and so forth. "In that" means at the time of the arising of the cognitions of the preceding and succeeding forms. Even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the single cause, the two cognitions would necessarily exist simultaneously. Why? Because that single, potent cause does not await auxiliary conditions (*sahakārī*). Consequently, it would follow—contrary to reason—that the two cognitions of the preceding and succeeding [moments] have a single object.

By all of this, it has been stated that the thesis is sublated by inference (*anumāna-bādhita*) when the cognition of the subsequent form and the cognition of the prior form have a non-different object. The inference is as follows: whatever occurs sequentially does not have a single object, just like the visual and auditory cognitions occurring in succession; and the prior and subsequent cognitions of the letter *a* occur sequentially. Since having a single object is pervaded by non-sequential occurrence, and sequential occurrence is the opposite of that, [the reason] is indeed contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha*).
If it is argued that, in this case, because the thesis is sublated by perceptual recognition (*pratyakṣapratyabhijñā*), there is no arising of the inference at all; [we reply: no.

No; for the cognition "this is that very same [thing]" has as its object a relation between prior and posterior times, and thus its object is difference. For the state of being related to a prior time is indeed one thing, and the state of being related to a posterior time is another. Otherwise, if there were no difference between the state of being related to a prior time and the state of being related to a posterior time, then because the latter would exist at the present moment, the manifestation of the entity [as it was] would not occur. Furthermore, the cognition "this is that very same [thing]" would arise, rather than the cognition "this is that."

Alternatively, if there were no difference between being related to a prior time and being related to a subsequent time, there would be no appearance of it as "prior," nor would there arise the cognition "this is that very same thing," but rather [the cognition] "this is it.

Therefore, that which is related to a prior time is not what is related to a subsequent time, and that which is related to a subsequent time is not what is related to a prior time. Since, by virtue of having as their objects things related to prior and subsequent times, they have difference as their object, how can there be a subversion of the thesis based on recognition?

Umbeka, however, says: "Even if there is a single experience in the form 'this is that very same [object],' nevertheless, this [experience] is perceived as grasping both the past state of being an object of cognition and the state of being manifest within a single substratum. Or, even if these are two distinct cognitions consisting of perception and recollection, nevertheless, this [pair] is distinct from the case of the uninterrupted arising of the recollection of a jar and the perception of a cloth, because it appears as having mutual objects. For indeed, the object itself appears in the recollection as qualified by the past cognition, and thus it appears as nothing other than manifest."

Furthermore, an object of past cognition is perceived as being present before one's eyes, because it appears in the form of the recognition "I remember this. Therefore, for a person whose vision is unblinking, the very determination that [an object] persists without arising or perishing is the sublater of the inference that proves momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

That is incorrect. Because each subsequent perception has as its object a successive difference in the state of the thing, the superimposition of identity—thinking "this is that very same thing"—is an error. For instance, in the perception of one who sees for the first time, the state appears as it is when not yet perceived, and not as the state that was the object of past cognitions. The same applies to one who sees it repeatedly; the thing exists in its present form, not in its former form.

Furthermore, when a form remains present, the very non-remaining of its prior form is what constitutes its destruction. For example, in the state of old age, the form of childhood is destroyed; the prior form is an object of past cognition, while the present form is directly perceived (*aparokṣa*). Now, since a person seen in the state of childhood is recognized (*pratyabhijñāyate*) in the state of old age, how can the status of being an object of past cognition and the state of being directly perceived appear as residing in a single substratum? Or else, how can it be said that an object which is itself directly perceived appears in memory as qualified by a past cognition? Such things are asserted [by the opponent].

Even in a case where there is a continuous determination [of an object] by one who gazes for a very long time with unblinking eyes, the object's state of being directly present (*aparokṣatā*) arises through its connection with a present perceptual cognition. Since the past cognition no longer exists, the status of being the object of that past cognition is likewise non-existent at present; this is precisely what constitutes "destruction. Therefore, how can it be said that the very determination of a continuous [object], which is devoid of both arising and destruction, subverts the inference of momentariness?

As for what is also said: "For one who asserts that there is difference at every moment, this is a sublation; however, if non-difference were established merely by recognition, then because the identity of even what has perished would be understood—as in the case of recognizing a dead person—"

That too is refuted, because non-difference itself does not exist. Nor can there be non-difference between that which has perished and that which has not perished, due to their contradiction. Furthermore, non-difference cannot be established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of identity, since such a cognition of identity is possible even through similarity. Moreover, the "that" component [of the recognition] is not perceptual, because its object is not present; and if this [cognition] were of the nature of memory, it would not grasp an object previously perceived, as there is an absence of clear manifestation.

If it were of the nature of memory because it determines an object already seen, it would be erroneous, since it determines the seen object as non-different from its own [present] form. Furthermore, the aspect "this" is held to be perception; thus, the unity of memory and perception is contradicted. Therefore, with respect to an object standing before one that is devoid of being the object of a previous cognition, the mind grasps it through the mental cognition "this is that very same thing," having superimposed the status of being the object of the previous cognition upon it by way of similarity.

By the power of superimposition, the state of being an object of past cognition and the state of being imperceptible appear as having a single substratum, just like the recognition of water in a mirage. In the absence of superimposition, however, these two appear as having distinct substrata, just like the recollection of water and the perception of a mirage.

Therefore, this remains established: because it is erroneous and because it is not a direct perception (*apratyakṣa*), there is no sublation of the inference of momentariness by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Consequently, the cognitions of the preceding and succeeding *a*-sounds have distinct objects. Likewise, the cognitions of the *ga*-sound and so forth—whether fast, medium, or slow—have distinct objects, because they take as their objective support a *ga*-sound differentiated by the distinctions of speed and so on. The cognition of the identity of the *ga*-sound—such as "the *ga*-sound itself is fast" or "the *ga*-sound itself is slow"—is based solely on similarity. Thus, as for what is said:
"For even when there is a difference in speed and other such qualities,

another distinct cow-individual (*gavyakti*)— separated from other cow-individuals— is not clearly perceived as already established. Therefore, because of the oneness of the phoneme (*varṇa*), a single cognition arises."
"The existence of a distinct cognition [of the letter *ga*] would arise from the difference in the manifestors (*vyañjaka*)"—this [argument] of Kumārila (p.

499) is refuted. For it is the specific sound (*dhvani*) itself that is called the phoneme (*varṇa*). Therefore, when uttered rapidly, the specific sounds are called the rapid manifestation (*gavyakti*) of the *ga*; when uttered at a medium pace, they are the medium manifestation; and when uttered slowly, the specific sounds are the slow manifestation of the *ga*. However, no *ga* appears as something other than the manifesting sounds. One perceives only a commonality of name among them, thinking "the *ga*, the *ga*."

Likewise, among the short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, there is not a single uniform form. This is because it is specifically particular sounds (*dhvani-viśeṣa*) employed for the duration of one *mātrā* that constitute the short vowel *a*; similarly, other particular sounds employed for the duration of two *mātrās* become the long vowel *ā*; and particular sounds employed for the duration of three *mātrās* become the protracted vowel. Therefore, only a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) of the short, long, and protracted vowels appears; the letter *a* does not appear as an undifferentiated entity within them.

However, when the sound *a* itself is uttered for the duration of one *mātrā* and so forth, it is perceived respectively as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*); thus, it is merely the sound itself. Therefore, it is said:
"In the doctrine of eternality, a distinction between short and so forth by its own nature is contradictory;
how can that which exists at all times be [said to be] 'possessing a measure' (*mātrika*) in itself?"
"Therefore, let its duration of pronunciation be understood as either two morae or three morae; the word itself is not inherently possessed of a mora. (Śloka-Sphoṭavāda 50, 51)

That too has been refuted; for the cognition and the designation "the vowel *a* or *u*" do not apply consistently across the short, long, and protracted [vowels]. Furthermore, it might be argued that because the cognitions occurring at the earlier and later times share the same name, they must have the same object.

Therefore, he says: "Depending on," and so forth. There is a difference in the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) between the two perceptions of the letter *a*—the preceding and the succeeding—by virtue of their being prior and subsequent in form. There is also a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) through distinctions such as fast, medium, or slow [articulation]. Even given this difference in perception, appearance, and intrinsic nature, it is illogical for them to have the same object simply because of the identity of their name, namely, "perception of the letter *a*. Why? Because it would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that this would apply even to jars and other such things.

If it is argued that the cognition of a jar occurring previously and the cognition of another jar occurring later would have the same object simply because they share the common name "cognition of a jar," and consequently, a single jar would follow everywhere; and if it is further argued that establishing oneness in such cases as jars involves a contradiction with perception, since jars and the like are observed to be many, and therefore oneness is not established therein— [The response follows: ... [as per the source text] ... [the argument fails].

In this case as well, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the absence of contradiction with observed reality established in proving the oneness of phonemes? Here too, the distinction [of organs] is indeed established through their difference for each person; the point is that the determination of oneness occurs due to similarity, just as in the case of hair that has been cut and grown back again.

The reason "because of the identity of name" is inconclusive; thus he says: "As far as... and so forth. "Being denotable in that way" means that the cognition of the letter *a* [is the same as] the cognition of the letter *ā*; such being the identity of name, the state of being denotable is not established by pervasion through a single object despite a difference in meaning. To that extent, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful. There may be identity of name and yet a difference [in meaning]. Furthermore:

If it is argued that sound, which possesses a distinct nature for each different person and for each different instrument of production, enters into and ascends upon auditory cognition (*śrotravijñāna*)—that is, the act of hearing—and is established as one, why then are jars and other such things not also established as having a single form? Let them too be so established. Or else, some distinction must be stated.

If it is claimed that even though sound is one, there is a difference in appearance due to the difference in its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), the author replies with the words "In that case also" (*tatrāpi*) and so forth. Even in the case of those distinct objects like jars and the like, it would be possible to object in this way—that there is a difference in appearance due to the difference in their manifestors. (266)

Furthermore, because sound is invariably perceived through the operation—characterized by vibration and so forth—of a complete set of causes, it follows that it is an effect. Why? Because such [invariable perception] is impossible in the case of a manifesting cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*), since it is impossible for the manifested object to be perceived with necessity [prior to the operation of the manifestor].

He explains [the point] with the words "na hi" and so forth. When the sense organs are active, there is never a non-perception of sound; rather, there is indeed perception. Nor does the operation of a manifestor necessarily cause the object to be perceived or grasped. What is the reason? Because in some places devoid of jars and the like, even when illumination characterized by lamps and such exists, jars and the like are not perceived. Therefore, for a person who possesses the auxiliary causes for the production of unimpaired cognition...

This perception of sound, which occurs invariably through the operation of that [cause], must result from the production of the sound by the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*). For this would be the case if sound were produced by the operation of the instrument; consequently, sound is indeed something produced (*janya*), not something manifested (*vyaṅgya*). [Objection: But was it not previously stated that a *kāraka* (productive cause) is defined merely by its capacity to generate [an effect], whereas a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is that which brings about production in such a way as to render [the object] fit for the generation of cognition? Therefore, it is logical that the palate and other [articulatory organs] are merely manifestors.

This is not a fault, because [it was said] with reference to the mere effect: a producer is so called by virtue of merely producing [something], whereas a manifestor is so called by virtue of being capable of generating cognition; however, this is not said with respect to a visible effect. For instance, in the case of a person whose auxiliary causes are complete, that which produces a lamp or the like is necessarily a producer of the perception of the lamp and so forth, and not a manifestor; thus there is no fault.

Furthermore, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not the agent of sound. Since it is impossible for that [sound] to be established through the operation of an instrument that is not its agent, it is impossible for sound to be established [by such means]. Sounds are pervasive and eternal; therefore, because sounds are pervasive and eternal, they are perceived everywhere due to the operation of the manifesting instrument (*vyañjaka-karaṇa*). However, jars and the like are neither pervasive nor eternal; therefore, they are not necessarily perceived through the operation of a manifesting instrument.

If this is so, what confidence can there now be regarding jars and the like? What certainty is there that they are neither eternal nor all-pervasive? For let them too be eternal and all-pervasive. If it is asked, "How is it that they are not perceived at all times?", this is equally true for sounds as well. Whatever rebuttal applies there, it will apply to jars and the like as well. If it is argued, "Because those jars and the like are not accepted as being all-pervasive and eternal," [then...]

Is sound intended to be all-pervasive and eternal? Why is it so intended? [Because it] has the same properties as that [space]. [But] it has the same properties as a jar and other such things. And since all-pervasiveness and eternity have already been refuted, this [argument] is trivial.

"Of jars and so forth," etc., says the opponent. There is no fault because there exists another manifestor distinct from the causal factors (*kāraka*). Thus, the fault of the undesirable consequence [of these factors] being identical to sound does not apply. Demonstrating that there is indeed another manifestor, he says: "For light, etc. Light is established in the world as the manifestor of these jars and so forth, not potters and the like. If potters and the like were manifestors, they would be exactly like that; that is, they would not invariably cause the perception of a jar, just as lamps and the like do not invariably cause the perception of a jar.

Because even when there is illumination, the jar may be absent; likewise, potters and the like would also [be manifestors], but this is not the case. Furthermore, potters and the like excel [others], because the jar and so forth exist at all times during the potter’s activity. Therefore, due to the excellence of the manifestor—because it functions as something distinct from the manifestor—potters and the like are indeed producers (*kāraka*). Why? Because for that which assists, there is no other possible mode of action; since there is no other category apart from being either a producer or a manifestor.

In that case, since the status of being a manifester has been refuted, it follows by elimination that potters and the like possess the status of producers (*kāraka*). However, no other means of manifestation distinct from the instrument (*karaṇa*) is established for sound such that the instrument itself could be postulated as its producer. Therefore, because of its difference from objects such as jars, sound is indeed only a manifested entity (*vyaṅgya*).

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says "that," and so forth. This possibility of other manifesting agents is equal even in the case of sound (*śabda*). Why? Because in that case too—regarding sound—it occurs due to the proximity of the object to a sense-faculty suitable for it, and so forth; specifically, because the sound resides in a location suitable for the auditory faculty. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), mental attention (*manaskāra*) is included. [It occurs] due to the excellence (*atiśaya*) of the instruments (*karaṇa*). If one asks, "How is there excellence? he says: "In the case of a jar, etc. The particle *ca* has the sense of "for" (*hi*).

The property of those complete causal factors (kārakas), such as the potter and so forth, which produce a jar—that is, their necessary production of their own effect—is observed in the case of the instruments (karaṇas). For these too, when they are active, necessarily produce sound. Therefore, these too are indeed causal factors, just like the potter and the rest.

And if, because there is no other manifestor for sound, its causes are accepted as its manifestors, then—since there is no other manifestor such as a lamp for that very manifestor [of taste, etc. with respect to another object—the causes of those [manifestors], namely the causes of the lamps and so forth, would themselves be the manifestors of these lamps and so forth. This is because there is no other manifestor for them.

Since this is so, the manifestation (*vyakti*) of sound does not result from the articulatory organs (*karaṇa*), but rather its production (*utpatti*) alone. Or, if manifestation were to occur from the articulatory organs, it would be of three kinds: (1) manifestation would be the possession of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) by the sound through the relinquishing of its prior state; (2) or it would be the removal of the obstruction to its perception; (3) or it would be the cognition (*vijñāna*) that has sound as its object. This is because there is no other possible alternative apart from these three modes.

(1) In that case, manifestation is not the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the sound, because that would entail its impermanence. If it is asked, "Let there be the production of an excellence; but how does that entail impermanence?", he replies: because that production of an excellence is characterized by the loss of the previous form and the arising of another, subsequent form.

(2) He states the second position, beginning with "atha" and so forth: The obstructions of that sound—which consist of the conjunctions of the particles of stagnant air and which obstruct its perception—are of a nature such that they impede its apprehension. Their removal is the separation [from those obstructions] by means of air impelled by effort. If this [removal] is what you, the Mīmāṃsaka, consider to be the manifestation (*vyakti*) of the sound, it has been said:
"The air within the chest, struck by effort, undoubtedly moves outward;
it follows along with the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other [articulatory organs]."
"And because it possesses momentum (*vega*), it necessarily persists as long as that momentum lasts.
Furthermore, due to its movement, conjunctions and disjunctions necessarily arise between its own constituent parts and the motionless air. (Śloka-vārttika, Śabdanityatā 122–24)

How can that manifestation be produced? Since the removal of an obscuration is a non-entity, how could the collection of instruments—that is, the assemblage of causal factors—have any efficacy toward it, given that it is in no way an effect? The meaning is: it certainly could not.

He explains with the words "for not," and so forth. This is what he says: when the nature of the obstruction has been established, the causal factors are indeed incapable of acting; they do not possess efficacy. Even upon the removal of the obstruction, they lack efficacy. For it has already been demonstrated in the investigation of efficacy that removal is a non-entity (*abhāva*), and a non-entity cannot be an effect.

This was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. Now he says "not even," etc., to show that this very [position] does not exist. Because an eternal sound cannot have any excellence added to it (*anādheyātiśayatvāt*), there is no obscuration whatsoever by which the removal of an obscuration could constitute its manifestation. What is the reason? It has also been stated that such an obscuration lacks efficacy with respect to an eternal entity. Since this is so, there is no application of causal instruments (*karaṇa*) toward an obscuration; the meaning is that one should not put forward the claim that "causal instruments effect the removal of an obscuration for sound."

Nor is it the case that the causal factors lack the capacity for sound. Why? Because when their activity is absent—that is, when the activity of the instruments is absent—sound is not perceived. Therefore, it is logical that these instrumental activities produce sounds.

Otherwise, if the instruments were not producers but merely manifestors, then since there would be no distinction regarding sound, it would follow as an absurd consequence that other things, such as jars and the like, would also be manifested by potters and so forth.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that even those [objects] such as jars are indeed manifested by potters and the like, then, by accepting that view, all causes would be rendered purposeless. For, regarding an object to be manifested, a manifestor must either produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in it, or produce the absence of an obscuration, or produce a cognition [of it]. Since neither an excellence nor the nature of manifestation itself can be produced, all manifestors and all producers of the intrinsic nature [of things] would be purposeless.

The explanation begins with the words "yadi" (if), etc. If the instruments [of sound] are its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), of what nature are they? They are "possessing the same properties as all causes"—the analysis of the compound being: those instruments which possess all the common properties (*samāna-dharma*) that belong to all causes. In that case, not even a jar or the like would now be the effect of any potter or other agent, because there would be no distinction from the case of sound. If it is argued that "the manifestation of everything is intended," this is not tenable.

What is the reason? Because it would follow that all causal factors—which are considered to be manifestors—would be rendered purposeless. For there are three possible alternatives regarding manifestors: a manifestor might exist by producing either an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the manifested entity, or the removal of an obscuration (*āvaraṇābhāva*), or cognition (*jñāna*).

A manifestor does not function by producing an excellence (*atiśaya*) in that which is manifested. Why? Because an entity whose nature is already established cannot have an excellence added to it. Nor does it function by removing an obscuration, because the absence of an obscuration is not something produced as an effect. Nor is it a manifestor by producing cognition, for what reason? Because, just like the object itself, the cognition of that object is also established as pre-existent according to the view of those who maintain that the effect exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*). If, on the other hand, it is held that cognition which was previously non-existent is produced, then if some factor is desired to be the causal agent (*kāraka*) with respect to that cognition—

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that other agents such as potters and the like—who possess the same properties as the agent of cognition—are likewise [cognized], which would entail that everything is an effect with respect to jars and so forth. Or else, some distinction must be stated by which there is agency with respect to cognition but not with respect to jars and the like; yet no other mode of manifestation is possible.

Therefore, this collection of factors intended as causal agents (*kāraka*) is not of any use whatsoever for the manifestation of a jar or similar object; for manifestation has been refuted on the grounds that a real entity (*vastu*) cannot possess any added particularity (*ādheya-viśeṣa*). Nor is it of use for the action itself, since the production of an effect is not admitted [in the case of manifestation]; thus, it would be entirely useless. And so, when there is such a deficiency of causal agents, this world would be "inactive" (*nirīha*), meaning devoid of operation (*nirvyāpāra*). What kind [of world]? It is "one in which there is neither the beneficiary nor the benefactor" (*anupakāryopakāraka*); the analysis of the compound is: that in which no beneficiary (*upakārya*) or benefactor (*upakāraka*) exists.

Furthermore, when the permanence of sound is to be proven, the proof accepted and intended is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), such as non-application (*aprayoga*) and so forth. For example: "Sound is permanent because it is recognized as being one and the same. As it has been stated: "Because of the absence of number. For people say, "The word 'cow' has been uttered eight times," and not "eight cow-words"; by this it is understood that they recognize [the same word]. Because of the application of what exists: that which is applied already existed previously, just as an axe or similar tool exists prior to the act of cutting.

And since a word is employed for the purpose of conveying meaning, it must therefore exist prior to that employment. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes such reasons as "because it is uttered for the sake of another. As it has been said: "But [the word] must be eternal, because its perception is for the sake of another. 'Perception' means utterance; that [utterance] is for the sake of another in order to convey a meaning. If the word were to perish immediately upon being uttered, it would not be able to convey the meaning thereafter; thus, it would not be uttered for the sake of another."

"Without an example" means without an illustration (*adṛṣṭānta*). For there is nothing permanent whatsoever upon which this proof could operate. Why? Because all entities are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Explaining this very point, he says: "For [things] are subject to momentary destruction," and so forth. It was stated previously that destruction is not produced, and it will be stated later as well. Having demonstrated impermanence by way of destruction, he now demonstrates it by way of origination as well, saying: "Origination," and so forth. Furthermore, because entities possess origination from an external cause, they are therefore not eternal. Why is it that they originate from another? Because it is impossible for existence (*sattā*) to be accidental.

It has already been stated that if things were to arise spontaneously (*ākasmikatva*), there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth. Therefore, "that"—namely, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) along with its application and other factors—is a logical mark (*liṅga*). It does not occur at all in a stable, unitary entity which serves as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Since transformation—meaning production through various and distinct natures—is observed, as in the case of lamps and the like, the logical mark of recognition and so forth is seen to be pervaded by difference; thus, it is indeed contradictory [to the existence of a stable entity]. Furthermore, recognition here is not caused by a universal such as "lamp-ness" (*dīpatva*), because the universal has already been refuted.

"No," and so forth, says the opponent. "Recognition is not contradictory. Why? Because recognition—which has its origin in that which is non-different, namely, that which is stable and of a single nature—occurs in the case of lamps and the like due to error (*bhrānti*). If it is asked, 'How is there error? [The answer is: because of deception by similarity; that is, because one is deceived by the similarity between the preceding and succeeding moments. This explains that non-erroneous recognition is what is intended as the logical mark (*liṅga*), and that such [non-erroneous recognition] does not exist at all in the case of lamps and the like.

The Teacher [Dignāga] says: "There is no recognition of an unchanging birth. On what basis, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is this recognition of an unchanging birth asserted? Because a permanent entity lacks causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*). And this same refutation should be seen to apply to recognition even when it is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that this is because the object being recognized appears as non-different, we say: no. For that very non-difference must be examined through its preceding and succeeding states even in the case of things such as diamonds and stones.

Just as in the case of diamonds and the like, one must consider whether their nature is the same later as it was before, or whether it is indeed different, such that the impression of identity arises merely due to similarity—as is the case with lamps and similar objects. If it is argued that just as the non-difference in diamonds and the like is to be considered, so too is their difference to be considered; then this must also be investigated: in what manner does difference manifest across the sequence of earlier and later moments?

The Teacher [Dignāga] says: "By that very [fact]. Since it is impossible to determine with absolute certainty whether there is difference or non-difference, let there be doubt due to that very lack of determination. Let there be doubt regarding difference and non-difference in objects that are being recognized. If it is argued that the ascertainment of identity arises from doubt itself because of the fact of recognition, he replies: "Nor is the establishment of the oneness of sound achieved through a probans consisting of recognition whose object is doubtful."

If it is argued that the identity of an entity across preceding and succeeding times is established because no distinction is perceived and no distinction appears between the preceding moment and the subsequent moment;

"No," and so forth, is the reply. By this, the meaning is as follows: for an entity, its manifestation at this very moment is precisely its manifestation as a moment, because it does not manifest as being connected to prior or subsequent times. And the manifestation of a moment in its own nature is precisely its manifestation as distinct from prior and other moments; it possesses a manifestation that is different [from them], rather than manifesting as inseparable (*avinābhāva*) from the manifesting prior and other moments. It is simply that this distinction is not apprehended; for that purpose, inference is set in motion.

Therefore, he says: there is no non-perception of non-distinction (*aviveka*) regarding diamonds and the like. What is the reason? Because the existence and non-existence of diamonds and so forth are established through the prior and posterior states of the cognitions of diamonds and the like; that is, by way of their sequence. For instance, a subsequent cognition having a diamond as its object establishes the prior non-existence of its own specific cause when it arises later, and its existence when it arises subsequently. Thus, because the existence and non-existence of diamonds and the like are established through the sequence of cognitions, there is indeed distinction (*viveka*), that is, the presence of difference (*bheda*).

Clarifying this very point, he says: "If," and so forth. Other cognitions that arise at a later time would have their causes present at the earlier time of the preceding cognition; they would thus have already been produced, just like the preceding cognition. But this is not the case. Therefore, those cognitions being unproduced prior [to the later time] indicate a deficiency in their own causes. Otherwise, if their cause were present even earlier, it would have to be either capable or incapable [of producing them]. If it were capable, it would have produced them even earlier.

What is the reason? Because that which is capable produces [the effect]. Now, if it were incapable, it would not produce it even later. Why? Because even for that which is incapable, since no excellence can be imparted to it, it cannot subsequently acquire capability from anything whatsoever. Or, if it were to acquire capability from something, then, upon the acquisition of that capability, stability would be impossible; for there would be the loss of the prior nature of incapacity and the arising of another, which is capable.

Therefore, since successive cognitions establish the succession of their own objects, the distinctness of all things is established, and thus their impermanence follows. As for the cognition "this is that very same thing," it is caused by the perception of similarity.

For this reason, even the second reason that is stated—namely, "this is the employment of what exists"—also refers only to the production of the sound. Why? Because the sound possesses efficacy with respect to the agent; the meaning is that the sound acquires its efficacy in the performance of the intended effect.

Otherwise, if tools such as an axe or a word were already capable of their respective effects prior to the operation of the user, then, since they would possess that capacity inherently, the user would be of no use; consequently, axes and the like would function by themselves, independent of persons. But this does not happen. Therefore, there is indeed "employment" (prayoga). Furthermore, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the desired or intended object—such as cutting—is defined as the very production of an axe or similar tool with a nature capable of that [action].

Of what nature is this production? It is "dependent on a homogeneous material cause" (*samānajātīyopādānāpekṣa*), meaning it depends upon a preceding moment that is of the same kind and serves as its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), just like the application of an axe or similar tools. This is because axes and such instruments, when employed for cutting and other tasks, depend upon their own preceding moments of a similar nature. Alternatively, it may be "independent of a material cause," as in the case of the application of [the initial] action (*karman*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of sounds from a lute and the like is intended. For when actions and such are first employed, there is no dependence upon a preceding similar moment.

As for the one who thinks: "Let there be no recognition [as a form of] inference because of its deviation; rather, that recognition which occurs with respect to an object situated right before one's eyes, being directly perceived, is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the stability of entities is established from this very means of knowledge, perception"—that too we shall refute later.

In this manner, the fallacious reason (*kuhetu*) adduced to establish stability (*sthairya*) is to be understood. For there exists no such property of the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*) that establishes stability and which follows after an object that is of a similar class and possesses a single, stable nature. Why? Because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) exist in this state; that is, because they have the nature of arising and ceasing through successive intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, every recognition of stability is contradicted by reasoning and contradicted by inference. How so? As has been stated.

Just as the proof for momentariness has been stated and will be stated here in this treatise, so too, due to the reason of contradicting logic, other reasons for proving stability imagined by others are also subject to the faults of verbal expression.

Thus, having begun with the position that a sentence is not a sequence of manifestations (*vyakti*), three types of manifestation have been postulated: the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the word, the removal of its obscuration (*āvaraṇavigama*), and cognition (*jñāna*). Among these, because the word is eternal, there is no production of an excellence; and since the absence of an obscuration is not something produced, the removal of an obscuration cannot be the manifestation. Thus, when these two alternatives have been rejected, it remains that cognition is the manifestation.
At that time, the sentence is a sequence of manifestations; that is, the sequential order of cognitions becomes the sentence.

And this is not tenable, because a sentence has the nature of non-intelligence (*abuddhi*). Nevertheless, it is stated even while [this objection] is admitted: if the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of a sentence consisting in the sequence of manifestations is to be proven, then the non-human origin of intelligence itself would be what is to be proven. In that case, if the non-dependence on a person—that is, the non-reliance on a person—of intelligence is to be proven, there is a contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñābādhā*). By what means? Simultaneously with what is accepted, what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣapratīta*), and what is inferred (*anumita*); that is, by what is accepted (*abhyupeta*), by what is perceived through direct perception, and by what is inferred.

In that case, the sequence of the sentence is the sequence of the cognitions; and since that [sequence] is not something distinct from the cognitions, if one were to establish that this sequence is not of human origin, it would be the cognition itself that would be established as being non-human. And in that regard, the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of this Mīmāṃsaka is contradicted. Why? Because, according to his own established doctrine, he accepts that cognitions are qualities of the person.

Demonstrating the contradiction by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), he says: "Indeed, this is directly perceived: that those cognitions arise from mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sense faculties (*indriya*) are included. From what kind of mental attention and so forth? From those for which the convention has been established as "person" (*puruṣa*) for the sake of linguistic brevity. This was stated according to his own view. Alternatively, "from the qualities (*guṇa*) of the person," which bypasses [the term] "of the person"; this, however, was stated according to the view of others.

Therefore, since the fact that cognition arising from mental attention and other such factors is an effect is established by direct perception, there is a contradiction with perception if its lack of human authorship (apauruṣeyatva) is what is being proven.

It might be thought: "Since the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*) is not perceived, there is no sublation by perception. To this he says: "But surely," and so forth. The existence [of the effect] only when the thing regarded as the cause exists, and its non-existence when that is absent—these two specific instances of presence and absence constitute the state of being an effect for a given entity; it is nothing other than these. That aforementioned existence is established by perception. If it is asked, "How is its non-existence when that [cause] is absent established by perception? he replies: "Non-existence, too."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "non-existence" (abhāva) is that whose characteristic (lakṣaṇa), or nature (svabhāva), is precisely non-apprehension (anupalabdhi). We shall also explain how this [non-existence] is established through the power of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Perception, by making known the very existence of a thing as distinct from others, leads to the cognition of non-existence by implication; thus, the term "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) has been employed. Furthermore, since the presence or absence of cognition occurs through the presence or absence of mental attention (*manaskāra*) and other factors, it is for this very reason—namely, because they arise when those [factors] are present—that the fact that cognitions are produced by human effort is to be inferred.

What is the reason? Because this state of being an effect possesses the logical mark (*liṅga*) of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus, by this, the sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādhā*) has been stated.

Now, one might argue: "The sentence is not the sequence of individual manifestations (*vyakti*), but rather the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*) is the sentence. To this he says: "Furthermore," and so forth. The difference of the sequence from the phonemes [is established] by means of the *sphoṭa*, according to the previously mentioned investigation of the *sphoṭa*. Even if [the sequence] were non-different [from the phonemes], that has already been refuted; moreover, there is no other possibility for a real entity (*vastu*) apart from difference and non-difference. In that case, the sequence of the all-pervading phonemes would have to be superimposed through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, how could it then be independent of a person? It must necessarily depend upon a person.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "varṇṇa" and so forth: "The sequence (*ānupūrvī*), which is distinct—that is, of a different nature—from the phonemes (*varṇa*), has already been refuted by the very same sequence of arguments used in the previous investigation of the *sphoṭa*.
[As stated: 'A sentence does not exist as something separate from the phonemes, because it is not perceived,' and so on; by such refutations, the sequence itself has also been rejected."

Nor is that [sequence] of the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*), because it would follow that there would be no difference in the cognition "it is water" (*saroruha*). Nor is it inexpressible in terms of identity or otherness, because the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) cannot transcend these two alternatives; for it does not transcend the conceptual alternatives of identity and otherness. Therefore, this delusion—that there is a sequence—must belong to a cognition that superimposes that form upon the phonemes, which are themselves devoid of such a form and lack any real, distinct sequential order, and which thus superimposes a sequential order.

And how can that sequence be non-human? It is indeed human. What is the reason? Because it is presented through the activity of the manifestation of the Buddha's cognition; for it has been shown [by him].

Furthermore, because there is no such thing as an eternal or absolute intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the sound (*dhvani*) or word (*śabda*) that exists must necessarily be non-absolute and unstable. That sound would either be without a cause, or it would have another cause distinct from the person (*puruṣa*). In the case of being without a cause, it would have to be eternal, since it would not depend on anything else. However, if it has another cause, it could not arise from the activity of a person; yet it does indeed arise from the activity of a person. Therefore, it is understood to be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).

"How so? and so forth asks the opponent. "How is it understood that sound, or anything else such as earth and so on, is not eternal? "Existence," says the Teacher (Dharmakīrti). "Because destruction is necessarily concomitant with mere existence. Therefore, the impermanence of sound follows from its cause; by the very fact of being existent, it does not fail to perish, nor does it depend upon any other cause. And sound is existent; therefore, it is not eternal—this is the meaning of the whole passage. Why is destruction necessarily concomitant with mere existence? He says: "For not," and so forth. Because for entities, what is called 'destruction' does not arise as some distinct property (*dharmāntara*) from any cause of destruction.

Since this is so, therefore (*tad*) destruction must be the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity. Why is this? Because the entity itself arises from its own causes as possessing that property—that is, as possessing the property of destruction. Destruction is precisely the state of having the property of existing for only a single moment; and that [property] arises from causes alone. This means that destruction belongs only to those things that are produced (*kṛtaka*), and not to other things that exist. As it has been said: "That which exists and is without cause is eternal."

And so forth. Nor is destruction the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of any particular entity. Why? Because that [position] will be refuted later. Therefore, destruction would have the nature of mere existence; it would have the nature of mere being (*sattā*). For that reason, sound or any other entity whatsoever is a vessel of existence, a substratum of existence—that is to say, it is "existent. Thus, it is established that it is not eternal.

The opponent says: "It is not established. For what reason? Because that very destruction is not established as having another birth (*apara-janman*). "Birth from another" is *parajanma*; "not birth from another" is *aparajanma*. This is because it is not established. That is to say, it is because the causelessness of destruction is not established.

For instance, wood is seen to be burned by fire and a jar broken by a staff; thus, causes of destruction such as fire and so forth are observed in relation to entities such as wood. Indeed, since the destruction of wood and other things occurs when fire and the like are present, and their non-destruction occurs when they are absent, there is a positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding destruction. And this, they say, is the defining characteristic of a cause and its effect, or of that which possesses a cause. As it has been said: "Without the presence of the conditions for destruction—namely, impact, contact with fire, and so forth—destruction does not enter into association with jars and the like. (2)

He refutes [this] with the words "no," and so forth. In the world, fire and the like are not perceived as causes of destruction by acting upon wood and other materials; rather, when each preceding moment of wood and so forth ceases of its own accord through its own inherent cessation, and another subsequent moment in the form of ash and so forth arises, fire and the like are recognized as the causes of the destruction of the wood and so forth—not because they perform an act of destruction.

But from what does that transformation arise? To this he says: "By a specific condition," and so forth. A specific condition, such as fire, acts as a cooperative cause; [the transformation occurs] by depending upon that. Even granting this for the sake of argument, we say: let fire be the cause of the destruction of the wood. That destruction has its birth from fire (*agni-ja*). The analysis of the compound is: "that whose birth is from fire. Now, is it the wood itself, or something other than the wood, that is the destroyer of the fire in that case?

If destruction, as a distinct entity, were to arise from the cause [of the wood], then the wood would still be visible. Why? Because [the wood] would not have been destroyed. What does this mean for the wood? It means that if destruction, as a distinct entity, were to arise—that is, be produced—from a cause distinct from the wood, then the wood would be called "non-existent" or "destroyed"; that is to say, it would simply no longer exist.

If it is argued that even though [the wood] has not perished, it is nonetheless seen because another object has arisen, he says: "Or it is not seen. Why is it not seen? It is indeed seen. However, if one thing were not seen because another thing had arisen and the former had perished, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For by the arising of just any other object whatsoever, everything would become non-existent, or else it would simply not be seen. But that very object which is born from fire is the one that perishes, not everything; for this wood is perceived in the world as having the nature of destruction—this is the meaning.

He explains this very statement of summary (*grahaṇakavākya*) with the words beginning "yadi" (if). "If that very thing produced by fire is the non-existence (*abhāva*), i.e., the destruction (*vināśa*) of the wood; 'tad' means therefore; because this wood has become [that non-existence], i.e., because it has been destroyed, it is not seen. He refutes this with the words beginning "bhavatu" (let it be). "Let there be this name or designation for that object produced by fire, namely 'non-existence' (*abhāva*). Nevertheless, how can one thing be the destruction of another merely by name? For it is not logical that the wood should cease to be seen merely by applying the name "destruction"—even though some object produced by fire has been given that name.
[Objection: But surely, because it is perceived as such, this is simply destruction itself; therefore, calling it "its destruction" is a mere matter of terminology. To this he says:

"Nor is one entity the destruction of another, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). All entities would then be the destruction of wood. This recalls exactly what was stated immediately prior. He thinks as follows: Just as all entities, being distinct things (*arthāntara*), are not perceived as having the nature of the destruction of wood, so too, since [the effect] produced by fire is a distinct thing, it would not be perceived as having the nature of the destruction of wood.

It might be argued as follows: "If, because it is a different entity (*arthāntara*), the effect produced by fire does not have the nature of destruction, then smoke too would not be an effect of fire, since it is likewise a different entity, like a jar. Yet, even though there is no difference in their being different entities, the destruction of wood—which is produced by fire—does indeed exist; therefore, [the fire's effect] will likewise have the nature of destruction."

Therefore, he says: "Because there is no distinction. This means that since that entity produced by fire—being a real thing (*vastu*)—is not distinct from other things such as jars and the like, there is no difference between them. The implication is: how can it have the nature of destruction? For destruction consists in cessation. As for smoke, however, even if it is a different entity, it is perfectly logical for it to be an effect of fire, because there is no contradiction between being a different entity and being an effect of fire; thus, this [objection] is trivial. If it is argued: "The nature of destruction produced by fire in wood is not universal, as it does not apply to jars and so forth; therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," [the response follows].

Regarding the claim that "this fire-induced destruction occurs in the wood," what relationship exists between the wood and its destruction? Since they do not stand in a relationship of mutual benefit or assistance, there is no relationship at all. If it is argued that the wood is the substratum (*āśraya*) and destruction is the dependent (*āśrayin*) because it possesses that substratum—and thus a relationship of substratum and dependent exists—this is not so, because that very relationship of substratum and dependent will be refuted later.

Destruction is something produced; wood is its producer. If, therefore, there exists a relationship of produced and producer between destruction and the wood, then what is meant by "from fire"? Why is it said that destruction arises from fire? What is the reason? Because that destruction comes into being—that is, originates—from the wood alone. If it is argued that there is no fault because the destruction arises from the wood in dependence upon fire (*tadapekṣāt agnyapekṣāt*), and thus the fault previously stated—that destruction would not be caused by fire—does not apply; [The response follows: ... [text continues] ... [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here].

What need is there for wood to depend upon fire, since it has already obtained its excellence from the fire? None at all. Or, if the wood were to obtain its excellence from the fire, then there would have to be the production of another, second wood designated as "excellence. And in that case, the original wood would be one whose cause of destruction does not exist; the analysis of the compound is: "that which has no cause of its own destruction. Consequently, it would be seen exactly as it was before.
