It might be argued: "Since the second piece of wood arises from that very fire which possesses an excellence [of heat], the destruction of the previous piece of wood occurs from that same fire. [To this we reply:

What is the connection between this destruction produced by the fire and the previous piece of wood? That same dilemma remains. It was stated immediately above what the connection with the "piece of wood" is.

Furthermore, if one resorts to a relationship such as that of substrate and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), then because that will be refuted later, the entire argument must be repeated, and the dilemma would become infinite.

"Therefore" (*tad*) means that, since fire necessarily assists toward a subsequent excellence in the wood which is capable of being connected with destruction, it produces a new wood altogether; thus, the previous wood would have to be seen remaining in its former state—this is the conclusion.

Furthermore, the so-called "destruction of wood" is said to be the non-existence (*abhāva*) of the wood; and non-existence is not an effect (*kārya*). For if one were to accept that it is an effect by way of positive affirmation (*vidhi*), it would follow that it is an entity (*bhāva*). Therefore, the statement "one produces non-existence" means "one does not produce an entity"; it is merely a negation of action (*kriyā-pratiṣedha-mātra*). And thus, since the agent of that [destruction] is an agent of non-existence—or rather, a non-agent—precisely because it is a mere negation of action, it was stated in the section on the consideration of the locus and the located regarding the universal and its instances (*sāmānya-tadvat*) that fire and other such factors need not be depended upon for the destruction of wood.

Furthermore, when the non-existence—that is, the destruction—of the intrinsic nature of wood and so forth is admitted to be distinct from that very intrinsic nature of wood and so forth, then the entity such as wood would be excluded from that non-existence which is a separate thing. Consequently, for that wood and so forth which is being excluded from existence, its own intrinsic nature alone would be established; for it follows that for that which is excluded from non-existence, existence itself is established. Thus, how could wood and so forth be said to have become non-existent through a destruction produced by fire and other causes?

Since this is so, there is no destruction of one thing by another; the meaning is that one entity does not constitute the destruction of another entity. Even granting [the opponent's position], we say: let there be a distinct destruction produced by fire as a separate entity, yet why is the wood not seen remaining in its very same state? Proving this very point, he says: "What is this contradiction?"—namely, between the existence of that distinct destruction produced by fire and the perception of the wood; for if that were the case, the wood would be seen in its original condition.

Now, one might object: "That entity which is a distinct thing produced by fire is the destruction of the wood, because it is perceived as having the nature of destruction. And destruction is non-existence; that which is the non-existence of the wood is indeed produced as having a form that is the opposite of the wood. Nor is this [destruction] impossible to produce in its opposite form simply because it is a distinct thing, like a jar. For smoke does not fail to be the effect of fire just because it is a distinct thing, like a jar."

"Therefore, just as smoke, although it is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), is produced by fire, so too is destruction produced as a contrary form (*virodhirūpa*). And since two things that are contradictory by way of mutual exclusion cannot both be present, how could there be the perception of wood when its contrary—namely, that other thing called 'destruction' which is produced by fire—is present? Thus says Śaṅkara. 1.

That is incorrect. For there is no contradiction between a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) and being an effect of fire; even though smoke is a distinct entity, its status as an effect of fire remains entirely uncontradicted. Furthermore, a distinct entity produced by fire possesses the nature of existence (*bhāvarūpatā*) because it has the property of coming into being (*bhavanadharmatā*). And how could that which is an existent (*bhāva*) be, for you, a non-existent (*abhāva*)? Since destruction (*vināśa*) is held to be a non-existent due to its contradiction [with existence], destruction would thus be contradictory to the existence of a distinct entity. Moreover, this is not so, because even a distinct entity appears in the form of destruction.

The nature of the destruction of wood and so forth consists in its being the cessation of its own essence (*svarasanirodha*). For it is this cessation of its own essence that is the cause for the appearance of destruction. However, if one does not accept the cessation of its own essence, how could even a distinct entity appear as having the nature of destruction? This has already been stated [above] regarding the fact that [destruction] would have the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) and so on. Therefore, how can it be said: "Because of the production of a distinct entity called 'destruction' which is its opposite, the wood is no longer perceived"? If destruction were formless (*nīrūpa*), then there would indeed be a contradiction between it and the existent entity; however, in that case too, it could not be a distinct entity nor produced by a cause, precisely because it is formless.

Therefore, if fire were to produce something else [than itself], the wood would be seen remaining in its original state. If it is argued that the wood is not seen because it is grasped—that is, appropriated—by that other entity produced by fire, then it follows that this other entity is an obscuration of the wood. But that is not logical; for it is not possible for that other entity to serve as an obscuration of the wood.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "yadi" (if). "By that" means by another object produced by fire. "That" refers to the other object produced by fire. Nor is it logical for this [non-perception] to be imagined as an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*). For an obstruction would indeed obstruct the perception of the object being obscured; it would not, however, obstruct the capacities of a substance such as impact and so forth. This is because we observe impact and the like in the case of jars and other objects enveloped in darkness. In this context, "impact" (*abhighāta*) is the obstruction of the arising of another [entity] in its own location.

By the word "etcetera," odors, tastes, and so forth are included. Now, if one were to maintain that the obstruction itself binds all functional capacity to the wood, then, while such a total impediment is admitted, it would not be by this very obstruction that the wood is destroyed, nor by fire. Why? Because its destruction would result from that [obstruction] alone, through the removal of all capacities of the wood. And that being the case, there would again follow the same consequence regarding that [destruction] as well—namely, that it would be distinct from the fire, just as in the case of fire being the cause of destruction for something else.

The fault that was stated in detail regarding the destruction of wood by fire would also apply if the destruction of the wood were produced by another entity [distinct from the wood] caused by the fire. And thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For by that other entity—the destruction caused by the fire—another entity called "destruction" would have to be produced, and by that yet another, leading to an infinite regress. Alternatively, to avoid this fault, one might claim that the capacities of the wood, such as its susceptibility to being struck, remain entirely unaltered.

Even then, since the wood’s capacity for being struck and so forth remains unimpaired, what has been destroyed by that other [entity] produced by fire, such that the obstruction would be removed and the wood be seen in that way? As for the phrase "if... and so on: the analysis of the compound is "that from which the arising of fire occurs. The meaning is: because of being grasped by an entity called destruction that has arisen from fire. In that case, destruction itself would be subject to destruction. What is the reason? Because of its production.

The meaning is that because it possesses origination, destruction itself would be destructible, just like wood. Consequently, due to the destruction of that destruction, there would be the seeing of the wood once again.

He explains this with the words beginning "necessarily" (*avaśyam*): being something that possesses origination, the destruction of the wood must necessarily perish. When that destruction of the wood has perished, there would be the re-emergence of the wood and so forth; its manifestation would occur.

With the words "the killer and the killed," etc., [the opponent] raises a further objection: Just as when the killer of Caitra is killed, there is the non-reappearance—that is, the non-arising again—of the killed Caitra; so too, here, even though the wood has perished, it is argued that there is likewise a non-reappearance of the wood.

He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning “of the killer” (*hantuḥ*) and so forth. This resolution is not tenable. Why? Because the killer does not possess the nature of death. For the killer of Caitra is not, by his own nature, death; rather, he is the slayer. Therefore, it is logical that upon the destruction of that [slayer], Caitra would not come into being again; however, since death has not ceased, there must necessarily be a coming into being again.

He explains [the point] with the words beginning "vināśa" (destruction). Even if there were a destruction of destruction, there would be no restoration of the entity—that is, no returning to its former state—because even when the killer is killed, one who was killed by that killer does not come back to life. This rebuttal is not tenable. Why? Because the killer is the cause of that killing; since Caitra’s death has him as its cause, yet that killer is not of the nature of death itself.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "No," and so forth. We do not say that when the causes of destruction—such as fire, a staff, or the like—have ceased, the entity must come into existence again because it was not destroyed. If one were to speak in such a manner, this [objection] would indeed be a valid rebuttal. What then? [We refer to] that non-existence of an entity, such as wood, which is produced by fire and the like. Of what kind is it? It is characterized by absolute non-apprehension (*atyantānupalabdhi*). And here, the action (*kriyā*) resides in the object (*karman*), namely, apprehension (*upalabdhi*).

By the negation of that [non-existence], absolute non-perception is said to be the absence of all causal capacity. When there is the cessation of such an absence, what other course remains for an entity than its abiding in its own nature? That is to say, its very abiding in its own nature is its course.

But when the killer has perished, it is not logical for [the victim] to come into being again; for the killer of Caitra is not equivalent to his destruction. What then? He is equivalent to a staff or similar instrument—meaning he is like a staff and so forth—because he is the cause of destruction. For the death of this Caitra is equivalent to his destruction. Upon the cessation of that [killer], which is equivalent to his destruction—that is, upon the cessation of that death—there would indeed be the rebirth of this Caitra. Thus far, the fault has been stated regarding the case where destruction is a distinct entity.

With reference to the state of non-difference, he says: "Even if there is no otherness," and so forth. Even if destruction were non-different from the entity, the wood itself would be the destruction; for that wood, having arisen from its own causes, exists [by virtue of those causes]. Since nothing further needs to be done by fire and the like, destruction—being of such a nature—is without a cause. Therefore, apart from the alternatives of identity or difference, there is no other possible way for destruction, which is a property of the entity, to exist.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "not a different thing" (*anarthāntara*). When destruction is not a different thing from the wood, then that very wood becomes the entity called its destruction. And since that wood and so forth already exist even prior to the presence of fire and other [causes], one must consider: what efficacy do fire and the like have here toward the wood and so forth which are to be destroyed? In some places, the reading is "of the staff and so forth" (*daṇḍādīnām*); however, that should be explained with reference to jars and the like. Therefore, because of its assistance (*tanmukhāt*).

In that regard, since the causes of destruction provide no assistance to the wood and so forth, those causes of destruction do not depend in any way whatsoever—by any form or manner—upon that wood and so forth. Nor does this fire and so forth deserve to have a relationship with the wood and so forth such that "this is the cause of destruction for that. Why? Because a relationship is based upon assistance; otherwise, if one were to postulate a relationship without assistance, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), whereby everything would be related to everything else.
It might be argued: fire and so forth do not directly benefit wood and so forth, but rather do so by producing a benefit that is related to them.

Therefore, he says: "By way of succession," and so forth. An assistance is produced by fire and the like for wood and the like as its correlate, but not directly. Even when such assistance is conceived as occurring through a succession, this dilemma necessarily follows: is that assistance, even through succession, a different entity (*arthāntara*), or is it that very same wood and so forth? In that regard, if the assistance were a different entity from that wood and so forth, what would be the connection between that [wood] and this assistance, such that one could say, "This is the assistance of that wood"?

In that case, regarding the wood and so forth, one must inquire into how that assistance produced by fire can itself be an assistant; for without it, there would be no connection. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is intended—namely, that in that case too another assistance would have to be postulated. Likewise, even if the assistance were non-different from the object, the aforementioned inquiry would remain: "Is it destruction, or is it the wood itself? and so on. Therefore, because an existing form (*rūpa*) cannot transcend being either identical to or different from its cause.

It might be argued: "Since an existing entity cannot transcend being either identical to or different from itself, the production of an auxiliary [effect] caused by a factor of destruction is simply non-existent.

To this he says: "The auxiliary," and so forth. This is because it is characterized by the production of a form; that is, it is characterized by the production of an existing form. Consequently, that entity must either be produced by that destroyer or something else. And in both cases, the aforementioned fault applies. Thus, a cause of destruction that is devoid of performing either that [very action] or another is not a producer at all; therefore, it is not the cause of anything. Furthermore, if it were not a cause, then things such as a staff would not be required by a perishable object such as a jar.
Therefore, this entity, by its very existence, possesses such-and-such a nature—that is, a perishable nature.

Anticipating an objection from another who takes "destruction" (*nāśa*) to mean "non-existence through annihilation" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), [the author] says: "Even if it were causeless," and so forth. For if it were causeless, it would have to be eternal; and because it would be eternal, destruction would exist even at the time of the entity's existence—thus, if you argue that there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the coexistence of the entity and its destruction, this is not a fault. Why? Because how could there be eternality for a non-existent destruction characterized by annihilation?

He explains this with the words "It might be thus," and so forth: "Even though for the proponent of momentariness destruction is causeless, nevertheless, because it is necessarily eternal, existence—characterized by the absence of that [destruction]—would consist in the non-cessation of destruction; and destruction—characterized by the absence of that [existence]—would consist in the cessation of existence. Thus, both would coexist in a single thing."

This is not so. Why? Because that non-existence, being a non-entity (*avastu*), cannot possess properties such as permanence and so forth. For when something is non-existent, this conceptual distinction between permanent and impermanent is impossible; for those two [categories] are properties of entities (*vastudharma*). Furthermore, destruction, which is characterized by the cessation of an entity, is a mere nothingness (*akiñcit*).

Furthermore, since that which is arising exists eternally, it would necessarily coexist with something; yet destruction does not occur. Rather, an entity whose nature is to abide in a single characteristic simply does not exist by itself; thus, this is merely a negation of activity. Therefore, the fault mentioned immediately above does not apply.

Furthermore, he anticipates the opponent's objection: "If destruction is non-existent, then since destruction is non-existent, there would follow the consequence that an entity is not destructible; that is, an entity would lack the property of being destructible. This consequence, too, is untenable, because we do not maintain that the destruction of an entity occurs through a destruction that is a separate entity.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "How? [The opponent asks: How could a non-existent destruction destroy an entity? For it is impossible for that which is non-existent to possess causal activity. Therefore, for this reason, the entity would be indestructible; thus, the undesirable consequence does not even arise. What is the reason? Because it is not admitted that an entity is destroyed by a destruction that is a distinct entity from itself. He supports this very point with the passage beginning with "For whoever... Whoever is a proponent who says, "Destruction is nothing at all"—how could he desire the destruction of an entity by means of that destruction which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? He would not so desire.

"How so? and so forth asks the opponent. If destruction (*vināśa*) does not exist—that is, if it is non-existent—how can there be such a state as "destroyed"? It would simply not have been destroyed at all. For instance, in the present state, things are characterized by non-existent destruction; the analysis of the compound is "those for whom destruction is non-existent. Indeed, they are not reckoned as being destroyed. And when the destruction of an entity has not occurred, how can it be designated by that [destruction] as "possessing destruction" (*nāśavān*)? For something that does not possess a certain intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be connected with it.

That entity is designated by that unrelated [property] in such a way; it is designated by the word as "possessing that" (*tadvān*), or it is apprehended by cognition. He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). Indeed, it is not the case that destruction does not exist for an entity; rather, destruction certainly exists. If so, why is it said that "it does not exist"? That destruction which belongs to the entity does not exist [as a separate thing]. If destruction does not come into being, then how is it said that "destruction exists"? He says: the entity itself has the property of abiding for a single moment; destruction is that which lasts for one moment.
If destruction is indeed the very nature of the entity (*bhāva*), how then does the world designate that "the destruction of the entity has occurred"?

To this he says: "In darkness," and so forth. People in worldly practice designate it according to their perception—having ascertained (*vibhāvayantaḥ*) that this entity, whose nature is to endure for only a single moment and which is characterized by the deception of the arising of a similar [moment], no longer exists at a later time due to its non-perception because the continuity (*santāna*) has been severed. It was stated previously that they designate it as "the destruction of this entity has occurred" in accordance with such a cognition.

For no other form whatsoever, called "destruction" or otherwise, ever arises in an entity that has already been produced. That very entity, being just as it was from its own causes, exists for only a single moment. Therefore, it does not come into being through anything called "destruction"; rather, that entity is what is termed "destroyed. What then? It is simply the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of this entity, characterized by a duration of only one moment, by virtue of which the entity is said to be "destroyed. Otherwise, if it did not possess that nature intrinsically, it would not perish even in the absence of another cause.

If that which is called "destruction" is nothing at all, then how can it be said by you that destruction is now causeless? For when something has no intrinsic nature whatsoever, what is the point of considering whether it is causeless or caused? Furthermore, how can there be a distinction such as "the destruction of an entity"?

He refutes this with the words beginning "perishing" (*naśyan*). A perishing entity is independent of another; that is to say, it does not depend upon an external cause of destruction. [The phrase] "not for the sake of making known" means not for the sake of making known its independence from another. That state of destruction has been described by us as being without a cause. By superimposing a distinction—that is, a difference—of that state of destruction onto the entity through the conceptualizing mind (*vikalpabuddhi*), the following is what is meant: "the destruction of an entity is causeless," which means its destruction does not possess a cause.

He explains this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). An entity (*bhāva*) that has already arisen does not obtain destruction from another cause of destruction. Why? Because such a thing—namely, that which possesses a perishable nature (*naśvara-svabhāva*)—arises by its very own existence-cause (*sattā-hetu*) alone. For this reason, it does not depend on another [cause] imagined to be a cause of destruction; thus, it is "independent of another" (*aparāpekṣa*). Such being the case, this phenomenon (*dharma*) called destruction is "an independent phenomenon" (*aparāpekṣa-dharma*); [the compound] is for the purpose of negating that [dependence].

This means for the purpose of refuting destruction that has a cause. "By making known its intrinsic nature" means by making known the perishable nature of the entity (*bhāva*). This connects with the phrase "its very nature is stated thus. "Stated thus" means it is stated that its destruction occurs without a cause. When there is a desire to know only that—namely, when there is a desire to know merely this much: "Does the destruction of an entity arise from something other than itself?"—in what manner is it stated?

Having mentally distinguished—by means of the intellect—as if it were a separate entity from the substratum (dharmin), a property called "destruction," and having made the division that "this is the destruction of this entity," [the author says: "even though non-perishability has been established in reality as non-distinct from non-existence according to the manner described above, those of dull intellect, by superimposing destruction as a quality or property, agitate themselves. This is the connection [of the sentence].

But why do they cause such confusion? He says: "In some cases," and so forth. Because in expressions such as "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), where a case-ending denoting separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) is employed, one observes such [a distinction]; that is, because a distinction between the two related entities is perceived. Here, people are deceived by the mere proclamation, "destruction (*nāśa*) occurs of an entity (*bhāva*"), having superimposed upon the entity a quality (*guṇa*) or property (*dharma*)—namely, destruction—which is distinct from it, and having further superimposed existence (*sattā*) or being upon that imagined quality.

Having superimposed that quality called "destruction"—whether it has a cause or no cause—through a distinction in their views, by means of a conceptualization of existence (*bhāva*) or a conceptualization of a real entity (*vastu*), [they do so] with what kind of [conceptualization]? With one in which reality (*tattva*) is not established; they agitate themselves with that [conceptualization] in which reality is not established. With the words "even from itself" (*svataḥ api*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's intention: even for one for whom destruction occurs spontaneously without a cause, if the existence of that very non-existence—that is, destruction—is admitted even from itself, then this conceptualization characterized as "identity" or "otherness" arises in the mind.

He explains with the words beginning "nanu" (surely). The meaning is that there is neither posteriority nor anteriority even in the case of causelessness. This alternative regarding identity or difference is the same for the destruction of an entity—that is, a real thing—which occurs by its own nature.

Is destruction a different entity from the object, or is it the object itself? In that regard, if it were a different entity, then why is the object not perceived while the destruction—that different entity—exists (i.e., has its being)? Alternatively, if destruction is not a different entity, then even though it is not different, that very thing such as the jar would be what is called "destruction. Therefore, since nothing at all has happened to this object, how can it be said to be "destroyed"?

He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely). In this context, it has been stated. What was stated? That for that entity (*bhāva*), there exists no property-form (*dharmarūpa*) called destruction (*vināśa*) that is distinct from it. If so, how can an entity be "destructible"? He says: it was previously stated that it simply does not exist [anymore].

Clarifying this very point, he says: "For indeed," and so forth. For this proponent of the destruction of what has not yet arisen does not claim that for an entity already produced by its own causes, there exists some property such as destruction—whether of the nature of an entity, the nature of a non-entity, or something else like persistence or alteration—but rather he says: "On the contrary, that very entity does not exist," thereby stating merely the cessation of the entity. Thus, the meaning is this: in the first moment, the entity comes into being as it did not previously exist.
In the second moment, for that [entity], there is neither existence nor non-existence; nor does its own-nature undergo destruction; it simply ceases by itself.

If, however, by the term "destruction" one were to speak of the existence—meaning the arising—of some dharma, then existence would not have been negated by this proponent; that is to say, the cessation of existence would not have been stated. And thus, while the cessation of existence is the subject at hand, because another distinct entity is being prescribed, only something irrelevant would have been said. Why? Because there is no such thing as an "existence" (a real entity) called destruction, or characterized by the cessation of existence, which could arise through its own arising, such that by the prescription of that [destruction] the existence itself would undergo its own cessation.

This is what is meant: just as when a thing exists within consciousness, the thing does not undergo transformation, but rather that consciousness alone becomes related to it; so too, if one accepts that the cessation of a thing occurs, then that very property called "cessation" would be related to it, but the thing itself would not cease. How, then, could there be its cessation? Therefore, at that time, that thing has not become ceased unless it ceases of its own accord.

Therefore, as for what is said: "If non-existence (*abhāva*) does not occur even when there is no [prior] existence (*bhāva*), then there would be no destruction; but if it does occur, would it be different from that [existence] or non-different? In either of these two cases, the existence would be perceived at all times because it has not been destroyed. Therefore, there is no destruction of non-existence. How then is existence not perceived at all times? Because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [This is the objection.]

That is refuted. For the existence of a perceptible object is pervaded by its being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, in the absence of that [means of cognition], there is non-existence. Or, if it exists, it must necessarily be an object of a means of valid cognition—so how can there be a lack of apprehension? If, on the other hand, its existence consists in its having an imperceptible nature, then in that case there is the cessation of its perceptible nature. And is that [cessation] distinct from the entity or non-distinct? In either of these two positions, the perception of the entity would still occur; thus the fault remains exactly as before. Therefore, there is neither the non-existence of the entity, nor the fault of its being indestructible, because it has ceased in its own form.

If it is argued that because the cessation of an entity is formless, it must be something other than the formal entity, we reply: how can there be "otherness" for that which has no form at all? Could it then be "oneness"? That too does not exist, because it lacks form. Therefore, with respect to the entity, one merely negates both its identity and its difference from this [cessation], just as in the case of a hare's horn.

But even so, how is it maintained that an entity does not exist in the second moment? For if the entity exists in the second moment, then how can it be maintained that it does not exist there, given the contradiction? If, on the other hand, it does not exist, then how can it be said that "the entity does not exist," since it is non-existent? That is incorrect. Because even regarding the first moment, it is said in common worldly usage that "the entity comes into being. And in that case, if the entity [already] exists, why is it said that it "comes into being"? Therefore, this [objection] is trivial; for in all cases, the linguistic conventions of affirmation and negation are established by taking the entity as it is presented to the mind.
Therefore, this remains established: at that time, that entity would not have existed if it were not itself existent.

One might object: "By this statement, 'it is not self-existent' (na svayambhāvaḥ), it is actually said that the non-existence of an entity occurs by itself; and in that case, the same fault [as before] would apply. To this he says: "And 'it does not exist,' etc. The word *ca* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*). Because the statement "an entity does not exist" is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation) and not a *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation). Where there is merely the cessation of what was [erroneously] presupposed, without any contact with a positive portion of a real entity, that is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*.

However, where the negation of one thing entails the affirmation of another, that is a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). Otherwise, even here in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), if there were the existence or affirmation of some entity, it would not be expressed by the word "negation. Why? Because in both cases—both the *prasajya* and the *paryudāsa*—the affirmation (*vidhi*) is primary.

And if there were a positive injunction even in the case of a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), then negation itself would not exist. And thus, because there would be no negation of anything, there could be no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) anywhere either. Why is that? For if some entity were to be excluded from something, then it would be distinct from that; it would be touched by the distinction from the entity being excluded, by way of the exclusion of that which is to be excluded.

Just as in the case of the command "Bring a non-Brahmin," there is contact with a Kṣatriya or the like through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of a Brahmin; yet that is not the negation (*nivartana*) of anything at all. Why? Because even when it is said that "in every case there is the negation of something," no exclusion of an entity (*bhāvavyavaccheda*) is perceived; rather, by the word "negation" (*nivṛtti*), one perceives only some positive entity (*bhāva*).

Moreover, by this proponent who asserts the cessation of an entity, even while speaking of cessation, no actual cessation has been stated; rather, it would be merely the existence of another thing that has been stated. And thus, when one thing is said to be distinct from another through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the mutual distinction between those two is not established. In the absence of such a distinction, there can be no exclusion, because exclusion is characterized by the apprehension of one thing through its distinction from what is other than it. Therefore, in the manner described above, since there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would also not exist.

The meaning is that there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*), which is the following or affirmation of some object. Why? Because that positive concomitance is characterized by the persistence of a single nature. And that persistence, as well as the stability of that single nature, could only occur when there is the exclusion or avoidance of what is other than it. Yet, according to your view, that exclusion of what is other does not exist. Consequently, the world would be devoid of engagement and withdrawal based on words; there would be an absence of the linguistic practice of affirmation and negation regarding verbal objects.

It is not the case that [the word "destruction"] does not function in this way; therefore, one must necessarily admit that for some things, what is expressed by a word is merely an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

And since this is so, when it is said that "the destruction of a certain entity occurs," it must mean that the entity itself does not exist; it is not that some other distinct property called "destruction" is being predicated of it. For just as there is a real distinction in the expression "Caitra’s son," so too in the expression "the destruction of an entity," the use of the genitive case is identical; thus he says, "No," and so forth.

Indeed, a rule observed in one context does not apply everywhere simply because of a similarity in the mere sound of the word "Caitra’s son. The real rule observed in the case of "Caitra’s son" is not necessarily applicable here as well, in the case of "the destruction of an entity," because a real-world application cannot be established by the mere occurrence of a word.

This very point is stated by the words beginning with "not indeed" (*na hi*). Because a certain person is given the name "donkey" (*gardabha*), the properties of a donkey (*bāleyadharma*)—that is, the properties of a donkey—are not to be applied even to that human being. Likewise, in the sentence "Caitra has a son," the rule observed—the prescription of another entity, namely a son—is not to be applied to destruction (*nāśa*). In the case of "the destruction of an entity occurs" (*bhāvasya nāśo bhavati*), here too, destruction must be prescribed as something distinct from the entity. What is the reason? Because of contradiction. It has been stated that since destruction is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), and non-existence is contradictory to coming into being (*bhavana*).
If destruction is not a distinct entity, why is it said that "destruction occurs of an existent"?

To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. Even when one speaks of "the destruction of an existent," the purpose [of such a designation] has already been explained; for it was stated in the passage beginning, "Even though a property is like a distinct entity from the substratum, when the mind distinguishes the property [from the substratum] and there is a desire to know that alone, it is the very nature [of the thing] that is spoken of in that way. Thus it has been made known.

Therefore, since non-existence (*abhāva*) is nothing at all, the conceptual distinction between identity and difference is not applicable to it. Consequently, this conceptual distinction between identity and difference would only apply to an entity (*bhāva*) when a thing comes into being. What is the reason? Because existence (*bhavana*), as a positive affirmation (*vidhi*), conforms to a real entity (*vastu*).

Now, even in the case of the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*), that very thing has produced its own excellence; so how can it be said to have perished? Therefore, this [entity] is not "perished" in the sense of remaining in that same state. It is "perished" because it no longer exists by itself. It is not "perished" due to the production of something else; for by the production of an excellence, it is not the case that the thing itself has ceased to exist. This is because non-existence is characterized by the exclusion of all properties of existence through the cessation of all designations of excellence, whereas existence is characterized by the inclusion of production.

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "existence" (*bhāva*). Existence (*bhāva*) means becoming (*bhavana*), that is to say, arising (*utpāda*). That [arising] necessarily depends on something else; it depends on an agent of becoming (*bhavitṛ*), because there is no such thing as becoming in the absence of an agent of becoming. And that existence is nothing other than the very nature (*svabhāva*) or the entity (*vastu*) itself in its operation (*vyāpāra*). What is the reason? Because that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) cannot be involved in anything such as "becoming" and so forth; for there would be no connection. Furthermore, what is called "operation" is not a separate entity.

However, "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is indeed the arising of a nature as it truly is, that is, the arising of a specific nature. And how could such an arising belong to a destruction that is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? If there is no engagement with activity for that which lacks intrinsic nature, how then can there be conventional usage such as "the non-existence of a rabbit's horn"? The meaning is that the conventional usage "the rabbit's horn becomes a non-existence" occurs by means of an activity characterized by "becoming. By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of [expressions] such as "the son of a barren woman becomes a non-existence" is intended.

He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). Indeed, it is not stated by way of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) that "the hare’s horn is something [existent], whether it be an absence or something else. Rather, by the sentence "in this way the hare’s horn is an absence," it is shown—by means of the phrase "of this [hare’s horn]"—that its absence occurs; that is, a negation of existence (*bhāvapratiṣedha*) is made, namely, "it does not exist as a positive entity. Furthermore, people who engage in worldly discourse (*vyavahartṛ*), having superimposed [this notion] as if it were an active operation, demonstrate that "this hare’s horn and so forth is thus an absence."

By some particular context—that is, by relying on the occasion of the inquiry as to whether things such as a rabbit’s horn are non-existent or not—that rabbit’s horn and so forth do not become non-existent or not [in that sense]. However, that rabbit’s horn and so forth does not, through mere conventional usage, come to possess such functional activity. This is because the reality (*tattva*) regarding that rabbit’s horn and so forth consists in the discernment of all objects as being devoid of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of any object;
there is no inclusion therein of any non-existent thing, such as coming into being or the like.

If it is argued that destruction, even if it has a cause, will be of such a nature [as non-existence], he says: "No," and so forth. In this way, destruction is held by others to be characterized by the absence of all objects, like the horn of a hare. What is the reason? Because that destruction arises—that is, comes into being—within a real entity (*vastu*). And how can that which comes into being be a non-entity (*abhāva*)? It would be a contradiction.

If, however, this destruction is indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and is merely described by speakers as if it possessed activity—saying "it happens thus"—but does not itself possess the property of occurring in that way because it is formless (*nīrūpa*), then even one who asserts "non-existence comes into being" while maintaining this view actually intends that "nothing at all comes into being," since this statement consists merely in the negation of an action.

Therefore, when an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) exists in some object by way of a form that is not superimposed by itself, it does not transcend two alternatives—namely, identity or otherness—because there is no other possible mode.

(280) If it is argued: "The person (*pudgala*) is neither the intrinsic nature of the aggregates such as form, nor is it other than form and the rest; therefore, its intrinsic nature indeed transcends identity and otherness," that is not so. Because what is called "otherness" of an intrinsic nature is simply its non-identity, which is precisely its lack of being that very intrinsic nature.

If the person (*pudgala*) does not have the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), then it must be something other than the aggregates. For it is not the case that even for form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), which are well-known to be distinct, their mutual distinctness consists in anything other than their having a different nature; rather, distinctness is simply the state of not having that [other's] nature. And since this [state of having a different nature] exists in the person as well, it too must be accepted as being other than the aggregates.

If it is argued that even if they do not have the same nature (*asvabhāvatva*), there is still a lack of mutual essential connection (*svabhāvāpratibandha*), which constitutes their being "other," [we reply: that very lack of connection exists between the person (*pudgala*) and the aggregates (*skandha*). Therefore, even though they do not have the same nature, the person would not be "other" than the aggregates. [The author] refutes this with the words beginning "What is this... and so forth. What is this so-called "connection" of the person with the aggregates, by virtue of which that connection would not exist? [For if it did not exist,] the person would neither have the nature of the aggregates nor a nature other than the aggregates. The compound *anyasvabhāva* is analyzed as: "that which has another nature" (*anyaḥ svabhāvo 'sya*).

If it is argued that the very birth of the person (*pudgala*) from the aggregates (*skandhas*) constitutes its causal connection, then—given this—it would follow that because the person is an effect of the aggregates, it is intended to be inexpressible as being either identical to or different from them. If that were the case, all causes would be mutually inexpressible [in terms of identity or difference]. And if that were so—that is, if inexpressibility follows from being an effect—then since everything is in some way useful to everything, whether directly or indirectly, there would be a causal relationship everywhere; consequently, nothing at all would be distinct from anything else.

And thus, by asserting "inexpressibility" through the definition of inexpressibility just mentioned, one would merely have stated the relationship of cause and effect in different words; there would be no difference in meaning whatsoever. Furthermore, otherness (*anyatva*) has certainly not been negated. For we define otherness as the mutual non-conformity and non-mingling of two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). And since that non-conformity of intrinsic nature exists among all things that possess such natures, there is indeed mutual otherness.

Nor is there any other relation of dependence (*pratibandha*) of the person (*pudgala*) upon the aggregates (*skandhas*). For there is no such thing as a "relation" other than the relation of essential nature (*svabhāvapratibandha*), which consists in the characteristic of birth—that is, the nature of arising. Why is this? Because that which is not dependent lacks a relation to it by way of origination; thus, there is no contradiction with the fact that there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between them. Therefore, due to the lack of a relation, the person is distinct from the aggregates. Furthermore, they are distinct because of the difference in their properties (*dharma*).
For instance, the property of the person is inexpressibility (*avācyatva*), whereas the property of the aggregates is mutual expressibility; thus, there is a difference in their properties.

If it is argued that although there is no bond based on birth (*janma-kṛta*), there is nevertheless a bond for the person (*pudgala*) with respect to the aggregates (*skandha*) based on cognition (*jñāna-kṛta*), [the response is: "It might be so," and so forth. This refers to the very same cognition which belongs to whichever person; because when those [aggregates] are perceived—that is, when form (*rūpa*) and so forth are perceived—the person necessarily appears. Thus, there is a bond based on cognition; for it is maintained that the person is apprehended precisely through the apprehension of form, sound, and so forth, since the person is what is to be cognized by the consciousnesses of the eye and the other senses. Therefore, due to this bond based on cognition...

That entity called the "person" (*pudgala*) cannot be described as being other than the aggregates (*skandha*), even though it does not possess their form and lacks the nature of the aggregates. [The author] refutes this with the words "No," and so forth. The cognition of the person is not inseparable from the apprehension of form and the other aggregates. What is the reason? Because that person, having abandoned the nature of form and the rest, is itself devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For that which appears in the form of form and so forth is indeed its very own nature.

Now, if the person (*pudgala*) has a nature distinct from form and so forth, then, given that its nature is other than form and so forth, it would follow that the person must appear separately, just as form and the rest do not possess that [person's] nature. Yet it does not so appear; therefore, the person simply does not exist, because that which is perceptible yet does not appear is non-existent. Alternatively, if the person is held to be imperceptible, then even if the person is accepted as imperceptible, since there would be no cognition of its form—meaning no cognition bearing the aspect of the person—of what would the apprehension depend? Of what would it be contingent? [It would be contingent on nothing.]

The meaning is that the cognition of a person (*pudgala*) is not invariably concomitant with the cognition of form and so forth. Thus, the implication is that there is no connection established by cognition.
If it is argued that the person does not appear as a separate entity precisely because its perception is dependent upon form and the rest—

He says: "And not," and so forth. The connection is as follows: when a thing (vastu) has its cognition dependent upon another, and its apprehension is necessarily bound to that [other], then the manifestation of its own nature (*svabhāva-pratibhāsa*) does not cease. To illustrate with an example, he says: "Like light," and so forth. Just as in the case of blue and other objects whose cognition is bound to light, even while the light is manifesting, their own manifestation does not cease; for they manifest even apart from the light. The same would apply to the person (*pudgala*).

Furthermore, what is the proximity or connection of that person (*pudgala*) to those aggregates (*skandha*), such that—by reason of which proximity—the person presents itself spontaneously when those aggregates, though devoid of self-nature and lacking the essence of a person, appear [to consciousness]? That is to say, it causes one to grasp them as a self.

For in this way there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, while that which is unconnected appears, the person (*pudgala*) were necessarily to appear, then the meaning would be that even when anything whatsoever appears, something absolutely unrelated is also perceived. If it is argued that the appearing person has a proximity consisting in being the material cause (*upādāna*) of form and so forth, [we ask]: what is this meaning of "material cause"? It cannot be the relationship of effect and cause between the person and form and so forth, respectively.

Because that [invariable concomitance] is not admitted. Or, even if a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) were admitted, there would be no necessary perception of the person (*pudgala*) upon the perception of form and so forth. Why? Because cause and effect do not bring about their mutual cognition in such a way that, just as the cause is cognized from the effect, the effect is likewise cognized from the cause—this is the meaning. It is not that the person is invariably concomitant with form and so forth; rather, it is the cognition of the person that is [not invariably concomitant]. If it is argued that its being invariably concomitant with form and so forth constitutes that very proximity (*pratyāsatti*):

[Objection: Is it not the case that this very [invariable] concomitance is established by perception? [Response: It is said that such a connection is not tenable for a person (*pudgala*) with respect to form and so forth.
[Objection: Even though the person and form and so forth are neither effect nor cause, there will nonetheless be a connection between them.

Therefore, he says: It has been stated more than once that there is no real, essential connection (*prativandha*) between what is not cause and effect; and as for what is also said—that a cognition is "invariably concomitant" with the object of its apprehension—that would apply only if there were a cognition of form and so forth distinct [from the person], or a cognition of a person (*pudgala*). But that does not exist. For, regarding a person (*pudgala*), if it does not appear in consciousness by way of its own nature—meaning, without being associated with its own nature and without being associated with anything else—then there is no cognition of it whatsoever. This is the connection [of the words].
Due to the absence of that—that is, due to the absence of the aforementioned knowledge—the characteristic of the ineffability of the object-entity known as the *pudgala* is not established.

Therefore, in reality and from the perspective of ultimate truth, that entity must exist somewhere as something possessing either identity with or difference from [its cause], because there is no other possible mode of existence for a real thing. However, for the proponent of momentariness who holds the view that when a perishing entity ceases, nothing at all comes into being, but rather that entity simply ceases to exist of its own accord—even by him who says "non-existence comes into being," only a negation has been stated, namely that the entity does not exist, and no affirmation of anything else has been made.
Therefore, [the opponent] considers that for the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), there is no room for the conceptual alternatives of identity or difference regarding non-existence.

He explains this with the words "And even though... and so forth: "Even though this proponent of momentariness says, by means of a word that seems to touch upon a positive injunction, 'The non-existence of an entity occurs,' what he actually says is simply 'The entity does not exist. For in this way, that entity is negated only if nothing else is positively enjoined. What is the reason? Because in a negation—which consists in the exclusion of a mere entity—no positive injunction is possible."

And since no real property whatsoever belongs to an entity that is perishing, for that very reason there is no cause for the destruction of this entity. For a cause of destruction other than the perishing entity itself would be required only if some effect were to be produced by it upon that entity; however, no such effect exists. Therefore, a cause of destruction is something that produces nothing. And whatever thing produces nothing—would that ever be required by anyone? It is certainly not required.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "sati" (when existing). For a causal factor (*kāraka*) exists only when there is something to be produced. And it has already been stated that for an entity that is perishing, there is no effect whatsoever. Therefore, whatever is called a cause of destruction does nothing to the entity; being thus ineffective, the cause of destruction is not to be depended upon. [The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. If no excellence (*atiśaya*) whatsoever arises in the entity as it perishes, then how now—[the analysis of the compound is: "one in whom no excellence has arisen"—can an entity that has not produced any excellence be said to have perished while remaining in that very same state, namely, the state of its former nature?

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) begins with "nanu" and so forth: Even if one were to admit that an excellence (*atiśaya*) arises in an entity from the cause of its destruction, that very excellence would be what is called "destruction. Since that [excellence] has arisen, how could that entity be said to have perished? For the destruction of one thing does not occur through the existence of another. Therefore, for that reason, this entity remains in its original state and is not called "destroyed. Rather, it is called "destroyed" because it no longer exists of its own accord; it is not because of the production of some other distinct entity called "destruction," as was stated immediately prior.

For it is not the case that the non-arising of the excellence known as "destruction" is itself non-existent. What is the reason? Because all excellences of a non-entity consist in capacity (*sāmarthya*), and by the cessation of those designations (*upākhyā*)—that is, by the cessation of all capacities and designations. This is because [non-existence] is characterized by the absence (*viveka*) or lack of every property of existence (*bhāvadharma*), which is to say, the property of being; whereas existence is characterized by the inclusion of arising.

Because it "comes into being," it is called a "becoming" (*bhāva*). Therefore, a becoming is that which is connected with origination. And since this is so, there is no "becoming" of another thing—that is, no arising of something else—when a becoming ceases; the meaning is that nothing at all comes into existence.

"By this" means by the demonstration of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Even if the causelessness of destruction is accepted, that destruction—since it comes into being after first not having existed—would possess existence (*sattā*) like a sprout and so forth, because of the fact that the destruction comes into being after not having existed. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and perishability": the objection concerning the faults of [both] existence and perishability has been refuted by this very same argument.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "yopi" and so forth: Even if destruction were causeless, its existence and impermanence would be unavoidable, because this destruction comes into being after not having existed. Furthermore, the claim that "coming into being after not having existed, it is causeless" is also contradictory, because there is no contradiction between something being occasional and being causeless. This objection has already been refuted by this very demonstration that destruction is formless (nīrūpa). Why? Because at the time of destruction, the existence of any property (dharma) whatsoever is not admitted.

Just as, despite the fact that they share the same ontological status, resistance—defined as the obstruction of another's arising in its own location—is observed only in certain produced things (*janmin*) that possess the quality of origination, and not in all; so too, let the nature of destruction belong only to those entities that possess origination, and not to non-originated things such as space (*ākāśa*). And thus, the principle that "whatever exists is momentary" would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*).

He explains with the words beginning "Now," and so forth: "Let it be granted that this is indeed the nature of things. [The opponent asks: "What is this nature? He replies: "Those which have the property of momentary duration. The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom momentary duration is the property. However, that nature of having the property of momentary duration will belong only to those entities that possess origination, and not to non-originated things such as space and the like.

For it is not the case that everything becomes the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of everything simply because it is an intrinsic nature; this is like the nature of resistance (pratighātmatā). The meaning is that just as the nature of resistance, despite being the intrinsic nature of a thing, does not belong to everything, so it is here.

The Master says: "It is true. It is indeed true that not everything is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of everything. Nevertheless, because there is a restriction of intrinsic nature based on the cause—which is a restriction of intrinsic nature such that "this is the producer of this which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), but this is not"—there is the distinction: "this is resistant, this is not. However, regarding impermanence, there is no difference in the form of produced things within the domain of impermanence by which one would [be excluded] from another.

533) [If] the nature [of things] were perishable, it could not be otherwise. What is the reason? Because there is an absence of causes that differentiate a thing whose nature is non-perishable; that is to say, because all [things] are produced with a perishable nature. Now, the objection raised was: "But surely the nature of destruction does not belong to entities that are unproduced. And the response given there—"In that case, there is no difference in form regarding impermanence, because there is an absence of differentiators"—is not tenable. For space and so forth do not have a perishable nature produced by their own causes, precisely because they are unproduced. Therefore, how is it that [the author] stated, "This is true," and so on?

He thinks as follows: Just as "existence" (*sattva*) was stated to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), so too one might suspect that even among things produced (*kṛtaka*), some are perishable while others are not. Therefore, there is no fault in stating "existence" and so forth at the very beginning, in order first to grasp the inconclusiveness of the property of being produced.

He explains [the verse] with the words "no," and so forth. "Other" refers to that which is visible (*sanidarśana*) and so on. "Arising without cause" means being restricted [to a specific place] even in the absence of a cause—meaning it might exist in some places and not in others. However, such a restriction to a specific object is due to the persistence of the capacity of a cause that generates properties such as resistance (*pratigha*). Since a result arises in accordance with the cause's capacity—that is, there is a restriction of capacity—it is accepted that the restriction of the nature of the result follows from the restriction of the nature of the cause.

But if [the destruction] were accidental—that is, causeless—then the fault already stated regarding the necessity of the nature of the effect would apply: that the restriction by place, time, and intrinsic nature would not be logical. Therefore, just as there is a specific restriction for its nature which is the cause of its state of resistance, we do not perceive any entity whose causal nature is restricted to the production of something perishable. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that entity whose nature is restricted to the production of something perishable, such that only a certain thing produces what is perishable, and not everything."

By whatever specific causal determination [it occurs]: that which has its birth from a cause that produces perishability would thus be perishable, and not anything else that is born from a cause possessing different characteristics. What is the reason?

The opponent objects with the words "nanu" and so forth: It is likewise impossible to ascertain that those entities which arise from causes possessing all possible aspects are subject to destruction. Why? Because those causal complexes (*hetusāmagrī*) cannot be seen in their entirety by those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*). If it is argued that because a certain causal complex producing perishable things has been observed, other unobserved instances are also ascertained to be of such a nature by virtue of belonging to that same class; [the response follows:]

He says, "Variegated," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: those whose power is variegated. Such causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) are observed. Among those causal complexes possessing variegated powers, there might perhaps be some complex that would produce an entity whose nature is imperishable. He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). Furthermore, this refutation applies to the fact that destruction is the very nature of entities, not to those things that do not arise [in the first place]. The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "if even... (*yadi... api*) should be understood as applying to the objection (*codya*), because it is common to both cases. This is not a fault. Why? Because the context concerns the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Clarifying this very point, he says: We maintain that for those objects which, having been known at some time in some place by some person, are not known again, there is a destruction that follows their continuum. And as for those [objects] which, being unknown, come to be known, or having been known, are no longer known—it is precisely these that are established as being produced and impermanent. By this, it is stated that the pervasion of "being produced" by "momentariness" is determined through the reason of "existence."
But surely, even if they are not perceived despite being existent as knowers, how can their impermanence be established?

To this he says: For it is impossible that those things which possess the nature of producing cognition—having remained previously and not having perished—should fail to produce [cognition] while remaining in that very same nature.
If it is argued that they do not produce it due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), [the response follows].

He says: "They would not depend on anything else. The connection [of the sentence] is that its occurrence is indeed impossible. What is the reason? Because its nature of producing that [cognition] has already been established. Now, it might be argued: even if they do not depend [on other conditions], the cognition of some thing might at some time cease; [rather,] they should produce cognitions of their own objects at all times for everyone. But this is not the case, because cognition is observed only occasionally. Therefore, it is understood that when they do not produce a cognition, they have deviated from their nature as producers. As for that which is then unknowable—whether produced or unproduced—that will not be like this.

Therefore, he says: "Not [so]," and so forth. There is nothing of such a nature that is unknowable. Why? Because every object is known by some person at some time. If, however, it were not to produce even that knowledge, then, being incapable of even the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consisting of cognition itself, the entity would not exist at all, being devoid of that capacity. For we shall state that the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of an entity is its capacity for causal efficiency.

Furthermore, since that entity capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) perishes without fail while performing its causal function sequentially, and since destruction is not caused by any external factor, it is established that destruction is necessarily concomitant with existence. For this very reason—namely, from the aforementioned proof of the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of all entities—the permanence of the relationship between word and meaning must also be rejected; it is to be refuted.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "not" (*na*) and so forth. Precisely for this reason—because destruction, as previously stated, is necessarily concomitant with any entity whatsoever—the eternality of the relation must also be rejected, just as the eternality of sound was refuted. Thus far, having assumed the relation to be distinct [from its relata], the fault has been stated; now it is shown that a non-distinct relation is likewise untenable.

He says: That which is described by the followers of Jaimini as the capacity (*yogyatā*) of a word—namely, that which is designated as capacity and serves as the basis for the comprehension of the object signified—is not indeed something distinct from the word itself. For it has been explained previously that the very excellence of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) of entities, which is capable of performing the intended causal function, is what constitutes capacity, as stated in the passage beginning, "The capacity of a word is its efficient form.
Therefore, the point is that if the word is impermanent, its capacity must also be impermanent, because there is no difference between them.

Or, let it be that *yogyatā* (fitness) is something distinct from the word; even so, the power (*śakti*) of the word must be understood as already refuted. By what? By the faults regarding the relation (*sambandha*) previously mentioned.

He explains this with the words beginning "for it has been said," and so forth. In the discussion that the relation is a distinct entity from the related terms (*sambandhin*), many kinds of faults have been stated, such as:

"Because the related terms are impermanent, the relation cannot possess permanence," and so on. Since the power of the word, which is likewise postulated in the form of a relation, is refuted by those very same previously mentioned faults, the fault is not stated separately once again.

Thus, the Veda is not authorless. Even if it were authorless, its truthfulness could not be ascertained; for, simply by virtue of being authorless, a Vedic statement is not a means for producing knowledge of things as they are, nor is it a cause for non-erroneous knowledge. This is because [authorless things] such as fire—and by the word "etcetera," moonlight and so forth—are seen to be uncorrupted by human faults (*puruṣāgasā*, i.e., *puruṣadoṣeṇa*), yet are also seen to be otherwise, namely, observed to be causes of false cognition. This is the meaning.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "Let it be so" (*bhavatu*). Let it be granted that Vedic words are indeed not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*); nevertheless, it is quite possible that these Vedic words are causes of erroneous cognition. For it is not only due to the imposition of human defects—that is, because of the imposition of human defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like—that there occurs a delusion of cognition, a perversion of cognition, among the words which are the signifiers regarding the objects to be signified; for it is also possible that [words] produce false knowledge by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*).

Because even for those things devoid of that [defect], such as lamps and the like—which are themselves free from the imposition of human defects—there arises cognition of an unreal object. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), moonlight and so forth are included. Where? In the case of blue lotuses and the like. For instance, at night, the moon is the cause of a cognition appearing as red in a blue lotus; and moonlight is the cause of a cognition of white in a yellow garment.

The connection is as follows: "Therefore" (*tad*), these Vedic words would be independent of human refinement; by their *prakṛti*—that is, by their very nature—they would be the causes of cognition, the causes of knowledge regarding objects. What is the reason? Because of a specific nature, that is, a specific intrinsic form (*svarūpa*). Like what? Like fire and so forth. Furthermore, they would necessarily have false manifestations. The analysis of the compound is: those words from which there arise false manifestations, i.e., false cognitions of objects.

If you argue that the reason for the claim that Vedic words always have false manifestations (*vitathavyakti*) does not exist—and therefore, due to the absence of a restrictive cause, it is unreasonable to imagine that Vedic words have only false manifestations—then we ask: what is the cause for your Mīmāṃsaka position that Vedic words are the causes of non-false cognition, such that there is this restriction to non-false manifestation? None at all.

Therefore, according to your own view, since there is a restriction to manifestation in accordance with reality (*yathārthavyakti*), why is a restriction to manifestation contrary to reality (*ayathārthavyakti*) not likewise imagined by nature (*prakṛti*) or by its very essence (*svabhāva*)?

Alternatively, just as fire and other such things serve respectively as causes for true, false, or indeterminate cognitions regarding objects such as jars or blue lotuses, so too might Vedic words—despite being non-personal (apauruṣeya)—serve as causes for both types of cognition, namely false and otherwise, regarding their referents; for even non-personal things like forest fires or moonlight do not [inherently] possess the nature of being causes for both [types of cognition].

Just as in one instance, such as a jar, things that are causes of true cognition during the day become likewise causes of true cognition at night even in the case of a blue lotus and so forth; similarly, for Vedic words as well, even if they are not of human origin, both would occur—namely, being causes of true cognition and being causes of false cognition.

"Let it be so," and so forth, says the opponent. Because fire and other such things are produced, they possess the quality of being caused; thus, according to their respective conditions, this [quality] exists. However, in the case of eternal sounds, there is no such capacity to cause false cognition through the power of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), because it is impossible for eternal things to function otherwise by virtue of auxiliary conditions.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says, "Is it not so," and so forth. "Of such a kind" means that there indeed exists a property (*dharma*) characterized by transformation into something else in objects through the power of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). "In that case too" refers even to Vedic words. What is the reason? It is because even those Vedic words undergo transformation into something else through the power of convention (*saṃketa*) that conforms to human intention; the meaning is that they produce a different cognition by virtue of the force of convention.

Now, if it is not accepted that there is a transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of these [Vedic words] with respect to their objects due to the power of convention (*saṃketa*), but rather that Vedic words possess by their very nature the capacity to produce cognitions of their own objects because they are eternal; then, since these Vedic words abide in that very nature of producing the effect—which is the cognition of their own objects—there is no dependence on convention or anything else, such as the operation of an instrument (*karaṇavyāpāra*), which would otherwise be required. This is the reason.

Consequently, from Vedic words, there would always arise for every person a cognition—that is, knowledge—regarding objects. Yet, such cognition of objects does not occur for everyone at all times. Therefore, Vedic words do not have a nature established in the cognition of objects; rather, they necessarily depend upon convention (*samaya*) and so forth. Thus, since they too are causes of false cognition, the aforementioned defect remains as it was.

Moreover, if that sound is held to be uncreated, it could not even be the cause of cognition; for nothing whatsoever—whether cognition or anything else—is produced from eternal things by way of the capacity of the thing itself, namely, through the capacity to impart its own nature.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "If [it were] unproduced": if the Vedic word were unproduced, then there would be no cognition at all regarding its referents. Why? [He says: "Regarding cognition," and so forth. The analysis of the compound *itaradajanmājanma* is "the other" (*itarat*) and "non-arising" (*ajanma*). Because those two times—the time of cognition and the other time—are of an identical nature due to the eternity [of the word], which implies being of a single form, it is impossible for there to be a possibility of efficacy for cognition at the time of its arising.

Because there is a contradiction in something being a producer while remaining in that very same nature which was its non-producing state at the time when cognition did not arise. Why? Because, in this way, one must distinguish between "this thing, though considered eternal, is a producer by virtue of this form" and "it is not a producer by virtue of this [other] form"; yet such a distinction of forms—that is, a distinction of natures—is absent. This is because an eternal entity is always of a single nature.
If it is argued that even a single-natured entity might be a producer previously and a producer later;

He says, "No," and so forth. It is not logical that this eternal [entity] should have the same nature as that which is a non-producer; for it is of a single form. To claim that it produces [an effect] later after obtaining an additional auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) is false. This is because dependence on another—that is, dependence on an auxiliary—has already been refuted in the case of the eternal. Therefore, eternal words do not possess the capacity to generate cognition in a person regarding any object whatsoever. Why? Because if they fail to produce cognition at one time, they would necessarily never produce it at any time, since their nature remains eternally the same.

Now, [the opponent might argue: "To avoid this fault, let it be accepted that they always perform their own function. This too is not the case; for their effect, which is the cognition of their own objects, is not observed to be continuous. Furthermore, it has already been stated that those sounds are not agents in any way whatsoever.
It might be argued: "Even from eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*), cognitions certainly arise for someone at some time."

Therefore, he says: "Even those cognitions or understandings that will arise regarding space and so forth, which are considered eternal—it is maintained that these too do not possess that [eternal] nature as their own being, nor is their birth dependent upon the nature of space and so forth. This is because for eternal things, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory both successively and simultaneously.
What, then, is the cause for their arising?"

He says: "Not indeed," and so forth. [These cognitions] arise from a latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is a capacity deposited by a beginningless conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a similar kind; they have emerged and originated from that. They have proceeded solely as having for their object a superimposed form such as space (*ākāśa*) and so on, in accordance with scripture—that is, they merely manifest those forms. They arise with respect to those things like space which are imagined as being external. However, those cognitions do not have external objects as their domain, nor do they have the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of space and so on as their objects.

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "svalakṣaṇa" (specific characteristic). For a cognition whose object is a specific characteristic necessarily conforms to the capacity—the efficacy and presence—of that specific characteristic; that is, it exists only when that [characteristic] exists. Since its cause, the specific characteristic, is capable and efficacious, when that cause is present and capable, that cognition necessarily arises.

Thus, this being the logical conclusion, if there were to arise in some person a cognition of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of eternal entities, then, because the cause would be constantly present, it would occur for every person at all times.

Nor can it be through dependence on auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) that eternal things ever produce a cognition for anyone at any time. For, in the case of those individuals (*vyakti*) which produce an effect by means of auxiliaries, these very individuals—being employed toward a certain effect under specific constraints of place, time, and state—attain the status of a cause. In the production of that effect, they possess an excellence (*atiśaya*) inherent to their own nature (*ātmabhūta*) which is capable of bringing it about; this is what is meant by an "auxiliary," namely, a particular entity (*vastuviśeṣa*) that serves as the cause for obtaining that excellence.

"Likewise" means like impermanence. An eternal entity (*bhāva*), being incapable of having any excellence (*atiśaya*) imparted to it by anyone, would—if it were to produce a perception for a person who perceives it—be dependent upon that cause [of perception], namely, dependent upon the auxiliary causes of perception.
