It would then be logical that it should be perceived by that person alone and not by another, due to the restriction of the auxiliary causes. However, such production through dependence on auxiliaries is impossible for an eternal thing. Why? Because its nature is fixed; that is to say, because no excellence can be imparted to an eternal thing by an auxiliary cause.

Furthermore, because it would remain eternally in its nature of being produced, it would be perceived at the same time by every person; or, because it would not be a producer for anyone, it would not be perceived. In that case, since that very nature belongs to it, it would never be perceived by any person whatsoever. For this reason, if an existent, permanent entity were seen by some yogi, then nothing could be permanent or beyond the senses, since everything would necessarily be seen by someone.

And thus, this [sound] would always be perceptible by the senses of all persons, because there is no difference in its capacity to produce cognition with respect to every person. Yet this universal perceptibility does not belong to that which is eternal. Therefore, [these cognitions] are independent of the capacity of the object and independent of the capacity of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of space and so forth; they have superimposed objects as their domain. The meaning is that they appear in the forms of space and so forth, as superimposed according to tradition (*āgama*).

Relying solely upon an internal material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), there occurs such an awakening of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This refers to the beginninglessness of the conceptualization of space and so forth. The "awakening" of that deposited predisposition is its orientation toward the production of an effect. Precisely because it does not depend on the efficacy of an external object, all people experience, regarding space and so forth, nothing but errors (*bhrānti*) that are empty of external objects.

This is established: there is no production of an effect from eternal things. However, since the effect of cognition is sometimes seen to arise from sound, sounds do not possess the property of non-reversion (*aparāvṛtti*). The analysis of the compound is: "those whose very nature is non-reversion due to their being of a single form. But each instance of cognition arises with a distinct operation toward its respective object. Now, if [sounds] were eternal and of a single form, whether that [single form] be the truth itself or simply a state of uniformity—how can it be maintained that Vedic words produce cognitions of objects that are not false? The analysis of the compound is: "those from which there arises a cognition of an object that is not false."
It might be thought: "Because Vedic statements such as 'Fire is the remedy for cold' are non-false, all [Vedic statements] are non-false."

Therefore, he says: "For not," and so forth. For in Vedic statements such as "Fire is not the remedy or the opposite of cold," the capacity of fire to counteract cold is made known even prior to the Vedic sentence, based on what is already well-known in the world according to convention; thus, every Vedic statement—even those whose objects are unperceived—is likewise [authoritative], that is, it becomes non-false. For in the case of an object well-known in the world, the worldly usage is observed to follow convention.

Therefore, because of the usage at the time of linguistic practice following that convention—which was established by people's own will—it is precisely a matter of doubt whether this person is conforming to, or following, his own convention.

From such sentences as "Fire is the remedy for cold," one understands that fire possesses the capacity to dispel cold; however, does one understand this because of a fixed nature inherent in the word itself—a restriction of capacity by the very essence or *prakṛti* of the word—or otherwise? The point is that when even in a directly perceived object the Vedic word's inherent power to convey meaning is doubted, then it is all the more impossible to conceive of such power in the case of an entirely imperceptible object.
Now, it is surely the case that the meaningfulness of Vedic words follows precisely from their conformity with the beginningless worldly convention, and no doubt appears there regarding this.

Therefore, he says: words are seen to be subject to change according to worldly desire; they are applied to objects as conventionally agreed upon, yet when there is a reversal of place and so forth, they are seen to be changed again by being applied to a different meaning. For this reason, even if one accepts conformity with worldly consensus, a transformation—and thus a falsity—of these Vedic words is indeed possible, because that very consensus is itself not fixed.

Therefore, even though no error is observed in some Vedic statements such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," the fact that all Vedic statements possess such a nature—that is, their truthfulness—is not established.
If it is argued that their truthfulness follows precisely from their being uncreated (*akṛtaka*), [we reply:]...

He says: If these Vedic words possess an uncreated intrinsic nature (*akṛtaka-svabhāva*), then there might be some word among them that is fixed upon a false object. For this reason, because one cannot determine the intrinsic nature of words through such a distinction as "this has a true object" or "this has a false object"—due to a lack of thorough knowledge of their nature—there would be doubt regarding every word. This is because, when the formal argument is made that "the Vedic sentence has a true object because it is uncreated," there is an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

He states the formulation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words beginning "falsity" (*mithyātva*). The connection is as follows: "If speech which is unproduced were to have a true object, because falsity is observed only in things that are produced. What is the reason? Because the negative concomitance pervades the contradictory. That is, the negative concomitance of the reason "unproducedness"—which is its opposite, namely "being produced"—pervades falsity, which is the contradictory of the probandum, "having a true object. The genitive case in "of the negative concomitance" (*vyatirekasya*) is used in the sense of the agent.

Because falsity, which is contradictory to having a true object, is pervaded by being produced—which is distinct from the [Vedic] cause—then in the case of Vedic speech, since it is unproduced, upon the cessation of being produced there follows the cessation of falsity; thus, its having a true object is indeed established.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "yathā" (just as): whatever speech has a false meaning, all of that—without exception—is produced (*kṛtaka*). This is on the basis of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya-vyatireka*)—namely, truthfulness—by means of the absence of the reason (*hetu-vyatireka*), namely, being unproduced (*akṛtakatva*), through its opposite, being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Since the probandum is truthfulness, its absence is falsity; because falsity is impossible elsewhere—in that which is unproduced—the reason is that what is unproduced must have a true meaning, even without a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

In the formal argument (*prayoga*) "the Vedic word has truth as its object because it is produced," although there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the meaning is that it is nevertheless established even without anvaya. This is because whatever object is characterized by falsity (*mithyātva*) is not pervaded by "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*); in that case, regarding that falsity, there is the absence (*vyatireka*) of that non-pervader—namely, the absence of "being produced"—since falsity is pervaded by "being produced."

Furthermore, there is no possibility of contradiction, because it is impossible for two contradictory properties—namely, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and not being produced (*akṛtakatva*)—to coexist in one and the same thing as false. Therefore, since falsity, which belongs to a different class, is impossible in that which is unproduced, and since there is no other alternative besides truthfulness and falsity, it must be true by virtue of its being unproduced. Thus, because the desired property characterized by truthfulness is established through the reason of being unproduced, what is the use of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?

And because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the means of proving that [object], and because the logical mark is the means of proving the desired object, the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is useless. Why? Because, according to the method already stated, the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone.
"This is true," says the Teacher.

It is true that if the exclusion [of the reason] from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) were established, the probandum would be established. This would be the case if the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between falsity and being produced—which are the counter-examples to "not being produced" and "truth"—were established. In that case, because it is pervaded by being produced, the non-produced would be excluded from falsity. However, that relationship of pervaded and pervader between the two counter-examples is not established. Why?

Because, when falsity is impossible for that which is unproduced (*akṛtakatva*), and no subverting reason (*bādhaka-hetu*) has been stated to account for the impossibility [of that falsity], the existence—that is, the reality—of that very unproducedness can be maintained even while it is false; for it could be both unproduced and have a false object. (290ab) But surely, falsity is observed in what is produced, and where there is production, how can there be non-production?

Therefore, he says: "Of contradictory [things]," and so forth. Even for contradictory entities, because of the observation of a single pervader; just as the impermanent things that follow either from effort or not from effort are pervaded by the single property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "yadi" [if]. If the absence of this reason called "uncreatedness" (*akṛtakatva*) in the counter-example of the probandum—namely, in the state of being false (*mithyārthatva*)—were established, then the probandum's "reversed form," which is falsity, would pervade the "reversed form of the reason," namely the reversal of the reason called uncreatedness, which is "createness" (*kṛtakatva*). However, we do not perceive any subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for that [absence] when uncreatedness is impossible in that state of falsity.
If it is argued that the Veda does not function toward falsity precisely because of its uncreatedness—

He says, "And not," and so forth. It is logical that the prescription of "uncreatedness" (*akṛtatva*), which is not contradictory to being false in its object, should be a means for establishing the falsity of a negation. Why? Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For in this way, by the prescription of anything whatsoever, the absence of anything whatsoever might be understood. If it is asked: "How can the falsity observed in what is created apply to what is uncreated?"

He said: It is not the case that what has been observed as falsity in one produced thing cannot possibly occur again elsewhere in an unproduced thing; rather, it is indeed possible. Why? Because we observe that even things which coexist with their opposites—meaning those that exist in the same locus despite having contradictory properties—can occur separately due to a difference in individual instances (*vyakti*). Just as in the case of impermanence, between that which follows immediately after effort and its opposite, the latter is that which does not follow immediately after effort.
Impermanence, which was previously observed in conjunction with being produced immediately after an effort, is now observed in conjunction with not being produced immediately after an effort.

If this were so, then because falsity is not observed in that which is unproduced (*akṛta*), it would follow that falsity is non-existent there. To this he says: "And it is not the case that for such a thing"—meaning for that which exists as unproduced—falsity is non-existent simply because it is not observed.

Since it was stated previously that the non-existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) cannot be established through non-perception in all cases, and since the non-existence of the reason in the counter-example is thus unestablished, its exclusion from the counter-example (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

He explains this with the words "For not... and so forth. This person who possesses only limited vision—that is, one of limited perception—is not capable of seeing every object, such that by the cessation of his own perception, [an object] would not exist for him; that is, it would not be unseen by him. For there is no person whose cognition does not deviate from the existence of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

If one were to say, "It exists," and thus cognition proceeds toward every object of knowledge (*jñeya*), then that cognition, being all-pervasive of its objects, would—in ceasing—cause the object of knowledge itself to cease as well. Therefore, one who says "it does not exist" on the grounds of non-perception might be justified; but [this does not apply] to everything. Consequently, these entities, even if they exist, would be unperceivable and thus subject to exclusion (*apohya*). How so? By way of the remoteness of intrinsic nature, place, and time.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), *deśa* (place), and *kāla* (time); *viprakarṣa* (remoteness) by these means constitutes "obstruction" (*vyavadhāna*). Even though something exists, it may be remote due to place, time, and intrinsic nature, like a *piśāca* or similar being. [Objection: But surely, since those things obstructed by time—namely the past and the future—are not perceived, their non-existence is logical, precisely because of their absence. [Reply: True. However, although the past and future are not perceived at present, they have existed at some point [in the past] and will exist at some point [in the future]; thus, there is no absolute non-perception of them.

The phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth makes this very point clear. For who—other than an omniscient being—is capable of conceiving or determining the correspondence of an unauthored statement regarding an entirely imperceptible object, or the non-correspondence of another, authored statement regarding an entirely imperceptible object? No one at all. Since the opponent accepts that an authored statement lacks correspondence, both [possibilities] have been stated. It might be argued: "Because correspondence is observed in one Vedic sentence, there is correspondence throughout the entire Veda."

Therefore, he says: "And this has already been established previously in the investigation of *śeṣavat* inference. He asks, "What was established? and replies with the words beginning with "in some cases" (*kvacid*). "In some cases" means in a certain place or time. "In that way" (*tathā*) refers to the alteration of things previously observed; it is the reversal from the form previously perceived. This very point is expressed by the words beginning with "just as" (*yathā*), [referring to] due to a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*), characterized by the preparation of milk, honey, and so forth.

And the connection is that in some regions *āmalakī* fruits are sweet; this is not so for one who does not see them, that is, for one who has not seen that those *nimba* fruits are sweet. Those *nimba* fruits, being sweet, must indeed be rejected [as such]. Likewise, even if the falsity of Vedic statements were actually observed, it still could not be rejected. Therefore, we see no contradiction between being unauthored and having false content; thus, something may be both unauthored and have false meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that because non-artificiality (*akṛtakatva*) is not perceived in the state of falsity (*mithyārthatā*), its absence [therein] is established? [Response: To this he says: "For this non-perception does not establish the absence of a thing in objects whose nature is invisible or whose nature is visible," as was stated previously. Since the absence of non-artificiality in falsity is thus not proven, therefore whatever is false is all of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). In this way, there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) of falsity by artificiality. What is the reason? Because of uncertainty (*aniścayāt*).

The meaning is that if the property of being uncreated were to have a false referent, there would be no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). And the establishment of the probandum cannot proceed from a reason whose negative concomitance is uncertain.

For instance, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason with its own probandum (*sādhya*) consists either in positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or in negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which is the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), or in the existence of the reason in the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*). This is the meaning of "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*). And if these three characteristics are established by means of cognitions that are valid instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then—provided they have the ascertainment of those [characteristics] as their result—those three characteristics become the proof of the intended probandum. (The compound *tanniścayaphalaiḥ* is analyzed as: those for whom the ascertainment of those three characteristics is the result. Only then do those three characteristics constitute the proof of the intended probandum.

As stated by Ācārya Dignāga: "That which expresses what is ascertained by both [parties]... That is to say, that which expresses an object possessing the characteristics of a valid reason (*hetu*) as ascertained by both the proponent and the opponent is a proof (*sādhana*). Conversely, a word that expresses an object possessing characteristics such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth, when employed by the opponent with the intention of refutation, is a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).

A statement based on what is established for only one of the two parties, or one that is doubtful, is neither a proof nor a refutation. This refers to any word that expresses something established for only one of the proponent or the opponent, or something that is doubtful for both or either of them. Why is this? Because it requires further proof; since that which is not yet ascertained must depend upon further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its ascertainment.

Furthermore, there is no certain contradiction between "being unproduced" (*akṛtaka*) and "having a false object" (*mithyārthatva*), by virtue of which the absence of falsity in the unproduced would be established.

Now, it might be argued that falsity does not occur in the Veda precisely because of its being unauthored (*akṛtakatva*). To this he says: "For who," and so forth. For what conscious person would reject the possibility of falsity—which is observed to be incompatible with being unauthored—in the case of Vedic statements? Therefore, this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "being unauthored" as it has been stated is not a proof. Why? Because of doubt. Furthermore, demonstrating that there is no negative concomitance for the reason, he says:

Furthermore, etc.: in whatever object the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the counter-instance of the probandum (*sādhya-vipakṣa*)—where the probandum is "truthfulness" and its counter-instance is "falsity"—is described, such as "whatever is not produced is not false," that very object which is the domain of the exclusion of falsity would be the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for this reason of being "produced. For this reason, every reason (*hetu*) is positive (*anvayin*), that is, it possesses both positive and negative concomitance; the meaning is that it is not merely negative (*vyatirekin*), since the context concerns negative concomitance.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a "similar instance" (sapakṣa)—an object similar by virtue of the general property to be proven—is called a "homologous example" (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta)? And since such a thing does not exist here, how can it be said that this very [subject] is its similar instance? [Response: True. A similar instance is called a "similar instance" precisely because it is the locus of the positive concomitance (anvaya) with the property to be proven. For this very reason, he says: "Therefore, every logical reason (hetu) possesses positive concomitance."

He explains this with the words beginning with "yat" (whatever). This would be the case if the absence of falsity were established. Why? Because if there is an absence of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), your [proposition] that falsity exists cannot be pervaded by that state of being produced. Therefore, one who desires pervasion must accept that the cessation of falsity follows from the cessation of being produced. And this very establishment of the exclusion of falsity and being produced—which belong to different classes from the probandum and the probans—is achieved through the exclusion of being produced. (p. ...)

547) "It ceases like that which has a false object"—this is the form [of the statement]. The establishment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of a reason that is itself produced (*kṛtaka*) by virtue of its having a true object is the "establishment of the positive concomitance" (*anvayavyavasthiti*). What is the reason? Because the property to be proven (*sādhya*), namely "having a true object," is characterized by the exclusion of the heterologue (*vipakṣa*). The heterologue is falsity; since being produced excludes that [falsity], the exclusion or absence of that [falsity] in what is produced is its defining characteristic.

Furthermore, falsity (*mithyārthatva*) is the negation of truthfulness (*satyārthatā*). When that falsity is negated in what is uncreated (*akṛtaka*), then two negations have occurred. Because of these two negations—which consist in the exclusion of truthfulness—the affirmation of truthfulness is established. For this reason, it is not "without positive concomitance" (*ananvaya*); rather, through the negative concomitance of the probans (*sādhana-vyatireka*)—namely, being uncreated—with the negative concomitance of the probandum (*sādhya-vyatireka*)—namely, falsity—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. Thus, the establishment of pervasion is certainly not "without positive concomitance."

Therefore, there is no such thing as a reason that lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*); rather, every [valid] reason possesses both positive and negative concomitance. Why is this? Because the exclusion of one [class]—namely, the exclusion of falsity in what is non-artificial—is inseparable from the establishment of its dissimilar class. That is to say, it is because the establishment of truthfulness, which is the dissimilar class to falsity, is necessarily concomitant with it.

If the exclusion of one thing is necessarily concomitant with the establishment of its dissimilar counterpart, then even in the case of the exclusion of "non-momentary," "selfless," and so forth—where "and so forth" refers to suffering and the like—the establishment of momentariness, selflessness, suffering, and the rest would follow. This would also be the case whenever an exclusion is made of something such as a rabbit's horn; for by the exclusion of "falsity," there would be the establishment of "truth," and likewise, by the exclusion of things dissimilar to momentariness and the rest, there would be the establishment of their opposites: permanence, possession of a self, pleasure, and so on. But this is not desired. Therefore, the opponent thinks that it should not be so in this case either.

He refutes [this objection] with the words "no" and so forth: "This is not a fault. Why? Because the exclusion of the distinct (*vyatireka-vyavaccheda*) is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*). Distinctness is non-existence (*abhāva*); and since the exclusion or cessation of non-existence is of the nature of a positive entity—meaning that the establishment of a positive entity occurs through the cessation of non-existence—the definition of a positive entity has been stated by this. From this very statement, it also follows by implication that the exclusion of a positive entity is of the nature of non-existence."

Thus, by this, the definition of both existence and non-existence has been stated. In that regard, [the author] says "not existence," etc., demonstrating that in which, when it is excluded, there is no implication of existence, and in which, when it is excluded, there is an implication of existence. When the intrinsic nature of existence is excluded, there is no implication of existence—that is, no entailment of existence—because only its negation is possible, as in the case of the statement "existence does not exist."

However, the exclusion of a mere absence—which has the nature of the exclusion of non-existence—necessarily entails the presence of an existent; that is, it implies an existent. What is the reason? Because the distinction and separation between existence and non-existence consist in their mutual negation; that is to say, because they have that as their very nature. The meaning is that the distinction from existence has the nature of non-existence, and the distinction from non-existence has the nature of existence.

Having thus explained how the exclusion of existence and non-existence respectively do and do not imply the presence of an entity, he applies this to the present subject with the words "But that which has the nature of non-existence," and so forth. The exclusion (*vyatireka*) of truthfulness, which is characterized by falsity, is itself of the nature of the absence of truthfulness. When that [exclusion] is being excluded—namely, when it ceases upon the cessation of "being produced"—it establishes the entity characterized by truthfulness in that which is unproduced.
(Note: *B* reads *bhāvānākṣepakatvamuktvā*.)

If, however, the opponent accepts that "falsity" (*mithyārthatva*) is the opposite of "truthfulness" (*satyārthatva*), then in the case of Vedic statements, once their status as products has been excluded, there would be no falsity at all, but rather truthfulness; consequently, [the opponent] will argue that they would be purposeless. Therefore, truthfulness must necessarily be a positive entity (*bhāvarūpā*). A property characterized by falsity must be admitted, and when that [property] is excluded, it establishes the positivity of truthfulness.

Selflessness and so forth are not of the nature of separation. What is the reason? Experience is the feeling of pleasure and pain; its basis is appropriation. In that regard, the self is indeed dependent and subject to another; it is selflessness (*nirātman*) by its very nature (*svabhāva*). The word "self" (*ātman*) is a synonym for "nature. Furthermore, what is the reason that such a nature is selfless? The word "self" is a synonym for "nature."

What, then, is the reason why such a nature is selfless (*nirātman*)? He says: "Because of its independence in that [basis]," and so forth. This is because the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that [self] imagined by others is independence with respect to that basis for action and experience. Precisely because of having that as its nature, the self imagined by others is independent; therefore, the intention is that by contrast with that, a nature that is not independent is selfless. 2: B. *mithyārthatvam eva* | 3: B. *rūpo* |

4. Because it is precisely the end [of existence], therefore form (*rūpa*) is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and selflessness (*nairātmya*) is not merely the cessation of a self. 5. Otherwise, if selflessness were merely a cessation, then, due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it would be utterly indefinable (*nirupākhya*). And since it is indefinable, there would be no application of a reason that is a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*)—such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), where the word "etc. includes "following immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) and so forth. Consequently, from such reasons as "being produced," there would be no understanding of selflessness, nor the establishment of selflessness.

And it is accepted [that this is so]. Therefore, for a Buddhist, *nairātmya* (selflessness) is not merely the absence of a self, nor is mere exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) intended to be expressed. Rather, because the word "selfless" refers to and denotes a real entity (*vastu*) that is devoid of a self by means of the exclusion of a self, the objection that "the realization of selflessness would not follow from [reasons] such as 'being produced'" is not a fault. Even so, since there is contact with a real entity through the negation of a self (*ātmaparyudāsa*), [the fault remains].

Thus, it has been stated by us that the nature of the object is the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of the intrinsic nature of existence (*bhāva*). Furthermore, in the exclusion of one entity, there is no necessary implication of another entity. Therefore, for the Buddhists, even though selflessness is excluded in the case of things such as a rabbit’s horn, this does not establish the existence of a self. Consequently, what was stated—that "the same would apply even when eternal selflessness is excluded"—is refuted.
[Note: B adds *nātmavyavacchedamātram*;
B reads *svātantryaḥ*.]

Even for those such as the Naiyāyikas, for whom the absence of self (*nairātmya*) is not of the nature of non-existence but rather the mere absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvābhāva*), there would be no establishment of the existence of a self (*ātman*) upon the exclusion of that Naiyāyika-style *nairātmya* which is itself of the nature of an entity. For this reason, even when *nairātmya* is excluded in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like, there is no consequence of the self’s positive concomitance (*anvaya*). The meaning is that there is no following along with, nor persistence of, the self.

And just as in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like, even though there is an exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmyavyavaccheda*), there is no positive concomitance (*anvayānugama*) of a self; so too, in the case of a living body, even though there is selflessness—or rather, the absence of selflessness—there would be no establishment of the existence of a self.

Alternatively, it is explained otherwise. In the context of refuting the *vyatirekin* (negative-only inference) as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas, [the author] says "yasyāpi" and so forth, in order to refute the *vyatirekin* as stated by the Naiyāyikas as well. For even for the Naiyāyika and others, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not of the nature of non-existence; rather, selflessness (*nairātmya*) is itself a positive entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*). For that Naiyāyika who speaks thus, if there were a distinction from the positive entity of selflessness, there would be no establishment of the existence of a self.

Because when one entity is excluded, there is no necessary implication of another entity; for this reason, where there is that which possesses breath and so forth, there is no implication of the concomitance "there is a self. And just as there is no such implication of concomitance, likewise, even in the case of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) being soulless (*nairātmya*), the establishment of the existence of a self would not occur even upon the cessation of soullessness.

Demonstrating that this very [inference] is preceded by formal application (*prayoga*), he says: "Just as," and so forth. "This living body is not soulless, because it possesses breath and so forth. Here, "breath" (*prāṇa*) refers to inhalation; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), exhalation and the rest are included. In this formal application, the possession of a soul (*sātmakatva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*) for the living body, and it is not established for both [the proponent and the opponent]. Since that soul, which constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*), does not exist [for the opponent], a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not considered.

When one considers the relationship between the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—namely, selflessness (*nairātmya*) and the lack of possession of breath and so forth (*aprāṇādimattva*), which are the two counter-examples (*vipakṣa*) to the soul (*ātman*) and the possession of breath and so forth (*prāṇādimattva*) as previously stated—it is observed that selflessness exists only where there is a lack of possession of breath and so forth. This is because, according to the logical principle, when the pervader (the lack of possession of breath and so forth) is absent, the pervaded (selflessness) is also absent; whereas in that which possesses breath and so forth, selflessness does not exist.

Even though selflessness (*nairātmya*) does not exist in itself, it does not establish its own presence within the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*), namely the self, as a reason for [the existence of] breath and so forth. This is because, even when selflessness—which is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*)—is excluded, there is no implication of a positive entity characterized by non-self (*anātma*). Therefore, since there is no connection with positive concomitance (*anvaya*) despite the existence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the reason such as breath is purely negative (*vyatirekin*); thus, by this much of the text, the Naiyāyika’s desired conclusion has been demonstrated.
(Note: B reads *apyātmalakṣaṇasya*.)

He states the fault in this assumption with the words "In that way," and so forth: Even though selflessness (*nairātmya*) is being excluded from the vital breaths and so on by the exclusion of the state of lacking vital breaths and so forth—just as it does not establish its presence in the *sapakṣa* (the similar instance), namely the self—in that same way, when selflessness is being dispelled from the living body by the reasons such as the vital breaths, it would merely be excluded from the probandum; it would not, however, establish the self.

Clarifying this very statement of the formal proposition (*grahaṇakavākya*), he says: "Because of their absence in selflessness," and so forth. Since vital breaths and the like are absent in selflessness, the vital breaths and so forth—by negating that [selflessness]—exclude only selflessness and do not establish a self. What is the reason? Because the existence of the vital breaths and so forth is unestablished in that which possesses a self. Nor is there an establishment of a self in a living body through the exclusion of selflessness, which is the opposite of a self.

What is the reason? Because even if one demonstrates the exclusion of breath and so forth from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of selflessness (*nairātmya*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that breath and so forth are established in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), namely, the self (*ātman*).

Since this is so, there is no pervasion by the absence of the contrary. The meaning is that there is no establishment of pervasion between "possessing a self" (*sātmakatva*) and "possessing breath, etc. (*prāṇādimattva*) within their respective counter-instances (*vipakṣa*), because [the latter] lacks a self (*nairātmyāt*). When? At the time when the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of breath, etc., from the lack of a self is not established. For in this way, the pervasion of the probandum’s counter-instance—the lack of a self—by the reason’s counter-instance—the absence of breath, etc.—would be established only if the lack of a self were excluded from breath, etc. And that exclusion would occur only if there were a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Thus it says: "And the establishment of that," and so forth. The very establishment of that negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because the latter is invariably connected (*nāntarīyaka*) with the former. Thus, the establishment of negative concomitance itself is stated to be the establishment of positive concomitance.

Now, if the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not accepted, then, given that positive concomitance is unestablished, even if the occurrence of its absence (*vyatireka-vṛtti*) were established—meaning that although the absence of that self (*ātman*) from breath and so forth, which constitutes the absence of self (*nairātmya*), might be established—the self, which is the subject of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), remains unestablished. Consequently, even if there were an exclusion of the absence of self in the living body (the locus of the probandum), it would follow that the self itself is unestablished.

Therefore, "that" means that there is no pervasion by way of absence (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) devoid of positive concomitance; that is to say, there is no pervasion between the probandum and the probans in the case of their dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

We say, "even granting this. Let it be granted that there is a negative pervasion (*vyatireka*) lacking positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Since no other alternative is possible for a living body, if selflessness (*nairātmya*) were excluded from a living body, it would follow that the living body possesses a self (*sātmakatva*). However, this mode of reasoning is not possible when the reason (*hetu*) is "being uncreated" (*akṛtaka*) in order to prove truthfulness; thus he says: "of falsity," and so forth.

However, even if falsity—which is the opposite of the probandum—is excluded from non-human [Vedic] speech by means of its cause, namely its pervasion with being human-made, it would still not be established that what is uncreated possesses truthfulness. Why? Because, apart from truthfulness, another alternative—namely, meaninglessness—is possible. This [conclusion] would hold for words only if there were two categories: truthfulness and falsity; for in that case, upon the exclusion of falsity, truthfulness would necessarily follow.

What is the reason? Because when one [of the two] is excluded—namely, the exclusion of falsity—there is no other possible alternative besides the presence of truthfulness. However, there is indeed a state of duality, since another alternative is possible; therefore, those words might even be meaningless, so that neither your desired goal is established, nor is the establishment of their truthfulness achieved.

If it is argued that words are not meaningless because they cause the cognition of objects, [we reply: this cognition of meaning is not inherent; rather, it must be a human activity. Convention (*saṃketa*) is a human activity, and since it is the result of that, it is spoken of non-differently as "human activity. The meaning is that [the cognition] would arise from human activity. How so? Like the conceptualization of another object based on a well-known object.

He explains this very point with the words "Just as," and so forth. According to the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas), although the deeds of Bharata, Urvaśī, and others do not have that [sacrificial] purpose as their actual meaning, they nevertheless interpret the life-story of Bharata, the life-story of Urvaśī, and—by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—the life-stories of others such as Purūravas, in another way. By the second use of "and so forth," it is meant that other Mīmāṃsakas explain things differently from what is well-known in the world, interpreting the specific states and actions of Bharata and the others as something other than mere biography; for instance, "Bharata is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," "Urvaśī is the vessel (*pātrī*)," or "the fire-drill (*araṇi*)," and so on.

If it is argued that there is no comprehension of meaning from what is conceptualized by the commentator, he says: "In accordance with that," and so forth. According to the meaning conceptualized by the commentators, comprehension certainly does arise for some listeners; this is just as in the case of the explanations of words such as *bharata*. Even in Vedic sentences which are inherently meaningless, the conceptualization of meaning would be produced by persons and not by the nature of the words themselves. What is the reason? Because, regarding the comprehension of meaning from Vedic [texts], a person such as Jaimini and others must depend upon instruction.

What is this like? It is just like [the case of] different meanings. The meaning is that it is like the conceptualization of different meanings for words such as "Bharata" or "Urvaśī. Furthermore, the claim that [words], even when revealing their objects by their very nature (*svabhāva*), would depend upon human instruction, is also false. For fire and the like, which illuminate objects through their primordial nature (*prakṛti*) or inherent essence (*svabhāva*), do not depend upon human instruction. Rather, it is the person who, by means of the power of his own conventional usage (*samaya-vyāpāra-saṃketa*), explains and instructs others.

It is logical that one should say, "This word has been employed by me in this meaning," but it is not logical that there should be instruction by a person regarding the manifestation of meaning through the inherent nature [of words].

Now, even if the Veda is established by nature as having meanings equivalent to those agreed upon by men, it nevertheless requires human instruction regarding its meanings. In that case, there is no distinction between an object that is agreed upon by a person—that is, conventionally designated—and an object that is established by nature or inherent essence, because both alike depend upon human instruction. Furthermore, there is no other distinguishing feature by which one might recognize, "This is agreed upon by a person," and "This is established by nature. For this reason, one [meaning] in the Veda would be natural.

In the expression *nisarge bhavaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *adhyātma*. Any other worldly word whose meaning is of human origin is difficult to determine; that is, it is hard to understand, because there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish its specific classification.

If it is argued that there is a distinction—that the Veda, established by its very nature, possesses some correspondence with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely, conformity with other means of knowledge, whereas that which does not do so is of human origin—this we shall refute later in the passage beginning with "there is no operation of other means of valid cognition regarding objects that are entirely beyond the senses. Furthermore, since the worldly and the Vedic are of equal character in their dependence on human instruction and so forth, if one were to postulate the non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda solely on the basis of this distinction of correspondence with other means of valid cognition, [it would be fallacious].

Now, one would have to postulate that a great many worldly sentences are non-human (apauruṣeya) simply because they are consistent with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvādya*). For there exist even some human-composed sentences—such as "Impermanent, alas, are conditioned phenomena"—which are of this kind, meaning they are consistent with valid cognition. Consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows that these too must be non-human.
(Dhammapada 278)

Now, if even worldly [words], though consistent with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), possess human authorship, then likewise for these Vedic words, their capacity to convey intended meanings would be both human-made and yet conforming to valid cognition, as well as being non-contradictory to valid cognition; thus, we perceive no distinction between Vedic words and worldly ones.

Showing that Vedic words are non-human (apauruṣeya) precisely because they are mantras, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth. "Contradictory" (*vyāhata*) means mutually opposed. For instance, if it were established by a proposition that mantras are the conventions of some person—that is, if they were established as being fixed by human agreement—then it would be logical for them to accomplish their purpose; that is, the accomplishment of the desired effect through the employment of the mantra would be logical.

The explanation begins with the words "If these," and so forth. The connection is with what will be said later: "If these mantras were the *samaya* (convention/pledge) of some powerful author. They are called *samaya* because they are established by convention (*samaya-vyavasthāpitatvāt*). To the question, "How then was this convention made for them? he says: "Devotion to the welfare of others," and so forth. "Devotion to the welfare of others" means having that as one's primary concern; that is to say, out of compassion (*kṛpālutā*). It may have been made out of compliance with that, or from some other cause such as fame, and the like.

He asks, "What kind of convention (*samaya*) is this? and replies with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathā*). Just as this statement composed by me—what is its nature? It is "bound to the intended object. The "intended object" of the mantra's author is a specific ritual procedure characterized by such acts as invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*); that in which such a thing is the "bond" (*nibandhana*), the factor for engagement, is described as such.

By the word "thus" (*evam*), there would be an agreement (*samaya*) on the part of one who employs [the mantra] in an unspoken manner, thinking: "I shall join this person—who is employing [the mantra]—with this purpose, which is the result desired by the person. Then, through the application of the mantra, at some point upon the completion of the ritual procedure, the accomplishment of the desired object would occur, just as in the case of a poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). For example, suppose someone, having composed a poem, makes such an agreement: "To whoever reads the poem composed by me, I must give this [reward]. In that case, for those who read the poem he has composed, there is the accomplishment of the promised object; it is just like that.

Now, if it is argued that the power of the entity (*bhāvaśakti*) is simply an inherent capacity of the word's own nature by which the desired result arises—not from a convention established by a person according to their whim—then this would also apply elsewhere, such as even from a mantra that has been recited in some arbitrary manner. What is the reason? Because there is no difference in the mantra when it consists of the phonemes (*varṇa*).

The explanation begins with "No," and so forth. Indeed, the accomplishment of a purpose from mantras does not arise from the convention of human beings; rather, this is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the mantra, which consists of the form of phonemes (*varṇa*). If mantras were not applied according to a specific procedure (*vidhi*), they would not yield results for anyone.

"Then that... and so forth [is said by] the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). "Then that nature of the phonemes called 'mantra' would be indistinct everywhere"—that is, at a time devoid of ritual injunction, or even in the case of an inverted or otherwise incorrect application. Consequently, the desired fruit would arise even from a mantra employed in any manner whatsoever, having transgressed both the sequential order of recitation and the ritual injunction. For it is the phonemes themselves that constitute the mantra, and nothing else exists apart from the phonemes.
If it is argued that "it is their sequence—the sequence of the phonemes—that is the mantra, and not the phonemes themselves," [the response follows].

That is incorrect; for the fact that the meaning [of a sentence] is distinct from the phonemes, as well as the view that a sentence is the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*), has already been refuted previously in this very context.

The explanation begins with "no" and so forth. Since the sequence is not distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), the mantras would be nothing but the phonemes themselves; and since those phonemes are indistinguishable everywhere—even in reverse recitation and the like—they would grant results in every way, however they were employed. Yet, they do not grant results. He states that they do not merely fail to grant results when there is a lapse in the ritual procedure, but rather that when employed [incorrectly], they actually produce harm, beginning with the words "upaplava" and so forth. *Upaplava* means an affliction (*upadrava*). The word "tu" (but) indicates an emphasis.

It is observed that even a slight deviation from the prescribed sequence [of ritual] results in failure; and this is logical if mantras are of human origin (*puruṣasamaya*), but not if they are of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

If it is asked, "Even if it is a matter of [following] a specific tradition (*samaya*), how can there be a disturbance (*upaplava*)?", he says: "Of someone," and so forth. Among the injunctions (*vidhi*) prescribed by the author of the mantra, through the performance of one particular injunction, the presence (*sannidhi*) of the deity occurs. Due to that presence, because another specific injunction is not fully accomplished—either through neglecting the deity or through causing her distress—a disturbance may arise. In that case, a deity who has not transcended passion, being offended, will herself bring about misfortune.
But those who are free from passion do not do it themselves; rather, it should be understood that other deities and so forth, who have faith in them, perform it.

As for the question of how it is when no ritual procedure whatsoever is prescribed in a mantra, he says: "In the case of the failure of all procedures," etc. However, when there is a lapse in all procedures, because one performs some specific rule established by the author of the mantra, there is neither benefit nor harm due to the non-presence of the deity.

With the words "Furthermore," etc., he states another fault: the distinctness of the sequence from its constituent parts has already been refuted. Or, let it be granted that the sequence is either distinct from or non-distinct from the phonemes. In that regard, if the sequence were non-distinct, the mantra would be identical in nature to the phonemes, having the very essence of the phonemes. But if it were distinct, it would have the nature of that sequence—that is, the nature of the sequence of phonemes.

Since that mantra—whether consisting of phonemes or consisting of their sequence—is eternal because it is not produced by causes, and since its presence is eternal for the sake of its meaning which is the cause of human goals, there would be the constant accomplishment of those goals; from those mantras, the fulfillment of human purposes would arise.

What is the reason? Because, from whichever causal power (*bhāvaśakti*) or mantra-power the production of the fruit to be accomplished by the mantra arises, that causal power is unfailing; thus, there would be no deficiency in the result. For it is not logical that when the completeness of the cause exists, there should be a deficiency—that is, the non-existence—of the effect. Why? Because it would follow that such a complete cause, if it were not to produce its effect, would forfeit its status as a cause.

Even if mantras were eternal, the accomplishment of the desired result does not follow from the mere employment of the mantra; rather, it results from its connection with the ritual injunction (*vidhi*). If one asks, "What is the reason?"—namely, that it is because that mantra depends upon the injunction—this is incorrect. For if it is admitted that the mantra depends upon the injunction, then that which is depended upon—the injunction and so forth—would lack efficacy with respect to the mantra, since no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be imparted to the mantra [by such an injunction].

He explains this with the words "If indeed," and so forth. By means of ritual injunctions and the like—where "injunction" refers to the *kalpa* (ritual manual) or from some other auxiliary cause such as a particular location—they might acquire or obtain some excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*). In that case, the auxiliary would be capable and thus relevant regarding that excellence of intrinsic nature produced in the mantra. However, it has already been stated previously that such production of an excellence is not possible in the case of eternal things.

Therefore, if this [agent] were incapable of producing an excellence (*atiśaya*) through the assistance of mantras, then, being independent of them, the mantras would either always produce the effect or never produce it at all; for its own nature, being without such an excellence, would remain identical at all times.

Furthermore, if such an intrinsic power of mantras were independent of ritual commitments (*samaya*), then those mantras would not be the causes of results for every person, even one joined with sins and the like. Now, it might be argued that they bestow results only when employed by the sacrificer himself.

Therefore, he says: "The distinction of the performer—the specific quality of being the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the dependence upon that—is not appropriate for a mantra that is not to be consecrated (*asaṃskārya*). If mantras were to yield results solely through their own inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*) without depending on convention (*samaya*), they would not exclude any person from granting those results; nor would they exclude another, such as a *śūdra* or the like. For it is not the case that the nature of mantras—which is the nature of performing an action—becomes a non-nature (i.e., a non-producing nature) with respect to someone else who is not the sacrificer."

What is the reason? Because that nature which produces [the effect] has not been diminished by that non-Brahmin—meaning it has not been impaired—and because it has not been enhanced by another, such as a sacrificer. For this reason, there is a connection between the mantras and a certain person in terms of the relation of cause and effect. Due to the absence of that [causal] connection, and because there is neither proximity nor distance between the mantras and either the Brahmin or the other [person] respectively, the mantras would accomplish everything.

For this very reason, because this mantra is not something to be refined (*asaṃskāryatvāt*), there is no one—whether a Brāhmaṇa or anyone else—who can be the *prayoktṛ* (the one who applies it) with respect to its effect; that is, there is no one who, as an *niyoktṛ* (the one who directs), might enjoy or obtain the fruit accomplished by the mantra. It is only a Brāhmaṇa, and no other. For instance, just as a Śūdra or others who do not recite [the Veda] do nothing and thus are not *prayoktṛ*s, so too is the Brāhmaṇa [incapable]. This is because he does not undergo the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, even for an entity that is to be modified and upon which a new quality is imposed, it is indeed a difference in the underlying reality (*vastu*)—that is, a difference in the cause—that constitutes the differentiator; there is no ultimate difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of Brāhmaṇas, Śūdras, and so forth. The distinction between Brāhmaṇas, Śūdras, and others is merely constructed by worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). Therefore, because the users of the Brāhmaṇas and others are distinguished only by worldly convention, a restriction regarding the application of mantras is not possible; by means of which [restriction] only a Brāhmaṇa would obtain the fruit and not a Śūdra. Where, then, could such a restriction exist?

He said: It would be by convention (*samaya*). When the mantra is a convention, then the agent of the convention performs the convention without regard for the intrinsic nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*). Just as in the world, there might be a restriction such as, "I shall grant the fruit only to those well-known Brahmins who are the practitioners, and not to others."

The explanation begins with the words "ādheya" and so forth. Those entities (*bhāva*) which possess a produced (*ādheya*) particularity (*viśeṣa*) are such that, when there is a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) due to that cause—the cause of the particularity—then, because they have acquired an excellence (*atiśaya*) from that cause of the particularity, they would be of one nature in one place and of another nature elsewhere in a different cause; however, there can be no change of nature if there is no difference in the cause. Why? Because when there is no difference in the cause, there is no difference in the effect.

Now, if there is a distinction in the effect despite the absence of a distinction in the cause, then, even if such a distinction in the effect is admitted, it follows—more or less as has already been stated—that this distinction would be without a cause.

Therefore, for this reason, these mantras—though they are produced and though they are impermanent—are fruit-yielding due to a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) brought about by their causes; yet they would not be otherwise, nor would they fail to yield fruit, even when employed by Śūdras and others. What is the reason? Because there is no difference in the intrinsic nature of the intellect, the sense faculties, or the bodies of those two persons who possess the designations or names "Śūdra" and "Brāhmaṇa. If it is argued that there exists a distinction of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) in each individual instance, we say: no.

Since this [distinction] occurs even among Brahmins on a per-individual basis, it is said that there is no distinction based on caste (*jāti*). [Objection: But surely in the world there is a difference in names, such as "this is a Brahmin" and "this is a Śūdra," as well as a difference in conduct regarding honor and so forth; therefore, a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is inferred. [Response: If this is argued...

He says: "Not indeed," and so forth. Because of the difference in names such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so on—which follow human desire—and because of the difference in conventional practices such as honor and so on, there is a change in things that are followed by a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) produced according to their causes, which are accompanied by a difference in intrinsic nature. The connection [of the sentence] is: "Indeed, there is no difference in intrinsic nature. If it is argued that there is a difference in caste (*jāti*) between those two persons, the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra;

That is not so; for it is said, "Indeed, that... and so forth. Since the universal (*jāti*) has already been refuted by the general negation, it is merely stated here while provisionally accepting it. Indeed, even if it exists, that particular universal is held to be threefold when there is a distinction in configuration (*ākṛti*), quality (*guṇa*), and capacity (*śakti*). "Like a cow and a horse" (*gavāśvavat*): this means "just as in the case of a cow and a horse. Among these, the distinction in configuration is a specific arrangement [of parts]; it is found to follow through all individual cows, despite their differences, but not in individual horses.

The distinction of qualities (*guṇabheda*) in milk and other substances—consisting in the difference of their taste, potency, post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and so forth—is observed to follow through individuals of the same class, but not through those of different classes. This distinction is characterized by the capacity for effects corresponding to a specific difference in power (*śaktibheda*); for example, the capacity for milking and so forth belongs to cows, but not to horses. Thus, since differences such as generic form (*ākṛti*) are observed to follow through individuals of the same class, one may indeed postulate a distinction of genus (*jātibheda*) among cows, horses, and the like.

Furthermore, one who has once acquired proficiency regarding cows and the like recognizes this distinction of genus even across differences of place, time, and so forth, without further instruction; that is, one understands "this is a cow" and "this is a horse" without needing repeated teaching. However, one does not understand the distinction between Brāhmaṇas and others in such a way without instruction. "In the same manner" means like cows and horses. We do not observe any fixed quality in these two—the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra—that resides only within individuals of the same genus. The mention of "quality" (*guṇa*) is illustrative [of other characteristics as well].

Thus, we do not perceive any fixed difference in physical form or difference in capacity. Not perceiving such differences in form and so forth, how could we establish a distinction in caste between a Śūdra and a Brāhmaṇa? The meaning is: "We certainly could not. For instance, every particularity such as Vedic study, purity, and conduct is subject to deviation; and as for the difference in appearance that is postulated—characterized by being fair-skinned, reddish-brown hair, and so on—that does not exist even among some Brāhmaṇas, yet it is found among some Śūdras.
If there is no difference in caste between a Brahmin and a Śūdra, how then does this distinct cognition arise from hearing words such as "Brahmin" and so forth?

He says: "Even that which... and so forth. This difference in cognition—the difference in perception such as "this is a Brāhmaṇa" or "this is a Śūdra"—which follows from a difference in names, is caused by specific designations like "Brāhmaṇa" and so on; it would occur even in the absence of a difference in genus (*jāti*), due to the performance of specific activities, namely the performance of specific rites such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*). And "due to lineage" means because of birth from a family that performs such activities, just like the designations "physician" or "merchant," and so forth.

Just as among those of the same genus, designations such as "physician" and so forth proceed from the performance of specific activities and from [the observation of] positive concomitance, yet there is no difference in genus [among them]—so too it would be in the case of Brāhmaṇas and others. *In the margin:* [The word *jāti* is used here in the sense of *gotra* (lineage).]

"Therefore" (*tat*) means: for this reason, these mantras, when employed by an undistinguished person such as a Brāhmaṇa or a Śūdra, acquire a nature that is likewise undistinguished from that of the Brāhmaṇa and others. For that reason, the conclusion is that they would yield results for Śūdras and others without distinction. Thus, there is no fault in the production of results through the inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*) of mantras; however, when a result is desired from these Vedic mantras or from other [non-Vedic] mantras based on the aforementioned human convention (*puruṣasamaya*), [then the fault applies].

In that case, there would be no fault in these [mantras] yielding results without distinction. What is the reason? Because the production of the result is restricted by the inclination (*ruci*) of the author of the convention (*samayakāra*), the composer of the mantra. It is the author of the convention who has thus resolved: "I am present to bestow the connection with the result only for one who possesses such a designation as 'Brāhmaṇa' and observes such a rule, and not for others"—thus, the restriction of the result is determined by this inclination. This is the objection.

For it is thus: entities that function by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*) are independent of human activity; the meaning is that they produce effects solely through the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*). They are subject to a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) by way of that [nature], namely, through the door of their own nature, as follows: "If this is so because of a specific nature, why does it not happen here as well? Entities that function according to human will do not admit such a *prasaṅga*. What is the reason? Because those humans, who act according to their own whims, may proceed in any manner whatsoever.

As for the claim that a distinguished practitioner attains the fruit of the mantra, we observe that even in that case, the "application" (*prayoga*) is characterized as follows: it is the production of that intrinsic nature of the mantra which is capable of achieving the human goal desired; and once produced, it is either the transformation of its continuum through the production of successive distinctions, or its alteration. Both of these—production or transformation—would occur only when there is the arising of a distinction, that is, when a specific excellence is produced.
Otherwise, if no distinction were produced, what could the practitioner do with mantras that admit no excellence? Nothing at all.

He explains this with the words beginning with "yeva" (only, etc.). For this reason—that from that application of mantras, a certain practitioner who is a Brāhmaṇa enjoys the fruit, while another, such as a Śūdra, does not—the application of mantras is not their production, but rather their manifestation; yet that manifestation has already been refuted previously in the discussion on universals (*sāmānya*).
He explains that [refutation]: it has been stated that for eternal entities, there is no manifestation whatsoever, by virtue of which a speaker could be the manifestor of a word.

Or let there be manifestation (*abhivyakti*). And that [manifestation] would be eternal due to the eternity of the capacity [of the sound]. However, manifestation is the cognition whose object is the word; if the person who is the speaker of that [cognition] were to be joined with the fruits of the mantra, then the hearer would also have a connection with the fruit. For even one who merely hears a mantra being recited by another would have a connection with the fruit of the mantra, and not the speaker alone.

Since the speaker is indeed the cause of manifestation and, as such, the cause of knowledge, he is connected with the result; and since that status of being the cause of knowledge regarding the subject matter of the mantra belongs equally to the listener as well, why is it that the listener also—as being effectively the "speaker"—is not connected with the result?

He explains this with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*). For an eternal word, manifestation is neither a transformation of its own nature—that is, a change in its essential form—due to some other cause, nor is manifestation the removal of an obscuration, because an obscuration is impossible for that which is eternal. Rather, manifestation is the cognition—the mental apprehension—of that object, namely the word. What is the reason? Because the designation "unmanifested" applies when the word is not being heard. Indeed, a word that is not being perceived is not said to be "manifested."

This being the case, if the speaker were the cause of the cognition whose object is sound, then that nature of being the cause of the cognition of sound—which is the defining characteristic of the speaker—would also exist in the listener; consequently, the listener too would obtain the desired result arising from the employment of the mantra, just like the speaker. For there is no other state belonging to the speaker than the state of being a speaker, which is nothing other than being the cause of that cognition, namely, the cause of the cognition of sound.

Therefore, since there is no difference between the speaker and the listener in their being the cause of the cognition of the word, the connection with the result would be equal for both. If it is argued that the distinction between the speaker and the listener lies in this: that the speaker is "another" (*para*), and that the cognition which has another as its causal condition (*upādhi*) is "cognition conditioned by another" (*paropādhibuddhi*), whereas the listener does not have a cognition conditioned by another—[we ask] what, then, is the utility or capacity of the speaker regarding the production of cognition in the listener, such that the speaker is accepted as a causal condition (*upādhi*) on account of that utility?
If it is argued that the hearing of sound—that is, the perception of sound—occurs for the listener from the presence of the speaker, and therefore that speaker is the limiting adjunct (upādhi).

Is it not precisely this that is being questioned: how does the hearing of the word by the listener arise from the speaker? And why would it not arise from him? Because of the absence of a relationship; because of the absence of a state of mutual benefit between the benefactor and the beneficiary. Demonstrating that very absence, he says: "By bringing the object near—that is, by placing the object in proximity—this speaker would be the one who makes this listener hear; he would be the communicator. But such a presentation is impossible for that word, because it is eternal and thus cannot undergo any transformation whatsoever, as there is no change in its nature.

If it is argued that the speaker would be of service by either effecting a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the listener’s sense organ or by accomplishing the removal of an obscuration (*āvaraṇavigamana*) of the sound, that is not so; for the refinement of the sense organ and other such [propositions] have already been stated and refuted, beginning with: “The sense organ would be refined, and thus one would hear everything” (PV 1.258). If it is argued that there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener according to their respective cognitions (*pratyaya*), since the listener has the cognition, “This speaker is making me hear,” and the speaker has the cognition, “I am making this listener hear”—then [the response follows]: [The verse: PV 1.258. ... [as previously cited]. ... [The commentary continues: If it is claimed that the difference between the speaker and the listener arises from these two cognitions as appropriate, [we reply: no, because the nature of the object remains the same. Just as when a single person, such as Devadatta, is seen at a distance and then recognized upon being approached, the object is not different despite the change in the cognitions, so too here. Furthermore, if the sound were produced anew for each listener, then the very same word-sound would not be heard by others; rather, it would be like the perception of a unique individual, such as Devadatta, which is not shared by others. Moreover, if the sound were produced by the speaker, it would follow that it is not perceived by others, just as the sound of a drum is not heard by those who did not strike it. Therefore, the claim that the speaker produces a refinement of the listener’s organ or removes its obscuration is untenable. Thus, the distinction between speaker and listener cannot be established on the basis of such a causal relationship.

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words beginning "anupakārya" (not being assisted). The notions "it makes me hear" and "I hear" are mere illusions (*bhrāntimātra*). Of what nature is this? It is that in which there exists neither an object to be assisted (*upakārya*)—namely, the listener—nor an assistant (*upakāraka*)—namely, the speaker. Since the word is eternal, when cognition arises in a person, there is an absolute absence of any operation; thus, the state of being neither assisted nor assisting has been established. Therefore, if that state [of hearing] were to exist, it would be due to such a mere illusion.

If there were no distinction between speaker and listener, there would be an over-extension [of the principle]: it would apply to everyone, even to one who does not hear or cause another to hear. Why? Because even in other cases, such as with those who are insane, one observes the cognition "I am hearing" and so forth through delusion, even without hearing a sound. Therefore, since there is no benefit whatsoever [to the listener], such a cognition—that is, the cognition "I am making [him] hear" and so forth—is not tenable.

What is the reason? Because for all things that are mutually neither benefactors nor beneficiaries, there would be the undesirable consequence [of such thoughts as] "I hear this from him" and so forth. If it is argued that just as cognitions arise through delusion regarding those who are insane, so too might they arise regarding eternal entities, [the author] says: "Delusion," etc. Even that delusion which occurs to an insane person arises only when, during a state of sanity, there has been some benefit received from another person, and when a cognition is produced accordingly by what was then instilled [in the mind].

Furthermore, by the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), even in another state of madness, and even for one who does not speak, [the cognition] occurs through some proximity or some similarity. That too would be an error; it could not exist with respect to eternal mantras, since they provide no assistance whatsoever, even indirectly. [In the margin:
3: In the margin.

With the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he concludes the subject at hand. According to the method described, if both the reciter and the listener were causes for the manifestation [of the mantra], then, because there would be no distinction in their being causes for the cognition of the sound, the connection with the fruit of the mantra would be the same for both. Furthermore, in the case of those [mantras] that are not audible, there is no manifestation whatsoever; this is stated merely by way of concession.

Furthermore, with the words beginning "api ca," he states another refutation: "Those organs, such as the palate and so forth, by which sound is not manifested—that is, not brought within the range of the sense of hearing—are 'anabhivyakta-śabdāni' (organs for which sound is unmanifested). The connection [of the sentence] is made by changing the gender: 'the employment, i.e., the operation, of those organs would be useless. The meaning of the sentence is that where a silent recitation (*upāṃśu-japa*) is performed merely by the movement of the lips and so forth, that [recitation] would be useless."

That in which there is not even the movement of the lips and so forth, but only the mental contemplation of the mantra, is *manojapa* (mental recitation). The word "or" (*vā*) is used for conjunction. Furthermore, mental recitation would be useless; for sound is within the range of the ear, and sound is indeed that which is grasped by the ear. Since a mantra has the nature of sound, and because in both whispered (*upāṃśu*) and mental (*mānasa*) recitations there is an absence of being grasped by the ear, they lack the quality of sound. And because they lack the quality of sound, they lack the status of being a mantra. How could one who recites [such] be fruitful? "Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means that which is grasped (*gṛhyate*).

The meaning is "perceptible by the ear. That sound which has that very [quality] as its characteristic is so described. Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For if one were to desire that even mental recitation (*manojapa*) and the like—which are of the nature of cognition—be considered sound, setting aside the sound perceptible by the ear, then taste (*rasa*) and other such things would also become sound.
[Objection: Even so, if that which falls within the range of the ear possesses the nature of sound, then it follows that the universal *śabdatva* (sound-ness) must also possess the nature of sound.

"No," says the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin). We do not say that sound is exclusively within the range of the auditory organ. Rather, we say that sound is necessarily characterized by that [auditory perception], namely, it is defined as being apprehended by the ear. Why? Because, apart from its being graspable by the ear, there is no other defining characteristic for that sound.

In this regard, if with respect to this specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound, the person who utters [the sound] is intended as the cause of manifestation for mantras—which possess the nature of sound and have sound as their essence—and as the cause of the cognition that grasps the form of the sound, such that he has a connection with the result; then, regarding those causes by which the word that is the object of hearing remains unmanifest—the analysis of the compound being "those causes by which the word, which is the object of hearing, is unmanifest"—he is the "utterer" (*prayoktṛ*) of those causes, meaning the one who activates them merely through the movement of the lips and so forth.

One who mutters in a whisper is not joined with the fruit of the mantra, nor is one joined with the fruit of the mantra by muttering mentally. For at that time, during the practice of whispered silence, we do not perceive or grasp any object called "sound" with the ear.

He says that mental muttering is also a mantra: "And a mental conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is not a mantra whose nature is non-sound. This is because sound is accepted as being perceptible by the ear, as being unauthored (*apauruṣeya*), and as being eternal, whereas a conceptualization is the opposite of that.

With the words "by way of tradition" (*pāramparyeṇa*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent’s objection: even that mental cognition which appears as a mantra at the time of silent mental recitation (*manojapa*) is a manifestation of that [word]; it is the cognition of the manifestation of that sound. Why? Because it is produced from that by way of tradition; that is, because it is born from the word. For instance, first there arises a cognition of the word, and for one whose latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been instilled by that cognition, a manifestation of the word arises gradually during mental recitation.

He explains with the words beginning with "no" (not so). For even when one meditates with the mind or mutters what appears to be a mantra, that cognition which is a mere semblance of a mantra does not exist without hearing; that is, without the hearing of the sound. Since it arises from the word—that is, its production is from the word—it follows that even at the time of mental recitation (*manojapa*), that cognition is simply the manifestation of the word, which is to say, it is the knowledge of the word itself.
