And thus, because it possesses the nature of a mantra, the practitioner of mental recitation and the like would be successful in attaining the fruit; this is the intended meaning. If it were otherwise, there would be an infinite regress regarding the status of being a mantra through such a succession.

He states this very point in the passage beginning with "from sound," and so forth. "Conceptual constructions of word and meaning" refers to conceptual constructions regarding the objects of words arising from sounds that possess the characteristics of mantras. For instance, when it is said, "Svāhā to Agni," conceptual constructions such as "Agni has a form that is blazing, radiant, and so forth" sometimes arise. Since these too have their origin in sound through a causal lineage, those conceptual constructions would likewise be characterized by the manifestation of mantra; they would thus be [mantric] applications (*prayoga*). Even though they originate from sound, that which has that [mantra] as its object—(p.)...

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has sound as its object is the meaning. If that very cognition were the manifestation of the mantra, then those conceptual constructions of meaning which have sound as their object would not exist. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says: "This is unestablished. The fact that conceptual construction of sound has the specific characteristic of sound (*śabdasvalakṣaṇa*) as its object is unestablished. Why? Because it follows from conceptualization; because it is caused by conceptualizations of its own kind. Conceptualizations of the mind have only superimposed forms as their objects.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*). We do not say that every cognition arising from a word is the manifestation (*vyakti*) of that [word], nor that it is the manifestation of the word itself. Rather, that conceptual cognition which has that [word] as its object—that is, which has the word as its object—is the manifestation of that word.

This is incorrect, because it is unestablished that mental consciousness has that [the word] as its object or has the word as its object. For we shall demonstrate that there is no application of words to particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). [Objection: If external objects are not the cause of conceptual cognitions, how then do they arise?

He says: "For those," and so forth. For those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise according to their own [respective] awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), which is the cause. This occurs because they are established within consciousness; that is, they arise from the awakening of the latent predispositions for conceptualization. The analysis of the compound is: "those by whom the proximity—that is, the presence—of an external object is not required. Why? Because of the phrase "external," and so forth. "Departure" (*apāya*) means cessation; "non-arrival" (*anāgama*) means non-arising. This is because conceptual constructions do not exist when external objects have ceased or fail to arise.

Since they occur even in the absence of an object, they do not have the object as their cause. Why? Because that which does not depend upon the presence (*sattopadhāna*)—that is, the proximity (*sattāsannidhāna*)—of something for its own existence, being independent, cannot be the cause of that [object]. And how could that which is not a cause be the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)? It is not at all. Since conceptual construction is thus not an object of words, mental conceptualization—characterized by mental recitation (*manojalpa*) and so forth—is not the manifestation of a word, nor is it that by which one possesses it. Consequently, a person would not be a "reciter of mantras" (*mantrajapa-vān*), meaning they would not be a user of mantras; that is to say, such a thing would simply not be the case.

In the margin: Even while accepting the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of sound, he states a fault: "The cognition produced by sound and having that [sound] as its object is the manifestation of the word; since the person is the substratum (*āśraya*) of that manifestation, he is therefore the 'user' (*prayoktṛ*). This has been stated even in this position. What was stated? That it would follow that the ear is the user. For the hearer too is the substratum of the cognition—which is produced by the sound and has that [sound] as its object—arising within his own continuum; and thus, he too would be joined with the fruit of the mantra. In the margin:

Furthermore, the application (*prayoga*) of eternal mantras does not consist in the production of some excellence; rather, the application is the knowledge directed toward them. And if that knowledge is accepted as the application, then the word (*śabda*) operates upon the person. How so? By generating knowledge in that person. The person does not operate upon the word. Why? Because no assistance whatsoever can be rendered by a person to the eternal nature of the word—that is, to the nature of the word itself. This is the reason.
Moreover, the claim that "the person is the user of words" is an unconventional usage. For in the world, whoever is actively engaged in something is called its "user.

The conclusion is stated with the words "in every way," etc. If "word-cognition" means a cognition produced directly from a word, or if it means [produced] through a succession [of cognitions], then, when the attainment of a result is desired through the employment of mantras whose nature is that of words—because they generate a cognition having those [words] as their object—mental recitation (*manojapa*) would be useless. Why? Because the conceptual construction characterized as mental recitation does not touch upon the actual form of the words.

To the question, "Even for one who [accepts] that the fruit arises from convention (*samaya*), how is mental recitation (*manojapa*) not futile? he says: The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound is its own intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva*), while the form appearing to conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is their universal nature (*sāmānyasvabhāva*). With the intention of expressing these individual and universal natures as a single entity—having unified the perceived object and the conceptualized image—the author of the convention (*samayakāra*) uttered the formulation of mantras; thus, there is no contradiction in saying that mental recitation would otherwise be futile. This is because the accomplishment of the fruit occurs through the fulfillment of the author of the convention's intended purpose.

But there is no lack of contradiction regarding the real entity; rather, there is indeed a contradiction. For instance, if the attainment of a result were to arise from the real entity that is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound, then mental recitation would be useless, because that [recitation] does not touch upon the real entity. He explains this with the words beginning "by convention" (*samaya*). One should, by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), combine—through conceptual thought—the specific characteristic of sound, which is the object of the auditory faculty, and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is the appearance in conceptualization, according to worldly usage, that is, without overstepping common worldly practice. Having unified the perceived and the conceptualized—the specific characteristic of sound and the form of the universal—one should announce the convention.

"One who performs the recitation of the mantra prescribed by me with both speech and mind—for such a person, this mantra shall accomplish its purpose according to the ritual agreement. Therefore, since it is said that for one who recites this mantra with speech and mind, it shall accomplish its purpose according to the agreement, there is no fault in mental recitation (*manojapa*) and the like. By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the inclusion of whispered application (*upāṃśu-prayoga*) and so forth is intended. However, if the production of the fruit from a mantra—which has the nature of sound as its essential property—is desired, then in the absence of contact with that [sound] nature, there would be no fruit in mental recitation and the like.

With the words "As has been said," etc., he anticipates the opponent's objection. Regarding what was stated in the intervening passage, "Mantras are indeed nothing but phonemes (*varṇa*)," and [the claim] that there is no sequence (*ānupūrvī*) other than the phonemes—[the opponent] objects: "If sequence does not exist, then when the word 'sara' is heard and when the word 'rasa' is heard, there would be no difference in their effects, characterized by a difference in cognition. To this we reply: For there is no difference whatsoever in the phonemes between words such as 'sara' and 'sara'. Indeed, the very same phonemes that are present in the word 'sara' here are the same as those in the word 'sara' there.

Nor is there any other distinct word-element (*pada*) from which a difference in effect—characterized by a difference in cognition—could arise; yet a difference in effect does exist. For we observe a distinct cognition or intuition (*pratibhā*) regarding those two words *sara* and *rasa*. We perceive that their sequence alone is unequal and different, while the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves remain the same. And it is not logical for there to be a difference in effect—characterized by a difference in cognition—in the absence of a difference in the cause, namely the phonemes.

Therefore, even though there is no difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), there exists a distinct cognition that possesses differentiation; this is *ānupūrvī* (sequential order). For, due to this sequential order which possesses differentiation in each word, there arises a difference in apprehension—that is, a difference in cognition—regarding words such as "sara" and so forth.

The proponent of the established doctrine says: "True. There exists a sequence for each individual word; however, that sequence is dependent upon human intention and is thus of human origin. It is not distinct from the phonemes themselves. Due to differences in their causes, the phonemes of each word arise as different ones; it is only because of their similarity that those of dull intellect determine them to be identical.

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth. This is the general meaning here: by means of the mind that gives rise to each preceding phoneme, which resides in the speaker, the mind that gives rise to each subsequent phoneme is produced; thus, due to the sequence of the producing minds, there is a sequence in the arising of the phonemes they produce. And by means of these phonemes, which have arisen in sequence, auditory cognitions whose objects are those [phonemes] are directly produced, occurring only in a sequential manner.

The recollections having the phonemes as their objects occur only in a sequence; therefore, by virtue of the sequence of the cognitions that produce those phonemes, there is a sequential nature of being an effect with respect to them. And that which is the sequential nature of being a cause with respect to the cognitions of their own objects is established as "sequence" (*ānupūrvī*).

Now the meaning of the term *apada* is analyzed: the connection is that "the sound which is lost. For example, in the word *sara*, the vowel *a* follows the letter *sa*. From what is it produced? It is produced from the cognition arising from the production of that letter. The letter existing at the prior time is the letter *sa*. And that which is this letter is "that-letter" (*yadvarṇa*). The production of that letter is its cause, because it is by means of this that [the subsequent sound] arises; thus, it is "the production of that letter" (*yadvarṇasamutthāna*).

The term *yadvarṇasamutthānañ ca tajjñānaṃ ca* is a *karmadhāraya* compound. From that [compound] arises the knowledge; that is, the knowledge produced from the knowledge of the origination of the respective phoneme (*yadvarṇasamutthānajñānajam jñānam*). It is produced from that knowledge. The meaning is: the knowledge which originates the letter *sa*, from that knowledge which originates the letter *a*—once it has arisen—the letter *a* is produced. In this way, it should be applied that each subsequent phoneme is produced from the knowledge produced by the knowledge of the origination of each preceding phoneme.

Thus far, it has been stated that sounds are effects because they arise sequentially from the knowledge of their motivation (*samutthānajñāna*) which resides in the continuum of the speaker. Now, showing that these sounds—having arisen sequentially—become the causes for the sequential cognitions of their own objects residing in the continuum of the hearer, and are thus known, he says: "Having that as its adjunct" (*tadupādhi*), etc. A preceding sound is the "adjunct" (*upādhi*), i.e., the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the subsequent sound; that [subsequent sound] is so described. That [subsequent sound], by means of "hearing" (*śruti*), i.e., auditory cognition (*śrotrajñāna*), is "ascertained" (*samavasīyate*), i.e., apprehended. *(Marginal note: In the preceding sound, the subsequent sound is qualified by the cognition of the former.)*

But surely, the preceding phoneme does not exist at the time of the succeeding phoneme; how then can the succeeding phoneme be apprehended as having that as its adjunct (*tadupādhi*), i.e., the preceding phoneme as its adjunct?

He replies: "by means of the cognition produced by the cognition of that. The analysis of the compound is: that which has a cognition of its own object produced by a cognition whose object was the preceding phoneme.

This is what is meant: when the auditory consciousness has the letter *sa* as its object, at that very moment, the letter *a* is produced by a mind that brings about the *a*. Thus, the letter *a* and the letter *sa* as its objective support (*ālambana*) are simultaneous conditions. In this context, the meaning is that while the auditory consciousness having the *sa* as its object acts as a cooperative cause, the letter *a*—producing a cognition of its own object—is said to be perceived as being conditioned by the preceding phoneme.

Thus, when the subsequent phoneme—such as the letter *sa*—is produced by the preceding cognition acting as its auxiliary cause, what is its state at the time of hearing? It is "one whose hearing is not sharp" (*apaṭuśruti*). This refers to when the phoneme is uttered slowly and without haste; at that time, the hearing—the auditory consciousness—is "not sharp," meaning it is slow-moving and perceives the individual phonemes with clarity. In other words, it is the state in which the distinct phonemes are clearly discerned.

This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating how, when [the sounds] are uttered too rapidly, there is no discernment of the distinct phonemes (*varṇa*), and thus how a sequential recollection can arise. The phrase "imperfect auditory apprehension" refers to this. What does such a phoneme do?

He says: depending upon that recollection—the recollection of the preceding phoneme—it subsequently produces a recollection within itself regarding its own object; this should be understood as occurring through a successive process (*pāramparyeṇa*).

By this, it has been stated that phonemes (*varṇa*) are the causes of cognitions regarding their own objects in a sequential order. This causal relationship, as described by the aforementioned sequence, resides "in the phonemes" (*varṇeṣu*), meaning it is based upon the phonemes, or rather, it belongs to the phonemes. The same applies even to human [speech]: in the world, it is said that the sequence is indeed created by a person (*puruṣakṛta*).

In response to the question, "With respect to what do the phonemes possess the status of being effects and causes? it is said: "of the cognitions that grasp their causes. This is a *dvandva* compound meaning "causes" (*hetavaḥ*) and "graspers" (*grāhīṇi*). Then, a genitive compound is formed with *teṣāṃ varṇṇānāṃ hetugrāhīṇi* ("the graspers of the causes of those phonemes"). Subsequently, a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) is formed with the word *cetas*. If the cognitions [arise] in sequence as the causes of the phonemes, then by virtue of their connection, the phonemes possess sequential causality; for the phonemes are produced by those cognitions. These are the cognitions which grasp those phonemes.
Through their connection, the phonemes possess causality in a sequential order, because those cognitions apprehending the phonemes are produced by the phonemes.

He explains by means of the words beginning with *citta*. That vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) for which the mind (*citta*) is the motivating cause (*samutthāna-kāraṇa*) is described as such. Speech itself is the intimation because it makes another understand. And that [speech] is threefold in the world; thus he says "phonemes" (*varṇa*) and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: that whose designations are phonemes (*varṇa*), phrases (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*). Among these, syllables are the phonemes (*varṇa*). A collection of phonemes delimited by meaning is a phrase (*pada*). A collection of phrases is a sentence (*vākya*). Regarding the passage beginning with "therein," in the word *sara*: ... In the word [“sarkāra”], there is the letter *yaṅ*, and the phoneme *sakāra* follows it; after that is the vowel *akāra*, then the *repha* (the sound *r*), after which is another *akāra*, and following that is the *visarjanīya*. In this context, the cause for the arising of the *sakāra* is the mind (*cetas*). By means of that mind acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—the term “immediately preceding” being used to exclude the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)—there arises the mind that brings about the *akāra*. That is to say, that mind by which the *akāra* is brought forth or produced is what is referred to here.

When it is said "so be it," the letter *repha*, the vowel *ā*, and the *visarjanīya* are successively produced by those mental states which have each preceding one as their condition (*pratyaya*). The analysis of the compound is: "those for which the preceding mind is the condition, that is, the cause. Among these, the *repha* arises through the mental state that produces the vowel *ā*; the vowel *ā* [arises] through the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the mental state that produces the *repha*; and the *visarjanīya* is produced by the mental state that produces the vowel *ā*.

Is it not the case that a word is uttered with the intention, "I shall utter this word"? Therefore, the sequence of phonemes is uttered by means of a single intention; it is not the case that each individual phoneme is preceded by its own separate intention, because such is not perceived. So how can it be said that the mind which originates the letter *sa* produces the mind which originates the letter *a*, and so forth?

He thinks as follows: In the pronunciation of individual phonemes (*varṇa*), this very sequence applies; and in the pronunciation of a word (*pada*), this same sequence applies at the outset. For instance, with the intention of pronouncing the letter *sa*, one pronounces the letter *sa*; likewise, with the intention of pronouncing each subsequent phoneme, one pronounces each subsequent phoneme. However, some maintain that in the case of the repeated pronunciation of a word, the sole cause is the intention to pronounce the word as a whole. Others, however, hold a different view: that in the pronunciation of a word, there is only a single intention [to pronounce the word] which serves as the cause.

This is true; however, at the time of the pronunciation of the letter *sa*, the mind must necessarily exist, otherwise death would follow. That very mind is said to be the producer of the letter *sa*, because the letter *sa* arises immediately after it. In this way, the status of being the producer of the mind should be understood for each subsequent phoneme as well.

And here, by the passage beginning with “by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) which is the consciousness that originates the letter *sa*,” etc., it is stated that the sequence of phonemes has a single agent as its cause for the cognition of meaning, and not different agents. Therefore, what is said by Maṇḍana—“If the sequence [of phonemes] is the causal relation between effect and cause, then the cause of that [sequence] would be either a difference in the self [of the cognizer] or a difference in the speakers; thus, even when there is a difference in speakers, the cognition [of the sequence] would occur” (Sphoṭasiddhi 31)—[is refuted].
That is refuted; for it is not admitted that the nature of cognitions apprehending distinct letters—which have different agents—is the cause of the cognition of meaning.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Maṇḍana: "Even if the cognition of meaning occurs through the sequence of phonemes [arising] from the sequence of the motivating mind (*samutthāpakacitta*), nevertheless, that sequence, being a signifier, depends upon a cognition. Moreover, the cognition of meaning is observed to arise from words uttered by a speaker who is concealed or obstructed; yet in such cases, no one is able to ascertain a causal relationship with the motivating mind. For that [causal relationship] could only be ascertained if the eye were the same [as the ear], without relying on the cognition of the word.
And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the identity of a speaker who is both concealed and obstructed."

This is correct; for even when [the speaker] is concealed or obstructed, his identity as a single speaker is indeed apprehended by some. For instance, in the world, activity is observed to be preceded by the recognition: "Devadatta is calling me, not Yajñadatta. Where there is no such ascertainment, there is no activity; thus, our desired conclusion is established.

Furthermore, even for the proponent of *sphoṭa*, how could there be a manifestation of the *sphoṭa* in cases such as when it is in a hidden state, given that the manifesting phonemes (*varṇa*) cannot be determined to have a single agent? Moreover, the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* must necessarily be accepted in those instances; otherwise, the comprehension of meaning would not occur—this is what some maintain. This is trivial. *(Note: The marginal note marked "fn. 1" reads: "In the margin.")*

The word "yad" means "therefore"; these phonemes have different causes. The meaning is that for each [phoneme], a distinct, arising cognition is the cause. Their own causes are precisely those cognitions which bring them forth; those whose birth follows a sequence—that is their "ānupūrvī"—are described as such. The meaning is that phonemes occur sequentially due to the sequence of their causes. By this much, the statement "the sound which is known from the cognition that brings forth a particular phoneme" has been explained.

Explaining the statement "[it is determined by hearing]," he says "śruti" and so forth. "Even at the time of hearing"—that is, even at the time of listening—"when they proceed slowly," meaning when they are pronounced not too rapidly. Those phonemes which depend upon that very cognition having the preceding phoneme as its object—which serves as a cooperative condition—are described in that way.

Being thus constituted, what do they do? They produce their own cognition, which has itself as its object, namely, auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*). For instance, at the very same time that auditory consciousness having *sa* as its object arises, the letter *a* is likewise produced by a mind that brings about the manifestation of *a*. Therefore, the letter *a* and the cognition having *sa* as its object exist simultaneously; consequently, the letter *a* produces its own object-cognition together with that cognition having *sa* as its object acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). This same principle should be applied to the other phonemes as well.

"At that time" means when they have produced the cognition of experience regarding their own objects; at that time, they "resort to memory," meaning they ascend into memory, precisely by depending upon that memory which has the preceding phonemes as its object. The meaning is that they are remembered in the very same sequence in which they were experienced. This is the connection: "this very nature of the phonemes is characterized by non-simultaneity. To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says: "distinct," and so forth. Because they are produced by preceding preceding cognitions, their state of being an effect is distinct.

Because they serve as the causes for each subsequent cognition, those cognitions that give rise to the phonemes beginning with *sa* possess a distinct causal relationship; these very [cognitions] are the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has as its nature (*svabhāva*) a property (*dharma*) whose very production (*nirvṛtti*)—that is, its arising (*utpatti*)—proceeds from them. By this, it is stated that phonemes are effects in relation to their causes, the cognitions.

With reference to the cognitions that apprehend them, he states their causality: the analysis of the compound is as follows—*jananam* (production) is the bringing about (*nirvarttanam*) of a distinct effect, which is consciousness; that very property (*dharma*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Such an intrinsic nature of the phonemes (*varṇa-svabhāva*), differentiated by the distinctions in human articulation (*puruṣa-saṃskāra-bheda*)—that is, differentiated by the distinctions in human effort—is called "sequence" (*krama*). [Objection: But sequence is a property (*dharma*) of the phonemes; how then can such an intrinsic nature of the phonemes itself be called "sequence"?

He thinks as follows: there is no sequence for those things that arise simultaneously, because such a sequence is not perceived. Therefore, sequence belongs only to phonemes (*varṇa*) that arise non-simultaneously. If phonemes are held to arise non-simultaneously, then that very [sequence] is the sequence in the world; it is not something distinct from the phonemes, because such a thing is not perceived. Nor is sequence a single property (*dharma*) belonging to them, because they do not exist together. Nor is it a property of each individual [phoneme], because sequence is not perceived in that way. Therefore, it has been stated that phonemes arising non-simultaneously themselves are called "sequence."

This convention regarding their sequence is merely a conceptual construction. Furthermore, the very sequence that is perceived in the world in the word *sara* is not the same as that in the word *rasa*. Nor is there any nature of the preceding and following phonemes apart from their sequence. Therefore, the nature of the phonemes is distinct for each individual word. And the world indeed perceives the difference between the word *sara* and the word *rasa*. Thus, as Maṇḍana says: "Let it be granted that the phonemes, being proponents of [their own] production, are distinct."

"But their uncommon difference is not the cause of the cognition of the object, because that [difference] is not determined and because it was not perceived at the time of the convention. (Sphoṭasiddhi 30) This is refuted because the sequence of phonemes "rasa" is indeed determined as distinct from the sequence of phonemes "sara"; nor do the phonemes appear apart from their sequence.

Therefore, the determination of the difference between phonemes is nothing other than the determination of the difference in their sequence; it is simply that the distinction between one word for "taste" (*rasa*) and another word for "taste" is not perceived due to their similarity. For this very reason, it is logical that [the word] conveys the meaning of the word "taste," because it was observed as such at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). This applies to other words as well; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "It is indeed something else," and so forth. Since the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*) as previously described is called "sequence" (*krama*), for that reason, even though the form of the phonemes is not determined to be one due to their similarity, the word (*pada*) in each instance—i.e., at every step—is indeed something else. What is the reason? Because it is distinct from the mental impression of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*). The agent is precisely the motivating consciousness; [the word] is distinct because of the difference in its capacities.

"Combined" (*sahitam*) means uttered according to the sequence of preceding and following [sounds]. "Effecting a distinction in the task" (*kāryabhedakṛt*) means it produces a distinction in cognition (*buddhibheda*). Now, it was already established previously that "phonemes (*varṇa*), being devoid of meaning... (1.241). Therefore, how can it be said that the nature of the phonemes, when combined, effects a distinction in the task? On this point, some think: "The nature of each phoneme is distinct and its denotative capacity is human-made (*pauruṣeya*), not non-human-made (*apauruṣeya*). As it has been said: "True; it exists, but it is dependent upon persons. (1.243)

That is incorrect, because letters—whether occurring together or separately—do not convey meaning. Therefore, this is the intended sense: if the sequence of letters existed in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then that [sequence], being conceptualized as the form of a single word or the like, would be the conveyor of meaning. However, since it is the letters in their sequential order, when made the object of a single conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), that serve as the conveyors, it is precisely because they appear within a single conceptual cognition.

It is said that the form of sequential phonemes, when combined, produces a distinction in the effect; thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, since there is a distinction [of the phonemes] due to the distinction of their originators, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phonemes is certainly not one and the same in words such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*. What is the reason? Because there is a distinction due to the distinction in the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the agent’s mind. The agent is the speaker, and there is a distinction in the mental impression of that which is known by his mind; because of the distinction in the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), there is a distinction in capacity (*śakti*), and thereby a distinction in the intrinsic nature of the phonemes.

And that distinct nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*), which consists of their sequential order, is mounted upon a single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). When combined with one another, they are the cause of a difference in effect—that is, a difference in the cognition whose object is the meaning.

This causal sequence, characterized as the specific order in which the phonemes proceed, has arisen from a person who is the "creator of the arrangement" (*racanākṛt*)—one who creates an arrangement. Why? He says: "By will," and so forth. Because there is no contradiction in the establishment of those phonemes according to human will, there would be a contradiction in an established order [if it were not created by such a person].

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "kārya" (to be produced). The analysis of the compound is: "those which are both effects and causes, and are also cognitions. It is the very minds that give rise to the phonemes (*varṇa*) that are so described; for they are effects in relation to the preceding consciousness and causes in relation to the subsequent consciousness. The specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṇa*) arising from them is called "sequence" (*ānupūrvī*). And since that sequence is produced by the initial and sustained mental applications (*vitarka-vicāra*) of a person, the phonemes do not have a fixed order.

*Vitarka* is a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) in the form of inquiry, such as "Is this it, or is that it? *Vicāra* is a conceptualization in the form of ascertainment, such as "This alone is it. Why is the sequence not fixed? [The author replies with the words] "by desire" (*icchā*), and so forth. A sequence whose establishment is not contradicted by desire is "one whose establishment is not contradicted by desire" (*icchā-aviruddha-siddhi*). Those sequences which possess this [quality] are described as such. Because of that state [of being], for instance, the sequence of phonemes is established according to one's wish.
What is it like? It is like the sequence of specific actions. Just as there is a sequence for specific actions such as contraction and so forth due to the determination of desire, so it is here.

With the words "na hi" and so forth, he states the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Regarding the phrase "of place and time": the connection is that it is not possible to perform a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the arrangement situated in a particular place; for it cannot be done by human will that "let the Vindhya mountain be in the place of Malaya, or let the Vindhya and so forth be in the place of Malaya," nor can it be done that "first let there be the sprout, and afterwards let that which produces it arise from the seed. However, phonemes (*varṇa*) can indeed be transposed according to one's desire. Therefore, phonemes do not have a fixed sequence. For this very reason... (308)

...because the sequence of phonemes exists when there is a sequence of conceptualizations (vikalpa) standing in a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhūta*), and because the sequence of phonemes does not exist when the sequence of conceptualizations is absent. In worldly sentences, the causal relationship between the person and the sequence of phonemes is established: the person is the cause, and the sequence of phonemes is the effect. Therefore, from the establishment of this causal relationship, it follows that all other Vedic phonemes [are likewise produced]; just as the logical principle holds that every fire is necessarily preceded by fuel.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with *sati*: "When fuel exists, burning occurs; that by which something is burned is called 'burning' (*daha*), which is to say, combustion itself. This is because when fuel is absent, there is no burning. If, in some cases, the causal relationship between fire and fuel were established, then even for a fire whose fuel is not perceived, it would follow that [it could burn]—because if the restriction of place and time for that fire, which lacks a cause, were impossible, it would exist everywhere and at all times. Now, if it were indeed restricted... (p. ...)

574) It is maintained that [fire] occurs in certain places and so forth. If a restriction regarding place and so forth is thus maintained for fire, then that very place and so forth would constitute the fuel. What is the reason? [The text says] "dahanasya" and so on. If the material cause (*upādāna*) of fire were independent [of anything else], a restriction of place and time would be impossible; likewise, this sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) would also be impossible if it did not depend upon the human effort that serves as its cause.

In that case, being without support and without basis, and independent of human effort, it would manifest by itself. Even if a person were to exert effort with the thought, "I am uttering the sequence of phonemes," it would still be impossible to manifest the sequence of phonemes. Why? Because the capacity for that sequence belongs to [the Veda]; if one were to assume that this capacity sometimes belongs to a person, then every sequence of phonemes in the Veda would likewise be of human origin. Why? Because it is observed even among worldly [utterances].

Furthermore, why is the status of being an effect not accepted for the person who exists when that [Veda] exists? In that case, another definition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would have to be stated, distinct from "existing when that exists," by the absence of which the Vedicists could not maintain a causal relation between the person and human effort. And there is no other definition of the causal relation.

Now, since the characteristic of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is the same [in both cases], if the worldly sequence of phonemes is held to be artificial, then [the following] consequences would follow: what is the reason? Because even in the case of jars and so forth, such a conceptualization is possible—just as in the case of the conceptualization regarding the sequence of Vedic words. Just as there is the conceptualization that "that very Vedic sequence is manifested by human activity," so too it could be for jars and the like. Furthermore, because there is no distinction [between the two].

If it is argued that there is no distinction [of the jar and so forth] from other things because they conform to human activity, he says: “Those too,” and so forth. Even those jars and such were previously seen to be the construction of others—earlier potters and the like. That [construction] was not seen before; rather, it means that one has seen them [being made]. A later potter and the like also produces them; it is not without instruction.

Furthermore, for those whose practice is preceded by the instruction of others, [the argument applies]. If [the Veda] were authorless, then the Vedic sequence would be accepted as being without an author because no author is remembered. If that is so, then even jars and the like have some authors who are unknown; jars and such things are seen in places concealed over vast periods of time, yet their authors are not remembered.

Therefore, since the dependence upon human activity is equal [in both cases], if the Vedic sequence were not of human origin, then all things such as pots would likewise be unproduced; or else, just as there is no production of the Vedic sequence due to the non-remembrance of its author, so too there would be the insistence on the non-production of certain things like pots at certain times when their authors are not remembered. But this is not the case. Therefore, the connection is that neither this worldly nor the Vedic sequence of phonemes is created by a person.

Why? He says: "Established," and so forth. "Establishment" (*prasiddhi*) refers to the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). [The compound is a] descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Their property (*dharma*) is the conformity to the presence and absence of their own causes; it is because of not transgressing that [property].

Precisely because these mantras are produced by persons (*pauruṣeya*), their commonality with and distinction from ordinary persons is established. Of whom? Of those men who perform the sequence known as "mantra"—that is, those who compose the sequence of phonemes designated as "mantra. What is their [power]? It is the thorough knowledge of the mantra, the capacity to accomplish the desired object, and its majesty (*prabhāva*). For what reason? Because they are not common to others; thus he says: because of the absence of both that knowledge and that majesty in other persons, such as ordinary people and the like.

He explains this with the words "this" (*ayam*) and so forth: if even an ordinary person were to know that "this specific sequence of syllables is capable of extracting poison and so on, and no other," then by means of that very same distinction, he would [attain the result]. (p.)

576) One should explain and practice [it], yet one does not practice it in this way. Therefore, even if this sequence of syllables called a *mantra* is accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas as being effective by its very nature, nevertheless, there must be some person endowed with a particular supersensuous power who has understood it; for thus there exists a person who perceives imperceptible objects, who knows the *mantra*, its efficacy, and its performance.

Although it has been stated that a *mantra* is speech that accomplishes a desired object for those possessing the power of truth and austerity, nevertheless, this is said even while granting that point: a *mantra* is a producer of effects by its very nature. By means of employing a *mantra* that produces an effect, or by means of knowing the capacity of a *mantra* to produce its fruit, an excellence of the person [who knows it] is established. To the objection that there can be no one who perceives the imperceptible because one cannot distinguish between what is a *mantra* and what is not a *mantra* through inference, he replies with the words "For not... and so forth.

The meaning is this: while a sequence of phonemes characterized by a specific order is capable of removing poison and the like, this [particular] sequence of phonemes is not so capable. Thus, it is not possible to understand [the efficacy] from a logical mark (*liṅga*). Why? Because a specific logical mark that is unmixed with the distinction between mantra and non-mantra is unestablished. [Objection:

But surely, when both the mantra and the non-mantra—consisting of the forms of the phonemes—are apprehended through perception, their power to bestow the fruit is also apprehended through perception, since that [power] is not distinct from them.

Therefore, he says: "Of two [perceptions] that are perceptible," and so forth. "Not taught" means that because they have not been described as "this is a mantra" or "this is not a mantra," there is no thorough knowledge [of them]. Because there is no certainty such as "this one is capable of removing poison and the like, while this one is incapable. Regarding the phrase "even if taught": even if it has been taught by someone that "this is a mantra which performs such an effect," nevertheless, because the specific distinction of the mantra's own nature is not perceived—that is, because it is not ascertained in any way whatsoever—[there is no certainty].

Because the instruction lacks authoritative validity, except insofar as there is a correspondence with the result. However, the certainty that "this is a mantra" would arise through the attainment of the effect to be accomplished by the mantra. And since that effect to be accomplished by the mantra cannot be perceived prior to its cause—that is, prior to the performance of the mantra—the implication is that it does not exist at that time. Furthermore, the performance of a mantra that has not been ascertained is not possible.

Therefore, one must necessarily accept a person who perceives supersensuous objects through the means of valid cognition (*mīmāṃsā*), who distinguishes between the nature of mantras and non-mantras; otherwise, the performance of mantras would not be possible.

Furthermore, this sequence of syllables called "mantra" does not, by its own nature, produce effects such as the removal of poison; rather, it does so through human convention (*puruṣasamaya*). Why is that? Because for one person who practices a mantra, the mantra may be effective quickly, whereas for another who performs the same ritual application of the mantra, it may take a long time to become effective. For if the result were granted by the mantra itself by its own nature, this difference in timing would not be possible, since no one can alter the inherent excellence or lack of excellence of the mantra.

Since the production of a result from a mantra for another person depends upon the performance of vows and other such practices, the mantra is not a causal agent by its own nature (*svabhāva*). "Vow" (*vrata*) refers to the restriction prescribed in the ritual manual of the mantra; "performance" (*caraṇa*) is its execution. By the word "also" (*api*), offerings (*homa*) and so forth are included. For if it were to grant a result by its own nature, what would be the need for the performance of vows and other practices? This is because no excellence (*atiśaya*) would arise from them.

Likewise, even from a single mantra-based rite such as recitation or fire-offering (*japa-homa*), although two persons may perform the identical procedure, one observes the result while the other observes no result; therefore, the fruit does not arise from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [of the rite]. For if it were produced by intrinsic nature, there would be an equal connection with the result for both. This applies even to those who are carrying [the load], as well.

Even for mantras that remove poison and so forth, when they are employed again at a later time by that same person, there may be a failure to produce some intended effect due to inconsistency. This mode of operation is not logical if it pertains to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing. Why? Because an intrinsic nature remains identical across all instances, including persons and other factors. For whatever is the intrinsic nature of something does not become that nature in dependence upon anything else. However, when the result is held to arise from a convention (*samaya*) established by a person, then this fault does not apply.

For instance, a person is the creator of the mantra-convention; since he acts according to his own will, it is logical that he favors one person and not another. For what reason? Because of a specific similarity of nature (*sattvasabhāgatā*). This refers to the similarity between the practitioner of the mantra-rite and the originator of the mantra, by virtue of their equal character, conduct, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of gifts and other such factors is intended. It is due to the influence of that [similarity], or due to affection for that [originator], or due to the excellence of service.

Through recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, she bestows grace upon a certain person who possesses a specific form of service (*sevā*) toward her; she does not [bestow it] upon another being who is devoid of such commonality of nature (*sattvasabhāgatā*) and other qualities.

With the words beginning with "vratena," he raises a further objection. "Vrata-caryā" (the practice of vows) refers to the performance of observances (*niyama*). The compound *vratacaryā-vratacaryābhraṃśa* is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an elliptical compound consisting of dissimilar members), meaning "the practice of vows and the failure of the practice of vows. The word "ādi" (etcetera) is connected to each member; thus, the meaning is "by means of the practice of vows, etc., and by means of the failure of the practice of vows, etc. The connection is that success (*siddhi*) occurs when there is an accumulation of merit (*dharma*) through the practice of vows and so forth. Likewise, success may occur for a person who is virtuous by nature (*prakṛtyā*) or by their very disposition (*svabhāvena*).

However, when there is an accumulation of unrighteousness (*adharma*) due to the violation of vows and so forth, or because a person is by nature unrighteous, the meaning of the statement should be applied as follows: "there is no success for that person. The opponent maintains that even if the fruit is produced from the mantra by its very nature, the distinction between success and failure will occur in the manner already described.

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words beginning "no," and so forth. The accomplishment of the fruit does not arise from a mantra that depends upon *dharma*. What is the reason? Because in the *Ḍākinī-bhaginī-tantra* and others, we observe vows (*vrata*) that are causes for the accomplishment of mantras even though they are contrary to *dharma*. In the *Ḍākinī-tantra*, in the *Catur-bhaginī-tantra*, and by the word "and others" (*ādi*), because they are observed among the causes of misconduct in the *Kambukinī-tantra* and others. He asks, "What, then, are those things contrary to *dharma*? and answers with the words beginning "cruelty" (*kraurya*).

Cruelty (*kraurya*) is the killing of living beings; theft (*steya*) is robbery; sexual union (*maithuna*) is the engagement of the two organs; and base actions (*hīnakarma*) include [acts such as] offering smoke from cat-feces and the like. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other things contrary to the Dharma are also included. Those observances (*vrata*) in which cruelty and the rest are prevalent—that is, abundant—are described in that way. And by means of those aforementioned observances, there is a specific accomplishment of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*). For instance, the rule regarding the commitments (*samaya-vyavasthā*) is stated in the *Ḍākinītantra*:

When one kills and eats a living being, one attains the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of mantras. Likewise, in the *Kambuki-nī-tantra*, it is stated that accomplishment comes from the practice of theft. Similarly, in certain other *bhaginī-tantras*, there is a rule (*samaya*) stating that some [accomplishment] bestows success through the practice of sexual intercourse. If it is argued that cruelty and such would indeed be the nature of Dharma, he says: "And not," and so forth. We shall explain later, as the occasion arises, how such a nature of Dharma characterized by cruelty and the like is impossible. Thus, for now, it has been shown that accomplishment is seen even from what is non-Dharma (*adharma*).

Since success is not seen even from [merely] dharma, he says "friendliness" (*maitrī*) and so forth. Friendliness (*maitrī*) is the thought for the welfare and happiness of sentient beings. Purity (*śauca*) is twofold: external and internal. External is bathing and so forth; internal is the cessation of theft and so forth. Dharma is the favoring of others through giving and so forth. Those for whom friendliness, purity, and dharma are their supreme gifts are described as such. [The term refers to] those persons who are of that nature.

Taking that very cause—namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth—as the causal basis for some specific accomplishment, there is the non-accomplishment of that which is obtainable through the reversal of loving-kindness; and conversely, there is accomplishment through its opposite, such as hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth. Thus, the attainment of the fruit does not depend on a mantra that merely accumulates merit (*dharmopacaya*). For even cruelty and the like, when originated from hatred and so forth, become true merit (*dharma*) when practiced according to the injunctions of the mantra.

Therefore, he says: "And not," and so forth. For it is logical that from a single-natured action characterized by killing and the like, there should arise a dharma that is opposed to the non-dharma which contradicts it; yet it is not logical that from that very same source—namely, killing and the like performed outside the context of the ritual injunction for mantras—there should also arise non-dharma. Indeed, dharma cannot arise from a cause of non-dharma because they are contradictory. To explain: by the very same intention of hatred and so forth with which one performs killing and the like outside the ritual injunction for mantras, non-dharma arises.

If, even when performing the application of mantras with that very same intention, acts such as violence are committed, how can that [violence] be a constituent part of dharma? (p. 579) If cruelty and the like, even when performed according to the ritual injunction of mantras, are indeed unrighteous because they are produced by hatred and so forth, then how can one who recites [mantras] enjoy the fruit of dharma—characterized by the experience of desired objects and so on—arising from a vow (*vrata*) whose nature is unrighteousness? By "vow" is meant that characterized by cruelty and the like; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), other inferior things such as the offering of impure incense and so forth are included. How does the reciter (*jāpī*) partake of the fruit of dharma, which is characterized by the enjoyment of desired things?

"No," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). It is not the maturation—that is, the fruit of action—of this [present] unwholesome nature such as the vow that constitutes its desired result; rather, it is the maturation of previously performed wholesome karma. To the question "In what way?", he replies: "Like the instruction for the killing of a Brahmin, through its performance—that is, its accomplishment—just like the acquisition of a village. For example, someone might employ another person, saying: "Kill this Brahmin, and I will give you a village."

By carrying out that command, he obtains the village; yet that is not the fruit of the murder of a Brahmin. Rather, having encountered as an auxiliary cause the person propitiated by the commission of that Brahmin-murder, his previous auspicious karma alone ripens in such a manner.

To the question, "What then is the fruit of that unrighteous vow for one whose nature is unrighteous? he says: "But for that vow characterized by cruelty and so forth, which is unrighteous in nature, the future fruit—that is, the fruit to be experienced in a subsequent birth—is undesirable, such as rebirth in hell and the like."

If it is argued that the desired fruit of a virtuous action is [attained] by means of some unrighteous person (*adharmātmā*) through the employment of mantras and the like—[the author] replies: "But he is unrighteous. [The term] *mantrādiprayoga* refers to the employment of mantras and so forth; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the employment of vows such as cruelty is included. [This refers to] that virtuous action which has a desired fruit—the analysis of the compound being: "that action whose fruit is desired. In some way, by some manner, because of providing assistance, he is a "ripening agent," that is, a giver of the fruit. But how can an unwholesome factor be an assistant to a wholesome one?

He said: Because the capacity for assistance is manifold. For the state of being a cooperative condition (*sahakāribhāva*) is indeed diverse. Sometimes the unwholesome (*akuśala*) is a cooperative condition for the wholesome (*kuśala*); likewise, the wholesome is a cooperative condition for the unwholesome. For example, when one performs exceedingly noble wholesome deeds, unwholesome karma that would otherwise result in the suffering of the hells and so forth does not bear its fruit; having encountered a wholesome cooperative condition, it is exhausted in this very life by yielding nothing more than the suffering of illness and the like. It has been stated that the practice of spells and the like, though consisting of non-dharma (*adharma*), somehow assists karma that possesses a desirable result.

Demonstrating the manner in which assistance is rendered in this regard, he says: the specific person who is the author of the mantra is himself the basis (*āśraya*); the maturation (*vipāka*) is the yielding of the fruit; that which has this as its nature is "that whose property is the maturation based on the person" (*puruṣāśrayavipākadharmā*). "Property" (*dharma*) refers here to a particular kind of merit (*puṇya*). "By him" means performed by that person in a previous birth. "In such a way through his propitiation" means that the merit [accrues] in such a way due to the practice of cruelty and so forth;
it bears fruit through "his propitiation," that is, through the propitiation of the person who composed the mantra.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "By that," and so forth. "By him" refers to the person who composed the mantra. "The practice" refers to the application of vows and the like associated with cruelty. "The nourishment of the action" means its fulfillment. "By that" refers to the ripening, which is the giving of the fruit; thus, it is "of such a nature" (*dharmiṇaḥ*), meaning its inherent quality (*dharma*) is the granting of results. Regarding the phrase "of that fruit": because the action that yields a desired fruit has been performed, it bears fruit through the propitiation of that [mantra].

Or, one might argue that even without a person who composed the mantra, the fruit arises from the mantra because it is assisted by that very ritual procedure (*yantra*) through its operation, such as recitation (*japa*). Consequently, the opponent considers the previously stated claim—that the fruit results from propitiating a person—to be incorrect.

"No," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). "This is not so. What is the reason? [He says: "The person," and so forth. The "form" (*ākāra*) of the person who composed the mantra refers to its color, shape, and so on. Its "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to its being peaceful, fierce, and so on. Its "conduct" (*caryā*) refers to activity characterized by the operations of body and speech. Because there would follow the consequence of the futility of the mental resolve (*adhimokṣa*)—that is, the conviction—regarding those forms and other qualities, [it follows that] if there were no person who is the empowerer (*adhiṣṭhātā*) of the mantra, for what purpose would one resolve upon its form and other qualities?

If it is maintained that even that person is a benefactor [of the mantra], then, when it is admitted that the person who composed the mantra is a benefactor with respect to the attainment of the fruit from the mantra, a person of extraordinary qualities is established. The analysis of the compound is: "one whose qualities are extraordinary" (*asādhāraṇā guṇā asya*). What is the reason? Precisely because of devotion to him—that is, precisely because of devotion to the conduct, nature, and form of that particular person—it is possible to perform acts such as those involving poison.

Therefore, even though mantras are composed by persons, they do not yield results by their own nature or inherent character independently of the application of that person, nor independently of the application of a specific person; rather, they depend precisely upon the application of a specific person—provided that the composer of the mantra is indeed a person possessing extraordinary qualities. [Objection: If this were so, how is it that those who know the tantras recite mantras even when they lack such specific powers and qualities?

Therefore, he says: "Even those who... and so forth. Treatises (*tantra*) are those scriptures bound by mantras; those who know them are "knowers of the treatises" (*tantravid*). Even today, some among them compose certain unprecedented mantras. Thus, it is not that they alone lack the capacity; rather, it is the power—the efficacy—of that preeminent person, the author of the treatise upon which they rely, who is their master and lord. Why? Because they proceed according to the principles (*nyāya*) taught by him.
Therefore, because they follow the rule—beginning with the covenant—that was taught to them by the Lord, the Lord, being pleased, consecrates even the mantras composed by them; such is the meaning.

With the words "Even the men of the street," etc., he explains the meaning of the verse by first presenting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). "Even the men of the street" means even ordinary people; some, such as snake-charmers (*gāruḍika*) and others who know the characteristics of mantras and tantras, perform certain actions characterized by the pacification of poison and so forth. Yet they are not superior [to the Buddha], because they do not practice the drinking of alcohol and other [forbidden acts]. Similarly, the author of the mantra—who is considered to possess such power—would also not be one who possesses any excellence.

And [the opponent] might think that one who is devoid of even a hundredth part of the power of a man on the street would be the author of mantras; thus, they believe that a powerful person is not established [as the author].

He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth: there is no composition of mantras by those devoid of power. As for those men—even those on the street—who compose mantras, it is because of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the author of the tantra (*tantra-praṇetṛ*) who possesses power that these men have the capacity to compose mantras.

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For it is produced by that," and so forth. By observing and protecting the convention established by that person who possesses extraordinary power (*prabhāvātiśayavat*), and by acting according to his instruction—that is, the instruction of the person endowed with power—[the practitioners] become capable of performing mantra-rites. Why is this so?

Regarding the passage beginning with *tat* (that) and so forth: by the power (*prabhāva*) of that [mantra], there is its *samaya* (observance) and its *upadeśa* (instruction). This is because men who are indifferent toward them lack the capacity for the composition of mantras. In this context, *samaya* is that through the transgression of which one must undergo re-entry into the mandala and so forth. Therefore, the distinction between these two lies in the fact that *upadeśa* is the instruction for those other than [the composers]. In that regard, even in the case of mantras composed by ordinary men on the street, [the result arises] solely from meditating on their form, provided they possess power.

And because of the man’s meditation on the form [of the deity], etc.—the word “etc. including meditation on the natural conduct (*svabhāvacaryā*)—and because of the application and setting in motion of the mantra; since this is so, therefore that very empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is the empowerment by a powerful person, must be inferred and understood as being of such a nature, namely, that they perform actions by means of mantras composed by themselves.

Moreover, by asserting that "certain experts in tantra compose mantras," one would actually be establishing the excellence of a person. For such an expert in tantra who is the author of a mantra is indeed possessed of power, because he possesses a unique capacity not shared by other persons who are unacquainted with tantra. And since it is only mantras presided over by a person that yield results...

Therefore, one who desires results should declare that mantras are produced and of human origin, and thus bestow fruits. For one who seeks results from mantras, mantras are not eternal; rather, they are produced. Even though they are produced, they are not independent of persons in the granting of fruits. To demonstrate these two points, both "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "of human origin" (*pauruṣeya*) are employed.

He explains this with the words beginning "na hi" (for not). For indeed, the employment—that is, the utterance—of eternal Vedic mantras is impossible, because they cannot have any excellence added to them (*anādheyātiśayatvāt*). And since there is no fruit from mantras that are not employed, one who desires a fruit from their employment must assert that mantras are produced (*kṛtaka*), and moreover, that they are human (*pauruṣeya*) and bestow fruits only when presided over by a person (*puruṣādhiṣṭhita*).

What is the reason? Because mantras—which have results that cannot arise from anything else such as the power of things (*bhāvaśakti*)—are seen to yield results only through the presiding influence of a person (*puruṣādhiṣṭhāna*), and not through the power of things. And how it is not the case that results arise from mantras by virtue of the power of things has already been demonstrated [in the verse]:
"If such were the power of things, then everyone would be accomplished," and so forth (1.267).

And he provides an illustration: "Just as in the case of poetry and so forth, where an agreement has been made such that 'I shall fulfill this purpose for whoever recites my poetry in this manner'—the word 'and so forth' [in the compound] including the arts (*śilpasthāna*) and the like—in that poetry and so forth which is subject to such an agreement, [the result follows] because of the presiding person; likewise, the meaning is that it is the same with respect to mantras."

Whatever proof of incapacity—that is, whatever proof of the inability of men to perceive objects beyond the senses—is asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas, all of that has been refuted by this very demonstration of the excellence of knowledge and power in those who employ mantras. He explains this with the words "For [it] has been established," and so forth. For it has been established that mantras are created by persons, and it has also been established that mantras bestow results because they are presided over by such [persons].

Furthermore, not all persons are capable of composing or presiding over mantras; therefore, there exists a certain person of superior excellence who is the author of the mantra. The arguments intended to refute that person of superior excellence have also been countered and rejected.

By this, it is not being suggested that the proof offered by the opponent for rejecting excellence lacks non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*); rather, it is stated under this pretext that there simply exist no proofs based on the force of reality (*vastubala*) for rejecting excellence in a person. For there is no proof whatsoever, grounded in the force of reality, that can negate the excellence of a person.

But surely this exists: "The person intended [as an authority] does not possess excellence, because he is intelligent, because he possesses sense faculties, because he speaks, and because he is male, like a man in the street."

Therefore, he says: "Intellect, sense-faculties," and so forth. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), sense-faculties (*indriya*), speech (*ukti*), and masculinity (*puṃstva*). From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should understand possession of vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other such qualities. As for that which is described as a means of proving the absence of any excellence in the person (*puruṣātiśaya*), all of that is a fallacy of proof (*pramāṇābhāsa*); that is to say, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). What is the reason? Because, due to the doubt regarding its presence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), everything [in such cases] is of the nature of the "remaining" (*śeṣavat*). Indeed, that which is "of the nature of the remaining" is inconclusive. There exists a non-erroneous understanding (*gati*) of the object to be inferred, which is the realization of the inferable (*anumeya*) exactly as it is.

He explains by means of the words "yat tu" and so forth. The connection is as follows: that which is the proof for the rejection of the excellence of a person (*puruṣātiśaya*) is indeed not a means of making reality known (*tattvagamaka*). Furthermore, that proof consists of [the arguments] beginning with "due to the conjunction of the intellect and the sense organs" (*buddhīndriyayogāt*). Why is it not a means of making [reality] known? He says: "pratikṣepa... and so forth. "Rejection" (*pratikṣepa*) and "generality" (*sāmānya*) constitute the compound *pratikṣepasāmānye*. Because those two are not applicable to the proof of those two [i.e., the specific excellence and the particular reality].

For instance, by means of a proof such as "possessing intelligence" and so forth, either the negation that "there is no superior person" would be established, or else, that which is a superior person would be established as being identical to street-urchins, thereby proving his commonality with other ordinary persons.

In this context, with the words "for not" (*na hi*) and so forth, he states the absence of a means for negation: for a negation by one who does not perceive those objects—that is, by one who does not see supersensible objects—is not possible regarding supersensible matters. What is the reason? Because even though these supersensible objects exist, they are unknown to one of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*). Therefore, the point is that there can be no negation based on mere non-perception.

Nor can there be a rejection of the excellence of the person (*puruṣātiśaya*) on the grounds of establishing a contradiction, because for that very reason—namely, because that excellence of the person is beyond the senses—both types of contradiction are unestablished with respect to reasons such as "being an intelligent being" (*buddhimattva*). Furthermore, as was stated previously, since there is no contradiction in the possibility of the excellence of the person coexisting in one and the same locus with non-contradictory properties such as "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*), etc.

With the words "Nor also," etc., he states the non-existence of a proof for [such] generality: nor can there be the establishment of generality—that is, the establishment of equality—of that person possessing excellence by another person who is a limited perceiver (*arvāgdarśin*). What is the reason? Because it is impossible to know the possibility of a specific quality characterized by the perception of supersensible objects and so forth. And this applies to such things as the perception of supersensible objects existing in the mental continuum of another, which are imperceptible to mere humans.

Whatever non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is employed to establish impossibility, its status as a logical reason (*hetu*) has already been rejected. Furthermore, even though there is equality in such factors as maleness, one observes an excellence in some individuals—such as superior wisdom—due to their respective mental cultivation (*saṃskāra*); thus, the possibility of excellence in others is likewise conceivable. Therefore, since persons who possess possible distinctions cannot be established as being identical to other ordinary persons when they lack possible distinctions, this too was stated previously.

Therefore, this is an inference by elimination (*śeṣavat*); however, since the occurrence [of the reason] such as "being a speaker" is not observed [in the subject], yet there is doubt regarding its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), it is incapable [of proving the conclusion].

Moreover, regarding the phrase "those who speak thus": the followers of Jaimini (*Jaiminīyas*), who maintain that there is no person capable of perceiving supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), contradict and subvert their own position by this very statement—"there is no person whatsoever who knows supersensible objects"—which asserts the existence of a superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*) through whom the meaning of the Vedas is understood. This is because, by rejecting a person of superior capacity, they render impossible the comprehension of the Vedic meaning. For instance:

Vedic words themselves do not declare, "This is our meaning; this is not our meaning. Therefore, whatever meaning is intended for the words of the *agnihotra* would have to be postulated by persons such as the Mīmāṃsakas; yet that is not the case. For those persons are possessed of passion and other afflictions (*rāgādi-saṃyuta*). Consequently, a meaning postulated by them is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, if it were to be postulated that some person such as Jaimini alone is the knower of the meaning of the Veda, then on what basis could it be established that this one specific individual is the one who knows reality (*tattvavid*), while no other person knows the true nature of the Veda’s meaning? There is no reason for this, since there is no distinction between persons; thus, either everyone knows it, or no one at all does—this is the sense.

Now, if it is argued that—despite the equality of being human and so forth—a certain person such as Jaimini is postulated as one who possesses extraordinary powers and knows the relationship between Vedic words and their supersensible objects, then [the opponent replies]: "In that case, just like Jaimini and others, why is it that no other person at all—who is equal in terms of being human (*puṃstva*)—is accepted by you as someone possessing superior knowledge? For what reason is another person not considered by you to be a possessor of knowledge, just like Jaimini and the rest? This is the sense.

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "no," etc.: "Come here, sirs, O Brahmins; this matter of ours is to be accepted by you and no other"—in this way, Vedic words do not cry out or speak so that an understanding of the meaning might arise from them. The word "kevalam" (only) is used for emphasis.

Only those words whose connection with specific meanings is unmanifested "attack" (*abhipatanti*) or "ascend" (*ārohanti*) upon the hearing—the auditory consciousness. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose connection, that is, relation, with specific meanings is unmanifested. In that case, regarding words whose connection with their meanings is unknown, as they are being heard, one person imagines some meaning according to his own whim, while another person imagines a different meaning; thus, there is simply no definitive determination of the word-meaning.

[The opponent argues: "The relationship between words and their objects is innate; therefore, there will be a fixed restriction to a single object. To this he says: "No," and adds: "Nor is there any innate restriction of words [to a single object], nor is there an inherent connection by nature (*prakṛti*) with objects, by virtue of which they would be seen as assuming that specific object as their denotatum (*vācya*) merely through the force of convention (*samaya*), even when there is the possibility of multiple meanings."

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: it is not logical that among those Vedic words, one person should explain the true meaning while another does not. Of what kind [are these words]? "Of those whose restriction of meaning is unknown"—this is the analysis of the compound: those for whom the restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*) is not known. What is the reason? Because of the penetration of that which is beyond the senses (*atyakṣāveśāt*). This is because [the words] have made for themselves as their object a matter such as heaven and the means to attain it, which is supersensible (*atīndriya*). For a person of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) is not capable of knowing the restriction of the meaning of a word whose referent is supersensible; in that regard, he is simply ignorant.

Someone—such as Jaimini or Śabarasvāmin—who is overwhelmed by defects such as passion and so forth, declares the true meaning of those words, saying, "This alone is its meaning, and not another. It is not logical to establish a distinction [between them] by claiming that another person, who is no different from Jaimini and others, does not declare the truth; for such a distinction lacks justification.

Now, if it is claimed that—due to some indefinable cause, such as the excellence of the cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*) and so forth (the word "and so forth" including the intensity of practice)—that very person, Jaimini and his like, knows the meaning of the Veda and no other ordinary person does, then from what source does this Jaimini and his peers derive this excellence of knowledge regarding that which transcends the senses? For how can there be an excellence of knowledge concerning the reality of the Vedic meaning, which is supersensible, for one who is not distinguished from others whose true nature remains unknown?

Or let it be that Jaimini and others are knowers of objects beyond the senses; likewise, why is another superior person (puruṣātiśaya) postulated by the Buddhists and others—who perceives objects remote in space, time, and nature—not possible? Why is such a person not observed to exist, such that he might be rejected? Let him too be accepted as a seer of supersensible objects; otherwise, let even the esteemed Jaimini and others not be [accepted as such]. For there are no means of proof for their rejection.

There exist certain proofs, such as "being a human being" (*puruṣatva*) and so forth, which are intended by the Buddhists and others to refute a superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*); yet these do not fail to apply to, nor do they exclude, Jaimini and others who discern the meaning of the Vedas—they certainly do apply to them as well, because they too possess the quality of being human beings and the like.

Now, even if the means such as being human (*puruṣatva*) and so forth are possible, if a distinction is sought for Jaimini and others—just as this distinction characterized by the discernment of the supersensible meaning of the Veda is desired for Jaimini and his followers, despite the possibility of those same means—then, even though the means for rejecting a person who perceives supersensible objects, such as being human, are possible, so too would there be the perception of supersensible objects for other persons as well; therefore, it is only right that you Mīmāṃsakas should abandon your dogmatic insistence.

It is not on the grounds that he is a seer of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārthadarśin*) that the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda by Jaimini and others is accepted; rather, if it is held that a person who possesses speech consistent with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇasaṃvādin*) is a knower of the Vedic meaning, then the opponent considers that the very words of Jaimini and others—who are engaged in discerning the meaning of the Veda—are indeed consistent with valid means of knowledge. "No," says the Teacher [Dharmakīrti]. This reply is not tenable, because there is no possibility of a valid means of knowledge regarding those objects of the Veda that are entirely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*), such as the fact that [certain rites] are the means for attaining heaven and so forth.

He explains this with the words "It might be thus," and so forth: "We do not adhere to the interpretation of the Veda by any person such as Jaimini on the grounds of that person's authority (*prāmāṇya*). What then? We adhere to the interpretation because of its correspondence with valid means of cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvāda*). He clarifies this very point: among many interpreters of the Veda, whichever interpreter correlates—that is, joins—the meaning as it has been interpreted with valid means of cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, such an interpreter is accepted and acknowledged, and no other."

He refutes this with the words "that is not so," and so forth. *Dharma* and *adharma* constitute the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [he refers to] those things beyond the senses that bring about results such as heaven. Since other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), do not operate regarding these, there is no statement concerning the subject matter of the Veda that is corroborated by any other means of valid cognition; for it is precisely because of that impossibility. Indeed, because direct perception and the other means of valid cognition are impossible regarding that which is absolutely beyond the senses, scripture (*āgama*) is sought—that is, requested—for the sake of cognizing that which is beyond the senses.
