"Otherwise" means: if even regarding an object that is to be understood through scripture, the ascertainment of the object occurs only through corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, even though that scripture exists, if there were a non-occurrence of another means of valid cognition with respect to the object to be understood from it, then—due to the non-occurrence of another means of valid cognition—one would have no comprehension from the scripture alone. And "consequently," because one would have comprehension of an object devoid of scripture solely from another means of valid cognition, scripture itself would not be a means of proof at all.

Because the existence or non-existence of the comprehension of an object depends precisely on the existence or non-existence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that the comprehension of supersensible objects occurs not only from scripture (*āgama*) independently, but also from other means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet that the comprehension of supersensible objects arises from perception and the rest only when accompanied by scripture—how so? asks the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). How can that which is called "supersensible," such as the means for the attainment of heaven and so forth, also be an object of perception and the like? This is a contradiction.

It might be thought: "Perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish an object that is entirely beyond the senses; rather, those very means—perception and the rest—are established as valid even with respect to their own respective objects only by depending upon scripture (*āgama*). Thus, the opponent maintains that scripture alone possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) replies with the words beginning "anāgama" [etc.]: "In this case, there would be no cognition of fire and so forth from a mark such as smoke, because it would be 'without scripture' (*anāgama*). This means that it would not exist since there is no scripture [authorizing it] in this instance.

"No," and so forth, says the opponent. "Indeed, when one engages with objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), a means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not sought regarding the domain of scripture (*āgama*). If that were the case, this fault would indeed arise; consequently, scripture would be a non-means of proof for understanding [those objects] solely on its own. Rather, it is simply that the engagement of scripture even with respect to supersensible objects is not known. Therefore, if it is argued that the operation of scripture depends upon direct perception and the like..."

Now, perception and the other means of knowledge are incapable [of establishing] that which transcends the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, perception and the rest, even if they were capable, would not establish the application of scripture (*āgama*) either; for just as the means of achieving heaven and so forth is beyond the senses, so too is that application of scripture connected with an object that transcends the senses. How could it be established by another means of knowledge, such as perception? It is certainly not established. Therefore, this claim that perception and the rest are sought for its sake is merely trivial.

Even among many commentators, one whose speech accords with valid means of cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is accepted; thus, for one who says this, since it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the definition of scripture (*āgama*) would be something other than [the traditional] definition of scripture. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*). Whosever word is in conformity with valid cognition—[it follows that] the speech composed (*saṃskṛta*) by that person, i.e., produced by that person, would be scripture (*āgama*).

Furthermore, the refinement of a statement consists in demonstrating that its meaning is supported by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is another characteristic of scripture (*āgama*). Thus, authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*), though intended as a characteristic of scripture, is both meaningless and useless.

He explains this with the words beginning "tulya" (equal). Even when there is an equality between an object postulated by one person through speech that accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvādi*) and that postulated by another, provided that the doctrine of scripture being non-human (*apauruṣeya*) is accepted, if—on the strength of valid cognition—the status of being scripture were desired for a certain portion of that non-human scripture which accords with valid cognition, then the characteristic of scripture would be "accordance with valid cognition," such as in the case of sentences regarding the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth; it would not be "non-human authorship. Thus, non-human authorship would not be the defining characteristic of scripture.

What is the reason? Because, although that non-human agency is equal with respect to all objects taught by humans—whether they are desired or undesired—it is accepted as a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) since it is not sublated by valid cognition.

This is what is meant: the meaning is that the acceptance of the understanding of the scripture’s content is due to its being in conformity with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvāditva*). Even if that [agency] exists—that is, even if the state of being non-human (*apauruṣeyatva*) is equal—in other cases where there is no conformity with valid cognition, such understanding is not accepted; therefore, conformity with valid cognition must be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a scriptural word.

Furthermore, if it were possible for knowledge independent of scripture to arise regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses—that is, if knowledge occurring without reliance on scripture were possible—then one might maintain one's own preferred position that there exists someone who knows objects beyond the senses.

If, however, it is asserted that for a person such as Jaimini, who explains the meaning of the Veda, there is a correspondence to reality (*yāthātathya*) and an absence of error (*avaiparītya*) in his knowledge concerning supersensible matters—the means for attaining heaven and so forth—without depending on scripture, then it would follow that other persons besides Jaimini and the like must also be admitted to be perceivers of supersensible objects.
It might be argued: "One does not know supersensuous objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but rather teaches them after having known them through inference (*anumāna*).

This is not so; because inferences and other means of knowledge are impossible without being preceded by direct perception. [The author] clarifies this very point with the words beginning with "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*). Since direct perception does not operate with respect to those supersensuous objects, other means of knowledge that are preceded by direct perception cannot exist.

"It is cognized as having that which is not its object" means that the object (*ālambana*)—that is, the domain (*viṣaya*)—of that [cognition], such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is not that [object]. "That which does not have that as its object" (*atadālambana*) refers to what is not the domain of direct perception and so forth; the ellipsis to be supplied is: "it is cognized" [as such], and for the sake of ascertainment, scripture (*āgama*) is sought after it. However, the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as inference (*anumāna*), regarding an object beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), draws upon—that is, establishes—the fact that direct perception has an object beyond the senses, because inference and the like are preceded by direct perception.

For this reason, a person who perceives objects beyond the reach of the senses would be impossible to refute by the Mīmāṃsakas; yet he has been refuted. Therefore, there is no operation of any other means of valid cognition regarding objects that transcend the senses.

"For this very reason" means that because there is no certainty regarding the operation of the scripture—the Veda—toward a specific object, namely the means for attaining heaven and so forth which transcend the senses, since that [operation] does not occur through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This person is Jaimini or another such as Śabarasvāmin and the like. "By himself" means independently of the instruction of others. He does not know the meaning of the Veda because he possesses passion and the like. Possessing passion and the like is the cause of non-comprehension.

Nor does anyone else know the meaning of the Veda, because this person [who would know it] is likewise possessed of passion and other defects. The Veda itself does not make known—that is, does not illuminate—its own meaning. Therefore, from what source could there be an understanding of the Veda’s meaning? There is no such understanding at all. For the analysis of the compound is as follows: "every person indeed has not transcended a distortion (viplava) produced by defects such as passion; that is, one whose cognition is erroneous. Thus, he himself does not know the specific determination of the Veda's supersensuous objects—that "this alone is its meaning, and not that."

Nor does one person perceive this person—who possesses passion and so forth—as another person; for that other person would face the same logical consequence. The meaning is that, because he too possesses passion and so forth, he likewise lacks knowledge [of it]. For a blind man, being led by another blind man who himself does not know the path, does not reach the way. Nor does the Veda reveal its own meaning independently of instruction. Why? Because it would follow that instruction is useless;
it would follow that the explanations of Jaimini and others are fruitless.

Therefore, this Veda, whose meaning is not fully understood, is a "goitre" (*gaḍu*) among words. A goitre is called a lump of flesh between the forehead and the crown of the head because it is fruitless; likewise, the Vedic word is a goitre because it is fruitless due to its meaning being uncomprehended. It is like a goitre because, through doubt—such as "Is its meaning this, or is it that?"—it becomes a cause of suffering for one who is intent upon it. Thus, it brings suffering and establishes it for that person who has accepted the Veda.

What kind of thing is this? It is nothing but a false view, acting as a sinew or a tendon; bound by that, even one who wishes to remove it out of compassion finds it difficult to extract—thus [the author] mocks [the opponent]. By the phrase "by that" (tena), he means: regarding the Vedic statement in the *Śruti* text, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," there is no proof whatsoever for the claim that its meaning is not "one should eat dog-meat," but rather some other intended meaning. There is simply no evidence at all.

He explains [the passage] beginning with *kvacid* (in some cases). Regarding the sentence “One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*,” there is an absence of both [proximity and remoteness] because of the rejection of a real relationship—whether it be proximity to the intended meaning as claimed by some, or the absence of remoteness from the unintended meaning.

We perceive no distinction between the meaning “one should pour clarified butter and the like, purified by mantras and so forth, into fire, which is a specific kind of element, as intended” and the meaning “one should eat dog-meat.”

But surely this [objection] applies equally to all human-authored scriptures as it was stated. Demonstrating that very point, he says: "The teacher is beyond perception; those words and scriptures [spoken by him] are so described. Their meaning is according to intention," that is, as intended by the teacher.

Now, since there is no fixed rule as to whether persons who have not seen the teacher follow and understand it correctly, or rather the opposite—understanding it contrary to the teacher's intention—there is doubt in every case. This is what is meant.

He refutes this with the words beginning "no," and so forth: "This undesirable consequence does not apply in all cases. By means of revealing the intention of the teacher—the author of the scripture—this [teacher], while first making it known, declares his own intention to the listeners present at that time, saying, 'This is the meaning of this statement. Those listeners, in turn, reveal it to others, and they to yet others; thus, since a tradition of oral instruction from teacher to student is possible, [the scripture remains authoritative]."
For this characteristic of expressing an intention is not possible for Vedic words that are non-instructive and thus authorless, because of the absence of an instructor.

For this reason as well, in the case of human compositions, the possibility of the meaning being as it is commonly known exists; because the author of a scripture intends to inform the world, thinking "I must make the world understand," he speaks while maintaining and protecting the established usage of a word for whatever meaning it has in the world. Otherwise, his revelation would be fruitless. Therefore, from that very maintenance of the convention established by the world, the establishment of that meaning follows.

The establishment of the meaning of a scripture composed by a person would be possible—by virtue of the word "also" [in the original verse] and because of the aforementioned possibility of a continuous tradition (*sampradāya*). However, for words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the meaning cannot be established in the manner described above. Why? Because among those Vedic words, there is an absence of any person’s intention (*samīhā*), and because there is an absence of the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), which is the cause of verbal expression.

Thus, it has been stated that since the comprehension of the meaning of a human-authored scripture is possible through the existence of a tradition and so forth, there is no parity of logical consequence [between the two cases].

(p. 592) Now, [the author] states "Moreover," etc., to show that the determination of the meaning of human compositions occurs precisely through reasoning (*nyāya*). Wise people who act with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*), adhering strictly to reasoning—that is, to logic—engage themselves with regard to what is to be abandoned and so forth. They proceed toward the abandonment of what is to be abandoned along with its basis, and toward the acquisition of what is to be acquired along with its basis. In this context, what is to be abandoned is suffering (*duḥkha*), and what is to be acquired is liberation (*mokṣa*). Their respective bases are, in due order, karma and the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

This is what is meant: although words may have multiple meanings, the followers of the Sugata determine the meaning of the scripture only as that which is logically consistent and conducive to human goals, and not merely by the instruction of others. Therefore, this is not a fault. He says exactly that: "not by mere report. It is not by mere report from the elders; thus, the [alleged] consequence is not the same. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate later, at the appropriate occasion, that engagement with scripture must indeed be preceded by the observance of logic (*nyāya*).

If the determination of the meaning of scripture were [possible] only through the adherence to logic regarding that which is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), then there would be no certainty regarding the meaning of scripture; thus he says: "But surely," and so forth. "The arrangement of the world and so forth" refers to the arrangement of the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*), such as the earth and so on. As it has been said:
"In that regard, they desire the arrangement of the receptacle-world to be below:
a wind-circle sixteen hundred thousand [yojanas] in depth and incalculable [in extent]," and so forth.
fn. 1: From the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter 3, etc.: "The giving of desired or undesired fruits by volitions such as generosity and non-violence," and so forth.

Even an object that is beyond the scope of logical reasoning—due to its remoteness in terms of place, intrinsic nature, and so on—is understood by you Buddhists. Why? Because of the words of a person who is worthy of trust. The word of one whose speech is non-contradictory regarding objects accessible through perception and inference is considered to have a true meaning in a third category [of objects]. Therefore, an object is understood from the words of a person who is worthy of trust.
And thus, since the engagement with the meaning of scripture is not preceded by the observance of logic, he considers that the same undesirable consequence applies equally.

He refutes this with the words beginning "no," and so forth: An object that is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*) is not understood from the word of a person. Why? Because of lack of trust (*apratyaya*), which means because there is no certainty due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object. [One might argue: "Since there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) in the case of objects such as perception, correspondence is also determined for what is absolutely beyond the senses. This too is not so; for it is not the case that because something is seen to be unerring in some instance within the domain of perception and so forth due to correspondence with a means of valid cognition, everything taught by that person—even that which is not accessible through reasoning—is likewise [true].

What is the reason? It is because of [the statement] "due to the occurrence of that," and so forth. This is because the occurrence of the speech of that superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*) is established through its pervasion by non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*), since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) for the opposite case. [Objection: But surely you yourself have accepted that the definition of scripture (*āgama*) consists in non-contradiction regarding at least one part, as stated in [verse 1.218]: "Non-sublation by both perception and the two kinds of inference," and so forth.

Therefore, he says: "And because there is no other way," and so forth. The definition of scripture (*āgama*) is that it is a non-contradictory statement even regarding extremely remote objects, by virtue of its non-contradiction with objects accessible through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is accepted as the definition of scripture because, when one acts on the basis of scripture due to having no other recourse, acting in this manner is preferable. However, from such a scripture as described above, there is no certain determination of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), because it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇya*). Thus, it was stated previously that scripture is not a valid means of knowledge.

Thus, for words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the knowledge of their meaning does not arise from the tradition of a teacher, because there is no instructor. Nor does it arise from reasoning (*yukti*), because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot function with respect to an object that is entirely beyond the senses. Nor is there comprehension of the meaning from common worldly usage (*loka*), because since these words are not employed to communicate with others, it is impossible to follow worldly conventions. Therefore, in the case of such non-human words, it is logical that there is simply no comprehension of their meanings. Nevertheless, regarding Vedic words, there is a well-known worldly convention, such as the fact that people act toward objects capable of burning or cooking when they hear words like "fire" (*agni*).

If it is argued that worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) is the cause for understanding the meaning of the Veda, the author provides the following reply, beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*): "In that case, if [convention] is ignorance (*avidyā*), what person is there who perceives objects beyond the senses (*atīndriyārtha*)? For by such a perceiver of supersensible objects—who, given that words have multiple meanings and lack a fixed restriction to a single meaning, might distinguish among the various possible meanings of Vedic words, declaring: 'This is the supersensible meaning; this is the specific meaning; this alone is its meaning, not that one'—there exists no such person at all."

He explains by means of the words beginning with "na hi" [not indeed]. For this worldly convention does not arise from a non-human, uncreated relationship between word and meaning; rather, it arises from a convention (*samaya*) characterized by the expression of intention. What is it like? It is like [the conventions] of the authors of their own treatises, and so forth. From the convention—that is, the linguistic agreement—of the authors of their own treatises, such as Pāṇini and others, there arise for those who follow that convention, such as the followers of Pāṇini, the usages of technical terms like *vṛddhi* and *guṇa*. Why is this? Because they depend upon instruction.

For if even worldly convention were established by nature, it would not depend upon instruction from others. Furthermore, just as the comprehension of meaning arises from a conventional relationship that depends on instruction, so too the comprehension of the Vedic meaning does not arise from an authorless relationship that likewise depends on instruction; for in that case of an authorless Vedic relationship between word and meaning, instruction from another is not tenable. What is the reason? Because no person whatsoever knows that Vedic meaning, and the Vedic meaning is beyond the senses for those who are ignorant. As it has been said:
"For it is from the Veda that the status of these [rites] as means to the highest good (*śreyas*) is eternally understood;
and since their nature as *dharma* consists in being such [means], they are therefore not within the scope of the senses. (Ślokavārttika 1.1.2.2, v.
14) For the highest good is indeed the pleasure of the person, and that [pleasure] is [brought about] by substances, qualities, and actions."
"Therefore, dharma is to be established by means of those [means] characterized by injunction (*codanā*). (Ślokavārttika, Codanā 191).

For if it were admitted that the meaning of the Veda is perceptible by the senses, it would follow that the meaning of the Veda could be understood even without instruction, just like color and other such objects; that is, just as color and so forth are understood without instruction because they are perceptible by the senses, so too would the Vedic meaning be.

Now, if it is admitted that instruction is accepted even regarding the supersensuous meaning of the Veda for the sake of certainty, then, regarding such instruction, there is no confidence and no certainty concerning the meaning of the Veda. This is because the men who instruct on the meaning of the Veda are independent [agents]; since they lack perfect knowledge due to being overcome by passion and other defects, and act according to their own whims, their instruction cannot be established as non-contradictory with reality. For those who are ignorant are not capable of instructing according to reality. It is not the case that these persons instruct according to their own will.

But if it is argued that, like the Veda itself, the commentary on the Veda is also authorless—having come down through an unbroken tradition characterized by a succession of instructions—and therefore the meaning of the Veda is established from such a Vedic commentary as described;

He states the answer with the words "of that too" (*tasyāpi*) and so forth. Even for that commentary on the Veda, if it consists of words—that is, if its nature is verbal—it is subject to the same critical inquiry as the Veda. How can the meaning of this non-human (apauruṣeya) commentary on the Veda be known? From what source, then, could there be a determination of the Veda’s meaning from it? However, this fault does not apply to a human-authored scripture (*āgama*), because a person—(p. [number])...

595) One may explain the meaning of words that have been personally composed and conventionally established by pointing them out directly—by saying, "This is the meaning of this word"—thereby instructing an ignorant person who does not yet understand. Thus, there exists a means for understanding the meaning, that is, for the cognition of the meaning, in the case of human-made words; however, such a means does not exist for non-human (apauruṣeya) words. For a non-human word does not act in this way, [saying]: "This is my meaning, and it should be grasped by one possessed of passion and so forth."

Furthermore, no person such as Jaimini or others—who possesses passion and other defects—is capable of knowing the fixed relationship of this non-human word with respect to any supersensible object; thus, there is simply a lack of comprehension regarding its meaning, that is, the meaning of the Veda.

Furthermore, even if the Veda and its commentary were indeed of non-human origin, nevertheless, when taught by a person possessed of passion and other defects to another person, the tradition would not continue unimpaired even to the present day; since there is no evidence for this, one must resort to conventions such as oaths and the like. By the passage beginning with "of those who cause the loss of the scripture," he establishes that, due to the interruption of the tradition, the possibility of a different composition [of the text] actually exists. This is because men who cause the loss of the scripture act otherwise.

The connection is that [the author] sees a composition contrary to the original arrangement. He states the reason for this alternative arrangement as "out of self-aggrandizement" (*āhopuruṣikayā*), and so forth. "Out of self-aggrandizement" means out of a sense of egoism (*ahaṃmānitva*). For example, Mādhava, the destroyer of Sāṃkhya, composed the Sāṃkhya-siddhānta-nyāya-bhūṣaṇa by arranging the tenets of Sāṃkhya differently; or because an alternative arrangement is possible through hatred for the system, such as the composition of other sūtras that are mere counterfeits of the Mahāyāna by those who hate the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of humiliating those who have accepted that [view]": it is the impossibility of formulating things otherwise for the sake of humiliating that person who has accepted that philosophical system. How exactly does this humiliation of those who have accepted it occur? Through the vice of being a rogue (*dhūrta*). This is the vice of rogues: that another must be humiliated. Or else, it is for the sake of some gain or other from somewhere else.

Furthermore, regarding this determination of the meaning of the Veda, you, O Vedavādin, out of attachment to your own doctrine, have surely forgotten your own position—that which is called "mukhavarṇa," so named because it describes and adorns its own face—when you seek the determination of the Veda’s meaning from persons defiled by passion and other such flaws.

With the words beginning with "puruṣa," he explains the nature of the person: since a person is overwhelmed by passion and other afflictions and is thus deluded, he might even speak what is untrue; therefore, the word of this person is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Why, then, is it not examined here as well—whether or not it is possible—that such untruthfulness exists in the person, such as Jaimini and others, who are performing the transmission of the meaning of the Veda?

For that very person, such as Jaimini and others, who possesses passion and other defects while teaching the Veda or the meaning of the Veda, might teach otherwise due to the cause of being afflicted by passion and so forth; thus, the suspicion that the content is false is never dispelled.

Demonstrating the very grounds for suspicion, he says: "For it is heard," and so forth. By certain persons such as Yājñavalkya and others, [the Vedic texts] were recovered from what had been lost. There are other branches (*śākhāntara*) of the Veda that had been lost, meaning they had become obsolete; they were recovered by being remembered again and again and then re-composed. And what is the proof here that these were recovered by being remembered according to their true nature? Even now, certain other branches such as the Āhūraka have only a few students.

[The various recensions] are seen to have few students. What is the proof for the claim that those few students do not teach [the text] by way of superimposition? Just as other recensions are seen to have sparse students, so too—in the case of other recensions that once had many students or even a great number of students—it is possible that, after some time has passed, because of the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), there might arise the possibility of having few students. This is because there is no evidence that they had many students even previously.

Now, if that is so, how is it that those [scriptures] have many students? To this he says: "Furthermore," and so forth. Because there is the possibility—contrary to the study by persons other than those [reputed authorities]—of them being studied due to the conviction (pratyaya) in the authority (prāmāṇya) of a person who is considered trustworthy at another time, there is no certainty [regarding their validity].

Furthermore, the connection is as follows: "because for those men who have become rare—the propagators of other branches—it is possible that they might teach otherwise. The intention is that, consequently, there would be no confidence [in their teachings]. Of what sort are these propagators? They are those who have at some time forgotten what they had studied (*adhītavismṛtādhyayana*). Those by whom the study (*adhyayana*) which was previously learned has been forgotten are so described. The meaning is that, having forgotten what was studied exactly as it was learned, they might propagate it in a different manner.

He asks, "For what reason? and says: out of fear of the loss of the great reputation that others—those who have faith in him and those who study under him—hold for that teacher. [He thinks: "If I were to teach otherwise, they would surely abandon their conviction in me as a reliable authority. By the word "etcetera," [the author] implies the possibility of teaching otherwise due to vanity and similar traits.

"Let them indeed recite [the Veda] otherwise; nevertheless, the students would not understand it accordingly. To this he says: "That," and so forth. Because of trust in that esteemed person, and because of what was spoken by him—among those who have faith in the esteemed author, there arises a transmission of a different kind through the study and practice of the Veda without critical investigation. Demonstrating that activity proceeds precisely from the authority of the person, he says: because in the world, among many students, one frequently observes activity [proceeding] from an esteemed person.

But surely, if one acts based on a person who is deemed reliable, there is indeed agreement [with reality]; to this he replies: "Even from such a person deemed reliable, for some reason—such as the fear of losing that reputation—there is the possibility of *vipralambha*, which is to say, deception or disagreement."

He states the cause for this accumulation—beginning with "Furthermore," and so forth: We hear from you Mīmāṃsakas that there is indeed a succession of those limited individuals who are the authors of the commentaries on the Veda. Among them, one might be a commentator on the Veda who is characterized by any of the qualities such as hatred and the like. One might be hostile toward the vision of the Veda and thus teach otherwise; likewise, one might be ignorant or a rogue. And in that case, there would be a lack of confidence in the commentary on the Veda.

Since this is so, the meaning of the Veda is not established through an authorless (apauruṣeya) commentary on the Veda, nor is it established through worldly usage that is conventional and based on linguistic convention, because the world is corrupted by passion and other defects.

Or, let us grant that Vedic words are established by their very nature (*nisargasiddha*) and independent of convention (*samaya*). Even so, if this independence from convention is accepted, since words such as "cow" (*go*) are seen to have multiple meanings in common usage, the suspicion regarding those [multiple meanings] does not cease even in the case of every Vedic word; this is the connection [of the argument]. The meaning is: because the suspicion of multiple meanings has not been removed. If it is argued that only worldly words possess multiple meanings and not Vedic ones, he says: "Of some," and so forth.

Even in the case of some Vedic word whose meaning is well-known—where the word is established but not its meaning—or in the case of a word that is itself unknown, the meaning must be inferred by persons through the demonstration of its etymology. This being so, since the doubt regarding multiple possible meanings is never removed in any instance as to whether a person teaches the true meaning of Vedic words exactly as it stands or otherwise, [the Veda cannot be a valid means of knowledge].

It is also untenable to claim that Vedic words do not produce cognition regarding an unintended object even when employed [for that purpose]. For, although all words—both worldly and Vedic—are restricted to their respective referents (this being an *avyayībhāva* compound with *vīpsā*: "in each and every referent"), they nevertheless generate cognition in those respective objects according to convention and according to the established linguistic agreement, provided there is no defect in the conditions. Furthermore, it does not produce a cognition contrary to the intended one in the case of an unintended object.

Because there is no distinction in the production of cognition regarding desired and undesired objects due to the absence of proximity or distance; therefore, among all Vedic words which are indistinguishable with respect to their objects, who could discern a single specific object—one whose connection with the word is beyond the senses (*atyakṣasaṃyoga*)—among ordinary persons who do not perceive what is beyond the senses (*anatyakṣadarśin*), that is, those of limited vision? No one at all could discern it, since the cognition [of such a thing] would have to arise from common worldly usage.

Furthermore, this person, Mīmāṃsaka, does not himself follow established usage (*prasiddhi*) everywhere in the Veda, such that the understanding of the Vedic meaning would arise from popular worldly parlance. What is the reason? Because words such as *svarga*, *urvaśī*, and so forth—where the word *svarga* [means heaven] and the word *urvaśī* [means a celestial nymph], and by the word "and so forth" [is meant] words like *nandanavana* and others—are seen by this proponent of the Veda to be described and explained as denoting meanings that are either conventional or otherwise not well-known.

For it is thus: those qualities which distinguish a person from ordinary men are his abode and place; it is a bliss transcending humanity, a superhuman bliss, and it is the foundation and support for that superhuman bliss. It is the common worldly saying that heaven (*svarga*) is "possessed of manifold implements," meaning it contains various kinds of articles and objects of enjoyment. And it is the common worldly saying that the celestial nymph (*apsaras*) dwelling there is named Urvaśī.

Disregarding that popular worldly notion, [the author argues that] heaven is simply unsurpassed delight among human beings, and Urvaśī is the lower fire-drill (araṇi), as indicated by the words "the upper fire-drill" (pātrī) and so forth. Since this Jaimini and others are formulating a conceptualization of meaning entirely different from what is commonly established in the world, how could they rely upon popular consensus when determining the meaning of other terms such as *agnihotra*? The point is that they would not rely on it at all.

If it is argued that in the case of words such as *agnihotra*, one accepts the very meaning as it is understood because there is no contradiction in postulating a meaning well-known in the world; whereas in the case of words such as *svarga* (heaven) and *urvaśī* (the nymph), one does not accept [a literal] meaning because accepting a well-known meaning would contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so the opponent thinks.

"No," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*), beginning with the word "no. The distinction just mentioned is appropriate because, even in this case, when words such as *svarga* (heaven), *artha* (wealth), and *aiśvarya* (sovereignty) are accepted as referring to objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) that are well-known in common worldly usage (*lokaprasiddha*), there is no contradiction established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For here, there exists neither perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor inference (*anumāna*) as a subverting means of valid cognition. The phrase "in other cases as well" refers to words such as *agnihotra* and so forth; for in those cases too, it is difficult to maintain the absence of contradiction when postulating meanings well-known in common usage. This is because, due to the absence of a proving means of valid cognition, [the alternative] is difficult to understand.

Establishing this very point, he says: there is doubt that perhaps even someone like Jaimini might not perceive the attainment of heaven from the Agnihotra, even though it is commonly accepted as contradictory—due to its slowness and so forth. Furthermore, contradiction and non-contradiction are not something other than this; rather, they are the operation of subverting and proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Contradiction is the operation of the aforementioned subverting means of valid cognition called "non-perception" (*anupalambha*).

The operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the cognition of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the inference (*anumāna*)—is non-contradiction (*avirodha*). These two possess the nature of contradiction and non-contradiction; they are the operations of the subverting (*bādhaka*) and establishing (*sādhaka*) means of valid cognition. This is not intended with respect to an object that is beyond perception (*atyakṣa*), that is, supersensible (*atīndriya*). For indeed, regarding things remote in space and so forth, such as the means for attaining heaven (*svarga*) and the like, neither a subverting nor an establishing means of valid cognition operates. And since this is so, how could it be "on account of that"? That is to say, on account of the force of contradiction and non-contradiction.

Due to contradiction, there is no cognition of the well-known meaning in words such as "heaven" (*svarga*), whereas due to the absence of contradiction, there is cognition of the well-known meaning in words such as "fire-sacrifice" (*agnihotra*).

Now, it might be thought: "The absence of contradiction is not the operation of a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding supersensible objects; rather, the very operation of the speech known as scripture—such as the injunctions for the fire-sacrifice and so forth—in its capacity to denote meanings well-known in the world is itself the absence of contradiction."

Therefore, he says: "And not," and so forth. There is no contradiction precisely because the application of statements such as those concerning the *agnihotra* is based on expressing meanings well-known in the world. What is the reason? Because even in other cases, words such as "heaven" (*svarga*) and "Urvaśī" are seen in common usage to apply only to specific places and celestial nymphs. Consequently, since there is no distinction between the two cases, let the meanings established in both [the worldly and the scriptural] contexts be accepted; yet, this is not the case even for one of them.

Furthermore, the scripture known as the Veda is said to be authorless; yet it does not reveal its own meaning by itself, but rather the establishment of that scripture's meaning is accepted on the basis of worldly consensus. However, even when such worldly consensus is admitted, if one were to investigate contradictions, there would be a lack of confidence in every scripture, because it is impossible to determine whether there is a contradiction or not regarding matters beyond the reach of the senses.

Establishing precisely this lack of confidence, he says: "Even though that," and so forth. Even if that non-human scripture exists, the object denoted by words such as "heaven" (*svarga*) is not as it [is claimed to be]. "As-it-is-ness" (*tathābhāva*) means being thus; for instance, because one grasps the meaning of "heaven" as it is well-known in the world, and because one grasps an unestablished meaning, other words such as *agnihotra* are also to be suspected of being otherwise. This is because [the objects] do not exist in that manner.

Is its meaning merely that which is well-known in the world, or is it something entirely different, like the words "heaven" (*svarga*) and so forth? Why is this so? Because of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For in this case, no means of valid cognition operates to establish the acceptance of a meaning well-known in the world.

The opponent says: "As for what was stated," etc.—namely, that in the sentence "One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," there might be the assumption (*vikalpa*) or conceptualization of an injunction to consume horse-flesh; that fault does not apply. Why? Because in another part of the Veda itself, it is explained (*vyākhyāna*) through such a discussion of the meaning of this *agnihotra* and other sentences that one should pour clarified butter and so forth into a specific kind of fire.

"No," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). This response is not tenable, because the meaning of that explanatory passage located in another section has not been fully understood. Consequently, by imagining such a meaning even for other explanatory passages located elsewhere, one would be unable to prevent the imagination of eating dog meat.

The passage beginning with "yadi" (if) is a further support for this very point. For if this collection of words called the Veda, which is non-human in origin, had its meaning known in some other section, then from that section whose meaning is known, there would arise a comprehension of the meaning of the remaining parts. However, since those Vedic words—even in their abundance—have their meanings unknown, they are all effectively blind; thus, they are composed and interpreted by humans according to their own whims.

Since this is so, therefore, regarding other words that are similar: let there be the same kind of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) for those sentences that serve as explanations of [the injunction] "One should offer the Agnihotra," and so forth. What kind? He says: "Just as the conceptual construction was made for the sentence 'One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra,' so too [should there be] the conceptual construction of eating dog-flesh in another context"—that is to say, it should be understood in the same way.

Moreover, common renown (*prasiddhi*) is not something other [than human speech]. What then? It is the talk (*vāda*) of men, of persons; and that talk is not accepted by you as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because all persons are afflicted by passion and the like. The word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) means "again. Consequently, since worldly talk has already been established as non-authoritative, how can it be that the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas arises from it simultaneously? For that very same thing which was hated for being non-authoritative—[now it is desired].
That very same thing is again desired and longed for as the cause of practice; thus, there is a mutual contradiction.

Established renown (*prasiddhi*) is not something other than popular report (*janapravāda*); rather, popular report itself is established renown. Furthermore, all those people are such that the truthfulness (*yāthātathya*)—meaning the state of being non-erroneous—of their speech cannot be relied upon. This is the analysis of the compound: "those whose speech has a truthfulness that cannot be relied upon. For what reason? Because they are overwhelmed by passion and ignorance; that is, because they are pervaded by passion and ignorance. Therefore, the report of these people is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The claim that the popular consensus (*tatpravāda*) is authoritative simply because of the multitude of people is also false. For, when not even a single individual among a great many people possesses correct realization, the mere majority of the world is neither meaningful nor purposeful. How so? As in the case of the Persians (*pārasīka*) and so forth: just as the practice of sexual intercourse with one's mother by many Persians does not thereby become logical, so too, despite their numerical majority, the word of those possessed of passion and other defects regarding supersensible objects (*atīndriya-artha*) is simply not authoritative.

Now, it might be argued that from the speech of those very persons possessed of passion and so forth, there is once again the comprehension of an object beyond the senses denoted by words such as "agnihotra. But how is it possible for that same [object] to be both hateful and desirable at one and the same time?

Having disregarded—that is, having abandoned—the meaning in which the word *agnihotra* and so forth are well-known in common usage, there is no basis or reason for postulating another meaning, such as the eating of dog-meat and the like. Therefore, the claim that "only what is well-known should be accepted" is also untenable; because since common usage (*prasiddhi*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), what would be the basis for accepting it? There is none at all. Thus, let there be no acceptance of even common usage.

With the words beginning "by means of attainment" (*prāptyā*), he first explains the first half [of the verse]. It is logical that, when one perceives merits and defects, there should be an engagement with another meaning that is not well-known, by way of rejecting an already established meaning through its reversal. This would be the case if one were to perceive defects in the established meaning and perceive merits in what is not established. If it is argued: "There is no perception of defects in the established meaning of words such as *agnihotra*, nor is there any perception of merits in what is not established; therefore, the connection (*anvaya*) follows only the established meaning."

He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth; this is an explanation of the second half [of the verse]. It is not thus. Why? Because attainment (*prāpti*) is characterized by the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it is said that the attainment of an object is determined by a proving means of valid cognition, and thus attainment is defined as the operation of a *pramāṇa*. Furthermore, common renown (*prasiddhi*) is not a *pramāṇa*, whereby an established object would be logically attained.

Consequently, for the Mīmāṃsaka who does not accept this well-known usage as authoritative, the cognition of an object denoted by words such as *agnihotra* that occurs through the medium of that popular usage is a mere grasping of something arbitrary, because it lacks a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The meaning is that its apprehension is achieved in some way or another [without justification]. Therefore, since the worldly-meaning of words like *agnihotra* is not established by logical necessity (*nyāya*), and because the attainment of the worldly-meaning is thus precluded by logic, the meaning of words such as *agnihotra* must be determined according to one's own will.

In this regard, regarding the meaning of words such as *agnihotra* that is postulated by the Mīmāṃsakas—characterized by fire, substances, and so forth—and that which is postulated by the opponent—characterized by the eating of dog-meat: whether both of these conceptualizations, one's own and the other's, are consistent with established usage (*prasiddhi*) or not, even so, since their application is equal insofar as they are adopted by mere whim due to a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), what adherence to established usage is there by which the postulation of a meaning based on established usage would be made?

Moreover, when the meaning of all words is determined by common usage alone, this suspicion has been raised on account of their having multiple meanings. For what reason? Because the occurrence of words such as "fire" (*agni*) in multiple senses is observed in that very common usage.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*). There is no determination of a single meaning for Vedic words based on common usage (*prasiddhi*). What is the reason? Because from that very same common usage, doubt arises. For instance, words such as "fire" (*agni*) are seen in the world to have multiple meanings. And that observation of multiple meanings is worldly discourse (*lokavāda*), worldly report (*lokapravāda*), and conventional understanding; it is precisely because of this worldly discourse that there is multiplicity of meaning. Therefore, given this worldly discourse, it is not logical to restrict Vedic words to a single meaning.

Strengthening the very point that the meaning is indeterminate, he says: "Otherwise," and so forth. This is because there is no impossibility of the contrary for a word—namely, *dhvani*—which by its own nature possesses manifold capacities and is capable of conveying multiple meanings. "Otherwise" refers to the occurrence [of a word] in a sense other than the intended one. "The impossibility of the contrary" (*anyathā-sambhava*) means the impossibility of that occurrence in another sense; since there is an absence of such impossibility, it follows that by means of two negations, an affirmation is accepted—that is to say, the possibility of the contrary does indeed exist.

Consequently, regarding Vedic words that function with respect to objects beyond the senses, there must necessarily be doubt due to their capacity for multiple meanings—for those persons who perceive no regulator and who perceive no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a specific, restricted object. (326)

Since this is so, therefore [the analysis is as follows]: "those for whom the distinction of meaning is unknown" (*aviditārthavibhāga*) is the grammatical analysis. Regarding those words whose distinctions of meaning are unknown, one assumes a single intended object. What is its nature? It is "beyond the range of the senses" (*atyakṣasaṃyoga*). The analysis is: that which has a connection with a word that is beyond the range of the senses (*atyakṣa*) and devoid of distinctions. It is called "thus" because it is a superimposition (*samāropa*) that is "without a basis" (*anālambana*)—meaning without a foundation—due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it is without any means of valid cognition.

Having thus determined that very matter as if it were a fact and explaining it under that pretext, Jaimini says, "The Veda says this," thereby stating his own opinion under the guise of the Veda; whereas another teacher (tīrthakara) speaks quite openly, saying, "I myself declare this. Therefore, we perceive no distinction between this Jaimini and other teachers.

Establishing this very point without distinction, he says: “For instance” (*tathā hi*), and so forth. That which is both "that" (*sa*) and "the object" (*artha*) is "that object" (*tadartha*); its "manifestation" (*prakāśana*) is speech (*vacana*). Its "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is its capacity (*sāmarthya*); [the Veda] is "devoid" (*śūnya*) or "lacking" (*rahita*) in that respect. "By the superimposition of that" (*tatsamāropeṇa*) means by the superimposition of the activity of manifesting the meaning. ... Thus, whatever designation there is of one who "speaks in such a way" (*evamvaktīti*)—[this refers to] his own statement (*svavacana*) itself; that is what it amounts to.

By one who acts thus—by Jaimini, who, while being devoid of the activity of speech, attributes to the Veda the activity of manifesting meaning—one would merely illuminate oneself as being falsely disciplined; there would be no distinction between this [Veda] and a human statement.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth. When asked, "Which is the path that goes to Pāṭaliputra?", a certain man replied: "I do not know; I myself merely say that this post is the path. Thus, one person indicates the path under the pretext of a post that is devoid of the capacity to instruct on the path. Another, however, says: "The post has no capacity for speech; I myself, having known it, declare that this is the path."
While they are speaking thus, let the discrepancy in their own statements be examined; the intention is to see whether such a discrepancy exists or indeed does not exist at all.

He explains by means of the words "without intention" (*nirabhiprāya*) and so forth. "Intention" (*abhiprāya*) is the volition: "I shall do this and that. The "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is the effort preceded by that [volition]. It is that which possesses neither intention, nor activity, nor speech; thus it is so described. The connection is as follows: having superimposed the quality of being a path-indicator upon such an inanimate post (*sthāṇu*), one instructs either a single independent person who does not depend on the post, or another person. Thus he instructs the path.

Between these two types of persons, there is no distinction whatsoever when they themselves accept [their own] words, except for the dull-wittedness of the fool; it is precisely the dull-wittedness of the foolish listener that is distinguished. For, when one understands the speech of a post—which is devoid of intention and so forth—one concludes, "The post itself speaks. In the same way, when the Jaiminiyas express their own doctrine under the pretext of the Veda, the fool, due to his dull-wittedness, understands: "The Veda itself speaks thus."

Moreover, if a Vedic word were restricted to a single meaning, Jaimini might recognize that restriction to a single meaning; however, since a word as a signifier is everywhere capable of being a signifier for any object, why would there not be a restriction to the illumination of a single meaning? For no meaning whatsoever is restricted to a word by its own nature or by innate establishment. What is the reason? Because a word is capable [of signifying] every object to be expressed.

Furthermore, if the word were not capable with respect to every object, then—given that incapacity does not depart from it because its nature is one of incapacity, and for the reason that this word does not deviate from that nature—it would be impossible to apply a word that is not subject to human control or dependence to some object by assigning it the status of a signifier (*vācaka*), nor to withdraw it once so assigned, saying, "Now this word is not a signifier. And yet, such things do occur. Therefore, since words are capable with respect to everything, there is no illumination of a single specific meaning.

Or, let there be for the Vaidikas a restriction to a single meaning; nevertheless, a person is incapable of knowing a restriction regarding meanings that transcend the senses. He says this very thing: "By what person could supersensuous objects be known? For Mīmāṃsaka does not accept anyone as a seer of supersensuous objects. Regarding the phrase "apart from the expression of the intention to speak" (*vivakṣāvacanād ṛte*): the non-expression of the intention to speak is like not speaking at all; thus, "apart from the expression of the intention to speak" means that without the speaker’s communication of his own intention, supersensuous objects are not known by anyone at all. This is the meaning.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "by a person" (*puruṣa*). When a word is produced and uttered by a person with a certain intention (*vivakṣā*), that person might at some time communicate that intention to a certain listener, saying: "This was intended by me as the thing to be expressed. Thus, a restriction regarding the meaning of words preceded by intention might indeed be perceived. But in the case of a non-human (apauruṣeya) word, which has not been employed by anyone preceded by intention, how could a restriction of meaning be known even if it existed? Not at all.

What is the reason? Because there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Indeed, there is no distinct intrinsic nature whatsoever belonging to a Vedic word that is restricted to a specific intended object, such that from the perception of it, the cognition of the desired object would arise. Or, even if there were a difference in intrinsic nature, that difference in intrinsic nature would have to be either perceptible or imperceptible. It cannot first be perceptible; why? Because if the intrinsic nature were perceptible independently of instruction, it would follow that it would be cognized by itself.

Now, [if it is argued that the object] is not perceptible: even if it is not perceptible, because there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be known by anyone who possesses only limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*).

This was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. Furthermore, there is no specific distinction whatsoever that is restricted to a single object; for all words are devoid of proximity to or remoteness from all objects.

For there are no words that are, in reality, either proximate or remote with respect to any given object; rather, since those words are by nature equal with regard to all objects, the cause for restricting them to a single meaning is the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). Convention (*saṃketa*) is the manifestation of that [intention]; thus, convention is the manifestation of that very intention. For it is through convention that one understands: "This is the object intended by him. And since that intention does not exist in the case of non-human (Vedic) speech, [it follows that... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the role of human intention and convention in linguistic meaning.)

606) From where does that aforementioned singularity of meaning (*ekārthatā*) of that non-human word come? It comes from nowhere at all. He explains this with the words beginning "for it is by intention" (*vivakṣā hi*). By means of intention acting as the cause, a word is restricted to objects such that "this [word] is the designator of this very object. But it is not so by way of its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). What is the reason? Because that word lacks a connection—due to being devoid of a relation—toward any given entity, and thus it is equal in respect to all objects. Even in cases where there is a connection of the word to the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the organs of production (*karaṇa*), because the words arise from or are manifested by those [articulations], [they remain unrestricted].

Because there is no rule that all words must denote those organs; for not all words are denoters of the organs alone. However, since a word denoting an organ might also convey the organs themselves, the term "all" is used [to exclude such cases].

Since this is so, a convention (*saṃketa*) is established in order to manifest the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). Of what nature is it? It is characterized by the communication of the intended meaning; that is, it is characterized by the manifestation of the speaker’s intention. However, in the case of words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), intention is not the regulator, nor does convention manifest such [an intention]. What is the reason? Because, due to the very absence of a person, there is no existence of any intention whatsoever; therefore, there is no restriction to a single meaning for Vedic words. Or, even if there were such a restriction—

There is no such knowledge for anyone, nor is there any knowledge restricted to a single object. By their very nature, Vedic words are restricted to a single object, not by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*).
Therefore, if a restriction by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is admitted, that word cannot be separated from that [single] object by means of that intention.

He explains this with the words beginning with "If": if it were logical for the word to be inherently attached to objects by its own nature, independent of convention (*saṃketa*), the answer to this has already been stated: "Because there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*) with any particular thing, it is unrestricted."

Moreover, if the relationship between the signifier and the signified were admitted to be intrinsic and established by nature (*svābhāvika*), then a word could not be employed at will by the speaker’s intention for another meaning. For it is not possible to employ the eye—which is naturally restricted to the illumination of form—for the illumination of sound. Yet, a word is employed at will; therefore, it is not restricted by nature, like the gesture of the hand. If words were restricted to their objects by nature, then convention (*saṃketa*) would be... [p. 10]... [omitted].

It would be meaningless and fruitless; for a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) or a specific quality of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is not accessible to the senses through its own perception by means of convention (*paribhāṣā*) and so forth. "Convention" (*paribhāṣā*) means linguistic agreement (*saṃketa*). By the word "and so forth," the recollection of that agreement and other such factors are included. What is it like? It is like the difference between blue and other colors. Just as specific qualities such as blue do not depend on convention and the like for their own perception, so it is here. However, those perceptions which depend [on such factors]—that is, perceptions which depend on convention—are not the actual intrinsic natures of things.

Particulars do not belong to an entity by way of natural establishment; rather, they are conventional, produced by social convention (*saṃketa*). How so? Like royal insignia and the like. Just as various distinctions of insignia, such as banners and so forth, are established by a king for his own recognition—the word "and the like" including hand gestures and so on—and whatever is conventional is logically restricted by its own nature, it is not logical that it be naturally established. What is the reason? Because that conventional [sign] proceeds according to the will of the person.

If it is argued that for a Vedic word, a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is fixed by its very essence regarding its meaning, but that [meaning] is merely manifested through convention (*saṃketa*), [the author] replies: "For this very reason," and so forth. Since convention functions according to desire, for this very reason, how could there be any necessity in the manifestation of a specific intrinsic nature restricted to a single object by means of convention? There is none at all.

He explains this as follows: A convention (*saṃketa*) is a matter of one's own will; it can be established here for a desired object and not elsewhere, so there is no obstruction. Nor is there any [intrinsic] denoter. Consequently, that convention, being created by persons according to their own will, manifests only that specific nature restricted to a single object and not any other; thus, there is no fixed necessity.

In a convention where there is freedom for desire, what indeed is a restriction? The meaning is that there is no restriction at all. For that reason—namely, this lack of restriction—the convention would not manifest the specific fitness of this Vedic word to refer only to its intended object. Thus, it has been demonstrated that being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) is not a defining characteristic of scripture (*āgama*).

(p. 608) Now, he introduces [the following] in order to refute the definition of scripture (*āgama*) as being non-contradictory in some respects: "Because," and so forth. The word *kila* indicates the [author's] intention. Fire is the source of cold, the remover of cold; by this, just as the statement "fire is the remedy for frost" is true, so too another statement such as "one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice" and so on is established as being non-false. "Because it is a part of the Veda" is the reason (*hetu*). Thus spoke another elder Mīmāṃsaka; he said.

He explains [the verse] with the words "But another," and so forth. But another, namely a Mīmāṃsaka, because he is afflicted by the aforementioned faults, abandons the definition of scripture as being authorless (*apauruṣeya*) and, desiring to establish the validity of the Veda in another way, says: "The non-false," and so forth. "In which there is no comprehension" means that those Vedic sentences regarding which the Buddhist has no comprehension of their being non-false are "non-false"; by this, a specific portion is made the subject (*pakṣa*). "Because they are a part of the Veda."

Because the universal is taken as the reason (*hetu*), the reason does not constitute a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*). This is like the statement, "Fire is the remedy for cold," or "it is the opposite," and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), statements such as "twelve months are a year" are included.

He states the reply: "Of that," and so forth. This proof of that proponent is *śeṣavat* (based on the remainder). Why? Because of its fallibility (*vyabhicāritva*). The connection is as follows: such an inference was rejected by the master Dignāga, the knower of logic, in his *Pramāṇasamuccaya*. To the question, "In what way is it like *śeṣavat*? he says: "Like [the taste of] juice," and so forth. Just as an un-eaten fruit is inferred to be similar [to a tasted one] because it possesses a form identical to that of the tasted fruit—this inference is *śeṣavat*—so too is this case.

"Even though unobserved, rice grains are cooked because they are cooked in the same vessel; this is like rice grains whose cooking has been observed. And just as there is such an inference based on being cooked in the same vessel, so too is the Mīmāṃsaka's position."

The explanation begins with the words "by himself" (*svayam*) and so forth. The connection is as follows: such an inference was stated by the Master himself to be a non-probative argument (*asādhana*). Where? In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, while exposing the fallibility (*vyabhicāra*) of the "inference based on the remainder" (*śeṣavat-anumāna*) of the Naiyāyikas. What is it like? Just as [the taste] of fruits that have not yet been tasted is established as having the same flavor as a fruit already tasted, by virtue of their identical form (*tulyarūpatā*) serving as the reason; and likewise by the reason [of being] "contained within the same vessel."

It is like the means for cooking rice that has not yet been seen, based on the example of rice that has already been seen to be cooked. As for the principle of its being a non-prover (*asādhanatva-nyāya*), this refers to the principle of why that *śeṣavat* inference is not a prover, which was already stated previously in the passage beginning with, "Because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is demonstrated by mere non-perception," and so forth. Now, one might object: did not the Master Dignāga also state that the definition of scripture (*āgama*) is the non-deviation from a portion [of it], in the passage beginning with, "The status of [scripture] as inference arises from its general non-deviation from the words of a reliable person" (*Pra.vā. 1.218*)?

He says: "And this has been stated," and so forth. And this has been stated in the intervening passage: "The definition of scripture (*āgama*) is that which is non-contradictory in at least one part; we are not capable of remaining without relying on the authority of scripture."

In this context, the definition of scripture (*āgama*) is not based on the truth of a single, extremely well-known object, but rather on the definition of a scripture of reality (*tattva*). This refers to that entire range of objects which can be determined through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by one of limited vision; the analysis of "the object whose investigation is possible" (*śakyo vicāro yasya*) is the grammatical breakdown of the compound.

Just as there is the establishment of what is accepted through injunctions and prohibitions by means of their respective valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), so too is there the status of being perceived for those things intended as objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the treatise; for example, the mental states (*buddhi*, etc. in the Buddhist tenets. Likewise, there is the status of being an object of inference based on the power of facts (*vastubalānumāna*) for those things intended as objects of inference arrived at through the force of reality; for example, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and so forth. And there is likewise the same state for those things intended as objects of inference dependent upon scripture (*āgama*).

The establishment of affirmation for each of the three kinds of objects occurs through its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The establishment of negation for each of the three kinds of objects—namely, the state of being an object of perception and so forth, which constitutes their status as perceptual and other such [objects]—occurs through their respective means of valid cognition.

When, in this manner, affirmation and negation have been established, regarding the remaining objects that are absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), even though words lack any internal correspondence and there is an absence of a [direct] relationship, it is better—as a last resort—that a person who is in doubt should act toward them; for in all such matters, since no deviation has been observed, it is possible that the scripture might occasionally be non-contradictory.

"Now, 'elsewhere' refers to those scriptures where, regarding the objects as previously described, there is observed by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) either a contradiction with perception and so forth, or where the activity of a person toward such [an object] is not tenable; it is in this sense that we have stated the definition of scripture (*āgama*). On the other hand, the Mīmāṃsakas and others hold that a statement such as ‘Fire is the remedy for cold’—which is a portion of the Veda—is true in its meaning because it expresses the capacity of fire, which is an object of ordinary persons, to ward off the sensation of cold."

Having presented this as an illustration, he states that the entire scripture characterized by the Vedas has true meaning: "What kind of scripture? Even regarding a subject that is determinable and accessible through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it contains much that is illogical due to contradiction with those very means of valid cognition—then a Mīmāṃsaka or similar proponent who asserts such a scripture would, through sheer audacity, defeat a harlot. This is the connection with what is to be said hereafter.

Showing that even more [of his claims] are improper, he says: "Of the eternal," and so forth. The word "asserting" (*vadat*) is to be connected with every [clause]. A scripture that asserts that there exists an eternal agent, a *puruṣa*, thus asserts the agency of an eternal person; likewise, it asserts that entities are eternal; it asserts that supersensible objects are not perceptible, yet asserts that they are sensible and perceptible; likewise, it asserts an inconsistent and improper cause for entities; and likewise, it asserts an inconsistent state of entities.

And he speaks of the irregular cessation of entities; this we shall clarify in the *Vṛtti*. Or, a thing other than what has been stated is "one whose scope is rejected" (*vyastagocara*). That is so called because its scope—its range—is rejected or excluded. By what is it rejected? He says: by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception and inference, the treatise speaks in contradiction [to them]. Thus, a proponent who asserts that such a treatise—which expresses many unreasonable matters—is a true authority, would be like one who, out of sheer audacity, claims to defeat a harlot.

To the question, "What is it that he fails to do when making his declaration? the author replies with the words beginning "contradiction" (*virodham*). This means: one who makes a declaration without having resolved—that is, without having removed—the contradiction of the treatise regarding a subject matter that is capable of investigation; and without having demonstrated the cause for the engagement of persons in the treatise, as well as the purpose of the treatise, which is characterized by the relationship [between the subject and the goal], the appropriate means, and the human aim.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "apracyuteḥ": the analysis of the compound is "one whose former nature has not fallen away and whose other nature has not arisen. Such a person, they say, is the successive agent of good and evil deeds (*karma*) and the enjoyer of the fruits of those deeds. To the question of in what manner he is the enjoyer and the agent, he says: the self (*ātman*) is the enjoyer of the fruits of deeds by way of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the consciousness of pleasure, pain, and so forth produced by prior deeds.
As it has been said: "The state of being an enjoyer consists in the inherence [of the self] with the consciousness of pleasure, pain, and so forth."
In the performance of wholesome and unwholesome actions, the self is the agent of action by virtue of being the substratum for knowledge, effort, and so forth. As it has been said:
"Its agency is said to consist in its connection with knowledge and effort.
By the inclusion of the phrase "and so forth," the self's status as an enjoyer is also understood, since even the formless self possesses consciousness. As it has been said:
"And [the self] is an enjoyer because of its connection with consciousness, but it is not consciousness by its own nature.

Thus, the Veda speaks of [the self] as being the locus of the inherent cause and so forth; however, this is largely shown to be untenable by the author of the treatise himself, who demonstrated that a causal relationship between eternal things is impossible. Furthermore, one should connect this by stating that the Veda declares the eternity of certain entities to be untenable. Why is it untenable? Because for that which is non-momentary, there is a contradiction with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—and thus it transgresses the very nature of a real entity.

For a real entity (*vastu*) is that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*). And since that capacity for causal efficiency is not possible for a non-momentary thing, it is simply non-existent; how then could it possess the properties of a real entity? [The opponent claims: "Universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth are indeed imperceptible. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he implies action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and the rest, asserting that they are perceptible according to the Veda. Furthermore, the Veda declares that birth, duration, and cessation are the diverse states of entities. Regarding the diversity of birth, the Sūtra states that the cause of entities is their object.

He states that very same discordant reason—beginning with "of that which cannot have anything added to it"—as follows: because it is eternal, it is incapable of having any excellence added to it; thus, being previously a non-producer at the time before its causal activity, it later becomes a producer through dependence on others—that is, through dependence on auxiliary causes. This is what the Veda asserts, and this has been established in detail as being logical.

With the words beginning “because of its production,” he states that the Veda expresses an inconsistent state: because it is produced from its own causes, the Veda asserts the persistence of an entity—which, being already established, is not of the nature of an effect—by means of a substratum. And this is illogical; it has been demonstrated previously that for an entity devoid of all dependence, there can be no persistence through the power of another. Showing an inconsistent cessation, he says: the Veda asserts that the destruction of entities occurs from a cause, namely, a cause of destruction. And that is illogical, as it has been demonstrated [in the section on] non-destruction.

The Veda declares that such things and others like them are existent. What kind of thing? That which has its opposite well-established. For non-existence is the opposite of existence. That whose opposite is well-established by what means? By perception and inference; the meaning is that the Veda declares the existence of that [which is thus opposed]. Regarding the *agnihotra* and so forth—the word "and so forth" including bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like—the Veda declares their capacity for purifying sin and other such qualities.

Here too, by the word "etcetera," [it is meant that] it is sublated by inference based on the scriptural tradition (*āgama*) concerning the accumulation of merit (*dharma*) and so forth. To explain: the scriptural system establishes that non-merit (*adharma*) consists of passion and the like, as well as the karma originating from them; yet neither of these two is contradicted by the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) and such rites. How, then, could there be purification of non-merit through that? Or how could there be an increase of merit from it? This is because merit has the nature of non-greed and the like, as well as the karma originating from them, whereas the various ascetic practices (*tīrtha*) and so forth do not have that nature.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other similar improper statements of this kind are also to be understood.
