For that very [proponent], regarding the Veda—in all cases, whether concerning objects of perception and so forth, or in all three types of the body of a treatise (*śāstra-śarīra*) and the subject matter propounded by the treatise—without having resolved or removed contradictions with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-virodha*), and without demonstrating those properties (*dharma*) which constitute the necessary factors for engaging with the treatise.

What, then, are those factors? He says: "The connection," and so forth. "Connection" (*sambandha*) is the state of the meanings of words being mutually coherent. "Effective means" (*upāya*) is a method that is capable of accomplishment; that is to say, a suitable method. This refers to that which is taught in the treatise as a means for accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), such that it can be accomplished by a person when observed. "Goals of human life" (*puruṣārtha*) refers to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). [The compound] "connection, suitable means, and goals of human life" is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. These are their designations.

[Objection: But has it not already been stated that the treatise is unacceptably because its internal contradictions have not been resolved? Why, then, was it stated that it does not demonstrate the properties of a treatise (*śāstradharma*)? [Response: It is thought as follows:

having demonstrated that [the treatise] is pure regarding the objects of perception and inference, one might at some point say something else regarding an object devoid of connection and so forth; therefore, the non-demonstration of the properties of a treatise was stated for the sake of such a purpose.

Thus, having demonstrated the characteristics of a treatise (*śāstra*) such as its connection (*sambandha*) and so forth, [the author] proceeds by means of merely stating the truthfulness of the subject matter, which is extremely well-known. An "extremely well-known subject" is, for example, the capacity of fire to dispel cold; the "statement of its truth" refers to the mere assertion of that truth. Because it is difficult to fathom even with superior wisdom, it is "difficult to grasp through the excellence of wisdom" (*prajñāprakarṣaduravagrāha*); for that very reason, it is "profound" (*gahana*). This refers to such a subject, meaning one that is entirely beyond the range of perception (*atyantaparokṣa*).

Desiring to establish that [the teaching] is free from defects and possesses the truth of reality, the Mīmāṃsaka first triumphs through audacity even over a prostitute (*bandhakī*). He demonstrates the nature of the prostitute he triumphs over with the words "any woman whatsoever" and so forth. A *bandhakī* is a woman of ill-conduct. Having been seen by her husband himself at the scene of a transgression, and having been reproached by him, saying, "You have consorted with another man," she replied to that husband:

On the contrary... [he asked]. To explain how he replied, he says: "Behold," and so forth. By the word "mothers" (*mātaḥ*), the women standing nearby are addressed. "O mothers, behold the perversity of this man, my master! Indeed, "behold" (*paśyata*) is the second person plural form of the imperative.

Consequently, even from the word *mātṛ*, the plural form alone is appropriate, namely *mātaraḥ*. Regarding this, some maintain that there exists a word *mātaḥ* which has the same meaning as the vocative singular *mātṛ*; this is according to the rule that particles (*nipāta*) are like vowels [in their phonetic form]. And because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it retains the same form across all grammatical numbers; thus, when connected with the word *paśyata* in the plural, it is employed precisely as *mātar*.

Others, however, read the text as *paśyata mātaraḥ puruṣasya*. [The term] *dharmapatnī* is a compound with the middle member elided (*madhyapadalopī samāsa*), meaning a wife who is a means for accomplishing dharma. The context is that, instead of placing his trust in that lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*), he places his trust in two things called eyes, which are like water-bubbles on the water—his own. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose designation (*abhidhāna*) is 'eye'. He states the reason why he does not associate with another man, beginning with the words "by him" (*tena*).

"Jaratkāṇa" means one who is both old (*jaraṃś*) and one-eyed (*kāṇaḥ*); that is to say, by an "old one-eyed man. In this context, by the mention of "old," the deficiency of age is expressed. Since the eye is the supreme locus of beauty, the mention of "one-eyed" expresses deformity due to its deficiency. By the mention of "rustic," the deficiency of qualities such as wit and charm is expressed. By the mention of "wood-gatherer," poverty is expressed because of a life of hardship. Thus, even though she was requested for the sake of union with a man endowed with such qualities as old age and so forth, [she did not consent].

"I was not previously united with him out of attachment to his form and qualities. 'Form' (*rūpa*) refers to physical beauty; 'qualities' (*guṇa*) refers to attributes such as wit and the like. 'Attachment to form and qualities' (*rūpaguṇānurāga*) means a longing or desire for them; it is by reason of that. Regarding the 'son of the chief minister' (*mantrimukhyadāraka*)—that is, the young son of the preeminent minister—the analysis of the compound is: 'he who is both the chief minister and a son. How can it be possible that I should desire such a son?"

In this regard, by way of the reversal of the four defects such as old age and so forth, four qualities are stated to exist in the son of the chief minister: through the mention of "form" (*rūpa*), there is comeliness; through the mention of "qualities" (*guṇa*), there is eloquence and the like; through the mention of "chief minister," there is power (*aiśvarya*); and through the mention of "son," there is the quality of youth. However, this was merely uttered out of the audacity of the procuress and is not logically sound; for form and the other [qualities] alone are the causes of desire, whereas old age and the like are not.

With the phrase "of such a kind" (*evaṃjātīyakam*) and so forth, he applies the meaning of the example to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). "Of such a kind" means similar to the reply of a harlot. This is the inference of the Veda’s non-contradiction regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). Of what sort of Veda? Of a Veda whose contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been observed in regard to a matter that is capable of investigation. The analysis of the compound is: "that of which a contradiction with valid cognition has been observed. The inference is by way of the example of fire dispelling cold; that is, by means of the statement that fire counteracts cold.

Just as the statement "fire is the remedy for cold" is non-contradictory, so too other Vedic statements are non-contradictory. In this context, the Veda stands in the place of a lawful wife; the description of the agency and other attributes of a man who is subject to conflicting views [regarding reality] is like his eyes; and perception and inference are like his eyes. Now, the word of a wife whose infidelity has been witnessed is not more authoritative than that of a man who—having observed such a conflict [between scripture and experience]—disregards his own observation and accepts her word as being true to the facts.

Thus, having established the invalidity of those two means of knowledge that contradict the meaning declared by the Veda, we shall not understand what is absolutely beyond the senses based on the words of the Veda—which stands in the position of a wife and whose deviation from reality has been observed. (336)

Right here he states another fault, beginning with "sidhyet" (it would be established): "In this way," meaning that if the entire Veda were established as authoritative merely by the statement of one truth as observed, then every person would be authoritative in every respect. For it is not the case that among the many things spoken by a person there is not even a single word whose meaning is true; rather, such certainly exists.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with “yathā” (just as). Just as this extreme state of being expressive—that is, speaking the truth exclusively—is exceedingly difficult to accomplish because it is achieved only with extreme hardship; likewise, the utterance of truth is exceedingly difficult. This being the established principle, how can there be a correspondence—even in some way according to the *kākatālīya* (coincidental) logic—with respect to a single statement, on the grounds of its having a true meaning?

Therefore, regarding that collection of words belonging to a person who is not distinguished [from others] by virtue of one of his statements being non-contradictory—that is, of that person whose single statement has been seen to be non-contradictory—if it were accepted that such a state of affairs constitutes non-contradiction, then no person whatsoever would fail to be authoritative (*āpta*); rather, everyone would be authoritative. But this is not the case. Consequently, validity does not arise from the non-contradiction of a single part.

Furthermore, whatever indeed makes something known must do so by being either of the same nature as it or produced from it; it cannot do so otherwise. Nor is this sound (*dhvani*) the nature of those things intended to be expressed (*vācya*). Why? Because sound resides in the speaker; for the nature of one thing does not exist in another. Nor is this sound the effect of those things. Why? Because the sound arises in the mind of the speaker. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that [the word] is dependent solely upon the speaker’s intention and not upon an external object [...]. Furthermore, there exists no non-deviation for an object that is distinct from those [two], namely, distinct from both essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).

He explains [the passage] beginning with "no" (*na*) and so forth. The word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates sequence. This speech residing in the speaker is neither the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the objects to be expressed (*vācya*), nor is it their effect (*kārya*). What is the reason? Because even in the absence of those [objects]—that is, even when things (*vastu*) do not exist—it arises through mere intention to speak (*vivakṣāmātra*). Furthermore, there is no cause other than an effect or an intrinsic nature that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) for anything. And since there is deviation [in the case of speech], the word can occur otherwise than that [i.e., otherwise than the presence of the object].

Therefore, "otherwise" means even in the absence of an external object. Because of its possibility—that is, because of the possibility of that word—cognition of that [object], namely cognition of an external object, is untenable due to the existence of that word.

It might be argued as follows: even if the word is a distinct entity from the object denoted (*vācya*), it is nevertheless a signifier (*gamaka*) precisely because it is the effect of that denoted object. For the activity of expressive words—whether their production or manifestation—is brought about by the perception of the denoted object. That is, when the denoted object exists, there is its perception; from that perception arises the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*); and from the intention to speak comes the word. Thus, through this causal succession, the word is the effect of the object. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

He explains [the opponent's position] with the words "It might be so," and so forth. [The opponent argues: "Therefore, because the expressive word functions by means of the perception of the expressed object... He refutes this with the words "If that were so," and so forth. [The meaning is: If all verbal activity were to function solely on the basis of an existing object, then how could there be such a verbal activity—expressing mutually contradictory meanings through different scriptural traditions (*āgama*) regarding a single referent? It could not be so at all; the implication is that in all doctrines, the verbal activity would necessarily have a single, identical meaning.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "yadi" (if). If this restriction were to hold—that a word does not function without another denotable object to be denoted—then, because they express mutually contradictory meanings, there would be no operation of speech through the superimposition or attribution of contradictory natures, such as permanence and impermanence, upon a single object amidst diverse doctrines and philosophical systems.

For this possibility does not exist: that a single word could be both eternal and non-eternal without distinction—that is, without any other mode. The mention of "word" (*śabda*) is for the sake of illustration; by it, even a jar or the like would [absurdly] be both eternal and non-eternal without distinction. And such a thing is simply impossible. Yet, there is the common usage that for some, such as the Sāṃkhyas, sound is eternal, while for others it is non-eternal; likewise for [the categories of] "having a self" (*sātmaka*) and "being selfless" (*nirātmaka*), and so forth. Therefore, there is no connection between words and external objects.

For this reason, the scriptures (*āgama*) of a person who practices—which are inseparable from, that is, invariably concomitant with (*avinābhāvin*), real entities—do not in any way establish those entities for that practitioner; therefore, based on those scriptures that are not invariably concomitant with reality, there is either no certainty regarding the object or [only] uncertainty. It is not everyone who seeks the authority of scripture, but rather the ignorant person. For what purpose does he seek it? For the sake of understanding the object indicated by it.

This is for the sake of understanding the meaning demonstrated by that scripture. What is the reason? It is because only the ignorant person investigates, and not anyone else. To this he says: "For those who have realized the suchness (*yāthātathya*)—that is, the non-erroneous nature of things—and who have thus attained the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no dependence upon the instruction of others. Furthermore, as for the ignorant person by whom [the truth] must be sought, his qualities are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyaguṇa*). That person whose qualities are beyond the senses is "one with qualities beyond the senses" (*atīndriyaguṇa*). And since the word "person" (*puruṣa*) is used here, it forms a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).

Because one lacks the capacity to perform such a discrimination—that this person is omniscient or otherwise, and that he is not a speaker of falsehood—how could one proceed by determining that a statement composed by such a person is an authoritative scripture (*āgama*)?

Furthermore, it is not the case that all words of everyone function in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*). For a person who perceives that even in the absence of the existence of an object desired and sought after by others, [words] still function, there must necessarily arise a doubt regarding speech: "Is this word true to reality, or is it not? Regarding whose speech? Even regarding the speech of those whose words have never been observed to deviate from reality; that is, even regarding the speech of those for whom their words have not been seen to be erroneous when the subject matter is capable of investigation.

Because of the word "also" (*api*), there is even greater suspicion regarding the speech of those whose words have been observed to deviate from the truth... for that reason—namely, because of this suspicion—it is not proper for a cognizer to determine any object whatsoever on the basis of the word of any person. And since there is no certainty, the non-existence of the entity intended by the proponent is not established through the negation of that cognition, nor even through the negation of its arrival.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "What was said," and so forth. What was stated previously: because scripture has all things as its object, and because it functions through non-contradiction when a thing exists; therefore, non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of that [scripture]—that is, non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of scripture—will establish the non-existence of even an object remote in terms of its own nature and so on. That, namely the state of being a determiner of non-existence, belongs to this scripture; yet for this scripture, there is no such thing as having all things as its object, because it does not take as its objects those things that are unrelated to human goals.

Even granting this, it is said: even if scripture (*āgama*) were to have all things as its object, if there were non-occurrence [of it], then—given that there is non-occurrence with respect to another entity—the non-perception characterized by the cessation of scripture would be determinative of non-existence; but that is not the case, because scripture does indeed occur with respect to other entities as well.

This being the case, it has been stated that for a person desiring to understand an object from a scripture that deviates from its referent, the intended object is not established. For that reason, regarding remote objects, the non-existence of a thing—which results in the certainty of its non-existence—is not established as a basis for the conventional usage of "non-existent.

Therefore, the conclusion is that even when the three means of valid cognition—namely those designated as perception, inference, and scripture—are absent, there is no certainty regarding objects remote in space, time, or nature.
Showing that the various non-Buddhist outsiders merely speak inappropriately, he says:

(1) "Veda" and so forth. Here, the word *iti* and the word *vāda* should be connected with what is to be stated later. By this, the meaning is as follows: [the Veda’s authority... is] the mark (*liṅga*) of dullness (*jāḍya*). Now, one might object: since there is a prohibition against a genitive compound with a quality (*guṇa*), it ought to be "the authority of the Veda" (*vedasya prāmāṇyam*). This is not a fault, because in that context only specific qualities well-known in common usage are intended by the term "quality. And the indication of the mark for this is the statement beginning with "in the determination of the extent of the subject matter" (*adhikaraṇaitāvatve*).

(2) The claim of certain Naiyāyikas and others that God is the creator of the principles of reality (*tattva*) and so forth is also a sign of stupidity. (3) The desire for merit through bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) is a sign of stupidity. [The other... delusion and so forth, as well as the physical and vocal actions produced by them, are what constitute "merit" (*dharma*); whereas bathing, characterized merely by contact with water, is the opposite of that. How, then, could merit be obtained from it? Furthermore, this doctrine of bathing at sacred sites has been refuted in detail by masters such as Vasubandhu and others, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

(4) Even in the absence of virtues such as moral discipline (*śīla*), the arrogance and pride consisting in the boastful claim of belonging to a caste, thinking "I am a Brahmin," is a sign of stupidity because it is irrational. For [if one were to argue that] such pride in claiming a caste could arise either by taking hold of [some essence], or by relying on the fact that one was produced in the womb of a Brahmin woman by a Brahmin father—of these two, the former position is not tenable because a real, substantial universal (*sāmānya*) has been refuted. Nor is the latter tenable, because the bodies of a Brahmin and a Brahmin woman are by nature impure and thus indistinguishable from other bodies.

(5) The infliction of pain upon the body through fasting and other such means is "torment" (*santāpa*); its undertaking or performance is for the sake of destroying evil. [Regarding] evil, [...]* is the mark of dullness (*jāḍya*). For instance, greed, hatred, and delusion are the causes of all evil. Since the undertaking of torment is not incompatible with these, how could there be purification of evil by means of it? *The ellipsis likely refers to the fact that the mark of dullness is the failure to perceive the faults of evil.*

These five are the signs of dullness (*jāḍya*). Of what kind of dullness? Of that dullness in which "wisdom" (*prajñāna*) has been destroyed. Wisdom is knowledge supported by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); that in which such wisdom has been destroyed is described as such. The meaning is: devoid of knowledge that conforms to logic (*nyāya*). It is stated as "five" because they are taken according to the specific context... [the word] "signs" (*liṅgāni*). 0.
Those who possess great discernment regarding Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara and others, whose minds are submerged within the ocean of Dharmakīrti— the mine of true reality—
and whose memory is capable of investigating the sequence of earlier and later [arguments], and whose wisdom is likewise preeminent.
Whatever has been said here will be understood by those who are themselves skilled.
In the successive expositions of its meaning, there is a great clarity of speech; therein, the excellence of the eloquent sayings of others is perceived,
as is the destruction of the doctrines of all the arrogant non-Buddhist teachers.
How could this commentary fail to attract those whose intellects have been awakened by its most excellent characteristics? ||0||
